Example 2.1 The measured error rate of the running example is the mean \(\bar X\) of \(n = 200\) independent errors, each 1 with probability 0.1 and 0 otherwise. Its mean is 0.1, and one error has variance \(0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09\). Markov’s inequality at the threshold 0.15 gives \(0.1/0.15 = 0.67\). Chebyshev’s inequality with the deviation \(t = 0.05\) gives \[\Pr[|\bar X - 0.1| \ge 0.05] \le \frac{0.09}{200 \times 0.05^2} = 0.18, \tag{2.10}\] which covers the upper tail you ask about, since reaching 0.15 is one way to be 0.05 away. Against the simulated \(9.6\times10^{-3}\), Markov is about 70 times too large and Chebyshev about 19 times, because neither uses more than one or two numbers about the distribution.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.2 The Chernoff method
Failure probabilities like \(10^{-5}\) are out of reach for polynomial bounds at sensible widths, as Table 2.2 showed. This section reaches them by applying Corollary 2.1 with an exponential, \(g(x) = e^{\lambda x}\), for a chosen \(\lambda > 0\). The average of \(e^{\lambda X}\) is the MGF \(M_X(\lambda) = \mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\) of Probability distributions, which contains every moment of \(X\) at once.
A larger \(\lambda\) weights large values of \(X\) more, which helps, but also enlarges \(M_X(\lambda)\), which hurts. With the log-MGF \(K_X(\lambda) = \ln M_X(\lambda)\), the bound is \(e\) to minus an exponent, and the best \(\lambda\) makes that exponent largest.

Theorem 2.3 (The Chernoff bound) Let \(X\) be a random variable, let \(t\) be a real number, and let \(\lambda > 0\) be such that \(M_X(\lambda)\) is finite. Then \[\Pr[X \ge t] \le e^{-\lambda t}M_X(\lambda) = \exp\big(-(\lambda t - K_X(\lambda))\big). \tag{2.11}\] Since this holds for every such \(\lambda\), \[\Pr[X \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\sup_{\lambda > 0}\big(\lambda t - K_X(\lambda)\big)\Big). \tag{2.12}\]


Proof. 

For \(\lambda > 0\) the function \(e^{\lambda x}\) is positive and strictly increasing, so Corollary 2.1 applies with \(g(x) = e^{\lambda x}\). Its numerator is \(M_X(\lambda)\) and its denominator is \(e^{\lambda t}\), which gives the first form.
Writing \(M_X(\lambda) = e^{K_X(\lambda)}\) gathers both factors into one exponent.
The bound holds for every allowed \(\lambda\), so it holds for the smallest of the bounds, which is the one with the largest exponent.


For large sums the best exponent is also the right one. For a sum of \(n\) independent copies of a variable, Cramér’s theorem says that the probability of a large deviation is \(e^{-n I}\) up to factors that grow slower than exponentially, where \(I\) is the optimized exponent for one copy, and Section F.2 in the appendices derives that matching lower bound. In practice every Chernoff bound in this chapter is computed by the same five steps:

Write down the MGF of \(X\).
If \(X\) is a sum of independent terms, factorize the MGF into one factor per term.
Bound each factor by something simple.
Minimize the exponent over \(\lambda\) by setting its derivative to zero.
Simplify the result into a usable form.

Figure 2.2 shows the trade-off in \(\lambda\) for a binomial count. The bound has a clear minimum, and bounding each factor with \(1 + x \le e^x\), as step 1 of the next proof does, costs a little but puts the minimizing \(\lambda\) in closed form.






Figure 2.2: The Chernoff bound \(e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb E[e^{\lambda S}]\) for \(S \sim \mathrm{Bin}(100, 0.1)\) and \(t = 20\), as a function of \(\lambda\), before and after the relaxation \(1 + x \le e^x\). Both stay above the exact tail.



The method is used most for a count of independent yes/no events, such as errors on a test set or records drawn into a batch. Each event is a variable \(X_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p_i)\), equal to 1 with probability \(p_i\), and the question is how likely the count \(S\) is to land a fraction \(r\) above or below its mean \(\mu\).

Theorem 2.4 (Chernoff bounds for a count) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent with \(X_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p_i)\), let \(S = \sum_i X_i\), and let \(\mu = \sum_i p_i\). For every \(r > 0\), the upper tail obeys \[\Pr[S \ge (1+r)\mu] \le \exp\big(-\mu[(1+r)\ln(1+r) - r]\big) \le \exp\left(-\frac{r^2\mu}{2+r}\right). \tag{2.13}\] For every \(0 < r < 1\), the lower tail obeys \[\Pr[S \le (1-r)\mu] \le \exp\left(-\frac{r^2\mu}{2}\right). \tag{2.14}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the MGF of the count by that of a Poisson count with the same mean, apply the Chernoff bound, choose the best \(\lambda\), and simplify. The lower tail repeats the same steps for \(-S\).

One factor. Each \(X_i\) is 1 with probability \(p_i\), so its MGF is \(p_ie^\lambda + (1 - p_i) = 1 + p_i(e^\lambda - 1)\). The inequality \(1 + x \le e^x\) holds for every real \(x\), because the convex curve \(e^x\) lies above its tangent line \(1 + x\) at 0 (Probability distributions). With \(x = p_i(e^\lambda - 1)\) it gives \[M_{X_i}(\lambda) \le \exp\big(p_i(e^\lambda - 1)\big). \tag{2.15}\] The right side is the MGF of a Poisson count with mean \(p_i\).
Product. The MGF of a sum of independent variables is the product of their MGFs, because the exponential turns the sum into a product and independence lets the average of that product split (Probability distributions). The exponents of step 1 then add up to \(\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\): \[M_S(\lambda) \le \exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\big). \tag{2.16}\]
Chernoff bound. Putting this into Equation 2.11 at \(t = (1+r)\mu\) gives \[\Pr[S \ge (1+r)\mu] \le \exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1) - \lambda(1+r)\mu\big). \tag{2.17}\]
Minimize. The derivative of the exponent, \(\mu e^\lambda - (1+r)\mu\), vanishes at \(e^\lambda = 1 + r\), so \(\lambda = \ln(1+r)\), which is positive as required. Substituting it turns the exponent into \(\mu r - (1+r)\mu\ln(1+r)\), which is the first upper-tail bound.
Simplify. A width needs the exponent solved for \(r\), and \((1+r)\ln(1+r) - r\) has no closed-form inverse. So replace the logarithm by the lower bound \(\ln(1+r) \ge 2r/(2+r)\), valid for \(r \ge 0\), which turns the bracket into a ratio of polynomials. The difference \(\ln(1+r) - 2r/(2+r)\) is 0 at \(r = 0\), and it never decreases, because its derivative is never negative: \[\frac{1}{1+r} - \frac{4}{(2+r)^2} = \frac{r^2}{(1+r)(2+r)^2} \ge 0. \tag{2.18}\] Putting the lower bound into the bracket gives \((1+r)\frac{2r}{2+r} - r = \frac{r^2}{2+r}\), which is the second upper-tail bound.
Lower tail. A small \(S\) is a large \(-S\). For \(\lambda > 0\) the function \(e^{-\lambda x}\) is decreasing, so \(S \le s\) exactly when \(e^{-\lambda S} \ge e^{-\lambda s}\). Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{-\lambda S}\), with steps 1 and 2 at \(-\lambda\) in place of \(\lambda\), gives \[\Pr[S \le s] \le e^{\lambda s}M_S(-\lambda) \le \exp\big(\lambda s + \mu(e^{-\lambda} - 1)\big). \tag{2.19}\]
Minimize. With \(s = (1-r)\mu\), the derivative \(s - \mu e^{-\lambda}\) vanishes at \(e^{-\lambda} = 1 - r\), that is, at \(\lambda = -\ln(1-r) > 0\). Substituting it gives \[\Pr[S \le (1-r)\mu] \le \exp\big(-\mu[r + (1-r)\ln(1-r)]\big). \tag{2.20}\]
Simplify. For \(0 < r < 1\), which keeps \(1 - r\) positive and the series below convergent, multiply the Taylor series \(\ln(1-r) = -\sum_{j \ge 1}r^j/j\) by \(1 - r\). Each power \(r^j\) with \(j \ge 2\) gets \(-1/j\) from the 1 and \(1/(j-1)\) from the \(-r\), together \(1/(j(j-1))\), so \[(1-r)\ln(1-r) = -r + \sum_{j \ge 2}\frac{r^j}{j(j-1)}. \tag{2.21}\] Every term of the sum is non-negative, so keeping only the first one, \(r^2/2\), gives a lower bound. Adding \(r\), the bracket is then at least \(r^2/2\), which is the lower-tail bound.


The bounds depend on the expected count \(\mu\), not on the number of trials \(n\), so a relative deviation \(r\) becomes unlikely only once \(\mu\) is large. Because step 1 keeps each \(p_i\), a small \(\mu\), and with it a small variance \(\sum_i p_i(1 - p_i) \le \mu\), gives a small MGF bound, which is why this bound will beat Hoeffding’s range-only bound of the next section. For large \(r\) the simplified upper-tail exponent \(r^2\mu/(2+r)\) grows like \(r\mu\), not \(r^2\mu\), so counts overshoot their mean more easily than they undershoot it.

Example 2.2 In the running example the number of errors \(S\) is a sum of 200 independent \(\mathrm{Bern}(0.1)\) variables, so \(\mu = 20\). A measured rate of 15% means 30 errors, which is \((1 + r)\mu\) with \(r = 0.5\). The simplified upper-tail bound gives \[\Pr[S \ge 30] \le \exp\left(-\frac{0.5^2 \times 20}{2.5}\right) = e^{-2} = 0.135. \tag{2.22}\] That is the best bound so far, below Chebyshev’s 0.18, but still 14 times the simulated \(9.6\times10^{-3}\). Part of the gap is the simplification in step 5 of the proof, and the rest is a factor in front of the exponential, shrinking like \(1/\sqrt\mu\), that the Chernoff method cannot see because it bounds only the exponent.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.3 Sub-Gaussian variables and Hoeffding
Redoing the Chernoff calculation for every new distribution is tedious. A normal variable \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\), has the MGF \(e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\) (Probability distributions), a quadratic log-MGF, and the Chernoff calculation for it uses nothing else. So this section defines a class of variables by that one property, proves tail and sum bounds for the class once, and applies them to bounded variables, which gives Hoeffding’s inequality for averages.

Definition 2.1 (Sub-Gaussian variable) A random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian if, for every real \(\lambda\), \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(X - \mu)}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}. \tag{2.23}\] The square \(\sigma^2\) is its variance proxy.

The next result shows that it is never smaller than the true variance, and it can be much larger, which is where these bounds lose accuracy.

Proposition 2.1 (Properties of sub-Gaussian variables) Let \(X\) be \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian with mean \(\mu\), and let \(t > 0\).

Its variance is at most \(\sigma^2\).
Its tails are no heavier than those of a normal variable with variance \(\sigma^2\): \[\Pr[X - \mu \ge t] \le e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \qquad \Pr[|X - \mu| \ge t] \le 2e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{2.24}\]
If \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are independent and each \(X_i\) is \(\sigma_i\)-sub-Gaussian with mean \(\mu_i\), their sum is \(\sqrt{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}\)-sub-Gaussian.
For a constant \(c\), the variable \(cX\) is \(|c|\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian. So the mean of \(n\) independent \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian variables is \((\sigma/\sqrt n)\)-sub-Gaussian.



Proof. 

Variance. Expand both sides of the definition around \(\lambda = 0\). The left side is \(1 + \lambda^2\operatorname{Var}(X)/2 + \dots\), with no linear term because \(X - \mu\) has mean 0, and the right side is \(1 + \lambda^2\sigma^2/2 + \dots\). Subtracting 1, dividing by \(\lambda^2/2\) and letting \(\lambda \to 0\) forces \(\operatorname{Var}(X) \le \sigma^2\).
Tail. Putting the bound of the definition into Equation 2.11 for \(X - \mu\) gives, for every \(\lambda > 0\), \[\Pr[X - \mu \ge t] \le \exp\big(-\lambda t + \lambda^2\sigma^2/2\big). \tag{2.25}\] The exponent is a parabola in \(\lambda\), whose derivative \(-t + \lambda\sigma^2\) vanishes at \(\lambda = t/\sigma^2 > 0\), and substituting it gives the exponent \(-t^2/\sigma^2 + t^2/(2\sigma^2) = -t^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Replacing \(\lambda\) by \(-\lambda\) in the definition shows that \(-X\) is also \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian, which gives the same bound for the lower tail, and adding the two gives the two-sided bound.
Sums. The centred MGF \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda(X - \mu)}]\) of a sum of independent terms is the product of their centred MGFs, as in step 2 of the proof of Theorem 2.4. Each factor is at most a normal MGF, and the exponents of those add up: \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda\sum_i(X_i - \mu_i)}\big] \le \prod_i e^{\lambda^2\sigma_i^2/2} = e^{\lambda^2(\sum_i\sigma_i^2)/2}. \tag{2.26}\]
Scaling and means. Multiplying \(X\) by \(c\) is the same as multiplying \(\lambda\) by \(c\), so the definition at \(c\lambda\) gives the bound \(e^{c^2\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\). The sum of \(n\) independent \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian variables is \(\sigma\sqrt n\)-sub-Gaussian by item 3, and dividing by \(n\) makes their mean \((\sigma/\sqrt n)\)-sub-Gaussian.


Hoeffding’s inequality also needs the fact that bounded variables are sub-Gaussian. A variable trapped in an interval cannot have a heavy tail, since it cannot go beyond the interval at all. The lemma makes this quantitative, with a variance proxy of half the interval’s length, squared.

Lemma 2.2 (Hoeffding’s lemma) Let \(X\) take values in an interval \([l, u]\) and have mean \(\mu\). Then \(X\) is \(\frac{u-l}{2}\)-sub-Gaussian, that is, for every real \(\lambda\), \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\big] \le \exp\big(\lambda^2(u-l)^2/8\big). \tag{2.27}\]


Proof. Shifting \(X\) and the interval by \(\mu\) changes neither side, so assume \(\mu = 0\). A variable with mean 0 takes values on both sides of 0, so \(l \le 0 \le u\). The plan is to bound \(e^{\lambda X}\) by a straight line in \(X\), whose average depends only on the mean, and then to show that the logarithm of the result is at most a quadratic.

Use convexity. On \([l, u]\) the convex curve \(e^{\lambda x}\) lies below the chord joining its values at the two endpoints. That chord is the weighted average of the endpoint values, with weights that say how close \(x\) is to each end: \[e^{\lambda x} \le \frac{u - x}{u - l}e^{\lambda l} + \frac{x - l}{u - l}e^{\lambda u}. \tag{2.28}\]
Take expectations. The right side is linear in \(x\), so its average needs only \(\mathbb E[X] = 0\): \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}] \le \frac{u}{u-l}e^{\lambda l} - \frac{l}{u-l}e^{\lambda u}. \tag{2.29}\] This is exactly the MGF of the two-point variable that sits at \(l\) or \(u\) with mean 0, so that variable is the worst case on the interval.
Reduce to one variable. Let \(p = -l/(u-l)\), a number in \([0, 1]\), so that \(\frac{u}{u-l} = 1 - p\). Write \(w = \lambda(u - l)\), so that \(\lambda l = -wp\) and \(e^{\lambda u} = e^{\lambda l}e^{w}\). Factoring \(e^{\lambda l} = e^{-wp}\) out of the right side of step 2 leaves \(1 - p + pe^w\), so that side equals \(e^{\Lambda(w)}\), where \[\Lambda(w) = -wp + \ln\big(1 - p + pe^w\big). \tag{2.30}\] It remains to show that \(\Lambda(w) \le w^2/8\), by a Taylor expansion around \(w = 0\).
Value and slope at 0. At \(w = 0\) the value is \(\Lambda(0) = \ln 1 = 0\). The derivative is \(\Lambda'(w) = -p + \frac{pe^w}{1 - p + pe^w}\), so \(\Lambda'(0) = -p + p = 0\).
Bound the curvature. Write \(v = \frac{pe^w}{1 - p + pe^w}\), a number in \([0, 1]\), so that \(\Lambda'(w) = -p + v\). By the quotient rule the derivative of \(v\) is \(v \cdot \frac{1 - p}{1 - p + pe^w} = v(1 - v)\), so \(\Lambda''(w) = v(1 - v)\). A product of two non-negative numbers that add up to 1 is largest when both are \(\frac12\), so \(\Lambda''(w) \le \frac14\).
Taylor with remainder. Taylor’s theorem gives \(\Lambda(w) = \Lambda(0) + w\Lambda'(0) + \frac{w^2}{2}\Lambda''(\xi)\) for some \(\xi\) between 0 and \(w\). With value and slope 0 and curvature at most \(\frac14\), this is at most \(w^2/8 = \lambda^2(u-l)^2/8\).


The constant \(\frac18\) cannot be improved. A fair coin on the two endpoints has variance \((u-l)^2/4\), and step 1 of Proposition 2.1 shows that no variance proxy can be below the variance. Combining the lemma with items 3 and 4 of Proposition 2.1 gives Hoeffding’s inequality: the mean of \(n\) bounded independent variables has a variance proxy that shrinks like \(1/n\).

Theorem 2.5 (Hoeffding’s inequality) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent, each with values in \([l, u]\), and let \(\bar X_n\) be their mean, with \(\mathbb E[\bar X_n] = \mu\). For every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\big[\bar X_n - \mu \ge t\big] \le \exp\left(-\frac{2nt^2}{(u-l)^2}\right). \tag{2.31}\] For every \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), \[|\bar X_n - \mu| < (u-l)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}}. \tag{2.32}\]


Proof. 

Each term. By Lemma 2.2 each \(X_i\) is \(\frac{u-l}{2}\)-sub-Gaussian.
The mean. By items 3 and 4 of Proposition 2.1 their mean is \(\frac{u-l}{2\sqrt n}\)-sub-Gaussian, with variance proxy \((u-l)^2/(4n)\).
Tail. Item 2 of Proposition 2.1 with this proxy in place of \(\sigma^2\) gives the exponent \(t^2 \big/ \big(2(u-l)^2/(4n)\big) = 2nt^2/(u-l)^2\), which is the one-sided bound.
Width. The two-sided bound is twice this. Setting it equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\), as in Lemma 2.1, gives the width.


Hoeffding’s inequality needs only the range, not the variance. That is its strength, since there is nothing to estimate, and its weakness, since it assumes the worst-case variance \((u-l)^2/4\) of the fair coin on the endpoints.

Example 2.3 Each error of the running example lies in \([0, 1]\), so \(u - l = 1\), and the deviation is \(t = 0.05\) with \(n = 200\). Hoeffding’s inequality gives \[\Pr[\bar X - 0.1 \ge 0.05] \le e^{-2 \times 200 \times 0.05^2} = e^{-1} = 0.37. \tag{2.33}\] That is worse than Chebyshev’s 0.18, because the true variance of one error, \(0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09\), is far below Hoeffding’s worst case of \(1/4\). Figure 2.3 puts the bounds side by side with the simulated tail.







Figure 2.3: Empirical tail of the mean of 200 Bernoulli(0.1) variables against the Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding and Chernoff bounds.



When the true variance is much smaller than the worst case, Bernstein’s inequality keeps it in the bound. Write \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of each term and \(R\) for the largest distance a term can be from its mean.

Theorem 2.6 (Bernstein’s inequality) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent, each with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) and with \(|X_i - \mu| \le R\), and let \(\bar X_n\) be their mean. For every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\big[\bar X_n - \mu \ge t\big] \le \exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2 + \frac23 Rt}\right). \tag{2.34}\] For every \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) the deviation \(\bar X_n - \mu\) is below \[\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ln(1/\beta)}{n}} + \frac{2R\ln(1/\beta)}{3n}. \tag{2.35}\]


The proof is the same Chernoff recipe, with a sharper bound on each factor’s MGF. Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart (ch. 2) give it, and Section F.1 in the appendices derives it and the width step by step. For small \(t\) the \(2\sigma^2\) term of the denominator dominates, and the bound looks Gaussian with the true variance. For large \(t\) the \(\frac23 Rt\) term dominates, and the bound decays like \(e^{-ct}\), more slowly than the \(e^{-ct^2}\) of the Gaussian regime.

Example 2.4 The variance matters most when the rate is near zero. A classifier makes 1 false positive on 1,000 negative records, and you want a 95% upper bound on its true false-positive rate, so \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\ln(1/\beta) = \ln 20 \approx 3.0\). Setting the one-sided bound of Theorem 2.5 equal to \(\beta\) gives the half-width \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)/(2n)} = \sqrt{\ln 20/2000} \approx 0.039\), added to the measured rate of \(0.001\), because Hoeffding assumes a variance of \(0.25\). Bernstein’s inequality with the variance \(\sigma^2 = 0.001 \times 0.999 \approx 0.001\) of the measured rate, \(R = 1\) and \(n = 1{,}000\) gives the width \[\sqrt{\frac{2\times0.001\times3.0}{1000}} + \frac{2\times3.0}{3000} \approx 0.0045, \tag{2.36}\] almost ten times tighter, though only as a heuristic, because \(\sigma^2\) was estimated from the same data. The exact Clopper–Pearson bound, the largest rate under which 1 or fewer false positives in 1,000 trials still has probability at least \(0.05\), is \(0.0047\).

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.4 Many estimates at once
A learner rarely relies on one estimate. It compares many models or runs many training steps, and it needs all of them to behave at the same time. The union bound says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their separate chances, because the sum counts an outcome that lies in several events several times. The running example is one estimate, so this section uses a training loop.

Lemma 2.3 (The union bound) For any events \(A_1, \dots, A_k\), independent or not, \[\Pr[A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_k] \le \sum_{i=1}^k \Pr[A_i]. \tag{2.37}\]


Proof. 

Compare indicators outcome by outcome. Where none of the events happens, the indicator of the union and the sum of the indicators are both 0. Where at least one happens, the first is 1 and the second counts the events that happen, which is at least 1. So at every outcome \[\mathbf 1[A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_k] \le \sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf 1[A_i]. \tag{2.38}\]
Average. Averages keep this order, and the average of each indicator is the probability of its event, as in the proof of Theorem 2.1.


If each of \(k\) estimates fails with probability at most \(\beta/k\), all of them succeed together except with probability at most \(k\cdot\beta/k = \beta\). In an exponential bound, asking for \(\beta/k\) instead of \(\beta\) replaces \(\ln(1/\beta)\) by \(\ln(k/\beta) = \ln k + \ln(1/\beta)\), and that is the \(\ln k\) cost.
The first use is a question every learner faces. A learner picks its model after seeing the data, so you need its training loss to be close to its population loss for every model it could pick, not just for one fixed model.

Corollary 2.2 (Uniform convergence over a finite class) Let \(\Theta\) be a finite set of models, and let the loss of each model on each record lie in \([0, 1]\). Let \(D\) be a dataset of \(n\) records drawn independently from a population \(\mathcal D\). Write \(\mathcal L(\theta; D)\) for the empirical risk of a model \(\theta\), its average loss on \(D\), and \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta)\) for its true risk, its average loss on the population. For every \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), \[|\mathcal L(\theta; D) - \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta)| \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2|\Theta|/\beta)}{2n}} \quad\text{for all } \theta \in \Theta. \tag{2.39}\]


Proof. 

One model. For a fixed \(\theta\), the empirical risk is a mean of \(n\) independent terms in \([0, 1]\) whose average is the true risk. So Theorem 2.5 with \(u - l = 1\), on both tails, gives \[\Pr\big[|\mathcal L(\theta; D) - \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta)| \ge t\big] \le 2e^{-2nt^2}. \tag{2.40}\]
All models. By Lemma 2.3 over the \(|\Theta|\) models, the chance that any of them is off by \(t\) or more is at most \(2|\Theta|e^{-2nt^2}\).
Invert. Setting this equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\), as in Lemma 2.1, gives the width.


The size of the class enters only through \(\ln|\Theta|\), so squaring the number of models only doubles that term.

Example 2.5 A training loop includes each of \(n = 60{,}000\) records in a minibatch independently with probability \(q = 0.01\), so the batch size \(B\) is a count with mean \(\mu = 600\). For a batch more than 20% off, \(r = 0.2\), \(r^2 = 0.04\) and \(2 + r = 2.2\), and the two tails of Theorem 2.4 give \[\Pr[B \ge 720] \le e^{-0.04 \times 600/2.2} = e^{-10.9} \approx 1.8\times10^{-5}, \qquad \Pr[B \le 480] \le e^{-0.04 \times 600/2} = e^{-12} \approx 6.1\times10^{-6}. \tag{2.41}\] The two events cannot happen together, so \(B\) stays within \(600 \pm 20\%\) except with probability about \(2.4\times10^{-5}\) per step. Over 1,000 steps, Lemma 2.3 adds the per-step failure probabilities, so every batch stays in that range except with probability about \(1{,}000 \times 2.4\times10^{-5} = 0.024\).

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.5 Gaussian and Laplace tails
The normal and Laplace distributions are the two standard models of additive noise, and later chapters add such noise to computed numbers on purpose, so they need to know how large it can be. Both densities are known exactly, so this section bounds their tails directly and more sharply, and gives the width of the largest of many draws. The running example is a count, not a noise model, so this section’s examples use the noise itself.
Write \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) for a standard normal variable and \(\varphi(z) = e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) for its density. Of the two bounds below, the second, the Mills ratio bound, named after the ratio of tail to density, is sharper far out. Its proof weights the density by a factor that is at least 1 on the tail and makes the integral easy.

Proposition 2.2 (Gaussian tail bounds) Let \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) have density \(\varphi\), and let \(t > 0\). Then \[\Pr[Z \ge t] \le \tfrac12 e^{-t^2/2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Pr[Z \ge t] \le \frac{\varphi(t)}{t}. \tag{2.42}\] If \(X_1, \dots, X_k\) each have the distribution \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), independent or not, then for every \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every \(|X_i|\) is below \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\).


Proof. Steps 1 to 3 prove the first bound, steps 4 and 5 the second, and step 6 the width.

Shift the tail to start at 0. Substituting \(y = z - t\) makes the tail integral run over \(y \ge 0\): \[\Pr[Z \ge t] = \int_0^\infty \varphi(t + y)\,\mathrm dy. \tag{2.43}\]
Split the density. Expanding \((t+y)^2 = t^2 + 2ty + y^2\) in the exponent splits the density into the factor \(e^{-t^2/2}\), a factor \(e^{-ty}\) and the density \(\varphi(y)\), which keeps the constant \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\): \[\Pr[Z \ge t] = e^{-t^2/2}\int_0^\infty e^{-ty}\varphi(y)\,\mathrm dy. \tag{2.44}\]
Drop the middle factor. The factor \(e^{-ty}\) is at most 1 for \(t, y \ge 0\), and the integral of \(\varphi\) over \(y \ge 0\) is \(\frac12\) because the density is symmetric about 0. Together they give the first bound.
Weight the density. On \(z \ge t\) the factor \(z/t\) is at least 1, so multiplying the density by it can only increase the integral: \[\Pr[Z \ge t] = \int_t^\infty \varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz \le \int_t^\infty \frac zt\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz. \tag{2.45}\]
Integrate. Differentiating the density gives \(\varphi'(z) = -z\varphi(z)\), so \(z\varphi(z)\) has the antiderivative \(-\varphi(z)\). The integral of step 4 is therefore \(\frac1t\big[-\varphi(z)\big]_t^\infty = \varphi(t)/t\).
Width of \(k\) draws. Each \(X_i\) is \(\sigma Z\), so the first bound, doubled for both tails, gives \(\Pr[|X_i| \ge t] \le e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Setting this equal to \(\beta/k\) gives \(t = \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\) by Lemma 2.1, and Lemma 2.3 over the \(k\) draws gives a total failure probability of at most \(\beta\).


A standard normal is 1-sub-Gaussian, since its MGF is \(e^{\lambda^2/2}\), so Proposition 2.1 gives the Chernoff bound \(e^{-t^2/2}\), and the first bound beats it by a factor of \(\frac12\). The ratio of the Mills bound to the exact tail tends to 1 as \(t\) grows, because the tail mass sits ever closer to \(t\), where the factor \(z/t\) is close to 1.

Example 2.6 At \(t = 3\) the exact standard normal tail is \(1.35\times10^{-3}\). Against it, Chebyshev’s inequality allows \(1/3^2 = 0.111\) and the Chernoff bound \(e^{-9/2} = 0.0111\), while the two bounds of Proposition 2.2 allow \(0.0056\) (the halved Chernoff bound) and \(\varphi(3)/3 = 0.00148\) (the Mills ratio). So the Mills ratio is within 10% of the exact tail, while the Chernoff bound is 8 times too large (Figure 2.4).







Figure 2.4: The exact standard normal tail against the Chebyshev, Chernoff, halved Chernoff and Mills-ratio bounds.



For the Laplace distribution the tail can be computed exactly, so no bound is needed. The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b > 0\) has density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|x|/b}\), symmetric around 0.

Proposition 2.3 (Laplace tails and widths) Let \(X \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and \(t \ge 0\). Then \[\Pr[X \ge t] = \tfrac12 e^{-t/b}, \qquad \Pr[|X| \ge t] = e^{-t/b}. \tag{2.46}\] For \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), one draw satisfies \(|X| \le b\ln(1/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). Draws \(X_1, \dots, X_k \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\), independent or not, all satisfy \(|X_i| \le b\ln(k/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. 

The tail. Integrating the density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-x/b}\) from \(t\) to infinity gives \(\frac12 e^{-t/b}\). The density is symmetric, so the two-sided tail is twice that.
One draw. Setting \(e^{-t/b} = \beta\) and solving gives \(t = b\ln(1/\beta)\).
Many draws. Setting \(e^{-t/b} = \beta/k\) gives \(t = b\ln(k/\beta)\), and Lemma 2.3 over the \(k\) draws gives a total failure probability of at most \(\beta\).


For independent draws the union bound is nearly exact, because they rarely fail together when each fails rarely. For \(k = 100\) draws of \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) at \(\beta = 0.05\), the width is \(\ln(100/0.05) = 7.60\), and simulated draws exceed it at the rate 0.0486, close to the target (Figure 2.5).






Figure 2.5: Left: the bound \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) grows like \(\ln k\). Right: the empirical probability that the maximum of \(k\) Laplace draws exceeds it stays at \(\beta = 0.05\).




2.5.1 Sums of Laplace variables
Noise is often added many times and summed, so how large can a sum of \(k\) Laplace draws get? The Laplace MGF is \(1/(1 - \lambda^2b^2)\) for \(|\lambda| < 1/b\) and infinite beyond (Probability distributions), so no bound of the form \(e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\) holds for every \(\lambda\), and a Laplace variable is not sub-Gaussian. For \(|\lambda| \le 1/(2b)\), though, its log-MGF is still at most a quadratic, and the proof of Proposition 2.4 below runs the Chernoff bound on that range only.

Lemma 2.4 (The Laplace MGF near zero) Let \(X \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\). For every \(\lambda\) with \(|\lambda| \le 1/(2b)\), \[M_X(\lambda) \le e^{2\lambda^2b^2}. \tag{2.47}\]


Proof. 

Rewrite the log-MGF. With \(x = \lambda^2b^2\), the log-MGF is \(-\ln(1 - x)\), and the condition on \(\lambda\) gives \(x \le \frac14\).
Compare series. The series \(-\ln(1 - x) = x + x^2/2 + x^3/3 + \dots\) is term by term at most \(x + x^2 + x^3 + \dots\), which is the geometric series \(x/(1 - x)\).
Bound the denominator. Since \(x \le \frac14\), the factor \(1/(1 - x)\) is at most \(\frac43\), rounded up to 2 to keep the constants simple, so the log-MGF is at most \(2x = 2\lambda^2b^2\).



Proposition 2.4 (Sums of Laplace variables) Let \(S\) be the sum of \(k\) independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variables, and let \(t > 0\). Then \[\Pr[S \ge t] \le \exp\left(-\min\left(\frac{t^2}{8kb^2},\ \frac{t}{4b}\right)\right). \tag{2.48}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the MGF of \(S\) on the range of \(\lambda\) where Lemma 2.4 applies, run the Chernoff bound with \(\lambda\) restricted to that range, and split by whether the best \(\lambda\) lies inside it.

The MGF of the sum. The MGF of \(S\) is the product of \(k\) factors, each at most \(e^{2\lambda^2b^2}\) by the lemma, so \(M_S(\lambda) \le e^{2k\lambda^2b^2}\) for \(0 < \lambda \le 1/(2b)\).
The unconstrained optimum. By Equation 2.11 the exponent to minimize is \(-\lambda t + 2k\lambda^2b^2\), a parabola whose derivative \(-t + 4k\lambda b^2\) vanishes at \(\lambda^* = t/(4kb^2)\).
Small deviations. The optimum \(\lambda^*\) is allowed exactly when \(t \le 2kb\). Substituting it gives the exponent \(-t^2/(4kb^2) + t^2/(8kb^2) = -t^2/(8kb^2)\), so the bound is \(e^{-t^2/(8kb^2)}\).
Large deviations. If \(t > 2kb\), the parabola is still decreasing at \(1/(2b)\), so the best allowed \(\lambda\) is that boundary, where the exponent is \(-t/(2b) + 2kb^2/(4b^2) = -t/(2b) + k/2\). In this regime \(k/2 < t/(4b)\), so the exponent is at most \(-t/(4b)\).
Combine. Since \(t^2/(8kb^2) \le t/(4b)\) exactly when \(t \le 2kb\), the minimum is \(t^2/(8kb^2)\) in the regime of step 3 and \(t/(4b)\) in that of step 4.


Small deviations look Gaussian, with a variance of order \(kb^2\), and large deviations decay only exponentially. That two-regime shape is what sub-exponential means.

Example 2.7 Take \(k = 10\) and \(b = 1\). The central limit theorem approximates the sum by a normal variable with the same mean 0 and variance \(10 \times 2b^2 = 20\), since one \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) draw has variance \(2b^2\). It matches the bulk, with \(\Pr[S \ge 10]\) equal to \(1.42\times10^{-2}\) in simulation and \(1.27\times10^{-2}\) from the normal. But \(\Pr[S \ge 20]\) is \(3.4\times10^{-5}\) in simulation and only \(3.9\times10^{-6}\) from the normal, a factor of 9 too small. Both deviations are in the Gaussian regime of Proposition 2.4, so the bound gives \(e^{-100/80} = 0.287\) at \(t = 10\) and \(e^{-5} = 6.7\times10^{-3}\) at \(t = 20\), loose but a guarantee (Figure 2.6).







Figure 2.6: Empirical tail of a sum of 10 Laplace(1) variables, against the sub-exponential bound and the normal approximation.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.6 Azuma and McDiarmid
So far every quantity was a sum of independent terms, and two common situations break that. In sequential procedures each step can be chosen after seeing earlier outcomes, so the terms are dependent and the MGF of their sum no longer factorizes. And the risk of a model trained on the data is a complicated function of all the records, not a sum of one term per record. Azuma’s inequality handles the first situation, and McDiarmid’s inequality, which follows from it, the second. Azuma’s needs a martingale, a running total whose next step is zero on average given the past, like your fortune in a sequence of fair bets that you choose as you go.

Definition 2.2 (Martingale) A sequence \(W_0, W_1, \dots, W_n\) of random variables is a martingale if each increment \(U_i = W_i - W_{i-1}\) has mean zero given the past, that is, given everything observed before step \(i\): \[\mathbb E[U_i \mid \text{past}] = 0, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n. \tag{2.49}\]

Azuma’s inequality says that the total drift \(W_n - W_0\) obeys the same tail bound as a sum of independent bounded terms, with the lengths of the steps’ intervals in place of the ranges.

Theorem 2.7 (Azuma–Hoeffding inequality) Let \(W_0, \dots, W_n\) be a martingale whose increments satisfy \(U_i \in [A_i, A_i + d_i]\), where the position \(A_i\) may depend on the past but the length \(d_i\) is fixed in advance, so that the bound of each step is a constant. For every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr[W_n - W_0 \ge t] \le \exp\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i d_i^2}\right). \tag{2.50}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound it one step at a time instead, starting from the last step and working back, and then to apply the Chernoff bound.

Bound one step given the past. Given the past, \(U_i\) is a variable with mean zero on an interval of length \(d_i\). So Lemma 2.2 applies to it, with every expectation taken given the past, and its proof runs unchanged: \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda U_i} \mid \text{past}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2d_i^2/8}. \tag{2.51}\]
Peel off the last increment. The tower property says that you can average in two stages, first over the last step with the past held fixed and then over the past, and get the ordinary average. Split \(W_n - W_0 = (W_{n-1} - W_0) + U_n\). With the past held fixed, \(e^{\lambda(W_{n-1} - W_0)}\) is a constant and comes out of the inner average: \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(W_n - W_0)}\big] = \mathbb E\Big[e^{\lambda(W_{n-1} - W_0)}\,\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda U_n} \mid \text{past}\big]\Big]. \tag{2.52}\] Step 1 bounds the inner average by a constant, because \(d_n\) is fixed in advance, and a constant comes out of the outer average: \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(W_n - W_0)}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2d_n^2/8}\,\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(W_{n-1} - W_0)}\big]. \tag{2.53}\]
Repeat. Applying the same step to \(W_{n-1} - W_0\), then to \(W_{n-2} - W_0\), and so on, \(n\) times, gives \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(W_n - W_0)}\big] \le \exp\Big(\lambda^2\sum_i d_i^2/8\Big). \tag{2.54}\]
Chernoff. By Equation 2.11 the exponent to minimize is \(-\lambda t + \lambda^2\sum_i d_i^2/8\). Its derivative vanishes at \(\lambda = 4t/\sum_i d_i^2\), and substituting this \(\lambda\) gives the exponent \(-2t^2/\sum_i d_i^2\).


Hoeffding’s inequality is the special case of independent increments.

Example 2.8 You have two coins, with heads probabilities 0.3 and 0.7. You flip 200 times, and before each flip you pick the 0.7 coin if the previous flip was heads and the 0.3 coin otherwise. The flips are dependent, so Hoeffding’s inequality does not apply. What you can control is how far the heads count drifts from what your own choices predicted. Let \(X_i\) be 1 if flip \(i\) is heads, and \(p_i\) the heads probability of the coin chosen for it. Let \(W_n = \sum_{i \le n}(X_i - p_i)\) be the number of heads minus the number you expected. Given the past the coin is fixed, so \(X_i - p_i\) has mean \(p_i - p_i = 0\) and lies in \([-p_i, 1 - p_i]\), an interval of length 1. So \(W\) is a martingale with \(d_i = 1\) and \(\sum_i d_i^2 = 200\). At \(t = 20\), Theorem 2.7 gives \[\Pr[W_{200} \ge 20] \le e^{-2 \times 400/200} = e^{-4} = 1.83\times10^{-2}, \tag{2.55}\] while simulation gives \(1.12\times10^{-3}\) (Figure 2.7). The bound pays for assuming the worst-case variance, exactly as Hoeffding’s does. Each step’s true variance is \(p_i(1 - p_i) = 0.21\), not the \(0.25\) the interval allows.







Figure 2.7: Empirical tail of the martingale in the adaptive coin game against the Azuma bound.



McDiarmid’s inequality says that a function of many independent inputs that no single input can move much concentrates as tightly as a sum of bounded terms would. The proof turns the function into a martingale by revealing the inputs one at a time and tracking your best guess of its value. Each revealed input moves the guess by a bounded amount, and Azuma’s inequality does the rest.

Theorem 2.8 (McDiarmid’s inequality) Let \(X = (X_1, \dots, X_n)\) have independent coordinates, and let \(f\) be a function of them such that changing only the \(i\)-th input, with all others held fixed, changes \(f\) by at most \(c_i\). For every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\big[f(X) - \mathbb E[f(X)] \ge t\big] \le \exp\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i c_i^2}\right). \tag{2.56}\]


Proof. 

Build the martingale. After seeing \(X_1, \dots, X_i\), your best guess of \(f(X)\) is its conditional average \(W_i = \mathbb E[f(X) \mid X_1, \dots, X_i]\). Before seeing anything the guess is \(W_0 = \mathbb E[f(X)]\), and after seeing everything it is \(W_n = f(X)\), so \(W_n - W_0\) is exactly the deviation to bound. By the tower property, averaging the next guess over the input not yet seen gives back the current guess, so each increment has mean zero given the past.
Bound the range of each increment. Because the inputs are independent, seeing \(X_1, \dots, X_i\) does not change the distribution of the others, so \(W_i\) is the average of \(f\) over fresh copies of the unseen inputs \(X_{i+1}, \dots, X_n\), with \(X_1, \dots, X_i\) fixed at their observed values. With \(X_1, \dots, X_{i-1}\) held fixed, changing \(X_i\) changes every term of that average by at most \(c_i\), so it moves the average by at most \(c_i\). So \(W_i\) stays in an interval of length at most \(c_i\) whose position depends on the past. Given the past, \(W_{i-1}\) is a fixed number, so \(U_i = W_i - W_{i-1}\) stays in an interval of the same length.
Apply Azuma. Theorem 2.7 with \(d_i = c_i\) gives the bound.


The bounded-difference constant \(c_i\) measures how much one input can move the output. Its real use is for functions that are not averages, such as the risk of a trained model (Algorithmic stability and generalization).

Example 2.9 One test example moves the running example’s error rate by at most \(c_i = 1/200\), so \(\sum_i c_i^2 = 1/200\). McDiarmid’s inequality at \(t = 0.05\) then gives \(e^{-2 \times 0.05^2 \times 200} = e^{-1} = 0.37\), which is Hoeffding’s bound of Example 2.3 again.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.1 KL divergence
Someone hands you a die that is either fair or loaded so that a six comes up half the time, and you may roll it as often as you like. How much does one roll tell you, on average, about which die you hold? How strongly can a single roll point the wrong way? How often can the best guess from one roll be right? Each answer is a divergence, a number that is zero when two distributions, call them \(P\) and \(Q\), are equal and grows as they become easier to tell apart. The same questions measure how far a fitted model is from the truth and how many samples an A/B test needs.
One idea organizes the answers. To decide which distribution produced an outcome \(x\), compare how likely \(x\) is under each. Write \(p\) and \(q\) for the probabilities, or densities, of \(P\) and \(Q\). Their quotient is the likelihood ratio \(r(x) = p(x)/q(x)\). Its logarithm \(L(x) = \ln r(x)\) is the evidence for \(P\), in nats, and it adds over independent observations. Every divergence is a summary of \(r\). The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence averages the evidence over draws from \(P\), the max-divergence takes its largest value, and the total variation (TV) distance measures the mass of \(p\) above \(q\). Processing data, such as binning it, can only average likelihood ratios together, so no divergence grows under processing, and this data-processing inequality is what later parts use most.
The running example is the die, with \(P\) loaded and \(Q\) fair (Table 3.1). A six is three times more likely under \(P\), evidence of \(\ln 3 = 1.10\) nats for “loaded”. Any other roll gives \(\ln 0.6 = -0.51\) nats, weak evidence for “fair”. Two continuous pairs recur, a normal and a Laplace density each against a shifted copy, whose evidence is unbounded and bounded (Probability distributions). Sums \(\sum_x\) are integrals for densities, and Table 3.2 lists the symbols.
Add up the evidence of \(n\) rolls of the die. With the loaded die the sum climbs, with the fair die it falls, and each family of runs drifts along a straight line (Figure 3.1). This section names its slope, the average evidence per roll, and proves the two facts every later use rests on: it is never negative, and it adds over independent observations.
That data from \(P\) cannot favour \(Q\) on average sounds obvious, but the proof needs a tool that compares a function of an average with the average of the function. A function \(f\) is convex when its graph bends upward, so that every chord lies above it, and strictly convex when the graph has no straight pieces. The next proof uses Jensen’s inequality at step 2, and later sections use it again.
For the die’s two ratios, 0.6 and 3 each with probability \(\frac12\) under \(P\), and \(f(x) = x^2\), the average is 1.8 and the two sides are \(1.8^2 = 3.24\) and \(\frac12(0.36 + 9) = 4.68\).
KL also measures a model’s fit. For a model \(q_\theta\) with parameter \(\theta\), only the term \(-\mathbb E_P[\ln q_\theta(X)]\) of \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q_\theta)\) depends on \(\theta\), so minimizing this forward KL is maximum likelihood. Because KL averages under its first argument, the forward fit must cover every region the data visit, while the reverse divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_\theta\|P)\) of variational inference may lock onto one mode (Figure 3.2).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
Figure 3.1: Cumulative evidence for “loaded” over 60 rolls of the loaded die (blue) and the fair die (orange).




Definition 3.1 (Kullback–Leibler divergence) The KL divergence of \(P\) from \(Q\) is the average evidence for \(P\) that one observation gives when it comes from \(P\): \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P[L] = \sum_x p(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. \tag{3.1}\] It is infinite when \(P\) puts mass where \(Q\) puts none.



Lemma 3.1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(f\) be convex and let \(X\) be a random variable with a finite average. Then \[f(\mathbb E[X]) \le \mathbb E[f(X)]. \tag{3.2}\] If \(f\) is strictly convex, equality holds only when \(X\) is constant. For a concave \(f\), whose graph bends downward, the inequality is reversed.


Proof. 

Use a tangent. A convex function lies above its tangent lines. Take the tangent at \(\mathbb E[X]\), with slope \(a\), so that \(f(x) \ge f(\mathbb E[X]) + a(x - \mathbb E[X])\) for every \(x\).
Average. Put \(x = X\) and average. The last term averages to 0, because \(X\) averages to \(\mathbb E[X]\), which leaves \(\mathbb E[f(X)] \ge f(\mathbb E[X])\).
Equality. A strictly convex graph touches the tangent only at \(\mathbb E[X]\), so equality forces \(X = \mathbb E[X]\) with probability 1. A concave function is minus a convex one, which flips the inequality.




Theorem 3.1 (Gibbs’ inequality and additivity) For any two distributions, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \ge 0\), with equality only if \(P = Q\). Write \(P_1 \times P_2\) for the distribution of a pair drawn independently from \(P_1\) and \(P_2\). Then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1 \times P_2\,\|\,Q_1 \times Q_2) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\|Q_1) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_2\|Q_2), \tag{3.3}\] so \(n\) independent samples carry \(n\) times the KL divergence of one.


Proof. The plan is to write KL as the average of a convex function and apply Jensen, then to split the evidence of a pair into a sum.

Flip the ratio. Since \(\ln(p/q) = -\ln(q/p)\), KL is the average under \(P\) of the strictly convex function \(-\ln\) of \(q/p\).
Apply Lemma 3.1. The average of \(-\ln\) is at least \(-\ln\) of the average: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \ge -\ln\mathbb E_P\Big[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\Big]. \tag{3.4}\]
The inner average. Each \(p(x)\) cancels, so it is \(\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0}q(x)\), the mass \(Q\) puts where \(P\) can land. That is at most 1, so minus its logarithm is at least 0.
Equality. Step 2 needs \(q/p\) constant where \(p > 0\), and step 3 needs \(Q\) to put no mass elsewhere. Two distributions with a constant ratio on the same outcomes are equal, because both sum to 1.
Additivity. Under a product distribution the probability of a pair is the product of the probabilities, so the evidence of a pair is the sum \(L_1(x_1) + L_2(x_2)\). Averages are linear, and the average of \(L_i(X_i)\) involves only \(P_i\), so it is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_i\|Q_i)\).









Figure 3.2: One Gaussian fitted to two bumps by forward and by reverse KL.




Example 3.1 Under \(P\) the five non-sixes together have probability 0.5 and evidence \(\ln 0.6\) each, and the six has probability 0.5 and evidence \(\ln 3\), so \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.5\ln 0.6 + 0.5\ln 3 = 0.5\ln 1.8 = 0.2939. \tag{3.5}\] In the other direction the fair die weights the non-sixes \(\frac56\) and the six \(\frac16\), and the evidence is for “fair”: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) = \tfrac56\ln\tfrac{1}{0.6} + \tfrac16\ln\tfrac13 = 0.4257 - 0.1831 = 0.2426. \tag{3.6}\] A loaded die gives itself away faster than a fair one proves its innocence, because its sixes carry strong evidence. In general, telling two distributions apart takes a number of observations of order \(1/D_{\mathrm{KL}}\), which Section 3.9 makes precise.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.2 Rényi divergence
KL is an average, so it cannot say how often the evidence is large, and later parts need that. Since \(e^{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\) is the geometric mean of \(r\) under \(P\), other means can weight large ratios more. The power mean with exponent \(\lambda\) raises each value to the power \(\lambda\), averages, and undoes the power: \[m_\lambda = \big(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda]\big)^{1/\lambda}. \tag{3.7}\] Exponent \(-1\) gives the harmonic mean, the limit 0 the geometric mean, 1 the arithmetic mean, and \(\lambda \to \infty\) the largest value (Table 3.3). The Rényi divergence takes the logarithm of the power mean with exponent \(\alpha - 1\), so its order \(\alpha\) is a dial from the typical evidence to the worst case.



Table 3.3: Means of the die’s likelihood ratio under \(P\). Their logarithms are the Rényi divergences of orders 0, 1, 2 and \(\infty\).











Mean of \(r\) under \(P\)
Value
Its logarithm

Harmonic, \(1/\mathbb E_P[1/r]\)

Definition 3.2 (Rényi divergence) For an order \(\alpha \in (0, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\), the Rényi divergence of \(P\) from \(Q\) is \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_x p(x)^\alpha q(x)^{1 - \alpha}. \tag{3.8}\] The max-divergence is \(D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_x r(x)\), an essential supremum for densities, and \(D_1\) is defined as \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\), which Theorem 3.2 shows is the limit at order 1.

The forms used below move an average under \(Q\) to one under \(P\): an outcome three times as likely under \(P\) must count three times as much.

Lemma 3.2 (Change of measure) Suppose \(Q\) gives positive probability to every outcome that \(P\) does. Then for any function \(g\), \[\mathbb E_P[g(X)] = \mathbb E_Q[r(X)\,g(X)]. \tag{3.9}\] In particular \(\mathbb E_Q[r] = 1\), and \(\Pr_P[A] = \mathbb E_Q[r\,\mathbf 1[A]]\) for every event \(A\), with \(\mathbf 1[A]\) equal to 1 on \(A\) and 0 elsewhere.


Proof. Multiply and divide each term of \(\sum_x p(x)g(x)\) by \(q(x)\). The special cases take \(g = 1\) and \(g = \mathbf 1[A]\).

A second form links the divergence to the Chernoff method of Concentration inequalities, which bounds tails through the logarithm of a moment generating function. For the evidence under \(P\) that logarithm, the cumulant generating function of Probability distributions, is \[K_L(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{\lambda L}\big]. \tag{3.10}\]

Proposition 3.1 (Three forms of the Rényi divergence) For every order \(\alpha \in (0, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big] = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P\big[r^{\alpha - 1}\big]. \tag{3.11}\] So the divergence is the logarithm of a power mean, and a chord slope of \(K_L\): \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \ln m_{\alpha - 1}, \tag{3.12}\] \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{K_L(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{3.13}\]


Proof. 

Each term \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\) equals \(q\,r^\alpha\), so the sum is \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha]\), and Lemma 3.2 with \(g = r^{\alpha - 1}\) turns it into \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}]\).
Dividing a logarithm by \(\alpha - 1\) takes the logarithm of the power \(1/(\alpha - 1)\), which gives Equation 3.12.
Since \(r^{\alpha - 1} = e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), the logarithm of \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}]\) is \(K_L(\alpha - 1)\), which gives Equation 3.13.


The behaviour of the family therefore follows from the shape of \(K_L\), and the limit at order 1 needs its slope at 0.

Lemma 3.3 (Shape of the log moment generating function) If \(K_L\) is finite near 0, then \(K_L(0) = 0\), \(K_L'(0) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\), and \(K_L\) is convex.


Proof. 

Value. \(K_L(0) = \ln\mathbb E_P[1] = 0\).
Slope. Differentiate the logarithm of the average, passing the derivative inside it: \[K_L'(\lambda) = \frac{\mathbb E_P\big[L e^{\lambda L}\big]}{\mathbb E_P\big[e^{\lambda L}\big]}. \tag{3.14}\] This is the average of \(L\) under the tilted distribution, which weights each outcome \(x\) in proportion to \(p(x)r(x)^\lambda\). At \(\lambda = 0\) there is no tilt, and the slope is \(\mathbb E_P[L]\), the KL divergence.
Curvature. Differentiating once more gives the variance of \(L\) under the tilted distribution, which is never negative, so \(K_L\) is convex.



Theorem 3.2 (Properties of the Rényi family) For any two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\):

Order 1. If \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) is finite for some \(\alpha > 1\), then \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) as \(\alpha \to 1\).
Order \(\infty\). \(D_\alpha \to D_\infty(P\|Q)\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\), and the max-divergence is the largest log-ratio over events: \[D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_{A:\,\Pr_Q[A] > 0}\frac{\Pr_P[A]}{\Pr_Q[A]}. \tag{3.15}\]
Order 0. \(D_\alpha \to -\ln\Pr_Q[p(X) > 0]\) as \(\alpha \to 0\).
Monotonicity. \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\).
Additivity. \(D_\alpha(P_1 \times P_2\|Q_1 \times Q_2) = D_\alpha(P_1\|Q_1) + D_\alpha(P_2\|Q_2)\) for every order.
Skew symmetry. For \(0 < \alpha < 1\), \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}D_{1 - \alpha}(Q\|P)\), so \(D_{1/2}\) is symmetric.



Proof. The plan is to take the limits from the forms of Proposition 3.1 and from the sum, monotonicity from Jensen, and the last two claims from the algebra of the sum.

Order 1. The assumption makes \(K_L\) finite near 0, so Equation 3.13 is a difference quotient of \(K_L\) at 0, and it tends to \(K_L'(0)\), which is KL by Lemma 3.3. Section F.4 in the appendices proves the limit from below without the assumption.
Order \(\infty\), upper bound. Let \(r_{\max}\) be the largest likelihood ratio on the support of \(P\). Every \(r \le r_{\max}\), so \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}] \le r_{\max}^{\alpha - 1}\), and Equation 3.12 gives \(D_\alpha \le \ln r_{\max}\) for \(\alpha > 1\).
Order \(\infty\), lower bound. Keep only the term of a point \(x^*\) where \(r = r_{\max}\), which makes the average smaller, so \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}] \ge p(x^*)r_{\max}^{\alpha - 1}\). Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\), \[D_\alpha \ge \ln r_{\max} + \frac{\ln p(x^*)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{3.16}\] The last term vanishes as \(\alpha \to \infty\), so steps 2 and 3 squeeze \(D_\alpha\) to \(\ln r_{\max}\). For densities, replace \(x^*\) by a set of positive probability on which \(r\) is within any margin of \(r_{\max}\).
Events. By Lemma 3.2, \(\Pr_P[A] = \mathbb E_Q[r\,\mathbf 1[A]] \le r_{\max}\Pr_Q[A]\), and the event \(\{x^*\}\) reaches the bound.
Order 0. As \(\alpha \to 0\), \(p^\alpha \to 1\) wherever \(p > 0\), so the sum tends to \(\Pr_Q[p(X) > 0]\), and its logarithm is divided by \(\alpha - 1 \to -1\).
Monotonicity, positive exponents. By Equation 3.12 it is enough that the power mean grows with its exponent. For \(0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2\) the function \(y \mapsto y^{\lambda_2/\lambda_1}\) is convex, so Lemma 3.1 applied to \(Y = r^{\lambda_1}\) gives \[\big(\mathbb E_P[r^{\lambda_1}]\big)^{\lambda_2/\lambda_1} \le \mathbb E_P[r^{\lambda_2}], \tag{3.17}\] and raising both sides to the positive power \(1/\lambda_2\) keeps the order, so \(m_{\lambda_1} \le m_{\lambda_2}\).
Monotonicity, other exponents. The logarithm is concave, so Jensen reversed gives \(\ln\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] \ge \lambda\,\mathbb E_P[\ln r]\). Dividing by \(\lambda\) puts \(\ln m_\lambda\) above the logarithm of the geometric mean when \(\lambda > 0\) and below it when \(\lambda < 0\). For two negative exponents the power \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1\) lies in \((0, 1)\), so the function is concave and step 6 reverses, but the negative power \(1/\lambda_2\) reverses it back.
Additivity. The evidence of a pair is the sum of two independent terms, and the moment generating function of such a sum is the product of theirs (Lemma 1.2). So \(K_L = K_{L_1} + K_{L_2}\), and Equation 3.13 divides by \(\alpha - 1\).
Skew symmetry. Swapping \(p\) with \(q\) and \(\alpha\) with \(1 - \alpha\) leaves each term \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\) unchanged. So the two sums are equal, and their logarithms are \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) and \(-\alpha D_{1 - \alpha}(Q\|P)\).


Figure 3.3 draws the chords for the die, and Figure 3.4 the tilted distribution with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\).






Figure 3.3: Left: \(K_L\) for the die, whose chord to \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) has slope \(D_\alpha\). Right: \(D_\alpha\) against \(\alpha\).









Figure 3.4: The tilted weights \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\) for a Gaussian pair (left) and a Laplace pair (right).



The family can also bound how often a sample from \(Q\) looks like strong evidence for \(P\). The tool is Markov’s inequality, which says that a quantity that cannot be negative exceeds a level with probability at most its average divided by that level.

Proposition 3.2 (Tail of the evidence) For every evidence level \(c\) and every order \(\alpha > 0\), \[\Pr_Q[L \ge c] \le \exp\big(-\alpha c + (\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)\big). \tag{3.18}\]


Proof. 

The quantity \(r^\alpha = e^{\alpha L}\) cannot be negative, and it is at least \(e^{\alpha c}\) exactly when \(L \ge c\), so Markov’s inequality gives \(\Pr_Q[L \ge c] \le e^{-\alpha c}\,\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha]\).
By Proposition 3.1, \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\), and at \(\alpha = 1\) it is 1 by Lemma 3.2.


At order 1 the bound is \(e^{-c}\) for every pair, and larger orders use more about the pair to do much better (Example 3.3).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.3 Two Gaussians with equal variance
The most common pair in practice is a distribution and a shifted copy of it, such as a feature before and after a drift. For two normals with equal variance every divergence has a closed form in the shift measured in standard deviations: KL is half its square, each Rényi divergence is \(\alpha\) times the KL, and the max-divergence is infinite, because the evidence is a line with no top.

Proposition 3.3 (Divergences of two shifted normals) Let \(P = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(s, \sigma^2)\), and write \(\mu = s/\sigma\) for the shift in standard deviations. Then for every order \(\alpha\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \frac{\mu^2}{2}, \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{\alpha\mu^2}{2}, \qquad D_\infty(P\|Q) = \infty. \tag{3.19}\] The same holds for any two means a distance \(s\) apart, since shifting both changes nothing.


Proof. The plan is to compute the evidence, average it for KL, and complete the square in the Rényi integral.

The evidence. The normal density with mean \(m\) is \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x - m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). The constants cancel in the ratio, and expanding \((x - s)^2\) cancels the \(x^2\) terms: \[L(x) = \frac{(x - s)^2 - x^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{s^2 - 2sx}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{3.20}\]
KL. The evidence is linear in \(x\), so its average under \(P\) is its value at the mean 0, which is \(s^2/(2\sigma^2) = \mu^2/2\).
Constants. The factors \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\) raised to the powers \(\alpha\) and \(1 - \alpha\) multiply back to one such factor. What remains of \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\) is \(\exp(-B(x)/(2\sigma^2))\), with \(B(x) = \alpha x^2 + (1 - \alpha)(x - s)^2\).
Complete the square around \((1 - \alpha)s\). The constant left over is \((1 - \alpha)s^2 - (1 - \alpha)^2s^2\), so \[B(x) = \big(x - (1 - \alpha)s\big)^2 + \alpha(1 - \alpha)s^2. \tag{3.21}\]
Integrate. The squared term, with the factor \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\), is the density of \(\mathcal N((1 - \alpha)s, \sigma^2)\) and integrates to 1, so \[\int p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\,\mathrm dx = \exp\Big(-\frac{\alpha(1 - \alpha)s^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{3.22}\]
Divide. Taking the logarithm and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(\alpha s^2/(2\sigma^2)\), since \(-\alpha(1 - \alpha)/(\alpha - 1) = \alpha\).
Max-divergence. The line \(L\) has a non-zero slope, so it is unbounded above.


Doubling the noise is the same as halving the shift. By additivity, independent coordinates with shifts \(s_i\) give \(\alpha\sum_i s_i^2/(2\sigma^2)\), which depends only on the length of the shift vector (Section E.1 in the appendices proves the rotation invariance behind this). Every finite order is finite while the worst case is infinite, because large ratios exist but are rare, and Equation 3.18 measures how rare.

Example 3.3 Take \(\mu = 1\), so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0.5\) and \(D_\alpha = \alpha/2\). How often does a draw from \(Q\) give at least \(c = 2\) nats of evidence for \(P\)? The evidence decreases in \(x\), so \(L \ge c\) exactly when \(x \le \frac s2 - \frac{c\sigma^2}{s}\). Under \(Q\), \(x = s + \sigma Z\) with \(Z\) standard normal. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, so that \(\Phi(z)\) is the probability that \(Z \le z\). Then \[\Pr_Q[L \ge c] = \Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac c\mu\Big) = \Phi(-2.5) = 0.0062. \tag{3.23}\] At order 1, Equation 3.18 gives Markov’s bound \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\). With \(D_\alpha = \alpha\mu^2/2\) the exponent of the bound is the parabola \(-\alpha c + \alpha(\alpha - 1)\mu^2/2\), smallest at \(\alpha = c/\mu^2 + \frac12 = 2.5\). There it equals \(-3.125\), so the bound is \(e^{-3.125} = 0.0439\), 7 times the exact value against 22 times for Markov’s.

title: 3  Divergences
section: 3.4 Two Laplace distributions with shifted location
text:
3.4 Two Laplace distributions with shifted location
The Laplace distribution, with density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|x - m|/b}\) for centre \(m\) and scale \(b\), is the other standard noise model. Its evidence against a shifted copy is bounded, so this section computes the whole Rényi family to see what a bounded ratio changes. The max-divergence turns out to be the shift in units of the scale, and KL slightly less.

Proposition 3.4 (Divergences of two shifted Laplace distributions) Let \(P = \mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\) with \(s \ge 0\), and write \(t = s/b\). Then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = t + e^{-t} - 1, \qquad D_\infty(P\|Q) = t, \tag{3.24}\] and for every order \(\alpha \ne \frac12, 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\right). \tag{3.25}\] At \(\alpha = \frac12\) the bracket is replaced by its limit \((1 + \frac t2)e^{-t/2}\).


Proof. The plan is to rescale, read the max-divergence off the evidence, average the evidence for KL, and integrate the Rényi sum piece by piece.

Rescale. Dividing by \(b\) is a bijection, which changes no divergence (apply Theorem 3.5 to it and to its inverse), so take \(b = 1\) and \(s = t\). The evidence is the difference of the exponents, \(L(x) = |x - t| - |x|\).
Max-divergence. Two numbers a distance \(t\) apart have absolute values that differ by at most \(t\), by the triangle inequality, so \(L \le t\). For \(x \le 0\) both \(x\) and \(x - t\) are negative, and \(L(x) = t\) exactly.
KL, set up. KL is \(\mathbb E[|X - t|] - \mathbb E[|X|]\) with \(X \sim \mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\), and the second average is 1, the mean of the exponential density of \(|X|\).
KL, remove the absolute value. Every number satisfies \(|y| = y + 2(-y)_+\). Put \(y = X - t\) and use \(\mathbb E[X] = 0\): \[\mathbb E[|X - t|] = -t + 2\,\mathbb E[(t - X)_+]. \tag{3.26}\]
KL, the positive part. \((t - X)_+\) is the length of the interval from \(X\) up to \(t\), so its average integrates the distribution function, \(\frac12e^x\) below 0 and \(1 - \frac12e^{-x}\) above, over \(x < t\): \[\mathbb E[(t - X)_+] = \int_{-\infty}^0\tfrac12e^x\,\mathrm dx + \int_0^t\big(1 - \tfrac12e^{-x}\big)\,\mathrm dx = t + \tfrac12e^{-t}. \tag{3.27}\] So \(\mathbb E[|X - t|] = t + e^{-t}\), and subtracting 1 gives the KL.
Rényi. The integral \(I(\alpha) = \frac12\int\exp(-\alpha|x| - (1 - \alpha)|x - t|)\,\mathrm dx\) has an exponent linear in \(x\) on each of the pieces \(x < 0\), \(0 \le x \le t\) and \(x > t\), which integrate to \(e^{-(1 - \alpha)t}\), \(\frac{e^{-\alpha t} - e^{-(1 - \alpha)t}}{1 - 2\alpha}\) and \(e^{-\alpha t}\). Adding the pieces and halving, \(e^{-\alpha t}\) gets the coefficient \(\frac12(1 + \frac{1}{1 - 2\alpha}) = \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}\), and \(e^{(\alpha - 1)t}\) gets \(\frac12(1 - \frac{1}{1 - 2\alpha}) = \frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}\). Then \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln I(\alpha)\) is Equation 3.25.


The worst case is not rare here: the evidence equals \(t\) on all of \(x \le 0\), which has probability \(\frac12\) under \(P\). Against a Gaussian pair of the same variance \(2b^2\), the Laplace pair is further apart at low orders, but the Gaussian \(D_\alpha\) grows linearly while the Laplace one levels off at \(t\), and at \(t = 1\) they cross at order 2.98 (Figure 3.5).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.5 Total variation
KL and Rényi divergences are convenient to compute, but total variation answers the operational questions. It says how well the best possible test tells \(P\) from \(Q\) with one observation, and how far any bounded statistic can move when \(Q\) is replaced by \(P\).

Definition 3.3 (Total variation distance) The total variation distance is the largest difference between the probabilities that \(P\) and \(Q\) give to one event: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \max_A\big|\Pr_P[A] - \Pr_Q[A]\big|. \tag{3.28}\]

The hockey-stick divergence of Section 3.6 asks the same question with a weight on \(Q\). Which event, or which soft event that includes each outcome with some probability, makes \(\Pr_P[A] - \gamma\Pr_Q[A]\) largest? The next lemma answers it once for both sections.

Lemma 3.4 (The best event) Let \(\gamma \ge 0\). The largest value of \(\Pr_P[A] - \gamma\Pr_Q[A]\) over events \(A\) is \[\max_A\big[\Pr_P[A] - \gamma\Pr_Q[A]\big] = \sum_x\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big)_+, \tag{3.29}\] reached at \(A^* = \{x : r(x) > \gamma\}\). A soft event, which includes each outcome \(x\) with probability \(\phi(x) \in [0, 1]\), does no better: \(\sum_x\phi(x)(p(x) - \gamma q(x))\) is at most the same sum.


Proof. 

The quantity is \(\sum_{x \in A}(p(x) - \gamma q(x))\), and an outcome adds a positive term exactly when \(p(x) > \gamma q(x)\). So the sum is largest when \(A\) holds those outcomes and no others.
Each term of the soft sum is \(\phi(x)\) times the bracket, which is at most the positive part of the bracket. So the soft sum is at most the sum of the positive parts.



Theorem 3.3 (Forms and uses of total variation) The total variation is the largest gap over events, the mass of \(p\) above \(q\), half the total absolute difference, and the average under \(Q\) of how far \(r\) exceeds 1: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \max_A|\Pr_P[A] - \Pr_Q[A]| = \sum_x(p - q)_+ = \frac12\sum_x|p - q| = \mathbb E_Q\big[(r - 1)_+\big]. \tag{3.30}\] The overlap is \(\sum_x\min(p, q) = 1 - \mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\). Moreover:

Bounded statistics. Every function \(g\) with values in \([0, 1]\) satisfies \(|\mathbb E_P[g] - \mathbb E_Q[g]| \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
Best single-shot test. If nature picks \(P\) or \(Q\) with probability \(\frac12\) each and shows you one draw, the best guess is correct with probability \[\Pr[\text{correct}] = \frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q). \tag{3.31}\]
Metric. TV is symmetric, zero only when \(P = Q\), at most 1, and satisfies the triangle inequality.



Proof. The plan is to get the forms from Lemma 3.4 with weight 1, then to treat the statistic and the test as soft events.

Forms. The lemma with \(\gamma = 1\) gives \(\max_A[\Pr_P[A] - \Pr_Q[A]] = \sum(p - q)_+\). The differences \(p - q\) sum to 0, so their positive and negative parts have equal mass. So the best event for \(Q\) over \(P\) gives the same value, which justifies the absolute value, and the half-sum of \(|p - q|\) is that common value. Since \(p - q = q(r - 1)\), the sum is also \(\mathbb E_Q[(r - 1)_+]\).
Overlap. At each \(x\), \(\min(p, q) = p - (p - q)_+\), and summing over \(x\) gives \(1 - \mathrm{TV}\).
Bounded statistics. The gap \(\mathbb E_P[g] - \mathbb E_Q[g] = \sum_x g(x)(p(x) - q(x))\) is a soft event, so the lemma bounds it by TV, and \(1 - g\) bounds the other sign.
Best test. Saying “\(P\)” on \(A\) is right with probability \(\frac12\Pr_P[A] + \frac12(1 - \Pr_Q[A])\), which is \(\frac12 + \frac12(\Pr_P[A] - \Pr_Q[A])\). Step 1 maximizes the bracket, and a randomized test is a soft event that does no better.
Metric. The half-sum is half the \(\ell_1\) distance between two probability tables, which has the three properties and is at most 1.


So no classifier beats \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\) accuracy from one draw, and a data shift of TV 0.01 moves any fixed classifier’s accuracy by at most 0.01. TV is not additive, so for \(n\) samples you compute KL and convert it with Section 3.9.

Example 3.5 On the die only the six has \(p > q\), so \(\mathrm{TV} = 0.5 - \frac16 = \frac13\). The best test says “loaded” exactly when it sees a six, and it is right with probability \(\frac23\). For the Gaussian pair the curves cross at the midpoint \(s/2\), so the best event is \(\{x < s/2\}\). It has probability \(\Phi(\frac\mu2)\) under \(P\) and \(\Phi(-\frac\mu2) = 1 - \Phi(\frac\mu2)\) under \(Q\), so \[\mathrm{TV} = 2\Phi\Big(\frac\mu2\Big) - 1. \tag{3.32}\] At \(\mu = 1\) this is 0.3829, and the best test is right with probability \(\Phi(0.5) = 0.6915\) (Figure 3.6, left). At \(\mu = 0.1\) it is only 0.0399.







Figure 3.6: Left: the total variation of a Gaussian pair, shaded. Right: the best accuracy for \(n\) samples (Example 3.10).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.6 Hockey-stick divergence
TV measures the mass of \(p\) above \(q\). Now scale \(q\) up by a factor \(\gamma \ge 1\) and measure the mass of \(p\) that still sticks out above \(\gamma q\) (Figure 3.7). Only likelihood ratios above \(\gamma\) count, so this measures how much of the difference comes from large ratios. It appears in tests with unequal priors, and in rejection sampling, which draws from a target \(p\) by proposing from \(q\) under an envelope \(\gamma q\).






Figure 3.7: The mass of \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) above \(\gamma\) times \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\): 0.3829, 0.1906 and 0.0692 at \(\gamma = 1, 2, 4\).




Definition 3.4 (Hockey-stick divergence) For \(\gamma \ge 1\), which makes it vanish when \(P = Q\), the hockey-stick divergence is \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \max_A\big[\Pr_P[A] - \gamma\Pr_Q[A]\big]. \tag{3.33}\]


Proposition 3.5 (Properties of the hockey-stick divergence) Let \(\gamma \ge 1\) and \(c = \ln\gamma\). Then:

Forms. \(E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \sum_x(p - \gamma q)_+ = \mathbb E_Q[(r - \gamma)_+]\), and \(E_1(P\|Q) = \mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
Shape. \(E_\gamma\) is non-increasing and convex in \(\gamma\), and it is 0 exactly when \(\gamma \ge e^{D_\infty(P\|Q)}\).
Tails. \(E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \Pr_P[L > c] - \gamma\Pr_Q[L > c]\).
Unequal priors. If \(P\) has prior probability \(\pi \le \frac12\), the smallest probability of a wrong guess from one observation is \(\pi(1 - E_\gamma(P\|Q))\) with \(\gamma = (1 - \pi)/\pi\), the prior odds against \(P\).



Proof. 

Forms. Lemma 3.4 with weight \(\gamma\) gives the sum, and \(p - \gamma q = q(r - \gamma)\) turns it into an average under \(Q\).
Shape. Each term \((r(x) - \gamma)_+\) is a descending line in \(\gamma\) that flattens at 0, so it is non-increasing and convex, and so is their average. All terms vanish exactly when \(\gamma\) is at least the largest ratio.
Tails. The terms are non-zero only on \(\{r > \gamma\} = \{L > c\}\), where \(p\) sums to \(\Pr_P[L > c]\) and \(\gamma q\) to \(\gamma\Pr_Q[L > c]\).
Priors. Guessing “\(P\)” on \(A\) errs when a draw from \(P\) falls outside \(A\) or one from \(Q\) falls inside it. Factoring out \(\pi\), the error is \[\pi(1 - \Pr_P[A]) + (1 - \pi)\Pr_Q[A] = \pi - \pi\big[\Pr_P[A] - \gamma\Pr_Q[A]\big], \tag{3.34}\] which is smallest when the bracket is largest, that is equal to \(E_\gamma\).


Always guessing \(Q\) errs with probability \(\pi\), and one observation removes a fraction \(E_\gamma\) of that error. For the shifted pairs, property 3 gives the whole curve in closed form, and later parts use exactly these two curves.

Proposition 3.6 (Hockey-stick divergence of the shifted pairs) Let \(\gamma \ge 1\) and \(c = \ln\gamma\). For the normal pair of Proposition 3.3, \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac c\mu\Big) - \gamma\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac c\mu\Big), \tag{3.35}\] which is positive for every \(\gamma\). For the Laplace pair of Proposition 3.4, \(E_\gamma = 0\) for \(\gamma > e^t\), and \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = 1 - e^{-(t - c)/2} \quad\text{for } 1 \le \gamma \le e^t. \tag{3.36}\]


Proof. 

Normal pair. The evidence is the line of Proposition 3.3, so \(L > c\) exactly when \(x/\sigma < \frac\mu2 - \frac c\mu\). Under \(P\), \(x/\sigma\) is standard normal, and under \(Q\) it is shifted by \(\mu\), so property 3 gives the formula. It is positive by property 2, because \(D_\infty = \infty\).
Laplace pair, the event. With \(b = 1\), the evidence is \(t\) on \(x \le 0\), \(-t\) on \(x \ge t\) and \(t - 2x\) in between. So for \(c < t\), \(L > c\) exactly when \(x < \frac{t - c}{2}\), a point above 0.
Laplace pair, the tails. That event has probability \(1 - \frac12e^{-(t - c)/2}\) under \(P\). Under \(Q\) it needs a \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) variable below \(-\frac{t + c}{2}\), which has probability \(\frac12e^{-(t + c)/2}\).
Laplace pair, combine. Since \(\gamma e^{-(t + c)/2} = e^{-(t - c)/2}\), property 3 gives the formula. Beyond \(e^t\), the largest ratio, property 2 gives 0.


The curve \(\gamma \mapsto E_\gamma\) starts at TV and reaches zero at the largest ratio, which the Gaussian curve never does (Figure 3.8).






Figure 3.8: \(E_\gamma\) against \(\ln\gamma\) for the die, a Laplace pair and a Gaussian pair.




Example 3.6 On the die, only the six has \(r > \gamma\) for \(1 \le \gamma < 3\), so \(E_\gamma = 0.5 - \gamma/6\) falls linearly to zero at \(\gamma = 3\), the largest ratio. In rejection sampling of the loaded die from fair rolls, an envelope \(2q\) leaves the mass \(E_2(P\|Q) = \frac16\) of the six uncovered, and the sampled six comes up 40% of the time instead of 50%. The error in TV is never more than \(E_\gamma\).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.7 f-divergences
KL, TV and \(E_\gamma\) were defined separately, but each is an average under \(Q\) of some function of the likelihood ratio. Naming that function gives one family, with one proof of non-negativity here and one of the data-processing inequality in Section 3.8. A ratio of 1 is no evidence either way, so the function must vanish there.

Definition 3.5 (f-divergence) Let the generator \(f\colon (0, \infty) \to \mathbb R\) be convex with \(f(1) = 0\). The f-divergence is \[D_f(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_Q\big[f(r(X))\big] = \sum_x q(x)\,f\Big(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Big). \tag{3.37}\]


Example 3.7 Table 3.6 lists the common generators with their values on the die. The generator \(u\ln u\) gives KL because \(\mathbb E_Q[r\ln r] = \mathbb E_P[\ln r]\) by Lemma 3.2.



Table 3.6: Common f-divergences, their generators, and their values for the loaded die against the fair die.

Rényi divergence is not a member, but it is an increasing function of one, so it inherits what the family proves.

Proposition 3.7 (Non-negativity, and Rényi as a transform) Every f-divergence satisfies \(D_f(P\|Q) \ge 0\), with equality when \(P = Q\). For \(\alpha > 1\) the generator \(u^\alpha - 1\), and for \(0 < \alpha < 1\) the generator \(1 - u^\alpha\), give f-divergences with \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big(1 + D_f(P\|Q)\big) \;\; (\alpha > 1), \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big(1 - D_f(P\|Q)\big) \;\; (\alpha < 1), \tag{3.38}\] each an increasing function of \(D_f\).


Proof. 

Non-negativity. By Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, \(\mathbb E_Q[f(r)] \ge f(\mathbb E_Q[r]) = f(1) = 0\), with equality when \(r = 1\) everywhere.
Orders above 1. The generator \(u^\alpha - 1\) is convex and gives \(D_f = \mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha] - 1\), so Proposition 3.1 gives the first formula.
Orders below 1. Now \(u^\alpha\) is concave, so \(1 - u^\alpha\) is convex, with \(D_f = 1 - \mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha]\). The logarithm decreases in \(D_f\) and \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\) is negative, so the second formula increases in \(D_f\).


A convex function is a sum of hockey-stick shapes weighted by its curvature, so every f-divergence is a weighted sum of the curves \(E_\gamma\), which therefore carry all the information about a pair.

Theorem 3.4 (f-divergences from the hockey-stick curves) If the generator \(f\) is twice differentiable, then \[D_f(P\|Q) = \int_1^\infty f''(\gamma)\,E_\gamma(P\|Q)\,\mathrm d\gamma + \int_0^1\gamma f''(\gamma)\,E_{1/\gamma}(Q\|P)\,\mathrm d\gamma. \tag{3.39}\]


Proof. The plan is to write \(f(u)\) as hockey sticks for each fixed \(u\), then put in \(u = r(X)\) and average under \(Q\).

Taylor’s theorem around 1. With an integral remainder, \(f(u)\) is its value at 1, plus the tangent line, plus the curvature accumulated between 1 and \(u\): \[f(u) = f(1) + f'(1)(u - 1) + \int_1^u f''(\gamma)(u - \gamma)\,\mathrm d\gamma. \tag{3.40}\]
Hockey sticks. The remainder equals \(\int_1^\infty f''(\gamma)(u - \gamma)_+\,\mathrm d\gamma + \int_0^1 f''(\gamma)(\gamma - u)_+\,\mathrm d\gamma\). For \(u \ge 1\) only the first integral is non-zero and it stops at \(\gamma = u\). For \(u < 1\), swapping the limits of \(\int_1^u\) gives the second.
Average. Put \(u = r(X)\) and average under \(Q\). The first two terms vanish, because \(f(1) = 0\) and \(\mathbb E_Q[r - 1] = 0\).
The two integrals. \(\mathbb E_Q[(r - \gamma)_+] = E_\gamma(P\|Q)\) by Proposition 3.5. Also \(\mathbb E_Q[(\gamma - r)_+] = \sum_x(\gamma q - p)_+ = \gamma\sum_x(q - p/\gamma)_+\), which is \(\gamma E_{1/\gamma}(Q\|P)\).


Each generator weights the ratio differently (Figure 3.9); the quadratic one of \(\chi^2\) lets large ratios dominate. An f-divergence can also be estimated from samples alone, through a variational form that a generative adversarial network (GAN) fits with a neural network, as in the f-GAN of Nowozin, Cseke & Tomioka (2016).






Figure 3.9: The generators of six f-divergences.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.8 The data-processing inequality
You rarely look at raw data. You bin it, compute features, or pass it through a randomized algorithm, and the data-processing inequality says that none of this can make two distributions easier to tell apart. When processing maps several inputs to one output, the output’s likelihood ratio is an average of theirs. Every f-divergence is a convex summary of the ratios, and by Jensen averaging first can only make it smaller.

Definition 3.6 (Channel) A channel \(K\) maps each input \(x\) to a distribution \(K(\cdot \mid x)\) over outputs \(y\). Feeding \(X \sim P\) through it gives the output distribution \(PK(y) = \sum_x p(x)K(y\mid x)\), and likewise \(QK\).


Theorem 3.5 (Data-processing inequality) For every f-divergence, every Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha\) including \(D_\infty\), and every channel \(K\), \[D_f(PK\|QK) \le D_f(P\|Q), \qquad D_\alpha(PK\|QK) \le D_\alpha(P\|Q). \tag{3.41}\] Equality holds when \(r(x)\) can be computed from the output, which is then a sufficient statistic.


Proof. The plan is to show that the output’s ratio is a conditional average of the input’s, apply Jensen conditionally, and average over the output.

The output’s ratio. Write \(p(x) = q(x)r(x)\) inside \(PK(y)\) and divide by \(QK(y)\): \[r_Y(y) = \frac{PK(y)}{QK(y)} = \sum_x\frac{q(x)K(y\mid x)}{QK(y)}\,r(x). \tag{3.42}\] By Bayes’ rule the weights are the probabilities of \(X\) given \(Y = y\) when \(X \sim Q\) goes through \(K\), so \(r_Y(y) = \mathbb E[r(X)\mid Y = y]\).
Jensen, conditionally. Lemma 3.1 for the distribution of \(X\) given \(Y = y\) gives \(f(r_Y(y)) \le \mathbb E[f(r(X))\mid Y = y]\).
Average over the output. Over \(Y \sim QK\) the left side averages to \(D_f(PK\|QK)\), and the conditional averages on the right average to \(\mathbb E_Q[f(r)] = D_f(P\|Q)\).
Rényi. \(D_\alpha\) is an increasing function of an f-divergence by Proposition 3.7, and \(\alpha \to \infty\) gives \(D_\infty\).
Equality. If \(r(x)\) is a function of \(y\), then \(r(X)\) is constant given \(Y = y\), and step 2 is an equality.


The channel may use its own randomness, as long as it is the same whether the input came from \(P\) or \(Q\). The coarsest processing reports only whether an event happened, and this gives a lower bound on KL from any single event.

Corollary 3.1 (KL bounds every event) For every event \(A\), write \(p_A = \Pr_P[A]\) and \(q_A = \Pr_Q[A]\). Then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \ge \mathrm{kl}(p_A\|q_A) = p_A\ln\frac{p_A}{q_A} + (1 - p_A)\ln\frac{1 - p_A}{1 - q_A}, \tag{3.43}\] where the binary KL \(\mathrm{kl}\) is the KL divergence between coins with heads probabilities \(p_A\) and \(q_A\).


Proof. Reporting whether \(A\) happened is the channel \(\mathbf 1[x \in A]\), which turns \(P\) and \(Q\) into those two coins, and Theorem 3.5 with the generator of KL bounds their divergence by \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\).

So if KL is small, no event can have very different probabilities under \(P\) and \(Q\), and Hypothesis testing uses this to bound the errors of any test.
