By Shannon leakage, reveal-low(9) is the leakier channel. By one-guess success, reveal-if-zero(3) is worse by a factor of \(0.125/(2.78\times10^{-17}) \approx 4.5\times10^{15}\). Smith (2009) used a pair of programs like these to argue that Shannon leakage is the wrong measure for one-try guessing.
The extreme case is \(j = w\), a channel that reveals the secret only if it is all zeros. For a 4-bit secret the Shannon leakage is \(h(1/16) = 0.3373\) bits, and the min-entropy leakage is exactly 1 bit, because the guesser wins on seeing 0000 and otherwise picks one of 15 values, so its success doubles to \(\frac1{16} + \frac{15}{16}\cdot\frac1{15}\). For a 32-bit secret the Shannon leakage falls to \(7.786\times10^{-9}\) bits, while the min-entropy leakage stays at 1 bit. Both numbers are small next to the 4 or 32 bits of the secret, and both miss that for the one secret value 0000 the channel reveals everything. Any measure that averages over the secret can hide a fully exposed value, so a worst-case question needs a worst-case measure, which later parts build.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.7 Fano’s inequality
Mutual information also gives lower bounds, statements that no estimator can do better than some error rate, which you need to show that a problem is hard rather than that a method is good. Fano’s inequality is the basic tool. It says that if \(X\) is still uncertain after seeing \(Y\), every guess of \(X\) from \(Y\) must often be wrong. The reason is that describing \(X\) once the guess is known takes only two pieces: whether the guess was right, and, when it was wrong, which other value \(X\) is.

Theorem 5.7 (Fano’s inequality) Let \(X\) take values in a finite set of \(k\) elements, and let \(\hat X\) be any estimate of \(X\) computed from \(Y\), possibly with extra randomness independent of \(X\) and \(Y\). Write \(P_e\) for its error probability, \[P_e = \Pr[\hat X \ne X]. \tag{5.32}\] Then \[H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log_2(k - 1), \tag{5.33}\] and as a consequence \[P_e \ge \frac{H(X \mid Y) - 1}{\log_2 k}. \tag{5.34}\]


Proof. The plan is to expand the uncertainty of the error together with \(X\) in two orders, bound the pieces of one order, carry the bound from \(\hat X\) to \(Y\), and weaken it. Write \(E = \mathbf 1[\hat X \ne X]\) for the error indicator, which is 1 when the guess is wrong.

Expand in two orders. Every entropy in steps 1 to 4 is conditioned on \(\hat X\). The chain rule Equation 5.7 holds given each value of \(\hat X\), so it also holds for the average over \(\hat X\), and revealing \(X\) first or \(E\) first gives \[H(X \mid \hat X) + H(E \mid X, \hat X) = H(E, X \mid \hat X) = H(E \mid \hat X) + H(X \mid E, \hat X). \tag{5.35}\] Given both \(X\) and \(\hat X\) you know whether they differ, so \(H(E \mid X, \hat X) = 0\).
Bound the error’s uncertainty. By Corollary 5.1, \(H(E \mid \hat X) \le H(E)\), which is \(h(P_e)\) because \(E\) is 1 with probability \(P_e\).
Bound what remains of \(X\). If \(E = 0\), then \(X = \hat X\) and no uncertainty is left. If \(E = 1\), then \(X\) is one of the \(k - 1\) other values, so its entropy is at most \(\log_2(k - 1)\) by Theorem 5.1. Averaging over \(E\) bounds \(H(X \mid E, \hat X)\) by \(P_e\log_2(k - 1)\).
Combine. Steps 1 to 3 give \[H(X \mid \hat X) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log_2(k - 1). \tag{5.36}\]
Replace \(\hat X\) by \(Y\). The estimate is computed from \(Y\), so \(X \to Y \to \hat X\) is a Markov chain, and Theorem 5.4 gives \(I(X; \hat X) \le I(X; Y)\). Writing both sides as \(H(X)\) minus a conditional entropy turns this into \(H(X \mid Y) \le H(X \mid \hat X)\), and the bound of step 4 carries over.
Weaken. Using \(h(P_e) \le 1\) and \(\log_2(k - 1) \le \log_2 k\) gives \(H(X \mid Y) \le 1 + P_e\log_2 k\), and solving for \(P_e\) gives Equation 5.34.


The right side of Equation 5.33 increases with \(P_e\) on \([0, (k - 1)/k]\), the range from a perfect estimator to blind guessing, because its derivative is positive there: \[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dP_e}\Big(h(P_e) + P_e\log_2(k - 1)\Big) = \log_2\frac{(1 - P_e)(k - 1)}{P_e} > 0. \tag{5.37}\] So the Fano bound, the smallest \(P_e\) that satisfies it, can be found by bisection. The bound is tight when step 3 is, that is when the true value after a wrong guess is uniform over the other values. The \(k\)-ary symmetric channel keeps its input with probability \(1 - p\) and otherwise outputs one of the other symbols uniformly. It has exactly this structure, and Fano’s inequality is an equality for it (Figure 5.6, left).
If errors go to a few wrong values, the bound is loose, because little uncertainty is left after a wrong guess. The shift channel outputs \(x + 1 \bmod k\) instead of \(x\) with probability \(p\), and given the output the input is one of only two values. With uniform \(X\), \(k = 8\) and \(p = 0.2\), both channels have MAP error 0.2000, because the best guess is the input that keeps the output unchanged, which is wrong with probability \(p\). The Fano bound matches it for the symmetric channel but is only 0.0954 for the shift channel (Figure 5.6, right). The weak form Equation 5.34 gives 0.0945 for the symmetric channel and 0 for the shift channel, whose \(H(X \mid Y)\) is below 1.






Figure 5.6: MAP error against Fano’s lower bound, for \(k = 8\) and a uniform \(X\), as the noise level \(p\) grows. Left: on the symmetric channel the bound is exact. Right: on the shift channel, where errors go to a single wrong value, the bound is loose and the weak form is zero.



The same idea shows that estimating a parameter needs many samples, by turning estimation into identification. Pick candidate parameter values far apart, so that estimating the parameter well would identify the candidate, yet with sample distributions close together. If the samples carry little information about which candidate produced them, no estimator can identify it.

Proposition 5.5 (Fano’s method) Let \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k\) be candidate parameter values, with distributions \(P_{\theta_x}\) for the samples. Let the index \(X\) be uniform on \(\{1, \dots, k\}\), and given \(X\) let the \(n\) samples \(Y^n = (Y_1, \dots, Y_n)\) be independent draws from \(P_{\theta_X}\). Suppose that a number \(\kappa\) bounds the divergence between any two candidates, \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,P_{\theta_{x'}}) \le \kappa \quad\text{bits for all } x, x'. \tag{5.38}\] Then every estimator of \(X\) from \(Y^n\) has error probability \[P_e \ge 1 - \frac{n\kappa + 1}{\log_2 k}. \tag{5.39}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the information in \(n\) samples by \(n\) times the information in one, to bound the information in one sample by \(\kappa\), and to put the result into the weak form of Fano’s inequality.

Information adds at most over samples. Equation 5.7, applied one sample at a time, splits \(H(Y^n \mid X)\) into the terms \(H(Y_i \mid X, Y_1, \dots, Y_{i-1})\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\). Given \(X\) the samples are independent, so each term is \(H(Y_i \mid X)\). Without \(X\), the chain rule splits \(H(Y^n)\) the same way, and Corollary 5.1 bounds each term only by \(H(Y_i)\). Subtracting the first from the second, and using that all samples have the same distribution, \[I(X; Y^n) \le \sum_i I(X; Y_i) = n\,I(X; Y_1). \tag{5.40}\]
Write one sample’s information as an average divergence. Let \(\bar P = \frac1k\sum_x P_{\theta_x}\) be the average of the candidate distributions, which is the distribution of \(Y_1\) when the index is random. With \(p(x, y) = P_{\theta_x}(y)/k\) and \(p(y) = \bar P(y)\), Equation 5.10 reads \[I(X; Y_1) = \frac1k\sum_x D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,\bar P). \tag{5.41}\]
Bound it by \(\kappa\). For any distribution \(Q\), and later for \(Q = P_{\theta_{x'}}\), splitting \(\log_2\frac{P_{\theta_x}}{Q} = \log_2\frac{P_{\theta_x}}{\bar P} + \log_2\frac{\bar P}{Q}\) and averaging over \(x\) gives \[\frac1k\sum_x D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,Q) = \frac1k\sum_x D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta_x}\,\|\,\bar P) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar P\,\|\,Q), \tag{5.42}\] and the last term is non-negative. So the average divergence to \(\bar P\) is at most the average divergence to any single candidate \(P_{\theta_{x'}}\), which is at most \(\kappa\).
Apply Fano. The index is uniform, so \(H(X) = \log_2 k\), and steps 1 to 3 give \(H(X \mid Y^n) = \log_2 k - I(X; Y^n) \ge \log_2 k - n\kappa\). Putting this into Equation 5.34 gives the bound.


The bound fades as \(n\kappa\) approaches \(\log_2 k\), the number of bits needed to name the candidate. Choosing the candidates is the art of the method, and Wainwright (2019) works through many cases.

Example 5.7 A label is uniform over \(k = 8\) classes, so it has 3 bits of entropy, and the features carry at most 1 bit about it. Then \(H(X \mid Y) \ge 2\) bits, so every classifier, however it is trained, errs at least as often as the \(P_e\) that solves \(h(P_e) + P_e\log_2 7 = 2\), which is 0.3730. The weak form gives \((2 - 1)/3 = 0.3333\).
For estimation, take \(k = 1024\) candidates, so \(\log_2 k = 10\) bits, within \(\kappa = 0.01\) bits of each other. Then \(n = 100\) samples leave \(P_e \ge 1 - (1 + 1)/10 = 0.8000\), and even 400 samples leave \(P_e \ge 1 - (4 + 1)/10 = 0.5000\).

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.10 References

Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed., 2006), ch. 2 (entropy, mutual information, data processing, Fano) and ch. 7 (channel capacity and the coding theorem): the standard textbook for every Shannon result here.
MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003), ch. 2 and 8–10: the same material with a machine-learning slant, free online.
Smith, “On the Foundations of Quantitative Information Flow” (FoSSaCS 2009): vulnerability, conditional min-entropy, and the argument against Shannon leakage for one-try guessing.
Braun, Chatzikokolakis & Palamidessi, “Quantitative Notions of Leakage for One-try Attacks” (MFPS 2009): min-capacity and the fact that the uniform prior attains it.
Alvim, Chatzikokolakis, McIver, Morgan, Palamidessi & Smith, The Science of Quantitative Information Flow (2020): the full theory of vulnerability, leakage and capacity.
Wainwright, High-Dimensional Statistics (2019), ch. 15: minimax lower bounds, including Fano’s method.
Yu, “Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam” (1997): the three classical lower-bound methods side by side.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.1 Convexity, Lipschitz continuity and smoothness
Training a model means minimizing an average loss over the training set, and two questions come up every time. The first is how fast the optimizer gets there: how many steps gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) need, and which learning rate to pick. SGD estimates the gradient from a few random records, so its steps are noisy and it needs more of them. The second is how much the answer depends on any one training record, which the next chapter turns into a guarantee that the model works on new data.
Both questions have the same kind of answer, because a few constants of the loss decide everything: how steep it can be, how sharply it can curve at most, how much it must curve at least, and how noisy SGD’s gradient estimates are. Every rate and bound in this chapter combines these four.
The running example is logistic regression, a linear classifier, trained on 1,000 records with five features, and each result of the chapter is checked on it. For example, after 10,000 steps of SGD its loss is within \(7.71\times10^{-4}\) of the minimum, while the guarantee of Theorem 6.2 only promises 0.050, and the chapter explains why the guarantee is so cautious. Table 6.1 lists the symbols.
Every guarantee below rests on assumptions about the loss, and four properties are enough. Lipschitz continuity bounds the slope and smoothness the curvature from above, while convexity and strong convexity bound the curvature from below. This section defines each, relates them, and checks them on the logistic loss.
The proofs use a second picture, through tangents. The tangent at \(\theta\) predicts the value at \(\theta'\) by adding to \(f(\theta)\) the inner product \(\langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle\) of the gradient with the step, and for a convex function this prediction never overshoots.
Every convex convergence proof below uses the lemma with \(\theta' = \theta^*\). Moving the inner product to the other side and flipping its sign, it says that \(\langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta - \theta^*\rangle\) is at least the current error \(f(\theta) - f(\theta^*)\). So the gradient points away from the minimizer, and the further \(\theta\) is from optimal, the more a small step against the gradient shortens the distance to \(\theta^*\). Section G.1 derives the converse, from tangents to chords.
The next result collects the working forms of these definitions, with a test of smoothness by the Hessian \(\nabla^2 f\), the matrix of second derivatives, whose eigenvalues are the curvatures of \(f\). The proof bounds inner products by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle a, b\rangle| \le \|a\|\,\|b\|\): an inner product is the product of the lengths times a cosine.
The converses hold too, for twice-differentiable \(f\): a \(\beta\)-smooth \(f\) has no Hessian eigenvalue above \(\beta\), and \(f\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex exactly when every eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2 f\) is at least \(\lambda\) (Nesterov 2018, §2.1; Section G.1). A Hessian with no negative eigenvalue likewise makes \(f\) convex. So the two constants sandwich the curvature, and \(\kappa \ge 1\).
Two consequences of strong convexity are used later, the first in Section 6.7 and the second whenever a ridge term \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) is added.
Neither of Lipschitz and smooth implies the other: \(|\theta|\) is 1-Lipschitz but not smooth, and \(\theta^2/2\) is 1-smooth but not Lipschitz (Figure 6.1). By part (a) of Corollary 6.1 the gradient of a strongly convex function grows at least like \(\lambda\) times the distance to the minimizer, so no strongly convex function is Lipschitz on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), and the strongly convex results below stay in a bounded set by the projection defined in Section 6.2.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
Definition 6.1 (Convex function) A function \(f\colon \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R\) is convex when the straight segment (the chord) between any two points of its graph never dips below the graph. That is, for all \(\theta, \theta'\) and every mixing weight \(s \in [0, 1]\), \[f(s\theta' + (1-s)\theta) \le s f(\theta') + (1-s) f(\theta). \tag{6.1}\]



Lemma 6.1 (A convex function lies above its tangents) If \(f\) is convex and differentiable, then for all \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\) \[f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle. \tag{6.2}\]


Proof. 

Shrink the chord to a short step. Write the mixed point as \(\theta + s(\theta' - \theta)\), a step of size \(s\) towards \(\theta'\), and the chord’s height there as \(f(\theta) + s(f(\theta') - f(\theta))\). Subtracting \(f(\theta)\) from both sides of the chord condition and dividing by \(s > 0\) gives \[\frac{f(\theta + s(\theta' - \theta)) - f(\theta)}{s} \le f(\theta') - f(\theta). \tag{6.3}\]
Let the step vanish. The left side is the average slope over a short step towards \(\theta'\). As \(s \to 0\) it becomes the slope in that direction, which for a differentiable \(f\) is the inner product \(\langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle\), and this gives Equation 6.2.




Definition 6.2 (Lipschitz, smooth and strongly convex functions) Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R\) be differentiable.

\(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz when it never changes faster than \(L\) per unit of distance: \(|f(\theta) - f(\theta')| \le L\|\theta - \theta'\|\).
\(f\) is \(\beta\)-smooth when its gradient is \(\beta\)-Lipschitz: \(\|\nabla f(\theta) - \nabla f(\theta')\| \le \beta\|\theta - \theta'\|\).
\(f\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, for some \(\lambda > 0\), when it lies above each tangent by at least a bowl of curvature \(\lambda\): \[f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle + \frac\lambda2\|\theta' - \theta\|^2. \tag{6.4}\]

For a function that is both smooth and strongly convex, \(\kappa = \beta/\lambda\) is its condition number, which Section 6.2 shows sets how slowly gradient descent converges.



Proposition 6.1 (Working forms of the constants) Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R\) be differentiable.

\(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz exactly when \(\|\nabla f(\theta)\| \le L\) for every \(\theta\).
If \(f\) is \(\beta\)-smooth, the error of its tangent grows at most like a parabola of curvature \(\beta\) (the descent lemma): \[f(\theta') \le f(\theta) + \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle + \frac\beta2\|\theta' - \theta\|^2. \tag{6.5}\]
If \(f\) is twice differentiable and every eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2 f\) lies in \([-\beta, \beta]\) everywhere, then \(f\) is \(\beta\)-smooth.
If \(f\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, its gradient is strongly monotone: \[\langle\nabla f(\theta) - \nabla f(\theta'), \theta - \theta'\rangle \ge \lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|^2. \tag{6.6}\]



Proof. Steps 1 to 4 walk along the segment \(\theta_s = \theta + s(\theta' - \theta)\), \(s \in [0, 1]\), and add up the changes by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Step 5 adds two inequalities.

A bounded gradient makes \(f\) Lipschitz. The change of \(f\) is the integral of the slope in the direction of travel, \[f(\theta') - f(\theta) = \int_0^1\langle\nabla f(\theta_s), \theta' - \theta\rangle\,\mathrm ds, \tag{6.7}\] and by Cauchy–Schwarz each inner product, and so the integral, is at most \(L\|\theta' - \theta\|\) in size.
A Lipschitz \(f\) has a bounded gradient. Where the gradient is not zero, take the unit vector \(u = \nabla f(\theta)/\|\nabla f(\theta)\|\). The Lipschitz condition says \(f(\theta + hu) - f(\theta) \le Lh\), and divided by \(h\) the left side tends to \(\langle\nabla f(\theta), u\rangle = \|\nabla f(\theta)\|\) as \(h \to 0\), so \(\|\nabla f(\theta)\| \le L\).
Smoothness gives the descent lemma. The error of the tangent is the integral of how much the slope has changed: \[f(\theta') - f(\theta) - \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle = \int_0^1\langle\nabla f(\theta_s) - \nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle\,\mathrm ds. \tag{6.8}\] At position \(s\) you are a distance \(s\|\theta' - \theta\|\) from \(\theta\), so by smoothness and Cauchy–Schwarz the integrand is at most \(\beta s\|\theta' - \theta\|^2\). Since \(\int_0^1\beta s\,\mathrm ds = \beta/2\), the error is at most \(\frac\beta2\|\theta' - \theta\|^2\).
A bounded Hessian gives smoothness. The change of the gradient is the integral of the Hessian applied to the direction of travel, \[\nabla f(\theta') - \nabla f(\theta) = \int_0^1\nabla^2 f(\theta_s)(\theta' - \theta)\,\mathrm ds. \tag{6.9}\] A symmetric matrix with eigenvalues in \([-\beta, \beta]\) stretches no vector by more than \(\beta\), and an integral is no longer than the integral of the lengths, so it has length at most \(\beta\|\theta' - \theta\|\).
Strong convexity gives strong monotonicity. Write the strong convexity inequality from \(\theta\) to \(\theta'\) and from \(\theta'\) to \(\theta\), and add the two. The function values cancel and the two bowl terms add up to \(\lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|^2\), which leaves \[0 \ge \langle\nabla f(\theta) - \nabla f(\theta'), \theta' - \theta\rangle + \lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|^2, \tag{6.10}\] and moving the inner product to the left gives Equation 6.6.





Corollary 6.1 (Two consequences of strong convexity) Let \(\lambda > 0\).

If \(f\) is differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex with a minimizer \(\theta^*\), then for every \(\theta\) \[\|\theta - \theta^*\| \le \frac{\|\nabla f(\theta)\|}{\lambda}, \tag{6.11}\] and in particular the minimizer is unique.
If \(f\) is convex and differentiable, then \(f(\theta) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex.



Proof. 

Part (a). The gradient of a differentiable function on all of \(\mathbb R^d\) vanishes at its minimizer. Put \(\theta' = \theta^*\) in Equation 6.6 and bound its left side by Cauchy–Schwarz: \[\lambda\|\theta - \theta^*\|^2 \le \|\nabla f(\theta)\|\,\|\theta - \theta^*\|. \tag{6.12}\] Divide by \(\lambda\|\theta - \theta^*\|\), or note that there is nothing to prove when \(\theta = \theta^*\). A second point with zero gradient would be at distance 0 from \(\theta^*\), so the minimizer is unique.
Part (b). Expanding a square gives \(\|\theta'\|^2 = \|\theta\|^2 + 2\langle\theta, \theta' - \theta\rangle + \|\theta' - \theta\|^2\). Multiplied by \(\frac\lambda2\), this says that \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\), whose gradient is \(\lambda\theta\), meets the strong convexity inequality with equality, term by term. Adding it to the tangent inequality Equation 6.2 of \(f\) gives that inequality for the sum.









Figure 6.1: Left: the slopes of \(|\theta|\) (bounded, jumps), \(\theta^2/2\) (unbounded) and the logistic loss (bounded, continuous). Right: the curvatures of the logistic loss and of the sigmoid loss of Section 6.6.




Example 6.1 In the running example, features have \(\|x\| \le 1\) and labels \(y \in \{-1, +1\}\). The margin \(m = y\langle\theta, x\rangle\) is positive when a record is classified correctly, and the logistic loss is \(\ln(1 + e^{-m})\). Write \(\operatorname{sig}(m) = 1/(1 + e^{-m})\) for the logistic function.
The derivative of \(\ln(1 + e^{-m})\) in \(m\) is \(-\operatorname{sig}(-m)\), so by the chain rule the gradient is \(-\operatorname{sig}(-m)\,y\,x\), of length at most 1, so the loss is 1-Lipschitz by part (a) of Proposition 6.1. Differentiating again, with \(\operatorname{sig}'(-m) = \operatorname{sig}(m)(1 - \operatorname{sig}(m))\), the Hessian is \(\operatorname{sig}(m)(1 - \operatorname{sig}(m))\,xx^\top\). Here \(xx^\top\) has eigenvalue \(\|x\|^2 \le 1\) along \(x\) and 0 across it, and the factor in front, \(p(1 - p)\) with \(p\) in \((0, 1)\), is at most \(\frac14\). So the loss is convex and \(\frac14\)-smooth by part (c), but not strongly convex, because its curvature is 0 across \(x\) and tends to 0 as the margin grows.
For \(x = (0.6, 0.8)\) and \(y = +1\), the loss, gradient norm and curvature are 0.6931, 0.5000 and 0.2500 at \(\theta = 0\), but 0.0067, 0.0067 and 0.0066 at \(\theta = (3, 4)\), where the margin is 5. Confidently classified records add almost no curvature, and at the minimizer most records are classified confidently. So on the running dataset, with features drawn on the unit sphere and labels from a logistic model, the Hessian of the average loss at \(\theta^*\) has smallest eigenvalue only 0.0233.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.2 Gradient descent and SGD
Gradient descent steps against the full gradient, which costs one gradient evaluation per record. SGD uses the gradient of one random record, or a small batch, which is cheap and right on average but noisy. This section defines both and shows on a quadratic what a fast rate looks like without noise, so that you can see later what the noise costs.

Definition 6.3 (Gradient descent and projected SGD) Gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta\) takes the step \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\).
Projected SGD runs inside a convex set \(\mathcal W\), such as a ball, that is closed (contains its boundary), and its projection \(\Pi(u)\) is the point of \(\mathcal W\) nearest to \(u\). At step \(t\) the algorithm draws an index \(i_t\) uniformly from \(\{1, \dots, n\}\), takes that record’s gradient \(g_t = \nabla\ell(\theta_t; z_{i_t})\), and updates \[\theta_{t+1} = \Pi(\theta_t - \eta_t g_t). \tag{6.13}\] With a minibatch of \(B\) indices, \(g_t\) is the average gradient over the batch. Plain SGD is the case \(\mathcal W = \mathbb R^d\).

With one record or a batch, the estimate is right on average. Write “past” for the random choices made before step \(t\), which fix \(\theta_t\); a uniform index averages to the full gradient, so \[\mathbb E[g_t \mid \text{past}] = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t). \tag{6.14}\]
On a quadratic risk the gradient is linear in the error \(\theta - \theta^*\), so each GD step multiplies the error by a fixed matrix, and the next theorem reads the rate off its eigenvalues.

Theorem 6.1 (Gradient descent on a strongly convex quadratic) Let \(\mathcal L(\theta) = \mathcal L^* + \frac12(\theta - \theta^*)^\top H(\theta - \theta^*)\), where the symmetric matrix \(H\) has eigenvalues in \([\lambda, \beta]\) with \(0 < \lambda \le \beta\), and let \(\kappa = \beta/\lambda\). Then GD with \(\eta = 1/\beta\) from any \(\theta_0\) satisfies \[\|\theta_t - \theta^*\| \le \left(1 - \frac1\kappa\right)^t\|\theta_0 - \theta^*\|. \tag{6.15}\]


Proof. 

One step multiplies the error by a matrix. The gradient is \(H(\theta - \theta^*)\), so subtracting \(\theta^*\) from both sides of the update gives \[\theta_{t+1} - \theta^* = (I - H/\beta)(\theta_t - \theta^*). \tag{6.16}\]
Find the factor in each direction. The matrix \(I - H/\beta\) has the principal directions (eigenvectors) of \(H\), and turns a curvature \(h \in [\lambda, \beta]\) into the factor \(1 - h/\beta \in [0, 1 - 1/\kappa]\).
Bound the shrinkage, then repeat. In the orthonormal basis of principal directions, each coordinate of the error is multiplied by its own factor, so the length is multiplied by at most \(1 - 1/\kappa\). Applying this \(t\) times gives Equation 6.15.


For any \(\beta\)-smooth risk, convex or not, a weaker statement holds, about the risk’s value rather than the distance, and Section 6.6 starts from it. The descent lemma puts the risk below a parabola that touches it at \(\theta_t\), and a step of \(1/\beta\) lands at that parabola’s lowest point, so the risk falls at least as much as the parabola does.

Proposition 6.2 (One gradient step lowers a smooth function) If \(\mathcal L\) is \(\beta\)-smooth, one GD step with \(\eta = 1/\beta\) satisfies \[\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) \le \mathcal L(\theta_t) - \frac{1}{2\beta}\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2. \tag{6.17}\]


Proof. 

Put the step into the descent lemma. With \(\theta_{t+1} - \theta_t = -\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)/\beta\), the tangent term of Equation 6.5 is \(-\frac1\beta\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2\), the progress. The parabola term is \(\frac\beta2\cdot\frac{1}{\beta^2}\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2\), the price of overshooting.
Add them. Their sum is \(-\frac{1}{2\beta}\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2\): the overshoot eats half of the progress.


Theorem 6.1 says that GD converges linearly, by a constant factor per step, and Section G.1 extends Equation 6.15 to every twice-differentiable strongly convex smooth risk. Since \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\), the factor after \(t\) steps is at most \(e^{-t/\kappa}\), so shrinking the error to a fraction \(\tau\) takes about \(\kappa\ln(1/\tau)\) steps. A large \(\kappa\) makes GD slow, because the step must stay small for the steepest direction, where the error is multiplied by \(1 - \eta\beta\), which must stay between \(-1\) and 1.
SGD with a constant step cannot do this: near \(\theta^*\) the gradients of single records do not vanish, so its iterates keep jumping around \(\theta^*\).

Example 6.2 The logistic risk is not a quadratic, so this example uses least squares, whose risk \(\frac1{2n}\sum_i(y_i - \langle\theta, x_i\rangle)^2\) is a quadratic with \(H\) the average of the \(x_ix_i^\top\). The script draws 200 records with \(x \sim \mathcal N(0, \mathrm{diag}(1, 0.1))\) and \(y = x_1 + x_2\) plus noise, and \(H\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda = 0.101\) and \(\beta = 0.969\), so \(\kappa = 9.58\).
From \(\theta_0 = (-1, 3)\), Equation 6.15 predicts that GD needs at most 126 steps to shrink \(\|\theta - \theta^*\|\) by \(10^6\), since \((1 - 1/9.58)^t \le 10^{-6}\) needs \[t \ge \frac{\ln(10^6)}{-\ln(1 - 1/9.58)} = \frac{13.8155}{0.11024} = 125.3. \tag{6.18}\] GD takes 122, close to the bound, because the starting error lies largely along the flat direction, which shrinks at exactly the worst-case rate. GD crawls along the flat valley while SGD jitters around \(\theta^*\) (Figure 6.2).







Figure 6.2: Gradient descent (step \(1/\beta\)) and single-record SGD (step 0.1) on the least-squares risk of Example 6.2, over its contours.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.3 SGD for convex Lipschitz objectives
The cleanest guarantee for SGD needs only convexity and bounded gradients, so it covers the logistic loss and, with the subgradients defined after the proof, losses with kinks. Its proof, the template for the rest of the chapter, follows the squared distance to the minimizer. It needs two tools first: the projection never undoes progress, and a random gradient behaves like the true one in the cross term \(\langle g_t, \theta_t - \theta^*\rangle\) but not in its squared length.
The first tool is used where the new point is pulled back into \(\mathcal W\). Seen from \(\Pi(u)\), the directions to \(u\) and to any \(\theta\) in the set make an angle of at least \(90°\), so, as in a right-angled triangle, \(u\) is farther from \(\theta\) than \(\Pi(u)\) is.

Lemma 6.2 (Projection never moves a point away from the points of the set) Let \(\mathcal W \subseteq \mathbb R^d\) be convex and closed, so that a nearest point exists, and let \(\Pi(u)\) be its point nearest to \(u\). Then for every \(u\) and every \(\theta \in \mathcal W\), \[\|\Pi(u) - \theta\| \le \|u - \theta\|. \tag{6.19}\]


Proof. 

Walk from the nearest point towards \(\theta\). Let \(p = \Pi(u)\). The points \(p + s(\theta - p)\), \(s \in [0, 1]\), lie in \(\mathcal W\) because it is convex, and their squared distance to \(u\) is \(r(s) = \|u - p - s(\theta - p)\|^2\).
The angle at \(p\) is obtuse. Since \(p\) is the closest point of the set, \(r\) is smallest at \(s = 0\), so its derivative there, \(r'(0) = -2\langle u - p, \theta - p\rangle\), is not negative. That says \[\langle u - p, p - \theta\rangle \ge 0. \tag{6.20}\]
Pythagoras. Expanding the square of \(u - \theta = (u - p) + (p - \theta)\) gives \[\|u - \theta\|^2 = \|u - p\|^2 + \|p - \theta\|^2 + 2\langle u - p, p - \theta\rangle, \tag{6.21}\] where \(\|u - p\|^2\) and, by step 2, the inner product are non-negative, so \(\|u - \theta\| \ge \|p - \theta\|\).


The second tool is used where the proof averages over the random index, and its second half is what every SGD rate pays for.

Lemma 6.3 (Unbiased gradients: the cross term averages out, the square does not) Let \(\mathbb E[g_t \mid \text{past}] = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\), and let \(v_t\) be a vector fixed by the past, such as \(\theta_t - \theta^*\). Then \[\mathbb E\langle g_t, v_t\rangle = \mathbb E\langle\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), v_t\rangle, \tag{6.22}\] and the mean squared length of \(g_t\) exceeds that of the true gradient by its variance, the mean squared error of the estimate: \[\mathbb E[\|g_t\|^2 \mid \text{past}] = \|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 + \mathbb E[\|g_t - \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \mid \text{past}]. \tag{6.23}\]


Proof. 

The cross term. Given the past, \(v_t\) is fixed and the inner product with it is linear, so the conditional expectation passes inside it: \[\mathbb E[\langle g_t, v_t\rangle \mid \text{past}] = \langle\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), v_t\rangle. \tag{6.24}\] Averaging this over the past gives the first claim.
The square. Write \(g_t = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t) + e_t\), with the error \(e_t\) of conditional mean zero, and expand \(\|g_t\|^2 = \|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 + 2\langle e_t, \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\rangle + \|e_t\|^2\). The middle term pairs the error with a vector fixed by the past, so by step 1 it averages to zero.


For three records \(z = (1, 2, 6)\) with the loss \(\frac12(\theta - z)^2\), at \(\theta = 4\) the single-record gradients \(\theta - z_i\) are 3, 2 and \(-2\). They average to the true gradient 1, but their squares average to \(17/3 = 1^2 + 14/3\), where \(14/3\) is the variance.
The guarantee below is for the average of the iterates, as step 7 of its proof explains, and it has two costs. Travelling the distance \(R\) takes long with small steps, while each step’s random error grows with \(\eta\), so the right step balances them.

Theorem 6.2 (SGD on convex objectives) Let \(\mathcal L\) be convex, and let projected SGD run in a closed convex set \(\mathcal W\) that contains \(\theta^*\), starting at \(\theta_1 \in \mathcal W\) with \(\|\theta_1 - \theta^*\| \le R\). Let the random gradients be unbiased with \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2 \le G^2\). With a constant step \(\eta\) for \(T\) steps, the averaged iterate \(\bar\theta_T = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\theta_t\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T)] - \mathcal L^* \le \frac{R^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{\eta G^2}{2}. \tag{6.25}\] The step \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) makes the right side \(RG/\sqrt T\). For an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss every per-record gradient has length at most \(L\), so the bound is \(RL/\sqrt T\).


Proof. We follow the squared distance \(a_t = \|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2\): convexity ties the cross term of one step to the error, and summing over the steps cancels the changes in distance.

Projection can only help. By Lemma 6.2, since \(\theta^* \in \mathcal W\), \[a_{t+1} \le \|\theta_t - \eta g_t - \theta^*\|^2. \tag{6.26}\]
Expand the square, with \(\theta_t - \theta^*\) and \(-\eta g_t\) as the two vectors: \[\|\theta_t - \eta g_t - \theta^*\|^2 = a_t - 2\eta\langle g_t, \theta_t - \theta^*\rangle + \eta^2\|g_t\|^2. \tag{6.27}\]
Isolate the progress. Steps 1 and 2, solved for the cross term, give \[\langle g_t, \theta_t - \theta^*\rangle \le \frac{a_t - a_{t+1}}{2\eta} + \frac\eta2\|g_t\|^2. \tag{6.28}\]
Take expectations. By Lemma 6.3 the inner product averages to that with the true gradient, and \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2 \le G^2\), so \[\mathbb E\langle\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), \theta_t - \theta^*\rangle \le \frac{\mathbb E a_t - \mathbb E a_{t+1}}{2\eta} + \frac{\eta G^2}{2}. \tag{6.29}\]
Convexity turns progress into error. By Lemma 6.1 with \(\theta = \theta_t\) and \(\theta' = \theta^*\), the error \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*\) is at most the inner product on the left, which can therefore be replaced by \(\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*]\).
Sum over \(t = 1, \dots, T\). The distance terms cancel in a chain (they telescope) to \(a_1 - a_{T+1} \le R^2\), and the noise term is added \(T\) times: \[\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*] \le \frac{R^2}{2\eta} + \frac{\eta TG^2}{2}. \tag{6.30}\]
Pass to the averaged iterate. Divide by \(T\). Jensen’s inequality (Lemma 3.1) says that a convex function of an average is at most the average of the function, so \(\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T) \le \frac1T\sum_t\mathcal L(\theta_t)\), which gives Equation 6.25.
Choose \(\eta\). The derivative in \(\eta\), \(-\frac{R^2}{2\eta^2T} + \frac{G^2}{2}\), vanishes at \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\), where both terms equal \(RG/(2\sqrt T)\).


For a loss with kinks, a subgradient replaces the gradient: any vector \(g\) such that the linear function \(\mathcal L(\theta) + \langle g, \theta' - \theta\rangle\) stays below the graph. Step 5 then holds by this definition. The rate cannot be improved, since some convex \(L\)-Lipschitz functions force every method that only sees gradients to an error of order \(RL/\sqrt T\) after \(T\) of them (Bubeck 2015, §3.5; Section G.4).
The guarantee is also a worst case. When the risk curves near the optimum, SGD does much better.

Example 6.3 On the running example the exact minimizer, found by Newton’s method, has \(\|\theta^*\| = 3.152\) and \(\mathcal L^* = 0.5198\). Projected SGD runs on the ball of radius 5 from \(\theta_1 = 0\), so \(\theta^*\) is inside and \(R = 5\). With \(L = 1\) the step is \(\eta = R/(L\sqrt T)\), 0.5 at \(T = 100\). Table 6.2 gives the mean over 20 runs.

The bound holds, loose by a factor of 11 at \(T = 100\) and 65 at \(T = 10{,}000\), \[\frac{0.500}{0.0444} = 11.3, \qquad \frac{0.050}{0.000771} = 64.9. \tag{6.31}\] The gap grows because, as \(T\) grows 100-fold, the error falls by \(0.0444/0.000771 = 57.6\), nearer the 100 of a \(1/T\) rate than the 10 of \(1/\sqrt T\). The risk curves near \(\theta^*\), with the curvature 0.0233 of Example 6.1, and the next section shows what curvature buys (Figure 6.3, left).







Figure 6.3: Left: projected SGD on logistic regression, averaged iterate, against \(RL/\sqrt T\). Right: with a ridge term \(\lambda = 0.1\), the uniform and the \(t\)-weighted averages and the last iterate, against the two bounds of Theorem 6.3.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.4 Strongly convex objectives
A convex loss plus a ridge term is strongly convex (Corollary 6.1), and strong convexity pulls the iterates towards \(\theta^*\), harder the farther they are. With steps that shrink like \(1/(\lambda t)\) and an average of the iterates, that turns the \(1/\sqrt T\) rate of Section 6.3 into \(1/T\). The two choices below differ in how much weight the average gives to later iterates.

Theorem 6.3 (SGD on strongly convex objectives) Let \(\mathcal L\) be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, let projected SGD run in a closed convex set \(\mathcal W\) that contains \(\theta^*\), and let the random gradients be unbiased with \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2 \le G^2\).

With \(\eta_t = \frac{1}{\lambda t}\) and the uniform average \(\bar\theta_T = \frac1T\sum_t\theta_t\), \[\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T)] - \mathcal L^* \le \frac{G^2(1 + \ln T)}{2\lambda T}. \tag{6.32}\]
With \(\eta_t = \frac{2}{\lambda(t + 1)}\) and the average \(\tilde\theta_T = \sum_t\frac{2t}{T(T+1)}\theta_t\), which weights iterate \(t\) in proportion to \(t\), \[\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta_T)] - \mathcal L^* \le \frac{2G^2}{\lambda(T + 1)}. \tag{6.33}\]



Proof. This is the proof of Theorem 6.2 with a better step 5, whose extra distance term makes the distances cancel completely. Write again \(a_t = \|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2\).

The per-step inequality. Steps 1 to 4 of that proof hold with a step \(\eta_t\) that changes over time: \[\mathbb E\langle\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), \theta_t - \theta^*\rangle \le \frac{\mathbb E a_t - \mathbb E a_{t+1}}{2\eta_t} + \frac{\eta_t G^2}{2}. \tag{6.34}\]
Strong convexity adds a distance term. Strong convexity at \(\theta = \theta_t\), \(\theta' = \theta^*\), rearranged as after Lemma 6.1, says that the inner product is at least \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^* + \frac\lambda2 a_t\). Using this and moving the distance term to the right, \[\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*] \le \Big(\frac{1}{2\eta_t} - \frac\lambda2\Big)\mathbb E a_t - \frac{1}{2\eta_t}\mathbb E a_{t+1} + \frac{\eta_t G^2}{2}. \tag{6.35}\]
Uniform schedule. With \(\eta_t = 1/(\lambda t)\) the two coefficients are \(\frac{1}{2\eta_t} - \frac\lambda2 = \frac{\lambda(t - 1)}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{2\eta_t} = \frac{\lambda t}{2}\), so the distance terms are \(\frac\lambda2[(t - 1)\mathbb E a_t - t\,\mathbb E a_{t+1}]\). Summed over \(t\), each term subtracted at step \(t\) is added back at step \(t + 1\), leaving \(\frac\lambda2[0\cdot a_1 - T\,\mathbb E a_{T+1}] \le 0\). The noise terms \(\frac{G^2}{2\lambda t}\) sum to at most \(\frac{G^2(1 + \ln T)}{2\lambda}\), because \(\sum_{t \le T}1/t\) is at most \(1 + \int_1^T\mathrm ds/s = 1 + \ln T\). Dividing by \(T\) and applying Jensen gives (a).
Weighted schedule. With \(\eta_t = 2/(\lambda(t + 1))\) the coefficients are \(\frac{\lambda(t - 1)}{4}\) and \(\frac{\lambda(t + 1)}{4}\). Multiply the inequality of step 2 by \(t\), which turns the coefficients into the consecutive products \((t - 1)t\) and \(t(t + 1)\), so the distance terms become \(\frac\lambda4[(t - 1)t\,\mathbb E a_t - t(t + 1)\mathbb E a_{t+1}]\) and telescope in the same way. The noise term becomes \(\frac{t}{t + 1}\cdot\frac{G^2}{\lambda} \le \frac{G^2}{\lambda}\), so no harmonic sum appears and the total is at most \(TG^2/\lambda\). Dividing by \(\sum_t t = T(T + 1)/2\) and applying Jensen with the weights \(2t/(T(T + 1))\), which are non-negative and sum to 1, gives (b).


The harmonic sum of step 3 is where the \(\ln T\) comes from: the early iterates, taken with huge steps, are bad, and the uniform average gives them full weight. The bound is divided by \(\lambda\), so with a weak regularizer it beats \(RG/\sqrt T\) only after many steps. The \(1/(\lambda T)\) rate is not an artefact of the proof. On the risk \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) with gradient noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), the last iterate of schedule (a) is minus the average noise divided by \(\lambda\), and its error is exactly \(\sigma^2/(2\lambda T)\).
The constant \(G\) depends on the set \(\mathcal W\). For \(\ell + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) with \(\ell\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, the gradient on the ball of radius \(R\) is at most \(L + \lambda R\).

Example 6.4 On the running example with \(\lambda = 0.1\), the minimizer has \(\|\theta^*\| = 0.839\), inside the ball of radius 5, and \(G = 1 + 0.1 \times 5 = 1.5\). After \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, averaged over 20 runs, the uniform average has error \(9.09\times10^{-5}\) and the weighted average \(7.85\times10^{-5}\), against the bounds of parts (a) and (b), \[\frac{G^2(1 + \ln T)}{2\lambda T} = \frac{2.25 \times 10.21}{2000} = 1.15\times10^{-2}, \qquad \frac{2G^2}{\lambda(T + 1)} = \frac{2 \times 2.25}{0.1 \times 10{,}001} = 4.50\times10^{-3}. \tag{6.36}\] The bounds are loose by factors of about 130 and 60, \[\frac{0.0115}{0.0000909} = 127, \qquad \frac{0.0045}{0.0000785} = 57, \tag{6.37}\] mainly because \(G\) is the worst case over the whole ball (Figure 6.3, right).

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.5 Gradient noise and minibatches
Every SGD bound so far paid for \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2\), which by Lemma 6.3 includes the variance. Variance comes from sampling records and, in later parts, from noise added on purpose, so this section asks how the batch size changes it and how the learning rate should follow it. Averaging \(B\) independent gradients divides their variance by \(B\), as for the mean of a sample, and drawing without replacement does a little better.

Proposition 6.3 (Minibatch variance) Fix \(\theta\), and let \(\sigma_1^2 = \frac1n\sum_i\|\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i) - \nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\|^2\) be the variance of a per-record gradient. The average gradient \(g_B\) of \(B\) indices drawn uniformly satisfies \[\mathbb E\|g_B - \nabla \mathcal L(\theta)\|^2 = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{B} & \text{with replacement,}\\[2ex] \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{B}\cdot\dfrac{n - B}{n - 1} & \text{without replacement.}\end{cases} \tag{6.38}\]


Proof. Write \(u_i = \nabla\ell(\theta; z_i) - \nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\) for the deviation of record \(i\), so that the \(u_i\) sum to zero and the mean of \(\|u_i\|^2\) is \(\sigma_1^2\), and let \(I_1, \dots, I_B\) be the indices drawn. We expand the squared mean deviation into squares and cross terms and average each.

Each square. Each draw on its own is uniform, so \(\mathbb E\|u_{I_j}\|^2 = \sigma_1^2\).
Cross terms with replacement. The draws are independent and each deviation has mean zero, so each cross term has mean zero.
Cross terms without replacement. Two draws form a uniform pair of distinct indices, so a cross term averages \(\langle u_i, u_{i'}\rangle\) over the \(n(n - 1)\) ordered pairs \(i \ne i'\). Expanding \(\|\sum_i u_i\|^2\) shows that the sum of these terms is \(\|\sum_i u_i\|^2 - \sum_i\|u_i\|^2 = 0 - n\sigma_1^2\), so \[\mathbb E\langle u_{I_j}, u_{I_k}\rangle = -\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n - 1}. \tag{6.39}\] Once a record that deviates one way is drawn, the rest deviate on average slightly the other way.
Add up. The squared length of \(\frac1B\sum_j u_{I_j}\) is \(\frac{1}{B^2}\) times \(B\) squares and \(B(B - 1)\) cross terms. With replacement this averages to \(\sigma_1^2/B\), and without replacement to \[\frac{1}{B^2}\Big[B\sigma_1^2 - B(B - 1)\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n - 1}\Big] = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{B}\cdot\frac{n - B}{n - 1}. \tag{6.40}\]


The factor \(\frac{n - B}{n - 1}\) is 1 for \(B = 1\) and 0 for \(B = n\). For the three records of Section 6.3 at \(\theta = 4\), \(\sigma_1^2 = 14/3\), and over the three possible batches of two the batch average has variance \(7/6\), half of the \(\sigma_1^2/2 = 7/3\) of drawing with replacement.
Noise added on top of the sampling, independent and with mean zero, simply adds its mean squared size to the mean squared length of the gradient.

Proposition 6.4 (SGD with added gradient noise) In the setting of Theorem 6.2 with an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss, let each per-record gradient be perturbed by noise \(\xi_t\), independent of everything else, with mean zero and \(\mathbb E\|\xi_t\|^2 = \sigma^2\) (here \(\sigma^2\) is the size of the added noise alone). Then Equation 6.25 holds with \(G^2 = L^2 + \sigma^2\), so the best step is \(\eta^* = R/\sqrt{(L^2 + \sigma^2)T}\) and the bound there is \(R\sqrt{L^2 + \sigma^2}/\sqrt T\).


Proof. 

The second moment. Expand the squared length of \(\nabla\ell + \xi_t\). The cross term has mean zero, because \(\xi_t\) is independent of the gradient and has mean zero, so \(\mathbb E\|\nabla\ell + \xi_t\|^2 \le L^2 + \sigma^2\), and the noisy gradient is still unbiased.
Substitute. Put \(G^2 = L^2 + \sigma^2\) into Equation 6.25 and choose \(\eta\) as in step 8 of that proof.


So noisier gradients call for smaller steps and longer runs. Setting the bound \(R\sqrt{L^2 + \sigma^2}/\sqrt T\) equal to a target error and solving for \(T\), the steps needed grow in proportion to \(L^2 + \sigma^2\), so noise of size \(\sigma = 3L\) multiplies them by 10. A batch of \(B\) costs \(B\) gradient evaluations to divide the variance by \(B\), so it pays off only through parallelism.

Example 6.5 At the logistic minimizer of the running example, \(\sigma_1^2 = 0.1722\). The script measures the variance of the average gradient over 4,000 batches of each size from 1 to 500, and Equation 6.38 matches it within the Monte Carlo error (Figure 6.4). At \(B = 500 = n/2\), for example, it measures \(3.47\times10^{-4}\) with replacement against \(3.44\times10^{-4}\) predicted. Without replacement it measures \(1.74\times10^{-4}\) against \(1.72\times10^{-4}\), half as much.
The script then adds Gaussian noise to every per-record gradient and runs projected SGD for \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, 10 runs per setting (against 20 in Table 6.2), over 17 values of \(\eta\) from \(10^{-3}\) to 10. With \(R = 5\) and \(L = 1\) the recommended step is \(\eta^* = 5/\sqrt{(1 + \sigma^2)\cdot 10^4}\) (Table 6.3).

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.6 Non-convex objectives
Neural network losses are not convex, and no gradient method can promise their global minimum. SGD can still guarantee a point with a small gradient, an approximate stationary point. As in Proposition 6.2, the descent lemma shows that each step lowers \(\mathcal L\) in proportion to the squared gradient, minus a penalty for the noise when the gradients are random. If the risk is bounded below, as the theorem assumes, it cannot fall forever, so the squared gradients must be small on average.

Theorem 6.4 (SGD on smooth non-convex objectives) Let \(\mathcal L\) be \(\beta\)-smooth and bounded below by \(\mathcal L_{\inf}\), and let \(\Gamma = \mathcal L(\theta_1) - \mathcal L_{\inf}\) be the most it can fall. Let the random gradients be unbiased with \(\mathbb E[\|g_t - \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \mid \text{past}] \le \sigma^2\). SGD without projection, with a constant step \(\eta \le 1/\beta\), satisfies \[\min_{t \le T}\mathbb E\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \le \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \le \frac{2\Gamma}{\eta T} + \beta\eta\sigma^2. \tag{6.41}\] With \(\eta = \min\big(1/\beta,\ \sqrt{2\Gamma/(\beta\sigma^2T)}\big)\) the right side is at most \(\frac{4\beta\Gamma}{T} + 2\sqrt{\frac{2\beta\Gamma\sigma^2}{T}}\).


Proof. Bound one step by the descent lemma, average over the random gradient, then sum so that the decreases telescope.

Descent lemma for one step. By Equation 6.5 with \(\theta' = \theta_t - \eta g_t\), \[\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) \le \mathcal L(\theta_t) - \eta\langle\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), g_t\rangle + \frac{\beta\eta^2}{2}\|g_t\|^2. \tag{6.42}\]
Average over the random gradient. By Lemma 6.3 the inner product averages to \(\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2\), and \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2\) is at most \(\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 + \sigma^2\). Collecting the squared gradients, \[\mathbb E\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) \le \mathbb E\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{\beta\eta}{2}\Big)\mathbb E\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 + \frac{\beta\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}. \tag{6.43}\]
Make sure the step makes progress. With \(\eta \le 1/\beta\) the factor \(1 - \beta\eta/2\) is at least \(\frac12\), so \[\frac\eta2\mathbb E\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \le \mathbb E\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathbb E\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) + \frac{\beta\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}. \tag{6.44}\]
Sum and telescope. Over \(t = 1, \dots, T\) the differences of \(\mathcal L\) add up to \(\mathcal L(\theta_1) - \mathbb E\mathcal L(\theta_{T+1}) \le \Gamma\), and the noise terms to \(T\beta\eta^2\sigma^2/2\).
Divide by \(\eta T/2\). This gives the average in Equation 6.41, and the minimum is at most the average.
Choose \(\eta\). If \(\sqrt{2\Gamma/(\beta\sigma^2T)} \le 1/\beta\), that step makes both terms equal to \(\sqrt{2\beta\Gamma\sigma^2/T}\). Otherwise \(\eta = 1/\beta\), the first term is \(2\beta\Gamma/T\), and the second, \(\beta\eta\sigma^2\), is \(\sigma^2\). Squaring the failed condition \(\sqrt{2\Gamma/(\beta\sigma^2T)} > 1/\beta\) gives \(\sigma^2 < 2\beta\Gamma/T\), so the sum is below \(4\beta\Gamma/T\).


This is the argument of Ghadimi and Lan (2013). Without noise the rate is of order \(\beta\Gamma/T\), that of GD, while with noise the \(\sqrt{\sigma^2/T}\) term dominates for large \(T\). The squared gradient then falls like \(1/\sqrt T\), so the gradient itself only like \(T^{-1/4}\).
A small gradient is all you get. A stationary point can be a local minimum, a saddle point or a flat region far from anything good, and nothing bounds \(\mathcal L(\theta_T) - \mathcal L^*\). Without convexity there is no tangent inequality (Lemma 6.1) to turn the progress into a gap in function value.

Example 6.6 The sigmoid loss \(\operatorname{sig}(-m)\), with the margin \(m\) of Example 6.1, is a smooth stand-in for the 0–1 loss, which counts misclassified records. It is not convex, since \(\operatorname{sig}\) curves both ways. The margin is linear in \(\theta\), so its Hessian is \(\operatorname{sig}''(-m)\,xx^\top\), and its smoothness constant is the largest \(|\operatorname{sig}''|\), reached where \(\operatorname{sig} = (3 \pm \sqrt3)/6\), which is \(\beta = \frac{1}{6\sqrt3} = 0.0962\). The loss lies in \((0, 1)\) and equals \(\frac12\) at \(\theta_1 = 0\), so \(\Gamma \le \frac12\). Every gradient has length at most \(\max\operatorname{sig}' = \frac14\), and a variance is at most the mean squared length, so \(\sigma^2 \le \frac1{16}\).
On the logistic data, with \(2\Gamma = 1\), the step of the theorem at \(T = 100\) is \(\sqrt{1/(0.0962 \times 0.0625 \times 100)} = 1.289\), well below \(1/\beta = 10.4\). Table 6.4 averages 5 runs.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.7 Sensitivity of regularized ERM
This section asks how much the minimizer itself depends on the data, which decides whether the model does as well on new records as on its training set (Algorithmic stability and generalization). Regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) returns the minimizer \(\theta^*(D)\) of the regularized empirical risk \[\mathcal L_\lambda(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2. \tag{6.45}\] If you replace one record, how far can the minimizer move? Later parts call this quantity sensitivity. Changing one record changes one of the \(n\) terms of the average, so the gradient of the objective moves by at most \(2L/n\), and strong convexity turns a small gradient into a small distance.

Theorem 6.5 (Sensitivity of regularized ERM) Let each loss \(\ell(\cdot; z)\) be convex, differentiable and \(L\)-Lipschitz, let \(\lambda > 0\), and let the datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) of size \(n\) differ in one replaced record. Then \[\|\theta^*(D) - \theta^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.46}\] The bound is reached by the linear loss \(\ell(\theta; z) = z\theta\) with \(d = 1\) and labels \(z \in \{-1, +1\}\).


Proof. Let \(D'\) replace \(z_i\) by \(z'\), and write \(\theta = \theta^*(D)\) and \(\theta' = \theta^*(D')\). We show that the old objective has a small gradient at \(\theta'\), which strong convexity turns into a small distance from \(\theta\).

The objectives differ by one term. The new objective is the old one plus \(\psi(v) = \frac1n\big(\ell(v; z') - \ell(v; z_i)\big)\). Each loss has gradient of length at most \(L\), so by the triangle inequality \(\|\nabla\psi(v)\| \le \frac{2L}{n}\).
At \(\theta'\) the old objective has a small gradient. The new objective has zero gradient at its minimizer \(\theta'\), so \[\nabla\mathcal L_\lambda(\theta'; D) = -\nabla\psi(\theta'), \tag{6.47}\] whose length is at most \(2L/n\).
The old objective is strongly convex. It is an average of convex losses plus \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\), so part (b) of Corollary 6.1 applies.
A small gradient means close to the minimizer. Part (a) of Corollary 6.1, for the old objective at the point \(\theta'\), gives \[\|\theta' - \theta\| \le \frac{\|\nabla\mathcal L_\lambda(\theta'; D)\|}{\lambda} \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.48}\]
Tightness. For the linear loss the objective is \(\bar z\theta + \frac\lambda2\theta^2\), with \(\bar z\) the mean label, so \(\theta^*(D) = -\bar z/\lambda\). Changing one label from \(+1\) to \(-1\) lowers \(\bar z\) by \(2/n\) and moves the minimizer by exactly \(2/(\lambda n)\): the two gradients, \(+1\) and \(-1\), are opposite and of full length, and the loss adds no curvature, so neither step 1 nor step 4 loses anything.


The move shrinks like \(1/n\), because one record carries weight \(1/n\). Each loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so the trained model’s loss on any record changes by at most \(L\) times the move, \(\frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}\), a bound called uniform stability, which the next chapter turns into a generalization bound.
The bound is loose in two places. It uses only the regularizer’s curvature, while real data add their own, and it uses the worst case \(2L\) for the gradient difference.

Example 6.7 The script solves regularized logistic regression exactly with Newton’s method, replaces one random record with a fresh one drawn the same way, solves again, and records the largest move over 20 replacements. The bound is \(2/(\lambda n)\), for example \(2/(0.1 \times 1{,}000) = 0.02\) (Table 6.5).

6.7.1 Without strong convexity
Convexity alone does not keep the minimizer from jumping, because a convex function can be flat, and on a flat stretch a tiny change in the data can move the minimizer far.

Proposition 6.5 (A convex Lipschitz loss whose minimizer jumps) Let \(\ell(\theta; z) = |\theta - z|\), which is convex and 1-Lipschitz, and let \(D\) hold \(n = 2k + 1\) values, \(k + 1\) of them 0 and \(k\) of them 1. Replacing one 0 by a 1 moves the minimizer of \(\frac1n\sum_i|\theta - z_i|\) from 0 to 1, for every \(n\).


Proof. 

The minimizer is the median. Moving \(\theta\) up a little increases \(|\theta - z_i|\) for each value below \(\theta\) and decreases it for each value above. So the risk falls while more values lie above \(\theta\), and stops falling when half lie on each side.
Before and after. In \(D\) the majority is 0, so the minimizer is 0. After the replacement the majority is 1, a move of 1 whatever \(n\) is.


With \(\frac\lambda2\theta^2\) added, Equation 6.46 caps the move at \(2/(\lambda n)\), with subgradients in place of gradients. The actual move is half of that, \(1/(\lambda n)\), where the new subgradient \(-1/n + \lambda\theta\) vanishes.
For a non-convex loss even a regularizer may not help. With labels \(z \in \{-1, +1\}\), the double-well loss \(\frac14(\theta^2 - 1)^2 - z\theta\) has the risk \(\frac14(\theta^2 - 1)^2 - \bar z\theta\): two valleys near \(\pm1\), tilted towards the sign of the mean label \(\bar z\). With 11 records, six labelled \(+1\), replacing one \(+1\) by \(-1\) flips that sign and moves the minimizer from \(1.0427\) to \(-1.0427\) (Figure 6.8), and with 1,001 records the move is still 2.0010. A ridge term fixes this only if it makes the objective convex, as step 3 of the proof of Theorem 6.5 needs. A fixed number of SGD steps from a fixed start, by contrast, is a composition of smooth maps of the records, so for fixed random indices it changes continuously with the data. That is why, for non-convex models, one studies the influence of a record on the algorithm.






Figure 6.8: A double-well empirical risk on 11 records before (\(D\), six labels \(+1\)) and after (\(D'\), five labels \(+1\)) one label changes. The dots mark the global minimizers, which jump from one well to the other.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.1 Risk, empirical risk and the gap
You train a model and its loss on the training data is low. Will its loss on new data be low too? The difference between the two is the generalization gap, and bounding it is the central question of learning theory. The classical answer counts the models an algorithm could output; this chapter looks at the algorithm instead.
The idea that organizes it fits in one sentence: a model generalizes when it does not depend much on any single training record. So if replacing one record can move the loss by at most \(\gamma\) at every test point, a property called uniform stability, the expected gap is at most \(\gamma\). The chapter computes \(\gamma\) for regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) and for stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and ends with the same bias reappearing when a holdout set is reused to choose what to measure.
The running example is logistic regression in ten dimensions. Features \(x\) are uniform on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^{10}\), and the label \(y = \pm1\) is \(+1\) with probability \(\sigma(5x_1)\), where \(\sigma(t) = 1/(1 + e^{-t})\) is the logistic function. The model is a weight vector \(\theta\), chosen to minimize the average logistic loss \(\ln(1 + e^{-y\langle\theta, x\rangle})\) plus a penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\). With \(n = 50\) records and \(\lambda = 0.01\), averaged over 100 training sets, the training loss is 0.4603 and the test loss is 0.5781. With \(n = 1{,}000\) records the gap shrinks to about 0.006, and the chapter explains why.
Before bounding the gap you need to say exactly what it is, and why it is not zero: training loss and future loss agree on average only for a model chosen before looking at the data.
The test loss cannot be computed, because \(\mathcal D\) is unknown, so the training loss stands in for it, and for a fixed model it does so without bias.
Step 2 is exactly what fails for the trained model \(\mathcal T(D)\). The record \(z_i\) helped to choose \(\mathcal T(D)\), so it is no longer an independent draw from the model’s point of view. The algorithm chose a model that does well on exactly these records, so the training loss is biased downward.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
Definition 7.1 (Risk, empirical risk and the gap) A training set \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\) is a list of \(n\) records drawn independently from a distribution \(\mathcal D\), the source of all data, past and future. A training algorithm \(\mathcal T\) maps \(D\) to a model \(\mathcal T(D)\), and a loss \(\ell(\theta; z) \ge 0\) says how badly the model \(\theta\) does on the record \(z\). The population risk, or test loss, of \(\theta\) is its average loss on a new record, and its empirical risk, or training loss, is its average loss on the training set: \[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta) = \mathbb E_{z \sim \mathcal D}\big[\ell(\theta; z)\big], \qquad \mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i). \tag{7.1}\] The generalization gap of the trained model is the test loss minus the training loss, \[\mathrm{gap}(D) = \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\mathcal T(D)) - \mathcal L(\mathcal T(D); D). \tag{7.2}\]



Proposition 7.1 (A fixed model’s training loss is unbiased) Let \(\theta\) be a model that does not depend on the training set \(D\). Then \[\mathbb E_D\big[\mathcal L(\theta; D)\big] = \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta). \tag{7.3}\]


Proof. 

The expectation of an average is the average of the expectations, by linearity, so \(\mathbb E_D[\mathcal L(\theta; D)] = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E[\ell(\theta; z_i)]\).
Each \(z_i\) is a draw from \(\mathcal D\) and \(\theta\) is fixed, so each term \(\mathbb E[\ell(\theta; z_i)]\) is the average loss of \(\theta\) on a draw from \(\mathcal D\), which is \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta)\). The average of \(n\) copies of it is itself.




Example 7.1 In the running example with \(n = 50\) and \(\lambda = 0.01\), the average training loss over 100 training sets is 0.4603 and the average test loss, computed by numerical integration (Section 7.9), is 0.5781. The expected gap is about 0.119, not exactly their difference, because Example 7.4 estimates it with less noise. With \(n = 1{,}000\) it is about 0.006.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.2 Uniform stability and the expected gap
text:
7.2 Uniform stability and the expected gap
To control the gap you need to say how much \(\mathcal T(D)\) depends on the training set: replace one record, retrain, and see how much the loss changes at any test point. This section turns that into a definition and proves that it bounds the expected gap.
The tool is a training set that differs from \(D\) in one record. The replace-one neighbour \(D^{(i)} = (z_1, \dots, z_{i-1}, z_i', z_{i+1}, \dots, z_n)\) is \(D\) with record \(i\) replaced by \(z_i'\). In probability statements, the replacements \(z_1', \dots, z_n'\) are fresh draws from \(\mathcal D\), independent of each other and of \(D\).

Definition 7.2 (Uniform stability) A training algorithm \(\mathcal T\) is \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable if for every training set \(D\), every index \(i\), every replacement \(z_i'\) and every test point \(z\), \[\big|\ell(\mathcal T(D); z) - \ell(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z)\big| \le \gamma. \tag{7.4}\] If \(\mathcal T\) is randomized, as SGD is through the order in which it visits records, the condition is on the expectation over its internal randomness: \[\big|\mathbb E_{\mathcal T}\big[\ell(\mathcal T(D); z) - \ell(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z)\big]\big| \le \gamma. \tag{7.5}\]

Usually \(\gamma\) falls with \(n\), because each record carries less weight in a larger training set (the literature writes it \(\beta\), which this book keeps for a failure probability). In Figure 7.1 one record’s label is flipped, and the fitted model moves a lot when the penalty \(\lambda\) is small and barely when it is large.






Figure 7.1: One-dimensional logistic regression on 30 points, fitted on \(D\) and on \(D^{(i)}\), where one positive record has its label flipped, at \(\lambda = 0.01\) (left) and \(\lambda = 1\) (right). The titles compare the weight change with the bound of Theorem 7.2.



The main result needs one fact about independent draws: swapping two of them changes no expectation. Step 2 of the proof below uses it to exchange a training record with a fresh one.

Lemma 7.1 (Swapping two independent draws) Let \(U\) and \(V\) be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and independent of a random variable \(W\). Then \((U, V, W)\) and \((V, U, W)\) have the same distribution, so \(\mathbb E[g(U, V, W)] = \mathbb E[g(V, U, W)]\) for every function \(g\) whose expectation exists.


Proof. 

By independence, the joint density of \((U, V, W)\) at \((u, v, w)\) is the product \(\rho(u)\,\rho(v)\,\rho_W(w)\), where \(\rho\) is the common density of \(U\) and \(V\), and \(\rho_W\) is that of \(W\). For discrete variables, read mass functions for densities.
Exchanging \(u\) and \(v\) leaves this product unchanged, because \(U\) and \(V\) share the density \(\rho\). So the swapped triple has the same distribution, and every expectation computed from it agrees.


The test loss of the trained model can be measured on a fresh point \(z_i'\), and swapping the roles of \(z_i\) and \(z_i'\) keeps its average while turning it into the loss on \(z_i\) of a model trained with \(z_i'\) in its place, which never saw \(z_i\).

Theorem 7.1 (The expected gap is an average replace-one effect) For any training algorithm \(\mathcal T\), with the records of \(D\) and the replacements \(z_1', \dots, z_n'\) all i.i.d. from \(\mathcal D\), and \(\mathbb E\) averaging over all of them and over any randomness of \(\mathcal T\), \[\mathbb E_D\big[\mathrm{gap}(D)\big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\Big[\ell\big(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z_i\big) - \ell\big(\mathcal T(D); z_i\big)\Big]. \tag{7.6}\] If \(\mathcal T\) is moreover \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable, then \[\big|\mathbb E_D[\mathrm{gap}(D)]\big| \le \gamma. \tag{7.7}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the expected test loss with a fresh point, exchange that point with a training record by Lemma 7.1, subtract the training loss, and bound each term by stability.

Write the test loss with a fresh point. The point \(z_i'\) is independent of \(D\) and has distribution \(\mathcal D\), so given \(D\) its average loss is the test loss of \(\mathcal T(D)\). Averaging over \(D\) too gives \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\mathcal T(D))\big] = \mathbb E\big[\ell(\mathcal T(D); z_i')\big] \quad\text{for every } i. \tag{7.8}\]
Exchange \(z_i\) and \(z_i'\). The two points are i.i.d. and independent of the other records, so by Lemma 7.1 exchanging them changes no expectation. The exchange turns \(D\) into \(D^{(i)}\) and \(z_i'\) into \(z_i\), so \[\mathbb E\big[\ell(\mathcal T(D); z_i')\big] = \mathbb E\big[\ell(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z_i)\big]. \tag{7.9}\]
Average over \(i\). Steps 1 and 2 hold for every \(i\), so the expected test loss is also the average \(\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E[\ell(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z_i)]\).
Subtract the training loss. By definition, the expected training loss is \(\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E[\ell(\mathcal T(D); z_i)]\). Both sums run over the same \(i\), so their difference is the average of the differences, which is Equation 7.6.
Bound each term. Uniform stability at the test point \(z = z_i\) puts each difference \(\ell(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z_i) - \ell(\mathcal T(D); z_i)\) in \([-\gamma, \gamma]\) for every outcome. Expectations and averages of numbers in that interval stay in it, which is Equation 7.7. For a randomized \(\mathcal T\), take the expectation over its randomness first.


The identity is not a bound. It says that the expected gap is the average replace-one self-influence, how much the loss on \(z_i\) rises when \(z_i\) leaves the training set. So a large gap means that the model fits many records only because they were there, and Section 7.7 measures this record by record.
The bound, by contrast, takes the worst case over everything, which is why \(\gamma\) can sit far above the true gap, and why weaker notions that average over the data exist (Bousquet & Elisseeff 2002; Shalev-Shwartz et al. 2010). No count of models appears in it, so it covers SGD on large models.

Example 7.2 Step 2 is clearest with every outcome listed. Take \(n = 1\): one record \(z_1 \in \{0, 1\}\) with \(\Pr[z_1 = 1] = 0.3\), and a fresh copy \(z_1'\). The algorithm shrinks the data towards zero, \(\mathcal T(D) = z_1/2\), and the loss is the squared error \(\ell(\theta; z) = (\theta - z)^2\). Table 7.1 lists the four outcomes with the three losses of the proof.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.3 Regularized empirical risk minimization
The bound of Theorem 7.1 is only as good as \(\gamma\), so the next question is which algorithms have a small one. Regularized ERM is the first answer. Its penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) makes the objective a bowl with curvature at least \(\lambda\), and one record, with weight \(1/n\) in the objective, can only tilt such a bowl so far.
A loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the weights (Definition 6.2) when moving the weights by a distance \(r\) changes it by at most \(Lr\) at every record, so its gradient never exceeds \(L\) in norm. Regularized ERM returns the minimizer \(\theta_D\) of the regularized empirical risk, \[\mathcal L_\lambda(\theta; D) = \mathcal L(\theta; D) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2. \tag{7.10}\] Replacing one record changes the objective’s gradient by at most \(2L/n\). The penalty makes the objective \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, curved by at least \(\lambda\) in every direction, so a point where its gradient is small lies close to its minimizer, and the Lipschitz constant turns the weight change into a loss change.

Theorem 7.2 (Stability of regularized ERM) Let \(\ell(\cdot; z)\) be convex, differentiable and \(L\)-Lipschitz for every record \(z\), and let \(\lambda > 0\). Then for every training set \(D\), index \(i\), replacement \(z_i'\) and test point \(z\), \[\|\theta_D - \theta_{D^{(i)}}\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n} \quad\text{and}\quad \big|\ell(\theta_D; z) - \ell(\theta_{D^{(i)}}; z)\big| \le \frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}. \tag{7.11}\] So regularized ERM is \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable with \(\gamma = 2L^2/(\lambda n)\). Its weights also satisfy \(\|\theta_D\| \le L/\lambda\), which bounds the loss in Example 7.5.


Proof. 

The weights. The first bound is the sensitivity of regularized ERM, Theorem 6.5, and its proof runs as follows. The two objectives differ only in the \(i\)-th term, and the gradient of the second is zero at its own minimizer \(\theta_{D^{(i)}}\). So there the gradient of \(\mathcal L_\lambda(\cdot; D)\) is the difference of two per-record gradients divided by \(n\), of norm at most \(2L/n\). A \(\lambda\)-strongly convex function’s minimizer lies within the gradient norm divided by \(\lambda\) of any point (Corollary 6.1), here \(2L/(\lambda n)\).
The losses. The loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so a weight change of at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\) moves the loss at every test point by at most \(2L^2/(\lambda n)\). This holds for every \(D\), \(i\), \(z_i'\) and \(z\), which is Definition 7.2.
The norm. The gradient of \(\mathcal L_\lambda(\cdot; D)\) is zero at its minimizer, so \(\lambda\theta_D = -\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell(\theta_D; z_i)\). The right side is an average of vectors of norm at most \(L\), so dividing by \(\lambda\) gives \(\|\theta_D\| \le L/\lambda\).


Doubling \(\lambda\) halves \(\gamma\), but a larger \(\lambda\) also pulls the solution away from the best fit, so the test loss is U-shaped in \(\lambda\) (Figure 7.3, right). The bound is loose in three places: it charges the gradient difference its worst case \(2L\), it ignores the curvature of the training loss \(\mathcal L(\theta; D)\) itself, and step 2 assumes the worst test point.

Example 7.3 By the chain rule, the gradient of the logistic loss is \(-y\,\sigma(-y\langle\theta, x\rangle)\,x\), of norm at most \(\|x\| = 1\), so \(L = 1\) and \(\gamma = 2/(\lambda n)\) in the running example.
