title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.4 High probability: the Bousquet–Elisseeff bound
Equation 7.7 controls the gap on average, but you train once, so you need the gap of your model to be small with high probability. The gap is a function of \(n\) independent records, and stability bounds how much one record can move it, which is the setting of McDiarmid’s inequality (Theorem 2.8). Suppose that changing only the record \(z_i\) changes a function \(g(D)\) by at most \(c_i\), whatever the values of the other records. Then for every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\big[g(D) - \mathbb E\,g(D) \ge t\big] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_ic_i^2}\Big). \tag{7.12}\] Setting the right side equal to a failure probability \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) gives the deviation \(t = \sqrt{\frac12\sum_ic_i^2\ln(1/\beta)}\).
The theorem below adds this deviation and \(\gamma\) to the training loss. It is Theorem 12 of Bousquet & Elisseeff (2002), who define stability by removing a record; replace-one stability is at most twice that.

Theorem 7.3 (Bousquet–Elisseeff bound) Let \(\mathcal T\) be \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable, let the loss take values in \([0, K]\), and let \(\beta \in (0, 1)\). Then with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) over the training set \(D\), \[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\mathcal T(D)) \le \mathcal L(\mathcal T(D); D) + \gamma + (2n\gamma + K)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{2n}}. \tag{7.13}\]


Proof. First bound how much one record can move the gap, then feed that to McDiarmid’s inequality with \(g = \mathrm{gap}\), and bound the mean by Theorem 7.1.

One record and the test loss. Replacing \(z_i\) moves \(\ell(\mathcal T(D); z)\) by at most \(\gamma\) at every \(z\), by uniform stability. The test loss is an average of these losses over \(z\), so it also moves by at most \(\gamma\).
One record and the training loss. The training losses on \(D\) and on \(D^{(i)}\) share \(n - 1\) terms. Each shared term \(\frac1n\ell(\cdot; z_j)\) is evaluated at the same point under two models, so by stability it moves by at most \(\gamma/n\). The two unshared terms are evaluated at different points, \(z_i\) and \(z_i'\), so stability says nothing about them, but both lie in \([0, K/n]\). The total change is at most \(\frac{n - 1}n\gamma + \frac Kn \le \gamma + \frac Kn\).
Bounded differences. The gap is the test loss minus the training loss, so by the triangle inequality its change is at most \(c_i = 2\gamma + K/n\). Uniform stability holds for every training set and replacement, so this holds for all values of the records, as McDiarmid’s inequality requires.
Apply McDiarmid’s inequality. All \(n\) constants are equal, so the deviation \(\sqrt{\frac12\sum_ic_i^2\ln(1/\beta)}\) is \(\sqrt n\,(2\gamma + K/n)\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)/2}\). Multiplying inside and out by \(\sqrt n\) rewrites it, so with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), \[\mathrm{gap}(D) < \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{gap}(D)\big] + (2n\gamma + K)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{2n}}. \tag{7.14}\]
Bound the mean. By Equation 7.7 the expected gap is at most \(\gamma\). Substitute it, and move the training loss to the right-hand side.


Call the width of the bound everything it adds to the training loss. Its part \(K\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)/(2n)}\) is what Hoeffding’s inequality gives for one fixed model. Its stability part, \(2n\gamma\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)/(2n)} = \gamma\sqrt{2n\ln(1/\beta)}\), goes to zero only if \(\gamma\sqrt n \to 0\). With \(\gamma\) of order \(1/n\), as for regularized ERM, the width falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), and with \(\gamma\) of order \(1/\sqrt n\) it does not fall at all (Figure 7.4).
The looseness comes from step 3, which charges every record the full \(2\gamma\) although their effects largely average out. Later work (Feldman & Vondrák 2018, 2019; Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy 2020) reached, for \(K = 1\) and up to constant factors (which is what \(\lesssim\) means), \[\mathrm{gap} \lesssim \gamma\ln n\,\ln(1/\beta) + \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{n}}, \tag{7.15}\] so that \(\gamma\) of order \(1/\sqrt n\) also gives a gap of order \(1/\sqrt n\) up to log factors.






Figure 7.4: Width of the high-probability bound, Equation 7.13, with \(K = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\), for stability \(\gamma = 1/n\), \(n^{-3/4}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\), against the Hoeffding width for a single fixed model.




Example 7.5 By Theorem 7.2, regularized logistic regression in the running example has \(\gamma = 2/(\lambda n)\) and weights of norm at most \(1/\lambda\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality with \(\|x\| = 1\), the margin \(y\langle\theta, x\rangle\) is at least \(-1/\lambda\), so the largest loss is \(K = \ln(1 + e^{1/\lambda})\). With \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) the common factor is \(\sqrt{\ln 20/20{,}000} = 0.01224\), and with \(2n\gamma = 4/\lambda\) the width is \(\gamma + (4/\lambda + K)\times0.01224\). At \(\lambda = 1\), with \(K = 1.313\), that is \(2\times10^{-4} + (4 + 1.313)\times0.01224 = 0.065\). At \(\lambda = 0.1\), with \(K = 10.000\), it is \(0.002 + (40 + 10)\times0.01224 = 0.614\).
In both cases the stability term, \(2n\gamma \times 0.01224\), is three quarters or more of the width, while the expected gap at \(\lambda = 1\) is only \(2.53\times10^{-4}\) even at the smaller \(n = 1{,}000\) (Table 7.3). So the bound is valid but loose.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.5 Stochastic gradient descent
Large models are trained by SGD, whose steps each pick one training record at random and move the weights a little against the gradient of its loss. Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016) showed that SGD is stable, with a \(\gamma\) that grows with the sum of the learning rates.
Two SGD runs, one on \(D\) and one on \(D^{(i)}\), can only drift apart on the steps that pick record \(i\). Each such step pushes them apart by at most \(2\eta_tL\), where \(\eta_t\) is the learning rate at step \(t\), and it happens with probability \(1/n\). On every other step both runs take a gradient step on the same loss, and the lemma below says that such a step never pushes two points apart. It needs the loss to be \(\beta_s\)-smooth: its gradient changes by at most \(\beta_s\) per unit of distance (Definition 6.2; the subscript keeps \(\beta\) for the failure probability).

Lemma 7.2 (A short gradient step is non-expansive) Let \(h\) be convex and \(\beta_s\)-smooth, let \(0 \le \eta \le 2/\beta_s\), and let \(\psi(\theta) = \theta - \eta\nabla h(\theta)\) be one gradient step. Then for all \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\), \[\|\psi(\theta) - \psi(\theta')\| \le \|\theta - \theta'\|. \tag{7.16}\]


Proof. We expand the squared distance after the step and bound its cross term by a property of the gradient.

Co-coercivity. For a convex \(\beta_s\)-smooth function, two gradients that differ by a lot must come from points far apart along the direction of their difference. Writing \(g = \nabla h(\theta) - \nabla h(\theta')\), \[\langle g, \theta - \theta'\rangle \ge \frac1{\beta_s}\|g\|^2. \tag{7.17}\] This is Theorem 2.1.5 of Nesterov (2004), and Section G.2 in the appendices derives it step by step.
Expand the square. The difference of the two steps is \((\theta - \theta') - \eta g\), so \[\|\psi(\theta) - \psi(\theta')\|^2 = \|\theta - \theta'\|^2 - 2\eta\langle g, \theta - \theta'\rangle + \eta^2\|g\|^2. \tag{7.18}\]
Use co-coercivity. Replacing the inner product by the smaller \(\|g\|^2/\beta_s\) of step 1 can only increase the right side, so \[\|\psi(\theta) - \psi(\theta')\|^2 \le \|\theta - \theta'\|^2 - \eta\Big(\frac2{\beta_s} - \eta\Big)\|g\|^2. \tag{7.19}\]
Conclude. When \(\eta \le 2/\beta_s\) the subtracted term is not negative, so the distance does not grow.


The condition on \(\eta\) is needed: on \(h(\theta) = \frac{\beta_s}2\theta^2\) the step multiplies distances by \(|1 - \eta\beta_s|\), which exceeds 1 when \(\eta > 2/\beta_s\).
The stability of SGD, Theorem 7.4, is Theorem 3.8 of Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016).

Theorem 7.4 (Stability of SGD) Let \(\ell(\cdot; z)\) be convex, \(\beta_s\)-smooth and \(L\)-Lipschitz for every record \(z\). Run SGD for \(T\) steps from a starting point \(\theta_0\). Step \(t\) draws an index \(I_t\) uniformly from \(\{1, \dots, n\}\), independently of the earlier steps, and updates \[\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \eta_t\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t}), \qquad \eta_t \le \frac2{\beta_s}. \tag{7.20}\] Let \(\theta_t'\) be the run on \(D^{(i)}\) with the same indices and starting point, and \(r_t = \|\theta_t - \theta_t'\|\) the distance between the runs. Then \(\mathbb E\,r_T \le \frac{2L}n\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t\), and the output \(\theta_T\) is uniformly stable in expectation over the indices, with \[\gamma \le \frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t. \tag{7.21}\]


Proof. We couple the two runs, bound the growth of their distance in one step, average over the index, and add up the steps. Sharing the indices is allowed because the stability condition involves only the difference of the two runs’ average losses, and each run’s average is the same whichever indices the other run uses. Both runs start at \(\theta_0\), so \(r_0 = 0\).

Same record picked. With probability \(1 - 1/n\), the index \(I_t\) is not \(i\), and both runs take a gradient step on the same loss. That step does not increase distances, by Lemma 7.2, so \(r_t \le r_{t-1}\).
Differing record picked. With probability \(1/n\), one run steps on \(z_i\) and the other on \(z_i'\), and the lemma does not apply. The new difference is the old one minus \(\eta_t\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i)\) plus \(\eta_t\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}'; z_i')\), and each gradient has norm at most \(L\), so the triangle inequality gives \[r_t \le r_{t-1} + 2\eta_tL. \tag{7.22}\]
Average over the index. The index \(I_t\) is drawn fresh, so it is independent of \(r_{t-1}\). Weighting the two cases by their probabilities, \[\mathbb E\,r_t \le \Big(1 - \frac1n\Big)\mathbb E\,r_{t-1} + \frac1n\big(\mathbb E\,r_{t-1} + 2\eta_tL\big) = \mathbb E\,r_{t-1} + \frac{2\eta_tL}n. \tag{7.23}\]
Add up the steps. Starting from \(r_0 = 0\) and adding the increments of steps 1 to \(T\) gives \(\mathbb E\,r_T \le \frac{2L}n\sum_t\eta_t\).
From weights to losses. The loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so at every test point the loss difference is at most \(L\,r_T\) in absolute value, and its expectation is at most \(L\,\mathbb E\,r_T\), which is Equation 7.21.


So stability degrades linearly with training time (Figure 7.5). With a constant step \(\eta\) and \(m\) epochs (passes over the data), so \(T = mn\) steps, the bound is \(\gamma \le 2L^2\eta m\), and for a fixed number of epochs it does not improve with more data. Training longer lowers the training loss but raises \(\gamma\), and the test loss is the training loss plus the gap, so there is a case for stopping early. Section G.3 in the appendices finds the training time that balances the two.
The bound is loose because step 1 only uses that a step does not expand distances. A step on a curved loss often contracts them, and a strongly convex loss makes the bound independent of \(T\).

Example 7.6 Take \(n = 100\) records of the running example, no penalty, and a constant step \(\eta = 0.25\). At margin \(t\) the logistic loss has second derivative \(\sigma(t)(1 - \sigma(t))\), a product of two numbers that sum to 1, so at most \(\frac14\). With \(\|x\| \le 1\) that gives \(\beta_s = \frac14\), and \(\eta \le 2/\beta_s = 8\) holds. The script averages over 100 coupled pairs of runs, with \(z_1\) replaced by a fresh draw, and with \(L = 1\) both bounds are \(0.5m\).

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.6 An unstable algorithm: 1-nearest neighbour
An algorithm without stability shows what stability rules out. The nearest neighbour (NN) rule with one neighbour, 1-NN, predicts the label of the closest training point, so it fits every training record by using that record itself. It is scored with the 0-1 loss, which is 1 for a wrong prediction and 0 for a right one. With \(p(x) = \Pr[y = 1 \mid x]\), the best rule, the Bayes classifier, predicts the more likely label at each \(x\), with error \(\mathbb E[\min(p(x), 1 - p(x))]\).

Proposition 7.2 (1-NN is maximally unstable) Score 1-NN with the 0-1 loss, and assume the training points are distinct. Then its training error is 0, and it is \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable only for \(\gamma = 1\), the largest possible value. If moreover the features take values in a closed and bounded set on which \(p\) is continuous, its expected test error tends to \(\mathbb E[2p(x)(1 - p(x))]\) as \(n \to \infty\) (Cover & Hart 1967). So when \(p(x)\) lies strictly between 0 and 1 with positive probability, its gap stays bounded away from zero.


Proof. 

Training error. Each training point is its own nearest neighbour, so it is predicted with its own label.
Stability. Take any \(D\) and the test point \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\). On \(D\) the prediction at \(x_i\) is \(y_i\), with loss 0. Replace \(z_i\) by \((x_i, -y_i)\), the same point with the opposite label. On \(D^{(i)}\) that point is the nearest neighbour of \(x_i\), so the prediction is \(-y_i\), with loss 1.
The limit. As \(n\) grows, the nearest neighbour of a test point \(x\) lies arbitrarily close to \(x\), so its label is \(+1\) with probability close to \(p(x)\). The test label is an independent draw with probability \(p(x)\), and the two disagree with probability \(p(1 - p) + (1 - p)p = 2p(1 - p)\). Making “arbitrarily close” precise is Cover and Hart’s theorem, which Section G.5 in the appendices proves under the stated assumptions.
The gap. By step 1 the gap equals the test error, whose limit is positive under that condition on \(p\).


So zero training error says nothing here. 1-NN is a reasonable classifier: \(2p(1 - p)\) is \(2\min(p, 1 - p)\) times \(\max(p, 1 - p) \le 1\), so its limiting error is within twice the Bayes error. But its training error does not tell you how close it gets. With \(\gamma = 1\), Equation 7.7 only says that the gap is at most 1, which every 0-1 loss satisfies anyway.
A majority vote over several nearest neighbours rarely changes when one record is replaced, although its worst-case \(\gamma\) is still 1, and notions of stability that average over the data capture its behaviour (Devroye & Wagner 1979).

Example 7.7 In the running example the Bayes error is 0.250 and the 1-NN limit \(\mathbb E[2p(1 - p)]\) is 0.338, both computed by numerical integration. Table 7.5 compares 1-NN with regularized logistic regression, averaging over 10 training sets, with 0-1 error measured on 2,000 test points.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.7 Memorization of individual records
Theorem 7.1 says that the expected gap is an average over training records of how much each record’s own loss rises when it is replaced. That quantity can be measured directly by retraining, and measuring it shows which records carry the gap.

Definition 7.3 (Self-influence) The self-influence, or memorization score, of training record \(i\) is its loss under the model trained with a fresh point in its place, minus its loss under the model trained with it: \[\mathrm{mem}_i(D) = \ell\big(\mathcal T(D^{(i)}); z_i\big) - \ell\big(\mathcal T(D); z_i\big). \tag{7.24}\]

By Equation 7.6, the expected gap is the average of the expected self-influences. Uniform stability caps each of them at \(\gamma\), but only their average matters. Feldman (2020) uses the same idea with removal instead of replacement and accuracy instead of loss.
The contributions are uneven. Typical records are fitted well whether or not they are present, because similar records carry the same information, while atypical records, such as mislabelled points, are fitted only if they are in the training set. Memorization can still be necessary: Feldman (2020) shows that when the data contain many rare subpopulations, each seen about once, an algorithm that does not memorize them loses accuracy on them. Deep networks even fit random labels (Zhang et al. 2017), and score highest on atypical images (Feldman & Zhang 2020).

Example 7.8 The script draws training sets of \(n = 40\) points and, for each \(i\), replaces \(z_i\) by a fresh draw, refits, and records \(\mathrm{mem}_i\). Over 100 training sets, with ± one standard error, the measured gap and the average self-influence agree, as the identity requires. At \(\lambda = 0.01\) they are \(0.1482 \pm 0.0073\) and \(0.1422 \pm 0.0025\), and at \(\lambda = 0.1\) they are \(0.0420 \pm 0.0017\) and \(0.0416 \pm 0.0003\).
To see which records carry the gap, split them by whether the label goes with the trend (\(y_ix_{i1} \ge 0\), the more likely label, since \(\sigma(5x_1) > \frac12\) exactly when \(x_1 > 0\)) or against it. About a quarter go against it (24% and 25% at the two values of \(\lambda\)). At \(\lambda = 0.01\) their average self-influence is 0.284, three times the 0.097 of the others. At \(\lambda = 0.1\) the two are 0.055 and 0.037, so regularization flattens the profile (Figure 7.8).







Figure 7.8: Self-influence of each training record against \(y_ix_{i1}\), which measures how typical its label is, for \(n = 40\) and two values of \(\lambda\). The dashed line is the average, which equals the expected gap.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.8 Choosing what to measure after looking
text:
7.8 Choosing what to measure after looking
A holdout set is a sample kept aside for judging models, and by Proposition 7.1 it judges a model fixed in advance without bias. In practice you look at its verdict, change a feature, and ask again, so each new question depends on the holdout set. This section shows that the guarantee then fails, and what restores it.

Definition 7.4 (Questions to a holdout set) A holdout set \(H = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\) is a list of \(n\) records drawn independently from \(\mathcal D\). A question is a function \(f\) that maps one record to a number in \([0, 1]\), such as “is this record classified correctly by a given model?”. Its answer on the holdout set, written \(f(H)\), and its true value are \[f(H) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(z_i), \qquad f(\mathcal D) = \mathbb E_{z \sim \mathcal D}\big[f(z)\big]. \tag{7.25}\] A question is fixed in advance if it was chosen before \(H\) was drawn, and chosen after looking if it may depend on answers already given on \(H\).

Many questions fixed in advance can share one holdout set, because the largest error among \(k\) answers grows only with the logarithm of \(k\). The proof needs Hoeffding’s lemma (Lemma 2.2): a centred random variable with values in an interval of length \(c\) has moment generating function at most \(e^{s^2c^2/8}\) at every real \(s\).

Theorem 7.5 (Questions fixed in advance) If \(k\) questions \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) are all fixed in advance, then \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j \le k}\big|f_j(H) - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{7.26}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the moment generating function of one error, combine the \(2k\) signed errors through the exponential of their maximum, and choose \(s\) to balance the two resulting terms.

One error. Write \(Z_j = f_j(H) - f_j(\mathcal D)\) for the error of question \(j\). Because \(f_j\) is fixed while the records are drawn, \(Z_j\) is an average of \(n\) independent values \(f_j(z_i)\) in \([0, 1]\) minus their common mean. Each centred term \(f_j(z_i)/n\) lies in an interval of length \(1/n\), so Hoeffding’s lemma bounds its moment generating function by \(e^{s^2/(8n^2)}\). Multiplying the \(n\) independent bounds gives, for every real \(s\), \[\mathbb E\big[e^{sZ_j}\big] \le e^{s^2/(8n)}. \tag{7.27}\] Since \(s\) may be negative, the same bound holds for \(-Z_j\).
The largest of \(2k\). The largest error is the maximum of the \(2k\) variables \(\pm Z_j\). For \(s > 0\), Jensen’s inequality for the convex function \(e^x\) moves the expectation inside the exponential, and the exponential of a maximum is at most the sum of the exponentials: \[e^{s\,\mathbb E\max} \le \mathbb E\big[e^{s\max}\big] \le \sum_{\text{all } 2k}\mathbb E\big[e^{\pm sZ_j}\big] \le 2k\,e^{s^2/(8n)}. \tag{7.28}\]
Take logarithms. Dividing the logarithm by \(s\) bounds the expected maximum by a sum of two terms, \[\mathbb E\max \le \frac{\ln(2k)}s + \frac s{8n}. \tag{7.29}\]
Balance. The two terms are equal, each \(\sqrt{\ln(2k)/(8n)}\), at \(s = \sqrt{8n\ln(2k)}\), and their sum is Equation 7.26. The argument never used independence between the questions.


Step 1 is where looking breaks the argument. A question chosen from earlier answers depends on \(H\), so its values on \(H\) are not independent draws, just as in Section 7.1, and Example 7.9 shows how large the error can be. The remedy is to never let a record answer a question it helped to choose.

Proposition 7.3 (Sample splitting) Split \(H\) into \(k\) disjoint parts \(H_1, \dots, H_k\) of \(n/k\) records each, and answer question \(j\) on \(H_j\) only. Let each \(f_j\) depend only on the answers on \(H_1, \dots, H_{j-1}\) and on randomness of the analyst that is independent of \(H\). Then, however the questions are chosen, \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j \le k}\big|f_j(H_j) - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{k\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{7.30}\]


Proof. 

Each question is fixed for its own part. Fix the parts \(H_1, \dots, H_{j-1}\) and the analyst’s randomness. Then \(f_j\) is fixed and \(H_j\) is independent of it, so step 1 of the proof of Theorem 7.5 holds given those parts, with \(n/k\) records in place of \(n\).
Remove the conditioning. That bound holds for every value of the earlier parts, so it holds after averaging over them.
Finish as before. Steps 2 to 4 of that proof then apply unchanged, with \(n/k\) in place of \(n\).


A question chosen with the holdout set’s help is like a model trained on it: the analyst is a learning algorithm whose input is \(H\), and the answer to the final question plays the part of a training loss, optimistic for the same reason. Splitting removes the bias at the price of a factor \(k\). If the questions come in \(r\) rounds, and every question of a round is fixed before that round’s answers are seen, one part per round suffices, and the factor \(k\) in front of \(\ln(2k)\) becomes \(r\). The classical rule is one round: keep a test set for one final verdict, and use it once.
An analyst’s choices (“keep the feature if it looks predictive”) are thresholds, which one record can flip, so analysts are rarely stable. A later chapter reuses one holdout set safely for many adaptive questions with a randomized form of stability.

Example 7.9 The script builds a holdout set of \(n = 1{,}000\) records with \(d\) random \(\pm1\) features and a random label independent of them all, so no rule beats an accuracy of \(\frac12\) on new data. An analyst measures how often each feature agrees with the label, which is \(d\) questions fixed in advance, An agreement rate of a feature independent of the label is an average of \(n\) fair coin flips, with standard deviation \(\sqrt{1/(4n)} = 0.0158\), and the analyst keeps the features more than that far from \(\frac12\). The kept features then vote. A feature that agreed less than half the time votes the opposite of its value, and a tie counts as \(+1\). Then the analyst asks one question chosen after looking: the vote’s accuracy on the same holdout set (Table 7.6, 100 repetitions).

text:

Bousquet & Elisseeff, “Stability and Generalization” (JMLR 2002): defines uniform and weaker stability notions; Theorem 12 is the high-probability bound.
Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning (2014), ch. 13: the clearest textbook treatment; Theorem 13.2 is Equation 7.6 and Corollary 13.6 the regularized-ERM bound. Chapter 14 covers SGD convergence.
Hardt, Recht & Singer, “Train Faster, Generalize Better: Stability of Stochastic Gradient Descent” (ICML 2016): SGD stability for convex (Theorem 3.8), strongly convex and non-convex losses.
Feldman & Vondrák, “Generalization Bounds for Uniformly Stable Algorithms” (NeurIPS 2018) and “High Probability Generalization Bounds for Uniformly Stable Algorithms with Nearly Optimal Rate” (COLT 2019): the improved high-probability bounds.
Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy, “Sharper Bounds for Uniformly Stable Algorithms” (COLT 2020): removes a log factor from the 2019 bound.

Cover & Hart, “Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification” (IEEE Trans. Information Theory 1967): the 1-NN limit.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.1 Distinguishers and advantage
Some computations must hide something, such as a key, a message, or a value split among several holders. What does it mean that an observer with limited computing power learns nothing it was not supposed to learn? This chapter gives cryptography’s answer as mathematics, with toy constructions you can run.
One idea organizes the answer: security is a game. A challenger flips a fair coin to pick one of two worlds, runs a procedure in that world, and shows the result to an adversary, who guesses the world. An adversary that learns nothing is right half the time, and its advantage measures how much better it does. A scheme is secure when every efficient adversary’s advantage is tiny. Proofs walk from one world to the other through intermediate worlds called hybrids, each differing from the next in one detail, and add up the advantage gained at each step.
Two examples run through the chapter. The first is a coin with heads probability 0.51, to be told apart from a fair coin. One flip gives an advantage of at most 0.01, and 10,000 flips give 0.683, far below the 1 that adding 0.01 per flip, as the hybrid argument does, would suggest. The second is the 128-bit size of keys and cipher blocks used in practice. Testing \(10^{18}\) keys a second for a year finds a 128-bit key with probability \(9.3\times10^{-14}\), yet a cipher that encrypts 128-bit blocks loses its security guarantee after about \(2^{64}\) blocks. Table 8.1 lists the symbols, with \(Q\) and \(\nu\) for the number of queries an adversary makes and its advantage, which cryptography texts call \(q\) and \(\varepsilon\).
Every definition in this chapter compares two worlds, so you first need a score for an observer who tries to tell them apart. This section defines that score and shows that it measures the same thing as winning a guessing game.
The coin in the game is fair, so an adversary with nothing to go on wins half the time whatever it answers. The next lemma turns win rates into advantages and back.
Write \(\mathrm{TV}(P_0, P_1)\) for the total variation (TV) distance, the sum, over the outcomes that \(P_1\) makes likelier than \(P_0\) does, of the extra probability \(P_1\) gives them. Divergences shows that the best distinguisher, which says 1 exactly on those outcomes, wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(P_0, P_1)\). Since an advantage \(\nu\) gives the win probability \(\frac12 + \frac\nu2\) by Lemma 8.1, no advantage exceeds the TV distance, however much time the distinguisher uses: \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathcal A}(P_0, P_1) \le \mathrm{TV}(P_0, P_1). \tag{8.4}\] Two worlds at TV distance 0 give perfect security, and at a small one statistical security. Cryptography’s main business is the third case, where the TV distance is large but no efficient distinguisher can exploit it.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
Definition 8.1 (Distinguisher and advantage) A distinguisher \(\mathcal A\) is any procedure, efficient or not, that receives one sample and outputs a bit. Its advantage in telling a distribution \(P_0\) from a distribution \(P_1\) is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathcal A}(P_0, P_1) = \big|\Pr[\mathcal A(P_1) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(P_0) = 1]\big|, \tag{8.1}\] where \(\Pr[\mathcal A(P_1) = 1]\) is the probability that \(\mathcal A\) outputs 1 on a sample from \(P_1\). In the distinguishing game, a challenger flips a fair bit \(b\) and gives \(\mathcal A\) a sample from \(P_b\), and \(\mathcal A\) wins if its guess \(b'\) equals \(b\).



Lemma 8.1 (Winning and advantage) For any distinguisher \(\mathcal A\) in the distinguishing game, \[\Pr[b' = b] = \frac12 + \frac12\big(\Pr[\mathcal A(P_1) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(P_0) = 1]\big). \tag{8.2}\] So a distinguisher with advantage \(\nu\), flipped if needed as in step 3 below, yields one that wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac\nu2\).


Proof. 

Split the win by world. Each world has probability \(\frac12\), and \(\mathcal A\) wins in world 1 by saying 1 and in world 0 by saying 0, so \[\Pr[b' = b] = \tfrac12\Pr[\mathcal A(P_1) = 1] + \tfrac12\Pr[\mathcal A(P_0) = 0]. \tag{8.3}\]
Count only the outputs of 1. Saying 0 is the complement of saying 1, so replacing \(\Pr[\mathcal A(P_0) = 0]\) by \(1 - \Pr[\mathcal A(P_0) = 1]\) and collecting terms gives Equation 8.2.
Flip a losing distinguisher. If the bracket is negative, the distinguisher that outputs the opposite bit negates the bracket, keeps the advantage, and wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac\nu2\).




Example 8.1 Let \(P_0\) be a fair coin and \(P_1\) a coin with heads probability 0.6. The distinguisher outputs 1 on heads. Each row of Table 8.2 is one outcome, with probability \(\frac12\) for the challenger’s bit times the probability of the coin’s outcome.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.2 Negligible functions
A key of 40 bits can be found by trying every key, and a key of 256 bits cannot. So security says how fast the attacker’s success shrinks as a security parameter \(\lambda\), the key length in bits, grows. Calling a scheme secure first needs a notion of efficient attackers and of tiny success probabilities.

Definition 8.2 (Efficient adversaries and negligible functions) An adversary is probabilistic polynomial time (PPT) if it is a randomized algorithm whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in \(\lambda\). A function \(\mu\colon \mathbb N \to [0, 1]\) is negligible if, for every exponent \(c\), it eventually falls below \(\lambda^{-c}\) and stays there: \[\forall c > 0\ \ \exists \lambda_0\ \ \forall \lambda \ge \lambda_0:\quad \mu(\lambda) < \lambda^{-c}. \tag{8.5}\] A scheme is secure if every PPT adversary has negligible advantage in its security game.

An efficient adversary can repeat its attack polynomially many times, which by the union bound of Concentration inequalities multiplies its success by at most that polynomial. So “tiny” must stay tiny after multiplication by any polynomial, and the next proposition says that it does.

Proposition 8.1 (Negligible functions survive polynomial repetition) If \(\mu\) is negligible and \(\mathrm{poly}\) is a polynomial, then \(\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\mu(\lambda)\) is negligible. The sum of two negligible functions is negligible.


Proof. 

Bound the polynomial by a power. A polynomial of degree \(c' - 1\) is eventually below \(\lambda^{c'}\), so \(\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \le \lambda^{c'}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda_1\).
Ask \(\mu\) for a steeper decay. Fix any \(c > 0\). Applying Equation 8.5 with the exponent \(c + c'\) gives \(\mu(\lambda) < \lambda^{-(c+c')}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda_2\).
Multiply the two bounds. For \(\lambda \ge \max(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)\), \[\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\mu(\lambda) < \lambda^{c'}\lambda^{-(c+c')} = \lambda^{-c}, \tag{8.6}\] and since \(c\) was arbitrary, the product is negligible.
Handle a sum. With the exponent \(c + 1\), each of two negligible functions is eventually below \(\lambda^{-(c+1)}\), so their sum is below \(2\lambda^{-(c+1)}\), which is at most \(\lambda^{-c}\) once \(\lambda \ge 2\).


Brute force, trying \(t\) of the \(2^\lambda\) keys, succeeds with probability \(t/2^\lambda\), negligible for polynomial \(t\) but never zero. In logarithms, \(\mu\) is negligible when \(-\log_2\mu(\lambda)\) outgrows every multiple \(c\log_2\lambda\). So \(2^{-\lambda}\), \(\lambda^{-\log_2\lambda}\) and \(2^{-\sqrt\lambda}\) are negligible, but \(\lambda^{-10}\), with \(-\log_2\mu = 10\log_2\lambda\), is never below \(\lambda^{-11}\).

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.3 Indistinguishability and the hybrid argument
Most security definitions say that two things look the same, such as a ciphertext and random bits. This section makes that precise and answers the first question every proof meets: if one sample cannot be told apart, can many?

Definition 8.3 (Computational indistinguishability) Two families of distributions \(P_0 = \{P_{0,\lambda}\}\) and \(P_1 = \{P_{1,\lambda}\}\), one distribution for each \(\lambda\), are computationally indistinguishable, written \(P_0 \approx_c P_1\), if every PPT distinguisher has negligible advantage \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathcal A}(P_{0,\lambda}, P_{1,\lambda})\). If their TV distance is negligible they are statistically indistinguishable, written \(\approx_s\), and if they are equal they are perfectly indistinguishable, written \(\equiv\).

By Equation 8.4, \(\equiv\) implies \(\approx_s\), which implies \(\approx_c\). A hybrid argument needs to know how advantages combine along a chain of worlds, and the next lemma says they add at most.

Lemma 8.2 (Advantages add along a chain) For any distributions \(H_0, H_1, \dots, H_Q\) and any distinguisher \(\mathcal A\), \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathcal A}(H_0, H_Q) \le \sum_{i=1}^Q \mathrm{Adv}_{\mathcal A}(H_{i-1}, H_i). \tag{8.7}\]


Proof. 

Telescope. In the sum over \(i\) of \(\Pr[\mathcal A(H_{i-1}) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(H_i) = 1]\), each intermediate probability appears once with each sign, so the sum is \(\Pr[\mathcal A(H_0) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(H_Q) = 1]\).
Take absolute values. The absolute value of a sum is at most the sum of the absolute values.


The hybrid lemma walks from \(Q\) samples of \(P_0\) to \(Q\) samples of \(P_1\) by swapping one sample at a time. If the two ends are \(\nu\) apart, the \(Q\) steps share that \(\nu\), so a step is worth \(\nu/Q\) on average, and since a step changes one sample, it is a one-sample problem. Write \(P^{\otimes Q}\) for \(Q\) independent samples from \(P\).

Theorem 8.1 (The hybrid lemma) Let \(P_0 \approx_c P_1\) be families that an efficient algorithm can sample from, and let \(Q = Q(\lambda)\) be a polynomial. Then \(P_0^{\otimes Q} \approx_c P_1^{\otimes Q}\). Quantitatively, a distinguisher with advantage \(\nu\) on \(Q\) samples yields a distinguisher with advantage \(\nu/Q\) on one sample, with about the same running time.


Proof. The proof builds a one-sample distinguisher that lands at a random link of a chain of hybrids, computes its advantage by telescoping, and concludes by contradiction.

Define the hybrids. Let \(H_i\) be \(Q\) independent entries, the first \(i\) from \(P_1\) and the rest from \(P_0\), so \(H_0 = P_0^{\otimes Q}\) and \(H_Q = P_1^{\otimes Q}\).
Build a one-sample distinguisher. On input \(w\), let \(\mathcal B\) pick a position \(i\) uniformly from \(\{1, \dots, Q\}\), draw the other entries itself as in \(H_i\), which needs efficient sampling, put \(w\) in position \(i\), and run \(\mathcal A\). The tuple is distributed as \(H_{i-1}\) if \(w\) comes from \(P_0\), and as \(H_i\) if it comes from \(P_1\).
Average over the position. Each \(i\) has probability \(\frac1Q\), so \[\Pr[\mathcal B(P_0) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal B(P_1) = 1] = \frac1Q\sum_{i=1}^Q\big(\Pr[\mathcal A(H_{i-1}) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(H_i) = 1]\big). \tag{8.8}\]
Telescope. As in the proof of Lemma 8.2, the sum equals \(\Pr[\mathcal A(H_0) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(H_Q) = 1]\), so \(\mathcal B\) has advantage \(\nu/Q\).
Conclude by contradiction. If \(\nu\) were not negligible, there would be a \(c\) with \(\nu(\lambda) \ge \lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). With \(Q(\lambda) \le \lambda^{c'}\), the efficient \(\mathcal B\) would then have advantage at least \(\lambda^{-(c+c')}\) for those \(\lambda\), which contradicts \(P_0 \approx_c P_1\).



Example 8.3 Let \(P_0\) be a fair coin and \(P_1\) the running example’s coin, with heads probability \(\frac12 + \xi\). One flip gives an advantage of at most \(\xi\), so the hybrid lemma, turned around, allows at most \(Q\xi\) from \(Q\) flips. The factor \(Q\) is pessimistic, because the best attacker pools its flips into one count of heads. Table 8.4 and Figure 8.2 compare that bound with the exact best advantage and with majority vote, which outputs 1 when more than half the flips are heads.

Majority vote’s 0.082, above the best possible 0.080, is simulation noise. Both counts of heads have a standard deviation of about \(\sqrt Q/2\), and their means differ by \(Q\xi\), so they are close to bell curves whose centres are \(2\xi\sqrt Q\) standard deviations apart. Two normal curves whose centres are \(\delta\) standard deviations apart have TV distance \(2\Phi(\delta/2) - 1\), with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, so the best advantage is about \[2\Phi(\xi\sqrt Q) - 1, \tag{8.9}\] which grows like \(\xi\sqrt Q\) rather than \(\xi Q\). Majority vote stalls near \(\frac12\), because its threshold sits at the centre of the fair count’s curve, so on fair flips it still says 1 about half the time.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.4 Concrete security
Real systems fix \(\lambda\), and a statement for all large enough \(\lambda\) does not say whether 128 is large enough. Concrete security replaces “efficient” and “negligible” by explicit numbers, so that a proof says how much a key can withstand.

Definition 8.4 (Concrete security and reductions) A primitive is \((t, Q, 
u)\)-secure if every adversary that runs in time at most \(t\) and makes at most \(Q\) queries to its oracles, the procedures the game lets it call, has advantage at most \(
u\). It has \(\kappa\)-bit security if, roughly, every adversary with time \(t\) has advantage at most \(t/2^\kappa\), as for brute force over \(\kappa\)-bit keys. A reduction turns an adversary that breaks a scheme with \((t, Q, 
u)\) into one that breaks a primitive the scheme is built from with \((t', Q', 
u')\), and it is tight when \(
u' \approx 
u\).

So a reduction says that a hard primitive makes a hard scheme, and a loose one costs bits. If an attack of advantage \(
u\) on the scheme gives only \(
u/2^{20}\) on a 128-bit primitive, the scheme keeps only \(128 - 20 = 108\) bits.

Example 8.4 An exascale machine that tests \(10^{18}\) keys per second for a year of about \(3.16	imes10^7\) seconds tries \(2^{84.7}\) keys. Against a 128-bit key it succeeds with probability \(2^{84.7 - 128} = 9.3	imes10^{-14}\), and trying all \(2^{128}\) keys would take \(1.08	imes10^{13}\) years.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Pseudorandom generators and functions
The schemes later in this chapter need many random-looking values from one short random key, because truly random bits are expensive to share. This section defines the two objects that supply them, generators and functions, and builds the second from the first.

Definition 8.5 (Pseudorandom generator) Write \(U_\ell\) for the uniform distribution on \(\ell\)-bit strings. An efficient deterministic map \(G\) from \(\lambda\)-bit strings to \(\ell(\lambda)\)-bit strings, with \(\ell(\lambda) > \lambda\), is a pseudorandom generator (PRG) if \[G(U_\lambda) \approx_c U_{\ell(\lambda)}. \tag{8.10}\]

Pseudorandomness is a statement about efficient distinguishers only, because the outputs of \(G\) form a tiny subset of all strings.

Proposition 8.2 (A pseudorandom generator is never statistically secure) For every \(G\) as in Definition 8.5, \(\mathrm{TV}(G(U_\lambda), U_\ell) \ge \frac12\).


Proof. 

An exhaustive distinguisher. Let \(\mathcal A\) output 1 exactly when its input equals \(G(u)\) for some seed \(u\). On \(G(U_\lambda)\) it always outputs 1.
Few strings are outputs. At most \(2^\lambda\) of the \(2^\ell\) strings are outputs, so on \(U_\ell\), \(\mathcal A\) outputs 1 with probability at most \(2^{\lambda - \ell} \le \frac12\).
Bound the distance. So \(\mathcal A\) has advantage at least \(\frac12\), and Equation 8.4 gives the bound.


This distinguisher loops over \(2^\lambda\) seeds, so it is not efficient,. A random function from a set \(\mathcal X\) to a set \(\mathcal Y\) gives each input its own independent, uniform output. A pseudorandom function must look like one even to an adversary who chooses its questions.

Definition 8.6 (Pseudorandom function) A keyed function \(F_K\colon \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y\), with a \(\lambda\)-bit key \(K\), is a pseudorandom function (PRF) if every PPT adversary has negligible advantage in this game. The challenger flips \(b\), and its oracle is \(F_K\) for a uniform key \(K\) if \(b = 0\) and a random function if \(b = 1\). The adversary sends \(Q\) queries, each of which may depend on earlier answers, and guesses \(b\).

A random function on 128-bit inputs is a table of \(2^{128}\) entries, which nobody can store, and a PRF gives the same appearance from a 128-bit key. The toy code uses the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC), a keyed hash that practice treats as a PRF.

8.5.1 The GGM tree
A PRF can be built from any PRG that doubles its input’s length. The construction of Goldreich, Goldwasser & Micali (1986), the GGM tree, uses the generator to grow a binary tree of keys, picking the left or right half of the output by the next bit of the input.

Theorem 8.2 (The GGM tree is a pseudorandom function) Let \(G\) map \(\lambda\) bits to \(2\lambda\) bits, with output halves \(G_0(u)\) and \(G_1(u)\). For an input \(x = x_1\cdots x_n\), start at the root \(K\), replace the current node \(v\) by \(G_{x_i}(v)\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\), and let \(F_K(x)\) be the leaf reached. With advantages in the games of Definition 8.6 and Definition 8.5 written \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}\) and \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\), for every adversary \(\mathcal A\) making \(Q\) queries there is a PRG adversary \(\mathcal B\) with about the same running time such that \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal A) \le nQ\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}(\mathcal B). \tag{8.11}\]


Goldreich (2001, §3.6) proves it, and Appendix Section I.1 derives it step by step. It makes the tree random one level at a time, and each of the \(n\) levels costs at most \(Q\) times the PRG advantage, because the queries reach at most \(Q\) nodes per level, which Theorem 8.1 swaps one at a time.

Example 8.5 On the 2-bit input \(10\), the tree computes \(G_1(K)\) and then outputs the left half of \(G\) applied to that node, \(G_0(G_1(K))\). For 128-bit inputs, one evaluation walks 128 levels and costs 128 generator calls.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 The birthday bound
The proofs of the next two sections fail only if two random values coincide, such as a repeated nonce, a random value meant to be used once, so you need the probability of a coincidence. Among \(Q\) values there are about \(Q^2/2\) pairs, and each coincides with probability \(1/N\), so collisions become likely after about \(\sqrt N\) draws rather than \(N\).

Theorem 8.3 (The birthday bound) Draw \(Q\) values independently and uniformly from a set of size \(N\). Then \[1 - e^{-Q(Q-1)/(2N)} \;\le\; \Pr[\text{collision}] \;\le\; \frac{Q(Q-1)}{2N} \le \frac{Q^2}{2N}, \tag{8.12}\] and the collision probability reaches \(\frac12\) after about \(1.18\sqrt N\) draws.


Proof. The upper bound counts pairs. The lower bound bounds the exact probability of no collision by an exponential.

Upper bound. Each of the \(Q(Q-1)/2\) pairs coincides with probability \(1/N\), so the union bound gives the upper bound.
Exact value. Draw the values one at a time. If the first \(i\) are distinct, the next avoids them with probability \(1 - i/N\), so \[\Pr[\text{no collision}] = \prod_{i=0}^{Q-1}\Big(1 - \frac iN\Big). \tag{8.13}\]
Lower bound. The inequality \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\) of Concentration inequalities bounds each factor, and the exponents add to \(Q(Q-1)/(2N)\). Subtracting from 1 gives the lower bound.
The 50% point. Setting the lower bound to \(\frac12\), with \(Q(Q-1) \approx Q^2\), gives \(Q^2/(2N) = \ln 2\), so \(Q \approx \sqrt{2N\ln 2} \approx 1.18\sqrt N\).


The two bounds are close, because \(1 - e^{-x}\) bends downwards and so lies above its chord \((1 - 1/e)x\) on \([0, 1]\), which makes the lower bound at least \(1 - 1/e\) times the upper one. With \(N = 2^{128}\), random 128-bit values start to collide after about \(2^{64}\) draws.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
section: 8.7 Block ciphers and the switching lemma
text:
8.7 Block ciphers and the switching lemma
A block cipher such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a keyed permutation, which never gives two inputs the same output, while most proofs assume a PRF. This section bridges the gap and turns the birthday bound into a limit on how much data one key may encrypt. A random function sometimes repeats an output and a random permutation never does, so an adversary can tell them apart only about as often as \(Q\) random values collide.

Definition 8.7 (Pseudorandom permutation) A keyed permutation of \(\mathcal X\) is a pseudorandom permutation (PRP) if it satisfies Definition 8.6 with the random function replaced by a uniformly random permutation of \(\mathcal X\).


Theorem 8.4 (The switching lemma) Let \(\mathcal A\) make \(Q\) queries, and write \(\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}}\) and \(\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RP}}\) for \(\mathcal A\) run with a random function and with a random permutation of \(\mathcal X\) as its oracle. Then \[\big|\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RP}} = 1]\big| \le \frac{Q(Q-1)}{2|\mathcal X|} \le \frac{Q^2}{2|\mathcal X|}. \tag{8.14}\]


Proof. The plan is to run both oracles from one pre-drawn list of answers and show that they behave identically unless the list has a repeat.

Simplify the adversary. Assume the \(Q\) queries are distinct, since both oracles answer a repeated query the same way.
Pre-sample the function’s answers. Draw \(Y_1, \dots, Y_Q\) independently and uniformly from \(\mathcal X\) and answer the \(i\)-th query with \(Y_i\). On distinct queries this is exactly a random function.
Do the same for the permutation. A random permutation answers each new query with a value uniform over those not yet used, so it can be run from a uniform list of \(Q\) distinct values.
Compare the two. Let \(\mathrm{Col}\) be the event that the list of step 2 has a repeat. Every list is equally likely, so conditioning on no repeat gives a uniform list of distinct values, exactly the permutation’s. Hence \(\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1 \mid \text{no } \mathrm{Col}] = \Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RP}} = 1]\), which we call \(\rho\).
Bound the difference. Splitting on \(\mathrm{Col}\), and using step 4 for the case without a repeat, \[\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1] = \Pr[\mathrm{Col}]\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1 \mid \mathrm{Col}] + (1 - \Pr[\mathrm{Col}])\rho. \tag{8.15}\] Subtracting \(\rho\) from both sides gives \[\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1] - \rho = \Pr[\mathrm{Col}]\big(\Pr[\mathcal A^{\mathrm{RF}} = 1 \mid \mathrm{Col}] - \rho\big), \tag{8.16}\] and the bracket is a difference of probabilities, so the whole is at most \(\Pr[\mathrm{Col}]\) in absolute value.
Count the repeats. Equation 8.12 with \(N = |\mathcal X|\) bounds \(\Pr[\mathrm{Col}]\).


Since \(\mathrm{Col}\) depends only on the pre-drawn list, step 4 holds even when each query depends on earlier answers (Bellare & Rogaway 2006). The bound is tight, because the adversary that outputs 1 when two answers collide does so with probability \(\Pr[\mathrm{Col}]\) against a function and never against a permutation.

Corollary 8.1 (A pseudorandom permutation is a pseudorandom function) A PRP with advantage at most \(\nu\) against \(Q\)-query adversaries is a PRF with advantage at most \(\nu + Q^2/(2|\mathcal X|)\).


Proof. Go from \(F_K\) to a random permutation, at cost at most \(\nu\) by assumption, and then to a random function, at cost at most \(Q^2/(2|\mathcal X|)\) by Theorem 8.4. By Lemma 8.2 the total is at most the sum.


Example 8.7 For a cipher on 128-bit blocks, the extra term \(Q^2/(2|\mathcal X|)\) of Corollary 8.1 after \(Q = 2^k\) blocks is \(Q^2/2^{129} = 2^{2k - 129}\). After \(2^{32}\) blocks of 16 bytes, which is 64 GiB, it is at most \(2^{-65}\), and after \(2^{48}\) blocks, about 4 PiB, at most \(2^{-33}\). At \(2^{64}\) blocks it reaches \(\frac12\), so keys must be changed long before.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
section: 8.8 Perfect secrecy and the one-time pad
text:
8.8 Perfect secrecy and the one-time pad
Encryption should hide the message. The strongest possible answer is a ciphertext that tells even an unbounded adversary nothing, and Shannon (1949) showed what it costs: a key as long as the data.

Definition 8.8 (Perfect secrecy) An encryption scheme turns a message \(m\) into a ciphertext \(\mathrm{Enc}_K(m)\) under a random key \(K\), and back. It has perfect secrecy if, for all messages \(m, m'\) and ciphertexts \(y\), \[\Pr[\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = y] = \Pr[\mathrm{Enc}_K(m') = y]. \tag{8.17}\]

Equivalently, by Bayes’ rule, seeing the ciphertext does not change the probability of any message, for any prior on messages that is independent of the key. The proof for the one-time pad rests on one counting fact, which secret sharing and learning with errors use again.

Lemma 8.3 (A bijection maps uniform to uniform) If \(U\) is uniform on a finite set \(S\) and \(f\colon S \to S\) is a bijection, then \(f(U)\) is uniform on \(S\).


Proof. Each \(t \in S\) comes from exactly one element, \(f^{-1}(t)\), so \(\Pr[f(U) = t] = \Pr[U = f^{-1}(t)] = 1/|S|\).


Theorem 8.5 (The one-time pad has perfect secrecy) For \(n\)-bit messages, let \(K\) be uniform on \(n\)-bit strings and \(\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = m \oplus K\), where \(\oplus\) is bitwise exclusive or (XOR). Then every ciphertext has probability \(2^{-n}\) for every message, so the scheme has perfect secrecy.


Proof. 

The pad is a bijection. For fixed \(m\), the map \(k \mapsto m \oplus k\) is its own inverse, since \(m \oplus m = 0\).
Apply the lemma. By Lemma 8.3, \(m \oplus K\) is uniform whatever \(m\) is.


No scheme can do better on key length, so a 128-bit message needs a fresh 128-bit key.

Proposition 8.3 (Perfect secrecy needs as many keys as messages) If a scheme with key set \(\mathcal K\) and message set \(\mathcal M\) has perfect secrecy and correct decryption, then \(|\mathcal K| \ge |\mathcal M|\).


Proof. 

Few messages reach one ciphertext. Fix a ciphertext \(y\) that occurs. Each key decrypts \(y\) to one message, so at most \(|\mathcal K|\) messages can produce \(y\).
Fewer keys break secrecy. If \(|\mathcal K| < |\mathcal M|\), some message never produces \(y\) while another does, so their ciphertext distributions differ.


The pad must also never be reused, because XOR-ing two ciphertexts under one pad cancels it and reveals \(m_1 \oplus m_2\). English text is so redundant that both messages can be pulled apart from \(m_1 \oplus m_2\).

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Chosen-plaintext security
Practical encryption accepts a negligible advantage in exchange for a short key. This section gives the definition used in practice, shows that it forces encryption to be randomized, and proves a randomized scheme secure. In the game, the adversary picks two messages and must say which one a ciphertext encrypts, which Goldwasser & Micali (1984) showed is equivalent to their semantic security, under which a ciphertext helps compute nothing about the message.

Definition 8.9 (Indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack) A scheme is indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack (CPA), or IND-CPA secure, if every PPT adversary has negligible advantage in this game. The challenger draws a key \(K\) and a fair bit \(b\). The adversary may ask for encryptions of messages of its choice at any time. It submits two messages \(m_0\) and \(m_1\) of equal length, receives the challenge \(y^* = \mathrm{Enc}_K(m_b)\), and outputs a guess \(b'\).

Taking \(b = 0\) and \(b = 1\) as the two worlds, Lemma 8.1 makes this advantage \(2|\Pr[b' = b] - \frac12|\). The messages have equal length because ciphertexts usually reveal lengths. If encryption always maps a message to the same ciphertext, the adversary can encrypt \(m_0\) itself and compare.

Proposition 8.4 (Deterministic encryption is never IND-CPA secure) If \(\mathrm{Enc}_K\) is a deterministic function of the message and decryption is correct, some adversary that makes one encryption query has advantage 1.


Proof. 

The attack. Ask for \(y_0 = \mathrm{Enc}_K(m_0)\), submit \(m_0\) and \(m_1\), and output 0 if \(y^* = y_0\) and 1 otherwise.
World 0. If \(b = 0\), determinism gives \(y^* = y_0\), so the guess is 0.
World 1. If \(b = 1\), correct decryption of the distinct messages forces \(\mathrm{Enc}_K(m_1) \ne \mathrm{Enc}_K(m_0)\), so the guess is 1.


The fix is a fresh pad for every encryption. Draw a uniform \(r\) from a set \(\mathcal R\), use \(F_K(r)\) as a one-time pad, and send \(r\) along. The scheme fails only if the PRF is distinguishable from random or the challenge reuses a seen \(r\), and the bound adds the two.

Theorem 8.6 (A randomized scheme from a PRF) Let \(\mathrm{Enc}_K(m) = (r,\ m \oplus F_K(r))\) with \(r\) uniform on \(\mathcal R\). For every adversary \(\mathcal A\) making \(Q\) encryption queries there is a PRF adversary \(\mathcal B\) with about the same running time such that \[\Pr[\mathcal A \text{ wins}] \le \frac12 + \mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal B) + \frac{Q}{2|\mathcal R|}. \tag{8.18}\]


Proof. The proof replaces the PRF by a random function at the cost of the PRF advantage, and then shows that the challenge is a one-time pad unless one bad event happens.

Two hybrids. Hybrid 0 is the real game, and hybrid 1 replaces \(F_K\) by a random function \(f\).
The step costs the PRF advantage. \(\mathcal B\) runs the game for \(\mathcal A\) with its own oracle in place of \(F_K\) and outputs 1 when \(\mathcal A\) wins. With oracle \(F_K\) it simulates hybrid 0, and with \(f\) hybrid 1, so the win probabilities differ by at most \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal B)\).
The bad event. Let \(E\) be the event that the challenge’s \(r^*\) equals one of the \(Q\) values \(r_i\) that the encryption oracle drew. Each equals it with probability \(1/|\mathcal R|\), so the union bound gives \(\Pr[E] \le Q/|\mathcal R|\).
Without it, a one-time pad. Then \(f(r^*)\) is uniform and independent of everything else \(\mathcal A\) sees, so by Lemma 8.3 the challenge is uniform whatever \(b\) is, and \(\mathcal A\) wins with probability \(\frac12\).
Combine. Bounding the win probability by 1 when \(E\) happens, \[\Pr[\text{win in hybrid 1}] \le \tfrac12\Pr[\text{not } E] + \Pr[E] = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\Pr[E] \le \tfrac12 + \frac{Q}{2|\mathcal R|}, \tag{8.19}\] and adding the loss of step 2 gives the bound.


By Lemma 8.1, in advantage units the bound is \(2\,\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} + Q/|\mathcal R|\), and the term \(Q/|\mathcal R|\) is real, not an artefact of the proof.

Example 8.9 Against the deterministic scheme \(m \oplus F_K(0)\), the attack of Proposition 8.4 has measured advantage 1.000 over 20,000 games for each \(b\). Against the randomized scheme with 8-bit nonces, \(|\mathcal R| = 256\), the adversary asks for \(Q = 16\) encryptions of \(m_0\), and XOR-ing each reply with \(m_0\) reveals its pad \(F_K(r_i)\). If \(r^*\) matches one of those nonces \(r_i\), it reads the challenge and outputs the true \(b\), and otherwise it outputs 1. So it errs only when \(b = 0\) and there is no match, and its advantage is \(1 - (1 - \Pr[E]) = \Pr[E]\). Since \(r^*\) misses each nonce with probability \(255/256\), \[\Pr[E] = 1 - (255/256)^{16} = 0.0607. \tag{8.20}\] The simulation measures 0.0605, and the bound \(Q/|\mathcal R|\) is 0.0625. With 128-bit nonces the same attack has advantage below \(16/2^{128} = 2^{-124}\).

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.10 The simulation paradigm
Encryption hides everything, but many procedures must reveal something, such as a participant’s own share of a secret, and nothing else. The simulation paradigm defines “nothing else” indirectly: whatever the participant sees, it could have produced by itself from what it is allowed to know (Lindell 2017).

Definition 8.10 (Revealing nothing beyond a leakage) A randomized procedure run on the inputs \(x\) of all participants gives one participant a view \(\mathrm{View}(x)\), everything it sees during the run. The participant is allowed to learn a function \(L(x)\), its leakage. The procedure reveals nothing beyond \(L\) if an efficient simulator \(S\) given only \(L(x)\) reproduces the view’s distribution: \[S(L(x)) \equiv \mathrm{View}(x) \quad\text{for every input } x. \tag{8.21}\] Replacing \(\equiv\) by \(\approx_s\) or \(\approx_c\) gives statistical or computational security.

The definition captures “nothing else” because anything computed from the view has the same distribution when computed from the simulator’s output, which uses \(L(x)\) alone. The simplest procedure it covers splits a number into random pieces that add up to it, in \(\mathbb Z_p\), the integers \(\{0, \dots, p - 1\}\) with arithmetic mod \(p\).

Definition 8.11 (Additive secret sharing) To share a secret \(x \in \mathbb Z_p\) among \(h\) holders, draw the shares \(z_1, \dots, z_{h-1}\) independently and uniformly from \(\mathbb Z_p\), and set \[z_h = x - (z_1 + \dots + z_{h-1}) \bmod p. \tag{8.22}\]

Any \(h - 1\) shares should look uniform whatever the secret is, because the missing share is what ties them to \(x\).

Theorem 8.7 (Any h − 1 shares reveal nothing) For every secret \(x\) and every coalition of \(h - 1\) holders, the coalition’s shares are independent and uniform on \(\mathbb Z_p^{h-1}\). So a simulator that outputs \(h - 1\) uniform elements of \(\mathbb Z_p\), with no leakage, satisfies Equation 8.21 with \(\equiv\).


Proof. 

The randomness is uniform. Each of the \(p^{h-1}\) tuples \((z_1, \dots, z_{h-1})\) has probability \(p^{-(h-1)}\).
The coalition’s shares determine the randomness. Fix \(x\) and a coalition that misses holder \(j\). If \(j = h\), the coalition holds \(z_1, \dots, z_{h-1}\) themselves. If \(j < h\), it holds \(z_h\) and every other \(z_i\), and the definition of \(z_h\) gives back \(z_j = x - z_h - \sum_{i \ne j, h} z_i\).
So the map is a bijection. The map from the randomness to the coalition’s shares can be undone, so by Lemma 8.3 every tuple of shares has probability \(p^{-(h-1)}\) for every \(x\).



Example 8.10 Table 8.7 makes step 3 concrete for \(h = 2\) and \(p = 5\), and the script checks the uniformity for \(h = 3\) by listing every case.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.11 Learning with errors
Every primitive so far is defined by what it hides rather than by how. Learning with errors (LWE), introduced by Regev (2005), is a specific hard problem with no known efficient attack even by a quantum computer, and encryption built on it lets you add ciphertexts. It is linear algebra with noise.

Definition 8.12 (Learning with errors) Fix a dimension \(d\), a modulus \(p\) and an error distribution \(\chi\) on small integers. Draw a secret \(s\) uniformly from \(\mathbb Z_p^d\). An LWE sample is a uniform \(a \in \mathbb Z_p^d\) together with the inner product \(\langle a, s\rangle\) plus an error \(e\) drawn from \(\chi\): \[\big(a,\ \langle a, s\rangle + e \bmod p\big). \tag{8.23}\] Search LWE asks for \(s\) from many samples. Decision LWE asks whether given pairs are LWE samples or uniform pairs.

Solving search solves decision, since you can check whether the residuals \(b - \langle a, s\rangle\) of a candidate \(s\) are small. Regev shows the converse for a prime \(p\) polynomial in \(d\), and Appendix Section I.2 derives it step by step. For suitably wide errors drawn from a normal distribution rounded to integers, Regev (2009) proves LWE as hard as the hardest instances of well-studied geometric problems on lattices, regular grids of points in \(\mathbb R^d\). These results are cited, not proved here, and they do not cover the uniform errors used in the toy scheme below.

Example 8.11 Without noise, LWE is a linear system that Gaussian elimination solves. Take \(d = 2\), \(p = 7\), \(s = (3, 5)\), \(a_1 = (1, 2)\) and \(a_2 = (3, 1)\), so the right-hand sides are \(13 \equiv 6\) and \(14 \equiv 0\). The second equation gives \(s_2 = -3s_1 \equiv 4s_1\), and the first then gives \(s_1 + 8s_1 = 9s_1 \equiv 2s_1 = 6\), so \(s_1 = 3\) and \(s_2 = 12 \equiv 5\). With the error \((1, 0)\) both right-hand sides are 0, and the same steps give \((0, 0)\), completely wrong, because elimination multiplies the error by the inverse matrix, which mod 7 sends \((1, 0)\) to \((4, 2)\), and \((3, 5) + (4, 2) \equiv (0, 0)\). At \(d = 16\) and \(p = 4096\) with 32 samples, the script’s elimination recovers all 16 coordinates of \(s\) without noise, and 0 with errors in \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\).

title: 8  Cryptography basics
section: 8.12 Regev encryption and its noise budget
text:
8.12 Regev encryption and its noise budget
The hardness of LWE becomes encryption once a message bit hides in a sample. Picture \(\mathbb Z_p\) as a clock, and move the sample’s second component halfway round if the bit is 1. Whoever knows \(s\) subtracts \(\langle a, s\rangle\) and sees whether the rest is near 0 or near halfway. This section proves the scheme correct and secure, and asks how many ciphertexts can be added.

Definition 8.13 (Regev’s bit encryption) Take \(p\) even and a key \(s \in \mathbb Z_p^d\). To encrypt a bit \(m\), draw a fresh uniform \(a\) and an error \(e\) from \(\chi\), and output \[\mathrm{Enc}_s(m) = \big(a,\ w = \langle a, s\rangle + e + m\cdot\tfrac p2 \bmod p\big). \tag{8.24}\] To decrypt, compute \(v = w - \langle a, s\rangle \bmod p\) and output 1 if \(p/4 < v < 3p/4\).


Proposition 8.5 (Correctness) Decryption returns \(m\) whenever \(|e| < p/4\).


Proof. 

Remove the inner product. By the definition of \(w\), \(v = e + m\frac p2 \bmod p\).
A 0 stays near 0. If \(m = 0\), then \(v \equiv e\) lies in \([0, p/4)\) or, for negative \(e\), in \((3p/4, p)\), and the output is 0.
A 1 stays near halfway. If \(m = 1\), then \(v = e + p/2\) lies in \((p/4, 3p/4)\), and the output is 1.


Without \(s\), an LWE sample looks uniform, so the bit is added to something that looks uniform, as in a one-time pad.

Proposition 8.6 (Security under decision LWE) If an IND-CPA adversary \(\mathcal A\) against Regev’s scheme has advantage \(\nu\), there is a decision-LWE distinguisher \(\mathcal B\) with about the same running time and advantage \(\nu/2\).


Proof. 

The distinguisher. \(\mathcal B\) runs the IND-CPA game for \(\mathcal A\), builds each ciphertext from one of its given pairs by adding \(m\cdot\frac p2\) to the second component, and outputs 1 when \(\mathcal A\) wins.
On LWE samples. The ciphertexts are real, so by Lemma 8.1 \(\mathcal B\) outputs 1 with probability \(\frac12 + \frac\nu2\).
On uniform pairs. Adding a fixed value is a bijection of \(\mathbb Z_p\), so by Lemma 8.3 each second component is uniform whatever \(m\) is, and \(\mathcal A\) wins with probability \(\frac12\). The difference is \(\frac\nu2\).


A ciphertext is linear in \(a\), the error and the encoded bit, so adding ciphertexts adds all three, and two half-turns make a full turn.

Proposition 8.7 (Adding ciphertexts) The componentwise sum of encryptions of \(m_1, \dots, m_k\) under one key is an encryption of \(m_1 \oplus \dots \oplus m_k\) with error \(e_1 + \dots + e_k\). If every \(|e_i| \le B\), it decrypts correctly whenever \[k < \frac{p}{4B}. \tag{8.25}\]


Proof. 

Linearity. By linearity of the inner product, \[\sum_i w_i - \Big\langle\sum_i a_i, s\Big\rangle = \sum_i e_i + \Big(\sum_i m_i\Big)\frac p2 \bmod p. \tag{8.26}\]
Only the parity survives. Because \(p\) is even, \(2\cdot\frac p2 \equiv 0\), so only \(m_1 \oplus \dots \oplus m_k\) remains in the last term.
Bound the error. By the triangle inequality the summed error is at most \(kB\) in absolute value, and by Proposition 8.5 \(kB < p/4\) suffices.


Equation 8.25 assumes that every error is as large as possible, with the same sign. Independent errors with mean zero mostly cancel, so \(k\) errors of standard deviation \(\sigma\) sum to a standard deviation of \(\sigma\sqrt k\). For \(\chi\) uniform on the \(2B + 1\) integers \(\{-B, \dots, B\}\) the variance is \(((2B+1)^2 - 1)/12 = B(B+1)/3\). By the central limit theorem, with \(Z\) a standard normal variable and the reduction mod \(p\) taken into \((-p/2, p/2]\), \[\Pr[\text{failure after } k \text{ additions}] \approx \Pr\Big[\big|Z\sqrt{kB(B+1)/3} \bmod p\big| > p/4\Big]. \tag{8.27}\]

Example 8.12 Take \(d = 3\), \(p = 4096\) and \(s = (5, 1000, 3000)\). Encrypting \(m = 1\) with \(a_1 = (17, 2, 1)\) and \(e_1 = -7\) gives \(\langle a_1, s\rangle = 5085 \equiv 989\) and \(w_1 = 989 - 7 + 2048 = 3030\), which decrypts to \(v = 2041\), near 2048, so to 1. Encrypting \(m = 1\) with \(a_2 = (1, 1, 1)\) and \(e_2 = 12\) gives \(\langle a_2, s\rangle = 4005\) and \(w_2 = 4005 + 12 + 2048 \equiv 1969\). The sum has \(a_1 + a_2 = (18, 3, 2)\), whose inner product with \(s\) is \(9090 \equiv 898\), and \(w_1 + w_2 \equiv 903\), so decryption finds \(v = 5 = e_1 + e_2\) and outputs \(0 = 1 \oplus 1\).
Table 8.8 and Figure 8.5 compare the worst case with the typical case for \(p = 4096\) and \(B = 32\), where Equation 8.25 guarantees \(k < 32\). The simulation adds \(k\) toy ciphertexts of random bits, with \(d = 4\), 20,000 times.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
Who this part is for
This part teaches you to break models before it teaches you to protect them. Every defence in the rest of the book is measured against an attack: a guarantee is only as meaningful as the strongest adversary it stops, and an evaluation is only as honest as the attack it runs. So you start here, with the adversaries, what they see, what they want, and how well the best of them can do.
You are expected to have read the Prerequisites, or to know their content. This part leans hardest on hypothesis testing (the Neyman–Pearson lemma, trade-off curves, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves read at a low false positive rate), on the total variation distance of Divergences, and on the link between stability and generalization. Information theory appears in the chapters on attribute inference, memorization and linkage. You should also be comfortable with logistic regression, gradients of a small neural network, and an n-gram language model at the level of writing them in NumPy.
Differential privacy, the defence most of the book is about, is introduced in the next part, and it is designed against exactly the games defined here. The only privacy definitions in this part are the syntactic ones of the last chapter, k-anonymity and its successors, and they appear as targets: the chapter shows what each one promises and the attack that breaks it.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
The common thread
Every attack in this part is the same object: a game in which a challenger trains or releases something that depends on a hidden secret, and an adversary guesses the secret from what the threat model lets it see. What changes from chapter to chapter is the secret: one bit of membership, a sensitive attribute, a memorized string, the whole dataset, a client’s input, a property of the population behind the data, or a person’s name. Table 1 lists them.



Table 1: The chapters of this part, the question each one answers, and the earlier chapters it uses.





Chapter
The question it answers
Builds on




Threat models and privacy games
What can an adversary see and do, and how is an attack stated and scored?
3, 4, 8


Membership inference

4, 7, 9


Attribute inference and model inversion
Does the model reveal a person’s sensitive attribute beyond what the population already does?
3–5, 9, 10


Property inference

1, 3, 4, 9, 10


Memorization and training-data extraction

4, 5, 7, 9, 10

6, 9


Linkage and re-identification

1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9


Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
What do k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness guarantee, and which attacks get past each?
1, 3, 5, 11, 15


Reconstruction attacks
How many accurate statistics does it take to rebuild a whole private dataset?
2, 5, 9






Two ideas run through all nine chapters. The first is that an attack is a hypothesis test. When the secret is one bit, the best attack is the likelihood-ratio test of the Neyman–Pearson lemma, its advantage (true positive rate (TPR) minus false positive rate (FPR)) is at most the total variation distance between the adversary’s two possible views, and its whole error trade-off is bounded by one curve. Membership inference, attribute inference and property inference are each this statement with a different pair of views. The strongest practical attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) on membership, are explicit approximations of the optimal test.
The second idea is that the worst case is not the average case. Attacks succeed first on outliers, on duplicated strings, on unique combinations of attributes and on the one example in a batch that a neuron isolates. An average over records can look harmless while a few records are fully exposed. This is why attacks are reported as the TPR at a low FPR rather than as accuracy or area under the curve (AUC), and why the defence of the next part has to hold for every record and every dataset.
A third idea closes the part and frames what comes after it. Reconstruction attacks show that answering too many statistics too accurately destroys privacy no matter how the answers are computed: this is the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery. Some noise is not optional, and the question becomes how little noise is enough.
The second half of the part also tells one story about releasing less. Releasing records with the names removed or replaced by codes fails to linkage. Releasing only coarsened records fails to attacks on the sensitive attribute. Releasing only statistics fails to reconstruction, and adding a fixed amount of noise to each statistic fails once enough of them are asked, as an attack on a deployed query system shows. A few hundred published averages can even reveal whether one person is in the data, the tracing attack of Lower bounds. Each step releases less and still fails, which is the motivation for the definition of the next part.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
How to read this part
Order. The part opens with chapter 9, which sets up the vocabulary, and then has two halves. Chapters 10 to 14 attack trained models, from the smallest secret to the largest: one bit of membership, a sensitive attribute, a property of the training population, memorized text, and whole inputs recovered from gradients. Chapters 15 to 17 attack released data, from the weakest defence to the strongest: names removed (linkage), records hidden in crowds (syntactic anonymity), and only aggregate statistics published (reconstruction).
Read chapter 9 first. It fixes the vocabulary (challenger, adversary, view, game, advantage, baseline) that the others use without redefining. Then read chapter 10, since membership inference is the reference attack that chapters 11, 12 and 13 extend. Chapters 11 to 14 can then be read in any order. Read chapters 15 to 17 in order: chapter 16 starts from the linkage game of chapter 15 and uses the imputation baseline of chapter 11, and chapter 17 shows that even exact aggregate statistics, with no records released at all, give the data away. Chapters 16 and 17 matter most for what comes next: the attacks of chapter 16 are the requirements the next part’s definition is built to meet, and the results of chapter 17 return as lower bounds there.
Structure of a chapter. Every chapter has the same shape as in the prerequisites. It opens with the question it answers and a running example, then gives one section per topic, whose definitions, theorems and worked examples are numbered, each theorem followed by its proof. A Code section, a Summary table of the chapter’s results and References close it.
Toy experiments, real pipelines. The attacks in the literature run on image classifiers and large language models trained on GPUs. Here every experiment is a NumPy toy that runs in seconds: logistic regression on synthetic data, Gaussian mean estimation, a small multilayer perceptron written by hand, an n-gram language model with planted canaries. Each toy is chosen so that the optimal attack can be computed exactly and compared with the practical one. Where the published experiment needs a full pipeline (such as LiRA with 16 shadow models on CIFAR-10), the chapter describes that pipeline in prose and runs a faithful scaled-down version.
Run the code. From the repository root, for example,
uv run python code/part02-attacks/membership_inference.py
The scripts use fixed seeds, so their output matches the tables in the text.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: What you will be able to do

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.1 Two-world games
A hospital trains a model on patient records and offers it to doctors through a web service. Is the model “private”? The question has no answer until you say against whom. Can the attacker only read predicted labels, or does it hold the weights? Does it know the other patients or only the population, and can it slip crafted records into the training data? And does it want to learn that one person was a patient, their diagnosis, or the whole training table? Without a threat model that answers them, “the model leaks” and “the model is safe” are claims nobody can test.
Once the threat model is fixed, an attack can be written down as a game, as cryptographers do for encryption. A challenger trains the model with a hidden secret, such as whether one patient’s record was used, and shows the adversary what the threat model allows, and the adversary guesses the secret. That is the one idea of this chapter: an attack is a guess about a hidden secret, made from a view that the threat model fixes. When the secret is one bit, an attack is a test between two hypotheses, so the limits that Hypothesis testing puts on every test, such as the total variation bound, become ceilings that no attack can break.
The running example is a count of people with a sensitive condition, published with standard normal noise. An adversary wants to know whether one person with the condition is in the dataset. If it knows the other 100 records, the best attack flags members at a rate 0.3829 higher than it flags non-members. If it does not know them, the best attack manages only 0.0779, because their unknown count varies far more than the one the target adds. That gap between the uninformed and the best-informed adversary runs through every later chapter of this part.
Before threat models can be compared, you need a way to score a guess. This section scores the simplest game, whose secret is one bit, and shows why the score is the advantage, defined below, rather than the accuracy.
The adversary wins a game when its guess matches the hidden bit. Play 1,000 games with an attack whose TPR is 0.6 and FPR is 0.2. Table 9.2 counts the wins for a fair bit, \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), and for a bit that is 1 only one time in ten.
The next result says the same in general.
An attack that ignores its view, such as a coin flip, says 1 equally often in both worlds, so its advantage is 0 and it wins half the games. A perfect attack has advantage 1 and wins every game. In between, the fair-bit form reads \(\mathrm{Adv} = 2\Pr[b' = b] - 1\), twice the amount by which the attack beats a coin flip.
Unlike the win rate, the advantage does not depend on the prior, because each of the two rates is measured inside one world. In the second row of Table 9.2, always saying 0 already wins 900 games of 1,000, so the attack’s 780 wins look worse than knowing nothing. Yet the attack still learns from its view exactly what it learns in the first row, and its advantage of 0.4 says so. Because the advantage measures only what the view reveals, every two-world game in this part is scored by it.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
Definition 9.1 (Two-world game) A challenger flips a hidden bit \(b\), equal to 1 with probability \(\pi_1\) and to 0 with probability \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1\). In the world \(b = 1\) the target’s record is in the training data (“member”), and in the world \(b = 0\) it is not. The adversary receives its view \(V\), which is everything it gets to look at (from Section 9.2 on, what it knew beforehand is written separately as \(S\)). The view has distribution \(P\) when \(b = 0\) and \(Q\) when \(b = 1\). The adversary outputs a guess \(b'\), where 1 means “member”. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it flags: \[\mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1], \qquad \mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]. \tag{9.1}\] Its advantage is how much more often it says “member” to members than to non-members, \[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}. \tag{9.2}\]





Table 9.2: Expected wins in 1,000 games of an attack with TPR 0.6 and FPR 0.2. The attack fixes the win rate in each world, and the prior decides how many games each world gets.

Proposition 9.1 (Winning probability) In a two-world game, the probability that the guess is right, over the challenger’s bit and everything else that is random, is \[\Pr[b' = b] = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,(1 - \mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.3}\] With a fair bit, \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), it equals \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\).


Proof. The plan is to split the games by the world the challenger chose, count the wins in each world, and add.

Split the win into the two worlds. A game is won when the bit is 1 and the guess is 1, or when the bit is 0 and the guess is 0. A game has only one bit, so the two cannot happen together, and the probability of one or the other is the sum: \[\Pr[b' = b] = \Pr[b = 1 \text{ and } b' = 1] + \Pr[b = 0 \text{ and } b' = 0]. \tag{9.4}\]
The member world. A joint probability is the prior times the conditional probability, so the first term is \(\Pr[b = 1]\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1]\), which is \(\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}\).
The other world. In the same way the second term is \(\pi_0\Pr[b' = 0 \mid b = 0]\). The guess is either 0 or 1, so \(\Pr[b' = 0 \mid b = 0]\) is \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), and adding the two terms gives Equation 9.3.
The fair bit. With \(\pi_0 = \pi_1 = \frac12\) the right side is \(\frac12\mathrm{TPR} + \frac12 - \frac12\mathrm{FPR}\), which is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\).





Example 9.1 A data team releases \(Y = c + b + Z\), where \(c = 50\) is the number of people with the condition among the 100 other records and \(Z\) is standard normal noise. The target has the condition, so it adds 1 to the count exactly when it is a member, \(b = 1\). The adversary knows the other records, so it knows \(c\), and it says “member” when \(Y > 50.5\), halfway between the two possible centres. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF). A member’s count, centred at 51, lands above 50.5 when \(Z > -\frac12\), which by the symmetry of the normal curve has probability \(\Phi(\frac12) = 0.6915\), the TPR. A non-member’s, centred at 50, needs \(Z > \frac12\), with probability \(1 - \Phi(\frac12) = 0.3085\), the FPR. The advantage is \(2\Phi(\frac12) - 1 = 0.3829\), and by Proposition 9.1 the attack wins with probability 0.6915. Over 200,000 simulated games in each world, it scores TPR 0.6901 and FPR 0.3092, an advantage of 0.3809 and a winning probability of 0.6905.
