title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.2 Threat models
Papers on privacy attacks report numbers such as “membership advantage 0.2”, which mean nothing until you know what the attacker was assumed to see, know and do. This section lists what a threat model has to specify, then proves the one ordering that always holds: more access never makes an adversary weaker.

Definition 9.2 (Threat model) A threat model answers five questions.

Goal: what is the secret? It can be whether a record was in the training data (membership), a sensitive field of a known record (attribute), the records themselves (reconstruction), or a statistic of the whole dataset (property).
Access: what does the adversary observe? From least to most, it sees the model’s decisions on inputs it chooses (label-only), the model’s scores on them, such as confidences or losses (black-box), the parameters \(\theta\) (white-box), or everything the training process exposed to it, such as per-step gradients (the transcript).
Behaviour: does it follow the rules? An honest-but-curious adversary follows the protocol and only analyses what it sees. A malicious adversary may deviate, for example by inserting crafted records into the training data (poisoning).
Trust: who sees the raw data? In the central model a trusted curator holds the data, and the adversary sees only what is released. In the local model nobody is trusted, and the adversary may be the party that collects the data. Distributed settings, where many parties each hold a slice, sit in between, because each party trusts itself with its own slice but nobody with the rest.
Side information: what does it know already? It may know the population, a public dataset, some or all of the other records, or the target’s non-sensitive fields.


Label-only and black-box access describe a model behind an application programming interface (API). White-box access describes released weights, and also federated learning, where devices train a shared model on their own data, send updates to a server and all receive the global model. The transcript describes that server, which sees each client’s updates, the setting of Gradient inversion.
Trust works differently from the other axes, because it decides who the adversary is rather than how strong it is. In the local model the collector may itself be the adversary, so protection has to be applied before data leave the user, and Part 3 compares the models. Side information is the hardest axis to bound, because the defender rarely knows what the adversary knows. A guarantee that survives the strongest assumption, “the adversary knows every record except the target’s”, survives every weaker one, so that is the assumption to design for (Section 9.5).
Of the five axes, access is the one with a natural order, because from the weights the adversary can compute any score, and from a score the label. The proof of the order uses one tool for each step down that chain: whatever the adversary computes from its view cannot raise its best advantage, because it could have computed the same thing itself. Write \(\mathrm{Adv}^*(V) = \max_{\mathcal A}\mathrm{Adv}(\mathcal A)\) for the best advantage of any attack \(\mathcal A\) whose input is the view \(V\).

Lemma 9.1 (Processing the view cannot help) Let \(V' = h(V, R)\) for a function \(h\) that the adversary knows and randomness \(R\) that it can draw itself, independent of \(b\) and \(V\). Then every attack on \(V'\) has the same TPR and FPR as some attack on \(V\). So \(\mathrm{Adv}^*(V') \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(V)\), and the best TPR at every FPR from \(V'\) is at most the best from \(V\).


Proof. 

Simulate the processing. Given an attack \(\mathcal A'\) on \(V'\), build an attack \(\mathcal A\) on \(V\) that draws \(R\), computes \(h(V, R)\) and runs \(\mathcal A'\) on the result.
Compare the rates. Because \(R\) does not depend on \(b\), the input that \(\mathcal A\) passes to \(\mathcal A'\) has the distribution of \(V'\) in each world. So \(\mathcal A\)’s guess has the same distribution as \(\mathcal A'\)’s in each world, with the same TPR and FPR.
Compare the best attacks. Every pair of rates that some attack on \(V'\) reaches is reached by some attack on \(V\), and a maximum over a larger set is at least as large.


This is the data processing inequality of Divergences, seen from the attacker’s side. So a service that adds noise to the scores it returns can only lower the best advantage.

Proposition 9.2 (More access never weakens the adversary) For the same model and the same side information \(S\), the best advantages of attacks that see the labels, the scores, the parameters and the training transcript are ordered: \[\mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{labels}, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{scores}, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\theta, S) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(\text{transcript}, S). \tag{9.5}\] The same chain holds for the best TPR at every FPR. More side information never lowers the best advantage, \(\mathrm{Adv}^*(V) \le \mathrm{Adv}^*(V, S)\), and neither does allowing malicious behaviour.


Proof. The plan is to compute each view from the next, so that Lemma 9.1 applies at every link.

Each view can be computed from the next. A label is a function of the scores, such as the class with the largest score. A score on a query \(x\) is a function of \(\theta\) and \(x\), and the adversary chose \(x\) itself. The final \(\theta\) is the last entry of the transcript.
The chain. Each view on the left of Equation 9.5 is \(h(V, R)\) for the view \(V\) to its right, so Lemma 9.1 orders their best advantages and their best TPR at every FPR.
Side information. The view \(V\) is what you get from the pair \((V, S)\) by forgetting \(S\), so Lemma 9.1 applies again.
Behaviour. This step needs no processing, because a malicious adversary changes the data rather than the view. An honest-but-curious adversary is a malicious one that chooses not to deviate, and a maximum over more strategies is at least as large.


The chain compares the best attacks at each level, not the attacks people actually run. In the example below, the gap between two attacks inside one access level is larger than the gap between levels.

Example 9.2 The noisy count has no weights, so this example uses the simplest model that has them. Take a centroid anomaly detector: the mean \(\theta = \frac1n\sum_ix_i\) of \(n = 100\) records \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\) with \(d = 50\) features. A point \(x\) is flagged when its anomaly score \(\|x - \theta\|^2\) exceeds \(d\), the typical squared distance from the centre. The adversary holds a target \(z\), which is one of the \(n\) records if \(b = 1\) and a fresh draw if \(b = 0\).
With the weights (white-box), the adversary knows \(\theta\), and it asks how much more likely this \(\theta\) is in the member world than in the other. Write \(q(\theta \mid z)\) and \(p(\theta \mid z)\) for the density of \(\theta\) given the target \(z\) in those two worlds. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing, no attack catches more members at a given false positive rate than one that thresholds this likelihood ratio. If \(z\) was used, then \(\theta = (z + W)/n\), where \(W \sim \mathcal N(0, (n - 1)I_d)\) is the sum of the other records. If it was not, then \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d/n)\). Expanding the squares in the two Gaussian densities gives the log of the likelihood ratio (Section G.7 does it step by step): \[\ln\frac{q(\theta \mid z)}{p(\theta \mid z)} = \frac{n}{2(n - 1)}\big(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\big) - \frac{\|z\|^2}{2(n - 1)} + \text{const}. \tag{9.6}\] The constant depends only on \(n\) and \(d\). The bracket grows when \(\theta\) points towards \(z\), which is what training on \(z\) does.
Black-box access gives only the score, \(\|z - \theta\|^2 = \|z\|^2 - \big(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\big)\). The adversary knows \(z\), so the calibrated score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\) gives back exactly the bracket. The log-ratio adds only the term \(-\|z\|^2/(2(n - 1))\), which shifts the best threshold slightly from one target to the next, so thresholding the calibrated score is almost the likelihood-ratio test. A simpler black-box attack says “member” when the raw score, the target’s loss, is low, and it is confused by targets far from the mean, which score high whether or not they were used. With only the flag (label-only), the adversary says “member” when \(z\) is not flagged. Table 9.3 reports the advantage of each attack at its best threshold, over 100,000 games in each world.
The best attacks at the label-only, black-box and white-box levels give \(0.0400 \le 0.2789 \le 0.2789\), so the chain holds, and the two best attacks agree to four decimals. But the large gap lies inside the black-box level: calibrating each target against its own distance from the mean, \(\|z\|^2\), multiplies the advantage by about seven, the idea behind the attacks of Membership inference. Sablayrolles et al. (2019) show that whenever training picks parameters with probability proportional to \(e^{-\text{training loss}}\), the best attack looks at the parameters mainly through the target’s calibrated loss (Section G.7). Figure 9.1 shows the best advantage climbing from 0.0326 at \(d = 1\) to 0.7407 at \(d = 500\), because with more parameters per record one record moves the model in more directions.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.3 Privacy games
Salem et al. (2023) write each attack in the literature as a game between a challenger and an adversary, because one name, such as “membership inference”, covers attacks with different assumptions and scores. This section defines the games of this part, then works out the best possible guess in two cases: a rare secret bit, for which Section 9.1 found no best guess, and many secret bits behind one aggregate.

Definition 9.3 (Privacy game) A privacy game has four steps. The challenger draws a secret \(s\) from a known distribution, together with a dataset \(D\) whose distribution may depend on \(s\). It trains \(\theta = \mathcal T(D)\) and gives the adversary the view \(V\) that the threat model allows, along with the side information \(S\). The adversary outputs a guess \(s'\) and earns a gain \(g(s, s')\), usually \(\mathbf 1[s' = s]\). The attack is compared with a baseline, the best expected gain of a guess made from \(S\) alone, without looking at \(V\).

Figure 9.2 draws the membership game, and Table 9.4 lists the others. Every row can be played at every access level, as in “label-only membership”.

Figure 9.2: The membership game. The challenger trains on a dataset, flips a bit that decides whether the target was in it, and shows the adversary the target and a view of the model.



Say the secret bit is rare, 1 with prior \(\pi_1 < \frac12\). Then the safe default is to guess 0, which already wins with probability \(\pi_0\). The view should overturn that default only where it is strong enough evidence to outweigh the prior odds \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\) against a 1, that is, where it is more than \(\gamma\) times as likely when the bit is 1 as when it is 0. How much those views add to the default’s wins is measured by the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences, the total by which the probability \(q\) of a view when the bit is 1 exceeds \(\gamma\) times its probability \(p\) when the bit is 0 (for continuous views, sums become integrals of densities): \[E_\gamma(Q\|P) = \sum_x\max\big(q(x) - \gamma p(x),\, 0\big). \tag{9.7}\] At \(\gamma = 1\) it is the total variation (TV) distance, half the total absolute difference between the two probability tables: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \tfrac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{9.8}\]

Proposition 9.3 (Bayes-optimal guess) In a two-world game with prior \(\pi_1 \le \frac12\) on \(b = 1\), so that guessing 0 is the default, write \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\). The best attack wins with probability \[\max_{\mathcal A}\Pr[b' = b] = \pi_0 + \pi_1\,E_\gamma(Q\|P), \tag{9.9}\] and it says 1 exactly on the views \(x\) where \(q(x) > \gamma p(x)\).


Proof. The plan is to write the winning probability of any attack as the baseline plus a sum over views, and then to choose the views that make the sum largest.

Write an attack as a set. A deterministic attack says 1 on some set \(A\) of views. By Equation 9.3 it wins with probability \(\pi_1Q(A) + \pi_0(1 - P(A))\).
Pull out the baseline. Factoring out \(\pi_1\) from the terms that depend on \(A\), with \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\), gives \[\pi_1Q(A) + \pi_0\big(1 - P(A)\big) = \pi_0 + \pi_1\big(Q(A) - \gamma P(A)\big). \tag{9.10}\]
Choose the best set. The bracket is a sum over the views in \(A\) of \(q(x) - \gamma p(x)\). It is largest when \(A\) holds exactly the views whose term is positive, and then it is the sum of the positive terms, which is \(E_\gamma(Q\|P)\). In words, the best attack says 1 when the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) exceeds the prior odds \(\gamma\) against the bit being 1.
Randomizing does not help. A randomized attack says 1 on view \(x\) with some probability \(\phi(x)\) and gets \(\sum_x\phi(x)(q(x) - \gamma p(x))\) in the bracket. This is also largest with \(\phi = 1\) on the positive terms and 0 elsewhere.


The first term of Equation 9.9 is the baseline of always guessing 0, and the second is everything the view adds. For a fair bit, \(\gamma = 1\) and \(E_1\) is the TV distance, so the best win probability is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\), and matching it with \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\) from Proposition 9.1 makes the best advantage the TV distance, a ceiling that Section 9.4 extends.
The reconstruction game has many secret bits rather than one. Its simplest case shows how little a single aggregate reveals about each record.

Proposition 9.4 (Reconstruction from one exact count) Let the secret be \(m\) independent uniform bits \(x_1, \dots, x_m\), and let the release be their sum \(K\). The best reconstruction recovers in expectation the fraction of the bits below, whose two forms agree because \(\max(k, m - k) = \frac m2 + |k - \frac m2|\): \[\frac{\mathbb E[\max(K, m - K)]}{m} = \frac12 + \frac{\mathbb E\big[|K - \frac m2|\big]}{m}. \tag{9.11}\] For large \(m\) this is close to \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\).


Proof. The plan is to find what the count says about each bit, guess each bit from that, and then average over the count.

What the count says about each bit. Given \(K = k\), every arrangement of \(k\) ones among \(m\) places is equally likely, so each bit is 1 with probability \(k/m\).
The best guess for each bit. The gain is the fraction of bits guessed right, so each bit can be guessed separately. The best guess is 1 when \(k/m > \frac12\) and 0 otherwise, so every bit gets the majority value, and the expected number right is \(\max(k, m - k)\).
Average over the count. The count \(K\) is \(\mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\), and averaging \(\max(K, m - K)/m\) over it gives the fraction in the statement.
How large the gain is. By the central limit theorem, \(K - \frac m2\) is approximately normal with standard deviation \(\sqrt m/2\). The average distance of a normal variable from its mean is its standard deviation times \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\), and dividing \(\frac{\sqrt m}{2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\) by \(m\) gives \(1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\). Section E.2 computes the fraction exactly, as \(\frac12 + \frac12\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}\) with \(j = \lfloor m/2\rfloor\), and proves the approximation without the central limit theorem.


A model that lets an attacker guess a rare diagnosis “with 90% accuracy” reveals nothing if 90% of people do not have that diagnosis. Many aggregates are a different matter: Reconstruction attacks shows how noisy counts over random subsets of the records, a few times as many as there are bits, give away almost every bit.
Attribute inference has two possible baselines. A guess from the population asks whether the model helps, while the attack’s success on non-members asks whether it helps because this person was in the training data. Only the second measures a breach of that person’s privacy, as Attribute inference and model inversion develops.

Example 9.3 Take the noisy count \(Y = c + b + Z\) of Example 9.1, with the rest of the count \(c\) known, and attack it in three games.
In the membership game, the count is \(\mathcal N(c, 1)\) without the target and \(\mathcal N(c + 1, 1)\) with it, and by Example 9.1 the best attack wins with probability \(\Phi(\frac12) = 0.6915\).
In the attribute game with a fair prior, the target is known to be in \(D\), and the secret is whether it has the condition. The count is \(c + 1 + Z\) if it does and \(c + Z\) if not, the same two distributions as before, so the best guess is again right with probability 0.6915 (0.6925 in 200,000 simulated games). Now make the condition rare, with prior \(\pi_1 = 0.1\), so that always guessing “no” wins with probability 0.9. By Proposition 9.3 the release overturns that guess only where the likelihood ratio exceeds \(\gamma = 9\). The ratio of the two normal densities at \(y\) is \(e^{-(y - c - 1)^2/2}/e^{-(y - c)^2/2} = e^{(y - c) - 1/2}\), so this happens where \(y > c + \frac12 + \ln 9\). A normal variable with mean \(\mu\) and variance 1 exceeds \(a\) with probability \(\Phi(\mu - a)\), so the world with the condition puts mass \(\Phi(\frac12 - \ln 9)\) there and the other world mass \(\Phi(-\frac12 - \ln 9)\), and \[E_9(Q\|P) = \Phi(\tfrac12 - \ln 9) - 9\,\Phi(-\tfrac12 - \ln 9) = 0.0134. \tag{9.12}\] The best accuracy is \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.0134 = 0.9013\) (simulated: 0.9028). The same release that lifts a fair guess from 0.5 to 0.69 lifts this one by about a tenth of a percentage point, because the likelihood ratio rarely overturns 9-to-1 odds.
In the reconstruction game, release the exact count of \(m\) uniform bits instead. By Proposition 9.4 the best reconstruction recovers a fraction 0.6230 of the bits for \(m = 10\) (0.6236 in simulation), 0.5398 for \(m = 100\) and 0.5126 for \(m = 1000\). The approximation \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\) gives 0.6262, 0.5399 and 0.5126.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.4 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve
text:
9.4 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve
A two-world game is a test of the hypothesis “not a member”, under which the view has distribution \(P\), against “member”, under which it has distribution \(Q\). So everything Hypothesis testing proved about tests becomes a statement about attacks. This section draws out three: a ceiling on the advantage, a ceiling on the whole receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and a warning about which point of that curve to report.
The first ceiling is the TV distance, which Proposition 9.3 already found for a fair bit. The second bounds the attack’s TPR at every false positive rate, not just where TPR − FPR is largest. It comes from the trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\) of Hypothesis testing. For each false positive rate, \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\) is the smallest fraction of members that any attack with that false positive rate must miss, so an attack can catch at most the rest.

Proposition 9.5 (Ceilings on every attack) For every attack in a two-world game with views \(P\) and \(Q\), \[\mathrm{Adv} \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \qquad \Pr[b' = b] \le \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \tag{9.13}\] where the second bound is for a fair bit, and \[\mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.14}\] All three bounds are attained by likelihood-ratio attacks, which flag first the views with the largest likelihood ratio \(q/p\).


Proof. 

The attack is a test. An attack says “member”, rejecting the hypothesis \(P\), with probability \(\phi(V)\). Its type I error is its FPR, and its type II error is \(1 - \mathrm{TPR}\).
The advantage ceiling. Every test has \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) at most \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\), with equality for the test that says “member” exactly where \(q > p\) (Hypothesis testing). That gives the first bound of Equation 9.13, and Proposition 9.1 turns it into the second.
The curve ceiling. By the definition of the trade-off function, no attack with false positive rate FPR misses fewer than \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\) of the members, so \(1 - \mathrm{TPR} \ge T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the attack that attains it flags views in decreasing order of the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) until its false positive rate reaches the chosen value, flagging the last views only at random if that is needed to hit it exactly.


The warning needs one more quantity, which answers the question a flagged person cares about: given that the attack says “member”, how likely is that to be true? The precision is the members’ share of everyone the attack flags.

Proposition 9.6 (Precision) An attack with rates TPR and FPR, in a game with prior \(\pi_1\), is right when it says “member” with probability \[\Pr[b = 1 \mid b' = 1] = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{9.15}\]


Proof. 

A conditional probability is a ratio. The precision is the probability that a target is a member and flagged, divided by the probability that it is flagged. The numerator is \(\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}\), as in step 2 of the proof of Proposition 9.1.
The denominator. A target is flagged either as a member, with probability \(\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}\), or as a non-member, with probability \(\pi_0\mathrm{FPR}\). The two cannot happen together, so the probability of being flagged is their sum.


The advantage is only one point of the ROC curve, the plot of an attack’s TPR against its FPR as its threshold varies. It is the largest height of that curve above the diagonal, reached at one threshold, so it says nothing about the low false-positive end, where an attack identifies people with confidence. An attack that flags 1% of members with no false alarms has an advantage of only about 0.01, yet it identifies those members with certainty. Carlini et al. (2022) argue from this that membership attacks should be reported by their TPR at a low FPR, such as \(10^{-3}\), on ROC curves with log axes, and the rest of this part does so. Precision points the same way when members are rare (Jayaraman et al. 2021), as Example 9.4 shows.
Both ceilings depend only on \(P\) and \(Q\), so they bound attacks nobody has invented yet, and a training pipeline whose ROC curve stays close to the diagonal for every target defeats every attack at once.

Example 9.4 In the noisy count of Example 9.1, \(P = \mathcal N(50, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(51, 1)\). The attack there says “member” exactly where \(q > p\), so by Proposition 9.5 its advantage 0.3829 is the TV distance, and no attack does better.
Now hold the false positive rate at \(10^{-3}\), so that the threshold \(\tau\) must rise until only one non-member in a thousand exceeds it. With \(\Phi^{-1}\) the inverse of \(\Phi\), \(\Pr[\mathcal N(50, 1) > \tau] = 10^{-3}\) gives \(\tau = 50 + \Phi^{-1}(0.999) = 50 + 3.0902 = 53.09\). A member’s count, centred one higher, exceeds \(\tau\) with probability \(1 - \Phi(3.0902 - 1) = 0.0183\). That is the TPR, and by Equation 9.14 it is the best possible at this FPR (simulated: 0.0184, at an FPR of 0.00109). The attack now catches fewer than 2% of members, but when it fires, Equation 9.15 gives a precision of \(0.0183/(0.0183 + 0.001) = 0.948\) at a fair prior. If only one target in a hundred is a member, the precision drops to \(0.01 \times 0.0183/(0.01 \times 0.0183 + 0.99 \times 0.001) = 0.156\).
The black curve in Figure 9.3 is this ROC curve on log axes, and the green one is the same game against an adversary who does not know the other records (Section 9.5).







Figure 9.3: Left: the released count in the two worlds when the other 100 records are known (solid) and unknown (dashed). Right: the membership ROC curves of the best attacks on log axes, exact (lines) and from 100,000 simulated games per world (dots). The dotted diagonal is random guessing.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.5 Average case and worst case
A membership game can be scored in two ways. In the average case, the data and the target come from the population, the adversary knows only the population, and the advantage is an average over all of that randomness. In the worst case, the adversary knows, or even picks, the rest of the data and the target, and the advantage is the maximum over those choices. Evaluations of real models usually measure the first, but privacy guarantees have to control the second, and the two can be far apart.
When the view depends on something the adversary does not know, such as the other records, not knowing it works like extra noise, because averaging two distributions can only blur their difference. Knowing it removes that noise, and choosing it picks the situation where the difference is largest. Call the unknown \(\omega\), taking finitely many values with probabilities \(w_\omega\) that sum to 1, and let \(P_\omega\) and \(Q_\omega\) be the views in the two worlds when the unknown is \(\omega\).

Lemma 9.2 (Mixing hides, and knowing the mixture undoes it) Let \(\bar P = \sum_\omega w_\omega P_\omega\) and \(\bar Q = \sum_\omega w_\omega Q_\omega\) be the views averaged over the unknown, and write \((\omega, V)_{b}\) for the distribution of the pair of the unknown and the view in world \(b\). The chain below has three links, and each step of the proof gives one: \[\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q) \;\le\; \sum_\omega w_\omega\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega) \;=\; \mathrm{TV}\big((\omega, V)_{b=0}, (\omega, V)_{b=1}\big) \;\le\; \max_\omega \mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega). \tag{9.16}\]


Proof. 

Averaging first can only cancel. The TV distance of the averages is half the sum over views of \(\big|\sum_\omega w_\omega(p_\omega(x) - q_\omega(x))\big|\). Differences can cancel when they are added before taking absolute values, but not after, by the triangle inequality. So this is at most half the sum over views of \(\sum_\omega w_\omega|p_\omega(x) - q_\omega(x)|\), and swapping the two sums gives the middle term.
Knowing the unknown. The pair \((\omega, V)\) has probability \(w_\omega p_\omega(x)\) in world 0 and \(w_\omega q_\omega(x)\) in world 1. Half the total absolute difference between these two tables is \(\sum_\omega w_\omega\mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega)\), which is the equality.
Choosing it. An average is at most its largest term, which gives the last inequality.


A tiny case shows how much the unknown can hide. Let there be one other record, whose bit \(\omega\) is 0 or 1 with probability \(\frac12\) each, and let the mechanism release the exact count \(\omega + b\). Knowing \(\omega\), the adversary subtracts it and reads off \(b\), so the TV distance is 1. Without it, the count is 0 or 1 in world 0 and 1 or 2 in world 1, each with probability \(\frac12\). Only the count 1 appears in both, so the TV distance is \(\frac12(\frac12 + 0 + \frac12) = \frac12\).
Now let \(\omega\) collect everything that the average-case game draws at random and that a worst-case adversary is allowed to fix: the other records, and the target, which until now was fixed. The three terms of Equation 9.16 are then the best advantages of three adversaries.

Proposition 9.7 (Average case against worst case) The best advantages of an adversary who does not know \(\omega\), one who knows it and one who chooses it are ordered: \[\underbrace{\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q)}_{\text{does not know }\omega} \;\le\; \underbrace{\mathbb E_\omega\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega)}_{\text{knows }\omega} \;\le\; \underbrace{\max_\omega\,\mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega)}_{\text{chooses }\omega}. \tag{9.17}\] The first gap can be extreme. For the exact count of \(m\) unknown fair bits plus the target’s membership bit \(b\), the middle term is 1 while the left term is \(\binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\), about \(\sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\).


Proof. The plan is to identify each term as a best advantage, so that Lemma 9.2 orders them, and then to compute the exact count.

Three adversaries, three views. An adversary that does not know \(\omega\) sees \(V\), distributed as \(\bar P\) or \(\bar Q\), so by Proposition 9.5 its best advantage is \(\mathrm{TV}(\bar P, \bar Q)\). One that knows \(\omega\) sees the pair \((\omega, V)\), and by the equality of Equation 9.16 its best advantage is \(\mathbb E_\omega\mathrm{TV}(P_\omega, Q_\omega)\). One that chooses \(\omega\) picks the most revealing value, which gives the maximum, and Equation 9.16 orders the three.
The exact count, known crowd. An adversary who knows the other bits subtracts their sum from the count and reads off \(b\), so the middle term is 1.
The exact count, unknown crowd. An adversary who does not know them sees \(K\) in world 0 and \(K + 1\) in world 1, where \(K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\) is the unknown sum. So with \(p(k) = \Pr[K = k]\), the other world has \(q(k) = p(k - 1)\), the same list of binomial weights shifted one place right. Their TV distance is the total excess of \(q\) over \(p\) where it is positive.
Telescope. The binomial weights rise up to the middle value \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) and fall after it (Section E.2 proves it). So \(q\) is larger exactly to the right of the middle, with excess \(p(k - 1) - p(k)\) at \(k\). Adding these differences from the middle to the end, every weight cancels except the one at the middle, which is the largest weight \(\binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\).
Its size. For large \(m\) the binomial is close to a normal curve with standard deviation \(\sqrt m/2\), whose peak height is \(\sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\), and this tends to 0 as \(m\) grows.


Averaging over datasets hides the target in a crowd, but only from an adversary who does not know the crowd, and a malicious adversary can plant the other records itself. Averaging over targets hides the worst-treated person in the same way. If a mechanism exposes one target in a thousand completely and the others not at all, the middle term is \(1/1000 = 0.001\) and the right term is 1. Outliers and duplicated records are the usual victims, as Membership inference shows.
An audit can estimate average-case numbers from data, but they are lower bounds on the worst case: an audit that reports advantage 0.01 shows only that the worst case is at least 0.01. An audit narrows the gap by planting canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible (Memorization and training-data extraction). A guarantee that holds for every pair of datasets differing in one record bounds the right side of Equation 9.17, and therefore bounds every game in this part whose two worlds differ in one record. The definition in Part 3 is a guarantee of this kind.

Example 9.5 Keep the noisy count of Example 9.1, with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\) and a target who has the condition, but now let the \(m = 100\) other bits be fresh \(\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)\) draws that the adversary does not see. The count is then \(K + b + Z\) with \(K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(100, \frac12)\), and its likelihood ratio between the two worlds increases with the observed count (Section F.6). So the best attack is still a threshold. The member world’s count is the other world’s shifted by 1, and both are symmetric, about 51 and 50, so their densities cross halfway, at 50.5. Table 9.5 compares the adversaries of Equation 9.17, and adds a target whose condition the adversary does not know, which it has with probability \(\frac12\).
Not knowing the crowd cuts the advantage by a factor of five, and a normal approximation explains why: treating \(K\) as \(\mathcal N(50, 25)\) makes the two worlds Gaussians with shift 1 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{25 + 1}\), which gives \(2\Phi\big(1/(2\sqrt{26})\big) - 1 = 0.0781\). When the target has the condition only half the time, the half without it gives the same count in both worlds, so only the other half of each world’s mixture differs, and the advantage halves to \(0.0779/2 = 0.0390\). At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) the average-case attack has TPR 0.0019 (simulated 0.0016), against 0.0183 for the adversary who knows the rest, and these are the green and black curves of Figure 9.3. Figure 9.4 shows the average-case advantage falling as the crowd grows, while the worst case does not move.

A small advantage is not always a small risk, even in the worst case, as a release of one record shows.

Example 9.6 A mechanism publishes one record of \(D\), chosen uniformly among \(n = 1000\) records that are all different. The attack says “member” if the published record is \(z\). If \(z\) is in \(D\), it is published with probability \(1/n\), so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.001\), and if not, it is never published, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\). Simulation gives \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.00098\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\) over 200,000 games per world. The advantage is \(1/n = 0.001\) for every target and every dataset, so the mechanism looks almost perfectly safe in the average case and in the worst case alike. Yet every run exposes one person completely, because when the attack fires its precision is 1. Only the low false-positive end of Section 9.4 reveals the problem. The published record is possible in one world and impossible in the other, so a guarantee has to bound how much more likely an output is in one world than in the other.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 The loss attack and the generalization gap
A hospital trains a model to predict a disease and publishes it. You hold one patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, you have learned that the patient was treated at that hospital for that disease, although the model never output a diagnosis. This is membership inference. It is the simplest question an attacker can ask about a trained model, which makes it the standard measure of how much a model leaks. An attack is scored by two rates. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags as members, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags.
The one idea of this chapter is that membership inference is a statistical test about one record. Training is random, because the rest of the training set is drawn at random and the optimization varies from run to run. So the model’s output on a record, such as its confidence in the record’s label, has one distribution over models trained with that record, its IN distribution, and another over models trained without it, its OUT distribution. The attacker sees one output and must say which of the two produced it. A typical record is predicted well either way, so its two distributions nearly coincide, while an atypical record is predicted badly unless the model saw it. An attack that says “member” whenever the model is confident therefore flags typical records, which get confident outputs even when never trained on, and the best attack compares each record’s output with that record’s own two distributions.
The running example is a scaled-down, linear version of an experiment by Carlini et al. (2022). A pool of 1,000 labelled points in \(\mathbb R^{100}\) holds 950 typical points and 50 outliers, whose labels nothing else in the data predicts. Logistic-regression models train on random halves of the pool. The attacker targets 128 of these models. Pairing a model with a pool point gives one guess, and each model trained on 500 of the 1,000 points, so there are \(128 \times 500 = 64{,}000\) member pairs and as many non-member pairs. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the attack that thresholds the loss flags a fraction 0.0009 of members, which is what flagging at random would do, since a random flag hits members and non-members at the same rate. The per-record test of Section 10.3 flags 0.0149, and 87% of the members it finds are outliers.
A model is fitted to its training data, so its loss on a training point is usually lower than on a fresh one. This section asks how much membership that difference alone gives away.
Attacks are scored in the membership game of Threat models and privacy games. A challenger draws a training set \(D\) and flips a fair coin for a hidden bit \(b\). If \(b = 1\), the target \(z = (x, y)\), a feature vector and its label, is drawn uniformly from \(D\); if \(b = 0\), it is a fresh record from the same population. The adversary sees \(z\) and the trained model, with weights \(\theta\), and guesses \(b'\). Half the games have \(b = 1\) and are won with probability TPR, and the other half are won with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). So by Proposition 9.1 the adversary wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\), where the advantage \(\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) measures how much more often the attack says “member” to members than to non-members.
Yeom et al. (2018) turned the lower loss on members into an attack. Its cleanest version turns the loss into a probability, so the loss must lie in a known range.
The randomized rule makes the probability of saying “member” linear in the loss, so, as the next proposition proves, the advantage is the difference between the average loss of non-members and of members, divided by \(B\). That difference is the generalization gap. Write \(\theta_D\) for the model trained on the training set \(D\), and \(\mathcal D\) (calligraphic) for the population it is drawn from. The gap is the model’s expected loss on fresh data, its population risk \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta_D)\), minus its average loss on its own training set, its empirical risk \(\mathcal L(\theta_D; D)\).
So overfitting implies leakage, by an amount the training and test errors give without any attack. By Theorem 7.1, the expected gap is the average self-influence of the training records (Definition 7.3): how much each record’s own loss rises when it is replaced in training by a fresh record. But a small gap does not mean a private model. The loss attack ignores which record it is looking at, and the per-record test of Section 10.3 beats it by a wide margin.
Each attack below reads one of three numbers from the model’s output on \(z\). The confidence \(p_y\) is the probability the model gives to the true label, and the usual classification loss is the cross-entropy \(\ell = -\ln p_y\). The logit of the confidence is the log of the odds the model gives to the true label, \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}. \tag{10.2}\] The confidence crowds against 1, while \(\phi\) keeps confident outputs apart. That matters because Section 10.3 fits bell curves to these values, and the next lemma shows why a bell curve fits \(\phi\): for logistic regression, \(\phi\) is linear in the weights. It also shows that a threshold on \(\phi\) is a threshold on the loss, so the rest of the chapter works with \(\phi\).

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
Definition 10.1 (Loss attacks) Let the loss \(\ell(\theta; z)\) of the model on the target take values in \([0, B]\). The bounded-loss attack says “member” with probability \(1 - \ell(\theta; z)/B\). The loss threshold attack says “member” when \(\ell(\theta; z) < \tau\), for a threshold \(\tau\) such as the mean training loss, which a model’s report often states.



Proposition 10.1 (The loss attack’s advantage is the generalization gap) In the membership game, with expectations over the training set, the training run and the target, the bounded-loss attack has an advantage that is first a difference of average losses and then, renamed, the generalization gap: \[\mathrm{Adv} = \frac{\mathbb E[\ell(\theta; z) \mid b = 0] - \mathbb E[\ell(\theta; z) \mid b = 1]}{B} = \frac{\mathbb E_D\big[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta_D) - \mathcal L(\theta_D; D)\big]}{B}, \tag{10.1}\] the expected generalization gap divided by \(B\). For the 0-1 loss, which is 0 on a correct prediction and 1 on a wrong one, \(B = 1\), the attack says “member” exactly when the model classifies \(z\) correctly, and its advantage is the test error minus the training error.


Proof. The plan is to write the TPR and the FPR as average losses, subtract them, and then recognize the two averages as the test loss and the training loss.

The TPR. Given \(b = 1\), the attack says “member” with probability \(1 - \ell/B\) for whatever loss the target has. Averaging over targets and training runs gives \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 1]/B\).
The FPR. The same calculation with \(b = 0\) gives \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \mathbb E[\ell \mid b = 0]/B\).
Subtract. The advantage is \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\). The two 1s cancel, which leaves the first form of Equation 10.1.
Name the two averages. When \(b = 1\), \(z\) is a uniformly chosen training point, so its expected loss is the expected empirical risk. When \(b = 0\), \(z\) is a fresh draw independent of \(D\), so its expected loss is the expected population risk. Substituting both gives the second form.
The 0-1 loss. With \(B = 1\), the probability \(1 - \ell\) is 1 on a correct prediction and 0 on a wrong one. So \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \text{train error}\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \text{test error}\), and their difference is the test error minus the training error.





Lemma 10.1 (For logistic regression, the logit of the confidence is the margin) Let a logistic-regression model with weights \(\theta\) give the true label \(y \in \{-1, 1\}\) of a record \(z = (x, y)\) the probability \(p_y = 1/(1 + e^{-y\langle \theta, x\rangle})\). Then \(\phi\) is the margin \(y\langle \theta, x\rangle\), how far the point lies on the correct side of the decision boundary, and \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y} = y\langle \theta, x\rangle \qquad\text{and}\qquad \ell = -\ln p_y = \ln\big(1 + e^{-\phi}\big). \tag{10.3}\] So a threshold on any of the confidence, the loss and \(\phi\) is a threshold on the others.


Proof. 

The odds. Write \(t = y\langle \theta, x\rangle\). Then \(1 - p_y = e^{-t}/(1 + e^{-t})\), so the factor \(1 + e^{-t}\) cancels in the ratio \(p_y/(1 - p_y)\), which leaves \(e^t\). Its logarithm is \(\phi = t\).
The loss. The reciprocal of the confidence is \(1/p_y = 1 + e^{-\phi}\), so the loss \(-\ln p_y\) is \(\ln(1 + e^{-\phi})\).
Monotone. The confidence rises with \(\phi\), and by step 2 the loss falls as \(\phi\) rises. So “\(\phi\) above a cut” is the same event as “loss below the matching cut”.



Example 10.1 In the running example, each of the 950 typical points has features \(x\) drawn from the normal distribution \(\mathcal N(0, I/100)\), with \(I\) the identity, so its 100 independent coordinates each have variance \(1/100\) and \(\|x\| \approx 1\). Its label \(y = \pm1\) follows the first coordinate with some noise, and the factor 30 makes it follow closely, since \(x_1\) is of order \(1/10\): \[\Pr[y = 1 \mid x] = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-30x_1}}. \tag{10.4}\] The 50 outliers have the same kind of \(x\) scaled by 5 and a label drawn by a fair coin, so a model gets an outlier’s label right only by fitting that point itself. Each model is logistic regression with the penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\), \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\), trained on a random half of the pool (\(n = 500\)). Each model trained on a random half is followed by one trained on the other half, so every point is a member of exactly half the models.
Over the 128 target models, the training error is 0.1495, and the test error, on the half of the pool each model did not see, is 0.2663. “Member if correctly classified” therefore has \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - 0.1495 = 0.8505\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - 0.2663 = 0.7337\). Its advantage, \(0.8505 - 0.7337 = 0.1168\), is exactly the gap \(0.2663 - 0.1495\).
The logistic loss is unbounded, so the bounded-loss attack needs it clipped: any loss above \(B = 2\) is replaced by 2. The mean clipped loss is 0.4158 on members and 0.5433 on non-members. So Equation 10.1 predicts an advantage of \((0.5433 - 0.4158)/2 = 0.0638\), and simulating the randomized attack gives 0.0639. The loss threshold attack at the mean unclipped training loss, \(\tau = 0.4159\) (almost the clipped mean, because few training losses exceed 2), has \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.5936\), \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.4834\) and advantage 0.1102.
By the win rate \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\), the three attacks win between 53% and 56% of the games. None of them identifies anyone with confidence, because each flags a large share of non-members too, with an FPR of 0.7337 for the error rule and 0.4834 for the threshold. Figure 10.1 shows why: the two distributions of \(\phi\) are shifted, but they almost entirely overlap.







Figure 10.1: Distribution of \(\phi\), the logit of the target model’s confidence in the true label, over member pairs and non-member pairs of the 128 target models. The dashed line is Yeom’s threshold: the attack says “member” to its right, where the loss is below the mean training loss.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.2 Shadow models
An attacker who wants a better rule than “low loss means member” has to know what members’ outputs look like. It has no labelled examples, because it does not know who is in the target’s training set. This section shows how the attacker can learn that from models of its own, whose training sets it chooses (Shokri et al. 2017), and what the best rule learned this way can achieve.

Definition 10.2 (Shadow models and the attack model) Suppose the attacker holds records from the target’s population. A shadow model is a model that the attacker trains like the target, with the same recipe, on a training set that includes each of its records with probability \(\frac12\). For each shadow model and record, the attacker keeps the shadow model’s output \(o\) on the record, such as its confidence, and the membership label \(m\), with \(m = 1\) for “in”. The attack model \(h(o) \in (0, 1)\) is a classifier trained on these pairs by minimizing the cross-entropy, \(-\ln h\) on “in” pairs and \(-\ln(1 - h)\) on “out” pairs. It says “member” when \(h(o)\) exceeds a threshold.

In the running example the output is \(o = (y, \phi)\), the record’s label and the logit of the confidence. With enough shadow data, the attack model learns the best rule available from \(o\) alone, as the next proposition proves.

Proposition 10.2 (The attack model is the best record-blind attack) Let \(q(o)\) and \(p(o)\) be the densities of the output for members and for non-members, each pooled over all the records that could produce \(o\) (they are unrelated to the confidence \(p_y\)), and let the attack model range over all functions of \(o\). As the number of shadow pairs grows, \(h(o)\) tends to the posterior probability of membership, and with a fair prior the posterior odds are the likelihood ratio: \[h(o) \to \Pr[b = 1 \mid o], \qquad \frac{\Pr[b = 1 \mid o]}{\Pr[b = 0 \mid o]} = \frac{q(o)}{p(o)}. \tag{10.5}\] So no attack that sees only \(o\) has a higher TPR, at any FPR, than a threshold on \(h\).


Proof. The proof has four links: the shadow pairs look like the real game, cross-entropy recovers the posterior, the posterior ranks outputs by the likelihood ratio, and a threshold on the likelihood ratio is optimal.

The shadow pairs have the right distribution. A shadow model is trained like the target, and each record is in or out with probability \(\frac12\). So a shadow pair \((o, m)\) has the same joint distribution as a pair of target output and membership bit in the game.
Cross-entropy is minimized by the posterior. Fix one output \(o\), and let \(\rho = \Pr[m = 1 \mid o]\) be the probability of “in” given that output. If the attack model predicts \(h\) there, its expected loss is \(-\rho\ln h - (1 - \rho)\ln(1 - h)\). This is convex in \(h\), and its derivative \(-\rho/h + (1 - \rho)/(1 - h)\) is zero at \(h = \rho\), so that is the minimum. The same holds at every \(o\) separately, so the best function is \(h(o) = \Pr[m = 1 \mid o]\), which by step 1 is \(\Pr[b = 1 \mid o]\).
Bayes’ rule. The joint probability of a world, \(b = 1\) or \(b = 0\), and an output is the prior of the world times the density of the output in that world. So the posterior odds are the prior odds times \(q(o)/p(o)\), and with a fair prior the prior odds are 1. The odds \(h/(1 - h)\) rise with \(h\), so a threshold on \(h\) is a threshold on \(q(o)/p(o)\).
Neyman–Pearson. The Neyman–Pearson lemma says that a threshold on the likelihood ratio has the highest TPR at its FPR among all tests that see the same observation.


The attack model is optimal for the wrong question. Seeing \((y, \phi)\) and not which record produced it, it cannot know that \(\phi = 2\) is high for one record and low for another. When members tend to have the higher \(\phi\) within each class, \(h\) rises with \(\phi\) there, so a threshold on \(h\) is a threshold on \(\phi\) and, by Lemma 10.1, on the loss: the loss attack with a threshold for each class.
What shadow models really buy is calibration. The attacker picks the threshold at which the desired fraction of its own shadow non-members pass, and trusts that real non-members behave the same way. Salem et al. (2019) found that one shadow model, or shadow data from another distribution, often suffices.

Example 10.2 For each class, the attack model is a logistic regression of “in” on \(\phi\) with an intercept, trained on the roughly 32,000 shadow pairs of that class (the 64 shadow models times the roughly 500 pool points with that label). Both slopes are positive, 0.238 for \(y = -1\) and 0.158 for \(y = +1\). So within each class the attack is a threshold on the loss.
To compare it with the loss attack over all thresholds, draw each attack’s receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, its TPR against its FPR as the threshold sweeps. The area under the curve (AUC) equals the probability that a random member scores higher than a random non-member (Hypothesis testing). The attack model and the loss attack both have AUC 0.577, and the same TPR at every FPR to within sampling noise (Table 10.3).
Calibration works: a threshold set on the shadow models for an FPR of 1% gives an FPR of 0.0095 on the 128 unseen target models. But the TPR there is 0.0098, no better than chance, because a threshold on \(\phi\) that ignores which record it sees cannot single out any member at a low FPR.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.3 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
text:
10.3 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
The attacks of the last two sections compare a record’s output with everyone else’s outputs. The right comparison is with the same record’s output under models that did and did not train on it. This section builds that test and proves that it is the best one.
Carlini et al. (2022) built the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) on that comparison. For a record \(z\), the attacker has a few dozen shadow values of \(\phi_z\), the logit of the confidence on \(z\), and summarizes them by bell curves, a shape justified after the theorem below.

Definition 10.3 (LiRA, online and offline) For a record \(z\), let \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z}\) be the mean and standard deviation of \(\phi_z\) over the shadow models that trained on \(z\), and \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) those over the shadow models that did not. Write \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) for the normal density at \(\phi\). Online LiRA scores the target model’s \(\phi_z\) by the log of the ratio of the IN fit to the OUT fit, \[\ln\Lambda_z(\phi_z) = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}, z}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}^2\big). \tag{10.6}\] Offline LiRA uses only the OUT fit, and scores how many OUT standard deviations the output lies above its usual value, \[\frac{\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{out}, z}}. \tag{10.7}\] Each says “member” when its score exceeds a threshold that is the same for every record.

Online LiRA needs shadow models that trained on each new target record, while offline LiRA’s OUT models can be trained once and reused. One threshold serves all records because, as the theorem below shows, the record is drawn the same way in both worlds, so it drops out of the likelihood ratio that the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1) thresholds.

Theorem 10.1 (One threshold on the per-record likelihood ratio is optimal) In the membership game, suppose the target record \(z\) is drawn from the same distribution whether \(b = 1\) or \(b = 0\), and let \(q_z\) and \(p_z\) be the IN and OUT densities of \(\phi_z\). Among all attacks that see \(z\) and \(\phi_z\), the highest TPR at each FPR is reached by saying “member” when \(\Lambda_z(\phi_z) = q_z(\phi_z)/p_z(\phi_z)\) exceeds one threshold, the same for every record. Online LiRA estimates this true ratio by its Gaussian fits, so when the fits are exact the test is online LiRA.


Proof. The plan is to write the density of the adversary’s view in each world, see that the record’s part cancels in the likelihood ratio, and apply the Neyman–Pearson lemma.

The view is a pair. The density of the pair is the probability of drawing the record, call it \(g(z)\), times the density of the output given the record. Write it as \(g(z)\,q_z(\phi)\) when \(b = 1\) and as \(g(z)\,p_z(\phi)\) when \(b = 0\).
The record’s factor is shared. By hypothesis, the record is drawn the same way whether or not it ends up in the training set, so \(g\) is the same function in both worlds. The running example satisfies this, since every pool point is a member of each model with probability \(\frac12\).
The ratio. Since the factor \(g(z)\) is the same in both worlds, it cancels: \[\frac{g(z)\,q_z(\phi)}{g(z)\,p_z(\phi)} = \frac{q_z(\phi)}{p_z(\phi)} = \Lambda_z(\phi). \tag{10.8}\]
Neyman–Pearson. The best test of the pair thresholds its likelihood ratio at one value, by Theorem 4.1. So different records are compared through their ratios, never through their raw \(\phi\). With exact Gaussian fits, the log of the ratio is Equation 10.6.


The hypothesis is needed, since if members came from one hospital and non-members from another, the record alone would reveal \(b\). The theorem is an instance of Lemma 9.2 in Threat models and privacy games, which says that an attacker who does not know a hidden part of the data does no better than one who knows it. An attacker that ignores the record sees the IN and OUT distributions averaged over all records, where the large shift of an atypical record is diluted among the small shifts of the typical ones. The bell-curve shape is justified because, by Lemma 10.1, \(\phi_z\) is linear in the weights. The regularized estimate \(\theta\) sets the gradient of the training objective to zero, and that gradient averages \(n\) independent per-record terms, so \(\theta\) is approximately Gaussian over the training randomness, by the central limit theorem that Section G.6 proves for such estimates. So \(\phi_z\) is close to normal, and for deep networks Carlini et al. found the same.
Offline LiRA is a weaker test, because without IN models it cannot write down \(q_z\). It only asks whether \(\phi_z\) lies unusually far above its OUT values, the direction in which training on \(z\) moves it, since fitting \(z\) raises its margin. The two scores can be compared exactly in the simplest case, where the IN and OUT fits have the same standard deviation \(\sigma_z\). Write \(t_z\) for the offline score, the output measured in units of \(\sigma_z\) from the OUT mean. Then \(t_z\) is standard normal under OUT, and under IN it is normal with variance 1 and mean the separation \[s_z = \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}}{\sigma_z}. \tag{10.9}\] Measured in \(t_z\), the OUT density is proportional to \(e^{-t_z^2/2}\) and the IN density to \(e^{-(t_z - s_z)^2/2}\), with the same constant, which cancels in Equation 10.6. Expanding the square leaves \(\ln\Lambda_z = s_zt_z - s_z^2/2\). For one record \(s_z\) is a fixed positive number, so both scores rank that record’s outputs alike. Across records they differ, because online LiRA weights each \(t_z\) by \(s_z\), while offline LiRA treats every \(t_z\) the same.
How much each record can be caught at a given FPR is then a question about two unit-variance Gaussians. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function, so that \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\) is the point a standard normal exceeds with probability \(\alpha\). Theorem 4.3 in Hypothesis testing shows that when an observation is \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) in one world and \(\mathcal N(s, 1)\) in the other, the most members any test can catch at FPR \(\alpha\) is \[\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s\big). \tag{10.10}\] At \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\) the cut-off is 3.0902. With a separation of 0.5, a member must still clear \(3.0902 - 0.5 = 2.59\) standard deviations above its own mean, so the TPR is \(1 - \Phi(2.59) = 0.0048\). With a separation of 4, the cut-off sits below the member mean, and the TPR is \(1 - \Phi(-0.91) = 0.8185\).

Example 10.3 On a population with two kinds of record, this formula shows in closed form how much the per-record comparison gains (Table 10.1). A typical record is predicted confidently whether or not the model trained on it. An atypical record has a negative \(\phi\), which means it is misclassified, unless the model trained on it.

Now set three attacks to an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) pooled over both kinds, that is, counted over all non-members together.
One threshold on \(\phi\) is the loss attack. Typical records make up 95% of non-members and their OUT values are high, so the threshold must sit high. Solving for the point that 0.1% of all non-members exceed puts it at \(\phi = 6.075\). Atypical members score around 2 and almost never pass it. Only typical members occasionally do, and the pooled TPR is 0.0048. That matches the typical kind’s best TPR alone, because typical records dominate the non-members, so the threshold sits almost where the typical kind alone would put it, at \(3 + 3.0902\).
One threshold on the z-score is offline LiRA. Each record is standardized against its own OUT distribution, so every record gets FPR \(10^{-3}\), at \(t \ge 3.0902\). Each kind then gets its own best TPR from the table, and the pooled TPR is their weighted average, \(0.95 \times 0.0048 + 0.05 \times 0.8185 = 0.0455\).
One threshold on \(\ln\Lambda\) is online LiRA. A one-dimensional numerical search for a pooled FPR of \(10^{-3}\) puts the threshold at 1.497. Since \(\ln\Lambda = st - s^2/2\), the cut \(\ln\Lambda \ge 1.497\) is the z-score cut \(t \ge (1.497 + s^2/2)/s\). That is \(t \ge 3.244\) for typical records, with an FPR of only \(5.90\times10^{-4}\). For atypical ones it is \(t \ge 2.374\), with FPR 0.0088. The pooled FPR is \(0.95 \times 5.90\times10^{-4} + 0.05 \times 0.0088 = 10^{-3}\), and the pooled TPR is 0.0503, the best possible at that FPR by Theorem 10.1.
The global threshold is ten times worse than either per-record test. The likelihood ratio beats the z-score because it spends its allowance of false positives where they pay. A typical record’s IN and OUT curves overlap, so admitting more of its false positives admits almost no extra members. An atypical record’s curves lie far apart, so a few more false positives there admit many members.


Example 10.4 Figure 10.2 shows the IN and OUT distributions of a typical point and an outlier of the running example. On the 128 target models, online LiRA reaches a TPR of 0.0149 at FPR \(10^{-3}\), against 0.0009 for the loss attack (Table 10.3).
With few shadow models, each record’s estimated standard deviations are noisy, and the noise hurts most at a low FPR. A record whose spread is underestimated has its OUT curve drawn too narrow, so an ordinary output looks far out in the tail and becomes a false positive at a strict threshold. Carlini et al. therefore recommend a global variance when shadow models are few: one IN variance and one OUT variance, each the average over all records (Figure 10.3 compares online and offline LiRA, each with both kinds of variance). With 16 shadow models, online LiRA with variances per record reaches 0.0023, barely above chance, while with a global variance it reaches 0.0151.







Figure 10.2: The logit \(\phi\) of one point over the 64 shadow models, split into the 32 that trained on it (IN) and the 32 that did not (OUT), with the fitted Gaussians. Left: a typical point, whose two distributions overlap. Right: an outlier, which the models predict wrongly unless they trained on it.









Figure 10.3: TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) of four LiRA variants on the 128 target models, as the attacker uses the first 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 of its shadow models. With a global variance the attack is strong even with few shadow models; with a variance per record it needs many. The dotted line is the loss attack, which needs no shadow models.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.4 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
text:
10.4 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
Older papers report an attack’s accuracy, which is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\) in the membership game, or its AUC, and both average over all members and non-members. This section asks which number says whether an attack is a threat, starting from the fact that a privacy breach is not an average. It happens when an attacker can say with confidence that a particular person was in the data, and that needs a low FPR, where almost every “member” verdict is right.

Definition 10.4 (TPR at a low FPR) An attack’s TPR at FPR \(\alpha\) is the height of its ROC curve at \(\alpha\), the largest fraction of members it flags with a threshold that flags at most a fraction \(\alpha\) of non-members. Carlini et al. (2022) report it at a low \(\alpha\) such as \(10^{-3}\), together with the whole ROC curve on log axes.

Two attacks can have the same AUC and best advantages (the largest TPR − FPR over all thresholds) within 0.015 of each other, yet TPRs at FPR \(10^{-3}\) that differ by a factor of 38. In the pair below, attack A exposes a few members completely and learns nothing about anyone else, while attack B learns a little about everyone.

Proposition 10.3 (Same AUC, different exposure) Let \(r \in (0, 1)\) be a fraction of members. Attack A gives a fraction \(r\) of members a score above every other record’s, and gives every other record, member or not, a random score from one common distribution. Attack B gives members a score \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) and non-members a score \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), with \(\mu > 0\). Then A has AUC \(\frac12 + \frac r2\), best advantage \(r\) and \[\mathrm{TPR}_A(\alpha) = r + (1 - r)\alpha, \tag{10.11}\] while B has AUC \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\), best advantage \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), and the TPR of Equation 10.10 with \(s = \mu\). The two AUCs are equal when \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2) = \frac12 + \frac r2\).


Proof. The plan is to compute each attack’s AUC from its definition as a ranking probability, A’s TPR by splitting members into recognized and not, and B’s best advantage from the total variation distance.

AUC of A. The AUC is the probability that a random member outscores a random non-member, with ties counted as one half (Proposition 4.2). With probability \(r\) the member is a recognized one, and it wins. Otherwise both scores have the same distribution, so the member wins with probability \(\frac12\). The total is \(r + (1 - r)\frac12 = \frac12 + \frac r2\).
TPR of A. At a threshold with FPR \(\alpha\), the recognized members always pass. The other members have the same score distribution as non-members, so they pass with the same probability \(\alpha\), which gives \(\mathrm{TPR}_A(\alpha)\). Then \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = r(1 - \alpha)\), which is at most \(r\).
AUC of B. A member outscores a non-member when the difference of their scores is positive. That difference is \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) minus an independent \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), so it is normal with mean \(\mu\) and variance 2, and it is positive with probability \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\).
Advantage of B. The best advantage of a test between two distributions is their total variation distance, the most by which the two can differ in the probability of one set of scores (Theorem 4.5). The best set is where the member density exceeds the non-member density, which for two unit-variance Gaussians at distance \(\mu\) is the scores above the midpoint \(\mu/2\). Its TPR is \(\Phi(\mu/2)\) and its FPR is \(1 - \Phi(\mu/2)\), and their difference is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\).


With \(r = 0.05\), both AUCs are 0.5250 when \(\mu = 0.0887\) (Table 10.2). At FPR \(10^{-3}\), A has TPR \(0.05 + 0.95 \times 10^{-3} = 0.05095\), while B has \(1 - \Phi(3.0902 - 0.0887) = 0.00134\), which is 38 times less.

Who is exposed matters more than how many. Only the low-FPR end of the ROC curve shows the difference, and only on log axes, since linear axes squeeze everything below FPR 0.01 into one pixel column (Figure 10.4).
Measuring a low FPR takes many non-members. An FPR is estimated by counting false positives, and a count of \(k\) events has a relative error of about \(1/\sqrt k\) (Hypothesis testing). To see \(k\) false positives at FPR \(\alpha\) you need about \(k/\alpha\) non-members, which is why the running example uses 64,000 non-member pairs.
A low FPR makes the verdicts reliable. With as many members as non-members, the precision, the fraction of “member” verdicts that are right, is \(\mathrm{TPR}/(\mathrm{TPR} + \mathrm{FPR})\), so a TPR of 0.05 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) gives \(0.05/0.051 = 0.98\).

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.5 Why outliers are most exposed
Example 10.3 showed that the low-FPR end of the ROC curve is made of the records with a large separation between their IN and OUT distributions. This section asks which records those are, and finds that they are the ones the model cannot predict without having seen them.

Proposition 10.4 (Exposure of one record) Let the IN and OUT distributions of \(\phi_z\) for a record \(z\) be Gaussian, with means \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) and a common standard deviation \(\sigma_z\). The best TPR of any test on \(z\) alone at FPR \(\alpha\) is \[\mathrm{TPR}_z(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s_z\big), \qquad s_z = \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}}{\sigma_z}, \tag{10.12}\] and the numerator \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) is the self-influence of \(z\) measured in \(\phi\): the average amount by which training on \(z\) raises the model’s \(\phi\) on \(z\).


Proof. 

The test. Standardizing the output, as in Section 10.3, gives a standard normal under OUT and \(\mathcal N(s_z, 1)\) under IN. So Equation 10.10 with \(s = s_z\) is the best TPR.
Self-influence. Definition 7.3 defines the self-influence of a training record \(z_i\) as \(\ell(\theta_{D^{(i)}}; z_i) - \ell(\theta_D; z_i)\). That is the loss of the model trained on \(D^{(i)}\), the training set with \(z_i\) replaced by a fresh record, minus the loss of the model trained on \(D\) itself. Measured with \(\phi\) instead of \(\ell\), the sign flips, because \(\phi\) rises where the loss falls.
Average it. Take \(z_i = z\) and average over the rest of the training set, the fresh record and the training run. The models trained on \(D\) contain \(z\), so they give \(\phi_z\) the mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z}\). The models trained on \(D^{(i)}\) do not, so they give \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\). The averaged self-influence in \(\phi\) is the difference of the two means.


Which records have a large self-influence? If the rest of the data already predict \(z\)’s label, \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) is high and training on \(z\) adds little. If they predict the opposite label, \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) is low, and the model must move toward \(z\) to fit it. The regularization limits how far the model can move. By Theorem 7.2, one record moves the weights of a regularized fit by at most \(2G/(\lambda n)\), where \(G\) bounds the length of a record’s loss gradient, and its proof shows that each record’s pull scales with the length of its own gradient. For logistic regression that gradient is \(x\) times a probability, so the pull of \(z\) scales with at most \(\|x_z\|\). A move of the weights changes the margin \(\phi_z = y\langle \theta, x_z\rangle\) by at most \(\|x_z\|\) times the length of the move. So a long \(x_z\) both pulls the weights harder and turns that pull into a larger change in its own margin, and the outliers of the running example have long features and unpredictable labels.
Leakage is concentrated. The loss attack’s advantage reflects the average self-influence, while the low-FPR end of the ROC curve is governed by the largest ones, because a strict threshold is passed only by the records with the largest separations. So a model with a small generalization gap can still expose a few records completely. Memorizing them can even be what makes it accurate: Feldman (2020) shows that on long-tailed data, a rare subpopulation seen once in training must be memorized for good test accuracy.
Removing the outliers does not fix it. Carlini et al. (2022b) removed the most exposed records and retrained, and the next layer of records became exposed, which they call the privacy onion effect. Exposure is relative to the rest of the dataset, because a record’s OUT distribution depends on what the other records predict about it. A guarantee that protects every record, the subject of Part 3, has to bound the self-influence of the worst record, not the average.

The outliers’ part of that is \(0.05 \times 2.0999 \approx 0.105\), a share of 0.552 of the total, from 5% of the points.
Outliers are the true positives. At FPR \(10^{-3}\), online LiRA flags 26% of outlier members and 0.2% of typical members. Each target model has about 25 outlier members and 475 typical members, so it finds about \(0.26 \times 25 = 6.5\) outliers and \(0.002 \times 475 = 0.95\) typical points, and over the 128 target models a share of 0.873 of the members it finds are outliers. title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.6 The full-size pipeline: LiRA on CIFAR-10
text:
10.6 The full-size pipeline: LiRA on CIFAR-10
The usual full-scale experiment runs LiRA with 16 shadow models on an image classifier for CIFAR-10, a benchmark of small colour images in ten classes. This section states the protocol and what changes at full size. The running example is this protocol at small scale, with logistic regression in place of a ResNet, a deep convolutional network.

Definition 10.5 (The LiRA evaluation protocol) The protocol has six steps.

Data split. Take the 50,000 CIFAR-10 training images as the pool, and give every model, target and shadows alike, a random half of it. One model plays the target and the others the shadows, and rotating the target gives many pairs to evaluate.
Training. Train every model with the target’s recipe, including its architecture (wide ResNets), optimizer, epochs and data augmentation, which is what gives the shadow pairs the target’s distribution (Proposition 10.2, step 1).
Statistic. For each model and image, compute the network’s raw class scores \(f\) on the image and on a few augmented copies, such as horizontal flips and small shifts. Convert each to \(\phi\) as \(f_y\) minus the log of the sum of \(e^{f_{y'}}\) over the other classes. This equals \(\ln(p_y/(1 - p_y))\), because the softmax sets \(p_y = e^{f_y}/\sum_{y'} e^{f_{y'}}\), but it never forms \(1 - p_y\), a number that rounds to 0 for a confident model.
Fits. For each image, fit IN and OUT Gaussians over the shadow models, with one mean per augmented copy and variances per record or global.
Scores. For each target model and image, compute the online score Equation 10.6 or the offline score Equation 10.7.
Evaluation. Pool all pairs of target model and image, sweep one threshold, and plot the ROC curve on log axes. Report the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\), with the number of non-member pairs it rests on.


With 16 shadow models, use a global variance, because each image is then out of only about 8 shadows, and Figure 10.3 shows that variances per record from so few values fail at the low-FPR end.
Carlini et al. report that online LiRA is about ten times more powerful than earlier attacks at a low FPR on CIFAR-10, and that the loss attack is close to chance there, as Table 10.3 shows in miniature. The auditing part of the book reuses this pipeline to measure privacy leakage. A privately trained model takes the place of the target, and inserted canaries, records such as mislabelled images chosen to be as exposed as possible, play the members.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 The attribute inference game
A hospital trains a model that predicts whether a patient will develop a lung disease from their age band and whether they smoke, and lets anyone query it. An insurer knows your age and, from a claim, that you have the disease. Can it use the model to find out whether you smoke? It can make a better guess than it could without the model, but that alone is not a privacy failure. If smokers get the disease more often, a published study would allow the same guess about everyone with the disease, whether or not their record was used. The question that matters for you is different: does the model reveal more about your attribute because your record was in its training data?
Attribute inference is the attack that recovers one sensitive field of a record, such as smoking status, a genotype or an income band, from the record’s other fields and access to a model. The one idea of this chapter is to compare every such attack with the imputation baseline, the success of a guesser who never sees the model but knows the population’s exact joint distribution of attributes, features and labels. A model trained without your record was built from other people’s data, so it can teach an attacker only what holds for the population at large, nothing about you beyond that. The chapter proves that, as a result, no attack beats the baseline on records outside the training set. Only on training records can an attack beat it, and that excess is the leak about individuals. The excess is a difference between the success on people who were in the training set and on people who were not, so attribute inference is a membership question in disguise, which ties this chapter to Membership inference.
The running example has two layers. A small smoking table, in which 30% of the population smokes, shows the baseline exactly: the best guess from age and diagnosis is right with probability 0.748, against 0.7 with no observation at all. A toy population with ten numeric features then shows an attack crossing the baseline. Its baseline is 0.7517, and the model inversion attack of Section 11.3, run against a logistic regression trained on 100 of its records, is right on 0.7832 of the training records, above that baseline, but on only 0.7262 of fresh records.
A claim such as “the attack recovered 78% of smoking statuses” means nothing until you know two more numbers. One is how often the attribute could be guessed without the model, and the other is how often the attack succeeds on people outside the training set. This section sets up the game of Yeom et al. (2018), a two-world game like those of Threat models, which measures the second and compares it with the success on people inside the training set. A challenger flips a coin to decide whether the target comes from the training set or fresh from the population. The coin is not a real-world event, but a way to run both situations under one set of rules, so that the attack’s success in one can be compared with its success in the other. The score subtracts the success on non-members from the success on members, and Section 11.2 proves that this difference is what the model reveals about its training records beyond the population.
Any attribute attack can be turned into a membership attack. If the attribute attack is right more often on members, then “the attack was right” is itself evidence of membership. A membership adversary may check this, because the membership game of Membership inference hands it the whole record, sensitive field included, and asks only whether the record was used. A membership attack is described by two rates. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the probability that it says “member” for a member, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the probability that it says “member” for a non-member. Its advantage is TPR minus FPR.
Membership attacks also have a known ceiling, which the reduction below, Proposition 11.1, passes on to every attribute attack. Hypothesis testing proves that no test, randomized or not, has an advantage above the total variation distance \(\mathrm{TV}\) between the two distributions it must tell apart. That distance is half the sum (an integral for continuous outcomes), over all outcomes, of the absolute differences between their two probabilities.
The subtraction in Equation 11.1 is what makes the advantage a measure of privacy. Success that comes from knowing the population, such as “people with the disease tend to smoke”, is the same for members and non-members, as Proposition 11.2 below proves, so it cancels. The cancelled part still matters to the people attacked, so report the success on members and on non-members as well, as a membership attack reports its TPR and FPR. The reduction also says that a model with no membership leak has no attribute leak. If \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\) are equal, Equation 11.3 forces the advantage of every attribute attack to 0. The converse fails. A model whose predictions do not depend on \(s\) at all gives no attribute attack anything to work with, yet it can still reveal who was in its training set, for example through a lower loss on its training records.
The membership test that the reduction builds is a weak one, though. It outputs a single bit, so all it can tell you is whether it fired, and how much a firing should raise your belief in membership is the likelihood ratio TPR/FPR, how many times more often it fires on members than on non-members. For an attack that is right on most of the population, members or not, that ratio is close to 1. To lower its FPR, a test that sees only this bit can only fire on a random share \(r\) of the right guesses. That multiplies both rates by \(r\), so the ratio stays near 1 and the TPR stays near the FPR. Membership inference judges attacks at a low FPR, because a few confident identifications are what harm people, and there the dedicated attacks do much better.
