title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
Definition 11.1 (The attribute inference game) Fix a training algorithm \(\mathcal T\), a population \(\mathcal D\), a training-set size \(n\) and an adversary \(\mathcal A\). The game has three steps.

The challenger draws a training set \(D \sim \mathcal D^n\) of \(n\) independent records from the population and trains a model \(\theta = \mathcal T(D)\) on it.
It draws a hidden bit \(b \in \{0, 1\}\), each value with probability \(\frac12\). If \(b = 1\), it picks the target \(z = (s, x, y)\) uniformly from \(D\), so the target is a member of the training set. If \(b = 0\), it draws \(z \sim \mathcal D\) afresh, so the target is a non-member.
The adversary receives the target’s public fields and label \((x, y)\), but not \(s\), and access to \(\theta\), either its weights or queries to it. It may also know the population \(\mathcal D\), fully or in part. This auxiliary knowledge is fixed before the game starts, so it is the same in both worlds. It outputs a guess \(\hat s\) of the sensitive attribute.

The attribute advantage of \(\mathcal A\) is its success rate on members minus its success rate on non-members, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}}(\mathcal A) = \Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 1] - \Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 0], \tag{11.1}\] where each probability is over everything random in the game.




Proposition 11.1 (Attribute advantage is membership advantage) Let \(\mathcal A\) be an adversary in the game of Definition 11.1. Let \(\mathcal B\) be the membership adversary that receives the whole record \(z = (s, x, y)\) and \(\theta\), runs \(\mathcal A\) on \((x, y)\) and \(\theta\), and says “member” exactly when \(\hat s = s\). Then \[\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathcal B} - \mathrm{FPR}_{\mathcal B} = \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}}(\mathcal A). \tag{11.2}\] Write \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\) for the distributions of the pair \((z, \theta)\), the target together with the model, over the draw of the training set, the target and the training randomness, when \(z\) is a member and when it is not. Then every adversary satisfies \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}}(\mathcal A) \le \mathrm{TV}\big(P_{\mathrm{in}}, P_{\mathrm{out}}\big). \tag{11.3}\]


Proof. The plan is to read off the two rates of \(\mathcal B\), subtract them, and then apply the bound by total variation.

The membership test fires when the guess is right. \(\mathcal B\) is given \(s\), so it can check whether \(\hat s = s\), and it says “member” on exactly that event.
Its two rates. The TPR is the probability of “member” when \(b = 1\), and “member” means that the guess was right, so the TPR is \(\Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 1]\). In the same way, the FPR is \(\Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 0]\).
Subtract. TPR minus FPR is then the right-hand side of Equation 11.1, term by term.
Bound by total variation. \(\mathcal B\) sees exactly the pair \((z, \theta)\), and it runs \(\mathcal A\) with the same auxiliary knowledge in both worlds, so it is a test between \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\), randomized by \(\mathcal A\)’s coins. Its advantage is therefore at most \(\mathrm{TV}(P_{\mathrm{in}}, P_{\mathrm{out}})\), and step 3 turns that into Equation 11.3.





Example 11.1 The toy experiment of this chapter (Section 11.5) has a binary sensitive attribute with prior \(\Pr[s = 1] = 0.3\), ten public features and a binary label. A logistic regression that keeps a separate weight vector for each value of \(s\), and predicts a record’s label with the vector of its \(s\), is trained on \(n = 100\) records, and this is repeated 200 times. Each time, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) inversion attack, which Section 11.3 defines and which queries the model at each candidate value of \(s\), guesses \(s\) for the 100 members and for 100 fresh records. It is right on 0.7832 of members and 0.7262 of non-members. The attribute advantage is their difference, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = 0.7832 - 0.7262 \approx 0.0569, \tag{11.4}\] where the last digit comes from the unrounded rates. The standard error of this average over the 200 models is 0.0045.
Read as a membership test, the same attack has TPR 0.7832 at FPR 0.7262. Its likelihood ratio when it fires is \(0.7832/0.7262 = 1.08\), so being right is barely more likely for a member than for a non-member. Its balanced accuracy is the average of its accuracy on members, the TPR, and on non-members, one minus the FPR. That average is \(\frac12(\mathrm{TPR} + 1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = \frac12 + \frac12(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR})\), one half plus half the advantage, here \(\frac12 + \frac12 \times 0.0569 = 0.5285\), hardly better than the \(\frac12\) of a coin flip. The attack is right on 0.7262 of people whose records the model never saw, so most of its 78% success would be there even if the person had never been in the training data.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 The imputation baseline
The game removes population inference by subtracting it. This section measures it directly, because it is the part of an attack’s success that any model trained on the same population would give, and so would published statistics about that population. The measure is the success of the best guess of \(s\) from \((x, y)\) by someone who knows the population distribution exactly. Statisticians call filling in a missing field from the others imputation, so this is the imputation baseline. Jayaraman & Evans (2022) found that many published attribute inference attacks do no better than imputation fitted on similar data, a practical estimate of this exact baseline, and argued that this is the baseline an attack must beat.
The best guess has a simple form. Whatever you answer after an observation is right exactly when the true \(s\) is your answer, so the best answer is the value of \(s\) with the largest joint probability \(p(s, o)\) with that observation, which is also the value with the largest posterior \(p(s \mid o)\). Information theory proves that this MAP guess beats every deterministic guessing rule. A randomized rule picks a deterministic rule with coins independent of the secret, so its success is an average of theirs and never above the best one.

Definition 11.2 (Vulnerability and the imputation baseline) Let \(S\) be a secret and \(O\) an observation with joint probability \(p(s, o)\). The vulnerability of \(S\) given \(O\) is the success of the MAP guess \(\arg\max_s p(s \mid o)\). Since \(p(s, o) = p(o)\,p(s \mid o)\) and the factor \(p(o)\) does not depend on \(s\), it can be summed as the largest joint probability per observation or averaged as the largest posterior: \[V(S \mid O) = \sum_o\max_s p(s, o) = \mathbb E_O\Big[\max_s p(s \mid O)\Big]. \tag{11.5}\] With \(S\), \(X\) and \(Y\) the sensitive attribute, features and label of a record drawn from \(\mathcal D\), the imputation baseline is \(V(S \mid X, Y)\). With no observation, the vulnerability is \(V(S) = \max_s p(s)\).

For continuous features the sum becomes an integral, while the second form, an average over records, covers both cases. For a concrete case, take no observation and a prior of 0.3 on smoking. The rule “always say non-smoker” is right 70% of the time and “always say smoker” 30%, so \(V(S) = 0.7\).
On a non-member, the model was trained without the target, so beyond what the adversary already knows about the population it should help no more than a coin the adversary flips before guessing. Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 11.1, below, needs that idea made precise: an observation that is independent of the secret cannot raise the best success.

Lemma 11.1 (An independent observation is useless) If an observation \(U\) is independent of the pair \((S, O)\), then \(V(S \mid O, U) = V(S \mid O)\).


Proof. 

Independence factorizes the joint. Independence means that the probabilities multiply, \(p(s, o, u) = p(s, o)\,p(u)\).
Pull \(p(u)\) out of the maximum. The factor \(p(u)\) is not negative and does not depend on \(s\), so Definition 11.2 with the observation \((o, u)\) gives \[V(S \mid O, U) = \sum_{o, u}\max_s p(s, o)\,p(u) = \sum_u p(u)\sum_o\max_s p(s, o). \tag{11.6}\]
The weights add up to one. The inner sum is \(V(S \mid O)\), and the \(p(u)\) sum to 1, so the whole is \(V(S \mid O)\).


The lemma turns the model into a useless observation for a fresh target. The best any adversary can do on a non-member is then the best guess from \((x, y)\) alone, which gives the non-member ceiling.

Theorem 11.1 (The non-member ceiling) For every adversary in the game of Definition 11.1, the success on non-members is at most the imputation baseline: \[\Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 0] \le V(S \mid X, Y) = \sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y). \tag{11.7}\] The bound also holds for an adversary that sees the whole training set \(D\) instead of the model, so even publishing the training data reveals nothing about outsiders beyond the population.


Proof. 

A non-member is independent of the model. When \(b = 0\), the target \(z\) is drawn afresh, separately from \(D\). The model depends only on \(D\) and the randomness of training, so \(\theta\) is independent of \(z = (s, x, y)\), and so is \(D\) itself. The adversary’s auxiliary knowledge and its own coins are fixed before the target is drawn, so they are independent of \(z\) too.
So the model is a useless observation. Lemma 11.1 with \(O = (X, Y)\) and \(U = \theta\) (or \(U = D\)) gives \(V(S \mid X, Y, \theta) = V(S \mid X, Y)\).
No rule beats the MAP guess. The adversary’s rule is a function of \((x, y, \theta)\), possibly randomized. By the optimality of the MAP guess, recalled before Definition 11.2, its success is at most the vulnerability given that observation, which step 2 showed is \(V(S \mid X, Y)\).


The ceiling is about non-members, while the next result is about attacks that never look at the model, on both kinds of target. A training record, picked at random from a training set drawn from the population, looks exactly like a fresh draw if you ignore the model, so such an attack cannot tell the two worlds apart.

Proposition 11.2 (Model-free attacks have zero advantage) If the guess \(\hat s = g(x, y)\) depends on \((x, y)\) only, and not on \(\theta\), then \(\Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 1] = \Pr[\hat s = s \mid b = 0]\). The Bayes imputation guess \(\arg\max_s p(s \mid x, y)\), which is the MAP guess of Definition 11.2 under the true population, has success exactly \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) in both worlds, so it attains the ceiling Equation 11.7 on non-members.


Proof. 

A member is a population record. \(D\) consists of \(n\) independent draws from \(\mathcal D\), and the target is one of them, chosen uniformly at random. Whichever one is chosen was drawn from \(\mathcal D\), so on its own, ignoring the model, the target has distribution \(\mathcal D\), the same as a fresh draw.
A rule that ignores \(\theta\) sees one distribution. Its success is \(\Pr[g(X, Y) = S]\) for a record drawn from \(\mathcal D\) in either world, so the two terms of Equation 11.1 are equal and the advantage is 0.
Imputation reaches the ceiling. With \(g\) the MAP guess under \(\mathcal D\), this common success is \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) by Definition 11.2.


On non-members, then, the model only teaches you the population. An adversary who does not know \(\mathcal D\) can learn it from the model, and so raise its success on non-members towards \(V(S \mid X, Y)\), but no further. This does not contradict Lemma 11.1, which takes the population as known: the model teaches what is true of everyone, never anything about this target beyond it. The smoking example in Dwork & Roth (2014, §1) makes the same point. A study that shows smoking causes cancer lets an insurer infer more about any smoker’s health, whether or not that smoker took part. The study disclosed a fact about the world, not about its participants, and a privacy definition that forbade this would forbid learning anything from data.
That does not make population inference harmless, since being guessed to be a smoker hurts whether or not the guess used your record. But no protection that limits what one record can change, such as differential privacy in Part 3, can prevent it, because the harm would be there with your record removed. Preventing it is a matter for policy and fairness, not for the defences against the attacks of this part. The ceiling is also a property of the population, not of the model, and it can be high. If \(x\) and \(y\) nearly determine \(s\), every model and every statistic about the population “reveals” \(s\), which is why attacks should be reported relative to it.

Example 11.2 Let \(s = 1\) mean “smoker”, \(x\) the age band (young or old) and \(y = 1\) “has the disease”. The population has \(\Pr[s = 1] = 0.3\). Among non-smokers a fraction \(\Pr[\text{old} \mid s = 0] = 0.4\) is old, and among smokers a fraction \(0.6\). The disease probabilities \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x, s]\) are 0.1 (young non-smoker), 0.3 (old non-smoker), 0.4 (young smoker) and 0.7 (old smoker). The probability of a full record is the chance of the smoking status, times the chance of the age band given it, times the chance of the disease outcome given both. Multiplying gives the joint table, Table 11.2. For example, \(p(\text{smoker}, \text{old}, \text{disease}) = 0.3 \times 0.6 \times 0.7 = 0.126\), and \(p(\text{non-smoker}, \text{young}, \text{no disease}) = 0.7 \times 0.6 \times 0.9 = 0.378\).

The last row is each column’s smoker entry divided by the column total. For young people with the disease, it is \(0.048/(0.042 + 0.048) = 0.5333\). Now watch the best guess improve as the guesser sees more.
With no observation, the best guess is “non-smoker”, right with probability \(V(S) = 0.7\).
With age alone, the guesser adds the two disease columns of each age band. The two disease probabilities add to 1, so each sum is the prior times the age probability. Young smokers have probability \(0.3 \times 0.4 = 0.12\) and young non-smokers \(0.7 \times 0.6 = 0.42\), so a young person is a smoker with probability \(0.12/0.54 = 0.2222\). Old smokers have \(0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18\) and old non-smokers \(0.7 \times 0.4 = 0.28\), so an old person is a smoker with probability \(0.18/0.46 = 0.3913\). Both are below \(\frac12\), so the guess stays “non-smoker” in both age bands and \(V(S \mid X) = 0.7\). Age changes the odds but never the decision, so it adds nothing to the success.
With age and disease, the posterior crosses \(\frac12\) in the two disease columns (Figure 11.1), so the MAP guess becomes “smoker” there. The success is the sum of the largest entry in each column, the bold ones, so \(V(S \mid X, Y) = 0.378 + 0.048 + 0.196 + 0.126 = 0.748\). The entry a guess misses in each column is the one not in bold, and the largest of these is the 0.084 of old non-smokers with the disease.
The min-entropy leakage of Information theory turns this gain into bits, a unit that compares leaks of secrets with different priors. It is the base-2 logarithm of how many times more likely the best guess is to succeed with the observation than without. Here seeing age and disease raises the success from 0.7 to 0.748 (age alone added nothing), a leakage of \(\log_2(0.748/0.7) = 0.0957\) bits.
Every one of these numbers comes from the population. A model trained on 10,000 patients from it, if it predicts well, lets an insurer reach 0.748 on anyone drawn from the population. The ceiling Equation 11.7 says that nobody outside the training set can be attacked more successfully than that.







Figure 11.1: The posterior probability of smoking in each cell of the smoking table, with each cell’s probability in brackets. Red bars cross \(\frac12\), where imputation guesses “smoker”. Switching these two cells to “smoker” gains \((0.048 - 0.042) + (0.126 - 0.084) = 0.048\) over the 0.7 of the blind guess.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 Model inversion
The imputation baseline assumes a guesser who knows the population exactly, and a real adversary does not. In particular, it usually does not know \(p(y \mid x, s)\), the link between the label and the sensitive attribute, and Bayes’ rule needs that link to compute the posterior of \(s\). But a model that predicts \(y\) from \(x\) and \(s\) is an estimate of exactly that link. Fredrikson et al. (2014) used this on a linear model that predicted the stable dose of the drug warfarin from demographics and two genetic markers, so that an adversary who knew a patient’s demographics and dose could infer their genotype. They called the attack model inversion, running the model “backwards” from its output to an input. This section states the attack as Bayes’ rule and shows when it is no more than imputation.
By Bayes’ rule, written out in the proof of Proposition 11.3, the value of \(s\) that best explains what you see has the largest product of two factors. The first is how plausible \(s\) is for someone with these features, and the second is how likely the observed label is if the attribute were \(s\). The adversary supplies the first factor from what it knows about the population. It gets the second by querying the model with each candidate value of \(s\), and Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) showed that models releasing confidences, the predicted probability of each label, make this much more effective, because a confidence says how likely the label is under each candidate, not just which label wins.

Definition 11.3 (MAP model inversion) Let \(p(s \mid x)\) be what the adversary knows about how \(s\) relates to the public features, and let \(f_y(x, s)\) be the model’s confidence in the observed label \(y\) when it is fed the candidate \(s\). The MAP inversion attack guesses \[\hat s_{\mathrm{inv}}(x, y) = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.8}\]

Fredrikson et al. (2014) used the marginal \(p(s)\) in place of \(p(s \mid x)\), which treats \(s\) as independent of \(x\). That throws away the evidence \(x\) carries about \(s\) and loses success even with a perfect model.
Even with \(p(s \mid x)\), a perfect model gives the attack nothing beyond imputation. If the model’s confidences were exactly the population’s probabilities, the second factor would be the true likelihood. This chapter calls a model with that property calibrated, a stronger demand than the usual meaning of calibration, that among inputs given confidence 0.7 about 70% have the label. For a calibrated model the attack is the imputation guess.

Proposition 11.3 (For a calibrated model, inversion is imputation) Suppose the adversary’s \(p(s \mid x)\) is the population’s, and that for every training set the model satisfies \(f_y(x, s) = p(y \mid x, s)\) for all \(s\), \(x\) and \(y\), so that its answers do not depend on which records it was trained on. Then \(\hat s_{\mathrm{inv}}\) is the Bayes imputation guess of Proposition 11.2. Its success is \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) on members and non-members alike.


Proof. The plan is to write the posterior of \(s\) by Bayes’ rule, drop the factor that does not depend on \(s\), substitute the model, and then apply the result on model-free attacks.

Bayes’ rule. The joint probability of \(s\) and \(y\) given \(x\) can be built in two stages, first \(s\) from \(x\) and then \(y\) from both, so \(p(s, y \mid x) = p(s \mid x)\,p(y \mid x, s)\). Dividing by \(p(y \mid x)\) turns it into the posterior of \(s\): \[p(s \mid x, y) = \frac{p(s \mid x)\,p(y \mid x, s)}{p(y \mid x)}. \tag{11.9}\]
The denominator does not depend on \(s\). It is the same number for every candidate, so it cannot change which candidate is largest. The MAP guess is therefore \(\arg\max_s p(s \mid x)\,p(y \mid x, s)\).
Plug in the model. Replacing the unknown \(p(y \mid x, s)\) by the model’s estimate \(f_y(x, s)\) gives Equation 11.8. For a calibrated model the replacement changes nothing, so \(\hat s_{\mathrm{inv}}\) is the MAP guess, with success \(V(S \mid X, Y)\).
Members and non-members. The guess uses \(\theta\) only through answers that are the same for every training set, so it is a fixed function of \((x, y)\). It is a model-free attack, so Proposition 11.2 gives equal success in both worlds.


Everything the attack does well or badly therefore comes from how the model’s \(f_y(x, s)\) differs from the population’s \(p(y \mid x, s)\), and the difference helps the attack on members and hurts it on non-members. On members, the model is too sure of the truth. Training lowers the log-loss \(-\ln f_y(x, s)\) on each training record at its true \(s\), which pushes \(f_y(x, s)\) up towards 1. The other candidate value \(s'\) was never paired with this record during training, so \(f_y(x, s')\) stays closer to an honest prediction. In the toy model the record never touches the weights used at \(s'\), because each value of \(s\) has its own weight vector. The ratio \(f_y(x, s)/f_y(x, s')\) that decides the attack is therefore tilted towards the truth for members. This is the generalization gap of Membership inference, the difference between a model’s loss on its training records and on fresh ones, seen through the sensitive attribute.
On non-members, an overfit model does worse than imputation. Its confidences carry the noise of a small training set rather than the population’s exact probabilities, so on some records its guess differs from the imputation guess, and by Theorem 11.1 no departure from imputation can win on average. More data closes both gaps, the excess on members and the shortfall on non-members. As \(n\) grows, a correctly specified model, one whose family contains the population’s \(p(y \mid x, s)\), approaches \(p(y \mid x, s)\), and both success rates approach \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) (Figure 11.3; Section G.6 in the appendices shows why the fit converges). The population inference on non-members gets better and the individual leak gets smaller.

Example 11.3 Start with a calibrated model on the smoking table, and take an old patient with the disease. From Example 11.2, the adversary knows \(\Pr[\text{smoker} \mid \text{old}] = 0.3913\), so \(\Pr[\text{non-smoker} \mid \text{old}] = 1 - 0.3913 = 0.6087\). It queries the model at both values of \(s\), and a calibrated model returns the population’s disease probabilities, \(f_1(\text{old}, \text{smoker}) = 0.7\) and \(f_1(\text{old}, \text{non-smoker}) = 0.3\). The scores of Equation 11.8 are \(0.3913 \times 0.7 = 0.2739\) for “smoker” and \(0.6087 \times 0.3 = 0.1826\) for “non-smoker”, so it guesses “smoker”. Dividing the smoker score by the sum of the two restores the normalization that step 2 of the proof dropped, and gives \(0.2739/(0.2739 + 0.1826) = 0.6000\), the posterior of Table 11.2. The attack is imputation.
The toy model shows what a trained model changes. Its population draws \(s\) with \(\Pr[s = 1] = 0.3\) and ten standard normal features, the first shifted by 0.5 when \(s = 1\). The label follows a logistic model with a different, fixed weight vector for each value of \(s\), listed in the script. Guessing from \(x\) alone is right 0.7045 of the time, and Bayes imputation, which knows the true logistic weights, is right 0.7517 of the time, both measured on a million fresh records. In the 200 games with \(n = 100\), imputation, which never looks at the models, is right on 0.7508 of the members and 0.7555 of the non-members. The difference, \(-0.0046\), is about one standard error of that difference from zero, as Proposition 11.2 predicts, and the 0.7555 on non-members sits above the ceiling of 0.7517 only by the same sampling noise.
The trained models overfit, with a mean log-loss of 0.2965 on members and 0.6690 on non-members. MAP inversion, given the population’s \(p(s \mid x)\) so that only the model’s contribution varies, and the trained models’ confidences, is right on 0.7832 of members, \(0.7832 - 0.7517 = 0.0315\) above the imputation ceiling, and on 0.7262 of non-members, 0.0254 below it (computed before rounding). The member success above the ceiling is something no population-level knowledge could produce, since the ceiling is the best that perfect population knowledge achieves.
Figure 11.2, from a separate, smaller run of 50 models that is enough to show the shape, shows where the excess on members comes from. It plots the attack’s evidence for the true value \(s\) over the other value \(s'\), the log of the ratio of their two scores, \(\ln\frac{p(s \mid x)f_y(x, s)}{p(s' \mid x)f_y(x, s')}\). The attack is right when this is positive. For members the distribution has a thinner left tail, because training has removed most of the cases where the model strongly prefers the wrong value.
Figure 11.3 repeats the game for training sets from 25 to 1600 records. At \(n = 25\) the attack is right on 0.8420 of members and 0.6810 of non-members, an advantage of \(0.8420 - 0.6810 = 0.1610\). At \(n = 400\) the advantage is 0.0111, and at \(n = 1600\) it is 0.0052.







Figure 11.2: The evidence of MAP inversion for the true attribute, the log of the score of the true value over the other, for members and non-members of 50 models trained on 100 records each. The attack is right when the evidence is positive; members have far fewer large negative values.









Figure 11.3: Success of MAP inversion on members and non-members against the training-set size \(n\), 40 models per point. Members start above the Bayes imputation ceiling and non-members below it; both converge to the ceiling as the model approaches the population.



The same idea can invert a whole input rather than one field. Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) also attacked a face recognition model in which each class is one person. They followed the gradient of a chosen class’s confidence with respect to the image, searching for the input that maximizes it, and obtained a recognizable, blurred image of that person. Here the whole input plays the role of \(s\). Nothing about the person is known beforehand, so an image regularizer that keeps the search among plausible images plays the role of the prior. What the attack recovers is a typical input of the class, which by this chapter’s measure is population inference about the class. It is still a privacy problem, because the class is a single person and its population is that person’s photos.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 Confidence masking
If confidences make inversion stronger, why release them? Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) suggested rounding the confidences an interface returns, and many deployed interfaces return only the top label. Such confidence masking is cheap and leaves the predicted label unchanged. This section asks whether it closes the leak. It shows that masking can never help the best attacker, but also that it need not shrink the gap between members and non-members.
Masking only coarsens what the adversary sees. The proof of Proposition 11.4 below needs the general form of that fact: whatever you compute from an observation, the best guess from the result is no better than the best guess from the observation itself.

Lemma 11.2 (Processing cannot help the best guesser) Let \(h\) be any function of an observation \(O\), possibly randomized with randomness independent of \((S, O)\). Then \(V\big(S \mid h(O)\big) \le V(S \mid O)\).


Proof. 

A rule on \(h(O)\) is a rule on \(O\). Whoever sees \(o\) can compute \(h(o)\), drawing any randomness itself, and then guess. So a rule \(g\) that guesses from \(h(o)\) is also a possibly randomized rule on \(o\), namely “apply \(h\), then \(g\)”.
No rule on \(O\) beats the MAP guess. By the optimality of the MAP guess recalled before Definition 11.2, none of the rules on \(O\) succeeds more often than \(V(S \mid O)\), and that includes every rule on \(h(O)\).


For example, rounding a confidence of 0.62 to 0.6 can only merge observations that a guesser could have told apart, and it never separates two that were the same. This is the guessing version of the data-processing inequality of Divergences.
To apply the lemma to masking, write \(f(x, s)\), without a label subscript, for the model’s whole vector of confidences over the labels at input \((x, s)\), whose entry for label \(y\) is \(f_y(x, s)\). Let \(F = \big(f(x, s)\big)_s\) be the list of these vectors that the adversary gets by querying the model at every candidate value of \(s\).

Proposition 11.4 (Masking cannot help the best attacker) Let \(h\) be any masking function applied to the answers \(F\), such as rounding, keeping only the top label or adding noise. In each world of the game separately, with \(V\) computed under that world’s joint distribution of the target and the model rather than under the population alone, the best attack on the masked answers does no better than the best attack on the full ones: \[V\big(S \mid X, Y, h(F)\big) \le V\big(S \mid X, Y, F\big). \tag{11.10}\]


Proof. 

A masked observation is a processed one. Anyone holding the full answers can apply the mask themselves, so \((x, y, h(F))\) is computed from \((x, y, F)\).
Apply the lemma. Lemma 11.2 with \(O = (X, Y, F)\) and the processing \((x, y, F) \mapsto (x, y, h(F))\) gives Equation 11.10. The argument never used which world the target came from, so it holds for \(b = 0\) and for \(b = 1\) separately.


The inequality says nothing about the difference between the two worlds, and labels alone still leak, because a label can still be checked at each candidate. With only the top label, the adversary still sees, for each candidate \(s\), whether the predicted label equals the known label \(y\), so the confidence factor of Equation 11.8 becomes 1 on a match and 0 otherwise. On a member, the model usually predicts the training label at the true \(s\), because it fit that record, while at the other value it gives an honest prediction that matches \(y\) less often. So a label that matches at only one candidate points to that candidate, and on members it usually points to the truth. A non-member rarely gets this help. Its two predicted labels usually agree, so both match or both miss, the confidence factors are equal, and the prior \(p(s \mid x)\) alone decides, which is the guess from \(x\) alone. This asymmetry is why masking hurts the population inference more than the individual leak.
Label-only membership inference (Choquette-Choo et al. 2021) exploits the same asymmetry between members and non-members.
Masking lowers the success in both worlds by amounts that depend on \(h\), and nothing forces the two drops to be equal, so the gap need not shrink, and Example 11.4 shows it growing. Do not read much into small changes either way. Equation 11.10 is about the optimal attacker, and MAP inversion with an overfit model is not optimal, so a particular mask can even raise its success slightly. Above all, masking is obfuscation, not a guarantee. It removes one attack’s input without bounding what any attack can learn about a member. Part 3 introduces differential privacy, which bounds the difference between members and non-members itself, for every attacker and every output format.

Example 11.4 The same 200 models as in Example 11.3, attacked through three interfaces, give Table 11.3 and Figure 11.4.

Rounding to one decimal changes almost nothing. The attack only compares the scores of the two candidates, and most confidences are far enough from the rounding boundaries that the comparison keeps its sign. With labels only, non-member success drops from 0.7262 to 0.7092, close to the 0.7045 of guessing from \(x\) alone. Member success drops less, to 0.7741, still \(0.7741 - 0.7517 = 0.0224\) above the imputation ceiling. So the advantage grows, from 0.0569 to 0.0650. The interface now leaks less about the population, while members are still guessed well above what the population allows.

11.5 Code
The script code/attribute_inference.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. It works out the smoking table exactly. For the toy model it samples the population and trains a ridge-regularized logistic regression with one weight vector per value of \(s\) by Newton’s method. It then plays the game, attacking the \(n\) members and \(n\) fresh non-members of each model with MAP inversion, Bayes imputation and the guess from \(x\) alone. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/attribute_inference.py

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 The property-inference game
A hospital trains a readmission model on its 1,000 patients and shares it with a research partner. Suppose you have checked that no attack on the model can tell, much better than a coin flip, whether any one patient was in the training set. The partner can still learn whether 45% or 55% of the hospital’s patients are over 65, and be right almost every time. That secret is not about a record but a property of the training set as a whole, a statistic of the dataset such as the fraction of records that belong to some subgroup. Property inference is the attack that recovers such a statistic from a trained model.
This chapter asks why an attacker can learn a property from a model when it cannot learn a record. The one idea is that a model behaves like a noisy average over its \(n\) records, which Section 12.3 makes precise for fitted models. Changing one record, whose values are bounded, moves an average by about \(1/n\), while the randomness of which records were sampled moves it by about \(1/\sqrt n\). So one record’s signal is about \(1/\sqrt n\) in units of the noise, and it shrinks as \(n\) grows. A property is different, because raising the subgroup’s share from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records at once, which together move the average by about the gap \(|t_1 - t_0|\). In units of the noise that is \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\), which grows with \(n\). So property inference gets easier with more data, while membership inference gets harder.
The running example is the hospital, whose records state each patient’s age group, and the secret is whether 45% or 55% of its patients are over 65. An attacker’s advantage is the probability that it answers “55%” when 55% is true minus the probability that it answers “55%” when 45% is true. At \(n = 1{,}000\), no attacker on any model trained on these records has advantage above 0.9985, a ceiling that simply publishing the number of patients over 65 reaches, while on the same published number the best attacker asking whether one patient took part has advantage 0.0126. Logistic regressions and small networks trained on a synthetic population then show the practical attack. Table 12.1 lists the symbols.
To ask whether an attacker can learn the property, you must fix who draws the data, what the attacker sees and knows, and how its guess is scored. Threat models and privacy games writes attacks as games between a challenger, who runs the training pipeline with a hidden secret, and an adversary, who tries to guess the secret (Salem et al. 2023). In the property game the secret is one bit, which of two subgroup shares the population that produced the training set has. This section sets up that game and finds its ceiling, against which every later attack is measured.
Records come from a population that mixes a majority group \(A\) and a subgroup \(B\). Write \(\mathcal D_A\) and \(\mathcal D_B\) for the distributions of a record from each group. A population in which a fraction \(t\) of people belong to \(B\) is the mixture \(\mathcal D_t = (1 - t)\mathcal D_A + t\,\mathcal D_B\). To draw a record from it, first pick \(B\) with probability \(t\) and \(A\) otherwise, then draw from that group.
With a fair bit, an attacker who learns nothing scores exactly \(\frac12\). Knowing \(\mathcal D_A\), \(\mathcal D_B\) and \(\mathcal T\) means, in practice, holding auxiliary data from both groups and being able to train models the way the victim does, as the attack of Section 12.3, which trains its own models on such data, requires. Suri & Evans (2022) call this game distribution inference.
An attack’s true positive rate \(\mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1]\) is how often it says 1 when the bit is 1, and its false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]\) is how often it says 1 when the bit is 0. Its advantage is \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\). Half the games have \(b = 1\), where the attacker wins with probability \(\mathrm{TPR}\), and half have \(b = 0\), where it wins with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). So its accuracy is
\[\Pr[b' = b] = \tfrac12\big(1 + \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\big). \tag{12.1}\]
Write \(P_{n,t}\) for the distribution of \(\theta\), over both the random data and the training randomness. Two results from Part 1 bound what the attacker can do. The first says that the best advantage at telling two distributions apart is their total variation (TV) distance, which is half the sum over all views of the absolute difference between their two probabilities, with an integral of densities in place of the sum for continuous views. The test that attains it says 1 wherever the second distribution is more likely than the first (Hypothesis testing).
The second result is the data processing inequality (Divergences). Passing a view through any random function whose behaviour does not depend on the secret cannot increase the TV distance between the view’s two distributions. Equality holds when the output is a sufficient statistic, meaning that the likelihood ratio of the view between the two worlds can be computed from the output alone. The best test only thresholds that ratio, so it loses nothing.
The model is computed from the data, so the attacker can never learn more from \(\theta\) than from \(D\) itself. When each record shows its group, the theorem also shows that only the count of subgroup records matters.
The theorem says that releasing the count is the worst case. When the group is visible in each record, no model trained on \(D\) can leak more about the share than the count does. A model that never takes the group as an input, like the logistic regression of Section 12.3, is still bound by this ceiling, since it is computed from the same records.
The ceiling bounds accuracy, which is also the right score here, because the secret belongs to a group, not a person. A membership attacker faces many targets, and exposing a few with high confidence is already a harm, so it is scored by its true positive rate at a low false positive rate, while here each dataset carries one secret.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
Definition 12.1 (Property-inference game) Fix a dataset size \(n\), two shares \(t_0 \ne t_1\), and a training algorithm \(\mathcal T\) that maps a dataset to parameters and may use random choices of its own, such as its initialization. The property-inference game runs in four steps.

The challenger draws a hidden bit \(b\), which is 0 or 1 with probability \(\frac12\) each.
It draws a dataset \(D \sim \mathcal D_{t_b}^n\) of \(n\) independent records and trains \(\theta = \mathcal T(D)\).
The adversary receives a view of \(\theta\): the parameters themselves (white-box), or the model’s predictions on inputs of its choosing (black-box). It knows \(\mathcal D_A\), \(\mathcal D_B\), \(n\), \(t_0\), \(t_1\) and \(\mathcal T\).
It outputs a guess \(b'\) and wins if \(b' = b\).









Theorem 12.1 (The ceiling on property inference) In the game of Definition 12.1, every adversary has \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \mathrm{TV}(P_{n,t_0}, P_{n,t_1}) \le \mathrm{TV}(\mathcal D_{t_0}^n, \mathcal D_{t_1}^n). \tag{12.2}\] If in addition \(\mathcal D_A\) and \(\mathcal D_B\) have disjoint supports, so that no record could come from both groups and each record shows its group, then the right-hand side equals \[\mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t_0), \mathrm{Bin}(n, t_1)\big). \tag{12.3}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the advantage by the TV distance of the models, then by that of the datasets, and then to show that with visible groups the count \(S\) of subgroup records carries everything the dataset says about the share.

The game is a test. The view has distribution \(P_{n,t_0}\) when \(b = 0\) and \(P_{n,t_1}\) when \(b = 1\). No test between two distributions has advantage above their TV distance, which gives the left inequality of Equation 12.2.
Training is a channel. The view is a randomized function of \(D\), and its randomness does not depend on \(b\). By the data processing inequality such processing cannot increase the TV distance, which gives the right inequality.
Write the likelihood ratio of a dataset. Let \(\mathcal D_A(x)\) and \(\mathcal D_B(x)\) also denote the two groups’ densities at a record \(x\). In general \(x\) has density \((1 - t)\mathcal D_A(x) + t\,\mathcal D_B(x)\) under \(\mathcal D_t\), but with disjoint supports one of the two terms is zero. So a record \(x\) from \(B\) has density \(t\,\mathcal D_B(x)\) under \(\mathcal D_t\), and a record from \(A\) has \((1 - t)\mathcal D_A(x)\). The records are independent, so the density of \(D\) is the product over its records. In the ratio of the density under \(t_1\) to that under \(t_0\), the factors \(\mathcal D_A(x)\) and \(\mathcal D_B(x)\) cancel. Each of the \(S\) subgroup records leaves a factor \(t_1/t_0\), and each of the \(n - S\) others leaves \((1 - t_1)/(1 - t_0)\), so the likelihood ratio is \[\Big(\frac{t_1}{t_0}\Big)^S\Big(\frac{1 - t_1}{1 - t_0}\Big)^{n - S}. \tag{12.4}\]
Conclude that the count is sufficient. The likelihood ratio depends on \(D\) only through \(S\), so \(S\) is sufficient, and the data processing inequality from \(D\) to \(S\) holds with equality. Each record is from the subgroup with probability \(t\), independently, so \(S\) has law \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t)\), and the TV distance between the datasets is Equation 12.3.





Example 12.1 If age group is part of each of the hospital’s \(n = 1{,}000\) records, Equation 12.3 gives the ceiling \(\mathrm{TV}(\mathrm{Bin}(1000, 0.45), \mathrm{Bin}(1000, 0.55)) = 0.9985\) for every model trained on the data. It is close to 1 because the count has mean 450 in one world and 550 in the other, with standard deviation \(\sqrt{1000 \times 0.45 \times 0.55} \approx 15.7\). The two means are more than six standard deviations apart, so the two distributions barely overlap.
At \(n = 100\) the means are 45 and 55 and the standard deviation is about 5, only two standard deviations apart, and Proposition 12.2 below turns that into a ceiling of \(0.6827\). Over 200,000 simulated games, the best test on the count has advantage 0.6811, within sampling error.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.2 Why a property leaks when no record does
text:
12.2 Why a property leaks when no record does
This section proves the opening’s claim, that more data hides each record better and the property worse, for the simplest release of all, the count \(S\) of subgroup records. Two attackers look at the same count, one asking whether a subgroup target is in \(D\) and the other whether \(D\) was drawn with share \(t_0\) or \(t_1\), and both best advantages can be computed exactly.
The membership attacker compares the count when a subgroup target is in \(D\) with the count when a fresh record takes its place. Its advantage, worked out in Proposition 12.1 below, comes down to how far the distribution of a count moves when the count is shifted by one, and that depends on the shape of the distribution. A probability mass function is unimodal if it rises to a most likely value, the mode, and then falls.

Lemma 12.1 (Shifting a unimodal count by one) Let \(X\) be an integer-valued random variable with finite support, whose probability mass function \(p_k = \Pr[X = k]\) is unimodal. Then \[\mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Law}(X + 1), \mathrm{Law}(X)\big) = \max_k p_k, \tag{12.5}\] where \(\mathrm{Law}(\cdot)\) means “the distribution of”.


Proof. 

Write the TV distance as steps. The shifted variable takes the value \(k\) with probability \(\Pr[X + 1 = k] = p_{k-1}\). So the TV distance is half the total size of the steps between neighbouring probabilities, \[\mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Law}(X + 1), \mathrm{Law}(X)\big) = \frac12\sum_k|p_k - p_{k-1}|. \tag{12.6}\]
Add the climb and the descent. Let \(k^*\) be the mode. The support is finite, so the probabilities start and end at 0. Up to \(k^*\) every step goes up, so the steps add to the climb from 0 to the top, \(p_{k^*}\). After \(k^*\) every step goes down, so they add to the descent back to 0, also \(p_{k^*}\).
Halve. The total is \(2p_{k^*}\), and half of it is \(p_{k^*} = \max_kp_k\). Table 12.2 walks through \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(4, \frac12)\).





Table 12.2: Shifting \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(4, \frac12)\) by one. The positive differences add up to \(6/16\), the height of the mode, and so do the negative ones. Half the total absolute difference is \(\frac12 \times \frac{12}{16} = \frac{6}{16} = 0.375 = \max_k\Pr[X = k]\).

Unimodality matters, because a distribution that rises twice climbs and descends twice, so its steps add up to more than twice its peak. The next proposition shows that the membership advantage is the height of the binomial’s most likely value times \(1 - t\), the chance that a fresh record is not from the subgroup. That height shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\), because the count’s standard deviation grows like \(\sqrt n\) and its probability is spread over that many likely values.

Proposition 12.1 (Membership from a released count) Let the dataset hold \(n - 1\) records from \(\mathcal D_t\) plus one more, either a target from the subgroup or a fresh record from \(\mathcal D_t\), and let the release be the count \(S\) of subgroup records. Write \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, t)\) for the count among the \(n - 1\) other records. The best advantage at telling the two cases apart is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{mem}}(n) = (1 - t)\max_k\Pr[X = k] \approx \frac{1 - t}{\sqrt{2\pi(n - 1)t(1 - t)}}. \tag{12.7}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the two views as distributions of the count, to notice that one of them is a mixture containing the other, and to reduce the TV distance to the effect of shifting a binomial by one.

Write the two views. With the target in \(D\), the count is \(S = X + 1\). With a fresh record, the count is \(X + 1\) when the fresh record is from the subgroup, which happens with probability \(t\), and \(X\) otherwise.
See the second view as a mixture. So the law of the second view is \(t\,\mathrm{Law}(X + 1) + (1 - t)\,\mathrm{Law}(X)\).
Mixing scales the TV distance. Write \(P = \mathrm{Law}(X + 1)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{Law}(X)\), with mass functions \(p\) and \(q\). In each term of the TV distance between \(P\) and \(tP + (1 - t)Q\), the difference is \(p(x) - tp(x) - (1 - t)q(x) = (1 - t)\big(p(x) - q(x)\big)\), so the factor \(1 - t\) comes out: \[\mathrm{TV}\big(P, tP + (1 - t)Q\big) = \frac12\sum_x(1 - t)|p(x) - q(x)| = (1 - t)\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q). \tag{12.8}\] The best advantage is this TV distance, so it is \((1 - t)\,\mathrm{TV}(\mathrm{Law}(X + 1), \mathrm{Law}(X))\).
Shift the binomial. A binomial mass function is unimodal, so Lemma 12.1 turns the TV distance into \(\max_k\Pr[X = k]\), which gives the exact form of Equation 12.7.
Estimate the height of the mode. By the normal approximation of Probability distributions, \(X\) is close to a normal with the same mean and variance \((n - 1)t(1 - t)\). A normal density with variance \(s^2\) has height \(1/\sqrt{2\pi s^2}\) at its peak. The probability of the most likely integer is close to that height, because the integers are spaced one apart and the density is nearly flat over a unit interval at the top. That gives the approximate form. Section E.2 proves both facts.


The property attacker sees the same count, but its two worlds centre the fraction \(S/n\) on \(t_0\) and on \(t_1\), with spread about \(\sqrt{t(1 - t)/n}\) at share \(t\). Its advantage therefore depends on how many spreads apart the two centres are, and that number grows like \(\sqrt n\). The best test cuts halfway between the centres, which is where the factor 2 below comes from.

Proposition 12.2 (The property from a released count) Let the release be the count \(S\) of a dataset drawn from \(\mathcal D_{t_0}^n\) or \(\mathcal D_{t_1}^n\), with the groups visible, and let \(\bar t = \frac{t_0 + t_1}2\) be the midpoint share. With \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, the best advantage is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{prop}}(n) = \mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t_0), \mathrm{Bin}(n, t_1)\big) \approx 2\Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big) - 1. \tag{12.9}\]


Proof. 

Start from the exact answer. The count is sufficient (Theorem 12.1), so the best advantage is the TV distance between the two binomials.
Approximate by two normals. By the normal approximation, \(S/n\) is close to \(\mathcal N(t, t(1 - t)/n)\). The two variances are close when the gap is small, so replace both by the one at the midpoint, \(\bar t(1 - \bar t)/n\). Measured in units of that standard deviation, the two means are a distance \[\gamma = \frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}} \tag{12.10}\] apart, so the problem is two unit-variance normals with means \(\gamma\) apart.
Use the Gaussian pair. For two unit-variance normals with means \(\gamma\) apart, the densities cross halfway between the means, and the best advantage is \(2\Phi(\gamma/2) - 1\) (Hypothesis testing). Substituting \(\gamma\) gives Equation 12.9.


The two results say that more data protects records and exposes properties. The membership advantage falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), a line of slope \(-\frac12\) on the log axes of Figure 12.1 (right). The property advantage climbs to 1 once \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\) is a few times \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\), sooner for a larger gap. Neither argument is special to counts, because models fitted by minimizing an average loss behave like averages of their records, as Proposition 12.3 shows.
The reason is that a property is a group of records. Moving from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, which for the hospital is \(1{,}000 \times 0.1 = 100\) of its 1,000 patients. A protection measured one record at a time says little about a change to 100 records at once, and Part 3 makes this precise with group privacy, which extends a guarantee for one record to a group at a cost that grows with the group’s size. To hide the property, a released count must carry noise of about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\), the distance between its values in the two worlds, and that much noise also hides the count the release was for.






Figure 12.1: Left: the released fraction \(S/n\) at \(n = 1{,}000\) under \(t = 0.45\) and \(t = 0.55\), and under \(t = 0.5\) with and without one target from the subgroup; the last two curves are indistinguishable. Right: the best property advantage for two gaps, and the best membership advantage of one record, against \(n\).




Example 12.2 Table 12.3 gives both advantages, and you can check the first row by hand. For the property, \(\bar t = 0.5\), so \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)} = 0.5\) and the argument of \(\Phi\) in Equation 12.9 is \(\sqrt{100} \times 0.1/(2 \times 0.5) = 1\). Then \(2\Phi(1) - 1 = 2(0.8413) - 1 = 0.6827\). For membership, Equation 12.7 gives \(0.5/\sqrt{2\pi \times 99 \times 0.25} = 0.5/12.47 = 0.0401\). Both approximations are within 1% of the exact values.
At \(n = 10{,}000\), an attacker who wants to know whether one patient is in the data has advantage 0.0040, so with a fair bit it is right with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12(0.0040) = 0.502\). An attacker who wants the share of patients over 65 has advantage 1.0000 to four decimals, though the data, the release and its knowledge are the same.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.3 Shadow models and meta-classifiers
For a real model nobody can write down \(P_{n,t}\), the distribution of the trained parameters, so the best test of Theorem 12.1 is out of reach. Ateniese et al. (2015) gave the recipe every later attack uses: if you cannot compute the two distributions, sample from them. This section states that recipe, and then answers the two questions it leaves open, which classifier to train and how accurate it can be.

Definition 12.2 (Shadow-model attack) The attacker draws many datasets of \(n\) records from \(\mathcal D_{t_0}\) and from \(\mathcal D_{t_1}\), using auxiliary data, and trains a shadow model on each with the victim’s algorithm \(\mathcal T\). It labels each shadow model’s parameters with the bit that produced them, trains a classifier on these labelled parameter vectors, the meta-classifier, and applies it to the victim’s model.

This is the shadow-model idea of Membership inference, with whole models as the data points. Choosing the best meta-classifier needs the distribution of the parameters, which the next proposition gives.
Let \(\theta\) minimize the average loss \(\frac1n\sum_i\ell(\theta; x_i)\) over the training records, and let \(\theta(t)\) minimize the expected loss under \(\mathcal D_t\), the model you would get from infinitely many records. How noisy \(\theta\) is around \(\theta(t)\) depends on two things. A sharply curved loss pins the minimizer down, and records whose gradients at \(\theta(t)\) point in different directions pull it about.

Proposition 12.3 (Fitted parameters are approximately Gaussian) Let the average curvature of the loss be \(H = \mathbb E_{\mathcal D_t}\nabla^2\ell(\theta(t); x)\) and the second moment of the per-record gradients \(G = \mathbb E_{\mathcal D_t}\big[\nabla\ell(\theta(t); x)\nabla\ell(\theta(t); x)^\top\big]\), with \(H\) invertible, and define the sandwich covariance \(\Sigma_1(t) = H^{-1}GH^{-1}\). Under the regularity conditions of van der Vaart (1998, ch. 5), roughly that the loss is smooth, \(\theta(t)\) is its unique minimizer and these moments exist, for large \(n\) \[\theta \approx \mathcal N\big(\theta(t), \Sigma_1(t)/n\big), \tag{12.11}\] meaning that \(\sqrt n\,(\theta - \theta(t))\) converges in distribution to \(\mathcal N(0, \Sigma_1(t))\).


Proof. This is the asymptotic normality of M-estimators, estimators defined as the minimizer of an average loss. The plan is to write the fit as a linear function of an average of per-record gradients, which is approximately Gaussian. Section G.6 proves each approximation for logistic regression.

The fit solves an average equation. At a minimizer the gradient is zero, so \(\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell(\theta; x_i) = 0\).
Linearize around \(\theta(t)\). For large \(n\), \(\theta\) is close to \(\theta(t)\), so a first-order Taylor expansion of the gradient is accurate. The sample average of the Hessians, taken at points between \(\theta\) and \(\theta(t)\), is close to its expectation \(H\) by the law of large numbers, so \(0 \approx \frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell(\theta(t); x_i) + H(\theta - \theta(t))\). Solving for \(\theta\), \[\theta - \theta(t) \approx -H^{-1}\,\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell(\theta(t); x_i). \tag{12.12}\] So the fit is an average, as in Section 12.2, in which each record pulls by its gradient scaled by the inverse curvature.
The average gradient has mean zero. \(\theta(t)\) minimizes the expected loss, so the expected gradient there is zero. Each gradient therefore has mean zero, so its second moment \(G\) is its covariance, and an average of \(n\) independent copies has covariance \(G/n\).
Apply the central limit theorem. The average gradient is approximately \(\mathcal N(0, G/n)\). Multiplying a Gaussian vector by the symmetric matrix \(-H^{-1}\) multiplies its covariance by \(H^{-1}\) on both sides, which gives \(\mathcal N(0, H^{-1}GH^{-1}/n)\).


Under the two hypotheses, then, the parameters are two Gaussians with nearly equal covariances when the gap is small, and the next lemma gives the best test between such Gaussians. In \(d\) dimensions the noise can be larger in some directions than in others, so a shift along a noisy direction counts for less than the same shift along a quiet one. The Mahalanobis distance measures a shift in exactly this way, in standard deviations of the noise along the direction of the shift.

Lemma 12.2 (Two Gaussians with a shared covariance) Let \(P = \mathcal N(m_0, \Sigma)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(m_1, \Sigma)\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) with \(\Sigma\) invertible, with densities \(p\) and \(q\), and let \[\gamma = \sqrt{(m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(m_1 - m_0)} \tag{12.13}\] be their Mahalanobis distance. Then the log-likelihood ratio is linear in \(\theta\), \[\ln\frac{q(\theta)}{p(\theta)} = \omega^\top\Big(\theta - \frac{m_0 + m_1}2\Big), \qquad \omega = \Sigma^{-1}(m_1 - m_0), \tag{12.14}\] and the best test with a fair bit has accuracy \[\Phi(\gamma/2). \tag{12.15}\]


Proof. The plan is to write out the two log-densities, let the quadratic parts cancel because the covariances are equal, and find the distribution of what is left.

Expand the two quadratics. A Gaussian log-density is \(-\frac12(\theta - m)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\theta - m)\) plus a constant that depends only on \(\Sigma\), so the constants cancel in \(\ln q - \ln p\). Multiplying out, the terms \(\theta^\top\Sigma^{-1}\theta\) appear with opposite signs and cancel too, which leaves \((m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}\theta - \frac12(m_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}m_1 - m_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}m_0)\).
Factor the constant. Because \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is symmetric, the cross terms \(m_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}m_0\) and \(m_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}m_1\) are equal, so the bracketed constant factors as \((m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(m_1 + m_0)\). With its factor \(-\frac12\) it becomes \(-(m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}\frac{m_0 + m_1}2\). Pulling out \(\omega^\top = (m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}\) gives the linear form.
Find its distribution. Call the linear form \(\Lambda\). As a linear function of a Gaussian it is Gaussian. Under \(Q\) the mean of \(\theta - \frac{m_0 + m_1}2\) is \(m_1 - \frac{m_0 + m_1}2 = \frac{m_1 - m_0}2\), so the mean of \(\Lambda\) is \(\omega^\top\frac{m_1 - m_0}2 = \frac{\gamma^2}2\), by the definition of \(\gamma\), and under \(P\) the same computation gives \(-\frac{\gamma^2}2\). Under both, its variance is \(\omega^\top\Sigma\omega = (m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(m_1 - m_0) = \gamma^2\).
Compute the accuracy. The best test says 1 where \(q > p\), that is, where \(\Lambda > 0\). Under \(Q\) the threshold 0 lies \(\frac{\gamma^2/2}{\gamma} = \frac\gamma2\) standard deviations below the mean, so the test is right with probability \(\Phi(\gamma/2)\). Under \(P\) it is right when \(\Lambda < 0\), which by symmetry has the same probability. Averaging the two worlds gives Equation 12.15.


The lemma and Proposition 12.3 together give the best attack on a fitted model, which is linear.

Theorem 12.2 (The best attack on a fitted model) Suppose the parameters satisfy Proposition 12.3 under both hypotheses, and that the gap is small enough to replace \(\Sigma_1(t_0)\) and \(\Sigma_1(t_1)\) by their average \(\bar\Sigma_1\). Then the best attack is a linear test in \(\theta\), and its accuracy, with \(\gamma\) the Mahalanobis distance of Lemma 12.2, is \[\Phi(\gamma/2), \qquad \gamma = \sqrt{n\,\big(\theta(t_1) - \theta(t_0)\big)^\top\bar\Sigma_1^{-1}\big(\theta(t_1) - \theta(t_0)\big)}. \tag{12.16}\] For a small gap, with \(\theta'(\bar t) = \frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt}\) the slope of the population fit at the midpoint, \[\gamma \approx \kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|, \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{\theta'(\bar t)^\top\Sigma_1(\bar t)^{-1}\theta'(\bar t)}. \tag{12.17}\]


Proof. 

Two Gaussians. Under the two hypotheses \(\theta\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(\theta(t_b), \bar\Sigma_1/n)\), for \(b = 0, 1\).
Apply the lemma. Lemma 12.2 with \(m_b = \theta(t_b)\) and \(\Sigma = \bar\Sigma_1/n\) says the best test is linear, with accuracy \(\Phi(\gamma/2)\). Since \(\Sigma^{-1} = n\,\bar\Sigma_1^{-1}\), the factor \(n\) comes out of the Mahalanobis distance, which gives Equation 12.16.
Linearize in the share. For a small gap the population fit changes almost linearly in \(t\), so \(\theta(t_1) - \theta(t_0) \approx \theta'(\bar t)(t_1 - t_0)\), and the covariance hardly changes, so \(\bar\Sigma_1 \approx \Sigma_1(\bar t)\). Substituting both into Equation 12.16 gives \(\gamma^2 \approx n(t_1 - t_0)^2\,\theta'(\bar t)^\top\Sigma_1(\bar t)^{-1}\theta'(\bar t)\), whose square root is Equation 12.17.


The count of Section 12.2 fits the same mould, which checks the theorem against an exact answer.

Corollary 12.1 (The released fraction) For the released fraction \(\theta = S/n\), the constant is \(\kappa = 1/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\), which is 2 at \(\bar t = \frac12\), and the advantage \(2\Phi(\gamma/2) - 1\) is Equation 12.9.


Proof. 

The fraction is a fitted model. Take the loss \(\ell(\theta; x) = \frac12(\theta - a)^2\), where \(a \in \{0, 1\}\) marks the subgroup. The minimizer of its average is the mean of the marks, \(\theta = S/n\), and its population version is \(\theta(t) = t\), so \(\theta' = 1\).
Compute the sandwich. The second derivative of the loss is \(H = 1\). The gradient \(\theta - a\), taken at \(\theta(t) = t\), is \(t - a\) and has variance \(G = t(1 - t)\), the variance of a \(\mathrm{Bern}(t)\) variable. So \(\Sigma_1 = t(1 - t)\), and Equation 12.17 gives \(\kappa = 1/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\).
Turn accuracy into advantage. Advantage is twice accuracy minus 1, so \(\Phi(\gamma/2)\) becomes \(2\Phi(\gamma/2) - 1\), which with this \(\kappa\) is Equation 12.9.


Two numbers set the leak. The slope \(\theta'\) says how much the property moves what the model learns, and \(\Sigma_1\) says how noisy that is. If the property does not affect what the model fits, then \(\theta' = 0\) and, to first order, nothing leaks however large \(n\) is. The constant also compares any model with the count. By Corollary 12.1 the count on \(n'\) records has \(\gamma = \sqrt{n'}\,|t_1 - t_0|/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\). Setting this equal to the model’s \(\kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\) and solving for \(n'\) shows that the model leaks as much as the count on \(n' = n(\kappa\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)})^2\) records, which is how Suri & Evans (2022) measure leakage.
The Gaussian picture fails where its approximations do. With small \(n\) the parameters are skewed, so the linear meta-classifier is no longer optimal. A meta-classifier trained on few shadow models also estimates the direction \(\omega\) with error, most of all when the effect is small and the shadow models’ noise swamps the shift.

Example 12.3 Each record has two features \(x \sim \mathcal N(0, I_2)\) and a label. The majority labels with \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x] = \sigma(2x_1 + x_2)\) and the subgroup with \(\sigma(2x_1 - x_2)\), where \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) is the logistic function. Think of a symptom \(x_2\) that raises risk in most patients and lowers it in a minority. The group is never a feature, so the model sees \((x_1, x_2, y)\) only. A logistic regression with weights \((\theta_1, \theta_2)\) and an intercept is trained on \(n\) records by Newton’s method, with a tiny ridge penalty \(10^{-3}\). The chapter’s script (Section 12.5) computes \(\theta(t)\), shown in Table 12.4, and \(\Sigma_1(t)\) to numerical precision, by Gauss–Hermite quadrature over \(x\) (a numerical rule for integrals against a Gaussian).
The property moves \(\theta_2\). At \(t = \frac12\) the two rules cancel in \(\theta_2\), because half the population pushes it up and half down. As \(t\) grows, the subgroup’s rule wins and \(\theta_2\) goes negative. The script computes the slope \(\theta'(\frac12) = (0, -1.704, 0)\) for \((\theta_1, \theta_2, \text{intercept})\). Mixing the rules also shrinks \(\theta_1\) from 2 to 1.704, but symmetrically in \(t\), so \(\theta_1\) is flat at \(\frac12\) and carries no information there. The intercept is 0 for every \(t\), by the label-flipping symmetry below, so it carries none either.
The noise \(\Sigma_1(\frac12)\) has diagonal \((12.59, 6.94, 6.04)\) and zero off-diagonal entries, by symmetry. A change of the data that leaves the population unchanged and flips the sign of one parameter makes that parameter’s covariance with the others equal its own negative, hence zero. Flipping the sign of \(x_2\) swaps the two groups’ rules, leaves the population at \(t = \frac12\) unchanged and flips only \(\theta_2\), and flipping the sign of \(x\) and swapping the labels flips only the intercept. Two thousand models trained on \(n = 1{,}000\) records at \(t = \frac12\) have variances, times \(n\), of \((11.92, 6.80, 6.08)\), and their mean \(\theta_1\) is 1.693, so the Gaussian picture is right to within about 5%. Most of the difference in the variance of \(\theta_1\) comes from the ridge penalty, which the population fit omits. The penalty is added to the average loss, so it does not fade as \(n\) grows, and including it lowers the predicted value from 12.59 to 11.83 (Section G.6).
Only \(\theta_2\) has a nonzero slope and \(\Sigma_1\) is diagonal, so Equation 12.17 reduces to the slope of \(\theta_2\) over its standard deviation, \(\kappa = 1.704/\sqrt{6.94} = 0.647\), against 2 for the count (Corollary 12.1). With \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)} = \frac12\), the formula for \(n'\) above says that the model leaks the property as well as \((0.647/2)^2 = 0.105\) of its records would, about one record in ten.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.4 Permutation invariance
A logistic regression has one parameter vector per function, since different weights give different predictions, but a neural network has many. Swap two hidden units, together with their incoming and outgoing weights, and the network computes exactly the same function. Ganju et al. (2018) observed that a meta-classifier fed the flattened weights then sees each unit in an arbitrary position of the vector, and does poorly. This section works out why for one hidden layer of tanh units, and which representations bring the property back.

Definition 12.3 (A one-layer tanh network and its symmetries) A network with \(h\) hidden units computes \[f_\theta(x) = \sigma\big(v^\top\tanh(Wx + \beta) + c\big), \tag{12.18}\] where row \(j\) of the matrix \(W\) and entry \(\beta_j\) of the hidden bias vector \(\beta\) compute unit \(j\)’s input, \(v_j\) is its outgoing weight, and \(c\) is the output bias. Unit \(j\)’s parameters are \(u_j = (W_{j\cdot}, \beta_j, v_j)\). A symmetry is a matrix \(g = F\Pi\), where the permutation matrix \(\Pi\) reorders the units and the diagonal matrix \(F\) with entries \(\pm1\) flips the sign of some of them. It acts on \(\theta\) by applying \(g\) to the rows of \(W\) and to the entries of \(\beta\) and \(v\), leaving \(c\) alone.

There are \(h!\) orders and \(2^h\) sign patterns, so a generic network, one whose units are nonzero and pairwise neither equal nor opposite, has \(h!\,2^h\) parameter vectors that compute the same function: \(4! \times 2^4 = 384\) for \(h = 4\). The next proposition shows that the symmetry of the function carries over to the distribution of the trained weights, provided training treats every arrangement of the units alike, and that this has a sharp consequence for a linear attacker.

Proposition 12.4 (Symmetries hide the property from raw weights) Every symmetry \(g\) leaves the network’s function unchanged, \[f_{(gW,\ g\beta,\ gv,\ c)} = f_{(W,\ \beta,\ v,\ c)}. \tag{12.19}\] Suppose the initial parameters have the same law as their image under every \(g\) (for example, independent entries drawn from a distribution symmetric about 0) and training is gradient descent. Then, under both hypotheses of the game,

the law of the trained parameters is invariant under every \(g\);
every coordinate of every \(u_j\) has mean zero, so the mean of a linear score of the raw parameters can differ between the hypotheses only through the output bias \(c\);
the sum of the units’ outer products, \(\sum_j u_ju_j^\top\), is invariant under every \(g\), so its entries can serve as features, the second-moment features.



Proof. The plan is to show that \(g\) passes through tanh, so it leaves the output unchanged, then that it passes through every step of gradient descent, and then to read off what this means for averages.

tanh commutes with \(g\). tanh acts entry by entry, so permuting its input permutes its output in the same way. tanh is odd, \(\tanh(-z) = -\tanh(z)\), so flipping the sign of an entry flips the sign of its output. Hence \(\tanh(gz) = g\tanh(z)\).
The output is unchanged. By step 1 the symmetry can be pulled out of tanh, and \(g^\top g = \Pi^\top F^2\Pi = I\), because each entry of \(F\) is \(\pm1\) and undoing a reordering gives back the original. So \((gv)^\top\tanh(gWx + g\beta) = v^\top g^\top g\tanh(Wx + \beta) = v^\top\tanh(Wx + \beta)\), which is Equation 12.19.
Gradient descent commutes with \(g\). Let \(\mathcal L\) be the training loss, and let \(g\) also denote its action on the whole parameter vector, which only reorders entries and flips signs, so it is linear and orthogonal. Step 2 says \(\mathcal L(g\theta) = \mathcal L(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\). Differentiating both sides with the chain rule gives \(g^\top\nabla\mathcal L(g\theta) = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\). Multiplying by \(g\), which undoes \(g^\top\) because \(g\) is orthogonal, gives \(\nabla\mathcal L(g\theta) = g\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\). One step with learning rate \(\eta\) from \(g\theta\) therefore lands at \(g\theta - \eta g\nabla\mathcal L(\theta) = g(\theta - \eta\nabla\mathcal L(\theta))\). Repeating, if \(T\) steps from \(\theta_0\) reach \(\theta_T\), then from \(g\theta_0\) they reach \(g\theta_T\).
The law is invariant. The initial parameters \(\theta_0\) have the same law as \(g\theta_0\). Training maps them to \(\theta_T\) and, by step 3, to \(g\theta_T\), so \(\theta_T\) and \(g\theta_T\) have the same law for every dataset, and averaging over datasets under either hypothesis keeps this. That is claim 1.
Raw means vanish. Take the \(g\) that flips unit \(j\) only. By claim 1, \(u_j\) and \(-u_j\) have the same law, so \(\mathbb E[u_j] = -\mathbb E[u_j]\), which forces \(\mathbb E[u_j] = 0\) under both hypotheses. A linear score \(w^\top\theta\) has mean shift \(w^\top(m_1 - m_0)\) between the hypotheses, where \(m_0\) and \(m_1\) are the mean parameter vectors, and \(m_1 - m_0\) is zero in every unit coordinate, so the score’s mean shift comes only from the output bias \(c\), which no \(g\) touches. That is claim 2.
Second moments are invariant. A permutation only reorders the terms of \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\), which does not change the sum. A sign flip turns \(u_j\) into \(-u_j\), and \((-u_j)(-u_j)^\top = u_ju_j^\top\). That is claim 3.


Raw weights hide the property because each position in the parameter vector holds a random one of the network’s units, with a random sign. The property changes the set of units the network learns, not their positions, so averaging position by position washes it out.
There are three ways to undo the symmetry. A canonical form picks one parameter vector per function: flip each unit so that \(v_j > 0\), then sort the units by \(v_j\). Sorting is the first remedy of Ganju et al., but it is fragile, because two units with nearly equal \(v_j\) swap places from one network to the next. A set representation feeds each unit through the same map \(\phi\), adds the results and applies a second map, \(\rho\big(\sum_j\phi(u_j)\big)\), which does not depend on the order (Zaheer et al. 2017). The features \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\) are the case \(\phi(u) = uu^\top\), with \(\rho\) the identity. Query features use the network’s outputs on probe inputs that the attacker fixes once, such as random points; they are invariant automatically and need only black-box access.
For the best attack, white-box access is never weaker, because whoever holds the weights can compute any query output. A fixed linear meta-classifier is not the best attack, though, and for it a better representation can matter more than more access, so in the example below black-box beats white-box.

Example 12.4 The data are as in Example 12.3, with \(t_0 = 0.2\) and \(t_1 = 0.8\). Each network has \(h = 4\) tanh units and is trained on \(n = 200\) records by 300 steps of full-batch gradient descent from a random start. For each hypothesis, 150 shadow networks fit the linear test of Lemma 12.2 and 150 target networks measure its accuracy; Figure 12.4 repeats this on a separate run of 100 each.
Each unit has four parameters (two input weights, a bias and an output weight), so the raw parameters number \(4 \times 4 + 1 = 17\) with the output bias. The symmetric second-moment matrix has 10 distinct entries, which with the output bias gives 11 features. Table 12.6 also reports each representation’s largest standardized mean gap: for each feature, the difference of its means under \(t_0\) and \(t_1\), divided by its pooled standard deviation.
Raw parameters are at chance, as claim 2 predicts. Their largest standardized gap, 0.34, is noise: a difference of two means of 150 standardized values has standard deviation \(\sqrt{2/150} = 0.115\), and by chance alone the largest of 17 such values is typically two to three times that. Canonical order lifts the accuracy to 0.807, mostly through one feature (Figure 12.4, left), and second moments reach 0.877 with fewer features, because they need no tie-breaking. Probe outputs do best, because they measure directly the function that the property changes.

12.7 References

Ateniese, Mancini, Spognardi, Villani, Vitali & Felici, “Hacking Smart Machines with Smarter Ones: How to Extract Meaningful Data from Machine Learning Classifiers” (International Journal of Security and Networks, 2015). The first property-inference attack: shadow models trained with and without the property, and a meta-classifier on their parameters.
Ganju, Wang, Yang, Gunter & Borisov, “Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations” (CCS 2018). The permutation problem for neural networks, neuron sorting, and the DeepSets meta-classifier.
Suri & Evans, “Formalizing and Estimating Distribution Inference Risks” (PoPETs 2022). The property game as a test between two training distributions, and leakage measured in records.
Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko, “Leakage of Dataset Properties in Multi-Party Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2021). Black-box property inference from query outputs alone.
Mahloujifar, Ghosh & Chase, “Property Inference from Poisoning” (IEEE S&P 2022). Adding a few records makes a property far easier to infer.
Melis, Song, De Cristofaro & Shmatikov, “Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning” (IEEE S&P 2019). Properties inferred from the updates of collaborative training.
Salem, Cherubin, Evans, Köpf, Paverd, Suri, Tople & Zanella-Béguelin, “SoK: Let the Privacy Games Begin! A Unified Treatment of Data Inference Privacy in Machine Learning” (IEEE S&P 2023). Property inference as one game among the others of this part.
