title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Verbatim, approximate, discoverable, extractable
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, API keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is” and it may finish the sentence with the real number. Nobody queried a database or broke into anything, because the number was stored in the weights and came out through the model’s normal interface. That is training-data extraction. Membership inference needs the record in hand and asks whether it was in the training set, while extraction gives the attacker the record itself, often without knowing that it existed.
The one idea of this chapter is the rank of a secret under the model. Fix the context in which the secret appears, say “my pin is”, and list every value that could fill it, here all five-digit pins, from most to least likely under the model. The rank of the true secret is its position in that list, which is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries the values in that order. Every measure in the chapter reads this rank. Greedy decoding, which always writes the most likely next symbol, reproduces the secret when each of its symbols is the most likely one at its step. Sampling at random from the model finds the secret quickly when it ranks near the top. Exposure counts in bits how far up the list the model has moved it.
The running example is a toy. The training set is a contact list, in which each line is a user name of three random syllables, a space and a five-digit pin, such as toneka 14524. There are 5,000 background lines, each seen once, and 600 secret lines, of which 100 each are inserted 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 times. The model is a character \(n\)-gram model, which predicts each character by counting what followed the last \(n - 1\) characters before it. Its order \(n\) plays the role of model size, because a higher order stores counts for more distinct \(n\)-grams, strings of \(n\) characters, from 2,734 at order 3 to 54,614 at order 8. When a context is written out, _ stands for a space, so gule_ is the five characters before the first digit of migule 16430.
“The model memorized its training data” can mean several things. Completing a famous quotation leaks nothing private, while emitting a phone number seen once in training does. Some definitions assume that the attacker knows the beginning of the training string, and others ask whether any prompt at all brings it out. You need to say which notion you measure, because one model can score very differently under two of them, as Example 13.4 shows. All of them rest on a language model’s probabilities, which come first.
A language model scores a string one symbol at a time, by giving the probability of each possible next symbol after the text so far, and the chain rule multiplies these into the probability of the whole string.
For the pin 16430 after the prompt migule, the model multiplies five numbers, the probabilities of 1 after migule_, of 6 after migule_1, and so on up to 0 after migule_1643.
The toy computes these probabilities by counting. An order-\(n\) model looks only at the last \(n - 1\) symbols, which it calls the context. The natural prediction is the fraction of times \(w\) followed the context in training. But that gives probability 0 to anything never seen, and one zero in the chain rule makes a whole string impossible. Smoothing removes the zeros by pretending that every symbol was seen a fraction of an extra time in every context.
The toy uses \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(V = 39\) symbols, which are the 26 letters, the 10 digits, the space, an end-of-line symbol and a start symbol, which pads the start of each line to give its first symbols a full context and has the lowest code.
A discoverable suffix is extractable, because its training prefix is one allowed prompt. The converse fails, because an extractable string may come out after some other prompt while its own prefix leads elsewhere. The most dangerous \(k\)-eidetic strings are those with \(k = 1\), because a string found in one document only is typically one person’s secret, and the model still gives it back.
The notions answer different threat models. Discoverable memorization assumes an attacker who holds the training prefix, which is strong but easy to measure, while extractable memorization fits the real attacker, who has only the model, but needs a search over all prompts. So papers report discoverable rates, and attacks then show how much of the discoverable text an outsider can reach. Verbatim matching also misses near copies, and Ippolito et al. (2023) bypass a filter that blocks verbatim training text by asking for a changed style, such as different capitalization, which returns the text with small edits the filter does not match. A verbatim rate is therefore a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it.
Greedy decoding is a convenience for measurement, while deployed systems sample, so you also need to know how many samples bring a string out. Each sample is an independent try, and the chance that all of them miss falls exponentially in their number.
The proposition converts a probability into an attack budget, so that a string with probability \(10^{-3}\) after its prefix comes out with 99% confidence (\(\beta = 0.01\)) within about 4,600 samples. It is slightly pessimistic, because it replaces \(1 - q\) by the larger \(e^{-q}\), but for rare strings it agrees closely with the exact budget, \(\ln\beta/\ln(1 - q)\) rounded up, the smallest \(m\) with \((1 - q)^m \le \beta\).

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
Definition 13.1 (Language model) A language model gives, for every preceding text \(c\) and every symbol \(w\), a probability \(p(w \mid c)\) that the next symbol is \(w\). Write \(x_{<t} = x_1\dots x_{t-1}\) for the symbols before step \(t\) of a string \(x = x_1\dots x_L\) of length \(L\). The probability of \(x\) after a prompt \(c\) is the product of its one-step probabilities, where \(c, x_{<t}\) means \(c\) followed by \(x_{<t}\), and on a log scale the product becomes a sum: \[p(x \mid c) = \prod_{t=1}^{L}p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t}), \qquad \ln p(x \mid c) = \sum_{t=1}^{L}\ln p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t}). \tag{13.1}\] Greedy decoding from a prompt \(c\) appends the most likely next symbol at each step, and \(\mathrm{greedy}(c)\) is the string it produces. Sampling draws each next symbol at random with the model’s probabilities, until an end-of-line symbol or a length limit.




Definition 13.2 (An n-gram model with add-α smoothing) Let the alphabet have \(V\) symbols, and let \(\alpha > 0\) be a smoothing constant. An order-\(n\) model stores, for every context \(c\) of \(n - 1\) symbols and every symbol \(w\), the count \(N(c, w)\) of times that \(w\) followed \(c\) in the training text. Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing adds \(\alpha\) to each of the \(V\) counts, so the total grows by \(\alpha V\): \[p(w \mid c) = \frac{N(c, w) + \alpha}{N(c) + \alpha V}, \qquad N(c) = \sum_wN(c, w). \tag{13.2}\] Each symbol has a code, its position in a fixed order of the alphabet, and greedy decoding breaks a tie toward the lower code.



Definition 13.3 (Notions of memorization) Let a language model be trained on a dataset of documents.

Extractable (Carlini et al. 2021). A string \(s\) of the training data is extractable if there is some prompt \(c\), any prompt at all, such that \(\mathrm{greedy}(c)\) begins with \(s\).
\(k\)-eidetic (Carlini et al. 2021). A string \(s\) is \(k\)-eidetically memorized if it is extractable and it appears in at most \(k\) documents of the dataset (in the toy, lines).
Discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023, named by Nasr et al. 2023). Suppose the training data contain a prefix \(c\) followed by a suffix \(x\). Then \(x\) is discoverably memorized if prompting with that same prefix makes greedy decoding produce the suffix, so that \(\mathrm{greedy}(c)\) begins with \(x\).
Approximate (Ippolito et al. 2023). The suffix \(x\) is approximately memorized if \(\mathrm{greedy}(c)\) is within distance \(\tau\) of \(x\) in some string distance. In the toy the distance is the number of wrong digits and \(\tau = 1\), so a pin with at most one wrong digit counts.

Notions 1 to 3 are verbatim, because the output must match exactly.





Proposition 13.1 (Samples needed to extract a string) Let \(q = p(x \mid c) > 0\) be the probability of the string \(x\) after the prompt \(c\), and let \(\beta \in (0, 1)\) be a failure probability. Draw \(m\) independent samples from \(c\) at temperature 1, that is, with each next symbol drawn with exactly the model’s probabilities. If \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{q}, \tag{13.3}\] then at least one of the samples begins with \(x\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. The plan is to compute the probability that every sample misses, bound it by an exponential, and solve for \(m\).

One sample hits with probability \(q\). A sample draws each next symbol \(x_t\) with probability \(p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t})\). By the chain rule, Equation 13.1, the chance that it begins with \(x\) is the product of those probabilities, which is \(q\).
All \(m\) samples miss with probability \((1 - q)^m\). Each sample misses with probability \(1 - q\), and the samples are independent, so the misses multiply.
Replace \(1 - q\) by an exponential. The curve \(e^{-q}\) is convex, and the line \(1 - q\) is its tangent at \(q = 0\), since both equal 1 there with slope \(-1\). A convex curve lies above its tangent lines, so \(1 - q \le e^{-q}\). Raising both sides to the power \(m\) keeps the order, because both are non-negative: \[(1 - q)^m \le e^{-mq}. \tag{13.4}\]
Solve for \(m\). The miss probability is therefore at most \(\beta\) as soon as \(e^{-mq} \le \beta\). Taking logarithms gives \(mq \ge \ln(1/\beta)\), and dividing by \(q > 0\) gives Equation 13.3.




Example 13.1 Take the secret line migule 16430, inserted 4 times, and prompt each model with its prefix migule. Greedy decoding gives only 07 and then ends the line at order 3, 81554 at order 4, 14032 at order 5, and the true 16430 at orders 6, 7 and 8. The switch happens at order 6 because an order-6 model reads five characters of context. From the first digit on, its contexts (gule_, then ule_1, and so on) occur in this line and nowhere else, as the script checks. In such a context the line’s own next digit has count 4 and every rival digit has count 0, so greedy decoding emits the line’s digit every time. Shorter contexts, such as the four characters ule_ that an order-5 model reads, are shared with other lines, whose digits can outvote the four copies.
Sampling gives a graded version of the same picture. At order 5, where greedy decoding fails for most secrets, the probability \(q\) that one sample from the true prefix reproduces a secret’s pin, averaged over the 100 secrets of each group, is \(1.4 \times 10^{-3}\) at 4 copies and \(0.142\) at 32 copies. With \(\beta = 0.01\), the exact budgets \(\ln\beta/\ln(1 - q)\) for these mean probabilities, computed before rounding \(q\), are 3,252 and 31 samples.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Duplication and model size
Example 13.1 showed one line becoming memorized as the model grew. This section asks which lines get memorized in general, because that decides which data a defence must protect first. Carlini et al. (2023) found that discoverable memorization grows linearly in the logarithm of how often a string is duplicated, of model size and of prompt length. Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel (2022) found that a sequence repeated 10 times is generated about 1,000 times more often than one seen once. The \(n\)-gram toy lets you derive why, for every line, from its counts.
The idea is a vote. Greedy decoding follows the largest count at each step, and each copy of a line adds one vote for the line’s own next symbol in every context the line passes through. The next lemma states how copies change the counts and which symbol wins a step, which the proof of Theorem 13.1 needs, and the size of one copy’s effect, which the canary of Section 13.3 uses.

Lemma 13.1 (What counting implies) In an order-\(n\) model with add-\(\alpha\) smoothing (Definition 13.2), the following hold.

Training on \(k\) copies of a line adds \(k\) to the count of a (context, next symbol) pair for each time the line passes through it, and changes no other count.
In a fixed context \(c\), the most likely symbol is the one with the largest count, that is, \(\arg\max_wp(w \mid c) = \arg\max_wN(c, w)\).
Suppose that a context \(c\) occurs in the training data only in the \(k\) copies of one line. Then the line’s own next symbol and each other symbol get, respectively, \[p(\text{true} \mid c) = \frac{k + \alpha}{k + \alpha V}, \qquad p(\text{other} \mid c) = \frac{\alpha}{k + \alpha V}, \tag{13.5}\] so the true symbol is \((k + \alpha)/\alpha\) times as likely as any other, whatever \(V\) is. A context never seen at all gives every symbol probability \(1/V\).



Proof. 

Training is counting. A line passes through a sequence of (context, next symbol) pairs, and training on it adds 1 to the count of a pair each time the pair occurs. Training on \(k\) copies repeats this \(k\) times.
Smoothing keeps the order. In a fixed context, Equation 13.2 adds the same \(\alpha\) to every count and divides by the same \(N(c) + \alpha V\). Both operations are increasing, so the symbol with the largest count still has the largest probability.
A context of one line. At such a context the line’s next symbol has count \(k\), every other symbol has count 0, and the total is \(N(c) = k\). Putting those counts into Equation 13.2 gives Equation 13.5, and the two probabilities share a denominator, so their ratio is \((k + \alpha)/\alpha\). A context never seen has all counts 0, which gives \(\alpha/(\alpha V) = 1/V\).


Table 13.2 evaluates Equation 13.5 for the toy. For one copy, \(\alpha V = 3.9\), so \(p(\text{true} \mid c) = 1.1/4.9 = 0.2245\) and \(p(\text{other} \mid c) = 0.1/4.9 = 0.0204\), a ratio of \(1.1/0.1 = 11\). The last column writes the ratio in bits, \(\log_2 11 = 3.46\), the unit that exposure uses in Section 13.3. That is the mechanism of memorization in this toy: a context that belongs to one training line alone, followed by that line’s next symbol.

To turn the vote into a number, count the rest of the corpus separately from the line’s copies. At each step, the gap is how far the strongest rival symbol is ahead of the true symbol in those counts. The copies must close the gap at every step, so the step where the rival is furthest ahead sets the number of copies needed.

Theorem 13.1 (Copies needed for greedy extraction) Let \(s\) be a training line made of a prefix \(c\) and a suffix \(x = x_1\dots x_L\), inserted \(k\) times into the training set of an order-\(n\) model with add-\(\alpha\) smoothing. Let \(c_t\) be the context at step \(t\), the last \(n - 1\) symbols of \(c\,x_{<t}\). Let \(N_-\) be the counts of the rest of the training set, without the copies of \(s\). Assume that each context \(c_t\) occurs only once within \(s\), so that a copy adds to no rival pair. The gap at step \(t\) is the bracket below, reduced by one at a step where the true symbol has a lower code than the strongest rival, because there a tie is already a win. Then greedy decoding from \(c\) emits \(x\) if and only if \(k \ge k^*(s)\), where \[k^*(s) = \max_{t \le L}\Big[\max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w) - N_-(c_t, x_t)\Big] + 1. \tag{13.6}\] A line in the training set has at least one copy, so a \(k^*\) below 1 counts as 1. A line whose contexts are unique to it, with \(N_- = 0\) at every step, has \(k^* = 1\), since the start symbol, with the lowest code, would win a tie at such a context. Over a population of lines, the fraction discoverably memorized at \(k\) copies is the fraction with \(k^*(s) \le k\).


Proof. The plan is to find when the true symbol wins one step, then require every step to win, and finally read off the special cases.

Greedy picks the largest count. By part 2 of Lemma 13.1, at context \(c_t\) greedy decoding emits the symbol with the largest count \(N(c_t, w)\).
What the copies add. By part 1 of Lemma 13.1, the \(k\) copies add \(k\) to \(N(c_t, x_t)\). Because \(c_t\) occurs only once in \(s\), they add nothing to a rival pair \((c_t, w)\) with \(w \ne x_t\). So the true symbol’s count is \(N_-(c_t, x_t) + k\), and each rival’s is still \(N_-(c_t, w)\).
Winning one step. The true symbol wins outright when its count beats the largest rival count: \[N_-(c_t, x_t) + k > \max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w). \tag{13.7}\] Moving \(N_-(c_t, x_t)\) to the right turns this into \(k > \text{gap}_t\), where \(\text{gap}_t\) is the bracket of Equation 13.6. Both sides are whole numbers, so this is \(k \ge \text{gap}_t + 1\). When the true symbol has the lower code, a tie already wins, which removes the \(+1\) at that step.
Every step must win. If some step loses, greedy decoding emits a wrong symbol there, so its output does not begin with \(x\). So \(x\) comes out exactly when \(k \ge \text{gap}_t + 1\) at every step, which is \(k \ge k^*(s)\).
Unique contexts. If \(N_-(c_t, \cdot) = 0\) at every step, every gap is \(0 - 0 = 0\), so \(k^* = 1\).
The population rate. Each line is memorized at \(k\) copies exactly when \(k^*(s) \le k\), so the fraction of lines memorized is the fraction for which this holds.


Figure 13.1 draws steps 3 and 4 for one line. Each copy counts at every step at once, because it adds one to every pair on the line’s path, so the largest gap decides and not the sum of the gaps.






Figure 13.1: One secret line inserted once, and an order-5 model. At each step of the pin, the bars show the count of the true next digit (blue) and of its strongest rival (orange) in the rest of the training set. The label is the gap plus one, the copies that step needs. The line needs as many copies as its hardest step.



Duplication works as a vote, and model size works by splitting the vote. A longer context occurs at fewer places in the training text, so its rival counts are smaller, while the line’s own \(k\) votes follow it into every context. In the limit every line has contexts of its own and \(k^* = 1\), which is the toy version of “larger models memorize more”. For the same reason rare data are exposed first, since a line whose name shares few syllables with other names reaches a context of its own at a lower order. Real models show the same pattern. The change in the loss on an example when that example leaves the training set is its self-influence (Definition 7.3 in Algorithmic stability and generalization), and atypical examples, the analogue of a line whose contexts nobody else shares, have the largest (Feldman 2020).
Deduplication is the cheapest defence, because it lowers \(k\) for every repeated string. Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often, without losing quality. By Theorem 13.1 it does nothing for singletons in a high-capacity model, where \(k = 1\) already and \(k^* = 1\).

Example 13.2 The script prompts each of the 600 secrets with its true prefix, decodes five symbols greedily, and compares them with the pin (Table 13.3). It also computes \(k^*\) for every secret from Equation 13.6, and the prediction \(\Pr[k^* \le k]\) matches the verbatim rate exactly in all 36 cells, as Theorem 13.1 says it must (the script also handles contexts that recur within a line).
Along a row of the table, more copies mostly means more memorization, so that at order 5 the rate climbs from 0 at one copy to 0.70 at 32, and the small dips, such as 0.99 to 0.97 at order 7, come from the different 100 secrets of each column. Down a column, a larger model memorizes more. A line seen once is safe at orders up to 5, memorized 8% of the time at order 6, 70% at order 7 and 98% at order 8. Those singletons of the order-8 model are 1-eidetic in the sense of Definition 13.3.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.3 Canaries and the exposure metric
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing. An auditor wants a graded answer: how much closer to the secret does the model put an attacker? Carlini et al. (2019, “The Secret Sharer”) proposed planting random secrets of a fixed format in the training data and measuring where the trained model ranks each among all secrets of the same format. Planting the secret gives the right answer and the size of the space, so memorization can be measured exactly.
An attacker who guesses from the highest score down needs as many guesses as the rank of the true secret. Without the model the attacker faces every candidate, so the ratio of the rank to the size of the space measures what the model gave away, and on a log scale it becomes a difference of bits.

Definition 13.4 (Canary, rank and exposure) A canary is a sentence with a hole, together with a randomness space \(\mathcal R\) of values that can fill the hole. In the toy, the sentence is “my pin is” followed by a value \(r\), one of the \(|\mathcal R| = 10^5\) pins. A value \(\hat r\) is drawn uniformly at random from \(\mathcal R\), and the sentence filled with \(\hat r\) is inserted \(k\) times into the training data. After training, the rank of a candidate \(r\) is the number of candidates at least as likely as it under the model, itself and every tie included: \[\operatorname{rank}(r) = \big|\{r' \in \mathcal R : p(r' \mid \text{sentence}) \ge p(r \mid \text{sentence})\}\big|, \tag{13.8}\] where \(p(r \mid \text{sentence})\) is the model’s probability of \(r\) in the hole, after the sentence’s text. The exposure of the canary is the number of bits of search the model saves: \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.9}\]

Ties are counted against the attacker, who may have to try every tied candidate first. Because the rank lies between 1 and \(|\mathcal R|\), the exposure lies between 0 and \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\). Solving Equation 13.9 for the rank gives \(2^{\log_2|\mathcal R| - \mathrm{exposure}}\) guesses instead of \(|\mathcal R|\), so each bit of exposure halves the work. The maximum, \(\log_2 10^5 = 16.61\) bits for a pin, is the min-entropy of a uniform canary, the base-2 logarithm of its number of equally likely values, in the sense of Information theory (Definition 5.5), so a canary at full exposure has lost all of it.
Exposure is an audit tool because you know how it behaves when nothing was memorized, as a space of four candidates shows. Suppose the model was trained without the canary and gives the four candidates different scores. The drawn value is then independent of the model’s order, so it is equally likely to sit at rank 1, 2, 3 or 4, and its exposure is \(2 - \log_2(\text{rank})\), as Table 13.4 lists.

The mean of the four is \(\frac14(2 + 1 + 0.415 + 0) = 0.854\). The probability of exposure at least 1 is \(\frac12 = 2^{-1}\), from ranks 1 and 2, and of exposure at least 2 is \(\frac14 = 2^{-2}\), from rank 1 only. The next theorem shows that the tail \(2^{-h}\) holds, as a bound, for every space.

Theorem 13.2 (Exposure of a canary that was not memorized) Suppose the model does not depend on the drawn value \(\hat r\), for instance because the canary was never inserted. Then for every threshold \(h \ge 0\), \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge h\big] \le 2^{-h}. \tag{13.10}\] If moreover no two candidates tie, the average exposure is \[\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r)\big] = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \frac{\log_2(|\mathcal R|!)}{|\mathcal R|}, \tag{13.11}\] which tends to \(\log_2e = 1.4427\) bits as \(|\mathcal R|\) grows.


Proof. The plan is to show that the canary lands at a uniformly random position in a fixed order, count the positions with high exposure, check that ties only help, and average the exposure over the positions.

The order is fixed. The model does not depend on \(\hat r\), so its scores \(p(r \mid \cdot)\) are fixed numbers before \(\hat r\) is drawn. With no ties they order \(\mathcal R\) into positions \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\).
The canary’s position is uniform. The value \(\hat r\) is uniform on \(\mathcal R\) and independent of the scores, so its position is equally likely to be any of \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\).
Count the positions with high exposure. By Equation 13.9, exposure at least \(h\) means \(\log_2\operatorname{rank} \le \log_2|\mathcal R| - h\), that is \(\operatorname{rank} \le |\mathcal R|2^{-h}\). There are \(\lfloor|\mathcal R|2^{-h}\rfloor\) such positions, each with probability \(1/|\mathcal R|\), so \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge h\big] = \frac{\lfloor|\mathcal R|2^{-h}\rfloor}{|\mathcal R|} \le 2^{-h}. \tag{13.12}\]
Ties keep the bound valid. With ties, break them in a fixed order to get positions as before. The rank counts every candidate at least as likely as \(\hat r\), so it is never below the position of \(\hat r\). A higher rank means a lower exposure, so the probability of a high exposure can only fall.
The mean. With the rank uniform on \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\), the average of \(\log_2\operatorname{rank}\) is \(\frac{1}{|\mathcal R|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal R|}\log_2 i\). A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of the product, and \(1 \cdot 2 \cdots |\mathcal R| = |\mathcal R|!\), so the average is \(\log_2(|\mathcal R|!)/|\mathcal R|\). Subtracting it from \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) gives Equation 13.11.
The limit. Stirling’s approximation of the factorial, derived in Section E.2, says that \(\ln(|\mathcal R|!)\) is \(|\mathcal R|\ln|\mathcal R| - |\mathcal R|\) up to a correction that grows no faster than a multiple of \(\ln|\mathcal R|\). Dividing by \(|\mathcal R|\ln 2\) turns this into base-2 logarithms per candidate, and \(1/\ln 2 = \log_2 e\), so \[\frac{\log_2(|\mathcal R|!)}{|\mathcal R|} = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2 e + O\Big(\frac{\ln|\mathcal R|}{|\mathcal R|}\Big). \tag{13.13}\] The correction vanishes as the space grows, so the mean exposure tends to \(\log_2 e\).


The bound is tight whenever \(|\mathcal R|2^{-h}\) is a whole number, as in the space of four. Read with \(h\) set to the observed exposure, it says that \(2^{-\mathrm{exposure}}\) is a p-value, the probability, if nothing was memorized, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. “Was this canary inserted?” is a membership question, and the test that says “inserted” when the exposure is at least \(h\) has false positive rate at most \(2^{-h}\), by Equation 13.10. Membership inference calibrates such tests with shadow models, trained with and without a record, but none are needed here, because Equation 13.10 already says how a random canary’s exposure behaves.
Canaries also test defences, because you can compare exposure across two training runs that differ in one thing, such as deduplication or unlearning. With differentially private training, which Part 3 defines and which limits how much any one record can change the model, exposure near the null mean says that the planted secrets were not memorized, as Carlini et al. (2019) found for their canaries under private training.

Example 13.3 The script plants “my pin is 58745” and computes the exact exposure by scoring all \(10^5\) pins, for orders 2, 3 and 4, which do not saturate at once (Table 13.5). At \(k = 0\) the canary is one draw that was never inserted, so its exposure is a single sample of the null distribution of Theorem 13.2. The jump from \(k = 0\) to \(k = 1\) copies depends on whether a digit of the canary sits in a context that only the canary’s copies fill. No background line contains s_, an s followed by a space, because names are built from consonant-vowel syllables and so end in a vowel.
At order 2 the first digit’s context is a single space, shared by all 11,300 lines, so one copy is a single vote among thousands and moves the exposure by \(0.41 - 0.40 = 0.01\) bits. At order 3 the first digit’s context is s_, which occurs only in the canary. By part 3 of Lemma 13.1, one copy then makes the first digit 11 times as likely as each other first digit, a factor worth \(\log_2 11 = 3.46\) bits. The exposure rises from 0.89 to 4.05, by \(4.05 - 0.89 = 3.16\) bits. That is close to 3.46 but not equal, because multiplying the canary’s probability by 11 does not divide its rank by 11. The rank falls only by the number of pins the canary overtakes, and that number depends on how densely the scores lie just above it. At order 4 the first two digits have the unique contexts is_ and s_5, worth about \(2 \times 3.46 = 6.92\) bits, of which the exposure, going from 3.76 to 9.98, gains \(9.98 - 3.76 = 6.22\). The remaining digits share their contexts with the 5,000 background pins, and they move only as the copies outvote them.

For orders 2, 3 and 4 the scores have no ties, so their exposures are exactly the uniform-rank values. Their mean is 1.443 bits, against 1.4426 from Equation 13.11, and a fraction \(0.03125 = 1/32 = 2^{-5}\) has exposure at least 5, exactly on the bound Equation 13.10. Ties work the other way, because the rank counts every tied candidate, so a model that ties many pins shows low exposure whatever it stores. The order-8 model trained on the contact list alone has never seen the contexts after “my pin is”, so it gives every pin the same probability, every rank is \(|\mathcal R|\) and every exposure is 0.

13.3.1 Estimating exposure in a large space
For a large space, such as 9-digit numbers, exposure has to be estimated from a sample of candidates. The counting estimate of \(\operatorname{rank}/|\mathcal R|\) is the fraction of sampled candidates at least as likely as the canary. With \(m\) samples its smallest non-zero value is \(1/m\), so it cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2m\). Extrapolation fits a distribution to the sampled scores and reads off its tail beyond the canary’s score, and Carlini et al. (2019) fit a skew-normal, a normal with one heavier tail. At order 3, the script estimates the canary’s exposure from 10,000 random pins in both ways, fitting a plain normal for the second (Table 13.6).

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.4 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.4 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
The attacker of Section 13.1 had the training prefix, but a real attacker has only the model. This section asks what such an attacker can extract, and how it tells memorized text from text that is merely likely. Carlini et al. (2021) answered with a three-stage attack on GPT-2, whose hard stage, the ranking, is a hypothesis test.

Definition 13.5 (Generate-rank-verify attack) The attacker generates a large number of samples from the model, ranks the distinct generations by a score of how likely each is to be memorized, and verifies the top of the ranking against a source of training text. Its quality is the precision of the top of the ranking, the fraction of the top-ranked generations that are real training data.

Verifying is a search, against the training data or public sources. Ranking needs more thought, because a string may be likely as ordinary text that any model finds likely, or because the target memorized it, and only the second is a leak. So for a generated string \(x\), the attacker tests the hypothesis \(H_0\), “\(x\) was drawn from common text”, against \(H_1\), “\(x\) was drawn from what the target memorized”. A reference model \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\), trained on data from the same distribution but not on the target’s training set, gives the distribution of common text, and the target model \(p_\theta\) itself stands in for \(H_1\), since it gives memorized strings high probability. The evidence for memorization is then the ratio of the two probabilities, a difference on a log scale.

Proposition 13.2 (Rank generations by the likelihood ratio) Suppose that under \(H_0\) a string has probability \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) and under \(H_1\) probability \(p_\theta(x)\). Call the fraction of \(H_0\) strings a test flags its false positive rate (FPR), and the fraction of \(H_1\) strings its true positive rate (TPR). Among all tests with a given FPR, the one with the highest TPR flags a string when the log-likelihood ratio \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x) \tag{13.14}\] is above a threshold. Ranking by \(\ln p_\theta(x)\) alone gives the same order when \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is constant.


Proof. 

The best test thresholds the ratio. The Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1) says that, among all tests with a given FPR, the one with the highest TPR flags \(x\) when the likelihood ratio \(p_\theta(x)/p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) is above a threshold. Each flagged string costs false positives in proportion to \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) and gains true positives in proportion to \(p_\theta(x)\), so for a fixed budget of false positives you catch the most by flagging the largest ratios first.
Take logarithms. The logarithm is increasing, so it keeps the order of the ratios, and thresholding the ratio is the same as thresholding its logarithm, Equation 13.14.
Raw likelihood. If \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is a constant, \(\ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) is the same for every string, so \(\Lambda\) and \(\ln p_\theta\) order the strings in the same way.


Ranking by raw likelihood, \(\ln p_\theta(x)\) alone, treats every string as equally common a priori. That assumption is wrong exactly for strings that are likely under any model, such as software licences, news boilerplate and number sequences, and those are the strings raw likelihood puts first. Extracting them reveals nothing, and since a reference model knows them too, their ratio is close to 1 and Equation 13.14 cancels them. Membership inference calibrates in the same way, comparing the target’s loss on a record, minus the log of its probability, with the loss from models that did not see it.
The reference can be crude. Carlini et al. (2021) used a smaller model of the same family, and also zlib, a general-purpose compressor whose output length on the text measures its predictability without any model and stands in for \(-\ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\). The attacker cares about precision more than recall, because it checks the top few candidates by hand. Ordinary generations vastly outnumber memorized ones, so flagging a few strings with high precision needs a tiny FPR, the same operating point that matters in membership inference.

Example 13.4 The attacker samples 20,000 lines from the order-6 model, starting each at the beginning of a line. To make ranking hard, 50 public lines, such as the entries of a published directory, are added 100 times each to the target’s training set. The reference model is trained on an independent contact list of 5,000 lines plus the same 50 public lines, 100 times each. A generation counts as a hit if it is a private training line, background or secret.
Of the 20,000 samples, 14,852 are distinct, and among them are 197 private training lines and all 50 public lines. By duplication group, the samples contain none of the secrets inserted 1, 2 or 4 times, 11% of those inserted 8 times, 86% of those inserted 16 times and all of those inserted 32 times. With the prefix, 8% of the singletons and 65% of the lines seen twice come out at order 6 (Table 13.3). Without the prefix, a sample must first produce the right name before it can produce the pin, and only heavily duplicated lines make their names likely enough.
Ranking decides the precision (Figure 13.5). Of the top 100 distinct generations by target likelihood, only 45 are private training lines, and the rest are mostly the 50 public lines, the most likely strings the model knows. Ranking by Equation 13.14, 85 of the top 100 are private training lines, because the reference model also finds the public lines likely and cancels them.







Figure 13.5: Fraction of the top-ranked distinct generations that are private training lines (solid) or public lines (dashed), from 20,000 samples of an order-6 model trained with 50 public lines repeated 100 times. Ranking by likelihood puts the public lines first, and ranking by the ratio to the reference model puts the private lines first.




13.4.1 The divergence attack on a production model
A chat model that has been aligned, further trained to answer as an assistant rather than continue documents, rarely emits training data when sampled, so the toy’s generate stage fails on it. Nasr et al. (2023) found a prompt that brings the data out anyway, verifying generations against the training sets of open models and, for closed ones, against a 9-terabyte corpus of public web text. Their divergence attack asked ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) to repeat a single word forever. After many repetitions the model left its chat behaviour and began to emit text from its pretraining data, the web text it learned from before alignment, much of it matching the web corpus verbatim. They report training data emitted about 150 times as often as in normal use, and over 10,000 unique memorized examples, including contact details, for about 200 US dollars.

text:
13.7 References

Carlini, Liu, Erlingsson, Kos & Song, “The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks” (USENIX Security 2019): canaries, the exposure metric, its estimation by sampling and skew-normal extrapolation, and extraction of planted secrets by search.
Carlini et al., “Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models” (USENIX Security 2021): extractable and \(k\)-eidetic memorization; the generate-rank-verify attack on GPT-2 with perplexity, reference-model, zlib and lowercase ranking.
Carlini, Ippolito, Jagielski, Lee, Tramèr & Zhang, “Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models” (ICLR 2023): memorization measured by prompting with training prefixes; log-linear growth with model size, duplication and prompt length.
Nasr et al., “Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models” (2023): discoverable against extractable memorization, measurement on open models against their training sets, and the divergence attack on an aligned chat model.
Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel, “Deduplicating Training Data Mitigates Privacy Risks in Language Models” (ICML 2022): how the rate of regenerated sequences grows with duplication.
Lee et al., “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better” (ACL 2022): near-duplicate detection at scale and its effect on emitted training text and model quality.
Ippolito et al., “Preventing Generation of Verbatim Memorization in Language Models Gives a False Sense of Privacy” (INLG 2023): approximate memorization and why verbatim filters fail.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020): why accuracy on rare examples requires memorizing them.
Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), ch. 3: \(n\)-gram language models, smoothing and perplexity.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 The reconstruction game
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type, but the raw text never leaves the phones. A server sends the current model \(\theta\) to each phone, the phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples, and only that gradient goes back. The server averages the gradients of many phones and takes a gradient step on the model. This is the setting of federated learning (FL), and it is often described as private because “the data stay on the device”. This chapter asks one question about it: what does a single client’s gradient reveal about the client’s data?
The answer is often everything, and one idea explains why. In a fully connected layer, each row of the weight gradient is the layer’s input multiplied by a single number, the rate at which the loss changes with that row’s output. The bias gradient is the list of those numbers, one per row. So with one example, dividing a row of the weight gradient by the matching entry of the bias gradient gives back the input exactly. The chapter takes four steps. First, one division recovers the input of one example. Second, the signs of the last layer’s gradient give its label, because the true class is the only one whose entry is negative. Third, for layers that offer no such division, such as convolutions, Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) searches for an input whose gradient matches the one observed. Fourth, the chapter asks which of these attacks survive when the client averages over a batch.
The running example comes in two sizes. A network with three inputs and two hidden units is small enough to compute by hand, and the division gives back its input \((0.5, 1, 0.2)\) exactly from each of its two hidden units. The experiments then use synthetic \(8\times8\) images and a network with 32 hidden units, whose gradient has 2,212 entries against 64 unknown pixels. There the division recovers an image to rounding error, DLG recovers one with about 13 correct digits after 600 steps, and in a batch of 4 the same division, applied at each unit that responds to only one image, still recovers all four images.
Before any attack can be judged, you need to know who sees what and what counts as success. This section fixes both for one round of federated training, in the vocabulary of Threat models and privacy games, and then fixes the network that every experiment uses.
The server is honest-but-curious in the sense of that chapter: it runs the protocol as specified and only analyses what it receives. Its access is the transcript. It sees each client’s own update, here the gradient the client sends, and it knows the architecture and every parameter of \(\theta\) because it chose them. The client’s loss is the average of the losses of its examples, and the derivative of an average is the average of the derivatives, so the gradient it sends is the average of its per-example gradients.
The relative error is 0 for a perfect reconstruction and 1 for a mistake as large as the input itself. The matching is needed because an average does not change when you reorder the examples, so the gradient carries no record of which example came first. The attacks below either recover the client’s exact pixels or, for large batches, produce blends, images that mix several of the client’s inputs.
All experiments use one small network, written in NumPy. Its first fully connected layer gives one number per hidden unit, the unit’s pre-activation, and an activation is applied to each unit. A second fully connected layer turns the result into one score per class, called a logit. The softmax turns the logits into probabilities by exponentiating and normalizing, so that every probability is positive and they sum to 1. The loss is the cross-entropy, minus the log of the probability the model gives to the true label, which is small when the model is confidently right.
The activation \(\sigma\) is either the ReLU \(\max(a, 0)\), which passes positive values and replaces negative ones by 0, or the sigmoid \(1/(1 + e^{-a})\), which squashes every value smoothly into \((0, 1)\).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
Definition 14.1 (The gradient reconstruction game) Fix a model \(\theta\), known to the server, and a population of labelled examples. The challenger, who holds the secret, is the client, and the adversary, who guesses it, is the server. The game has three steps.

The challenger draws a batch of \(B\) labelled examples \((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_B, y_B)\) from the population. The inputs are the secret.
The client sends the gradient of its average loss with respect to all the parameters, \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i). \tag{14.1}\]
The adversary sees \((\theta, g)\) and outputs reconstructions \(\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B\).

Each true input \(x\) is matched to its closest reconstruction \(\hat x\) in Euclidean distance (two inputs may share one), and the pair is scored by its relative error \(\|\hat x - x\|/\|x\|\).




Definition 14.2 (The network) An input \(x \in \mathbb R^d\) has a label \(y\), one of \(K\) classes. It passes through a first layer with weights \(W_1 \in \mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and biases \(b_1\), one per hidden unit. An activation \(\sigma\) is applied to each of the \(m\) hidden units. A second layer with weights \(W_2 \in \mathbb R^{K\times m}\) and biases \(b_2\) gives one logit per class, and then \[a = W_1x + b_1, \quad h = \sigma(a), \quad z = W_2h + b_2, \quad p = \mathrm{softmax}(z), \quad \ell = -\ln p_y, \tag{14.2}\] where the softmax has entries \[p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{k'}e^{z_{k'}}}. \tag{14.3}\] The backward signals are the rates at which the loss changes with each hidden unit’s pre-activation and with each logit, \(\gamma_1 = \partial\ell/\partial a\) and \(\gamma_2 = \partial\ell/\partial z\).



Example 14.1 The client’s inputs are synthetic \(8\times8\) grey-scale images, so \(d = 64\). Each shows one of \(K = 4\) shapes (a horizontal bar, a vertical bar, a diagonal and a square outline), shifted at random and with pixel noise. The network has \(m = 32\) hidden units and is at its random initialization, as in the first round of training. The first layer has \(64\cdot32\) weights and 32 biases, and the second has \(32\cdot4\) weights and 4 biases, so the network has \[64\cdot32 + 32 + 32\cdot4 + 4 = 2{,}212 \tag{14.4}\] parameters. The server receives 2,212 numbers about an example that has only 64 unknown pixels.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 What a gradient is made of
text:
14.2 What a gradient is made of
Every attack in this chapter reads the input out of the gradient, so you first need to know where in the gradient the input sits. Two results answer this, one placing the input in every row of the weight gradient and one giving the backward signals that scale those rows.
The reason the input appears is the chain rule. The weight \(W_{jk}\) multiplies the input \(x_k\) and feeds only the output \(a_j\), so the loss changes with it at the rate at which the loss changes with \(a_j\), times \(x_k\). So the gradient of a weight is the signal flowing backward into its output times the input flowing forward into it. Collected over all \(j\) and \(k\), these products form a matrix whose \((j, k)\) entry is \(\gamma_jx_k\), called the outer product of \(\gamma\) and \(x\).

Proposition 14.1 (The gradient of a fully connected layer is an outer product) Let a fully connected layer compute \(a = Wx + b\) with \(W \in \mathbb R^{m\times d}\), and let the loss \(\ell\) depend on \(W\) and \(b\) only through \(a\), with backward signal \(\gamma = \partial\ell/\partial a\). Then \[\nabla_W\ell = \gamma\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_b\ell = \gamma. \tag{14.5}\]


Proof. 

Each weight feeds one output. Written out, output \(j\) is \(a_j = \sum_kW_{jk}x_k + b_j\). The weight \(W_{jk}\) appears in \(a_j\) only, with coefficient \(x_k\), so \(\partial a_j/\partial W_{jk} = x_k\).
The chain rule multiplies the two rates. The loss depends on \(W_{jk}\) only through \(a_j\), so \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial W_{jk}} = \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a_j}\,\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial W_{jk}} = \gamma_jx_k, \tag{14.6}\] which is the \((j, k)\) entry of \(\gamma x^\top\).
The bias has coefficient 1. The bias \(b_j\) enters \(a_j\) with coefficient 1, so the same rule gives \(\partial\ell/\partial b_j = \gamma_j\).


Row \(j\) of the outer product is the input multiplied by the number \(\gamma_j\). The signal \(\gamma\) depends on everything above the layer (the rest of the network, the loss, the label), but the factor \(x^\top\) does not. So the rest of the network can only rescale the rows, never change their direction.
To use Proposition 14.1 at the first layer you need its backward signal \(\gamma_1\), and the chain rule obtains it by sending the last layer’s signal \(\gamma_2\) back through the network. At the last layer the signal has a simple form. Raising the logit of a wrong class \(k\) raises the loss at the rate \(p_k\), the probability the model already gives that class, and raising the logit of the true class lowers the loss at the rate \(1 - p_y\). Each hidden unit then collects the logits’ signals, weighted by its connections to them, and multiplies by the slope of its activation.

Proposition 14.2 (The backward signals) For the network of Definition 14.2, write \(e_y\) for the one-hot vector of the label, with 1 in position \(y\) and 0 elsewhere, and \(\odot\) for the entrywise product of two vectors. Then \[\gamma_2 = p - e_y, \tag{14.7}\] so the entry of \(\gamma_2\) at the true label is negative and every other entry is positive, and \[\gamma_1 = (W_2^\top\gamma_2)\odot\sigma'(a). \tag{14.8}\]


Proof. The plan is to differentiate the loss in the logits, read off the signs, and then pass the result back through the second layer and the activation.

Remove the fraction. Since \(p_y = e^{z_y}/\sum_ke^{z_k}\), taking minus its log gives \[\ell = -z_y + \ln\sum_ke^{z_k}. \tag{14.9}\]
Differentiate in one logit. The first term depends only on \(z_y\), so it contributes \(-1\) when \(k = y\) and 0 otherwise. The second term is the log of a sum, whose derivative is the derivative of the sum, \(e^{z_k}\), divided by the sum itself, which is \(p_k\). Together, \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k} = p_k - \mathbf 1[k = y], \tag{14.10}\] which is entry \(k\) of \(p - e_y\).
Read off the signs. Every \(e^{z_k}\) is positive, so every \(p_k\) lies strictly between 0 and 1. The entry at the label is \(p_y - 1 < 0\), and every other entry is \(p_k > 0\).
Pass back through the second layer. Logit \(k\) is \(z_k = \sum_jW_{2,kj}h_j + b_{2,k}\), so \(h_j\) enters each logit with coefficient \(W_{2,kj}\), and the chain rule sums over the logits: \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial h_j} = \sum_k\gamma_{2,k}W_{2,kj} = (W_2^\top\gamma_2)_j. \tag{14.11}\]
Pass through the activation. The output \(h_j = \sigma(a_j)\) changes with \(a_j\) at the rate \(\sigma'(a_j)\), so multiplying step 4 by it gives entry \(j\) of Equation 14.8.


For ReLU the slope is \(\sigma'(a_j) = \mathbf 1[a_j > 0]\), which is 1 if the unit is switched on and 0 if it is switched off. So a unit that is switched off on an input has \(\gamma_{1,j} = 0\) and, by Proposition 14.1, a zero row in the first-layer weight gradient.

Example 14.2 Take \(d = 3\) inputs, \(m = 2\) ReLU units and \(K = 2\) classes, with \[W_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.4 & -0.2 & 0.1\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.4\end{pmatrix},\quad b_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.1\\ -0.1\end{pmatrix},\quad W_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix},\quad b_2 = 0, \tag{14.12}\] and the example \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\) with label \(y = 1\), the first class. Table 14.2 walks through the forward pass, the backward pass and the gradient.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
The server sees \(g\). Is there any computation, without a search, that gives back the client’s input? For a fully connected first layer with a bias, the most common kind, there is one division, which Phong et al. (2018) pointed out for this federated setting.
By Proposition 14.1, row \(j\) of the first-layer weight gradient is \(x\) scaled by \(\gamma_{1,j}\), and entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is that same number, so dividing removes the scale.

Theorem 14.1 (Exact recovery from one example) Suppose the client sends the gradient of a single example, and the first layer is fully connected with a bias, \(a = W_1x + b_1\), whatever the layers above it and the loss. Then for every unit \(j\) with \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j \ne 0\), \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.13}\] Moreover, if \(\gamma_1 \ne 0\), the matrix \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\) has rank one, and its row space is the line through \(x\).


Proof. 

Write out what the server sees. Proposition 14.1 applied to the first layer gives \((\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:} = \gamma_{1,j}\,x^\top\) and \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j = \gamma_{1,j}\).
Divide one by the other. When \(\gamma_{1,j} \ne 0\), the ratio is \(\gamma_{1,j}x^\top/\gamma_{1,j} = x^\top\). Nothing about the rest of the network enters, because the depth, the activations above, the loss and the label all sit inside the number \(\gamma_{1,j}\), and that number cancels.
Read off the rank. All rows of \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \gamma_1x^\top\) are multiples of the same vector \(x^\top\), and at least one is nonzero when \(\gamma_1 \ne 0\). A matrix whose rows are all multiples of one nonzero vector has rank one, and its row space is spanned by that vector.


The attack is exact and needs no optimization, no prior knowledge of the data and no label. It also checks itself, because every usable unit must give the same answer.
Four things get in its way, and only one stops it fully. With ReLU, switched-off units give nothing, but one active unit is enough. Without a bias there is no denominator, but the rank-one structure still gives the direction of \(x\), so only the scale remains unknown, one number that matching gradients as in Section 14.5 finds. A convolutional first layer really breaks the outer-product form. It applies the same small filter at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum of outer products over all the image patches, and only the search of Section 14.5 can undo it. A batch of more than one example also breaks the formula, but only partly, as Section 14.6 shows.






Figure 14.1: Exact recovery from the first-layer gradient of a ReLU network with 32 hidden units. Left: the client’s \(8\times8\) input. Middle: \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\), one row per hidden unit and one column per pixel (blue positive, red negative), next to \(\nabla_{b_1}\ell\). Right: one row divided by its bias entry, the input exactly.




Example 14.3 In the hand network of Example 14.2, the server never sees \(a\), \(h\), \(z\) or \(p\). It sees only the gradient rows of Table 14.2. Dividing the first row by \(-0.3279\) and the second by \(0.9838\) gives \((0.5, 1, 0.2)\) both times, which is the input.
On the images, Figure 14.1 shows the attack on one input. Of the 32 ReLU units, 13 are switched on and have a nonzero bias gradient. Every one of the 13 ratios equals the image to a relative error of at most \(6.7\times10^{-17}\), which is rounding error. To check the rank, look at the singular values of \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\). They measure how much of the matrix lies along each of its independent directions, so a rank-one matrix has exactly one that is not zero. The largest is \(1.6155\) and the second is \(9.5\times10^{-17}\) times the first, so the gradient is rank one, as Theorem 14.1 says.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
The gradient depends on the label too, and the label is often the most sensitive part: the diagnosis, the word typed next, the class of a photo. Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen (2020) noticed that the label can be read off the last layer in closed form. Their attack, iDLG (“improved DLG”), then searches only for the input, which makes the gradient-matching search of Section 14.5, below, easier and more reliable.
The next result gives three rules, one from the bias, one from the weights and one for batches. All three come from Proposition 14.2, which says that the last layer’s backward signal is a vector of probabilities with 1 subtracted at the true label. A batch gradient averages these vectors. Before the division by the batch size, the subtracted 1s in each position add up to the number of examples of that class.

Proposition 14.3 (Labels from the last layer) Let the network of Definition 14.2 keep its last-layer bias \(b_2\). For a single example, the label is the position of the only negative entry of the last-layer bias gradient, \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.14}\] If in addition the hidden activations satisfy \(h \ge 0\) and \(h \ne 0\), as for ReLU or the sigmoid, then row \(y\) of \(\nabla_{W_2}\ell\) is the only row whose entries are all non-positive, and the only row with a negative sum.
For a batch of \(B\) examples, write \(n_k\) for the number of examples of class \(k\) and \(p_{ik}\) for the probability the model gives class \(k\) on example \(i\). Then \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.15}\]


Proof. 

The bias rule. Proposition 14.1 at the last layer gives \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = \gamma_2\), and Proposition 14.2 gives \(\gamma_2 = p - e_y\), with entry \(p_y - 1 < 0\) at the label and \(p_k > 0\) elsewhere. The smallest entry is therefore at \(y\).
The weight rule. Proposition 14.1 gives \((\nabla_{W_2}\ell)_{k,:} = \gamma_{2,k}\,h^\top\). With \(h \ge 0\), row \(y\) is a negative number times non-negative entries, so it is non-positive entrywise, and every other row is \(p_kh^\top \ge 0\). Summing a row multiplies \(\gamma_{2,k}\) by \(\sum_jh_j\), which is positive because \(h \ge 0\) and \(h \ne 0\), so the sum keeps the sign of \(\gamma_{2,k}\).
The counts. The batch gradient is the average of the per-example ones, so \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = \frac1B\sum_i(p_i - e_{y_i})\). The vector \(e_{y_i}\) has a 1 in position \(k\) exactly when example \(i\) has class \(k\), so \(\sum_ie_{y_i}\) counts the examples of each class, and entry \(k\) is \[(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k = \frac1B\Big(\sum_ip_{ik} - n_k\Big). \tag{14.16}\] Multiplying by \(B\) and solving for \(n_k\) gives Equation 14.15.


For one example the bias rule makes no errors, at any point of training, because the sign argument never depends on how good the model is. A confident model gives a tiny negative entry, which floating point hides only when \(p_y\) rounds to 1 and the entry becomes 0. That is one reason attacks are run on models early in training. Without a bias, and even for an activation such as tanh whose outputs can be negative, step 2 of the proof still shows that row \(y\) of \(\nabla_{W_2}\ell\) is a negative multiple of \(h\) and every other row a positive one, so the label’s row points the opposite way.
For a batch, the gradient leaks the label histogram. Equation 14.15 is exact, so the only unknown is the total prediction \(\sum_ip_{ik}\), and the attacker can estimate it well. If it holds data of its own from a similar population, which this attack assumes, it can run the model on them and average the predictions into a guess \(\bar p\), then replace the total by \(B\bar p_k\) and round. The true counts are integers, so rounding gives them exactly whenever the estimate of the total is off by less than \(\frac12\) for every class. The cruder guess \(\bar p_k = 1/K\) of evenly spread predictions does worse, because even an untrained network favours some classes over others.






Figure 14.2: Labels from the last-layer bias gradient. Left: for one example, \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = p - e_y\) has a single negative entry, at the true label (red). Right: for a batch of 16, the counts \(B(\bar p - \nabla_{b_2}\ell)\) with \(\bar p\) the model’s average prediction on the attacker’s own images (green) are close to the true counts (grey); with \(\bar p = 1/K\) (orange) they are off by up to about half an example.




Example 14.4 In the hand network of Example 14.2, the last-layer bias gradient is \(\gamma_2 = (-0.6559, 0.6559)\). Its smallest entry is the first, so the server reads off the label 1. On 1,000 random images and random networks, both the bias rule and the weight rule name the label correctly in a fraction 1.000 of the trials.
For a batch, take 16 images with true counts \((4, 2, 4, 6)\) over the four shapes. Table 14.3 reads them off the bias gradient of the 32-unit ReLU network, with three guesses for the total prediction in Equation 14.15.

With the averaged guess every estimate is within \(\frac12\) of the truth, the largest miss being \(4.19 - 4 = 0.19\), so rounding fixes it. With the uniform guess the first class is off by \(4 - 2.12 = 1.88\), and rounding cannot help.
Over 200 random batches and networks, the averaged guess gets all the rounded counts right in 1.000 of batches of 4 and 0.975 of batches of 16. For batches of 64 the rate falls to 0.525, and with the uniform guess the three rates are 0.925, 0.095 and 0.000. The rates fall because the error of the estimate is a sum of \(B\) deviations, one per example, and that sum grows with \(B\). At \(B = 16\) the largest error over the four classes, before rounding, has a median over batches of 0.233 with the averaged guess, against 1.102 with the uniform one.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Deep Leakage from Gradients
The closed forms need a fully connected layer with a bias. Most image models start with convolutions, and many architectures have layers that rescale or mix their inputs, such as normalization and attention, or no biases at all. Zhu, Liu & Han (2019) gave a generic attack that needs none of these: guess an input, compute its gradient, and move the guess until the gradients match. Zhu et al. also searched for a soft label, a probability vector standing in for the unknown label, and that joint search often failed. With the label fixed by Equation 14.14, the search is over the input only.
DLG measures how badly a guess matches by one number, the squared distance between the gradient the guessed batch would produce and the observed gradient, summed over all the gradient’s entries. It is zero for a perfect match and positive otherwise.

Definition 14.3 (Deep Leakage from Gradients) Given the model \(\theta\), the observed gradient \(g\) and the labels \(y_1, \dots, y_B\), write \(G(x') = \frac1B\sum_i\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i)\) for the gradient that a guessed batch \(x' = (x_1', \dots, x_B')\) would produce. The matching loss is \(R(x') = \|G(x') - g\|^2\), and DLG outputs \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\|\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\|^2, \tag{14.17}\] searching by a gradient method that starts from random noise and repeatedly moves the guess a little downhill on \(R\).

For a batch, the label rules of Proposition 14.3 give only the counts of each class, not which example has which label. That is enough, because the guesses are interchangeable: the attacker hands out the recovered labels to the guesses in any order, and each guess is then pulled towards a true example with its label.
Two facts make this a sensible search. The true batch scores the best value the matching loss can take, and the slope of the matching loss can be computed, as long as the network can be differentiated twice. The second fact needs the second derivatives because \(G\) is itself made of first derivatives of the network.

Proposition 14.4 (The true batch is a global minimizer) The true batch \((x_1, \dots, x_B)\) has \(R = 0\), the smallest value \(R\) takes. If the network is twice differentiable, then \(R\) is differentiable in the guess, with \[\nabla_{x'}R = 2\,J_G(x')^\top\big(G(x') - g\big), \tag{14.18}\] where \(J_G\) is the Jacobian of \(G\), the matrix of rates at which each gradient entry changes with each input pixel.


Proof. 

The true batch is a global minimizer. \(R\) is a squared length, so \(R \ge 0\) for every guess. Plugging in the true inputs reproduces \(g\) exactly, so \(R = 0\) there, and no guess can do better.
The slope of a squared length. A squared length \(\|u\|^2\) changes with \(u\) at the rate \(2u\). Here \(u = G(x') - g\), and \(g\) does not depend on the guess.
The chain rule passes the slope back to the guess. \(u\) changes with \(x'\) at the rates collected in \(J_G(x')\), so the chain rule multiplies the transpose of that matrix by \(2u\), which is Equation 14.18. The entries of \(J_G\) are derivatives of the gradient, so they are second derivatives of the network, and they exist because the network is twice differentiable.


The need for second derivatives is why Zhu et al. replaced ReLU by the sigmoid, and why the experiments here do the same. The gradient \(G\) contains the factor \(\sigma'(a)\) of Equation 14.8, and the search differentiates \(G\), so it differentiates that factor too. The ReLU’s slope is 0 or 1, constant on each side of zero, so the factor does not change as the guess moves, and the part of the slope of \(R\) that would flow through it is zero. The sigmoid’s slope varies smoothly, so that part is not lost.
Nobody builds \(J_G\) itself, which has one row per parameter and one column per pixel. Automatic-differentiation libraries instead differentiate the gradient computation, running backpropagation through the backward pass, which is called double backpropagation. That needs only a twice-differentiable network, not a fully connected first layer, so DLG also works for convolutional networks and on real images. Zhu et al. recover pictures from the CIFAR-100 image dataset and text tokens from single-example gradients.
Proposition 14.4 does not say that the search finds the true batch. \(R\) is not convex in the guess, and for such a function Optimization shows that a gradient method with a suitable step only drives the slope to zero. That gives a stationary point, where the surface is flat, which may or may not be the global minimum, so success is an empirical question. The final value of \(R\) tells you which case you are in: \(R = 0\) up to rounding means an exact match, while a value stuck well above zero means the search is stuck, and restarts or image priors, penalties that favour natural-looking images, may help.
The minimizer is also plausibly unique, since matching \(g\) imposes one equation per parameter, 2,212 here against \(64B\) unknown pixels, though that count is not a proof. For a single example the sigmoid network still has a fully connected first layer with a bias, so Theorem 14.1 shows that its gradient determines the input. Geiping et al. (2020) improved the search by comparing gradients by a cosine distance and penalizing differences between neighbouring pixels, and so recovered recognizable images from trained networks and from batches.






Figure 14.3: Deep Leakage from Gradients on one \(8\times8\) image, sigmoid network with 32 hidden units. Top: the reconstruction \(\hat x\) at selected iterations of the Adam optimizer (Example 14.5), starting from uniform noise, and the true input. Bottom: the matching loss \(R(\hat x)\) and the relative error, on a log scale. Both fall geometrically until they reach rounding error.




Example 14.5 The chapter’s script (Section 14.8) runs DLG on one image with the sigmoid network of 32 hidden units, computing the slope of Equation 14.18 by double backpropagation written out by hand. A finite-difference check, which nudges one pixel slightly and sees how much \(R\) changes, agrees with it to within \(1.2\times10^{-10}\). The search starts from uniform noise and runs 600 steps of the Adam optimizer, with learning rate 0.05 decaying linearly to 0. Adam is a variant of gradient descent that scales each pixel’s step by a running estimate of the size of that pixel’s gradient. The label comes from Equation 14.14.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Batches and averaging
Clients rarely send the gradient of one example. They send the average over a batch, or the change in parameters after several local training steps, which the end of this section treats. Averaging is often said to protect the individual examples, and this section measures that claim. Averaging does destroy the one-line formula of Equation 14.13, and it does make DLG harder. But the span of the batch survives, and so does every example to which some hidden unit responds alone.
The structure of a batch gradient follows from Proposition 14.1. Each example contributes one outer product, whose rows are multiples of its own input, so every row of the sum is a weighted combination of the \(B\) inputs.

Proposition 14.5 (The gradient of a batch) Take a batch of \(B\) examples and a fully connected first layer, and write \(\gamma_{1,i}\) for the backward signal of example \(i\) at that layer, with entries \(\gamma_{1,ij}\), one per unit \(j\). Then \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\gamma_{1,i}\,x_i^\top, \tag{14.20}\] so \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\) has rank at most \(B\), and every row lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{x_1, \dots, x_B\}\). For every unit \(j\) with \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j \ne 0\), the unit ratio is a weighted combination of the inputs, \[\frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j} = \sum_{i=1}^B\frac{\gamma_{1,ij}}{\sum_{i'}\gamma_{1,i'j}}\,x_i^\top, \tag{14.21}\] with weights that sum to 1 (some may be negative). It equals \(x_i\) exactly when \(\gamma_{1,ij} \ne 0\) and \(\gamma_{1,i'j} = 0\) for every \(i' \ne i\).


Proof. 

A sum of outer products. The batch gradient is the average of the per-example gradients, and by Proposition 14.1 each of those is \(\gamma_{1,i}x_i^\top\).
Rank and span. Stack the \(x_i^\top\) as the rows of a matrix \(X\) with \(B\) rows, and the \(\gamma_{1,i}^\top\) as the rows of a matrix \(\Gamma\). The sum of outer products is then the product \(\frac1B\Gamma^\top X\). A product has rank at most that of either factor, and \(X\) has only \(B\) rows, so the rank is at most \(B\). Row \(j\) of the product is \(\frac1B\sum_i\Gamma_{ij}x_i^\top\), a combination of the inputs, so it lies in their span.
The ratios. By Proposition 14.1 again, entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is \(\frac1B\sum_i\gamma_{1,ij}\). Dividing row \(j\) by it cancels the factors \(\frac1B\) and gives Equation 14.21. The weights are each example’s share of the same total, so they sum to 1, and if only \(\gamma_{1,ij}\) is nonzero the weight on \(x_i\) is 1 and all the others are 0.


For ReLU the condition for exact recovery, that only example \(i\) has a nonzero signal at unit \(j\), has a simple form. By Proposition 14.2, \(\gamma_{1,i'j} = 0\) whenever unit \(j\) is switched off on \(x_{i'}\), so a unit that is switched on for example \(i\) and for no other example gives back \(x_i\) exactly. Such a unit isolates example \(i\), and Section 14.7 asks how often that happens.
The span leaks even when nothing is isolated. When the gradient has rank \(B\), as it does for the batch of 4 below, its rows span exactly the span of the inputs. Every example is then a combination of \(B\) directions the attacker can read off the gradient, so a search such as DLG can look for each example as \(B\) unknown coefficients of those directions instead of \(d\) unknown pixels. That is 4 unknowns instead of 64 here, or of hundreds of thousands for real images.
Local steps do not help either. If the client takes several steps of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on its batch and sends the total change in parameters, only the backward signals change from step to step. For one example and a learning rate \(\eta\), step \(s\) changes \(W_1\) by \(-\eta\gamma_1^{(s)}x^\top\) and \(b_1\) by \(-\eta\gamma_1^{(s)}\), where \(\gamma_1^{(s)}\) is that step’s backward signal. Summed over the steps, the change in \(W_1\) is the vector \(-\eta\sum_s\gamma_1^{(s)}\) times \(x^\top\), still rank one, and the change in \(b_1\) is that same vector. So the scale still cancels and Equation 14.13 still recovers \(x\) exactly.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.7 How often a unit isolates an example
text:
14.7 How often a unit isolates an example
Every isolated example comes out exactly, so the share of a batch that a gradient exposes is the share isolated by at least one unit. How does that share depend on the batch size and on the width of the layer? To answer, you need a model of when units switch on, and the simplest one treats each unit’s response to each example as a fair coin.
For a single unit, the coin model is exact in one case. Suppose the first-layer bias is zero and the inputs are drawn from a distribution that is symmetric about zero, such as \(\mathcal N(0, I)\). Unit \(j\), with weights \((W_1)_{j,:}\), is on for \(x_i\) when \((W_1)_{j,:}\,x_i > 0\). With the weights fixed, symmetry makes this product equally likely to be positive or negative, it is exactly zero with probability 0, and independent inputs make the signs independent across the batch. So each unit’s on/off pattern over the batch is a sequence of fair coin flips. Different units look at the same inputs, though, so independence between units is only approximate, and real data are not symmetric at all.

Proposition 14.6 (Isolation under independent units) Take a ReLU first layer with \(m\) units and a batch of \(B\) examples. Suppose that each unit is on for each example with probability \(\frac12\), independently across examples and across units, and that every unit \(j\) active on an example \(i\) passes on a nonzero backward signal, \((W_2^\top\gamma_{2,i})_j \ne 0\), where \(\gamma_{2,i}\) is the last-layer signal of example \(i\). That fails only by coincidence. Then each example of the batch is recovered exactly by some unit ratio with probability \[P_{\text{iso}}(B, m) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m. \tag{14.22}\]


Proof. 

One unit. By Proposition 14.5 and the ReLU slope, unit \(j\) gives back \(x_i\) exactly when it is on for \(x_i\) and off for each of the other \(B - 1\) examples, since an active unit has a nonzero signal by hypothesis. Each of these \(B\) events has probability \(\frac12\), and they are independent, so their probability together is \(2^{-B}\).
Many units. The example is missed only if all \(m\) units miss it. The units are independent by hypothesis, so this has probability \((1 - 2^{-B})^m\), and subtracting from 1 gives Equation 14.22.


The formula pits an exponential in \(B\) against a count that grows linearly in \(m\). A unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-B}\), so among \(m\) units the expected number that isolate it is \(m2^{-B}\), and almost every example is isolated when \(m\) is much larger than \(2^B\). To find the width that gives an even chance, require the miss probability \((1 - 2^{-B})^m\) to be at most \(\frac12\) and take logs. The log of \(1 - 2^{-B}\) is negative, so dividing by it flips the inequality and gives \[m \ge \frac{\ln2}{-\ln(1 - 2^{-B})}. \tag{14.23}\] At \(B = 10\) the denominator is \(-\ln(1 - 2^{-10}) = 0.000977\), close to \(2^{-10}\) itself, and the bound is \(0.6931/0.000977 \approx 709.4\), so you need \(m \ge 710\) units. Real first layers have thousands of units, so if units behaved like these coins, batches of 10 would not be safe from this attack.
Data whose examples resemble one another, such as images of a few shapes, are easier for the attacker, not harder. With such images, a unit tends to fire on many examples of a batch or on few. The number of examples it fires for is more spread out than the coin model predicts, which statisticians call overdispersion. In particular some units fire only on rare inputs, and when such a unit fires on a large batch it usually fires on just one example, so isolation is much more common at large \(B\). Take one extreme model, in which each unit has its own firing rate \(r\), drawn uniformly between 0 and 1. A unit with rate \(r\) isolates a given example with probability \(r(1 - r)^{B-1}\), and averaging over \(r\) gives \(\int_0^1r(1 - r)^{B-1}\,dr = 1/(B(B + 1))\). That shrinks only like \(1/B^2\) instead of halving with each extra example.
The game of this chapter has an honest-but-curious server. A malicious server does better still, because it chooses \(\theta\) to attack rather than at random. It can plant first-layer units that fire on rare inputs only (“trap weights”, Boenisch et al. 2023), or that sort inputs into bins by a feature such as brightness (Fowl et al. 2022), so that most examples of even a large batch are isolated by construction.

Filled circles: Gaussian inputs and zero first-layer bias. Open squares: the \(8\times8\) images, where isolation decays much more slowly.

All 4 of the 4 images were recovered.
