title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
A hospital shares its discharge records with researchers, after deleting the names and keeping ZIP code, date of birth, sex and diagnosis. Is anyone in the file identifiable? Usually, yes, because most people are the only person with their combination of ZIP code, birth date and sex, so anyone who holds a voter roll with names and those three columns can join the two tables and name most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification. Unlike the rest of this part, it attacks the data itself rather than a trained model.
The one idea of the chapter is that identifying information is measured in bits, and bits add up. Picking one person out of \(n\) takes \(\log_2 n\) bits, because each bit halves the number of candidates, so 27.9 bits single out one of the 248.7 million people in the United States in 1990, the census year of the classic study below. An attribute with 12 equally likely values, such as a birth month, cuts the candidates twelvefold and so carries \(\log_2 12 \approx 3.6\) bits. When attributes are independent their cuts multiply, so their bits add. Once the attributes you know carry a few bits more than \(\log_2 n\), almost everyone is unique.
The running example is a synthetic census of \(n = 10{,}000\) people with eight attributes, which an adversary learns one at a time. Once the known attributes carry 12.90 bits, an average over people that Section 15.4 defines, a third of the people are already unique, even though that is below the \(\log_2 n = 13.29\) bits needed to name one person, because skewed attributes leave some people in rare combinations. At 20.39 bits 97.5% are unique.
Data protection practice sorts a table’s columns into three kinds. Direct identifiers, such as a name, name a person on their own, while sensitive attributes, such as a diagnosis, are what must not be tied to a person. Between them sit quasi-identifiers, such as a birth date. Each names nobody alone, but together they often single out one person, and they appear next to names in other datasets. “De-identification” usually removes only the direct identifiers. This section scores a join on the quasi-identifiers with a game in the style of Threat models, in which a challenger hides a secret and an adversary guesses it.
A target in a class of \(k\) look-alikes is found one time in \(k\), but it lands in that class \(k\) times as often as in a class of one, so each class adds the same \(1/n\) to the success, whatever its size.
Each unique record is a sure win, so the fraction of unique records is a lower bound on the success. Conversely, if every class has at least \(k\) records, then \(n\) records fill at most \(n/k\) classes, so \(J \le n/k\) and the success is at most \(1/k\), the idea that Syntactic anonymity studies.
The game assumes the adversary knows that the target is in the release. Otherwise a unique match may belong to someone who is not in \(R\), and whether that doubt protects anyone is the question of Section 15.6.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
Definition 15.1 (The linkage game) A release \(R\) holds \(n\) records, each with quasi-identifiers and a sensitive attribute. Records with identical quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class, and the \(J\) classes have sizes \(k_1, \dots, k_J\). A challenger draws a target uniformly from the \(n\) records and gives the adversary the target’s quasi-identifiers, as a voter roll would. The adversary outputs one record of \(R\) and wins if it is the target’s. The linkage attack outputs a record drawn uniformly from the target’s class.



Proposition 15.1 (Linkage success) In the game of Definition 15.1, the linkage attack wins with probability \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac1n\sum_{j=1}^J k_j\cdot\frac{1}{k_j} = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] the number of distinct quasi-identifier combinations divided by the number of records. No adversary that sees only the target’s quasi-identifiers does better.


Proof. 

Condition on the target’s class. A target in class \(j\) shares its quasi-identifiers with \(k_j - 1\) other records, so picking one of the \(k_j\) at random wins with probability \(1/k_j\).
Nothing beats this. Within a class, the target is equally likely to be any of the \(k_j\) records, because it was drawn uniformly and the adversary sees only quasi-identifiers, which are identical within the class. So every guess within the class wins with probability exactly \(1/k_j\). A guess outside the class never wins, since its quasi-identifiers differ from the target’s.
Average over the target. The target lands in class \(j\) with probability \(k_j/n\), so the success is \(\sum_j\frac{k_j}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{k_j} = \frac Jn\).

The join gives Ana’s asthma, Carla’s depression and Dan’s pneumonia with certainty, because each of them matches exactly one record. Ben matches two records, his own and a stranger’s with the same quasi-identifiers, so the adversary is right about him with probability \(\frac12\). The three records born on 1990-01-01 count too, since a target drawn from them is found one time in three, though this part of the roll names none of them. With \(J = 5\) classes for \(n = 8\) records, Equation 15.1 gives a success of \(5/8 = 0.625\).
This is, in miniature, how the computer scientist Latanya Sweeney re-identified the governor of Massachusetts in the late 1990s: in the Cambridge voter roll, six people shared his birth date, three of them were men, and only one lived in his ZIP code.
Sweeney (2000) then estimated from 1990 census tables that 87% of the US population were likely unique on {5-digit ZIP code, date of birth, sex}. The bits explain why (Figure 15.1). Treating each attribute as uniform gives an upper bound on its bits, because equally likely values are the hardest to guess, so about 40,000 ZIP codes, \(365 \times 80 = 29{,}200\) birthdays in about 80 birth years, and two sexes carry at most \[\log_2 40{,}000 + \log_2 29{,}200 + 1 = 15.3 + 14.8 + 1.0 = 31.1 \text{ bits}, \tag{15.2}\] against the 27.9 bits needed to single out one American, which leaves room for most people to be unique.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers
Deleting an identifier also deletes the ability to follow one person through the data. A common alternative is to replace the identifier by a code that stays the same on all of that person’s records, often its MD5 hash, a standard 128-bit hash. This section shows two separate ways in which the code fails to hide the person.

Definition 15.2 (Pseudonyms) A pseudonym replaces an identifier \(x\) by a code that is the same on every record of the same person. A hashed pseudonym is \(h(x)\) for a public hash function \(h\) that anyone can compute. A keyed hash mixes a secret key into \(h\), so that only the key holder can compute it.

A good hash cannot be run backwards, so the way to invert it is to hash candidate inputs until one matches, and an identifier with a public format can be guessed by listing every value. Even a pseudonym that nobody can invert has a second weakness, because all of one person’s records carry it.

Proposition 15.2 (Two ways a pseudonym fails) Suppose the identifiers come from a public set of \(N\) values.

If the pseudonyms are \(h(x)\) for a public hash with 128-bit outputs that behaves like a random function, giving each input an independent uniform output, an adversary who computes \(h\) on all \(N\) values recovers the identifier behind every pseudonym. It fails only if two identifiers share a hash, which has probability at most \(N^2/2^{129}\). The cost is \(N\) hash computations for the whole release, which doubles with each bit of the identifier.
Whatever the pseudonyms, an adversary who links any one record to a person learns that person’s pseudonym, and with it every record that carries it.



Proof. 

Part 1: the adversary can list every pseudonym. With no secret key, the possible pseudonyms are the values \(h(x)\) over the \(N\) identifiers, which take \(N\) computations. The adversary keeps a table from each value back to its identifier.
Each pseudonym maps back to one identifier. Two identifiers with the same hash would make the lookup ambiguous. The birthday bound, Theorem 8.3, says that \(N\) values of a random function with \(2^{128}\) outputs collide with probability at most \(N^2/(2 \cdot 2^{128}) = N^2/2^{129}\).
Part 2: a consistent pseudonym groups a person’s records. It is the same on every record of one person, so learning it from one record identifies all of them.


Hashing therefore protects only identifiers that are already hard to guess. Phone, licence and identity numbers carry between about 20 and 33 bits (ten-digit phone numbers carry 33.2), and a laptop computes millions of MD5 hashes a second, so it lists any of these sets in seconds to hours. A keyed hash stops the enumeration, but not the second failure. Keeping a person’s rows together, the reason to use a pseudonym, makes them one long record, which Section 15.5 shows to be identifying.

Example 15.2 In 2014 a freedom-of-information request obtained every New York City taxi trip of 2013, about 173 million trips, with each medallion number, the permit number of a cab, and each driver’s licence number replaced by its MD5 hash. One hashed licence seemed to earn thousands of dollars a day. Its code, cfcd208495d565ef66e7dff9f98764da, is the MD5 of the string “0”, as the script of Section 15.7 confirms, the placeholder that every trip with a missing licence carried, so the codes were plain MD5 with no key.
Vijay Pandurangan then inverted all the pseudonyms, as part 1 of Proposition 15.2 predicts. Licence numbers have six digits, or seven starting with 5, about 2 million possibilities or 20.9 bits, and medallion numbers, which follow a few fixed patterns of letters and digits, about 22 million or 24.4 bits. He hashed every possibility in minutes. In miniature, the script hashes all \(10^6\) six-digit numbers, 19.9 bits’ worth, and recovers five secret identifiers.
Passengers had no pseudonym, yet each trip is itself a record of rare details, of the kind Section 15.5 studies. A pickup minute (one of 525,600 in the year) carries 19.0 bits and a pickup square of 100 metres (one of 78,000) carries 16.3 bits, together at most 35.3 bits, more than the 27.4 bits that single out one trip among 173 million. Anthony Tockar showed this in 2014 with photographs of celebrities entering taxis. And by part 2 of Proposition 15.2, a passenger who finds their own trip and knows who drove it learns the driver’s pseudonym, and with it the year’s trips and income.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 How many people are unique
A custodian, the organization that holds and releases data, can count the unique records in its own table, but not in the population behind it, nor for columns an adversary might combine from elsewhere. So it needs a model that predicts the count. It is the birthday problem of Cryptography basics asked the other way round: how many people share their cell with nobody?

Definition 15.3 (Cells and uniqueness) A population has \(n\) people, and a release may cover all of them. A person’s combination of attribute values is their cell. Under the population model, each person falls in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), independently of everyone else, and \(K\) is the number of cells. A person is unique when nobody else is in their cell, and \(U\) is the number of unique people.

A person is unique when all the others avoid their cell, and averaging that chance over the person’s own cell gives the expected fraction unique.

Theorem 15.1 (Expected fraction unique) Under the population model of Definition 15.3, the expected fraction of unique people is \[\frac{\mathbb E[U]}{n} = \sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.3}\]


Proof. The plan is to write \(U\) as a sum of one 0/1 counter per person, find the chance that one person is unique, and add.

Count with indicators. \(U\) is the sum over people of \(\mathbf 1[\text{person } i \text{ is unique}]\). The mean of a sum is the sum of the means even when the terms depend on each other (Lemma 1.1), and the mean of an indicator is its probability. So \(\mathbb E[U]\) is the sum of the \(n\) probabilities, which are equal because everyone draws a cell from the same probabilities.
Condition on the person’s own cell. Call it \(c\), which has probability \(p_c\).
Ask the others to stay away. Given \(c\), the person is unique if each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands outside \(c\). They are independent and each avoids \(c\) with probability \(1 - p_c\), so this has probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\).
Average over the cell. One person is unique with probability \(\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}\), and by step 1, \(\mathbb E[U]\) is \(n\) times this.


When all \(K\) cells are equally likely, the formula is a single power, close to \(e^{-n/K}\) because \(1 - p\) is close to \(e^{-p}\) when \(p\) is small, and the proof of Corollary 15.1, after the next lemma, needs to know how close.

Lemma 15.1 (A power and its exponential) For \(0 \le p < 1\) and any exponent \(\ell \ge 0\), \[e^{-p\ell/(1-p)} \le (1 - p)^\ell \le e^{-p\ell}. \tag{15.4}\]


Proof. 

Take logarithms. The power becomes \(\ell\ln(1 - p)\), so the claim is \(-\frac{p}{1 - p} \le \ln(1 - p) \le -p\).
The upper bound. The logarithm is concave and \(x - 1\) is its tangent line at \(x = 1\), so \(\ln x \le x - 1\) for every \(x > 0\). With \(x = 1 - p\) this is \(\ln(1 - p) \le -p\).
The lower bound. With \(x = \frac1{1 - p}\) the same inequality gives \(\ln\frac1{1-p} \le \frac1{1-p} - 1 = \frac{p}{1-p}\), and flipping the sign gives \(\ln(1 - p) \ge -\frac{p}{1-p}\).



Corollary 15.1 (Uniform cells) If all \(K\) cells are equally likely, write \(b = \log_2 K\) for the bits a cell carries. The expected fraction unique is \((1 - 1/K)^{n-1}\), and it equals the exponential below up to a relative error of order \(1/K + n/K^2\), \[\frac{\mathbb E[U]}{n} \approx e^{-n/K} = \exp\big(-2^{\log_2n - b}\big). \tag{15.5}\]


Proof. 

Substitute uniform cells. With \(p_c = 1/K\), Equation 15.3 has \(K\) equal terms \(\frac1K(1 - \frac1K)^{n-1}\), which add up to \((1 - \frac1K)^{n-1}\).
Replace the power by an exponential. Lemma 15.1 with \(p = 1/K\) and \(\ell = n - 1\) puts the power between \(e^{-(n-1)/(K-1)}\) and \(e^{-(n-1)/K}\). These exponents differ by \(\frac{n-1}{K(K-1)}\), of order \(n/K^2\), and replacing \(n - 1\) by \(n\) moves the exponent by only \(1/K\). Two exponentials whose exponents differ by a small amount \(u\) differ by a factor \(e^u \approx 1 + u\), a relative error of \(u\).
Write the exponent in bits. The average occupancy is \(n/K = 2^{\log_2n}/2^b = 2^{\log_2n - b}\).


For uniform cells, then, the fraction unique depends only on \(b - \log_2n\), the bits beyond those needed to name one person, and the curve is the same for a town and for the planet (Figure 15.2, right). Setting \(\exp(-2^{\log_2 n - b})\) equal to a fraction \(f\) and solving gives \(b - \log_2 n = -\log_2\ln(1/f)\), so half the people are unique once \(b\) exceeds \(\log_2n\) by 0.53 bits, 90% at 3.25 bits more and 99% at 6.64 bits more.
Real attributes are skewed, and skew usually lowers uniqueness, because many people crowd into a few common cells while many rare cells stay empty. This is not a theorem. With 10 equally likely cells and 100 people, nobody is unique, but making one cell rare lets the few people in it be unique.

Example 15.3 Sweeney’s three attributes have \(K = 40{,}000 \times 29{,}200 \times 2 = 2.34\times10^9\) cells for \(n = 248.7\) million people, so \(n/K = 0.106\) people per cell. If everyone fell into a uniformly random cell, Equation 15.5 says that a fraction \(e^{-0.106} = 0.899\) would be unique. Sweeney’s 87% is a little lower because ZIP codes and birth years are not equally common. Golle (2006) repeated the estimate with the 2000 census and found 63%, and both estimates depend on how they spread birth dates within age groups, since the census publishes only the groups.
The often-quoted “33 bits identify anyone” is the point \(b = \log_2 n\). With \(2^{33}\) uniform cells for 8 billion people, \(n/K = 8\times10^9/2^{33} = 0.93\), and only a fraction \(e^{-0.93} = 0.394\) is unique; 99% needs \(32.9 + 6.64 = 39.5\) bits. The running census is skewed, so uniform cells misjudge it, and Section 15.4 compares it with the exact formula.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.4 Uniqueness from marginals and from one population
text:
15.4 Uniqueness from marginals and from one population
Theorem 15.1 needs every cell probability, and there can be billions of cells, while a custodian often knows only how common each value of each attribute is. Its answer is also an average over imagined populations, while the custodian has one. This section closes both gaps, with a floor from the per-attribute frequencies and a bound on how far one population strays.
The floor uses the chance that two random people share a cell. Both land in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c \cdot p_c\), so this collision probability is \(\sum_cp_c^2\), a measure of how crowded a typical cell is.

Proposition 15.3 (A floor from the collision probability) Under the population model, for any cell probabilities, \[\frac{\mathbb E[U]}{n} \ge \Big(1 - \sum_cp_c^2\Big)^{n-1}. \tag{15.6}\] If a cell is a combination of independent attributes, and attribute \(j\) takes the value \(v\) with probability \(p_j(v)\), then \(\sum_cp_c^2 = \prod_j\sum_vp_j(v)^2\). So the floor needs only each attribute’s frequencies, its marginal.


Proof. The plan is to write Equation 15.3 as the average of a convex function, move the average inside the function, and factorize what is left.

Write the fraction as an average. Draw a random person and note the probability of the cell they landed in. That number is random, and it equals \(p_c\) with probability \(p_c\). With \(g(x) = (1 - x)^{n-1}\), Equation 15.3 is the average of \(g\) at that probability.
Check that \(g\) bends upwards. Its second derivative, \((n-1)(n-2)(1 - x)^{n-3}\), is never negative on \([0, 1]\) when \(n \ge 2\), so \(g\) is convex there.
Apply Jensen’s inequality. A convex curve lies above its tangent line at the average point, so the average of \(g\) is at least the average of the tangent line. A line’s average is its value at the average point, which is \(g\) of the average.
Compute the inner average. The average cell probability is \(\sum_cp_c\cdot p_c = \sum_cp_c^2\), which gives Equation 15.6.
Factorize for independent attributes. Then \(p_c = \prod_jp_j(c_j)\), where \(c_j\) is the value the cell gives attribute \(j\). Expanding the product of sums gives one term per choice of a value for each attribute, that is, one term per cell, and that term is \(\prod_jp_j(c_j)^2 = p_c^2\): \[\prod_j\sum_vp_j(v)^2 = \sum_c\prod_jp_j(c_j)^2 = \sum_cp_c^2. \tag{15.7}\]


Step 3 is an equality when all cells with positive probability are equally likely, so the floor is tight for uniform cells. It is loose when a few crowded cells push the collision probability up while people in rare cells stay unique.
The entropy \(H = \sum_cp_c\log_2(1/p_c)\) is the average number of bits a cell carries, and it adds over independent attributes, by the chain rule of Information theory, Theorem 5.2. The entropy rule \(e^{-n2^{-H}}\) replaces the cells by \(2^H\) equally likely ones. It is not a bound in either direction, but it is often closer to the exact value than the floor.
The second gap is that the custodian has one population, in which no single person moves the fraction unique by much. McDiarmid’s inequality, Theorem 2.8, makes this a bound. If changing input \(i\) alone moves a function of independent inputs by at most \(d_i\), it strays more than a margin \(\gamma > 0\) above (or below) its mean with probability at most \(\exp(-2\gamma^2/\sum_id_i^2)\).

Proposition 15.4 (One population is enough) Under the population model, for every margin \(\gamma > 0\), \[\Pr\Big[\Big|\frac Un - \frac{\mathbb E[U]}{n}\Big| \ge \gamma\Big] \le 2e^{-n\gamma^2/2}. \tag{15.8}\]


Proof. 

Change one input. \(U\) is a function of the \(n\) independent cells. Moving one person from cell \(u\) to cell \(u'\) changes only the counts of those two cells.
Bound the change. A cell holds a unique person exactly when its count is 1. The move can switch that on or off in each of the two cells, so \(U\) changes by at most 2 and \(U/n\) by at most \(d_i = 2/n\).
Apply McDiarmid. With \(d_i = 2/n\) for all \(n\) people, \(\sum_id_i^2 = 4/n\), so each tail is at most \(\exp(-2\gamma^2 n/4) = e^{-n\gamma^2/2}\). The two tails give the factor 2.


Setting the right side equal to a failure probability \(\beta\) says that the fraction unique is within \(\sqrt{2\ln(2/\beta)/n}\) of its expectation with probability \(1 - \beta\). The bound is loose, because it charges every person the worst case, while most moves change \(U\) by 0 or 1.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Sparse, high-dimensional data
In 2006 Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings by 480,189 subscribers, with names replaced by random numbers. Each record is a set of (movie, rating, date) triples, 209 on average out of 17,770 movies. There are no columns to join on, and what an adversary knows about a person is partial and noisy. Narayanan & Shmatikov (2008) still matched Netflix records to named reviews on the Internet Movie Database. This section asks how to match noisy information to a record, and when to trust the match.
No record matches exactly, so the attack scores how well each record agrees with what the adversary knows, item by item. An agreement on a film that half the subscribers rated says little, while one on an obscure film says a lot, so rarer items get larger weights.

Definition 15.4 (The Narayanan–Shmatikov score) The adversary’s auxiliary information \(\mathrm{aux}\) is a set of items \(i\), such as films, with approximate values \(\mathrm{aux}_i\), such as ratings. For a record \(r\) with value \(r_i\) on item \(i\), the agreement \(\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i)\) is 1 if \(r\) rated \(i\) within one star of \(\mathrm{aux}_i\), and 0 otherwise. With a weight \(w_i\) for each item, the score of the record is \[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{aux}, r) = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{aux}}w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i). \tag{15.9}\] Narayanan and Shmatikov use \(w_i = 1/\ln\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\), where the support \(\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\) is the number of records that rated item \(i\). Their attack also scores dates, which this chapter leaves out.

The weights can be derived. For each record, the adversary weighs “this record is the target” against “this record is someone unrelated” by the likelihood ratio, the probability of what it observed under the first explanation divided by that under the second. For independent items its logarithm is a sum over items, the form of Equation 15.9.

Proposition 15.5 (The score is a log-likelihood ratio) Suppose an unrelated record agrees with item \(i\) of the auxiliary information with probability \(s_i\), and the target’s record with probability \(1 - \rho\), independently across items, where \(\rho\) covers wrong or stale information. Then the logarithm of a record’s likelihood ratio is its score Equation 15.9 with the weights \[w_i = \ln\frac{1 - s_i}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \rho}{\rho} \approx \ln\frac{1}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \rho}{\rho}, \tag{15.10}\] plus a constant that is the same for every record; the approximation holds for rare items. If also the target is one of the \(n\) records, each equally likely a priori, and records are independent given which is the target, so that the patterns of all records multiply, then record \(t\) is the target with posterior probability \[\Pr[\text{target} = t \mid \text{data}] = \frac{\mathrm{LR}(t)}{\sum_j\mathrm{LR}(j)}, \tag{15.11}\] where \(\mathrm{LR}(t)\) is the likelihood ratio of record \(t\). So the top-scoring record is the most probable target.


Proof. The plan is to write a record’s pattern of agreements under both explanations, take the log of the ratio, drop the terms shared by all records, and apply Bayes’ rule.

Record the agreements. Write \(a_i(r) \in \{0, 1\}\) for whether record \(r\) agrees with the auxiliary information on item \(i\).
The pattern under each explanation. If \(r\) is the target, each item agrees with probability \(1 - \rho\), independently, so the pattern has probability \(P_1(r) = \prod_i(1 - \rho)^{a_i}\rho^{1 - a_i}\), the exponents picking the right factor. If \(r\) is unrelated, it has probability \(P_0(r) = \prod_is_i^{a_i}(1 - s_i)^{1 - a_i}\).
Take the log of the ratio. The logarithm turns the ratio of products into a sum over items: \[\ln\frac{P_1(r)}{P_0(r)} = \sum_i\Big[a_i\ln\frac{1 - \rho}{s_i} + (1 - a_i)\ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\Big]. \tag{15.12}\]
Keep what depends on the record. Collecting the terms with \(a_i\) leaves \(\sum_ia_i\big[\ln\frac{1-\rho}{s_i} - \ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\big]\) plus \(\sum_i\ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\), which is the same for every record. Splitting each logarithm of a ratio turns the bracket into \(\ln\frac{1-s_i}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}\), which is Equation 15.10.
Bayes’ rule. If \(t\) is the target, record \(t\)’s pattern follows \(P_1\) and every other record’s follows \(P_0\), so all the patterns together have probability \(P_1(t)\prod_{j \ne t}P_0(j)\). The prior is the same for every \(t\), so the posterior of \(t\) is proportional to this. Dividing by \(\prod_jP_0(j)\), which does not depend on \(t\), leaves \(\mathrm{LR}(t) = P_1(t)/P_0(t)\), and normalizing gives Equation 15.11.


For rare items these weights are about \(\ln(1/s_i)\). They and the Narayanan–Shmatikov weights both grow as an item gets rarer, at different rates, and Example 15.5 compares the two. For one record, “target or unrelated” is a hypothesis test, and by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, Theorem 4.1, thresholding the likelihood ratio is the most powerful test.
Because the score adds up evidence, noise costs little: with a wrong item the target loses one term, while unrelated records rarely gain one. What decides success is the bits, and each item contributes its surprisal \(\log_2(1/s_i)\), the bits that single out an event of probability \(s_i\).

Proposition 15.6 (False matches and bits) Take reliable information (\(\rho \to 0\)) with exact agreement required. If an unrelated record agrees on each item \(i\) of a set \(I\) independently with probability \(s_i\), the expected number of the \(n\) records that agree on all of \(I\) by chance is \[n\prod_{i\in I}s_i = 2^{\log_2n - \sum_{i\in I}\log_2(1/s_i)}. \tag{15.13}\]


Proof. 

One record. By independence, an unrelated record agrees on every item of \(I\) with probability \(\prod_{i\in I}s_i\).
All records. The expected number of false matches is the sum of these probabilities over records (Lemma 1.1), \(n\) times step 1.
Write it in bits. Writing \(n = 2^{\log_2 n}\) and \(s_i = 2^{-\log_2(1/s_i)}\) turns the product into a power of 2.


So false matches vanish once the items’ bits exceed \(\log_2n\), as in Section 15.3. A film that 1% of subscribers rated carries \(\log_2100 = 6.64\) bits, and three of them carry \(3 \times 6.64 = 19.9\) bits, more than the \(\log_2480{,}189 = 18.9\) bits that single out one Netflix subscriber. This is why sparsity is the weakness: most items are rated by few people, so each one a person rated is worth many bits.
The top score is the best guess if the target is in the release. If it may not be, the adversary must also decide whether to trust the guess, and a real match should stand out from the other scores.

Definition 15.5 (The eccentricity test) Let \(\mathrm{top}_1 \ge \mathrm{top}_2\) be the two largest scores and \(\sigma\) the standard deviation of all the scores. The eccentricity is the gap between them in units of \(\sigma\), and the eccentricity test declares a match to the top record only if it clears a threshold \(\tau\), \[\frac{\mathrm{top}_1 - \mathrm{top}_2}{\sigma} \ge \tau, \tag{15.14}\] and otherwise says “no match”. Narayanan and Shmatikov used \(\tau = 1.5\).

How often the top score stands out by chance depends on the shape of the score distribution, so \(\tau\) has to be calibrated by running the test for people known to be absent from the release, at a small false positive rate (Hypothesis testing). On Netflix, Narayanan and Shmatikov found that 8 ratings, 2 of them wrong, with dates known to within 14 days (their score uses dates), identify 99% of records, and 2 ratings with dates within 3 days identify 68%.

Example 15.5 The script draws a scaled-down Netflix of 5,000 users and 4,000 items, with 203,029 ratings and density 0.0102 (the share of user–item pairs rated), close to Netflix’s 0.0118. An item drawn from a random user’s record carries a median of 5.83 bits, against \(\log_2 5000 = 12.29\) bits needed.
The auxiliary information is a few items from the target’s record, with the rating off by one star half the time, and in the noisy setting a quarter of the items are replaced by random popular items. Table 15.3 gives the fraction of 400 targets whose record gets the top score. The third weighting is Equation 15.10 in its approximate form, with \(s_i = \lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert/n\) and \(\rho = \frac12\), which makes the term in \(\rho\) zero.

Two items carry about \(2 \times 5.83 = 11.7\) bits, a little under \(\log_2n\), and re-identify about 43% of targets, while four carry about 23 bits and re-identify 93%. With 8 items of which 2 are wrong, the rarity weightings re-identify 98–99%, as Narayanan and Shmatikov found. Equal weights fall to 94%, because a wrong popular item helps many unrelated records. The two rarity weightings differ by less than two standard errors, each \(\sqrt{0.98 \times 0.02/400} = 0.007\). The derived weighting of Proposition 15.5 trails with 2 and 4 items, by \(0.440 - 0.402 = 0.038\) and \(0.941 - 0.924 = 0.017\), within two standard errors, since its \(\rho = \frac12\) and independence model do not describe this noise.
To test the eccentricity (Figure 15.3), the script also scores 400 outsiders drawn from the same model, so that any match declared for them is false. With 8 items, 2 of them wrong, and \(\tau = 1.5\), 94.8% of insiders, the targets in the release, are correctly re-identified, but 26.3% of outsiders are also “matched”. The median eccentricity is 7.32 for insiders and 0.72 for outsiders, but the outsiders’ distribution has a long tail. Holding false matches to 1% of outsiders takes \(\tau = 4.83\), which still re-identifies 73.0% of insiders (Figure 15.4).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Does releasing a sample protect?
Statistical agencies often release a sample, such as 1% of a census. The argument is plausible deniability: a record unique in the sample need not be unique in the population, because the person you have in mind may share their attributes with someone who was not sampled. Yet Rocher, Hendrickx & de Montjoye (2019) predicted, from a statistical model of the population fitted to a sample, that 99.98% of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset with 15 demographic attributes. This section derives when a match found in a sample can be trusted.
Each of \(n\) people is in the release independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate. Take a cell with probability \(p\), and let \(\lambda = (n - 1)p\) be the expected number of other people in it. The adversary can start from a person or from a record.
From a person, the adversary knows a target’s cell and finds exactly one record there. Either the target was sampled and no one else in the cell was, or exactly one other person was sampled instead, which grows more likely in a crowded cell.

Proposition 15.7 (A match from a person) Given that the target’s cell holds exactly one record of the release, that record is the target’s with probability \[\kappa = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{(n-1)p(1 - q)}{1 - pq}} \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - q)}, \tag{15.15}\] where the approximation holds for small \(p\).


Proof. The plan is to compute the right and the wrong story given the number of others in the cell, and then average both over that number.

Name the crowd. Each of the \(n - 1\) others is in the target’s cell with probability \(p\), independently, so their number is \(W \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, p)\).
The two stories. Given \(W\), the right match needs the target sampled and none of the others, with probability \(q(1 - q)^W\). The wrong one needs the target unsampled and exactly one of the \(W\) others sampled, with probability \((1 - q)\cdot Wq(1 - q)^{W-1} = Wq(1 - q)^W\).
Condition on one match. By the definition of a conditional probability, a correct match has probability \(\Pr[\text{right}]/\big(\Pr[\text{right}] + \Pr[\text{wrong}]\big)\), and each of these unconditional probabilities is its story averaged over \(W\). The factor \(q\) cancels, leaving \[\kappa = \frac{\mathbb E[(1 - q)^W]}{\mathbb E[(1 + W)(1 - q)^W]}. \tag{15.16}\]
The two averages. Both come from the generating function \(\mathbb E[z^W]\). Each of the \(n - 1\) others contributes an independent factor \(z\) to \(z^W\) if it is in the cell and 1 if not, so \(\mathbb E[z^W] = (1 - p + pz)^{n-1}\), which is \((1 - pq)^{n-1}\) at \(z = 1 - q\). For the second average, \(Wz^W = z\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dz}z^W\), and the derivative of \((1 - p + pz)^{n-1}\) is \((n-1)p(1 - p + pz)^{n-2}\), so multiplying by \(z\) and setting \(z = 1 - q\) gives \(\mathbb E[W(1 - q)^W] = (n-1)p(1 - q)(1 - pq)^{n-2}\).
Simplify. The denominator of step 3 is the first average plus the second. Dividing both by \((1 - pq)^{n-1}\) turns the first into 1 and the second into \(\frac{(n-1)p(1-q)}{1 - pq}\), which gives Equation 15.15. For small \(p\), \(1 - pq \approx 1\) and \((n-1)p = \lambda\).


From a record, the adversary takes a record alone in its cell in the release and looks the cell up in a population register, such as a voter roll. Being alone in the sample says that nobody else in the cell was sampled, so what remains is whether anyone in the cell was left out.

Proposition 15.8 (A match from a record) A record that is alone in its cell in the release is alone in the population with probability \[\xi = \left(\frac{1 - p}{1 - pq}\right)^{n-1} \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{15.17}\]


Proof. 

Sort the others into three groups. Each other person is, independently, in the cell and sampled (probability \(pq\)), in the cell and not sampled (\(p(1 - q)\)), or outside the cell (\(1 - p\)).
Condition on being alone in the sample. This rules out the first group for every other person. People are independent, so for each of them the chances of the other two groups are divided by their total, \(1 - pq\).
Ask that nobody hides in the cell. All \(n - 1\) others must be outside the cell, with probability \(\big(\frac{1-p}{1-pq}\big)^{n-1}\). Subtracting the numerator from the denominator writes the ratio as \(1 - \frac{p(1 - q)}{1 - pq}\), close to \(1 - p(1 - q)\) for small \(p\), so by Lemma 15.1 the power is about \(e^{-\lambda(1 - q)}\).


Over a whole release, the share of sample-unique records that are unique in the population compares two expected counts, each a sum of indicators as in Theorem 15.1.

Proposition 15.9 (Sample uniques that are real) Under the population model, the expected number of records unique in both the release and the population, divided by the expected number unique in the release, is \[\frac{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}}{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_cq)^{n-1}}. \tag{15.18}\] It tends to the population’s fraction unique, Equation 15.3, as \(q \to 0\) and is 1 at \(q = 1\).


Proof. 

Records unique in both. A population unique is unique in the sample if it is sampled, and sampling is independent of the cells. So the expected number is \(q\) times that of population uniques, \(nq\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}\) by Theorem 15.1.
Records unique in the sample. Person \(i\) in cell \(c\) is sampled, and each other person must be outside \(c\) or unsampled, which rules out only being in \(c\) and sampled, probability \(p_cq\). Adding over people gives \(nq\sum_cp_c(1 - p_cq)^{n-1}\).
Divide. The factor \(nq\) cancels. As \(q \to 0\) the denominator tends to \(\sum_cp_c = 1\), and at \(q = 1\) the two sums are equal.


Sampling only helps people in crowded cells. It enters Equation 15.15 and Equation 15.17 through the factor \(1 - q\) on \(\lambda\), so for rare combinations, \(\lambda \ll 1\), both are close to 1 whatever \(q\) is. Since shrinking \(q\) only raises \(\lambda(1 - q)\) towards \(\lambda\), neither falls below its value at \(q = 0\): \(\kappa \ge 1/(1 + \lambda)\) and \(\xi \ge e^{-\lambda}\).

So a 1% sample gives deniability only to the people who were not unique anyway. The adversary can also estimate each record’s \(p\) from the sample and compute \(\xi\), which tells it which matches to trust.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 k-anonymity
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table. The columns that remain, such as age, ZIP code and sex, are quasi-identifiers. None of them names anyone, but together they single out most people, so anyone with a list of names and the same columns can join that list to the release. Between 1998 and 2008, researchers answered with definitions that constrain the released table itself. k-anonymity hides every record in a crowd of at least \(k\) records with the same quasi-identifiers. l-diversity asks each crowd to hold several different values of the sensitive column, such as a diagnosis, and t-closeness asks each crowd to have the same mix of those values as the whole table. They are called syntactic because each is a property of the published table that you can check by reading it. Statistics offices and open-source anonymization tools such as ARX still use them, so you need to know where each promise ends.
The one idea of this chapter is that a syntactic definition fixes the adversary’s knowledge in advance. k-anonymity assumes that the adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and nothing else, l-diversity lets it also rule out a few of the target’s sensitive values, and t-closeness lets it know how the sensitive values are spread over the whole table. Each attack below gives the adversary one piece of knowledge more than its definition assumes, and the guarantee then no longer applies. A second release, the most ordinary extra knowledge there is, breaks all three definitions.
The running example is a synthetic hospital table of 10,000 patients, with age, ZIP code and sex as quasi-identifiers and one of eight diagnoses as the sensitive attribute. Released with exact quasi-identifiers, it lets an adversary who knows a random patient’s three columns pick out that patient’s record with probability 0.933, guessing at random among the records that share those values. Two independent anonymized releases of it reveal more than three times as many diagnoses as either alone.
Sweeney and Samarati’s 1998 answer to the linkage attack is to make sure that every combination of quasi-identifiers in the release is shared by at least \(k\) people. The data holder, the custodian, gets there by generalizing, so that age 37 becomes 35–39 and ZIP code 02139 becomes 021**, and by suppressing the few records that still stand out. This section asks what the definition buys against linkage, and what it costs in the detail the quasi-identifiers can keep.
The linkage game of Linkage and re-identification draws a target uniformly from a release of \(n\) records and gives the adversary the target’s quasi-identifiers, and the adversary wins if it picks out the target’s record. It finds the target’s class but cannot tell the records inside apart, so it guesses one of them at random. In a class of \(\lvert E\rvert\) records it is then right with probability \(1/\lvert E\rvert\), and the target lands there with probability \(\lvert E\rvert/n\). So each class contributes \(1/n\), and summing over \(J\) classes gives the success \(J/n\) of Equation 15.1. For a fixed \(n\), large classes mean few classes, and that is the whole guarantee.
The guarantee is about identity only. Equation 16.1 bounds the chance of picking out the target’s record, and says nothing about the sensitive attribute, which the next two sections attack. It also needs the right columns treated as quasi-identifiers. In data with many columns and few filled entries, such as movie ratings, every column is one, because a few ratings already single a person out (Section 15.5). Every column must then be coarsened until \(k\) records agree on all of them, which leaves little of the table (Aggarwal, 2005).
Coarse quasi-identifiers protect more but say less, so the next question is how coarse they must be. Suppose the generalized quasi-identifiers split \(n\) people into \(K\) cells, each person falling into a cell independently and every cell equally likely, and no record is suppressed, so each cell is a class. Naming a person’s cell then takes \(\log_2 K\) bits, to compare with the \(\log_2 n\) bits that single out one person of \(n\). Each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands in a given person’s cell with probability \(1/K\), so the number of others there is a \(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1/K)\) count. With many people and many cells, Theorem 1.2 in Probability distributions shows that this count is close to a Poisson count with the same mean, \((n - 1)/K \approx n/K\).
So k-anonymity costs more than the naive \(\log_2 k\) bits below \(\log_2 n\), which is what exactly \(k\) people in each of \(K = n/k\) cells would allow. Cells vary in size around their mean, and the unlucky small cells violate the definition, so you need \(\lambda_k\) people per cell on average, more than \(k\). For \(k = 2\) a person violates the definition when \(N = 0\), which has probability \(e^{-n/K}\). Setting \(e^{-n/K} = 0.01\) gives \(\lambda_2 = \ln 100 = 4.61\), more than twice \(k\).
Real tables are not uniform, so real anonymizers search for a generalization that works on the data at hand. This chapter’s script uses the algorithm of LeFevre, DeWitt & Ramakrishnan (2006).
Because Mondrian splits until a half would fail the criterion, its classes stay close to size \(k\). With no tied values they have between \(k\) and \(2k - 1\) records, because a box of \(2k\) or more records splits at its median into two halves of at least \(k\).

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
Definition 16.1 (k-anonymity) A generalization replaces each quasi-identifier of a record by a coarser value, such as an age by a range or a ZIP code by a prefix, and different records may be coarsened differently. Suppression deletes records. An equivalence class \(E\) of the released table is a set of records with the same generalized quasi-identifiers, and \(\lvert E\rvert\) is its number of records. A release is k-anonymous if every equivalence class has at least \(k\) records.



Proposition 16.1 (k-anonymity caps linkage) If a release of \(n\) records is k-anonymous, then the adversary’s success in the linkage game is at most \(1/k\): \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.1}\]


Proof. 

Count records by class. The \(J\) classes split the \(n\) records between them, each record in exactly one class, so \(n = \sum_j\lvert E_j\rvert\).
Use the definition. Every class has at least \(k\) records, so the sum is at least \(Jk\). Then \(n \ge Jk\), which is \(J/n \le 1/k\).
Read off the linkage success. Equation 15.1 says that the linkage success is \(J/n\), so it is at most \(1/k\).





Proposition 16.2 (The cost of k-anonymity for uniform cells) Suppose \(n\) people fall independently into \(K\) equally likely cells, and treat the number of other people in a person’s cell as a \(\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K)\) count. A person’s class is smaller than \(k\) when at most \(k - 2\) others share the cell, so the expected fraction of people in classes smaller than \(k\) is \[\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K) \le k - 2]. \tag{16.2}\] Suppose the custodian accepts that in expectation at most 1% of records fall in such classes, to be suppressed. Let \(\lambda_k\) be the mean at which the fraction is exactly 1%, that is \(\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_k) \le k - 2] = 0.01\). The fraction falls as the mean grows, so it is at most 1% exactly when \(n/K \ge \lambda_k\), and the quasi-identifiers may carry at most \[\log_2 n - \log_2\lambda_k \text{ bits.} \tag{16.3}\]


Proof. The plan is to compute the chance that one person’s class is too small, note that this chance is also the expected fraction of such people, and then solve for the coarseness.

The size of a person’s class. A person’s class is their cell, which holds the person plus \(N\) others, with \(N\) a \(\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K)\) count by assumption.
When it is too small. The class is smaller than \(k\) when \(1 + N \le k - 1\), that is when \(N \le k - 2\), which has probability \(\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K) \le k - 2]\).
From one person to the fraction. The expected number of people in small classes is the sum, over people, of each one’s chance of being in one, because the expected count of events is the sum of their probabilities. Every person has the same chance, so the sum is \(n\) times it, and the expected fraction is that chance.
Solve for the coarseness. A Poisson count with a larger mean is more likely to exceed any fixed level, so the chance that it is at most \(k - 2\) falls as the mean grows. The fraction is therefore at most 1% exactly when \(n/K \ge \lambda_k\), that is \(K \le n/\lambda_k\). Taking \(\log_2\) of both sides gives \(\log_2 K \le \log_2 n - \log_2\lambda_k\).




Example 16.1 Table 16.2 applies Equation 16.2 to a population of \(n = 10{,}000\), with \(\log_2 n = 13.29\) bits. For \(k = 2\), \(\lambda_2 = 4.61\) from the calculation above, \(\log_2 4.61 = 2.20\), and \(13.29 - 2.20 = 11.08\) bits are allowed.

At the other extreme, Section 15.3 showed that 99% of people are unique once the quasi-identifiers carry \(\log_2n + 6.64\) bits. Hiding 99% in pairs needs 2.20 bits below \(\log_2 n\), so only \(6.64 + 2.20 = 8.84\) bits, about 9, separate “almost everyone is unique” from “almost everyone is hidden in a pair”, and every published attribute uses some of those bits.

Definition 16.2 (Mondrian) Given a table and a criterion that a class must meet, such as having at least \(k\) records, Mondrian starts with the whole table as one box. Each quasi-identifier is coded as ordered numbers (ZIP codes in a fixed order, sex as 0 and 1). Mondrian splits a box at the median of the quasi-identifier whose values in the box span the largest share of their full range, as long as both halves still meet the criterion. If that split fails, it tries the next widest quasi-identifier, and a box whose every split fails is final. Each final box is a class, published as a range per quasi-identifier.



Example 16.2 In the hospital table of \(n = 10{,}000\) patients, age runs from 0 to 89, the ZIP code takes 800 values with a few areas far more common than the rest, and sex has two values. title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.2 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
Machanavajjhala, Kifer, Gehrke & Venkitasubramaniam (2006) pointed out that k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to but not what it says. The release exists to show a sensitive attribute \(S\), such as a diagnosis. This section asks what an adversary learns about a target’s sensitive value from a k-anonymous release, and what condition on the classes limits it. Table 16.4 is a 3-anonymous release that shows the two attacks.



Table 16.4: A 3-anonymous release with three classes of three records. Age 3* means 30–39, and 4* means 40–49.

Both attacks, and the guarantee that answers them, compute the adversary’s posterior, its belief about the target’s sensitive value after it has seen the release.

Lemma 16.1 (Within a class, the posterior is the frequency) Suppose the adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers, knows that the target is in the release, and knows nothing else about the target. Let \(E\) be the target’s class, and let \(n_E(v)\) be the number of records of \(E\) with sensitive value \(v\). Then the adversary’s posterior is the class’s frequency of \(v\), \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert} = P_E(v). \tag{16.4}\] If the adversary also knows that the target’s value is not in a set \(B\) of values, then for every value \(v\) outside \(B\), \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, S_{\text{target}} \notin B] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert - \sum_{u \in B}n_E(u)}. \tag{16.5}\]


Proof. 

Every record of the class is equally likely to be the target’s. All records of \(E\) show the same generalized quasi-identifiers and differ only in the sensitive value, which the adversary does not know. The adversary knows nothing else about the target, so, as for a target drawn at random, it has no reason to favour any record, and each has probability \(1/\lvert E\rvert\).
Count the records with value \(v\). The target has value \(v\) exactly when its record is one of the \(n_E(v)\) records with that value. Adding \(1/\lvert E\rvert\) over them gives \(n_E(v)/\lvert E\rvert\).
Cross out the excluded values. Knowing that the target’s value is not in \(B\) rules out the records with values in \(B\). The records that are left still look alike, so the adversary spreads its belief evenly over them. There are \(\lvert E\rvert - \sum_{u \in B}n_E(u)\) of them, and step 2 applied to these records gives the second formula.


Alice is 26 and lives in ZIP code 13053, so her class is the first. Every record in it says heart disease, and by Lemma 16.1 her posterior for heart disease is \(\frac33 = 1\), so the homogeneity attack discloses her diagnosis without re-identifying anyone. Bob is 35, lives in 13068, and is in the third class, where two of three records say cancer, so his posterior for cancer is \(\frac23\). His neighbour knows that Bob never had flu that season and rules it out. Crossing out the flu record leaves two cancer records, and cancer then has posterior \(\frac22 = 1\), which is the background knowledge attack.
Both attacks work because one value dominates the class, either from the start or after a few values are ruled out. l-diversity therefore asks for enough different values in each class, and its three versions differ in how they measure “enough”. Sort a class’s value counts from largest to smallest as \(r_1 \ge r_2 \ge \dots \ge r_m\), so that \(r_1\) is the count of the most common value. The entropy \(H(P_E) = -\sum_v P_E(v)\log_2 P_E(v)\) measures in bits how spread out the values are, and \(\ell\) equally common values have entropy exactly \(\log_2 \ell\). The third version is built to survive the background knowledge attack.

Definition 16.3 (l-diversity) A class \(E\) is

distinct \(\ell\)-diverse if it holds at least \(\ell\) different values;
entropy \(\ell\)-diverse if \(H(P_E) \ge \log_2\ell\), so that the class is at least as spread out as \(\ell\) equally common values;
recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse if \(r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + r_{\ell+1} + \dots + r_m)\), so that the most common value has fewer than \(c\) times as many records as all the values outside the \(\ell - 1\) most common have together.

A release is \(\ell\)-diverse in one of these senses if every class is.

The right-hand side of the recursive condition is \(c\) times the tail, the records left after the \(\ell - 1\) most common values are set aside. The guarantee allows the adversary to rule out \(\ell - 2\) values, the most any guarantee can allow, since ruling out \(\ell - 1\) values of a class with exactly \(\ell\) values leaves one. Ruling out values only removes counts, so the top count cannot grow and the rest cannot shrink below the tail.

Proposition 16.3 (What recursive diversity guarantees) Let a class be recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse, and let the adversary know, besides the target’s quasi-identifiers, that the target’s value is not one of some \(\ell - 2\) values. Then every remaining value \(v\) has \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, \text{background}] < \frac{c}{1 + c}. \tag{16.6}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that the defining inequality survives elimination, and then let Lemma 16.1 turn it into a posterior.

What is left. Rule out a set \(B\) of \(\ell - 2\) values, all occurring in the class (a value that does not occur removes nothing, and leaves more counts in the tail). The remaining \(m - \ell + 2\) values keep their original counts. Call the largest of them \(r'_1\), and the total of the other \(m - \ell + 1\) remaining values \(R\).
The top does not grow. Ruling out values removes records but never adds any, so \(r'_1\) is one of the original counts. No original count exceeds \(r_1\), so \(r'_1 \le r_1\).
The tail does not shrink below the original tail. \(R\) is a sum of \(m - \ell + 1\) of the original counts. The smallest such sum is that of the \(m - \ell + 1\) smallest counts, which is \(r_\ell + \dots + r_m\). So \(R \ge r_\ell + \dots + r_m\).
Combine with the definition. Chaining step 2, the definition and step 3 gives \[r'_1 \le r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + \dots + r_m) \le c\,R. \tag{16.7}\]
Turn counts into a posterior. By Lemma 16.1, after elimination the posterior of a remaining value is its count over the total count left, \(r'_1 + R\), so it is at most \(r'_1/(r'_1 + R)\). The share \(x/(x + R)\) grows with \(x\), like a larger slice of a pie whose other part is fixed. With \(r'_1 < cR\) from step 4, the share is therefore below \[\frac{cR}{cR + R} = \frac{c}{1 + c}. \tag{16.8}\]


l-diversity rules out certainty but still allows high likelihood. The bound \(c/(1 + c)\) is \(\frac12\) at \(c = 1\), \(\frac23\) at \(c = 2\) and \(\frac34\) at \(c = 3\), so even recursive diversity lets the adversary be fairly sure. Distinct \(\ell\)-diversity only says that the adversary must rule out \(\ell - 1\) values to be certain, while one value can still hold all but \(\ell - 1\) of the records. Entropy \(\ell\)-diversity does not limit the top value’s share directly either. An entropy 3-diverse class over 8 values can have one value in 73% of its records, because the other 27% spread evenly over seven values give entropy \(-0.73\log_2 0.73 - 0.27\log_2\frac{0.27}{7} = 1.60\) bits, above \(\log_2 3 = 1.58\).
The guarantee assumes how much the adversary knows rather than limiting it. It covers \(\ell - 2\) ruled-out values, and one more can give certainty whatever \(c\) is. An adversary who knows something softer, such as “probably not flu”, is not covered either.
Some tables cannot be made diverse at all. The whole table’s distribution \(P\) is the average of its classes’ distributions \(P_E\), each weighted by the class’s share of the records. In entropy, such an average is at least as spread out as its parts are on average, so a concentrated table forces some class to be concentrated too.

Proposition 16.4 (A table with low entropy has no entropy-diverse release) If the whole table’s distribution \(P\) of the sensitive attribute has entropy below \(\log_2\ell\), then no partition of the table into classes is entropy \(\ell\)-diverse.


Proof. 

The table is a mixture of its classes. Pick a record uniformly at random, and let \(C\) be its class and \(S\) its sensitive value. Then \(S\) has distribution \(P\), and given that \(C\) is the class \(E\), it has distribution \(P_E\).
Conditioning lowers entropy on average. Information theory proves in Corollary 5.1 that \(H(S \mid C) \le H(S)\). Here \(H(S \mid C)\) is, by the definition of conditional entropy, the average of the class entropies \(H(P_E)\), weighted by the class shares, and \(H(S)\) is \(H(P)\).
Conclude. If every class had \(H(P_E) \ge \log_2\ell\), their weighted average would too, and step 2 would give \(H(P) \ge \log_2\ell\), against the hypothesis.



Example 16.3 In Table 16.4 the three classes hold 1, 3 and 2 different values, so they are distinct 1-, 3- and 2-diverse. The largest \(\ell\) for which a class is entropy \(\ell\)-diverse is \(2^{H(P_E)}\), because \(\ell\) equally common values have entropy \(\log_2\ell\). The first class has one value, entropy 0 and \(\ell = 1.00\), and the second has three equally common values and \(\ell = 3.00\). The third, \(\frac23\) cancer and \(\frac13\) flu, has entropy \(\frac23\log_2\frac32 + \frac13\log_2 3 = 0.918\) bits and \(\ell = 2^{0.918} = 1.89\). The release as a whole is only 1-diverse, because of Alice’s class.
In the hospital table, the “certain disclosure” column of Table 16.3 counts the patients in homogeneous classes, 28.0% of all patients at \(k = 2\) and 2.3% at \(k = 5\), which is 232 patients whose diagnosis the release states outright. Knowing a patient’s age never gives that certainty, since at no age does the population’s distribution give any diagnosis more than 0.705.
A posterior has to be read against what the adversary would believe with no release, since 0.6 for a diagnosis is no leak if the population already gives 0.6 to people of the target’s age. The right comparison is the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion, the best guess from the target’s own quasi-identifiers when the population is known exactly. Here the diagnosis depends only on age, so imputation guesses from age alone. Guessing the most common diagnosis of the whole table is right for 18.5% of patients. Imputation is right for 53.6% (Figure 16.2, right). A 5-anonymous release is right for 59.3%. So most of what the release teaches the adversary is the age–diagnosis pattern, which any useful study of this table would report. The excess over imputation, \(0.593 - 0.536 = 0.057\) at \(k = 5\), comes from classes so small that their most common diagnosis is often the member’s own, and it is down to \(0.540 - 0.536 = 0.004\) at \(k = 20\).

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
l-diversity counts values, but what matters is how far the adversary’s belief moves. Li, Li & Venkatasubramanian (2007) found two attacks that diversity does not see. In the skewness attack, 1% of the table has HIV, and a class that is half HIV is 2-diverse in every sense, yet by Lemma 16.1 it raises the belief that a member has HIV fifty-fold. In the similarity attack, a class holds gastric ulcer, gastritis and stomach cancer, so it is 3-diverse, and still reveals a stomach disease. This section measures a class by its distance from the whole table’s distribution, and asks what a bound on that distance guarantees.

Definition 16.4 (t-closeness) Let \(d\) be a distance between distributions on the values of the sensitive attribute. A release is t-close if every class’s distribution is within distance \(t\) of the whole table’s, that is \(d(P_E, P) \le t\) for every class \(E\).

The first choice of distance is total variation. Theorem 3.3 in Divergences proves that the total variation (TV) distance, half the total absolute difference between two probability tables, equals the largest difference between the probabilities the two tables give to one set of values: \[\mathrm{TV}(P_E, P) = \frac12\sum_v\lvert P_E(v) - P(v)\rvert = \max_A\,\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert. \tag{16.9}\] Here the maximum is over all sets of values \(A\), and \(P_E(A)\) is the probability under \(P_E\) that the value lands in \(A\).

Proposition 16.5 (What t-closeness in total variation guarantees) If a release is t-close with the total variation distance, then for every class \(E\) and every set of values \(A\), \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.10}\] In particular, guessing the most common value of the target’s class is right with probability at most \(\max_vP(v) + t\), the best guess from the table alone plus \(t\).


Proof. 

A distance bound is an event bound. By Theorem 3.3, \(\mathrm{TV}(P_E, P)\) is the largest of \(\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert\) over all sets \(A\), so a bound \(t\) on the distance bounds every one of them by \(t\).
The adversary’s belief is the class distribution. By Lemma 16.1, the adversary’s belief about a target in class \(E\) is \(P_E\). So every question it can ask about the target’s value, “is it in \(A\)?”, gets an answer within \(t\) of the answer from the table as a whole.
Apply it to the best guess. Take \(A = \{v\}\) for the class’s most common value \(v\). Then step 1 gives \(P_E(v) \le P(v) + t\), and \(P(v)\) is at most \(\max_uP(u)\).


The bound is additive, but rare values need a ratio. Equation 16.10 lets a 1% value rise to \(1\% + t\), which at \(t = 0.15\) is 16%, a sixteen-fold increase. A guarantee for rare values has to bound the ratio of the adversary’s beliefs with and without the release, not their difference, and that is the shape of differential privacy, the definition of Part 3.
Total variation treats every pair of values as equally different, so it does not see the similarity attack. The earth mover’s distance (EMD), the choice of Li et al., makes similar values close. Think of each distribution as piles of sand on the values, and of a ground distance between values as the cost of moving a unit of sand from one to the other.

Definition 16.5 (Earth mover’s distance) Given a ground distance between values, the earth mover’s distance \(\mathrm{EMD}(P_E, P)\) is the least total cost of moving the mass of \(P_E\) until it becomes \(P\), where moving mass \(f\) from value \(i\) to value \(j\) costs \(f\) times their ground distance.

For ordered values, such as salary bands or age groups, the least cost has a closed form. On a line, sand can only get from one side of a gap to the other by crossing it, so the work can be counted gap by gap.

Proposition 16.6 (Earth mover’s distance on ordered values) Number \(m\) ordered values \(1\) to \(m\), and place them at ground distance \(\lvert i - j\rvert/(m - 1)\), so that the two ends are distance 1 apart. Then \[\mathrm{EMD}(P_E, P) = \frac{1}{m - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\Big\lvert\sum_{j \le i}\big(P_E(j) - P(j)\big)\Big\rvert. \tag{16.11}\]


Proof. 

Cost per gap. A move from \(i\) to \(j\) crosses each of the \(\lvert i - j\rvert\) gaps between them once, so its cost is \(1/(m - 1)\) per unit of mass per gap crossed.
How much must cross each gap. Look at the gap between values \(i\) and \(i + 1\). The values up to \(i\) hold \(\sum_{j \le i}P_E(j)\) under the class and must end up holding \(\sum_{j \le i}P(j)\). Their excess, or shortfall, is \(\sum_{j \le i}(P_E(j) - P(j))\), and that net mass has to cross the gap, rightwards if it is positive and leftwards if it is negative. So any plan moves at least this much across the gap.
A plan that does no more. Move exactly the net amount of step 2 across each gap, between neighbouring values. Value \(i\) then gains the net mass entering through its two gaps, which is \(P(i) - P_E(i)\), so the plan turns \(P_E\) into \(P\). So the least cost is \(1/(m - 1)\) times the sum, over the \(m - 1\) gaps, of the absolute net mass that crosses each one, which is Equation 16.11.


The choice of distance is a choice of what counts as similar. EMD with a ground distance that puts diagnoses of the same organ close together treats gastritis and gastric ulcer as close, so a class full of stomach diseases is far from the table and fails the definition. On salary bands, if the table is spread evenly, a class bunched at the low end is farther from it than a class spread across the range.

Example 16.4 Take total variation first. In Table 16.4, the table’s distribution is \(\frac49\) heart disease, \(\frac39\) cancer and \(\frac29\) flu. Both distributions sum to 1, so the excesses and shortfalls are equal, and the half-sum of absolute differences is the total excess of the class over the table. Alice’s class is all heart disease, an excess of \(1 - \frac49 = \frac59 = 0.556\). The second class is \(\frac13 = \frac39\) of each value, an excess of \(\frac39 - \frac29 = \frac19 = 0.111\) on flu only. Bob’s class, \(\frac69\) cancer and \(\frac39\) flu, has excesses \(\frac39\) and \(\frac19\), together \(\frac49 = 0.444\). So the release is \(t\)-close only for \(t \ge 0.556\).
For the skewness attack (Figure 16.3), the class that is 50% HIV is at total variation \(0.50 - 0.01 = 0.49\) from a table with 1% HIV, the excess on HIV. A class with 10% HIV is at \(0.10 - 0.01 = 0.09\), which passes \(t = 0.1\), and still makes HIV ten times as likely for its members.

16.4 The composition attack
Every definition so far is about one release, and Ganta, Kasiviswanathan & Smith (2008) asked what happens when there are two. Two hospitals in one city publish their patient tables, each properly k-anonymous or \(\ell\)-diverse, with no coordination, and a patient treated at both appears in a class of each.

Definition 16.6 (The composition attack) Let a target appear in two releases, in class \(E_1\) of the first and class \(E_2\) of the second. The attack’s candidates are the values that appear in both classes, \[\{v : n_{E_1}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_2}(v) > 0\}. \tag{16.12}\] The target’s value is pinned down when a single candidate is left.

The true value is always a candidate, because the target’s own record carries it in each class, so a single candidate is the truth. None of the three definitions composes, that is, survives the combination of two releases, because each is a condition on one table, and nobody checked the intersection of two classes. To prevent it, a hospital would have to check its classes against every other release, which it cannot see, so a definition that survives must bound what two releases leak together, whatever the adversary knows. Differential privacy, the subject of Part 3, does.
To see how often the attack succeeds, model the classes as random. Let the target’s class have \(k_1\) records in the first release and \(k_2\) in the second, and let the values of the other members be independent draws from the population, with \(p_v\) the probability of value \(v\). Given the true value \(v\), let \(W_1\) be the set of wrong values, those other than \(v\), that appear among the \(k_1 - 1\) other members of the first class, and \(W_2\) the same for the second. These are the wrong values each release leaves open, and the target is pinned exactly when no wrong value is left open by both. Write \(p(W) = \sum_{u \in W}p_u\) for the probability of a set of values \(W\). The formula below fixes what the first class leaves open and asks whether the second class avoids it.

Proposition 16.7 (How often two releases pin down a value) In this model, the probability that the two releases pin down the target’s value is \[\Pr[\text{pinned}] = \sum_vp_v\,\mathbb E\big[(1 - p(W_1))^{k_2 - 1}\big], \tag{16.13}\] where the expectation is over the random set \(W_1\) for the given \(v\). For every set \(W\) of values other than \(v\), the probability that \(W_1\) is exactly \(W\) is \[\Pr[W_1 = W] = \sum_{T \subseteq W}(-1)^{\lvert W\rvert - \lvert T\rvert}\big(p_v + p(T)\big)^{k_1 - 1}. \tag{16.14}\]


Proof. The plan is to fix the true value and what the first class contains, compute the chance that the second class avoids it, and then average.

Condition on the true value. The target’s true value is \(v\) with probability \(p_v\). Everything below is for a fixed \(v\), and the outer sum \(\sum_v p_v(\cdot)\) averages over it.
When the value is pinned. The candidates are \(v\) itself together with the wrong values that appear in both classes, the set \(W_1 \cap W_2\). So the value is pinned exactly when \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are disjoint.
Fix what the first class leaves open. Condition on \(W_1 = W\) for a particular set \(W\). The \(k_2 - 1\) others of the second class are independent draws, and each avoids \(W\) with probability \(1 - p(W)\), so \[\Pr[W_2 \cap W = \emptyset] = (1 - p(W))^{k_2 - 1}. \tag{16.15}\] Averaging over the possible sets \(W\), weighted by \(\Pr[W_1 = W]\), gives the expectation in Equation 16.13.
The distribution of the first class’s set. \(W_1 = W\) means two things. Every one of the \(k_1 - 1\) draws lands in \(W \cup \{v\}\), and each value of \(W\) is hit at least once. For any set \(T\), the event that all draws land in \(T \cup \{v\}\) has probability \((p_v + p(T))^{k_1 - 1}\). Inclusion–exclusion then handles the second requirement. Start from “all draws land in \(W \cup \{v\}\)”, subtract the cases where some value of \(W\) is missed, which means all draws land in a smaller set, add back the cases subtracted twice, and continue alternating over every number of missed values. Each term is labelled by a subset \(T\) of \(W\) that the draws are allowed to hit, and the values of \(W\) outside \(T\) are the ones forced to be missed. The sign \((-1)^{\lvert W\rvert - \lvert T\rvert}\) is plus when an even number are missed and minus when an odd number are.


For a single wrong value \(u\), the sum has two terms, \[\Pr[W_1 = \{u\}] = (p_v + p_u)^{k_1 - 1} - p_v^{k_1 - 1}. \tag{16.16}\] That is the probability that every draw is \(v\) or \(u\), minus the probability that every draw is \(v\), in which case \(u\) was never hit.
The model understates the risk, because it draws the other members of a class from the whole population. In real releases a class collects people of similar ages, who are more likely to share a diagnosis, so each class holds fewer distinct wrong values and the intersection is smaller.
The sum over subsets grows quickly with the number of values, so a simpler bound helps. The target escapes only if some wrong value turns up in both classes, and the chance of “some” is at most the sum of the chances of each.

Proposition 16.8 (A union bound on pinning) In the same model, \[\Pr[\text{pinned}] \ge 1 - \sum_vp_v\sum_{u \ne v}\big(1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_1 - 1}\big)\big(1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_2 - 1}\big). \tag{16.17}\]


Proof. 

When it fails. Given \(v\), the value is not pinned when some \(u \ne v\) is in both \(W_1\) and \(W_2\).
The chance for one wrong value. The value \(u\) is missing from the first class when all \(k_1 - 1\) others avoid it, which has probability \((1 - p_u)^{k_1 - 1}\). So \(u\) is in \(W_1\) with probability \(1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_1 - 1}\), and likewise for \(W_2\). The two classes are drawn independently, so the probability that \(u\) is in both is the product.
Add over wrong values. The expected number of wrong values in both sets is the sum of these products, because the expected count of events is the sum of their probabilities. A count that is at least 1 whenever the event happens has an expectation at least the event’s probability, so the chance that there is at least one shared wrong value is at most this sum. Subtracting from 1 and averaging over \(v\) gives Equation 16.17.


The union bound charges every wrong value separately, so it is accurate only when two wrong values rarely turn up in both classes at once. With classes of 2, each class holds at most one wrong value, and the bound is exact. With classes of 5, the sum in Equation 16.17 already exceeds 1, so the bound is negative and Equation 16.13 is needed.

Example 16.5 With the population’s diagnosis distribution of the hospital table, the model’s probability that two releases pin down the diagnosis is 0.8734 for classes of 2, 0.1615 for classes of 5, 0.0288 for classes of 7 and 0.0015 for classes of 10. It falls fast because a larger class contains more wrong values, and each one is another chance for the two classes to share one. Simulation agrees to within 0.001 (Figure 16.4, left). The union bound gives 0.8734 at \(k = 2\) and is negative from \(k = 5\) on.
The script then runs the attack. A city has 15,000 people drawn from the model of the hospital table. Two hospitals each treat a random 10,000 of them, so 6,649 people are treated at both. Each hospital publishes a 5-anonymous Mondrian release of its own patients. Table 16.7 gives what the adversary learns about the 6,649.

At \(k = 5\) a patient’s class has 6.8 records, averaged over patients rather than over classes, so the nearest model case is classes of 7, and it predicts only 2.9%. The release does better because real classes gather similar ages, as noted after Proposition 16.7. With distinct 3-diversity, no single release pins anyone down, and the two together pin down 18 patients (0.27% of 6,649).

Machanavajjhala, Kifer, Gehrke & Venkitasubramaniam, “l-Diversity: Privacy Beyond k-Anonymity” (ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data, 2007; ICDE 2006): the homogeneity and background knowledge attacks, and the three versions of l-diversity.
Li, Li & Venkatasubramanian, “t-Closeness: Privacy Beyond k-Anonymity and l-Diversity” (ICDE, 2007): the skewness and similarity attacks, and the earth mover’s distance.
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan & Smith, “Composition Attacks and Auxiliary Information in Data Privacy” (KDD, 2008): the intersection attack on independent releases, and why a definition must survive other releases.
Aggarwal, “On k-Anonymity and the Curse of Dimensionality” (VLDB, 2005): why high-dimensional data cannot be k-anonymized without destroying it.
Prasser, Kohlmayer and colleagues, the ARX data anonymization tool (arx.deidentifier.org): an open implementation of these criteria.
