title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.8 Why δ must be much smaller than 1/n
text:
18.8 Why δ must be much smaller than 1/n
How small must \(\delta\) be? A deliberately terrible mechanism shows the danger. It is DP with \(\varepsilon = 0\) and yet publishes records verbatim, because over a whole dataset its small chances add up.

Proposition 18.3 (Release each record with probability δ) The mechanism that publishes each record of the dataset, in full, independently with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP under add/remove. On a dataset of \(n\) records it publishes \(n\delta\) records on average, and at least one record with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}, \tag{18.27}\] so \(\delta = 1/n\) exposes someone with probability about \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.632\).


Proof. The plan is to run the mechanism on \(D\) and on \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\) with the same coins, so that the outputs differ only through one extra coin, and then to count the exposures.

Couple the two runs. Run the mechanism on \(D'\) by first running it on \(D\) and then tossing one more coin for \(x\). The two outputs are equal unless that coin publishes \(x\), which happens with probability \(\delta\).
Bound one direction. The output on \(D'\) lands in an event \(S\) either because the output on \(D\) did or because the extra coin changed it, so \[\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta. \tag{18.28}\]
Bound the other direction. With probability \(1 - \delta\) the extra coin does nothing, and a probability is at most 1, so \[\Pr[M(D') \in S] \ge (1 - \delta)\Pr[M(D) \in S] \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S] - \delta. \tag{18.29}\] Both directions match Equation 18.1 with factor \(e^0 = 1\) and slack \(\delta\).
Count the exposures. The number of records published is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, \delta)\), with mean \(n\delta\), and none is published with probability \((1 - \delta)^n\). For small \(\delta\), \(\ln(1 - \delta) \approx -\delta\), which gives \[(1 - \delta)^n = e^{n\ln(1 - \delta)} \approx e^{-n\delta}. \tag{18.30}\]


So \(\delta\) is a per-person budget for catastrophe. Pick it well below \(1/n\), with \(n\) the number of people rather than records. A common choice is \(\delta = 1/n^{1.5}\), and fixed values need checking: Abadi et al. (2016) used \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for 60,000 training examples, so \(n\delta = 0.6\).
One pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) can describe mechanisms that fail in very different ways (Figure 18.7). The Gaussian count with \(\sigma = 2\) is \((1, 6.830\times10^{-3})\)-DP, and its loss exceeds 3 with probability \(4.462\times10^{-9}\). Publishing a person’s bit with probability \(6.830\times10^{-3}\), and otherwise running randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\), gives the same pair, with the whole \(\delta\) on outputs of infinite loss. From the pair alone, Equation 18.24 at level 3 allows \[\Pr[L > 3] \le \frac{6.830\times10^{-3}}{1 - e^{1 - 3}} = 7.899\times10^{-3}, \tag{18.31}\] and the catastrophic mechanism comes close to it. So read a quoted pair pessimistically unless you know the whole curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).






Figure 18.7: The tail \(\Pr[L > c]\) of two \((1, 0.0068)\)-DP mechanisms on a log scale. Blue: the Gaussian count, whose tail falls fast. Red: publish the bit with probability \(\delta\), else randomized response; its tail stays at \(\delta\). Dotted: the largest tail the pair allows, from Equation 18.24.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.9 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
18.9 What differential privacy does not protect
The definition compares two worlds that differ in one record, not the world before and after the release. Kifer & Machanavajjhala (2011) showed that no definition can block every inference without assumptions on how the data were generated. Four limits matter in practice.
Population inference. Suppose the cancer rate among smokers is 0.1 or 0.3, equally likely, so your belief that Alice, a smoker, will get cancer is 0.2. A study that excludes her reveals the rate 0.3, and your belief rises to 0.3. Yet the study never saw her record, so nothing happened to her because she took part.
Correlated records. If \(k\) records move together, as in a household, their joint privacy loss can reach \(k\varepsilon\), so the unit of privacy must match the unit of correlation.
Everything outside the mathematical mechanism. Floating-point leaks (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), timing side channels and other releases need separate care.
Tasks about one person. Contact tracing must find whom one infected person met, so its output must depend on that person, which DP forbids. DP protects your contribution, not secrets that other people’s data reveal.

Example 18.9 A count with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) meets a household of \(k = 5\) people who always answer alike. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script finds a largest privacy loss of 5.0000 for the household, which is protected only as if by a 5-DP mechanism. The exact best advantage against it is \(1 - e^{-5/2} = 0.9179\), under the 5-DP bound \(\tanh(5/2) = 0.9866\). An attacker who asks whether the household took part is right with probability up to 0.959, although each record is “protected at \(\varepsilon = 1\)”.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.10 Is it a privacy violation?
Some reported privacy failures show that a release reveals something about the people whose data it used, and others that it reveals something true about the world, which then applies to particular people. DP is designed to stop only the first kind. Three questions from Kamath’s course on private data analysis sort a claim into one kind or the other.

Does it depend on this person’s record? DP bounds an inference’s probability by \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability without the record, plus \(\delta\), so it has nothing against an inference that is as likely without the record.
Does the inference succeed exactly when the model is accurate? Then it comes from patterns shared by many records, and blocking it is a decision not to learn.
When, and by whom, was the information given up? An inference from what the person disclosed elsewhere, such as her purchases, is the same whether or not her record was used.

The first question decides, and the other two explain a no. To measure a claimed attack, compare its success on members with its success on non-members, because only the excess can be a privacy loss (Attribute inference). An inference that is no violation can still be unacceptable, since norms of information flow (Nissenbaum, 2004) cover far more than DP.

Example 18.10 Train a regression model on points that all lie on the line \(y = x + 1\), among them \((2.7, 3.7)\). Asked about \(x = 2.7\) it answers the training label 3.7, which looks like a leak. But without that point the line and the answer stay the same, so the first question says no. Table 18.7 applies the test to four well-known cases.

Dwork, Kenthapadi, McSherry, Mironov & Naor, “Our Data, Ourselves: Privacy via Distributed Noise Generation” (EUROCRYPT 2006). Introduces approximate \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), ch. 2: the definition, randomized response, what DP promises and does not (§2.3), and the “release a random record” argument for small \(\delta\). The standard reference for this whole chapter.
Warner, “Randomized Response: A Survey Technique for Eliminating Evasive Answer Bias” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1965). The original spinner design, which answers truthfully with a known probability, and its estimator.
Boruch, “Assuring Confidentiality of Responses in Social Research: A Note on Strategies” (The American Sociologist, 1971). The forced-response design, of which the two-coin protocol is an instance.
Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy” (2017), §1.6. Why a purely additive (total variation) definition cannot be both useful and private.
Wasserman & Zhou, “A Statistical Framework for Differential Privacy” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2010). DP as a bound on the power of tests.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015). The hypothesis-testing characterization Equation 18.17 and its use for optimal composition (Advanced and optimal composition).
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS Series B, 2022). Trade-off functions as the privacy definition itself (\(f\)-DP); Equation 18.18 is their \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\).
Kasiviswanathan & Smith, “On the ‘Semantics’ of Differential Privacy: A Bayesian Formulation” (Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2014). The posterior reading for arbitrary priors, and the bad-set argument for approximate DP.
Yeom, Giacomelli, Fredrikson & Jha, “Privacy Risk in Machine Learning: Analyzing the Connection to Overfitting” (CSF 2018). Membership advantage and the bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\).
Kifer & Machanavajjhala, “No Free Lunch in Data Privacy” (SIGMOD 2011). Why DP cannot protect correlated data without assumptions on how it was generated.
Desfontaines & Pejó, “SoK: Differential Privacies” (PETS 2020). A map of the many variants of the definition, including the choice of neighbouring relation.
Abadi et al., “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016). Example-level DP for training neural networks, with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for 60,000 examples.
Kamath, “Algorithms for Private Data Analysis” (University of Waterloo, recorded lectures, 2020). The three-question test for privacy violations, and the catastrophic and graceful readings of \(\delta\).
Kosinski, Stillwell & Graepel, “Private Traits and Attributes Are Predictable from Digital Records of Human Behavior” (PNAS, 2013); Duhigg, “How Companies Learn Your Secrets” (New York Times Magazine, 2012). Inferences from public or volunteered data, the “not a violation” side of Table 18.7.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Post-processing
You have proved that one mechanism satisfies differential privacy (DP), and now you use it: you round its output, you protect users who each contributed fifty records, and you answer a hundred queries rather than one. So three questions come up. Is a processed output still private? What does a guarantee about one record give for a group of \(k\) records? And what is the guarantee of many mechanisms run on the same data?
The answers are the three properties that make DP usable as an engineering tool. Two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ by adding or removing one record, unless a section says otherwise. One idea organizes all three properties, the privacy loss of an output \(y\) from the definition of differential privacy, the log of how much more likely \(y\) is on \(D\) than on \(D'\): \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{19.1}\] Here \(p_{M(D)}\) is the probability, or density, that the mechanism \(M\) gives to \(y\) on \(D\). Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the case \(\delta = 0\) of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, keeps this loss within \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\) for every output and every neighbouring pair. When you walk through several datasets, or run mechanisms whose coins (their internal randomness) are independent, likelihood ratios multiply, so privacy losses add, and that is what costs. Processing instead merges outputs and averages their likelihood ratios, which is free.
The running example is randomized response at level \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\): a person whose record is one private bit reports it truthfully with probability \(\frac34\) and flips it with probability \(\frac14\). If the bit is 1 the report 1 has probability \(\frac34\), and if it is 0 it has probability \(\frac14\), a ratio of 3, while the report 0 has the ratio \(\frac13\). So the privacy loss is \(\pm\ln 3\) on every output. The output distributions \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) are written \(P\) and \(Q\), with mass functions or densities \(p\) and \(q\), and a sum over continuous outputs means an integral.
A private output is rarely published as is. You round a noisy count, fit a model to noisy marginals, or let an analyst decide what to do next, each time without looking at the data again. This section asks whether such processing can undo the protection. It cannot, because a processed output merges outputs, and its likelihood ratio is an average of theirs, which stays in the band \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\). For approximate DP the privacy loss is not bounded, so the proof works with events and needs one small lemma first.
In its event form, from the definition chapter, \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP says that \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S] + \delta\) for every set \(S\) of outputs and every ordered neighbouring pair. Step 1 of the proof of post-processing turns an event about the processed output into a soft rule on the original output, one that accepts each output with some probability, and the lemma says that soft rules obey the same bound.
The lemma is the randomized version of the worst-event argument of Divergences. The largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\) over events \(S\) is the hockey-stick divergence, \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+, \tag{19.3}\] where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) keeps the positive parts. So \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when that divergence is at most \(\delta\) for every ordered neighbouring pair. The smallest such \(\delta\) at each \(\varepsilon\) is the privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of \(M\), and the script computes it exactly for every mechanism in this chapter.
To cover randomized processing, describe it as a channel \(K\): \(K(z \mid y)\) is the probability that the processing outputs \(z\) when its input is \(y\). A deterministic function \(f\) is the case \(K(z \mid y) = \mathbf 1[z = f(y)]\), which is 1 when \(z = f(y)\) and 0 otherwise. The processed output on \(D\) has the distribution \(PK(z) = \sum_y p(y)K(z \mid y)\), which weights each \(y\) by how likely it is to become \(z\), and \(L^f_{D,D'}(z)\) is its privacy loss. The theorem says that processing never makes \(D\) and \(D'\) easier to tell apart.
So nothing downstream needs a new proof. A model trained on DP statistics, or a plot of them, never reads the data again and inherits the guarantee. Attackers are covered too: a membership-inference attacker of Part 2 applies a channel to \(y\), so the bounds of the definition chapter on its error rates hold for every attack. An analyst who picks the next question from earlier private answers is post-processing them, though answering that question is a new mechanism (Section 19.3; Adaptive data analysis).
Invertible processing, such as a change of units, keeps the privacy loss exactly, since nothing is averaged. Processing that merges outputs with different losses lowers it, though usually only a little. The one condition is that \(f\) must not read the data, because step 1 needed the same \(g\) under \(D\) and \(D'\). Looking up the exact count of the noisy winning category is therefore a second, non-private mechanism (Section 19.5).

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
Lemma 19.1 (Soft tests obey the definition) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, fix a neighbouring pair with output distributions \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), and let \(g\) be any function of the output with values in \([0, 1]\). Then \[\mathbb E_P[g(Y)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_Q[g(Y)] + \delta. \tag{19.2}\]


Proof. 

Write the gap as a sum. The difference \(\mathbb E_P[g] - e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g]\) equals \(\sum_y g(y)\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)\), a sum in which each value \(g(y)\) multiplies a fixed bracket.
Push it to the extreme. The sum is largest when \(g(y) = 1\) wherever the bracket is positive and \(g(y) = 0\) wherever it is negative, because any value in between gives up part of a positive term or adds part of a negative one. That choice of \(g\) is the indicator of the event \(B = \{y : p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\}\), so the sum is at most \(\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\).
Apply the definition to the event \(B\), which bounds \(\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\) by \(\delta\).





Theorem 19.1 (Post-processing) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and let \(f\) be any randomized function of its output whose coins are independent of the data and of \(M\)’s coins. Then \(f \circ M\), the mechanism \(D \mapsto f(M(D))\), is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. In terms of the channel \(K\) of \(f\), for every neighbouring pair the hockey-stick divergence can only go down, and so can the largest privacy loss: \[E_{e^\varepsilon}\big(PK\,\|\,QK\big) \le E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q), \qquad \max_z\big|L^{f}_{D,D'}(z)\big| \le \max_y\big|L_{D,D'}(y)\big|. \tag{19.4}\]


Proof. The plan is to turn any event about the processed output into a soft test on the original output and apply Lemma 19.1, then to show the privacy-loss form by the averaging argument of the data processing inequality (DPI).

Fix an event \(S\) of processed outputs. Let \(g(y) = \sum_{z \in S}K(z \mid y)\), the probability that processing \(y\) lands in \(S\). It is a probability, so it takes values in \([0, 1]\), and it does not depend on the data, because \(f\) does not look at the data: the same \(g\) serves for \(D\) and for \(D'\).
Average over the output. To land in \(S\), the mechanism first produces some \(y\), and then processing sends it into \(S\) with probability \(g(y)\), so \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] = \sum_y p(y)g(y) = \mathbb E_P[g(Y)]\), and the same with \(q\) for \(D'\).
Apply the lemma to \(g\). Lemma 19.1 gives \(\mathbb E_P[g] \le e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g] + \delta\), that is \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[f(M(D')) \in S] + \delta\). This holds for every \(S\) and every ordered neighbouring pair, which is the event form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for \(f \circ M\). The hockey-stick inequality of Equation 19.4 is the same statement for the worst event \(S\).
The privacy-loss form. The likelihood ratio of \(z\) is \(PK(z)/QK(z)\). In the numerator, for outputs with \(q(y) > 0\), write each \(p(y)\) as \(q(y)\) times its likelihood ratio \(e^{L(y)} = p(y)/q(y)\). That turns the ratio into a weighted average of the likelihood ratios of the \(y\) that can produce \(z\): \[e^{L^f(z)} = \frac{PK(z)}{QK(z)} = \sum_y\frac{q(y)K(z \mid y)}{QK(z)}\,e^{L(y)}. \tag{19.5}\] The weight of each \(y\) is the share of the \(D'\)-probability of \(z\) that comes through \(y\). The weights are non-negative and sum to 1, because \(\sum_y q(y)K(z \mid y) = QK(z)\). So \(e^{L^f(z)}\) lies between the smallest and the largest \(e^{L(y)}\), and \(|L^f(z)|\) is at most the largest \(|L(y)|\), which is the second inequality of Equation 19.4. This is step 1 of the DPI derivation in Divergences.





Example 19.1 Collect answers with randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) and then, before publishing, flip each answer with probability \(r = \frac14\) using a fresh coin. The published answer \(z = 1\) can be reached in two ways: the first answer was 1 and was kept, or it was 0 and was flipped. Each path’s probability is the product of its two steps, and Table 19.1 follows both paths.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.2 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but people are not rows. A user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages, and a household shares an address. To bound what an adversary learns about all \(k\) records of one user, you need a guarantee for datasets that differ in \(k\) records. Group privacy derives it from the one-record guarantee, at a price that is linear in \(k\) for \(\varepsilon\) and exponential in \(k\) for \(\delta\).
Say that \(D\) and \(D''\) are at distance \(k\) if a path \(D = D_0 \sim D_1 \sim \dots \sim D_k = D''\) joins them, changing one record per step. The idea is to apply the one-record guarantee once per step. Each step multiplies the bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) and adds a slack \(\delta\), which later steps multiply again, so the slacks pile up in a geometric sum.

Theorem 19.2 (Group privacy) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Then for every pair of datasets \(D\) and \(D''\) at distance \(k\) and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{19.6}\] In particular, pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP gives pure \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for groups of size \(k\).


Proof. The plan is to prove the pure case through the privacy loss, which adds along the path, and the approximate case through events, chaining the one-step bound \(k\) times.

Pure DP: telescope the likelihood ratio along the path. Multiply and divide by the densities at the intermediate datasets \(D_1, \dots, D_{k-1}\). Each appears once in a numerator and once in a denominator, so they cancel and only the two ends remain: \[\frac{p_{M(D_0)}(y)}{p_{M(D_k)}(y)} = \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{p_{M(D_{i-1})}(y)}{p_{M(D_i)}(y)}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad L_{D_0,D_k}(y) = \sum_{i=1}^k L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y). \tag{19.7}\]
Bound each term. Each pair \(D_{i-1} \sim D_i\) is neighbouring, so \(|L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) by pure DP.
Add. A sum of \(k\) terms, each between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\), lies between \(-k\varepsilon\) and \(k\varepsilon\), so \(|L_{D_0,D_k}(y)| \le k\varepsilon\) for every \(y\), which is pure \(k\varepsilon\)-DP.
Approximate DP: one step. With \(\delta > 0\) the privacy loss is no longer bounded, so there is nothing to add up, and the proof chains the event form instead. Fix an event \(S\) and write \(s_i\) for the probability \(\Pr[M(D_i) \in S]\). The definition applied to the neighbouring pair \(D_{i-1} \sim D_i\) gives \(s_{i-1} \le e^\varepsilon s_i + \delta\).
Substitute the next step into the right side. The bound on \(s_1\) goes in place of \(s_1\): \[s_0 \le e^\varepsilon s_1 + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\big(e^\varepsilon s_2 + \delta\big) + \delta = e^{2\varepsilon}s_2 + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon). \tag{19.8}\]
Repeat \(k\) times. By induction, \(s_0 \le e^{k\varepsilon}s_k + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon + \dots + e^{(k-1)\varepsilon})\). Each new \(\delta\) enters before \(k - 1, k - 2, \dots, 0\) more multiplications by \(e^\varepsilon\), which is where the geometric sum comes from.
Simplify. The geometric sum is \(\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\), because multiplying it by \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) cancels all terms but the first and last. Each of its \(k\) terms is at most the largest one, \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), which gives the simpler but looser \(k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta\).


No better bound holds for all \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms. The mechanism below shows it, because it has an event on which every one-step bound of steps 4 to 6 is an equality.

Proposition 19.1 (The alarm mechanism attains the bound) Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) and a cap \(K\) on the count of some kind of record. On a count \(c \le K\) the alarm mechanism outputs “alarm” with probability \[a_c = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{K-c-1}e^{j\varepsilon} \tag{19.9}\] and “quiet” otherwise, and on a count above \(K\) it always outputs “quiet”. If \(a_0 \le (e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for neighbouring counts, which differ by 1, and for the counts \(0\) and \(k \le K\) it meets Equation 19.6 with equality on the event “alarm”.


Proof. 

One step is tight. Pulling the first term \(\delta\) out of the sum and a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) out of the rest shows that \(a_c = e^\varepsilon a_{c+1} + \delta\) for \(c < K\). So each neighbouring pair meets the event form with equality on “alarm”.
The mechanism is private. The other three checks, “alarm” in the reverse order and “quiet” in both orders, hold exactly when \(a_0 \le (e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). Section J.8 in the appendices proves it, and a simpler sufficient condition is \(a_0 \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\). For \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the condition allows \(K \le 21\).
The chain is tight. Along the path of counts \(0, 1, \dots, k\), step 5 of the proof of Theorem 19.2 substitutes equalities into equalities, so \(a_0 - e^{k\varepsilon}a_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta_k\).


Pure DP degrades linearly. A \(0.1\)-DP guarantee per record is \(10\)-DP for a user with 100 records, which is almost nothing, since a likelihood ratio of up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\) lets an adversary be nearly certain. This is the formal version of the “correlated records” caveat of the definition chapter. For approximate DP the \(\delta\) term grows exponentially: with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 10\) it is \(\delta_k = \frac{e^{10} - 1}{e - 1}\,\delta = 12818.3\,\delta\). Since \(\delta\) must already be much smaller than \(1/n\) for \(n\) records (the definition chapter), group privacy for large groups is often vacuous.
A specific mechanism can do much better than the generic bound. With Gaussian noise on a count, a group of \(k\) records shifts the count by \(k\), so its exact group profile is that of a Gaussian pair with a larger shift (Part 4). The better fix is often to define neighbours as datasets that differ in one user’s records, bound each user’s contribution, and prove DP at that level.

Example 19.2 For randomized response a group of \(k\) records is \(k\) people, and the reports in which all \(k\) favour the same side have privacy loss exactly \(k\ln 3\), so the pure bound is exact. A noisy count shows the telescoping of step 1 at work. Take \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise and the path of counts \(0, 1, 2, 3\), so \(k = 3\). With density \(\frac12e^{-|y - c|}\) at true count \(c\), the privacy loss between counts \(c\) and \(c + 1\) is \(L_{c,c+1}(y) = |y - c - 1| - |y - c|\), how much farther \(y\) is from \(c + 1\) than from \(c\). title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.3 Basic sequential composition
An analyst asks \(k\) queries of the same dataset, each with fresh noise. Each output alone is private, but an adversary sees all of them. This section asks what guarantee holds for the whole transcript \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\), even when each mechanism is chosen after seeing the previous outputs. For pure DP the answer rests on one fact about independent coins, which step 2 of the proof needs and parallel composition reuses: probabilities multiply, so privacy losses add.

Lemma 19.2 (Privacy losses of independent outputs add) Let \(Y = (Y_1, Y_2)\), where \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are produced with independent coins, so that \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)\) on \(D\) and likewise \(q(y_1, y_2) = q_1(y_1)q_2(y_2)\) on \(D'\). Then the privacy loss of the pair is the sum of the privacy losses of its parts, \[L(y_1, y_2) = \ln\frac{p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)}{q_1(y_1)q_2(y_2)} = L_1(y_1) + L_2(y_2). \tag{19.10}\] The same holds when the second output depends on the first, with the conditional probabilities \(p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\) and \(q_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\) in place of \(p_2(y_2)\) and \(q_2(y_2)\).


Proof. 

Independent outputs. The probability of seeing both outputs is the product of their probabilities, and the logarithm of a product of two ratios is the sum of the two logarithms.
Dependent outputs. The chain rule of probability writes any joint probability as “first, times second given first”, \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), and the same on \(D'\). The same logarithm then gives the same sum, with the conditional loss \(\ln\frac{p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)}{q_2(y_2 \mid y_1)}\) as its second term.


In the theorem below, each mechanism \(M_i\) may also read the previous outputs, the way an analyst picks the next query after reading the last answer. This is adaptive composition, and non-adaptive composition is the case where \(M_i\) ignores them. The condition is that each step is private however the earlier outputs turned out. Section B.1 in the appendices derives the theorem from scratch, with worked numbers.

Theorem 19.3 (Basic composition) Let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) run on the same dataset with independent coins, where \(M_i\) may read the previous outputs \(y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}\). If, for every fixed value of the previous outputs, \(D \mapsto M_i(D; y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP, then the mechanism that releases \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.11}\] For pure DP the bound \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) is the exact worst-case privacy loss whenever each \(M_i\) attains its own worst case at outputs that can occur together.


Proof. The plan is to prove the pure case by adding privacy losses with Lemma 19.2. The approximate case takes two mechanisms, since induction on \(k\) does the rest. That case splits an event over the first output, applies the second mechanism’s guarantee for each value of it, and applies the first mechanism’s guarantee to what is left, a soft test of the first output.

Pure DP: factor the probability of a transcript. By the chain rule, the probability of \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is the probability of \(y_1\), times that of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), and so on. On \(D\), \[p_D(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k p_{M_i(D;\,y_{<i})}(y_i), \tag{19.12}\] where \(y_{<i} = (y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) and each factor uses fresh coins. The same holds on \(D'\), with the same previous outputs plugged in.
Take the log-ratio. By Lemma 19.2, applied \(k - 1\) times in its dependent form, \(L_{D,D'}(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k L^{(i)}(y_i;\,y_{<i})\), where \(L^{(i)}\) is the privacy loss of \(M_i\) with its previous outputs fixed.
Bound each term and add. For the fixed \(y_{<i}\), \(M_i\) is \(\varepsilon_i\)-DP by assumption, so \(|L^{(i)}| \le \varepsilon_i\), and the sum is at most \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) at every transcript, which is pure \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\)-DP. When every \(M_i\) attains \(\varepsilon_i\) at outputs that can occur together, the sum is attained, which is the exactness claim.
Approximate DP: split an event over the first output. Take \(k = 2\), and write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distribution of the transcript \((Y_1, Y_2)\) on \(D\) and on \(D'\). For a set \(S\) of transcripts, let \(S_{y_1} = \{y_2 : (y_1, y_2) \in S\}\), the second outputs that complete \(y_1\) into \(S\). The transcript lands in \(S\) when the first output is some \(y_1\) and the second lands in \(S_{y_1}\), so \[P(S) = \sum_{y_1}p_1(y_1)\,P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}), \tag{19.13}\] where \(p_1\) is the mass function of \(M_1(D)\) and \(P_2^{y_1}\) the distribution of \(M_2(D; y_1)\). Write \(q_1\) and \(Q_2^{y_1}\) for the same objects on \(D'\).
Apply the second mechanism’s guarantee inside the sum. For each \(y_1\), \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) + \delta_2\), and also \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le 1\) because it is a probability. So \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le g(y_1) + \delta_2\) with \[g(y_1) = \min\big(1,\ e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\big) \in [0, 1]. \tag{19.14}\]
Sum over \(y_1\). The weights \(p_1(y_1)\) add up to 1, so \(\delta_2\) comes out once: \(P(S) \le \mathbb E_{p_1}[g] + \delta_2\).
Apply the first mechanism’s guarantee to \(g\). The function \(g\) takes values in \([0, 1]\), which is why it was capped at 1, so Lemma 19.1 gives \(\mathbb E_{p_1}[g] \le e^{\varepsilon_1}\mathbb E_{q_1}[g] + \delta_1\).
Undo the cap. Since \(g(y_1) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\), the average \(\mathbb E_{q_1}[g]\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\sum_{y_1}q_1(y_1)Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\), which by step 4 on \(D'\) is \(e^{\varepsilon_2}Q(S)\).
Combine. Steps 6 to 8 give \(P(S) \le e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}Q(S) + \delta_1 + \delta_2\). Nothing used that \(M_2\) ignores \(y_1\), so this covers adaptive composition.


Basic composition is exact for the worst case, and the worst case is rare. For \(k\) randomized-response answers about the same bit, “every answer is true” has loss \(k\ln 3\) but probability \((\frac34)^k\). Typical transcripts mix truths with lies, whose losses cancel. Under \(D\), each answer contributes \(+\varepsilon_0\) when it tells the truth, with probability \(t = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), and \(-\varepsilon_0\) otherwise. The mean of each answer’s loss is therefore \(\varepsilon_0(2t - 1)\), which is \(\varepsilon_0/2\) for \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\). A sum of \(k\) such independent terms stays within a spread of order \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt k\) of its mean (Concentration). An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee may ignore losses above \(\varepsilon\) that occur with probability at most \(\delta\), so a small \(\delta\) writes off the unlikely tail, and the \(\varepsilon\) you need grows like \(\sqrt k\) rather than \(k\), which is the advanced composition of Advanced and optimal composition.
The \(\delta\)s add without the inflation of group privacy, because each mechanism compares the same pair \(D, D'\), and step 6 of the proof just averages the second slack. Adaptivity is free, but only with budgets fixed in advance. Choosing the budgets from the outputs (“stop when the answer is good enough”) needs the privacy filters of Advanced and optimal composition.

Example 19.3 Start with an adaptive survey. Ask a person for a randomized-response answer with \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln 3\), then ask again with \(\ln 3\) if the answer was 1 and with \(0.5\) if it was 0. Level \(0.5\) tells the truth with probability \(e^{0.5}/(1 + e^{0.5}) = 0.6225\). So the second step depends on \(y_1\), but it is at most \(\ln 3\)-DP for each value of \(y_1\). In Table 19.5 each probability is the product of the two steps. For example, \((0, 1)\) under bit 1 is a lie and then the truth, \(\frac14 \times 0.6225 = 0.1556\).

If \(j\) answers equal 1, the privacy loss is \((2j - k)\ln 3\), and \(j\) is binomial with \(k\) trials and success probability \(\frac34\) when the bit is 1, or \(\frac14\) when it is 0. title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Parallel composition
A histogram counts people in disjoint bins. Sequential composition would charge \(d\varepsilon\) for \(d\) bins, which is far too pessimistic, because one person’s record lands in one bin only. Parallel composition makes that precise, with care about the two common neighbouring relations. Under add/remove, neighbours differ by adding or removing one record. Under replace, neighbours have the same size and differ in the content of one record, which is a removal followed by an addition.
Split the data universe into disjoint parts \(U_1, \dots, U_d\) by a rule that may depend on a record’s content but not on the rest of the dataset, and run \(M_i\) on \(D \cap U_i\), the records in part \(i\). A changed record touches only its own part, so you pay only that part’s budget.

Theorem 19.4 (Parallel composition) Let \(U_1, \dots, U_d\) be a partition of the data universe fixed in advance, and let \(M_i\) run on \(D \cap U_i\) with independent coins, each \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove. Then the release \((M_1(D \cap U_1), \dots, M_d(D \cap U_d))\) is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{19.15}\] Under replace, a record that moves from part \(a\) to part \(b \ne a\) costs \((\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_b, \delta_a + \delta_b)\), and one replaced within part \(a\) costs that part’s guarantee for two add/remove steps, at most group privacy with \(k = 2\); for pure DP with equal budgets both cases give \(2\varepsilon\). If the parts are fixed slots, so that record \(i\) always goes to part \(i\), a replacement changes one part only and the cost is \((\max_i\varepsilon_i, \max_i\delta_i)\) again.


Proof. 

Add/remove changes one part. If \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\), then \(x\) lies in exactly one part \(U_j\), because the parts are disjoint and cover the universe. For \(i \ne j\), \(D \cap U_i = D' \cap U_i\), so \(M_i\) gets the same input and has the same output distribution on both.
Pure DP: the other losses are zero. By Lemma 19.2 the privacy loss of the whole release is \(\sum_iL^{(i)}\), and \(L^{(i)} \equiv 0\) for \(i \ne j\) because the two distributions are equal and their ratio is 1. So \(|L| = |L^{(j)}| \le \varepsilon_j \le \max_i\varepsilon_i\).
Approximate DP: condition on the unchanged parts. Let \(W\) be the outputs of the parts \(i \ne j\), which have the same distribution on \(D\) and \(D'\) and are independent of \(Y_j\). Given \(W\), the release lands in an event \(S\) when \(Y_j\) falls in \(S_W\), the set of \(y_j\) completing \(W\) into \(S\). So the probability of \(S\) is the average over \(W\) of \(\Pr[Y_j \in S_W]\). Inside that average, \(M_j\)’s guarantee bounds the probability on \(D\) by \(e^{\varepsilon_j}\) times that on \(D'\), plus \(\delta_j\), and averaging over the same \(W\) carries the bound to \(S\).
Replace changes up to two parts. If \(D'\) replaces a record \(x \in U_a\) by \(x' \in U_b\), then \(D \cap U_a\) loses a record and \(D \cap U_b\) gains one: two add/remove steps on two independent mechanisms, which is a composition of two mechanisms (Theorem 19.3, with the other parts handled as in step 3), giving \((\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_b, \delta_a + \delta_b)\). If \(a = b\), part \(a\) sees a removal and an addition, two neighbouring steps, which is Theorem 19.2 with \(k = 2\) inside one part. In fixed slots a replacement changes only slot \(i\), and steps 1 to 3 apply again.


So a histogram costs one \(\varepsilon\), not \(d\). Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on each of \(d\) bins is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove, because adding a record changes one bin by 1. Under replace it is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP, since moving a record changes two bins, which is why a histogram’s sensitivity is quoted as 2 under replace (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
The partition must not depend on the data. “Split the data at its median” changes when one record changes, which can move many records between parts, and then step 1 of the proof fails. Use fixed bins, or account for the data-dependent split as a mechanism of its own.

Example 19.4 Local randomized response composes in parallel. Each of \(n\) people reports their own bit at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), and each person is one slot, so the whole vector of \(n\) reports is \(\ln 3\)-DP for any \(n\), not \(n\ln 3\), under either neighbouring relation.
A two-bin histogram shows the factor of 2. Give each bin rounded \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise, and let the script compute the exact pure \(\varepsilon\) of the pair under each relation. Adding or removing a record changes one bin by 1, so only that bin contributes privacy loss, and \(\varepsilon = 1.0000\). Replacing a record in bin 1 by one in bin 2 moves bin 1 up by 1 and bin 2 down by 1. The worst output then has both noisy counts far out on the side that favours \(D\), where both step losses equal 1 at once, so \(\varepsilon = 2.0000\).

19.5 What composes and what doesn’t
The three properties hold under weak assumptions, which makes it tempting to apply them where even those fail. Each assumption appeared in a proof. Post-processing needs \(f\) not to read the data, composition needs independent coins and one neighbouring relation, and group privacy and composition need budgets fixed in advance. Table 19.8 collects the ways these break in practice, and the section then proves that the commonest break, two releases sharing one noise draw, is a total failure.



Table 19.8: What composes and what doesn’t.

When two releases share one noise draw, the noise can be subtracted away, and privacy fails completely.

Proposition 19.2 (Shared noise is not private) Release two counts with the same Laplace draw \(Z\) of scale \(b\): \(c_1(D) + Z\) and \(c_2(D) + Z\), where removing some record lowers \(c_1\) by 1 and leaves \(c_2\) unchanged. Each count alone is \(1/b\)-DP, but the pair is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta < 1\).


Proof. 

The difference is noise-free. \((c_1 + Z) - (c_2 + Z) = c_1(D) - c_2(D)\), a deterministic function of the data.
It changes between neighbours. If the difference is \(c\) on \(D\), it is \(c - 1\) on the neighbour \(D'\) without that record, since removing the record lowers \(c_1\) by 1 and leaves \(c_2\).
One event separates the two. The event “the difference equals \(c\)” has probability 1 on \(D\) and 0 on \(D'\), so the event form \(1 \le e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 + \delta\) fails for every \(\varepsilon\) unless \(\delta \ge 1\).


What broke is step 1 of the proof of Theorem 19.3: the transcript’s probability is no longer a product of the two mechanisms’ probabilities. So fresh randomness is part of the mechanism. Seeding two mechanisms with the same seed, re-adding a cached noise draw to a related query, or reusing noise across shards are all the shared-noise bug. An exact total published elsewhere can be differenced against a DP release in the same way.
The neighbouring relation is part of the budget too. A guarantee proved under add/remove and reported under replace can be off by a factor of 2, and mixing the two inside one accountant, the code that totals the budget, is a bug that comes back in Subsampling.

Example 19.5 Randomized response survives shared coins, because a second answer that reuses the first answer’s coins repeats it, which is post-processing. Additive noise does not. The script simulates the differencing attack of Proposition 19.2 on two Laplace counts, the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or over. Alice is a smoker aged 30, so she counts only in the first. She is in the data with probability \(\frac12\), and the attacker guesses “in” when the difference of the two counts exceeds the midpoint of its two possible true values. Over 200,000 runs with \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise, the attack with shared noise has accuracy \(1.0000\), because the difference is exact.
With fresh noise the same attack has accuracy \(0.6206\). The second count no longer depends on Alice, so the best any attack can reach is that of the first count alone, \(\frac12\) plus half the total variation distance between what it sees in the two cases (Divergences). For \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1)\) the best event is “the output is above \(\frac12\)”, whose probabilities differ by \(1 - e^{-1/2}\), so the best accuracy is \(\frac12 + \frac12(1 - e^{-1/2}) = 0.6967\). The difference attack falls short of it because it adds the noise of the second count.

19.8 References

Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014): Proposition 2.1 (post-processing), Theorem 2.2 (group privacy, pure), Theorem 3.16 (basic composition, with the proof for approximate DP in Appendix B), and §3.5 for composition in general. The standard reference for every statement here.
Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (TCC 2006): the paper that defined DP, where the guarantee for groups of records first appears.
McSherry, “Privacy Integrated Queries” (SIGMOD 2009): parallel composition, and a system built on post-processing and composition as its only rules.
Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy” (2017), the opening sections: the basic properties of DP (post-processing, group privacy, composition) with careful proofs, at a more theoretical level than Dwork & Roth.
Near & Abuah, Programming Differential Privacy, chapters on the properties of DP: sequential and parallel composition and post-processing, with code.
Kifer & Machanavajjhala, “No Free Lunch in Data Privacy” (SIGMOD 2011): why correlated records defeat a per-record guarantee, the problem group privacy addresses.
Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (FOCS 2010), and Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015): advanced and optimal composition, the subject of Advanced and optimal composition.
Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, “Privacy Odometers and Filters: Pay-as-you-Go Composition” (NeurIPS 2016): what changes when the budgets themselves are chosen adaptively.

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.1 Sensitivity
You run a hospital database and want to publish how many patients have diabetes, with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. The definition of differential privacy says what the release must satisfy: changing one person’s record must barely change the distribution of what you publish. It does not say how to build such a release. The two mechanisms of this chapter are the answer used almost everywhere. Both compute the exact answer, call it \(f(D)\) for the dataset \(D\), and blur it with random noise \(Z\) drawn fresh each time, so that what you publish is \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{20.1}\] If the noise is wide compared with how far one person can move the answer, an observer cannot tell from the output whether that person was there.
Three questions decide everything. The first is how much one record can move the answer, the sensitivity of \(f\), which sets the scale of the noise. The second is which noise distribution to use. Laplace noise gives pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, while Gaussian noise gives only \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but scales better when many numbers are released at once. The third is how much noise exactly. Laplace noise needs a one-line formula, while for Gaussian noise the textbook formula is loose, and the exact answer comes from solving one equation numerically.
The running example is the hospital’s count: 1,234 of its \(n = 10{,}000\) patients have diabetes, and the count must be released under add/remove neighbours.
To hide one record, the noise has to cover the largest change one record can make to the answer. That change is the sensitivity, and it is the first thing to compute for any release. It depends on the query, on the norm you measure the change in, and on the neighbouring relation of the definition of differential privacy: under add/remove a neighbour has one record more or less, so the dataset size changes, and under replace one record is swapped for another, so the size \(n\) is fixed and public.
For a vector answer you need a way to measure a change, and two are used. The \(\ell_1\) norm \(\|v\|_1 = \sum_i|v_i|\) is the total change summed over coordinates, and Laplace noise is calibrated to it. The \(\ell_2\) norm \(\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_iv_i^2}\) is the straight-line length, and Gaussian noise is calibrated to it.
The two sensitivities are never far apart, and how far depends on how one record’s change spreads over the coordinates. The next result says exactly how far, and Section 20.5 turns it into the rule for choosing between the two mechanisms.
The sensitivities of the standard queries follow by asking what the single worst record can do. Table 20.1 collects them; records take values in a domain \(\mathcal X\), and \(B\) bounds a numerical record.
Sensitivity is a worst case over datasets. It does not depend on the data you hold, only on what the domain allows, which is why it can be computed before looking at the data. It is also why the sum of arbitrary real numbers has infinite sensitivity, since one record can be as large as it likes; clipping, in Beyond global sensitivity, forces a finite \(B\). The neighbouring relation changes the answer by up to a factor of 2, because replacing is removing one record and adding another, so a guarantee stated without its neighbouring relation is ambiguous by that factor in \(\varepsilon\).

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
Definition 20.1 (Sensitivity) Let \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) be a query with values in \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(p \in \{1, 2\}\), the \(\ell_p\) sensitivity of \(f\) is the largest distance between its answers on two neighbouring datasets, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \sim D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p. \tag{20.2}\]



Proposition 20.1 (The two sensitivities) For every query \(f\) with values in \(\mathbb R^d\), \[\Delta_2f \le \Delta_1f \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2f. \tag{20.3}\] The left bound is reached when one record moves a single coordinate, the right one when it moves all \(d\) coordinates equally.


Proof. 

Fix a vector \(v \in \mathbb R^d\). Squaring the sum \(\sum_i|v_i|\) gives every \(v_i^2\) plus cross terms that are never negative, so \(\|v\|_2^2 \le \|v\|_1^2\), that is \(\|v\|_2 \le \|v\|_1\).
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the sum \(\sum_i 1\cdot|v_i|\) gives \(\|v\|_1 \le \sqrt d\,\|v\|_2\).
Both inequalities hold for the change \(v = f(D) - f(D')\) of every neighbouring pair, so they hold for the maximum over pairs. If only one coordinate of \(v\) is non-zero, both norms equal its absolute value; if all \(d\) coordinates equal \(c\), then \(\|v\|_1 = dc\) and \(\|v\|_2 = \sqrt d\,c\).

Proposition 20.2 (Sensitivities of the standard queries) The sensitivities in Table 20.1 hold, and each is reached by some neighbouring pair.


Proof. 

Count. Adding or removing a record changes \(|D|\) by exactly 1. Replacing a record leaves it unchanged, which is why under replace the size is not private and a count of all records needs no noise.
Sum. Adding a record \(x \in [0, B]\) changes the sum by \(x \le B\), and replacing \(x\) by \(x'\) changes it by \(|x - x'| \le B\). Both bounds are reached with \(x = B\) and \(x' = 0\).
Mean with public \(n\). Under replace the mean is the sum divided by the fixed \(n\), so its sensitivity is the sum’s divided by \(n\), which is \(B/n\). Under add/remove the denominator moves too, so there is no such simple bound; the remedy is to release a noisy sum and a noisy count instead.
Histogram. Under add/remove the record lands in one bin, so that bin changes by 1 and the others not at all. The change vector is \(\pm e_j\), where \(e_j\) has a 1 in bin \(j\) and 0 elsewhere, and both of its norms are 1. Under replace one bin loses 1 and another gains 1, so the change is \(e_{j'} - e_j\), with \(\ell_1\) norm \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(\ell_2\) norm \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2\).
Threshold counts. The count for threshold \(j\) is the number of records with \(x \ge j\), so a record \(x\) adds 1 to every count with \(j \le x\). A record with \(x \ge d\) moves all \(d\) counts by 1, so the change vector is \((1, \dots, 1)\), with \(\ell_1\) norm \(d\) and \(\ell_2\) norm \(\sqrt d\). Under replace, changing \(x\) to \(x'\) moves only the counts with \(j\) between the two values, at most \(d\) of them, by 1 each, so the same bounds hold.




Example 20.1 The hospital also releases the mean age of its \(n = 10{,}000\) patients, with ages clipped to \([0, 100]\), under replace neighbours. By row 3 of Table 20.1 the sensitivity is \(B/n = 100/10{,}000 = 0.01\) year, so one patient can move the mean by at most a hundredth of a year, however old they are. For the diabetes count under add/remove, row 1 gives a sensitivity of 1.

text:
20.2 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism is the first mechanism to try (Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith 2006). It adds independent Laplace noise to each coordinate, with scale proportional to the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. Section A.3 in the appendices derives the same result from scratch for a single count, with every number shown.
Everything rests on the privacy loss of the definition of differential privacy. For an output \(y\), it is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is when the data are \(D\) than when they are \(D'\), \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}, \tag{20.4}\] where \(p_{M(D)}\) is the density of the published output on dataset \(D\). Write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the two output distributions \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\). In its section on pure DP being pointwise, that chapter proved that a mechanism whose loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) at every output, for every ordered neighbouring pair, is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The Laplace mechanism is proved private exactly this way.
For additive noise the loss has a simple shape. On neighbouring datasets the mechanism outputs \(f(D) + Z\) and \(f(D') + Z\), the same noise placed around two different centres, so the density of \(Q\) is the density of \(P\) slid over by the shift \(f(D') - f(D)\). How far apart two distributions are, at a factor \(\gamma \ge 1\), is measured by the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences, \(E_\gamma(P\|Q)\), the largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - \gamma\Pr_Q[S]\) over events \(S\). At \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) it is the smallest \(\delta\) that works for the pair. The first result says that under this measure the true answer drops out, and only the shift matters. That tells you what the Laplace scale must cover, and Section 20.4 uses the same lemma to compute the Gaussian mechanism’s exact \(\delta\).

Lemma 20.1 (Additive noise reduces to one shifted pair) Let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\), where \(Z\) has a density on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(v = f(D') - f(D)\) be the shift between the two answers on a neighbouring pair. Then for every \(\gamma \ge 1\), \[E_\gamma\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big) = E_\gamma\big(Z\|Z + v\big). \tag{20.5}\]


Proof. 

The map \(y \mapsto y - f(D)\) sends \(M(D)\) to \(Z\) and \(M(D')\) to \(Z + v\), and it is a bijection: every output corresponds to exactly one relabelled output, and back.
So an event \(S\) about \(M\)’s output is the same as the event \(S - f(D)\) about the relabelled output, with the same probability under each dataset. The hockey-stick divergence is a maximum of \(\Pr_P[S] - \gamma\Pr_Q[S]\) over events, and both sides range over the same values, so they are equal.


For the hospital’s count, the true value 1234 drops out and only the shift \(v = 1\) remains. Privacy is a property of the noise and of the set of shifts that neighbouring datasets can produce, which Section 20.1 bounded. The Laplace mechanism chooses its scale so that the largest shift one record can cause, divided by the scale, is exactly \(\varepsilon\).

Theorem 20.1 (The Laplace mechanism) The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b > 0\) has density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), a two-sided exponential peaked at 0. Let \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) have \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1f\) and let \(\varepsilon > 0\). The Laplace mechanism \[M(D) = f(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_d), \qquad Z_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Lap}(b), \quad b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \tag{20.6}\] is \(\varepsilon\)-DP (i.i.d. means independent and identically distributed). Its error per coordinate is about \(b\), and for every failure probability \(\beta \in (0, 1)\) the largest error over the \(d\) coordinates obeys \[\mathbb E[|Z_i|] = b, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z_i) = 2b^2, \qquad \Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{20.7}\] The scale is the smallest that works in general: for a count, \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise with \(b < 1/\varepsilon\) is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to write the privacy loss down and bound it at every output by the triangle inequality, then to read the error off the Laplace distribution, and finally to exhibit an event on which the privacy bound is reached.

Write the two densities. Fix \(D \sim D'\) and write \(a = f(D)\) and \(a' = f(D')\) for the two true answers. The coordinates of the noise are independent, so the density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is the product \(\prod_i\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|y_i - a_i|/b}\), and that of \(M(D')\) is the same with \(a'\) in place of \(a\).
Take the log-ratio. The constants \(\frac1{2b}\) cancel, and the log of a product of exponentials is the sum of the exponents, so \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \frac1b\sum_{i=1}^d\big(|y_i - a'_i| - |y_i - a_i|\big). \tag{20.8}\]
Bound each term. The distance from \(y_i\) to \(a'_i\) is at most the distance from \(y_i\) to \(a_i\) plus the distance from \(a_i\) to \(a'_i\), by the triangle inequality \(|y_i - a'_i| \le |y_i - a_i| + |a_i - a'_i|\). So each term of the sum is at most \(|a_i - a'_i|\), whatever \(y\) is.
Add the terms. Summing over \(i\) gives the \(\ell_1\) norm of the shift, which is at most the sensitivity, so for every \(y\) \[L_{D,D'}(y) \le \frac{\|a - a'\|_1}{b} \le \frac{\Delta_1f}{b} = \varepsilon. \tag{20.9}\] The same bound for the swapped pair gives \(L_{D,D'}(y) \ge -\varepsilon\), so \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) at every output, and the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by the pointwise criterion recalled above.
Accuracy. The absolute value \(|Z_i|\) has density \(\frac1be^{-z/b}\) on \(z \ge 0\), an exponential distribution with mean \(b\) and second moment \(2b^2\); since \(Z_i\) has mean 0, that gives \(\mathbb E[|Z_i|] = b\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_i) = 2b^2\). Integrating the same density from \(t\) to infinity gives the tail \(\Pr[|Z_i| > t] = e^{-t/b}\).
All coordinates at once. Give each coordinate a share \(\beta/d\) of the failure probability: setting \(e^{-t/b} = \beta/d\) gives \(t = b\ln(d/\beta)\). The probability that at least one of the \(d\) coordinates fails is at most the sum of their failure probabilities, by the union bound, which is \(d\cdot\beta/d = \beta\).
Tightness. The outputs where the loss is largest are those left of both answers, so take a count with \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\) and the event \(S = \{y \le 0\}\). Under \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = \Pr[Z \le 0] = \frac12\) by the symmetry of the noise about 0, and \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = \Pr[Z \le -1] = \frac12e^{-1/b}\) from the tail of step 5. So the ratio of the two probabilities is exactly \(e^{1/b}\), and on \(S\) the bound of step 4 holds with equality at every point. If \(b < 1/\varepsilon\), the ratio exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) and the definition fails on this event.


The noise does not depend on \(n\). A count gets noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) whether the database has a hundred records or a hundred million, because one record moves a count by 1 either way. The relative error of a count of size \(n\) is therefore about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\), so large populations are cheap to protect and small subgroups are expensive. The worst case is not rare, either: the privacy loss equals \(\varepsilon\) on the event \(S\) of step 7, which has probability \(\frac12\) (Figure 20.1, left), so the guarantee is tight in the strongest sense and not just at some unlikely output.






Figure 20.1: Left column: a count released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) noise on neighbouring datasets with true counts 0 and 1, and the privacy loss \(L(y)\). It equals \(+\varepsilon\) for every \(y \le 0\) and \(-\varepsilon\) for every \(y \ge 1\), never more. Right column: the same count with \(\mathcal N(0, 2^2)\) noise. The privacy loss is a straight line, and exceeds \(\varepsilon = 1\) on the shaded tail, which has probability 0.0401 under \(M(D)\). The exact \(\delta(1) = 0.0068\) is smaller, because the hockey-stick subtracts \(e^\varepsilon\) times the mass of \(M(D')\) on the same tail.



Two more facts about the Laplace mechanism matter later. Drawn as a random number, the privacy loss of an output from \(M(D)\) never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\). It has an atom of probability \(\frac12\) at \(+\varepsilon\), an atom of probability \(\frac12e^{-\varepsilon}\) at \(-\varepsilon\), and a continuous ramp between them (Figure 20.2, left), and Part 4’s accountants track exactly this distribution. The mechanism also satisfies a whole curve of weaker guarantees. For every \(\varepsilon' < \varepsilon\) it is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\), the hockey-stick divergence of two shifted Laplace distributions from Divergences, drawn as the dashed curve of Figure 20.3.
As for the shape of the noise, the proof used only that the log-density changes by at most \(\varepsilon/\Delta_1f\) per unit of shift, and the Laplace log-density \(-|z|/b\) has exactly that slope everywhere. Other shapes are slightly better for large \(\varepsilon\) (Geng & Viswanath’s staircase mechanism), but the Laplace is within a small factor and is the standard choice.






Figure 20.2: The privacy loss distribution under \(M(D)\) for a count, with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\). The loss never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\); it has an atom of probability 0.5000 at \(+\varepsilon\), an atom of 0.1839 at \(-\varepsilon\), and a continuous ramp of total probability 0.3161 in between (density shown). Right: Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. The loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\), here \(\mu = 0.5\), and exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability 0.0401 (shaded).




Example 20.2 Release the diabetes count, 1,234 of \(n = 10{,}000\) patients, with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) under add/remove. The sensitivity is 1, so the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\) and the expected absolute error is \(b = 10\) (simulated over a million releases: 9.978). For a 95% guarantee take \(d = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) in the accuracy bound. With probability 0.95 the error is then below \(b\ln20 = 29.96\) (simulated 95th percentile: 29.85), a relative error of \(29.96/1234 = 0.0243\).
To see the privacy loss itself, take a count with \(b = 1\), so \(\varepsilon = 1\), and true answers 0 and 1. Table 20.2 evaluates the two densities and the loss at a few outputs. Left of both true answers the ratio of the densities is stuck at \(e\), right of them at \(e^{-1}\), and in between the loss falls linearly from 1 to \(-1\). Once \(y\) is past both centres, moving it further away multiplies both densities by the same factor, so however far out an output lands, it never favours one dataset by more than a factor of \(e\). A million simulated draws reproduce the tight event’s probabilities to three decimals (Table 20.7).

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.3 The Gaussian mechanism: classic calibration
Gaussian noise is the other natural choice. It has lighter tails than Laplace noise, a sum of independent Gaussians is again Gaussian, and it is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. The price is that its privacy loss is a straight line in the output and so is unbounded (Figure 20.1, right), so the pointwise criterion never applies and Gaussian noise cannot give pure DP. Instead you accept a small probability \(\delta\) that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\). This section derives the calibration found in the textbook of Dwork & Roth and in many papers and libraries, and shows where it is loose; Section A.6 in the appendices derives the same formula from scratch, with worked numbers.
The smallest \(\delta\) that works for one pair is its hockey-stick divergence at \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\), and the largest of these over all pairs, as a function of \(\varepsilon\), is the privacy profile \(\delta_M(\varepsilon)\) of \(M\). The first tool says which event is the worst one: the set of outputs where the loss is too large.

Lemma 20.2 (The bad event and the exact δ) Fix a neighbouring pair, write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distributions of \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\), with densities \(p\) and \(q\), and let \(L\) be the privacy loss. Call \(B = \{y : L(y) > \varepsilon\}\) the bad event, the outputs that favour \(D\) over \(D'\) by more than a factor \(e^\varepsilon\). Then \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B] \le \Pr_P[B] = \Pr_{y \sim P}[L(y) > \varepsilon]. \tag{20.10}\] Equivalently, writing \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) for the positive part, \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_Q[(e^L - e^\varepsilon)_+] = \mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]. \tag{20.11}\]


Proof. 

The quantity \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\) is the integral over \(S\) of \(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\). To make the integral as large as possible, include every output where the integrand is positive and no other. The integrand is positive exactly where \(p > e^\varepsilon q\), that is where \(L > \varepsilon\), which is \(B\). This is the argument of Divergences for the worst event of a hockey-stick divergence, and it gives the equality.
The inequality drops the term \(e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\), which is never negative.
For the expectation forms, the hockey-stick is the integral of \((p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\). Factoring out \(q\) gives \(q\,(e^L - e^\varepsilon)_+\), and factoring out \(p\) gives \(p\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\); integrating each against its density is the stated expectation.


So the bad event’s probability is always a valid \(\delta\), though usually a loose one, and the last form needs only the distribution of the loss under \(P\), the starting point of Numerical accounting. For Gaussian noise that distribution is itself normal.

Lemma 20.3 (The privacy loss of Gaussian noise) Let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\), that is \(d\) independent normal coordinates with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\), and let \(v = f(D') - f(D)\) be the shift of a neighbouring pair. Write \(\mu = \|v\|_2/\sigma\) for the shift measured in standard deviations of the noise. Under \(M(D)\) the privacy loss is normal, \[L \sim \mathcal N\Big(\frac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2\Big), \tag{20.12}\] and under \(M(D')\) it is \(\mathcal N(-\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\).


Proof. 

Under \(M(D)\), write the output as \(y = f(D) + z\), where \(z\) is the noise. The density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is proportional to \(e^{-\|z\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and that of \(M(D')\) to \(e^{-\|z - v\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), since \(y\) sits at distance \(z - v\) from \(f(D')\). The log of their ratio is the difference of the exponents, and expanding \(\|z - v\|^2 = \|z\|^2 - 2\langle z, v\rangle + \|v\|^2\) gives \[L(y) = \frac{\|v\|^2 - 2\langle z, v\rangle}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{20.13}\]
The loss depends on \(z\) only through the inner product \(\langle z, v\rangle = \sum_iz_iv_i\), the component of the noise along the shift. That is a sum of independent normals, so it is normal, with mean 0 and variance \(\sum_i\sigma^2v_i^2 = \sigma^2\|v\|^2\).
A constant minus a multiple of a normal is normal, so \(L\) is normal with mean \(\|v\|^2/(2\sigma^2) = \mu^2/2\) and variance \(4\sigma^2\|v\|^2/(4\sigma^4) = \mu^2\). The other \(d - 1\) directions of \(z\), perpendicular to \(v\), do not enter.
Under \(M(D')\) the noise is centred one shift further along \(v\), which lowers \(\langle z, v\rangle\) by \(\|v\|^2\) on average and so lowers the loss by \(\mu^2\); the variance is unchanged.


Unlike the Laplace loss, the Gaussian loss has no atoms and no largest value (Figure 20.2, right). The classic calibration bounds \(\delta\) by the probability that it exceeds \(\varepsilon\) and chooses \(\sigma\) to make that tail small.

Theorem 20.2 (Classic Gaussian calibration) Let \(f\) have \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2f\), and let \(\varepsilon \in (0, 1)\) and \(\delta \in (0, 1)\). The Gaussian mechanism \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\) and \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon} \tag{20.14}\] is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP (Dwork & Roth 2014, Theorem A.1).


Proof. The plan is to bound \(\delta\) by the bad-event probability of Lemma 20.2, which by Lemma 20.3 is a normal tail, and to show with a standard tail bound that this tail is below \(\delta\) for the \(\sigma\) above. The route is Dwork & Roth’s, in a one-sided form that is a little shorter. Write \(c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\), so \(\sigma = c\,\Delta_2f/\varepsilon\).

Bound \(\delta\) by the bad event. By Lemma 20.2, \(\delta \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\). By Lemma 20.3 the loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\), so \(L > \varepsilon\) exactly when a standard normal exceeds \((\varepsilon - \mu^2/2)/\mu = \frac\varepsilon\mu - \frac\mu2\). Writing \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), and using its symmetry \(\Phi(-t) = 1 - \Phi(t)\), \[\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(-t), \qquad t = \frac\varepsilon\mu - \frac\mu2. \tag{20.15}\]
Take the worst shift. A larger shift makes the bad event more likely, because \(t\) decreases as \(\mu\) grows. So the worst neighbouring pair has the largest shift, \(\|v\|_2 = \Delta_2f\), that is \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma = \varepsilon/c\), and then \(t = c - \frac{\varepsilon}{2c}\).
Bound the normal tail. The Mills-ratio bound of Concentration inequalities says \(\Phi(-t) \le \varphi(t)/t\) for \(t > 0\), where \(\varphi(t) = e^{-t^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) is the standard normal density. The reason is that beyond \(t\) every point \(z\) has \(z/t \ge 1\), so \(\int_t^\infty\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz \le \int_t^\infty\frac zt\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz\), and since the derivative of \(\varphi\) is \(-z\varphi(z)\) the right side integrates to \(\varphi(t)/t\).
Expand \(t^2\). Squaring \(t = c - \varepsilon/(2c)\) gives \(t^2 = c^2 - \varepsilon + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4c^2} \ge c^2 - \varepsilon\), dropping the last term because it is positive. By the definition of \(c\), \(e^{-c^2/2} = \delta/1.25\), so \[e^{-t^2/2} \le \frac{\delta}{1.25}\,e^{\varepsilon/2}. \tag{20.16}\]
Combine. Steps 3 and 4 give \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\,e^{\varepsilon/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi}\,t)\), which is at most \(\delta\) when \(t \ge e^{\varepsilon/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi})\). For \(\varepsilon \le 1\) the right side is at most \(e^{1/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi}) = 0.5262\).
Check that \(t\) is large enough. For \(\varepsilon \le 1\), \(t = c - \varepsilon/(2c) \ge c - 1/(2c)\), and this lower bound grows with \(c\). It equals 0.5262 at the positive root of \(c^2 - 0.5262c - \frac12 = 0\), which is where \(\delta = 1.25e^{-c^2/2} = 0.7448\); since \(c\) grows as \(\delta\) shrinks, \(t \ge 0.5262\) for every \(\delta \le 0.7448\), and every \(\delta\) of practical interest qualifies.


The constant 1.25 absorbs \(e^{\varepsilon/2} \le e^{1/2}\) and the \(1/(t\sqrt{2\pi})\) factor of step 5, and the condition \(\varepsilon < 1\) keeps \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) under control. The proof made three approximations in a row, the bad-event bound, the Mills ratio and the constants, and the example follows the chain to see what each one costs.

Example 20.3 Release the diabetes count with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The sensitivity is 1, so \(c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25\times10^5)}\) gives \(\sigma = 4.8448\) and \(t = c - 1/(2c) = 4.7416\). Table 20.3 follows the proof step by step.

The classic \(\sigma\) delivers a \(\delta\) about 240 times smaller than asked for, since \(10^{-5}/(4.11\times10^{-8}) \approx 243\). Most of the slack is in two places. The bad-event bound throws away the \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B]\) correction, a factor of \(1.06\times10^{-6}/(4.11\times10^{-8}) \approx 26\) here, and the constants of steps 4 and 5 lose another factor of \(10^{-5}/(1.10\times10^{-6}) \approx 9\). The Mills ratio itself costs almost nothing.

So you could use less noise for the same \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and Section 20.4 finds exactly how much less. The classic theorem is stated for \(\varepsilon < 1\), and its constants are designed for that range. The formula does not fail immediately above 1: at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the classic \(\sigma\) still gives a valid guarantee up to \(\varepsilon = 8.42\) and violates it beyond (Figure 20.4, right), because the classic \(\sigma\) shrinks like \(1/\varepsilon\) while the exact one shrinks more slowly. Nothing in the classic proof tells you that, so for \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) you need the exact curve.

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.4 The exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism
text:
20.4 The exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism
Lemma 20.2 says that the smallest valid \(\delta\) is the bad-event probability minus the correction \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B]\), and Lemma 20.3 says that for Gaussian noise both terms are normal tail probabilities. So the exact \(\delta\) has a closed form, the one Divergences computed for two Gaussians with the same variance. Balle & Wang (2018) turned that observation into a calibration: instead of bounding \(\delta\), compute it exactly, and pick the smallest \(\sigma\) for which it is below the target. Section A.7 in the appendices derives the formula from scratch, with worked numbers.

Theorem 20.3 (Exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism) Let \(f\) have \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2f\), reached by some neighbouring pair, and let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\). Write \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\). Then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if and only if \(\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\), where \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{20.17}\] The function \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\) and strictly increasing in \(\mu\). At \(\varepsilon = 0\) it is the total variation (TV) distance \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) between the two output distributions, and it tends to 0 as \(\varepsilon \to \infty\).


Proof. The plan is to reduce the worst pair to one dimension, apply the two lemmas there, and show that the largest shift is the worst one; the monotonicity claims then follow from the formula.

Reduce to a shifted pair. By Lemma 20.1, for a neighbouring pair with shift \(v\) the smallest \(\delta\) at this \(\varepsilon\) is \(E_{e^\varepsilon}\big(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\|\mathcal N(v, \sigma^2I_d)\big)\).
Reduce to one dimension. Rotate coordinates so that \(v\) points along the first axis. A rotation is a bijection, so as in Lemma 20.1 it changes no divergence, and the normal distribution with independent equal-variance coordinates looks the same after any rotation (Section E.1 in the appendices proves it). Now both distributions are products: the first coordinate is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) or \(\mathcal N(\|v\|_2, \sigma^2)\), and the other \(d - 1\) coordinates have the same density \(h\) under both. The hockey-stick is the integral of \((p - \gamma q)_+\), and \((p_1h - \gamma q_1h)_+ = h\,(p_1 - \gamma q_1)_+\) because \(h \ge 0\), so integrating out the last \(d - 1\) coordinates leaves \(E_\gamma\) of the first coordinate alone. Coordinates that are identical under both hypotheses carry no evidence.
Use the two lemmas. By Lemma 20.2, \(E_{e^\varepsilon} = \Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\) with \(B = \{L > \varepsilon\}\). By Lemma 20.3 with \(\mu_v = \|v\|_2/\sigma\), the loss is \(\mathcal N(\mu_v^2/2, \mu_v^2)\) under \(P\) and \(\mathcal N(-\mu_v^2/2, \mu_v^2)\) under \(Q\), so standardizing each tail gives \[\Pr_P[B] = \Phi\Big(\frac{\mu_v}2 - \frac\varepsilon{\mu_v}\Big), \qquad \Pr_Q[B] = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\mu_v}2 - \frac\varepsilon{\mu_v}\Big). \tag{20.18}\] This is Equation 20.17 with \(\mu_v\) in place of \(\mu\).
The worst pair has the largest shift. A smaller shift is harder to detect, and the proof shows that the pair with a smaller shift is a post-processing of the pair with a larger one, which cannot help anyone tell them apart. Let \(\mu' < \mu_v\), take \(Y\) from the unit-variance pair with shift \(\mu_v\), and output \(Y' = \frac{\mu'}{\mu_v}Y + W\) with independent \(W \sim \mathcal N(0, 1 - \mu'^2/\mu_v^2)\). If \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) then \(Y'\) has mean 0 and variance \(\mu'^2/\mu_v^2 + (1 - \mu'^2/\mu_v^2) = 1\); if \(Y \sim \mathcal N(\mu_v, 1)\) the mean becomes \(\mu'\) and the variance is still 1. By the data-processing inequality of Divergences, the hockey-stick of the post-processed pair is no larger, so \(\delta_{\mu_v}(\varepsilon)\) is non-decreasing in \(\mu_v\) and the maximum over neighbours is at \(\|v\|_2 = \Delta_2f\), that is at \(\mu\).
If and only if. The hockey-stick at \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) is the smallest \(\delta\) that works for one pair, and steps 1 to 4 show that the pair at shift \(\Delta_2f\) is the worst. So \(\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is sufficient, since it covers the worst pair and hence all, and necessary, since any smaller \(\delta\) fails on that pair.
Monotone in \(\varepsilon\) and in \(\mu\). Differentiating Equation 20.17 gives \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\varepsilon}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = -e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) < 0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\mu}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) > 0\).
The two ends. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is 1 and Equation 20.17 reads \(\Phi(\frac\mu2) - \Phi(-\frac\mu2) = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), which is the TV distance because the TV distance is the hockey-stick with \(\gamma = 1\). As \(\varepsilon \to \infty\) the first term \(\Phi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\) goes to 0 and the second is non-negative, so \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) \to 0\).


Because \(\delta_\mu\) grows with \(\mu\), less noise always means a larger \(\delta\), and there is a single noise level that hits the target exactly.

Corollary 20.1 (Analytic calibration) For \(0 < \delta < 1\) the equation \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \delta\) has exactly one root \(\mu^*\) in \(\mu\), and \[\sigma^*(\varepsilon, \delta) = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*} \tag{20.19}\] is the smallest \(\sigma\) for which the Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

As a function of \(\mu\), \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is continuous, tends to 0 as \(\mu \to 0\) (both arguments of \(\Phi\) go to \(-\infty\), since there is no signal) and to 1 as \(\mu \to \infty\) (the first \(\Phi\) goes to 1 and the second to 0), and is strictly increasing by Theorem 20.3. So it crosses every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) exactly once.
By Theorem 20.3, a noise level \(\sigma\) works exactly when \(\delta_{\Delta_2f/\sigma}(\varepsilon) \le \delta\), that is when \(\Delta_2f/\sigma \le \mu^*\), so the smallest such \(\sigma\) is \(\Delta_2f/\mu^*\).


The root is found by bisection: start with an interval of \(\mu\) whose ends put \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) on either side of \(\delta\), evaluate at the midpoint, and keep the half where the sign changes. Monotonicity is what makes this safe, since there is exactly one crossing to find. The script halves in \(\ln\mu\), because \(\mu^*\) ranges over several orders of magnitude, and 60 halvings pin it to machine precision.

Example 20.4 Release the diabetes count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with Gaussian noise. The sensitivity is 1, so the analytic calibration gives \(\sigma^* = 30.75\), the row \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) of Table 20.5. A normal variable stays within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean with probability 0.95, so the 95% error is \(1.96\sigma^* = 60.27\), against 29.96 for Laplace noise with \(\delta = 0\): for a single count, Laplace noise is better on both error and guarantee, and Section 20.5 says when the Gaussian earns its place.
To see the two terms of Equation 20.10 at work, take \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) and measure the noise \(z\) in units of \(\sigma\). With \(\mu = 1\) the loss is \(L = \frac12 - z\), so the bad event \(B = \{L > 1\}\) is \(\{z < -\frac12\}\). Under \(M(D)\) the noise is standard normal, so \(\Pr_P[B] = \Phi(-0.5)\); under \(M(D')\) the output is centred one unit higher, so in the same coordinates \(z\) is \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) and \(\Pr_Q[B] = \Phi(-1.5)\). Table 20.4 evaluates both, and the integration and Monte Carlo checks of Table 20.7 agree with the result.
