Dashed: the weak triangle inequality with \(u = v = 2\). Dotted: Proposition 2’s bound \(3\varepsilon(2\beta)\), drawn from \(\beta = 2\), where its condition \(\alpha = 2\beta \ge 4\) starts to hold.




Example 29.4 Post-processing first. Pass the output of randomized response with \(t = 0.75\) through a channel that flips it with probability 0.2. When the bit is 1, the final output is 1 if the first output was 1 and kept, or 0 and flipped, which has probability \(0.75 \times 0.8 + 0.25 \times 0.2 = 0.65\). When the bit is 0, the same event has probability \(0.25 \times 0.8 + 0.75 \times 0.2 = 0.35\). So the two output distributions are now closer, and \(D_2\) drops from 0.8473 to \(\ln\big(0.65^2/0.35 + 0.35^2/0.65\big) = 0.3333\), and \(D_\infty\) drops from 1.0986 to \(\ln(0.65/0.35) = 0.6190\).
For group privacy, check the first row of Table 29.6 by hand, two records at \(\beta = 2\) with \(\sigma = 1\). The exact value is \(2 \cdot 2^2/2 = 4\). The weak triangle inequality gives \(\frac{1.5}{1}\varepsilon(4) + \varepsilon(3) = 1.5 \times 2 + 1.5 = 4.5\), and the theorem gives \(3\varepsilon(4) = 3 \times 2 = 6\), which is \(6/4 = 1.5\) times the exact value. Figure 29.3 draws the whole two-record case. The weak-triangle bound hugs the exact line \(2\beta\) for \(\beta \ge 3\) and blows up near \(\beta = 1\), where its factor \(\frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1}\) does. For the Laplace mechanism with \(b = 1\) at order 2, two records apart, the exact value is 1.5958, the weak triangle inequality gives 1.9674 and the theorem 2.4411, while the pure DP group bound \(2/b = 2\) beats the theorem.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.5 The moments accountant
Abadi et al. (2016) introduced the moments accountant to train neural networks with DP, before RDP existed, and many libraries still describe their accounting in its terms. For each \(\lambda > 0\), in practice the integers up to 32, it tracks the logarithm of the moment generating function of the privacy loss, adds these numbers over the training steps, and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with a tail bound. This section shows that it tracks the same object as the RDP curve, so everything in this chapter applies to it.

Definition 29.2 (Log-moment of a mechanism) For \(\lambda > 0\), the log-moment of a mechanism \(M\) is the cumulant generating function of the privacy loss of the worst pair of neighbours, \[K_M(\lambda) = \sup_{D \sim D'}\ln\mathbb E_{Y \sim M(D)}\big[e^{\lambda L(Y)}\big]. \tag{29.21}\] Abadi et al. write it \(\alpha_M(\lambda)\), which clashes with the Rényi order.

The moment inside the logarithm is the one in Equation 29.1 with \(\alpha - 1 = \lambda\). So the log-moment is the RDP curve one order up, multiplied by \(\lambda\).

Proposition 29.2 (The moments accountant is RDP) For every mechanism \(M\) and every \(\lambda > 0\), \[K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \frac{K_M(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.22}\]


Proof. 

The moment is a Rényi moment. Fix neighbours. By Equation 29.1 at the order \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\), \(\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}] = e^{\lambda D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\), and its logarithm is \(\lambda D_\alpha(P\|Q)\).
Take the supremum. The factor \(\lambda > 0\) does not change which pair of neighbours is worst, so the supremum of the left side is \(K_M(\lambda)\) and that of the right side is \(\lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1)\).


So the two parts of Abadi et al.’s Theorem 2 are results of this chapter. Composability, \(K_M(\lambda) \le \sum_i K_{M_i}(\lambda)\), is Equation 29.11 at order \(\lambda + 1\) multiplied by \(\lambda\). The tail bound says that \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta = \min_\lambda\exp\big(K_M(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon\big)\). It is the conversion proved in the next section, Section 29.6, read in the other direction, fixing \(\varepsilon\) and solving for \(\delta\). So the two accountants give the same numbers with different bookkeeping.
The identity itself is simple, so what was new in 2016 was a bound on \(K_M(\lambda)\) for the subsampled Gaussian step of private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, in which each step uses a random fraction of the data. Amplification by subsampling derives it in RDP form.

Example 29.5 For randomized response with \(t = 0.75\) at \(\lambda = 1\), the moment \(\mathbb E_P[e^L] = 0.75 \times 3 + 0.25 \times \frac13\) has the same two terms, 2.2500 and 0.0833, as the last column of Table 29.2, so its logarithm is \(1 \cdot \varepsilon(2) = 0.8473\). At \(\lambda = 2\), the direct sum and \(2\varepsilon(3)\) both give 1.9136.
For the Gaussian pair \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), the privacy loss under \(P\) is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\) (Lemma 20.3). A normal variable with mean \(m\) and variance \(s^2\) has the cumulant generating function \(m\lambda + s^2\lambda^2/2\), so \[K(\lambda) = \lambda\frac{\mu^2}{2} + \frac{\lambda^2\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\cdot\frac{(\lambda + 1)\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1), \tag{29.23}\] with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), as Equation 29.22 says. At \(\mu = 1\) the formula gives \(K(1) = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1.0000\) and \(K(2) = 1 + 2 = 3.0000\). Averaging \(e^{\lambda L}\) over a million draws gives 1.0000 and 3.0003.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.6 From RDP to (ε, δ)
After composing, you hold a curve, but what you report is an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair, because that guarantee has a direct meaning for every event. The conversion rests on one observation. Outputs whose privacy loss is at most some threshold \(c\) already satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, so only outputs with a larger loss can break it, and their total probability can be charged to \(\delta\). That probability is a tail of the privacy loss. The Chernoff bound controls a tail with an exponential moment, which is exactly what each point of the RDP curve provides.
The tool is the Chernoff bound of Theorem 2.3 in Concentration inequalities. For any random variable \(X\), any level \(c\) and any \(\lambda > 0\), it says that \(\Pr[X \ge c]\) is at most \(e^{-\lambda c}\,\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\). The converted \(\varepsilon\) is then the RDP value plus a tail term, which pays for \(\delta\) and shrinks as the order grows. This is Mironov (2017), Proposition 3, and Section D.3 in the appendices derives it from scratch.

Theorem 29.5 (From RDP to (ε, δ)-DP) Let \(M\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for some order \(\alpha > 1\). Then for every \(0 < \delta < 1\), \(M\) is \((\varepsilon_\delta, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_\delta = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.24}\] If you hold the whole curve, the best order gives \(\varepsilon_\delta = \min_\alpha\big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\big]\).


Proof. The plan is to split every event into outputs with small loss, which satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, and outputs with large loss, whose probability is a tail, and then to bound the tail with Chernoff. Fix neighbours with privacy loss \(L\), and a threshold \(c\) to be chosen.

Split the event. For any event \(S\), \(\Pr_P[S] = \Pr_P[S \cap \{L \le c\}] + \Pr_P[S \cap \{L > c\}]\).
Small losses. On \(\{L \le c\}\) the definition of \(L\) gives \(p \le e^c q\). Integrating over \(S \cap \{L \le c\}\), the first term is at most \(e^c\Pr_Q[S]\).
Large losses. The set \(S \cap \{L > c\}\) lies inside \(\{L > c\}\), so the second term is at most \(\Pr_P[L > c]\).
Chernoff on the loss. Apply Theorem 2.3 to \(L\) under \(P\) with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\): \[\Pr_P[L > c] \le e^{-(\alpha-1)c}\,\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]. \tag{29.25}\] By Equation 29.1 the average is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\), at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\), so \[\Pr_P[L > c] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c)}. \tag{29.26}\]
Choose the threshold. Setting \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c) = \ln\delta\) gives \(c = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). Then \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^c\Pr_Q[S] + \delta\) for every event and every pair of neighbours, which is \((c, \delta)\)-DP.


For the Gaussian curve the best order has a closed form, because the curve grows with \(\alpha\) while the tail term falls, and the minimum is where they balance.

Corollary 29.1 (The best order for a Gaussian curve) For the Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) and \(0 < \delta < 1\), the right side of Equation 29.24, over all real orders \(\alpha > 1\), is smallest at \[\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}, \qquad \varepsilon_\delta = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}. \tag{29.27}\]


Proof. 

Substitute. Write \(a = \alpha - 1 > 0\) and \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). The Gaussian curve is \((a + 1)/(2\sigma^2)\), so Equation 29.24 becomes \(\varepsilon_\delta(a) = \frac{a + 1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\ell}{a}\).
Set the derivative to zero. The derivative \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\ell}{a^2}\) vanishes at \(a = \sigma\sqrt{2\ell}\). The function is a line plus \(\ell/a\), whose second derivative \(2\ell/a^3\) is positive, so this is the minimum.
Evaluate. At that \(a\), both \(\frac{a}{2\sigma^2}\) and \(\frac{\ell}{a}\) equal \(\frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{2\sigma}\), so they add to \(\sqrt{2\ell}/\sigma\). With the constant \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\), this is Equation 29.27.


The conversion gives something away in two places. Step 3 of the conversion’s proof charges the whole tail \(\Pr_P[L > c]\) to \(\delta\). The exact smallest \(\delta\) at level \(c\) is the average \(\mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{c - L})_+\big]\) (Lemma 21.1), which charges an output with loss above \(c\) only the fraction \(1 - e^{c - L}\) of its probability. Step 4 then bounds the tail with a Chernoff bound, which overestimates it. From RDP to (ε, δ) and to tests removes much of both losses with sharper conversions.
The order trades two terms against each other. Small orders make the curve small but the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) large, and large orders do the opposite (Figure 29.4, left). A steeper composed curve makes large orders more expensive, so at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 20\) wants \(\alpha \approx 97\) while 1000 such steps want \(\alpha \approx 4\). Because the best order ranges this widely, this part optimizes over one fixed grid that spans the range: 99 orders from 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, the 52 integers from 12 to 63, and 128, 256 and 512, which is 154 orders:
ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + list(range(12, 64)) + [128, 256, 512]






Figure 29.4: Left: converting the curve of 1000 Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The converted \(\varepsilon\) (black) is the sum of the RDP curve (dashed) and the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) (dotted). Its minimum over the grid, 8.84 at \(\alpha = 4\), sits above the exact value 7.51 (green). Right: total \(\varepsilon\) against the number of steps \(k\) on log axes, for advanced composition, RDP with Mironov’s conversion, and the exact value.




Example 29.6 Take one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Here \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\) and \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = 4.7985\). The curve is \(\alpha/2\), and Equation 29.24 adds \(11.5129/(\alpha - 1)\). At \(\alpha = 2\) the sum is \(1.0000 + 11.5129 = 12.5129\), dominated by the tail term, and at \(\alpha = 20\) it is \(10.0000 + 0.6059 = 10.6059\), dominated by the curve. The grid’s best order is 5.8, next to the continuous optimum \(\alpha^* = 1 + 4.7985 = 5.7985\), and both give \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\). The exact \(\varepsilon\) comes from the privacy profile of Theorem 20.3 with \(\mu = 1/\sigma = 1\). Solving \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) by bisection gives 4.3772, so the conversion is 21% too large (\(5.2985/4.3772 = 1.21\)). Read the other way, the mechanism at \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) has \(\delta = 1.300 \times 10^{-7}\), which is 76.9 times smaller than the conversion promises.
Now the opening’s problem, \(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table 29.7 compares four ways to account for them. The exact value is available because \(k\) steps are one Gaussian with \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\). The two routes of Part 3 turn each step into one point \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) of its exact curve and compose the points. Basic composition (Theorem 19.3) spends \(\delta/k\) per step and reports \(k\varepsilon_0\). Advanced composition in its sharp form (Equation 21.17) spends a fraction \(s\) of \(\delta\) on the \(k\) per-step slacks and the rest on the tail of the summed loss. The script picks the best \(s\) on the grid Part 3 uses, and at every \(k\) it lands on \(s = 10^{-1/4} \approx 0.56\).

Advanced composition is 5 to 9 times the exact value, and it gets looser as \(k\) grows, because each step’s curve was collapsed to one point before composing. At \(k = 1\) it is even worse than basic composition, because it pays for the tail of a sum that has only one term. RDP is 18% to 57% above exact, and it gets tighter as \(k\) grows. Only at \(k = 1\) does the grid cost anything, 0.251 against 0.241 at the continuous optimum 97.0, because the grid jumps from 63 to 128. The remaining gap is the conversion’s slack, which depends on the composed \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\). At the continuous optimum, Mironov’s conversion is 1.07 times exact at \(\mu = 10\), 1.21 at \(\mu = 1\), 1.42 at \(\mu = 0.1\) and 1.76 at \(\mu = 0.01\), so the most private composed mechanisms, with small \(\mu\), pay the most.

DP-SGD is private only because each step touches a random 1% of the data, and Amplification by subsampling computes the curve of such a step.

Mironov, “Rényi Differential Privacy” (IEEE Computer Security Foundations Symposium, CSF 2017; arXiv:1702.07476). The source of this chapter: the definition (Definition 4), adaptive composition (Proposition 1), weak group privacy (Proposition 2), the conversion (Proposition 3), the curves of randomized response, Laplace and Gaussian (Table 2, Corollaries 2 and 3) and the weak triangle inequality (Proposition 11, Corollary 4). Short and readable.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.1 Where Mironov’s conversion loses
Privacy accountants track Rényi differential privacy (RDP), because it composes by adding curves (the previous chapter). Take two neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) that differ by adding or removing your record, with \(D'\) the one that holds it. A mechanism \(M\) then produces two output distributions, \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\). For each order \(\alpha > 1\) the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) measures how far apart they are, and the RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds it over all neighbouring pairs. But nobody reports the curve. A paper, a model card or a regulator asks for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP), or for a statement about attacks: how much better than guessing can a test tell whether your record was used? So every RDP analysis ends with a conversion, and the conversion decides the number you publish. This chapter asks how much the standard conversion loses and where, which \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) a curve supports at best and at which order, and what a curve says about tests.
One idea organizes the answers. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln(P(y)/Q(y))\), the logarithm of how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). The first section recalls two facts about it. The smallest \(\delta\) at a given \(\varepsilon\) is an average of a function of the loss, while the RDP curve records only a few other averages of it, the values of its moment generating function (MGF). So a conversion asks for the largest \(\delta\) consistent with those few averages. The classic answer, Mironov’s conversion, wastes much of what the curve says, and a sharper one recovers almost all of it. The last section shows that what remains, 5 to 10% of \(\varepsilon\) for the Gaussian mechanism, belongs to the curve itself and not to any formula.
The running example is the Gaussian mechanism on a query of sensitivity 1, with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) (the noise multiplier), run \(k\) times. After dividing by \(\sigma\), each output shifts by \(1/\sigma\) between the two datasets, so the \(k\) outputs differ by a vector of length \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\). Only the component along that vector carries evidence, so the composed mechanism is equivalent to the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) (Theorem 20.3), and its RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), the sum of \(k\) single-step curves \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) (Rényi DP). At \(\mu = 1\), a single release at \(\sigma = 1\), the exact answer at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is \(\varepsilon = 4.377\) (Theorem 20.3), while Mironov’s conversion gives 5.299 and the improved one 4.729. Every number uses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and the part’s grid of 154 orders: 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, every integer from 12 to 63, then 128, 256 and 512.
Rényi DP derived Mironov’s conversion, the one in the original moments accountant and in much older code. Before you can improve it, you need to know where it loses. This section rewrites its proof as two inequalities on the privacy loss, so that the cost of each can be measured on the Gaussian. Section D.3 in the appendices derives the same conversion from scratch, with the Gaussian’s best order in closed form.
Two results from earlier chapters turn a conversion into a statement about the loss. The first says what \(\delta\) is. For one pair of datasets, taken in the order \((D, D')\), the smallest \(\delta\) at level \(\varepsilon\) is the hockey-stick divergence, the largest value of \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over sets \(S\) of outputs. Writing \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) and factoring \(P\) out of \((P - e^\varepsilon Q)_+\) turns it into an average of a function of the loss (Lemma 21.1). The outputs that contribute are those with \(L > \varepsilon\), which gives the second form (Lemma 20.2): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{30.1}\] So an output contributes to \(\delta\) only if its loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then only the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. An output with loss \(\varepsilon + \ln 2\) contributes half its probability, and only an output with infinite loss contributes all of it. For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), a Riemann sum of the average and the closed form Equation 20.17 both give \(\delta = 1.2694\times10^{-1}\).
The second result says what an RDP curve knows. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is \(1/(\alpha - 1)\) times the logarithm of \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) (Equation 3.13), so a bound \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) on it is a bound on the MGF of the loss at the point \(\alpha - 1\): \[\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{30.2}\] Every conversion bounds the average in Equation 30.1 using only the averages in Equation 30.2. A DP guarantee is the largest of these \(\delta\) over all neighbouring pairs, taken in both orders. RDP also bounds the divergence in both orders, so every bound below, proved for one pair \((P, Q)\), holds just as well for \((Q, P)\) and for every other pair.
Mironov’s proof makes two moves. It replaces \(\delta\) by the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then it bounds that probability by the MGF.
The two steps lose in different places. Step 1 ignores how far past \(\varepsilon\) the loss goes, so an output with loss just above \(\varepsilon\) counts fully toward the tail but almost nothing toward \(\delta\). It is tight only when every output with \(L > \varepsilon\) has infinite loss, as for a mechanism that sometimes publishes the record outright. Step 2 replaces a tail by an MGF, and Markov’s inequality is tight only for a variable that puts all its mass on 0 and on the level itself. A smooth loss distribution is nothing like that.
For the Gaussian, the loss under \(P\) is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\) (Lemma 20.3). The tail \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\) reaches \(10^{-5}\) at 4.2649 standard deviations above the mean. Minimizing Mironov’s \(\varepsilon\) over the order, which Rényi DP did in closed form (Corollary 29.1 with \(\sigma = 1/\mu\)), gives \(\mu^2/2 + \mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\), which sits \(\sqrt{2\ln(10^5)} \approx 4.799\) standard deviations above the mean. So step 2 moves the level up by a fixed \(4.799 - 4.2649 \approx 0.534\) standard deviations, and in units of \(\varepsilon\) its cost grows like \(\mu\).

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
Proposition 30.1 (Mironov’s conversion, in two steps) Let \(M\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for some order \(\alpha > 1\), and fix a neighbouring pair with privacy loss \(L\). For every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) \;\overset{(1)}{\le}\; \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \;\overset{(2)}{\le}\; e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}. \tag{30.3}\] Hence, for every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\), the mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.4}\]


Proof. 

Drop the fraction. Inequality (1) rounds the fraction of Equation 30.1 up to 1. The positive part \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) is 0 when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and below 1 otherwise, so it is at most the indicator \(\mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]\). Averaging both sides under \(P\) gives (1).
Bound the tail by the MGF. Inequality (2) is Markov’s inequality (Theorem 2.1): a quantity that cannot be negative exceeds a level with probability at most its average divided by the level. The quantity \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) exceeds \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) exactly when \(L > \varepsilon\), so \[\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}, \tag{30.5}\] and Equation 30.2 bounds the average by \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\).
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Setting the right side of (2) equal to \(\delta\) and taking logarithms gives \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon) = -\ln(1/\delta)\), which rearranges to Equation 30.4. The same argument applied to \((Q, P)\) covers the other order of the pair.





Example 30.1 You release a statistic of sensitivity 1 with the Gaussian mechanism at \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). Mironov’s conversion gives \(\alpha/2 + \ln(10^5)/(\alpha - 1)\) at each order. The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so the best order lies in between. Over all real orders it is \(\alpha = 5.799\), with \(\varepsilon = 5.299\), and the grid’s order 5.8 gives the same 5.299. The exact answer, from Equation 20.17, is 4.377, so Mironov’s number overstates \(\varepsilon\) by 0.921.
Table 30.1 splits that excess between the two steps, and repeats the split for 100 such releases, where \(\mu = 10\). Its first three rows give the \(\varepsilon\) at which each member of Equation 30.3 equals \(10^{-5}\), and the last two their differences. The middle row needs the tail. Under \(P\) the loss is \(\mu^2/2 - \mu y\) with \(y\) standard normal, so \(L > \varepsilon\) when \(y < \mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\), and \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. This tail equals \(10^{-5}\) when \(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu = -4.2649\), which puts the level at \[\varepsilon = \frac{\mu^2}{2} + 4.2649\,\mu, \tag{30.6}\] about 4.765 at \(\mu = 1\) and 92.649 at \(\mu = 10\).

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.2 The improved conversion
Both of Mironov’s steps together replace the integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) of Equation 30.1, as a function of a loss value \(z\), by an exponential \(c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) that lies above it. The bound has to be an exponential, because that is the only function of the loss whose average Equation 30.2 tells you. Mironov’s constant \(c = e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) makes the exponential equal 1 at \(z = \varepsilon\), so it passes through the corner of the indicator. But the integrand is well below 1 near \(\varepsilon\), so a lower exponential still lies above it. This section finds the lowest one, and that is the whole improvement.
The result was found three times. It is Theorem 21 of Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato (2020) and Proposition 12 of Canonne, Kamath & Steinke (2020), who also give the \(\delta\) form, and Asoodeh, Liao, Calmon, Kosut & Sankar proved it independently (2020, Lemma 1). Its \(\delta\) is Mironov’s multiplied by a factor below 1 that depends only on the order.

Theorem 30.1 (The improved conversion) Let \(M\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for some order \(\alpha > 1\). For every \(\varepsilon\), the mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\delta = \frac{e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}}{\alpha}\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big)^{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.7}\] Equivalently, for every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\), it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.8}\]


Proof. The plan is to reduce the conversion to one constant, find the smallest constant for which the exponential stays above the integrand, and then solve for \(\varepsilon\).

Reduce to a constant. Suppose \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+ \le c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) for every real \(z\). Then the same holds with \(z\) replaced by the random loss \(L\), and averaging under \(P\) keeps the inequality. The left side averages to \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) by Equation 30.1, and the right side to at most \(c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\) by Equation 30.2, so \[\delta(\varepsilon) \le c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{30.9}\]
Write the smallest constant. The condition of step 1 says that \(c\) is at least \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)z}\) at every \(z\), so the smallest valid constant \(c^*\) is the largest value of that expression. It is 0 for \(z \le \varepsilon\), and for \(z > \varepsilon\) it is \[g(z) = e^{-(\alpha - 1)z} - e^{\varepsilon - \alpha z}. \tag{30.10}\]
Find the maximum. To locate the peak of \(g\), differentiate it and factor out \(e^{-\alpha z}\): \[g'(z) = e^{-\alpha z}\big(\alpha e^\varepsilon - (\alpha - 1)e^z\big). \tag{30.11}\] The bracket equals \(e^\varepsilon > 0\) at \(z = \varepsilon\) and decreases as \(z\) grows, so \(g\) first rises and then falls. Its maximum is where the bracket vanishes, at \(e^{z^*} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}e^\varepsilon\), that is at the point \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\).
Evaluate it. Write \(g(z^*) = e^{-\alpha z^*}(e^{z^*} - e^\varepsilon)\). At \(z^*\) the difference \(e^{z^*} - e^\varepsilon\) is \(e^\varepsilon/(\alpha - 1)\), and the first factor is \(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon}(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha\). Multiplying the two gives \[c^* = \frac{e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}}{\alpha - 1}\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big)^\alpha. \tag{30.12}\]
Collect. Step 1 with \(c = c^*\) bounds \(\delta\) by \(c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). Since \((1 - 1/\alpha)/(\alpha - 1) = 1/\alpha\), the constant in front simplifies to \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), which is Equation 30.7.
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Setting Equation 30.7 equal to \(\delta\) and taking logarithms gives \[\ln\delta = (\alpha - 1)\big(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon\big) - \ln\alpha + (\alpha - 1)\ln\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big). \tag{30.13}\] Dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) and solving for \(\varepsilon\), with \(\ln(1 - 1/\alpha) = \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha}\), gives Equation 30.8. As for Mironov’s conversion, the pair \((Q, P)\) follows from the same curve.


Figure 30.1 draws the two exponentials. Mironov’s passes through the corner of the indicator at \(z = \varepsilon\), while the lowest one touches the integrand at \(z^*\), slightly to the right of \(\varepsilon\). The chapter’s script (Section 30.6) checks step 4 by brute force: at \(\alpha = 6\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\) the formula gives \(c^* = 1.380552\times10^{-10}\) at \(z^* = 4.1823\), and the maximum of \(g\) over a grid of two million points agrees to all seven digits. One practical point remains. When \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is tiny, Equation 30.8 can be negative, and then you report 0, as the script and Canonne et al. do. That is safe because \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) only falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows, so a bound at a negative level also holds at 0.






Figure 30.1: The hockey-stick integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) (black) at \(\varepsilon = 3\), the indicator \(\mathbf 1[z > \varepsilon]\) that Mironov’s step 1 replaces it with (dashed), and the two exponentials of order \(\alpha = 6\) that bound it: Mironov’s, through the corner of the indicator (red), and the smallest one, which touches the integrand at \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\) (blue). The shaded curve is the density of the Gaussian privacy loss at \(\mu = 1\): the conversions average the exponentials against it.



Both conversions add a term to the same \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), so their difference at one order does not depend on the mechanism. That difference is what an accountant gains by switching.

Corollary 30.1 (What the improved conversion saves) At every order \(\alpha > 1\), for every RDP curve and every \(\delta\), the improved \(\varepsilon\) of Equation 30.8 is smaller than Mironov’s Equation 30.4 by \[s(\alpha) = \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.14}\] At a fixed \(\varepsilon\), the improved \(\delta\) is Mironov’s times \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\). Over a grid of orders, the best improved \(\varepsilon\) is below the best Mironov \(\varepsilon\) by at least \(s(\alpha_M)\), where \(\alpha_M\) is the order Mironov’s conversion picks.


Proof. 

The saving in \(\varepsilon\). Subtracting Equation 30.8 from Equation 30.4 at the same order cancels both \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) and \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). What remains is \(\ln\alpha/(\alpha - 1) - \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha}\), which is \(s(\alpha)\).
The factor in \(\delta\). Mironov’s \(\delta\) at level \(\varepsilon\) is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}\), the right side of Equation 30.3, and Equation 30.7 multiplies it by the stated factor.
Over a grid. The improved conversion takes its own best order, so its minimum is at most its value at \(\alpha_M\). By step 1 that value is Mironov’s minimum minus \(s(\alpha_M)\).


The factor in \(\delta\) behaves like \(1/(e\alpha)\) for large orders, because \((1 - 1/\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\) tends to \(1/e\). So at large orders the gain is large in \(\delta\) but small in \(\varepsilon\). Table 30.2 gives values. At order 2, for instance, the factor is \(\frac12\cdot\frac12 = 0.25\) and the saving is \(\ln 2 + \ln 2 = 1.3863\). If two accountants report \(\varepsilon\) about 0.4 apart from the same curve at a best order near 10, one of them uses Mironov’s conversion. Opacus and dp_accounting both use the improved one.

Corollary 30.1 promised at least \(s(5.8) = \frac{\ln 5.8}{4.8} + \ln\frac{5.8}{4.8} = 0.555\). The actual saving is a little more, because the improved conversion moves to a better order. title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 30.3 RDP as a constraint on tests
text:
30.3 RDP as a constraint on tests
An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee limits attacks through a single straight line in the plane of a test’s two errors, and an RDP curve says more. A test looks at the output and decides between the hypothesis “it came from \(P\)”, so your record was not used, and “it came from \(Q\)” (Definition 4.1). Its two errors are usually written \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), but \(\alpha\) is the Rényi order on this page, so they are written by their names. Its false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is the probability that it rejects \(P\) although the output came from \(P\). Its false negative rate \(\mathrm{FNR}\) is the probability that it accepts although the output came from \(Q\), and its power is \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\). This section finds the region of error pairs that an RDP curve allows, following Balle et al. (2020), and from it the best possible conversion.
The tool is data processing. A test turns the output into a coin, and that is post-processing, which cannot increase a Rényi divergence (Theorem 3.5). So each order of the curve constrains the coin, and through it the pair of errors. The trade-off function \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\) of Definition 4.2 is the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) that any test reaches at false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\), so it describes the most powerful attack at each rate.

Theorem 30.2 (The test region of an RDP curve) Let \(M\) have RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\cdot)\) at the orders of a grid, and let \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) on neighbouring datasets. Every test between \(P\) and \(Q\), with errors \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\), satisfies at every order \(\alpha\) of the grid \[\mathrm{FPR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FNR})^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^\alpha \mathrm{FNR}^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}, \qquad (1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + \mathrm{FNR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{30.15}\] Call the set of pairs \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) that satisfy all of these the RDP privacy region, and let \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) be the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) in it at false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\). Then:

Trade-off bound. For every \(\mathrm{FPR}\), \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}) \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\), so no test is more powerful than the region allows.
Optimal conversion. Every pair consistent with the curve has \[\delta(\varepsilon) \le \delta_{\mathrm{opt}}(\varepsilon) = \max_{\mathrm{FPR}}\big[1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\big], \tag{30.16}\] and some two-outcome pair consistent with the curve attains it. So \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}\) is the best \(\delta\) that any conversion using only these RDP values can certify.



Proof. The plan is to compute the Rényi divergence of a test’s outcome and apply the curve to it, which proves claim 1, and then to rewrite \(\delta\) as a statement about tests, which the region bounds.

The outcome of a test is a coin. Table 30.3 lists its distribution under each hypothesis.



Table 30.3: The outcome of a test with errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), as a two-point distribution under each hypothesis.





Outcome
Probability under \(P\)
Probability under \(Q\)




reject

\(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\)


accept
\(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\)

Compute its Rényi divergence. For a two-point distribution, the sum in the definition of \(D_\alpha\) has one term per row of Table 30.3: \[D_\alpha(\text{coin under } P\,\|\,\text{coin under } Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big[\mathrm{FPR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FNR})^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^\alpha \mathrm{FNR}^{1 - \alpha}\big]. \tag{30.17}\]
Apply the curve. By data processing this divergence is at most \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\), which is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\). Multiplying by \(\alpha - 1 > 0\) and exponentiating gives the first inequality of Equation 30.15. The second comes the same way from the bound on \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\), as the same sum with the columns of the table swapped. So every test’s errors lie in the region, and its \(\mathrm{FNR}\) is at least \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) at its \(\mathrm{FPR}\), which is claim 1.
Write \(\delta\) as a best test. Let \(S\) be the set of outputs on which a test accepts, so that \(P(S) = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) and \(Q(S) = \mathrm{FNR}\). By Lemma 20.2, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the largest \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over all events, so \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \max_{\text{tests}}\big[1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FNR}\big]. \tag{30.18}\] Every test has \(\mathrm{FNR} \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) by step 3, and replacing \(\mathrm{FNR}\) by \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) can only increase the bracket. That gives the bound in Equation 30.16.
Attain the bound. Let \((\mathrm{FPR}^*, \mathrm{FNR}^*)\) maximize Equation 30.16, with \(\mathrm{FNR}^* = f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR}^*)\). Build a mechanism whose output is just the coin of Table 30.3 with these errors: on \(D\) it accepts with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}^*\), and on \(D'\) with probability \(\mathrm{FNR}^*\). By step 2, its Rényi divergences in both directions are the logarithms of the left sides of Equation 30.15, divided by \(\alpha - 1\), at a point of the region, so the mechanism satisfies the curve. The test that accepts exactly when the coin shows “accept” has errors \((\mathrm{FPR}^*, \mathrm{FNR}^*)\), so by step 4 this mechanism’s \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is at least \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}^* - e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FNR}^*\), which is \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}(\varepsilon)\).


Computing \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) uses the shape of the constraints. For a fixed \(\mathrm{FPR}\), both left sides of Equation 30.15 equal 1 at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), where the test ignores the output and the two coins are identical. Elsewhere they are at least 1, because each is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha}\) for a divergence that is never negative, so that point is their minimum. Both are also convex in \(\mathrm{FNR}\), because each term has the form \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\), which is jointly convex for \(\alpha > 1\) (Section F.5 proves it). So on \([0, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}]\) they decrease, the constraints hold above a cut-off and fail below it, and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) is that cut-off. The script finds it by bisection.
The region is an intersection of convex sets, so \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is convex and the objective of Equation 30.16 is concave in \(\mathrm{FPR}\), which a one-dimensional search maximizes. For a single order this optimum is close to the improved conversion. At order 2, where \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\) for the running example, Mironov gives \(1 + \ln(10^5) = 12.513\), the improved conversion 11.127 and the optimum from that one value 10.668. At orders 8 and 32 the improved conversion and the optimum agree to three decimals (5.214 and 16.228). Balle et al. indeed derive the improved conversion as the straight line that just touches the region of one order, the same tangency that Figure 30.1 shows between the exponential and the integrand.
The region is not the set an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee allows. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair says that every test has \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FNR} + \delta\), and the same with the two errors swapped: straight lines, and the best it can do is touch the curved region at one point. A whole trade-off curve is the envelope of such lines, one for each \(\varepsilon\), which is the duality that Gaussian DP develops. Nor does the region characterize RDP. A test squeezes the output into one bit, and information spread over many outputs is lost when they are merged into “accept” and “reject”. So a pair can have every test inside the region and still violate the curve: the region is what RDP implies about tests, not an equivalent definition.

Example 30.3 For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\) the true trade-off curve is known, so you can see how loose the region is. The best test between \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) rejects when the output exceeds a threshold, because the likelihood ratio increases with the output (Theorem 4.1). Its false negative rate at false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is the Gaussian trade-off function of Theorem 4.3, \[G_1(\mathrm{FPR}) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - 1\big). \tag{30.19}\] At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\), \(\Phi^{-1}(0.9) = 1.2816\), so \(G_1 = \Phi(0.2816) = 0.6109\) and the true power is 0.3891. Figure 30.2 plots the largest power the RDP curve allows against this true power, and Table 30.4 compares them at three rates. The curve allows 1.24 to 1.36 times the power the Gaussian has; at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\), for instance, \(0.48376/0.38914 = 1.24\).

Left: linear axes. Right: log axes, with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) line \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \le e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) from the improved conversion (grey), which touches the red curve.

Each order guards a different range of \(\mathrm{FPR}\). At small \(\mathrm{FPR}\) the second constraint of order \(\alpha\) keeps its first term, \((1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha\mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha}\), below \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). So the power is at most a constant times \(\mathrm{FPR}^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\), a line of slope \((\alpha - 1)/\alpha\) on log axes. As \(\mathrm{FPR}\) shrinks, a line of slope near 1 falls faster than one of slope near \(\frac12\), so the constraint of a large order is the tighter, or binding, one at small \(\mathrm{FPR}\), while small orders bind in the bulk. At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\), order 2 alone allows power \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\) and order 8 allows \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\). At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\) the roles swap, with 0.4932 for order 2 and 0.9838 for order 8. The exact boundaries of the two orders cross at \(\mathrm{FPR} \approx 1.87\times10^{-4}\), and at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-3}\) the binding order of the grid is 3.7.
Now suppose an auditor runs a membership test against the mean released with \(\sigma = 1\), at false positive rate \(10^{-3}\). The RDP curve alone guarantees that no test detects membership with probability above \(2.4910\times10^{-2}\), and the true best test reaches \(1.8298\times10^{-2}\). The \((4.729, 10^{-5})\) guarantee of the improved conversion only caps the power at \(e^{4.729}\times10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.1131\), more than four times the region’s bound. Reading an RDP result through one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair throws away most of what it says about low false positive rates.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.4 Choosing the order
Both conversions hold at every order, so you take the best one. Each converted \(\varepsilon\) is the RDP curve, which grows with the order, plus a term in \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), which shrinks with it, so the best order balances the two. An accountant evaluates the curve only on a grid of orders, and where the best order falls tells you what that grid must contain. For the Gaussian the curve is a line through the origin, and the best order has a closed form or nearly so.

Proposition 30.2 (Best orders for a linear curve) Let \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\) with slope \(\rho > 0\), which is \(\rho = \mu^2/2 = k/(2\sigma^2)\) for the composed Gaussian, and let \(0 < \delta < 1\). Over real orders \(\alpha > 1\), Mironov’s conversion is smallest at \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\), where it equals \[\varepsilon^* = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{30.20}\] The improved conversion is convex for \(1 < \alpha < 1/\delta\), and its smallest value there is at the root of \[\rho(\alpha - 1)^2 = \ln\frac{1}{\alpha\delta}. \tag{30.21}\]


Proof. Each step sets a derivative to zero, as for any smooth minimum, and the last checks that the stationary point is a minimum.

Mironov. The derivative of \(\rho\alpha + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is \(\rho - \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)^2\), which is increasing in \(\alpha\). Setting it to zero gives \((\alpha - 1)^2 = \ln(1/\delta)/\rho\), which is \(\alpha^*\). At \(\alpha^*\) the curve term is \(\rho\alpha^* = \rho + \sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\), and the second term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha^* - 1)\) is \(\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) too, so the two contribute equally beyond \(\rho\).
Improved, the derivative. Write Equation 30.8 as \(\rho\alpha + \ln(1 - \frac1\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\) and differentiate term by term. The middle term has derivative \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}\), and by the quotient rule the last one has derivative \[-\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)} - \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{(\alpha - 1)^2}. \tag{30.22}\] The terms \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}\) cancel, leaving \(\rho - \ln(1/(\alpha\delta))/(\alpha - 1)^2\). Setting it to zero gives Equation 30.21.
A minimum. The derivative of the expression of step 2 is \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)^2} + \frac{2\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))}{(\alpha - 1)^3}\), which is positive whenever \(\alpha < 1/\delta\). So the objective is convex there, and its stationary point is its minimum.


The script solves Equation 30.21 by iterating \(\alpha \leftarrow 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))/\rho}\) from Mironov’s \(\alpha^*\). The only difference from Mironov’s condition is the extra \(\alpha\) inside the logarithm, which pulls the best order slightly lower. Ignoring that slowly varying \(\ln\alpha\), the best order is \[\alpha^* - 1 \approx \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\rho}} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{k}}. \tag{30.23}\] More steps or less noise push the best order toward 1, with \(\alpha^* - 1\) shrinking like \(1/\sqrt k\). A smaller \(\delta\) pushes it up, but only through \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\): at \(\mu = 1\), moving from \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-10}\) doubles \(\ln(1/\delta)\) but moves the improved best order only from 5.432 to 7.483. Figure 30.3 shows the two converted curves for \(\mu = 1\). Both are U-shaped, and the improved one sits below Mironov’s everywhere by \(s(\alpha)\) of Equation 30.14.






Figure 30.3: Converted \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for each order of the grid, for the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), with Mironov’s conversion (red) and the improved one (blue). Dots mark the best order of each. The dashed line is the exact \(\varepsilon\), and the grey curve is the RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) that both conversions add to.

Mironov’s best order is then \(1 + \sqrt{\ln(10^5)/0.005} = 1 + \sqrt{2302.6} = 48.985\), and the improved conversion’s extra \(\ln\alpha\) brings it down to 40.525.

You plan \(k = 100\) full-batch noisy gradient steps at \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\rho = 100/2 = 50\). Equation 30.21 puts the best order at 1.472, and the grid’s 1.5 costs \(96.116 - 96.035 = 0.081\) in \(\varepsilon\). A single release at \(\sigma = 10\) instead wants order 40.525, and the grid’s integer orders match it to three decimals of \(\varepsilon\). One grid serves both because it is dense near 1 and runs from 1.1 to 512.
The grid needs orders near 1 for long runs with little noise. At \(\rho = 5000\) the best order is 1.048, below the grid’s smallest order 1.1, and the grid’s answer is \(5611.778 - 5475.791 = 135.987\) larger than the continuous optimum. title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.5 The slack no conversion removes
The improved conversion beats Mironov’s, and the optimal conversion of Equation 30.16 is the best possible from the curve. Yet for the Gaussian both stay above the exact \(\varepsilon\). Is that a weakness of the formulas, or of the curve as a summary? This section shows that it is the summary. A different mechanism satisfies the same curve and has a larger \(\delta\), and a conversion that sees only the curve must cover both. It also looks at the opposite direction, from \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) to RDP, which matters when one analysis mixes pure-DP and RDP components.
The idea is to build the worst mechanism the curve allows and compute its \(\delta\). By Theorem 30.2, the largest \(\delta\) consistent with a set of orders is attained by a two-outcome pair. Table 30.6 shows one, for the Gaussian’s curve at \(\mu = 1\) and the level \(\varepsilon = 4.377\) where the Gaussian has \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Like the coin of Table 30.3, it has two outcomes: a rare one, much likelier under \(D\), that betrays \(D\), and a common one that carries almost all the mass. The privacy loss column is \(\ln(P/Q)\) for each outcome. For the rare outcome it is \(\ln(2.2779\times10^{-4}/2.2998\times10^{-6}) = 4.5956\), and for the common one it is a tiny negative number, because \(P\) puts slightly less mass there than \(Q\).

Proposition 30.3 (The curve does not determine δ) The two-outcome mechanism of Table 30.6 satisfies \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \alpha/2\) and \(D_\alpha(Q\|P) \le \alpha/2\) at every order \(\alpha > 1\) that the script scans, and its \(\delta\) at \(\varepsilon = 4.377\) is \(4.4698\times10^{-5}\). So no conversion that sees only the RDP curve \(\alpha/2\) can certify \((4.377, 10^{-5})\)-DP, although the Gaussian mechanism at \(\mu = 1\) satisfies it.


Proof. The plan is to build the pair from the optimal conversion, push it strictly inside the curve at every real order, check that numerically, and compute its \(\delta\).

Build the pair. On the part’s grid, at \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4.377\), the pair that attains Equation 30.16 has \(\delta = 4.4700\times10^{-5}\). But it satisfies the curve only at the grid’s orders, because its Rényi divergence is a smooth function of the order and can poke above \(\alpha/2\) between two grid orders. So the script recomputes \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}\) with the constraints of a dense set of orders, steps of 0.002 from 1.01 to 30 and every integer up to 512. It then raises the probability of the rare outcome under \(Q\) by a relative \(10^{-5}\), which pushes the pair strictly inside the curve.
Check the curve. On a scan of \(\alpha\) from \(1 + 10^{-8}\) to \(10^6\), refined around the maximum, the largest value of \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) - \alpha/2\) is \(-9.97\times10^{-6}\), at \(\alpha = 5.0955\), so the curve holds everywhere scanned. The reverse divergences stay about 0.5 below the curve. Beyond the scan, \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) tends to the largest privacy loss, 4.5956, while \(\alpha/2\) grows without bound. The rounded values in the table also satisfy the curve.
Compute its \(\delta\). By Equation 30.1 only outcomes with \(L > \varepsilon\) contribute, and here that is only the rare outcome. So \(\delta(4.377) = P(\text{rare}) - e^{4.377}\,Q(\text{rare})\). With \(e^{4.377} \approx 79.6\) this is \(2.2779\times10^{-4}\) minus about \(1.831\times10^{-4}\), which is \(4.4698\times10^{-5}\) with unrounded values.
Conclude. A certificate computed from the curve alone must also hold for this pair, which has about 4.5 times the Gaussian’s \(\delta\) at the same \(\varepsilon\). So no such certificate can give \((4.377, 10^{-5})\). For comparison, the improved conversion’s \(\delta\) at that \(\varepsilon\) is \(4.4701\times10^{-5}\), within \(10^{-8}\) of this pair’s.


The pair puts almost all its mass at a loss near 0 and a sliver at 4.5956, where the improved conversion’s exponential nearly touches the integrand, so for this pair that bound is nearly an equality. It is very unlike the Gaussian loss, which spreads its tail smoothly over all large values. The RDP curve cannot tell the two apart, because it only sees MGF values (Equation 30.2).
The opposite direction asks when a guarantee of another kind gives an RDP curve, so that a pure-DP or \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) component can join an RDP analysis.

Proposition 30.4 (From (ε, δ) and from ε-DP to RDP)  

For every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\), some mechanism is \((0, \delta)\)-DP and has \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \infty\) at every order \(\alpha > 1\). So \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta > 0\) implies no RDP bound at any order.
Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\alpha, \min(\varepsilon, \alpha\varepsilon^2/2))\)-RDP for every \(\alpha > 1\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 3.3).



Proof. 

A rare catastrophe. Take the mechanism that outputs nothing, except that with probability \(\delta\) it publishes your record. Order the pair with the dataset that holds you first, \(P = M(D')\) and \(Q = M(D)\), which a guarantee must also cover. Then \(P\) puts mass \(\delta\) on an output that \(Q\) never produces, and otherwise matches \(Q\). Moving mass \(\delta\) changes the probability of any event by at most \(\delta\), so \(P(S) \le Q(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\), and the mechanism is \((0, \delta)\)-DP.
Its divergence is infinite. The sum \(\sum P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\) in the Rényi divergence contains the term \(\delta^\alpha\cdot 0^{1 - \alpha}\) for the published record. For \(\alpha > 1\) that term is infinite, so \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \infty\) at every order.
The bound \(\varepsilon\). An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism has privacy loss at most \(\varepsilon\) at every output, so \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) everywhere. Its average under \(P\) is then at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\). That average is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\) (Equation 3.13), so taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon\).
The bound \(\alpha\varepsilon^2/2\). This bound says that the logarithm of the MGF of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP loss grows at most quadratically. Concentrated DP proves it with Hoeffding’s lemma, together with the sharper bound \(\alpha\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), which randomized response attains as \(\alpha \to 1\).


So RDP, like pure DP, rules out catastrophic events however rare, and to get a curve from an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) mechanism you need to know how its \(\delta\) arises. For randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), the bound of claim 2 is 0.2500 at order 2 and 0.5000 at orders 4 and 10. The script gives \(D_2 = 0.2273\), \(D_4 = 0.3519\) and \(D_{10} = 0.4473\), each below its bound.

Example 30.5 Table 30.7 and Figure 30.4 compare all four answers for the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 10\) per step. Over \(k = 1\) to \(10{,}000\) steps, \(\mu = \sqrt k/10\) runs from 0.1 to 10 and the exact \(\varepsilon\) from 0.341 to 91.817, the range where accounting choices matter. Because everything depends only on \(\mu\), the row \(k = 100\), where \(\mu = 1\), repeats the single release at \(\sigma = 1\) of the earlier sections.

Over the whole grid, unlike at the single order 2 of Section 30.3, the optimal and improved conversions coincide: at \(\mu = 1\) they are 4.728505 and 4.728507, a difference of \(2\times10^{-6}\). The optimal conversion can use all orders at once, but that helps only if more than one order holds back the worst mechanism. For the worst pair at \(\varepsilon = 4.377\), only the constraint at order 5.1 is active, and at every other order of the grid the pair’s divergence stays at least 0.0011 below the curve. Mironov’s excess shrinks fast with \(k\), from 42% to 7%, and the unavoidable excess slowly, from 10% to 5%, because for large \(\mu\) the term \(\mu^2/2\) that every method shares dominates.
Suppose your paper reports \((4.729, 10^{-5})\)-DP from an RDP accountant for this mechanism, and a reviewer asks whether a better conversion would lower it. The answer is no, by Proposition 30.3. The same construction at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives a pair inside the curve at every real order whose \(\delta\) reaches \(10^{-5}\) only at \(\varepsilon = 4.728376\). The improved conversion at the best real order, 5.4318, gives 4.728387, which is a valid certificate. So the best value any method can certify from the curve lies between 4.728376 and 4.728387, which is 4.7284 to four decimals, and a method that sees only the grid’s orders must report at least 4.728505. A lower number needs an accountant that sees the mechanism, and for the Gaussian that number is 4.377.

When the slack matters, change the summary, not the formula. To get the exact 4.377 you must track more than an MGF: the trade-off function (Gaussian DP) or the full privacy loss distribution (numerical accounting). The 5 to 10% is for the plain Gaussian. Subsampled Gaussian steps, as in private training, have curves that are not lines, and there the gap to the exact value can be much larger, as choosing an accountant measures.

30.8 References

Mironov, “Rényi Differential Privacy” (IEEE CSF 2017): the definition, composition, the Gaussian and Laplace curves, and the conversion of Equation 30.4 (Proposition 3).
Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato, “Hypothesis Testing Interpretations and Rényi Differential Privacy” (AISTATS 2020; arXiv:1905.09982): privacy regions of divergences, the test region of Equation 30.15 (§5.1.1), and the improved conversion as a tangent line (Theorem 21).
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020; arXiv:2004.00010): the short proof of the improved conversion through the optimal constant \(c^*\) (Proposition 12), and its use for concentrated DP (Corollary 13).
Asoodeh, Liao, Calmon, Kosut & Sankar, “A Better Bound Gives a Hundred Rounds: Enhanced Privacy Guarantees via f-Divergences” (IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory, ISIT 2020; arXiv:2001.05990): an independent proof of the improved conversion (Lemma 1, Eq. 20), applied to noisy gradient descent.
Asoodeh, Liao, Calmon, Kosut & Sankar, “Three Variants of Differential Privacy: Lossless Conversion and Applications” (IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Information Theory, 2021; arXiv:2008.06529): the optimal conversion from one Rényi order through the joint range of two \(f\)-divergences, and RDP as a trade-off between the two errors of a test.
Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016): \(\varepsilon\)-DP implies \(\varepsilon^2/2\)-zero-concentrated DP (Proposition 3.3) and the standard zero-concentrated conversion.
Steinke, “Composition of Differential Privacy & Privacy Amplification by Subsampling” (2022 survey, arXiv:2210.00597): a unified treatment of privacy loss, RDP, conversions and their tightness.
Opacus (opacus/accountants/analysis/rdp.py) and Google’s dp_accounting (rdp_privacy_accountant.py): production implementations of the improved conversion.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.1 The definition of zCDP
The first chapter of this part describes a mechanism by a whole curve. Take two neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\), which differ by adding or removing one record. At each order \(\alpha > 1\), the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is the largest Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha\) between the output distributions \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) over all such pairs. For the Gaussian mechanism, which adds normal noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) to a query that one record moves by at most 1, the curve is the line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), fixed by its slope. This chapter asks when one number can stand for the whole curve, and what that number buys.
The answer is zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), the most widely used form of concentrated differential privacy (CDP). A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when its RDP curve lies under the line \(\rho\alpha\). RDP curves add under composition, and lines through the origin add to a line, so composition adds the parameters. Every section asks how well a line fits the curve. It fits the Gaussian exactly. A pure differential privacy (DP) mechanism has a curve that flattens at \(\varepsilon\), because no Rényi divergence exceeds its largest log-ratio of probabilities, so a line fits it only near \(\alpha = 1\). For the subsampled Gaussian of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD for short, the line fits so badly that zCDP throws away everything subsampling gained. Truncated CDP repairs this by asking for the line only on small orders.
Two running examples carry the chapter. The first is one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\), which is \(0.5\)-zCDP; at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) its exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(4.377\), and zCDP reports \(4.728\). The second is a DP-SGD run of \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, each on a random sample that includes each record with probability \(q = 0.01\), with \(\sigma = 1\). At the same \(\delta\), RDP accounting puts that run at \(\varepsilon = 6.719\), while zCDP reports \(5475.8\).
You add Gaussian noise to a count, a mean or a gradient, again and again, and you want one number that says how much privacy you have spent so far. Bun and Steinke (2016) turned the Gaussian’s straight RDP curve into a definition: describe a mechanism by the slope of a line that lies above its RDP curve.
The name comes from what the definition says about the privacy loss: it is concentrated around its mean like a normal variable, and “zero” says the line has no intercept. Fix a neighbouring pair and write \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), with \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\) their probabilities or densities at an output \(y\). Capital letters are used because \(q\) is the sampling rate later in this chapter. The privacy loss \(L(y) = \ln(P(y)/Q(y))\) says how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\), and drawing \(y\) from \(P\) makes it a random variable \(L\). Divergences shows that the Rényi divergence is a rescaled logarithm of the moment generating function (MGF) of this loss (Equation 3.13): \[(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]. \tag{31.2}\] So zCDP bounds every exponential moment of the loss, and exponential moments control how often the loss is large.
Three properties make the definition useful, and each is inherited from a property of the Rényi divergence.
For the Gaussian the definition holds with equality in every moment. Its privacy loss is normal with mean \(\rho\) and variance \(2\rho\) (Lemma 20.3), and the logarithm of the MGF of that normal at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) is \(\lambda\rho + \lambda^2\rho = (\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho\). So a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is one whose privacy loss is, in every exponential moment, no worse than \(\mathcal N(\rho, 2\rho)\). For other mechanisms the smallest valid \(\rho\) is the largest ratio \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\), the rest of the curve is forgotten, and the later sections measure that cost.
The tail bound Equation 31.4 is loose only by a polynomial factor. For the Gaussian the exact tail is a standard normal tail at \(z = t/\sqrt{2\rho}\), while the bound is \(e^{-z^2/2}\). The Mills ratio of Concentration says that a normal tail at \(z\) is about \(e^{-z^2/2}/(z\sqrt{2\pi})\), so the exact tail divided by the bound is about \(1/(z\sqrt{2\pi}) = \sqrt{\rho/\pi}/t\).

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
Definition 31.1 (Zero-concentrated differential privacy) A mechanism \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP if, for all neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) and all orders \(\alpha > 1\), \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\alpha. \tag{31.1}\]



Proposition 31.1 (The moment and tail form) If \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP, then for every neighbouring pair the privacy loss \(L\) satisfies \[\ln\mathbb E\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] \le (\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho \quad\text{for all } \alpha > 1, \tag{31.3}\] and its upper tail falls off like a normal tail around \(\rho\): \[\Pr[L > \rho + t] \le e^{-t^2/(4\rho)} \quad\text{for all } t > 0. \tag{31.4}\]


Proof. 

The moment form. Multiply Equation 31.1 by \(\alpha - 1\), which is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction. By Equation 31.2 the left side becomes \(\ln\mathbb E[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\), which gives Equation 31.3.
A tail bound at each order. The positive variable \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) is large exactly when \(L\) is, so the Chernoff bound (Theorem 2.3) applies Markov’s inequality to it. For any level \(\tau\), it gives \[\Pr[L > \tau] \le \mathbb E\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]e^{-(\alpha - 1)\tau}, \tag{31.5}\] which Equation 31.3 bounds by \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\alpha\rho - \tau)}\).
The best order. Use the order that gives the smallest bound. Put \(\tau = \rho + t\) and write \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), so that \(\alpha\rho - \tau = \lambda\rho - t\). The exponent becomes \(\lambda^2\rho - \lambda t\), a parabola in \(\lambda\) whose smallest value, at \(\lambda = t/(2\rho)\), is \(-t^2/(4\rho)\).




Theorem 31.1 (The Gaussian mechanism, composition and post-processing)  

The Gaussian mechanism, which adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) noise to a query \(f\) with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\), is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = (\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). With the part’s noise multiplier, which measures \(\sigma\) in units of the sensitivity, \(\rho = 1/(2\sigma^2)\).
If \(M_1\) is \(\rho_1\)-zCDP and \(M_2\) is \(\rho_2\)-zCDP, possibly chosen after seeing the output of \(M_1\), the pair is \((\rho_1 + \rho_2)\)-zCDP.
Any function of the output of a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP.



Proof. 

The Gaussian. For two normal distributions with the same variance \(\sigma^2\), \(D_\alpha\) is \(\alpha\) times the squared distance between the means, divided by \(2\sigma^2\) (Equation 3.19). This holds in any dimension, because rotating the coordinates so that the means differ along one axis leaves the other axes identical under both, and identical independent coordinates add nothing (additivity in Theorem 3.2). On neighbours the distance is at most \(\Delta_2 f\), which gives the claimed \(\rho\).
Composition. The RDP curves of an adaptive composition add (Rényi DP), so the pair’s curve is at most \(\rho_1\alpha + \rho_2\alpha\), a line of slope \(\rho_1 + \rho_2\).
Post-processing. The Rényi divergence obeys the data-processing inequality (Theorem 3.5), so passing the output through any function cannot raise the curve.





Example 31.1 One Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) is \(0.5\)-zCDP, and ten of them are \(5\)-zCDP. A million simulated privacy losses (seed 0) have mean \(0.4990\) and variance \(1.0013\), against \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(2\rho = 1\). Their \(\ln\mathbb E[e^L]\) is \(1.0000\), against \((\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho = 1\) at \(\alpha = 2\). Table 31.1 compares the tail with its bound. At \(t = 4\) their ratio is \(0.094\), against \(\sqrt{0.5/\pi}/4 = 0.100\) from the Mills ratio.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.2 Pure DP implies zCDP
A real pipeline mixes Gaussian steps with \(\varepsilon\)-DP ones, such as a Laplace count, a randomized-response survey bit or an exponential-mechanism selection. To put them in one budget, you need their \(\rho\). The privacy loss of such a mechanism lies in \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\), and a bounded variable has Gaussian-like tails, so \(\rho\) should be of order \(\varepsilon^2\). The question is the constant.
The tool is Hoeffding’s lemma from Concentration (Lemma 2.2). A variable \(X\) confined to an interval of length \(w\) has an MGF no larger than that of a normal variable with the same mean and variance \(w^2/4\): \[\ln\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda X}\big] \le \lambda\mathbb E[X] + \frac{\lambda^2w^2}{8} \quad\text{for every real } \lambda. \tag{31.6}\] Applied once to bound the mean of the loss and once to bound its exponential moments, it gives the constant \(\frac12\).

Theorem 31.2 (Pure DP implies zCDP) If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.4), and its RDP curve lies under both the line and the cap \(\varepsilon\): \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \min\Big(\varepsilon,\ \frac{\alpha\varepsilon^2}{2}\Big). \tag{31.7}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the mean of the loss with Hoeffding’s lemma, then its exponential moments with the same lemma, and add the two. The cap comes separately.

The loss is bounded. Pure DP holds output by output (Proposition 18.1), so \(\varepsilon\)-DP for both orders of the pair gives \(e^{-\varepsilon} \le P(y)/Q(y) \le e^\varepsilon\) wherever either probability is positive. So \(L \in [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\), and \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same support.
The mean is at most \(\varepsilon^2/2\). Apply Hoeffding’s lemma to \(X = -L\), which lies in an interval of length \(2\varepsilon\), with \(\lambda = 1\): \[\ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{-L}\big] \le -\mathbb E_P[L] + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}. \tag{31.8}\] The left side is 0, because \(e^{-L} = Q(Y)/P(Y)\) averages to 1 under \(P\) when the supports agree (Lemma 3.2). So \(\mathbb E_P[L] \le \varepsilon^2/2\).
The exponential moments. Apply the lemma again, now to \(L\) itself with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\): \[\ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] \le (\alpha - 1)\mathbb E_P[L] + \frac{(\alpha - 1)^2\varepsilon^2}{2}. \tag{31.9}\]
Combine. Putting the mean bound of step 2 into step 3 bounds the right side by \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon^2/2 + (\alpha - 1)^2\varepsilon^2/2 = (\alpha - 1)\alpha\,\varepsilon^2/2\). By Equation 31.2, that is \(D_\alpha \le \alpha\varepsilon^2/2\).
The cap. \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\) and tends to the max-divergence \(D_\infty\), the largest log-ratio of probabilities over events (Theorem 3.2). \(\varepsilon\)-DP bounds that log-ratio by \(\varepsilon\).


Hoeffding treats the loss as an arbitrary bounded variable. A sharper route uses the fact that randomized response, which reports a bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flips it otherwise, is the worst \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism: every other one is a post-processing of it. Its MGF is a ratio of hyperbolic cosines, and step 3 of the proof below bounds it with one inequality: \(\ln\cosh x\) is a concave function of \(x^2\), so it lies below its tangent.

Lemma 31.1 (A tangent bound for ln cosh) For every \(a > 0\) and every real \(x\), \[\ln\cosh x - \ln\cosh a \le (x^2 - a^2)\frac{\tanh a}{2a}. \tag{31.10}\]


Proof. 

Change variable. Let \(h(s) = \ln\cosh\sqrt s\) for \(s \ge 0\), so that the claim is \(h(x^2) - h(a^2) \le (x^2 - a^2)h'(a^2)\). By the chain rule, \(h'(s) = \tanh(\sqrt s)/(2\sqrt s)\), which at \(s = a^2\) is \(\tanh(a)/(2a)\).
The derivative decreases. The function \(\tanh(y)/y\) decreases for \(y > 0\), because its derivative has the sign of \(y - \sinh y\cosh y\), which is negative. So \(h'\) decreases, and \(h\) is concave.
Tangent line. A concave function lies below each of its tangent lines, and the claim is the tangent at \(s = a^2\).



Theorem 31.3 (The sharp constant) Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\)-zCDP: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \alpha\,\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{31.11}\] No smaller \(\rho\) holds for randomized response. More generally, the exact RDP curve of randomized response is a valid RDP curve for every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.


Proof. The plan is to reduce every \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair to randomized response, compute its MGF exactly, bound it with Lemma 31.1, and show that the bound is reached as \(\alpha \to 1\).

Reduce to randomized response. Let \(P^\star\) and \(Q^\star\) be the output distributions of randomized response on the bits 0 and 1. Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair is a post-processing of them: there is a channel \(K\) with \(P = P^\star K\) and \(Q = Q^\star K\) (Theorem 21.2 with \(\delta = 0\)). By the data-processing inequality (Theorem 3.5), \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le D_\alpha(P^\star\|Q^\star)\) at every order, which is the last claim.
The MGF of randomized response. Under \(P^\star\) the truthful answer has probability \(p = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and likelihood ratio \(p/(1 - p) = e^\varepsilon\). So the loss is \(+\varepsilon\) with probability \(p\) and \(-\varepsilon\) otherwise. With \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), averaging \(e^{\lambda L}\) over the two values gives \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda L}\big] = \frac{e^{(\lambda + 1)\varepsilon} + e^{-\lambda\varepsilon}}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{31.12}\] Factoring \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) out of the numerator and the denominator turns each into twice a hyperbolic cosine: \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda L}\big] = \frac{\cosh\big((\lambda + \frac12)\varepsilon\big)}{\cosh(\varepsilon/2)}. \tag{31.13}\]
Bound it. Take \(x = (\lambda + \frac12)\varepsilon\) and \(a = \varepsilon/2\) in Lemma 31.1. Then \(x^2 - a^2 = \varepsilon^2\lambda(\lambda + 1)\) and \(\tanh(a)/(2a) = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)/\varepsilon\), so \[\ln\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda L}\big] \le (\alpha - 1)\alpha\,\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{31.14}\] By Equation 31.2 and step 1, this gives Equation 31.11.
No smaller \(\rho\). As \(\alpha \to 1\), any RDP curve tends to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, the mean loss (Theorem 3.2). For randomized response that mean is \(\varepsilon(2p - 1) = \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1) = \varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\). So \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\) tends to \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), and any smaller slope fails near \(\alpha = 1\).


Since \(\tanh x \le x\), the sharp constant is below \(\varepsilon^2/2\), and the two agree as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the sharp \(\rho\) is \(0.1225\) against \(0.1250\), and at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is \(0.4621\) against \(0.5000\). Mechanisms other than randomized response can need less: the Laplace mechanism needs \(0.3679\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\).
Any line fits poorly far from \(\alpha = 1\), because the true curve flattens at the cap (Figure 31.2). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the line \(\alpha\varepsilon^2/2\) crosses the cap at \(\alpha = 2\), and at \(\varepsilon = 3\) its slope \(4.5\) puts it above the cap at every order. Since every \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair is a post-processing of randomized response, an RDP accountant can instead charge a pure-DP step the curve of randomized response, while a zCDP accountant can keep only a line. For large \(\varepsilon\), as in local DP, account the mechanism by its curve or by \(\varepsilon\), not by a \(\rho\).






Figure 31.2: The RDP curve of randomized response (black) against the zCDP line \(\alpha\varepsilon^2/2\) (dashed), the sharp zCDP line \(\alpha\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) (dash-dotted) and the pure-DP cap \(\varepsilon\) (dotted), for \(\varepsilon = 1\) (left) and \(\varepsilon = 3\) (right). The grey line is the KL divergence \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), the curve’s value at \(\alpha \to 1\).



The exponential mechanism, which selects one candidate and favours those with higher scores, costs four times less than \(\varepsilon^2/2\). Its privacy loss on a neighbouring pair lies in an interval of length \(\varepsilon\), not \(2\varepsilon\), which is the bounded-range property of Durfee and Rogers (2019). Hoeffding’s lemma then pays a quarter of the variance term.

Proposition 31.2 (Bounded-range mechanisms) If, for every neighbouring pair taken in either order, the privacy loss of \(M\) lies in an interval of length \(\varepsilon\), then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon^2/8)\)-zCDP. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP exponential mechanism has this property, so it is \((\varepsilon^2/8)\)-zCDP (Cesar & Rogers 2021).


Proof. 

The mean. The loss is finite in both orders, so \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same support and \(\mathbb E_P[e^{-L}] = 1\), as in step 2 of Theorem 31.2. Hoeffding’s lemma with length \(\varepsilon\) and \(\lambda = 1\) then gives \(0 \le -\mathbb E_P[L] + \varepsilon^2/8\).
The exponential moments. The lemma with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) adds \((\alpha - 1)^2\varepsilon^2/8\) to \((\alpha - 1)\mathbb E_P[L]\).
Combine. With step 1 the sum is at most \((\alpha - 1)\alpha\,\varepsilon^2/8\), which by Equation 31.2 is \(D_\alpha \le \alpha\varepsilon^2/8\).



Example 31.2 Randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\) reports the truth with probability \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\). Table 31.2 compares its exact curve with the bounds. The third column puts the sharp mean bound \(\varepsilon\tanh(1/2) = 0.4621\), which holds for every \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair (Theorem 21.3), into step 4 of the Hoeffding proof in place of \(\varepsilon^2/2\). That line starts lower but keeps the slope \(0.5\), which comes from Hoeffding’s variance term, so it sits \(0.5 - 0.4621 = 0.0379\) below the zCDP line at every order.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.3 From zCDP to (ε, δ)
Whatever you account in, you report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Mironov’s conversion turns an RDP curve into such a guarantee (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests). At each order \(\alpha\), a mechanism with curve value \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is \((\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1), \delta)\)-DP, and you take the best order. The improved conversion of the same chapter avoids part of the slack of Markov’s inequality, and subtracts \(\ln(\alpha)/(\alpha - 1) - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\) from this. For a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism the curve is the line \(\rho\alpha\), so the best order can be found by hand. Section D.4 in the appendices derives the result from scratch, with worked numbers.

Theorem 31.4 (From zCDP to (ε, δ)) A \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{31.15}\] reached at the order \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.3). It is also \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with the smaller value \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha > 1}\left[\rho\alpha + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big) - \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\right] \tag{31.16}\] (Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020, Proposition 12 and Corollary 13).


Proof. Write \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\).

Plug in the line. Mironov’s conversion with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\) says that every \(\alpha > 1\) gives a valid \(\varepsilon\): \[g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \frac{\ell}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{31.17}\] The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so the best order lies in between.
Minimize. The derivative \(\rho - \ell/(\alpha - 1)^2\) is zero at \(\alpha - 1 = \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\). Both terms of \(g\) are convex for \(\alpha > 1\), so this stationary point is the minimum.
Evaluate. At \(\alpha^*\) the first term is \(\rho + \sqrt{\rho\ell}\) and the second is \(\ell/\sqrt{\ell/\rho} = \sqrt{\rho\ell}\), and their sum is Equation 31.15.
The improved form. Putting \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\) into the improved conversion gives the bracket of Equation 31.16 at each order, and every order is valid.


For calibration you need the reverse: the largest \(\rho\) whose conversion stays within a target \(\varepsilon\) at a given \(\delta\). The simple \(\varepsilon\) grows with \(\rho\), and solving Equation 31.15 for \(\rho\) shows that the target is met by every \[\rho \le \Big(\sqrt{\varepsilon + \ln(1/\delta)} - \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\Big)^2. \tag{31.18}\] Keep budgets in \(\rho\) and convert once, at the end: \(\varepsilon\) grows like the square root of \(\rho\), so adding the \(\varepsilon\)’s of two halves of a budget overstates the whole.
How much do the conversions lose? The Gaussian answers this, because the zCDP line is exact for it, so any gap is the price of the conversion alone. After dividing by \(\sigma\), a \(\rho\)-zCDP Gaussian mechanism is the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\), and Theorem 20.3 gives its exact smallest \(\delta\) at each \(\varepsilon\) (Equation 20.17). At \(\rho = 0.5\) the simple formula is 21% too large (\(5.299/4.377 = 1.210\)), and the improved conversion 8% (\(4.728/4.377 = 1.080\)), and both gaps shrink as \(\rho\) grows (Figure 31.3). The part’s accountants minimize over a fixed list of orders, ORDERS, and the improved conversion on that list agrees with a fine grid to within \(0.001\) for \(\rho \le 1\).

Right: each conversion divided by the exact Gaussian value.




Example 31.3 \(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 1\) are \((k/2)\)-zCDP, since each costs \(\frac12\) and composition adds.
