title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.4 Group privacy
A household or a user with many records contributes several records at once. Group privacy asks how the guarantee degrades for datasets joined by a chain of \(m\) neighbouring steps, writing \(m\) because \(k\) counts composed mechanisms. For pure DP the answer is \(m\varepsilon\) (Theorem 19.2). For RDP the chain needs a triangle inequality, which the Rényi divergence lacks at a fixed order, so Mironov’s group bound gives up orders: for a group of \(2^c\), a curve value \(\varepsilon\) at order \(\alpha\) becomes \(3^c\varepsilon\) at order \(\alpha/2^c\) (Rényi DP). zCDP constrains every order at once, so it can pay for the chain with higher orders.
The proof walks along the chain one record at a time. Each step must pass from \(P\) to \(Q\) through an intermediate distribution \(R\), and the tool is a triangle-like inequality that pays for the detour with higher orders on the two legs (Bun & Steinke 2016, Lemma 5.2).

Lemma 31.2 (A triangle-like inequality for Rényi divergence) For distributions \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), every order \(\alpha > 1\) and every \(m > 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}D_{\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}}(P\|R) + D_{m\alpha}(R\|Q). \tag{31.19}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the sum that defines \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) as an average under \(R\) of a product of two ratios, split the product with Hölder’s inequality, and recognize each factor as a Rényi divergence of one leg.

Insert \(R\). Assume \(R\) is positive wherever \(P\) or \(Q\) is, since otherwise the right side is infinite. Multiplying out one term shows \(R \cdot P^\alpha R^{-\alpha} \cdot R^{\alpha - 1}Q^{1 - \alpha} = P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\). So the sum that defines the divergence is an average under \(R\) (Lemma 3.2), with the ratios evaluated at an output drawn from \(R\): \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \sum_y P(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1 - \alpha} = \mathbb E_R\big[(P/R)^\alpha(R/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\big]. \tag{31.20}\]
Split with Hölder. Hölder’s inequality bounds the average of a product of two positive variables \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) by a product of power means, for exponents \(u\) and \(v\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\): \[\mathbb E[X_1X_2] \le (\mathbb E[X_1^u])^{1/u}(\mathbb E[X_2^v])^{1/v}. \tag{31.21}\] The second average will be a divergence of order \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1\), so choose \(v = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha - 1}\) to make that order \(m\alpha\), and the matching \(u = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha(m - 1)}\). Then \[\mathbb E_R\big[(P/R)^\alpha(R/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\big] \le \big(\mathbb E_R[(P/R)^{u\alpha}]\big)^{1/u}\big(\mathbb E_R[(R/Q)^{v(\alpha - 1)}]\big)^{1/v}. \tag{31.22}\]
Recognize two divergences. Write \(\alpha_1 = u\alpha = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}\) and \(\alpha_2 = v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = m\alpha\). Multiplying out as in step 1, the first average is \(\sum_y R^{1 - \alpha_1}P^{\alpha_1} = e^{(\alpha_1 - 1)D_{\alpha_1}(P\|R)}\), and the second is \(\sum_y R^{\alpha_2}Q^{1 - \alpha_2} = e^{(\alpha_2 - 1)D_{\alpha_2}(R\|Q)}\).
Take logarithms and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). The second leg contributes \(D_{m\alpha}(R\|Q)\), since \((\alpha_2 - 1)/v = \alpha - 1\). The first contributes \(D_{\alpha_1}(P\|R)\) times \(\frac{\alpha_1 - 1}{u(\alpha - 1)}\). Since \(\alpha_1 - 1 = \frac{m(\alpha - 1)}{m - 1}\), that coefficient is \(\frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}\), which gives Equation 31.19.



Theorem 31.5 (Group privacy) If \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP and \(D\), \(D'\) are joined by a chain of \(m\) neighbouring steps, then for every \(\alpha > 1\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le m^2\rho\,\alpha, \tag{31.23}\] so \(M\) is \(m^2\rho\)-zCDP for groups of size \(m\) (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.9). The Gaussian mechanism attains the bound.


Proof. The proof is by induction on \(m\), and the case \(m = 1\) is the definition.

Split the chain. Let \(\hat D\) be \(m - 1\) steps from \(D\) and one step from \(D'\). Apply Equation 31.19 with \(P = M(D)\), \(R = M(\hat D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\).
The group of \(m - 1\). By the induction hypothesis at order \(\alpha_1 = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1}\), the first term is at most \(\frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1}(m - 1)^2\rho\,\alpha_1 = m(m - 1)\rho\alpha\). The factor \(m\alpha - 1\) in \(\alpha_1\) cancels the coefficient’s denominator.
The last step. The second term is a single neighbouring step, so \(\rho\)-zCDP at order \(m\alpha\) bounds it by \(m\rho\alpha\). The sum is \((m^2 - m + m)\rho\alpha = m^2\rho\alpha\).
Tightness. For the Gaussian mechanism a group of \(m\) shifts the mean by \(m\Delta_2 f\), so Equation 3.19 gives exactly \(\alpha m^2(\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2) = m^2\rho\alpha\).


The bound is quadratic in \(m\), which matches pure DP: with \(\rho \approx \varepsilon^2/2\), the group’s \(m^2\rho\) is about \((m\varepsilon)^2/2\). The RDP route multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by \(3^c\) while dividing the order by \(2^c\), so its slope is \(6^c\rho\) instead of \(m^2\rho = 4^c\rho\) (Table 31.4). The induction can raise the order at each step only because zCDP controls every order; a bound known only up to some order would run out.
Strong group privacy is also a weakness. Bun and Steinke use it to prove lower bounds on the sample size of zCDP algorithms as strong as those for pure DP. These rule out stability-based algorithms, which release an exact answer when the data are far from any dataset where it would change, and Section 31.5 weakens the definition to escape them.

Example 31.4 Table 31.4 takes the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\rho = 0.5\)) and groups of size \(m\). The RDP route starts from a high order, 64, where \(\varepsilon(64) = 0.5 \times 64 = 32\). For \(m = 2^c\) it gives order \(64/2^c\), \(\varepsilon = 3^c \times 32\) and slope \(6^c \times 0.5\). The triangle-like inequality is an equality along the chain of normals with means 0, 1 and 2, where both sides of Equation 31.19 are 6 at \(\alpha = 3\) and \(m = 2\).



Table 31.4: Group privacy of the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\). zCDP gives slope \(m^2\rho\) at every order, and its conversion is within about 8% of the exact value. Mironov’s RDP group bound, started from order 64, gives slope \(6^c\rho\) and only on orders up to \(64/m\).

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.5 Approximate zCDP
Some useful mechanisms are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but not zCDP at all. Propose-test-release and stability-based histograms are of this kind: they fail with probability about \(\delta\). The lower bounds of Section 31.4 rule them out of zCDP, yet you still want them in one budget with Gaussian steps. Bun and Steinke’s answer is to let zCDP fail on an event of small probability.

Definition 31.2 (Approximate zCDP) A mechanism \(M\) is \(\delta\)-approximately \(\rho\)-zCDP if, for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), there are events \(E\) and \(E'\) of probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for the runs on \(D\) and on \(D'\), such that for every \(\alpha > 1\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)|_E\,\|\,M(D')|_{E'}\big) \le \rho\alpha \quad\text{and}\quad D_\alpha\big(M(D')|_{E'}\,\|\,M(D)|_E\big) \le \rho\alpha. \tag{31.24}\] Here \(M(D)|_E\) is the output distribution conditioned on \(E\), and the events may depend on the mechanism’s internal randomness, not only on its output (Bun & Steinke 2016, Definition 1.12).

Three properties make it a ledger with two columns, \(\rho\) and the probability \(\delta_a\) that zCDP fails.

Proposition 31.3 (The approximate zCDP ledger)  

An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \(\delta\)-approximately \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.13 and Corollary 8.7).
A \(\delta_1\)-approximately \(\rho_1\)-zCDP step followed by a \(\delta_2\)-approximately \(\rho_2\)-zCDP step is \((\delta_1 + \delta_2 - \delta_1\delta_2)\)-approximately \((\rho_1 + \rho_2)\)-zCDP (their Lemma 8.2). For many steps the failure probability is \(1 - \prod_i(1 - \delta_i) \le \sum_i\delta_i\).
A \(\delta_a\)-approximately \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta')\)-DP, where \(\varepsilon\) is any conversion of \(\rho\)-zCDP at \(\delta'\) (their Lemma 8.8).



Proof. The first two parts have short reasons. For the third, the usual conversion applies on the good event, and the bad event can add at most its probability.

Absorbing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP pair behaves, with probability \(1 - \delta\), like an \(\varepsilon\)-DP pair, which Theorem 31.2 turns into \(\varepsilon^2/2\). Section J.2 in the appendices derives the decomposition and the composition of mixed pipelines.
Composition. The conditioned mechanisms compose as zCDP (Theorem 31.1), and both good events hold with probability at least \((1 - \delta_1)(1 - \delta_2) = 1 - (\delta_1 + \delta_2 - \delta_1\delta_2)\).
Split on the event. Let \(\Pr[E], \Pr[E'] \ge 1 - \delta_a\), fix a set \(S\) of outputs, and write \(P_E(S) = \Pr[M(D) \in S \mid E]\). The probability of \(S\) outside \(E\) is at most 1, so \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le P_E(S)\Pr[E] + 1 - \Pr[E] = 1 - \Pr[E](1 - P_E(S)). \tag{31.25}\] This bound shrinks as \(\Pr[E]\) grows, so it is at most its value \(P_E(S)(1 - \delta_a) + \delta_a\) at the smallest allowed \(\Pr[E]\).
Use the conditional zCDP. The conditioned pair is \(\rho\)-zCDP, so \(P_E(S) \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E'] + \delta'\).
Remove the conditioning on \(D'\). Dropping the outputs outside \(E'\) can only lower a probability, so \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \ge (1 - \delta_a)\Pr[M(D') \in S \mid E']\).
Combine. Putting step 4 into step 3 and using step 5 gives \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + (1 - \delta_a)\delta' + \delta_a. \tag{31.26}\]


The \(\rho\) column composes like zCDP, so after conversion \(\varepsilon\) grows like the square root of the number of steps, while the \(\delta_a\) column adds up like \(\delta\) in basic composition. The ledger is worth keeping only when some steps are genuinely \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and not zCDP.

Example 31.5 A pipeline runs 10 stability-based steps, each \((0.5, 10^{-7})\)-DP, and 10 Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 1\). Each stability step enters the \(\rho\) column as \(0.5^2/2 = 0.125\) and the \(\delta_a\) column as \(10^{-7}\). The totals are \(\rho = 10 \times 0.125 + 10 \times 0.5 = 6.25\) and \(\delta_a = 1 - (1 - 10^{-7})^{10} = 1.0000 \times 10^{-6}\). The improved conversion at \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - \delta_a\) gives \(\varepsilon = 22.100\), with total \(\delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta' \le 10^{-5}\). Without the ledger you would convert the Gaussians alone to \(\varepsilon = 19.119\) at the remaining \(\delta = 10^{-5} - 10^{-6} = 9 \times 10^{-6}\) and add the stability steps by basic composition, for \(19.119 + 5 = 24.119\). The ledger saves about 2, because each \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) step costs \(\varepsilon^2/2\) in \(\rho\), not \(\varepsilon\).

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.6 Subsampling, and truncated CDP
DP-SGD, the running example of this part, runs each step on a Poisson sample of the data, in which each record is used independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate. Subsampling makes a step much more private than the Gaussian it contains, because a record is usually not in the batch. This section asks whether zCDP sees that gain, and what to do when it does not.
Take add/remove neighbours, sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma\), in one dimension, which is enough because only the shift along the record’s direction carries evidence. Without the record the step outputs \(Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). With it, the record is in the sample with probability \(q\), shifting the mean by 1, so the output is the mixture \(P = (1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The RDP curve is \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\), because the other order is never larger (Amplification by subsampling, Equation 33.17; Section L.1). On integer orders it has a closed form. The divergence averages a product of \(\alpha\) likelihood ratios, as if the step ran \(\alpha\) times, and the term \(j\) below collects the runs in which the record was sampled \(j\) times.

Lemma 31.3 (The subsampled Gaussian on integer orders) For every integer \(\alpha \ge 2\), the curve is a binomial sum: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha, \qquad A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^{\alpha}\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big) \tag{31.27}\] (Mironov, Talwar & Zhang 2019).


Proof. 

Write the ratio. Let \(r\) be the likelihood ratio of \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) to \(Q\). Then \(P/Q = 1 - q + q\,r\), and writing the divergence as an average under \(Q\) of the ratio to the power \(\alpha\) (Proposition 3.1) gives \(A_\alpha = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \mathbb E_Q[(1 - q + q\,r)^\alpha]\).
Expand. For integer \(\alpha\), the binomial theorem expands the power into the terms \(\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\,\mathbb E_Q[r^j]\).
Each moment. By the same form of Proposition 3.1, \(\mathbb E_Q[r^j] = e^{(j - 1)D_j}\) for the two normals, and Equation 3.19 gives \(D_j = j/(2\sigma^2)\), so the moment is \(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}\).



Proposition 31.4 (No amplification for zCDP) For the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with any \(q \in (0, 1]\), the smallest \(\rho\) with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha > 1\) is \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), the same as without subsampling. On integer orders the curve obeys \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \ge \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{31.28}\]


Proof. Write \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\) for the slope without subsampling. The plan is to show that \(\rho_0\) is enough, because subsampling never hurts, and that nothing smaller is enough, because at large orders subsampling stops helping.

Upper bound, by convexity. The ratio \(1 - q + q\,r\) is an average of 1 and \(r\), and \(x \mapsto x^\alpha\) is convex, so the \(\alpha\)-th power of that average is at most \((1 - q) + q\,r^\alpha\). Averaging under \(Q\), with \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha] = e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}\) from the Gaussian curve, gives \[A_\alpha \le 1 - q + q\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}. \tag{31.29}\] An average of 1 and a number at least 1 is at most that number, so \(A_\alpha \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}\), that is \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \rho_0\alpha\).
The other order. zCDP needs both orders of the pair, so \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\) needs the same bound. The sum \(\sum_y V(y)(U(y)/V(y))^\alpha\) is jointly convex in the pair of distributions \((U, V)\): its value at a mixture of pairs is at most the mixture of its values (Section F.5 proves it). Writing \((Q, P)\) as the mixture \((1 - q)(Q, Q) + q\,(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2))\), and using the Gaussian curve for the second pair, gives the same bound.
Lower bound, by one term. Every term of Equation 31.27 is positive, so keeping only \(j = \alpha\), the runs in which the record was always sampled, gives \(A_\alpha \ge q^\alpha e^{(\alpha^2 - \alpha)\rho_0}\). Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation 31.28.
Let the order grow. Dividing Equation 31.28 by \(\alpha\) gives \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha \ge \rho_0 + \ln q/(\alpha - 1)\), which tends to \(\rho_0\), because the penalty for a rarely sampled record, \(\ln q/(\alpha - 1)\), vanishes as the order grows. So a line above the whole curve needs \(\rho \ge \rho_0\), and step 1 shows that \(\rho_0\) suffices.


The curve bends, and a line cannot (Figure 31.4). For \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), the curve up to \(\alpha = 8\) is tiny and almost linear, with slope close to \(q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2 = 8.5914 \times 10^{-5}\). Expanding \((1 + q(r - 1))^\alpha\) in powers of \(q\) instead, the linear term averages to 0, so \(A_\alpha - 1\) starts with \(\binom\alpha2 q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and dividing its logarithm by \(\alpha - 1\) gives that slope. Between \(\alpha = 8\) and \(\alpha = 16\) the curve jumps by more than three orders of magnitude, and beyond that it follows Equation 31.28, which turns positive at \(\alpha = 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q) = 10.21\). A line above the whole curve needs the slope \(\rho_0 = 0.5\). A line that only has to clear the curve up to \(\alpha = 8\) can have slope \(1.1171 \times 10^{-4}\), which is \(4476\) times smaller.
Only the small orders matter for DP-SGD. After \(T\) steps the curve \(T\varepsilon(\alpha)\) stays small up to the bend, while the conversion’s term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) falls with the order, so Mironov’s and the improved conversion both pick an order just below the bend, \(\alpha = 4\) on the integer orders of ORDERS. The large orders that set the zCDP slope are never used.






Figure 31.4: The RDP curve of one Poisson-subsampled Gaussian step with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on integer orders (black), against the best zCDP line \(\rho\alpha\) with \(\rho = 1/(2\sigma^2) = 0.5\) (red dashed), which is the unsubsampled Gaussian’s line \(\alpha/2\), and the tCDP line on orders up to \(\omega = 8\) (blue). Both axes are logarithmic.




Definition 31.3 (Truncated concentrated differential privacy) A mechanism is \((\rho, \omega)\)-tCDP if, for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all orders \(\alpha \in (1, \omega)\) below the cut-off \(\omega > 1\), \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\alpha \tag{31.30}\] (Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke 2018, Definition 1). Plain zCDP is the case \(\omega = \infty\).

Composition and conversion work as for zCDP, on the covered orders.

Proposition 31.5 (Composition and conversion of tCDP) A \((\rho_1, \omega_1)\)-tCDP step followed by a \((\rho_2, \omega_2)\)-tCDP step is \((\rho_1 + \rho_2, \min(\omega_1, \omega_2))\)-tCDP (their Lemma 2). A \((\rho, \omega)\)-tCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \begin{cases}\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)} & \text{if } \ln(1/\delta) \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho,\\[2pt] \rho\omega + \dfrac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\omega - 1} & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \tag{31.31}\] (their Lemma 6).


Proof. 

Composition. On orders below both cut-offs the two curves add (Rényi DP), and above the smaller cut-off one of them says nothing.
The endpoint counts. \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing and lower semicontinuous in \(\alpha\), so \(D_\omega \le \lim_{\alpha \uparrow \omega}D_\alpha \le \rho\omega\), and Mironov’s conversion may use every order in \((1, \omega]\).
Constrained minimum. As in Theorem 31.4, the conversion is the convex function \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). If its minimizer \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\) is at most \(\omega\), which is the first condition, it gives Equation 31.15. Otherwise \(g\) decreases on all of \((1, \omega]\), since a convex function decreases before its minimizer, and the best order is \(\omega\).


Unlike zCDP, tCDP is amplified by subsampling, provided the cut-off stays below about \(\ln(1/q)/\rho\). The theorem uses sampling of a fixed size, not the Poisson sampling of DP-SGD, so it is a guide rather than an accountant here.

Theorem 31.6 (Subsampling amplifies tCDP) Let \(\rho, q \in (0, 0.1]\) with \(\ln(1/q) \ge 3\rho(2 + \log_2(1/\rho))\), and let \(M\) be \((\rho, \omega')\)-tCDP with \(\omega' \ge \ln(1/q)/(2\rho) \ge 3\). Running \(M\) on a uniformly random subset of a fraction \(q\) of the records, of fixed size and without replacement, is \((13q^2\rho, \omega)\)-tCDP with \(\omega = \ln(1/q)/(4\rho)\) (Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke 2018, Theorem 11).


The proof, in Section 3 of that paper, expands the Rényi sum of the two mixtures in powers of \(q\). The second-order term carries the factor \(q^2\), and the higher terms can be controlled only up to orders of about \(\ln(1/q)/\rho\), which is where the cut-off comes from. Because the theorem covers every tCDP mechanism, its constant 13 is generous: with \(\sigma = \sqrt5\) and \(q = 0.01\) its \(\rho\) is about 11 times what the subsampled curve needs.

title: 31  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
31.9 References

Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016; arXiv:1605.02065). The source for this chapter: the definition (1.1), the Gaussian (1.6), pure DP to zCDP (1.4, proved as 3.3), conversion (1.3, 3.5, 3.6), group privacy (1.9, 5.3), approximate zCDP (1.12, Section 8), and the lower bounds. Read Sections 1–3 first.
Dwork & Rothblum, “Concentrated Differential Privacy” (2016, arXiv:1603.01887). The original two-parameter definition and its motivation from advanced composition.
Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke, “Composable and Versatile Privacy via Truncated CDP” (STOC 2018). Truncated CDP: definition, composition, conversion (Lemma 6), amplification by subsampling (Theorem 11) and the sinh-normal mechanism.
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020). The discrete Gaussian and its zCDP guarantee, and the improved conversion from RDP and zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) (Proposition 12, Corollary 13), with a numerically stable way to compute it.
Cesar & Rogers, “Bounding, Concentrating, and Truncating: Unifying Privacy Loss Composition for Data Analytics” (Algorithmic Learning Theory 2021). Composition of pure DP, bounded-range (exponential mechanism) and CDP steps in one analysis, including the \(\varepsilon^2/8\) bound for bounded-range mechanisms.
Durfee & Rogers, “Practical Differentially Private Top-k Selection with Pay-what-you-get Composition” (NeurIPS 2019). Introduces the bounded-range property of the exponential mechanism.
Dong, Durfee & Rogers, “Optimal Differential Privacy Composition for Exponential Mechanisms” (ICML 2020). Exact composition of bounded-range mechanisms, and the mean bound that Cesar & Rogers use.
Mironov, “Rényi Differential Privacy” (CSF 2017). The RDP framework this chapter restricts to lines, and the RDP group-privacy bound used for comparison.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (2019, arXiv:1908.10530). The subsampled-Gaussian curve Equation 31.27.
Abowd et al., “The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2022; arXiv:2204.08986). zCDP accounting with the discrete Gaussian at national scale, and the role of invariants.

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.1 f-DP
Every privacy definition in this part answers one question. How well can an adversary who sees the output of a mechanism \(M\) tell whether it ran on a dataset \(D\) or on a neighbour \(D'\) with one record added or removed? Differential privacy (DP) in its \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form answers with two numbers, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) with a curve over orders \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP), and concentrated DP with one number \(\rho\) (concentrated DP). But Part 1 already gave the complete answer. It is the trade-off function, which gives for each rate of false alarms the smallest rate of misses any test can reach (Hypothesis testing). This chapter makes that curve the privacy guarantee itself.
The one idea is that the whole trade-off curve between \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) is the most informative description of a mechanism’s privacy, and every other notion is a lossy summary of it. Two facts make the curve practical. Gaussian noise gives a one-parameter family of curves \(G_\mu\) that is closed under composition, and a central limit theorem (CLT) says that composing many mechanisms that each leak little gives a curve close to some \(G_\mu\).
Throughout, \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are the two output distributions. Their densities, or probabilities for discrete outputs, are written \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\), since the letter \(q\) is kept for the sampling rate. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\). The Rényi order needs the letter \(\alpha\), so this chapter writes the type I and type II errors of a test as its false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and false negative rate \(\mathrm{FNR}\).
The running example is a count released with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1, so one record moves the centre of the output by one standard deviation. An attacker who accepts 5% false positives then misses the record with probability 0.7405, and the release is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP (Section 32.3 derives both numbers). The last sections carry the same reasoning to private training, with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\) and up to 10,000 steps.
A definition of privacy should say what an adversary cannot do. The strongest such statement bounds the adversary’s type II error at every type I error from below: however it tunes its test, it must miss at least this often. That bound is a curve, so the definition takes a curve as its parameter.
A test \(\phi\) looks at the output \(y\) and fires, deciding that the data was \(D'\), with probability \(\phi(y)\). So \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathbb E_P[\phi]\) and \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathbb E_Q[\phi]\). The trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\) gives the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) at each \(\mathrm{FPR}\) (Definition 4.2). Part 1 proved that it is non-increasing, convex, continuous and at most \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) (Theorem 4.2). Every function with these properties is the curve of some pair (Section K.1 in the appendices), and is called a trade-off function.
The definition is Dong, Roth & Su’s (2022, Definition 2.3), cited as Dong et al. from here on, and the curve inequality holds at every \(\mathrm{FPR}\). The old definition is a special case of it, because Part 3 proved that \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when the curve of every neighbouring pair lies above two straight lines (Theorem 18.3), \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\mathrm{FPR}) = \max\big(0,\; 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR},\; e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big). \tag{32.2}\] So \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\)-DP (Wasserman & Zhou 2010; Dong et al., Proposition 2.5). The second line is the first reflected across the diagonal \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathrm{FNR}\), and setting \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}\) shows that they meet there at \(\mathrm{FPR} = \frac{1 - \delta}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\). The curve starts at \(1 - \delta\) on the \(\mathrm{FNR}\)-axis, not at 1, and that gap is what \(\delta\) means: a test may catch \(D'\) with probability \(\delta\) at no cost in false alarms.
Because the neighbouring relation is symmetric, a guarantee for \((D, D')\) also holds for \((D', D)\), and the next result turns that into a guarantee with the reflected curve. The inverse \(f^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}) = \inf\{t \in [0, 1] : f(t) \le \mathrm{FPR}\}\) has the graph of \(f\) reflected across the diagonal. A curve with \(f = f^{-1}\) is symmetric, as \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) is.
Post-processing can only raise the curve, and Blackwell’s theorem (Dong et al., Theorem 2.10) gives the converse: \(T(P, Q) \le T(P', Q')\) exactly when some randomized map sends \(P\) to \(P'\) and \(Q\) to \(Q'\) at once. A divergence also shrinks under such maps, but it is one number computed from the pair, so it is a coarser summary than the curve.

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
Definition 32.1 (f-DP) Let \(f\) be a trade-off function. A mechanism \(M\) is \(f\)-differentially private (\(f\)-DP) if no neighbouring pair is easier to tell apart than \(f\) allows, \[T\big(M(D), M(D')\big) \ge f \quad\text{for all neighbours } D \sim D'. \tag{32.1}\]




Proposition 32.1 (Symmetry and post-processing) If \(M\) is \(f\)-DP, then \(M\) is \(\max(f, f^{-1})\)-DP. If \(K\) is a randomized map that does not look at the data, the mechanism that outputs \(K(M(D))\) is also \(f\)-DP.


Proof. 

Swap the roles. Since \(D' \sim D\) is also a neighbouring pair, \(T(Q, P) \ge f\). A test \(\phi\) of \(P\) against \(Q\) with errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) gives the opposite test \(1 - \phi\) of \(Q\) against \(P\), whose errors are \((\mathrm{FNR}, \mathrm{FPR})\). So \(T(Q, P)\) is the inverse of \(T(P, Q)\).
Reflect. A curve lies above \(f\) when its achievable error pairs sit inside the region above \(f\), and reflecting both regions across the diagonal keeps that inclusion. So \(T(Q, P) \ge f\) turns into \(T(P, Q) \ge f^{-1}\), and with \(T(P, Q) \ge f\) this gives \(\max(f, f^{-1})\). That maximum keeps all four properties of a trade-off function.
Post-processing. A test \(\phi\) on the processed output is the test \(y \mapsto \mathbb E[\phi(K(y))]\) on the raw output, with the same two errors. So the curve after processing is no lower than before (Dong et al., Lemma 2.9).




Example 32.1 Three mechanisms carry the label “\(\varepsilon = 1\)”. Binary randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\) reports the true bit with probability \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\) (randomized response). With bit 0 under \(D\) and 1 under \(D'\), the only useful test fires on output 1, with \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathrm{FNR} = 0.2689\). Mixing it with “never fire” and “always fire” gives a curve with one corner at \((0.2689, 0.2689)\), exactly the corner \(1/(1 + e)\) of \(f_{1,0}\). title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.2 Gaussian differential privacy
The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse of private machine learning, so its curve deserves a name. This section shows that Gaussian noise always produces one of Part 1’s Gaussian curves, a family with one parameter. Using that family as the yardstick gives Gaussian differential privacy (GDP), a one-number definition that is exact for the Gaussian mechanism.
Part 1 found the curve of two shifted normals (Theorem 4.3). The best test of \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) fires when the output exceeds a threshold, and it misses when a draw from the shifted normal stays below it. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function and \(\Phi^{-1}\) for its inverse.

Definition 32.2 (Gaussian differential privacy) For \(\mu \ge 0\), the Gaussian trade-off function is \[G_\mu(\mathrm{FPR}) = T\big(\mathcal N(0, 1), \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\big)(\mathrm{FPR}) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big). \tag{32.3}\] A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP if it is \(G_\mu\)-DP (Dong et al., Definition 2.6).

The Gaussian mechanism releases a vector, while Part 1’s curve is for one number. The proof that the mechanism is GDP needs a step that reduces the vector to one number, and the next lemma provides it. With independent noise of equal variance in every coordinate, only the direction of the shift carries evidence.

Lemma 32.1 (A Gaussian shift in d dimensions is a shift in one) Let \(I_d\) be the \(d \times d\) identity matrix. For every \(m \in \mathbb R^d\), \[T\big(\mathcal N(0, I_d), \mathcal N(m, I_d)\big) = G_{\|m\|_2}. \tag{32.4}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that the likelihood ratio depends on one number, find that number’s law, and read off Part 1’s curve.

Write the likelihood ratio. Expanding \(\|y - m\|^2 = \|y\|^2 - 2\langle m, y\rangle + \|m\|^2\) in the two normal densities cancels \(\|y\|^2\), which leaves \[\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = \exp\Big(\langle m, y\rangle - \frac12\|m\|^2\Big). \tag{32.5}\]
One number decides. The ratio depends on \(y\) only through \(s = \langle m, y\rangle/\|m\|\), the projection of \(y\) on the direction of the shift. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1) the best tests are thresholds on \(s\).
Find the law of \(s\). The inner product of a unit vector with a standard normal vector is standard normal, since its variance is the squared length of the unit vector. So \(s \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) under the first hypothesis, and the mean \(m\) adds \(\langle m, m\rangle/\|m\| = \|m\|\) under the second.
Read off the curve. Every best test is a threshold test of \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\|m\|, 1)\), whose curve is \(G_{\|m\|}\) by Theorem 4.3.


In two dimensions the best boundary is perpendicular to the shift (Figure 32.3, left). The Gaussian mechanism adds noise to a query, written \(g\) because \(f\) already names a trade-off function. Write \(\Delta_2 g\) for its \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the largest \(\|g(D) - g(D')\|_2\) over neighbours, and \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier, the noise standard deviation in units of \(\Delta_2 g\).

Theorem 32.1 (The Gaussian mechanism is GDP) The mechanism \(M(D) = g(D) + \mathcal N\big(0, \sigma^2(\Delta_2 g)^2 I\big)\) is \(1/\sigma\)-GDP. This is tight: a neighbouring pair with \(\|g(D) - g(D')\|_2 = \Delta_2 g\) has trade-off function exactly \(G_{1/\sigma}\).


Proof. The plan is to turn the two outputs into the pair of Lemma 32.1 by invertible maps, which cannot change any test’s errors, and read off the shift.

Standardize and centre. Divide the output by \(\sigma\Delta_2 g\) and subtract \(g(D)/(\sigma\Delta_2 g)\). Both maps can be undone, so no test’s errors change. Now \(P = \mathcal N(0, I)\), and Lemma 32.1 gives \(T(P, Q) = G_\nu\) with \(\nu = \|g(D) - g(D')\|_2/(\sigma\Delta_2 g)\).
Bound the shift. By the definition of sensitivity, \(\nu \le 1/\sigma\).
Compare curves. \(G_\mu\) decreases as \(\mu\) grows, because \(\Phi\) is increasing, so \(G_\nu \ge G_{1/\sigma}\) for every neighbouring pair.
Tightness. A pair at full sensitivity has \(\nu = 1/\sigma\) and gives equality.


For the Gaussian mechanism, \(\mu\)-GDP is not a bound with slack; it is the curve, and every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair follows from it (Section 32.3). The parameter \(\mu\) is the distance between the two output means in units of the noise standard deviation, set by the worst pair. Doubling it to \(\mu = 2\) cuts the miss rate of the best test at a 5% false-alarm rate from 0.7405 to 0.3612. Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing (their discussion after Definition 2.6).

Example 32.2 A count query has \(\Delta_2 g = 1\), since adding or removing one record changes the count by 1. Released with \(\sigma = 1\) it is 1-GDP, and with \(\sigma = 4\) it is 0.25-GDP. For \(\sigma = 1\), Table 32.2 evaluates \(G_1\). At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.01\), for example, the threshold is \(\Phi^{-1}(0.99) = 2.3263\), and subtracting the shift gives \(G_1(0.01) = \Phi(1.3263) = 0.9076\).

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.3 Duality with (ε, δ)
Regulators, papers and libraries report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). So you need to turn a curve into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs without losing anything, and you need the profile of \(\mu\)-GDP in closed form. This section does both.
The idea is geometric. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee is the line \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}\) and its mirror image, and a curve satisfies it when it lies above the line. For a slope \(-e^\varepsilon\), the smallest \(\delta\) that works is the one where the line just touches the curve. The line of slope \(u\) through the point \((\mathrm{FPR}, f(\mathrm{FPR}))\) meets the \(\mathrm{FNR}\)-axis at \(f(\mathrm{FPR}) - u\,\mathrm{FPR}\), and the touching line has the lowest of these intercepts. Minus that intercept is the convex conjugate \[f^*(u) = \sup_{\mathrm{FPR} \in [0, 1]}\big(u\,\mathrm{FPR} - f(\mathrm{FPR})\big). \tag{32.6}\]

Theorem 32.2 (Duality between f-DP and (ε, δ)-DP) Let \(f\) be a symmetric trade-off function. A mechanism is \(f\)-DP if and only if it is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), where \[\delta(\varepsilon) = 1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon). \tag{32.7}\] For any pair \(P, Q\), symmetric or not, \(1 + T(P, Q)^*(-e^\varepsilon)\) is the hockey-stick divergence \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\), the largest amount by which an event’s probability under \(Q\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under \(P\).


Proof. The plan is to find the smallest \(\delta\) for one line, show that the lines rebuild the curve, and identify the conjugate as a divergence (Dong et al., Propositions 2.11 and 2.12).

One pair is one line. By Equation 32.2, \(f \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) requires \(\delta \ge 1 - f(\mathrm{FPR}) - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}\) for every \(\mathrm{FPR}\). The smallest such \(\delta\) is the supremum of the right side, which is \(1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon)\). The mirror line gives the same condition, because \(f\) is symmetric.
\(f\)-DP implies every \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\). If \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f\) and \(f \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\), then \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)}\).
The lines rebuild the curve. The line for \(\varepsilon\) touches \(f\) where its slope is \(-e^\varepsilon\), and as \(\varepsilon\) runs over \([0, \infty)\) these slopes cover every value from \(-1\) down. A symmetric curve crosses the diagonal with slope \(-1\), or at a corner whose slopes include \(-1\), and is steeper to its left, so the lines and their mirror images touch every point. A convex function is the supremum of its touching lines, so \(\sup_{\varepsilon} f_{\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon)} = f\), and a mechanism with every \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\) has \(T \ge f\).
The conjugate is a hockey-stick divergence. If each detection of \(D'\) earns one unit and each false alarm costs \(\gamma \ge 1\), a test’s gain is \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} - \gamma\,\mathrm{FPR} = \int\phi\,(Q - \gamma P)\). The best test fires exactly where \(Q > \gamma P\) and gains \(E_\gamma(Q\|P)\), by Part 1’s best event (Lemma 3.4) with \(Q\) in the place of \(P\). The same maximum can be taken in two stages: at each \(\mathrm{FPR}\) the largest power is \(1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\), and then the best \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is chosen, so \[\max_{\mathrm{FPR} \in [0, 1]}\big(1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}) - \gamma\,\mathrm{FPR}\big) = E_\gamma(Q\|P). \tag{32.8}\] With \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) the left side is \(1 + f^*(-e^\varepsilon)\).


The whole privacy profile \(\varepsilon \mapsto \delta(\varepsilon)\) loses nothing, because its lines rebuild the curve, while one point keeps only one touching line (Figure 32.2, right). So “1-GDP” is stronger than “\((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP”, the point the example below computes: at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\) the single point allows \(\mathrm{FNR} = e^{-4.3772}(1 - 10^{-5} - 0.1) = 0.0113\), while \(G_1(0.1) = 0.6109\).
For \(G_\mu\) the touching point has a closed form, found with Part 1’s slope rule: the slope of a curve at a test’s threshold \(\tau\) is minus the likelihood ratio there (Proposition 4.1). The result is the exact Gaussian profile that Part 3 derived as a hockey-stick divergence (Theorem 20.3), and Section D.5 in the appendices derives it from the threshold test in plain steps.

Corollary 32.1 (The privacy profile of μ-GDP) A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP if and only if it is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), with \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{32.9}\]


Proof. The plan is to check that Theorem 32.2 applies, find the test where \(G_\mu\) has slope \(-e^\varepsilon\), and read off its errors (Dong et al., Corollary 2.13).

The curve is symmetric. The reflection \(y \mapsto \mu - y\) swaps \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), and swapping the pair inverts the curve (Proposition 32.1, step 1), so \(G_\mu = G_\mu^{-1}\) and \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the maximum of \(1 - G_\mu(\mathrm{FPR}) - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}\).
Find the touching point. That expression is concave, so its maximum is where \(G_\mu' = -e^\varepsilon\). By Proposition 4.1 this happens where the likelihood ratio \(Q/P\) at the threshold, \(e^{\mu\tau - \mu^2/2}\) by step 1 of the proof of Lemma 32.1, equals \(e^\varepsilon\), so \[\tau = \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}. \tag{32.10}\]
Read off the errors. The test fires when \(y > \tau\), so \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = \Phi(-\tau)\), and its power is \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}^* = \Phi(\mu - \tau)\).
Substitute. Putting these into \(\delta = 1 - \mathrm{FNR}^* - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}^*\) gives Equation 32.9.


At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the profile is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), the total variation (TV) distance, which is the best \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \mathrm{FNR}\) of any test (Theorem 4.5). For small \(\delta\), the first term of Equation 32.9 must be a small normal tail, which needs \(\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\) of about \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). So the \(\varepsilon\) you pay grows roughly like \(\mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). At \(\mu = 1\), the targets \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-5}\) and \(10^{-6}\) give \(\varepsilon\) = 3.8044, 4.3772 and 4.8866, and at \(\mu = 2\) the increments are about twice as large.

Example 32.3 For the running example, \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) put the touching threshold at \(\tau = 1.5000\). The best test there has type I error \(\Phi(-1.5) = 0.066807\) and power \(\Phi(-0.5) = 0.308538\), so \(\delta(1) = 0.308538 - e \times 0.066807 = 0.308538 - 0.181601 = 0.126937\). Part 3’s Table 20.4 has the same two numbers as the probability under \(P\) that the loss exceeds 1 and \(e\) times that probability under \(Q\); here they are the best test’s power and the price of its false alarms. Maximizing \(1 - G_1(\mathrm{FPR}) - e\,\mathrm{FPR}\) over a grid of 20,001 values gives the same 0.126937, at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.0668\).
Going from a target \(\delta\) to \(\varepsilon\) has no closed form. But \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) decreases in \(\varepsilon\), so the chapter’s script (Section 32.8) solves for it by bisection (Table 32.3).

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.4 Composition
Training runs a mechanism thousands of times on the same data. Composing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees directly is lossy (composition). This section shows that composing curves is exact, and that for Gaussian curves it is a one-line formula.
An adversary who sees two outputs, drawn with independent randomness, faces a pair of joint distributions: \(P_1 \times P_2\), both drawn on \(D\), against \(Q_1 \times Q_2\), both drawn on \(D'\). The curve of that pair defines the composition of curves.

Definition 32.3 (Tensor product) The tensor product of trade-off functions \(f_1 = T(P_1, Q_1)\) and \(f_2 = T(P_2, Q_2)\) is \(f_1 \otimes f_2 = T(P_1 \times P_2, Q_1 \times Q_2)\).

It does not depend on which pairs represent \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) (Dong et al., Definition 3.1; Section K.2 in the appendices proves it). The theorem below says that this product is the exact guarantee of a composition. Its Gaussian case follows from Lemma 32.1, because independent Gaussian coordinates form a Gaussian vector.

Theorem 32.3 (Composition of f-DP) If each mechanism \(M_i\) is \(f_i\)-DP, even when it is chosen adaptively from the earlier outputs, then \((M_1, \dots, M_k)\) is \(f_1 \otimes \dots \otimes f_k\)-DP, and no better bound holds in general. For Gaussian curves the shifts add like the sides of a right-angled triangle: \[G_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes G_{\mu_k} = G_\mu, \qquad \mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}. \tag{32.11}\]


Proof. The plan is to prove the non-adaptive case through Blackwell’s theorem, cite the adaptive case, show tightness, and compute the Gaussian product (Dong et al., Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3).

Non-adaptive composition. Let \((\tilde P_i, \tilde Q_i)\) be a pair whose curve is exactly \(f_i\). Since \(f_i \le T(P_i, Q_i)\), the pair with the lower curve can be processed into the other: by Blackwell’s theorem some randomized map \(K_i\) sends \(\tilde P_i\) to \(P_i\) and \(\tilde Q_i\) to \(Q_i\). Applied to the coordinates independently, the maps send the product pair \((\prod\tilde P_i, \prod\tilde Q_i)\) to \((\prod P_i, \prod Q_i)\). Post-processing cannot help a test (Proposition 32.1), so \(T(\prod P_i, \prod Q_i) \ge \bigotimes f_i\).
Adaptive composition. When \(M_2\) depends on the output of \(M_1\), step 1 does not apply. Instead, fix the first output and look at the attacker’s test on the second. Replacing it by the best test of a fixed pair with curve \(f_2\), at the same type I error, keeps that error and does not raise the type II error, because \(M_2\) is \(f_2\)-DP on every branch. So the attacker does no better than on the product pair. Section K.2 in the appendices derives this step by step, as Dong et al. do in their Appendix C.
Tightness. If the mechanisms ignore each other and some neighbouring pair attains each \(f_i\), the composed pair is the product pair.
Gaussian curves. \(\bigotimes G_{\mu_i}\) is the curve of \(\mathcal N(0, I_k)\) against \(\mathcal N(m, I_k)\) with \(m = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k)\). By Lemma 32.1 this is \(G_{\|m\|_2}\).


Under composition \(\mu^2\) adds, just as variances of independent noises add. Full-batch noisy gradient descent with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) composes \(T\) mechanisms that are each \(1/\sigma\)-GDP, so it is \(\sqrt T/\sigma\)-GDP, and by step 3 no accountant can improve on that. Zero-concentrated DP is the same arithmetic with \(\rho = \mu^2/2\) (concentrated DP), but \(\mu\) gives the exact curve and \(\rho\) only an RDP bound on it (Section 32.7).
For other curves the tensor product is hard. For \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) curves it is the optimal composition theorem (Theorem 21.4). When the \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) differ, computing it exactly is #P-complete (Murtagh & Vadhan 2016), a class of counting problems believed to have no efficient algorithm. So numerical accountants compute \(\bigotimes f_i\) another way. The composed privacy loss is the sum of the per-step losses (Lemma 21.2), so the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountants of numerical accounting discretize its law and convolve.

Example 32.4 By Equation 32.11, two releases of the running example compose to \(G_{\sqrt 2} = G_{1.4142}\), and four to \(G_2\). A hundred releases with \(\sigma = 10\) give \(G_{\sqrt{100 \times 0.01}} = G_1\). A simulation of the threshold test on the projection, with \(\mu = (1, 1)\) at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.05\) gives \(\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}} = 0.0497\) and \(\widehat{\mathrm{FNR}} = 0.5913\), against \(G_{\sqrt2}(0.05) = 0.5912\). That sits between one release, \(G_1(0.05) = 0.7405\), and one release with twice the shift, \(G_2(0.05) = 0.3612\) (Figure 32.3).
Curves of the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) family, by contrast, leave that family under composition. Run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on the same bit twice, the product Part 3 read as a sum of privacy losses (Table 21.1). The output 00 has probability \(e^2/(1 + e)^2 = 0.5344\) under \(P\) (bit 0) and \(1/(1 + e)^2 = 0.0723\) under \(Q\) (bit 1), and Table 32.4 lists all four outputs.

The best tests add outcomes in decreasing order of \(Q/P\), each raising \(\mathrm{FPR}\) by its \(P\) and lowering \(\mathrm{FNR}\) by its \(Q\). So \(f_{1,0}\otimes f_{1,0}\) is the polygon through \((0, 1)\), \((0.0723, 0.4656)\), \((0.2689, 0.2689)\), \((0.4656, 0.0723)\) and \((1, 0)\), with three slopes, \(-e^2\), \(-1\) and \(-e^{-2}\). An \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) curve has only two, so no single pair describes it. Each segment lies on a line of one such curve: the two outer ones on \(f_{2,0}\), and the middle one on the line \(1 - 0.4621 - \mathrm{FPR}\) of \(f_{0,0.4621}\). So the polygon is the supremum of these two curves, with \(0.4621 = \tanh(1/2)\).

Giving each release a quarter of the \(\delta\) budget turns it into the point \((4.6902, 2.5\times10^{-6})\) of 1-GDP, and adding the points gives \(\varepsilon = 18.7607\) at the same total \(\delta\), almost twice as large; Part 3’s Figure 21.4 shows the loss for many steps.

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
section: 32.5 The central limit theorem for composition
text:
32.5 The central limit theorem for composition
Most mechanisms are not Gaussian, so Equation 32.11 does not apply to them. But the loss of a composition is a sum of independent per-step losses, and such sums are nearly normal. This section turns that into a statement about curves, which is what lets one \(\mu\) summarize a long training run.
A CLT needs the mean, the variance and a third moment of the loss. Dong et al. write them as integrals of the log-slope of the curve, because the slope encodes the privacy loss.

Definition 32.4 (Moment functionals of a curve) For a trade-off function \(f\) define (Dong et al., §3.2) \[\mathrm{kl}(f) = -\int_0^1\ln|f'(t)|\,\mathrm dt, \qquad \kappa_2(f) = \int_0^1\ln^2|f'(t)|\,\mathrm dt, \tag{32.12}\] \[\kappa_3(f) = \int_0^1\big|\ln|f'(t)|\big|^3\,\mathrm dt, \qquad \bar\kappa_3(f) = \int_0^1\big|\ln|f'(t)| + \mathrm{kl}(f)\big|^3\,\mathrm dt. \tag{32.13}\]

The proof of the CLT starts by reading these as moments of the privacy loss random variable (PRV), the loss of an output drawn from \(P\) (Definition 21.1), using Part 1’s slope rule (Proposition 4.1).

Lemma 32.2 (The functionals are moments of the privacy loss) For \(f = T(P, Q)\), with \(L\) the privacy loss of an output drawn from \(P\), \[\mathrm{kl}(f) = \mathbb E_P[L] = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q), \quad \kappa_2(f) = \mathbb E_P[L^2], \quad \kappa_3(f) = \mathbb E_P|L|^3, \quad \bar\kappa_3(f) = \mathbb E_P\big|L - \mathbb E_PL\big|^3. \tag{32.14}\]


Proof. 

The slope is the threshold loss. A small loss means a large ratio \(Q/P\), so the best test with \(\mathrm{FPR} = t\) fires when \(L\) is below its \(t\)-quantile \(l(t)\) under \(P\). By Proposition 4.1 the slope there is minus the likelihood ratio \(Q/P = e^{-L}\), so \(|f'(t)| = e^{-l(t)}\) and \(-\ln|f'(t)| = l(t)\).
Integrate over quantiles. If \(U\) is uniform on \([0, 1]\), then \(l(U)\) has the law of \(L\), as when uniform numbers fed into an inverse distribution function produce samples. So \(\int_0^1 h(l(t))\,\mathrm dt = \mathbb E_P[h(L)]\) for any function \(h\).
Take moments. The choices \(h(x) = x\), \(x^2\), \(|x|^3\) and \(|x - \mathbb E_PL|^3\) give the four identities; the first is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence.


The theorem matches the composition to the Gaussian curve whose loss has the same ratio of mean to standard deviation. For \(k\) curves, collect each functional into a vector, \(\mathrm{kl} = (\mathrm{kl}(f_1), \dots, \mathrm{kl}(f_k))\) and so on, and write \(\|\cdot\|_1\) for the sum of the entries and \(\|\cdot\|_2^2\) for the sum of their squares.

Theorem 32.4 (Central limit theorem for composition) Let \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) be symmetric trade-off functions with \(\kappa_3(f_i) < \infty\), and put \[\mu = \frac{2\|\mathrm{kl}\|_1}{\sqrt{\|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2}}, \qquad \xi = \frac{0.56\,\|\bar\kappa_3\|_1}{\big(\|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2\big)^{3/2}}. \tag{32.15}\] If \(\xi < \frac12\), then for all \(\mathrm{FPR} \in [\xi, 1 - \xi]\) the composed curve lies in a band around \(G_\mu\), shifted by \(\xi\) both across and up or down: \[G_\mu(\mathrm{FPR} + \xi) - \xi \le f_1 \otimes \dots \otimes f_k(\mathrm{FPR}) \le G_\mu(\mathrm{FPR} - \xi) + \xi. \tag{32.16}\]


Proof. The plan is to find the mean and variance of the composed loss, approximate it by a normal with an explicit error, and match a Gaussian pair (Dong et al., Theorem 3.4 and Appendix D).

Add the losses. For product distributions the densities multiply, so the composed loss is a sum of independent per-step losses. By Lemma 32.2 it has mean \(K = \|\mathrm{kl}\|_1\) under \(P\) and variance \(V = \|\kappa_2\|_1 - \|\mathrm{kl}\|_2^2\).
Approximate by a normal. The Berry–Esseen theorem bounds the gap between the distribution function of a sum and the matching normal by a constant times the summed third central moments over \(V^{3/2}\). With the constant 0.56 that is \(\xi\).
Match a Gaussian pair. Swapping \(P\) and \(Q\) negates the loss, and a symmetric curve is unchanged by the swap, so by Lemma 32.2, step 2, the loss under \(Q\) has the law of minus the loss under \(P\), with mean \(-K\). The best tests therefore compare two nearly normal laws \(2K/\sqrt V\) standard deviations apart. The pair behind \(G_\mu\) has loss \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\) under \(P\) (Lemma 20.3), whose two laws are \(\mu\) standard deviations apart, so the match is \(\mu = 2K/\sqrt V\).
From the loss to the curve. A best test’s two errors are values of the two distribution functions of the loss, each within \(\xi\) of a normal value by step 2. Eliminating the threshold gives the band, as steps 3 to 6 of Section K.4 in the appendices show.


As the number of curves grows, each leaking less, the band closes and the composition converges to some \(G_\mu\) (Dong et al., Theorem 3.5). For \(k\) pieces that are \((\varepsilon_i, 0)\)-DP, with \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i^2 \to \mu^2\) and \(\max_i\varepsilon_i \to 0\), the limit is \(G_\mu\) (their Theorem 3.6), the \(\sqrt k\) behaviour of advanced composition with the exact constant. That is why GDP is the natural family, while two runs of randomized response already leave the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) family (Table 32.4).
The band \(\xi\) is a bound but a wide one, so in practice \(G_\mu\) itself is used as the estimate, and that is an approximation, not a bound. It can lie above or below the true curve, and its error is largest in the tails, where small \(\delta\) lives.

Example 32.5 Take \(k\) mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP with \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/\sqrt k\), so that the limit is the running example’s \(G_1\). For randomized response the summed loss is \(\varepsilon_0\) times the number of truthful runs minus the number of flipped ones, so the exact profile is a finite binomial sum (Table 32.5).

title: 32  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
32.6 The subsampled Gaussian and DP-SGD
Private training runs stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy, DP-SGD for short (subsampling). Each of its \(T\) steps puts each record in the batch independently with probability \(q\), clips the gradients and adds Gaussian noise with noise multiplier \(\sigma\). A step leaks little when \(q\) is small, so the CLT should apply, and this section finds the \(\mu\) it gives.
Under add/remove neighbours, one step reduces to a Gaussian against a mixture, because the added record shifts the sum by at most one sensitivity with probability \(q\) (subsampling derives it). In units of the sensitivity the pair is \(P = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), the record absent, and \(Q = (1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), the record present.

Theorem 32.5 (The subsampled Gaussian CLT) Under add/remove neighbours, let \(T \to \infty\) and \(q\sqrt T \to c\) with \(\sigma\) fixed. Then the trade-off curve of \(T\) steps of this subsampled Gaussian mechanism converges to \(G_\mu\) with \[\mu = q\sqrt{T\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}. \tag{32.17}\]


Proof. The plan is to compute the mean and variance of one step’s loss for small \(q\), add them over \(T\) steps, and use \(\mu = 2K/\sqrt V\) from Theorem 32.4 (Bu, Dong, Long & Su 2020, Theorem 5).

Write the likelihood ratio. The ratio of the \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) density to the \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) density is \(e^{(y - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\), by the cancellation of squares in Lemma 32.1. So \[\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = 1 + qW(y), \qquad W(y) = e^{(y - 1/2)/\sigma^2} - 1, \tag{32.18}\] where \(W\) measures how much the output favours “the record was in the batch”.
Find the moments of \(W\) under \(P\). The mean is 0, because averaging a density ratio under its denominator gives 1. The moment generating function \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda Y}] = e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\) of \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), at \(\lambda = 2/\sigma^2\), gives \(\mathbb E_P[(W + 1)^2] = \mathbb E_P[e^{2Y/\sigma^2}]\,e^{-1/\sigma^2} = e^{2/\sigma^2}e^{-1/\sigma^2} = e^{1/\sigma^2}\). Expanding the square, \[\mathbb E_P[W^2] = \mathbb E_P[(W + 1)^2] - 2\,\mathbb E_P[W + 1] + 1 = e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1. \tag{32.19}\]
Expand the loss. For small \(q\), \(L = -\ln(1 + qW) = -qW + \frac{q^2W^2}{2} + O(q^3W^3)\). The first term has mean 0, so \(\mathbb E_P[L] \approx \frac{q^2}{2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and to leading order \(\operatorname{Var}_P(L) \approx q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).
Sum over \(T\) steps. Means and variances of independent losses add, so \(K \approx \frac{Tq^2}{2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) and \(V \approx Tq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Then \[\mu = \frac{2K}{\sqrt V} = \frac{Tq^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}{q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}} = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}. \tag{32.20}\]
Justify the limit. With \(q\sqrt T \to c\), each step’s moments are \(O(1/T)\) and \(\sum\kappa_3 = O(Tq^3) \to 0\), the conditions of the limit form of the CLT. That form assumes symmetric curves, and this pair is not symmetric, so Section K.5 in the appendices treats \(P\) and \(Q\) separately, bounds the remainders by \(O(q^3)\) and proves the limit.


Subsampling buys a factor of about \(q\): full batches give \(\sqrt T/\sigma\)-GDP, and Equation 32.17 multiplies this by \(q\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), which is \(q \times 1.3108\) at \(\sigma = 1\). The neighbouring relation matters here: Dong et al. (Corollary 5.4) analyse fixed-size batches under replace-one neighbours, where a neighbour swaps one record for another, and get a different constant, \(\mu = 1.7101\) at \(T = 10{,}000\) in the running example (subsampling explains why not to mix them).
The result is a limit, used as an approximation at finite \(T\), and it is not a bound. The errors of the CLT and of the expansion in step 3 add up, and neither is controlled in the tail where \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) lives. Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz (2021) showed that the CLT value can lie below the true \(\varepsilon\), and the example confirms it. Numerical accounting computes certified values, and choosing an accountant compares the accountants on this example.

Example 32.6 The running DP-SGD example has \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Then \(\sqrt{e - 1} = \sqrt{1.7183} = 1.3108\), so \(\mu = 0.01 \times 1.3108\sqrt T\), which is 0.1311 at \(T = 100\). Table 32.7 turns each \(\mu\) into \(\varepsilon\) with Equation 32.9 and compares it with a numerical accountant.

section: 32.7 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve
text:
32.7 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve
Rényi DP tracks \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) over orders \(\alpha > 1\), and Conversions (Section 30.3) turned it into the region of test errors it allows. This section reads that region as \(f\)-DP, to see why RDP accounting leaves slack.
The construction rests on one observation. A test maps \(P\) to a coin \(\mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FPR})\) that lands 1 with probability \(\mathrm{FPR}\), and \(Q\) to the coin \(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FNR})\). Processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence (Theorem 3.5), so the two coins must stay within the RDP budget at every order. The lowest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) that passes this check is the curve that RDP certifies.

Theorem 32.6 (What an RDP curve certifies) Let \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) be an RDP curve, known at the orders of the part’s grid (the fixed list of orders its accountants evaluate), for both \((D, D')\) and \((D', D)\). Let \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) be the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) with \[D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FPR})\,\big\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FNR})\big) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) \quad\text{and}\quad D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FNR})\,\big\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FPR})\big) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) \tag{32.21}\] at every order \(\alpha\) of the grid (Equation 30.15). Then:

The trade-off curve of a pair determines its RDP curve.
\(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is a symmetric trade-off function, and a mechanism with this RDP curve is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\)-DP. At each \(\mathrm{FPR}\), no higher value follows from the RDP values alone.
The optimal conversion Equation 30.16 of Conversions is the privacy profile \(1 + f_{\mathrm{RDP}}^*(-e^\varepsilon)\) of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).



Proof. The plan is to read the RDP curve off the law of the loss, push each test through the data-processing inequality, check the shape of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), exhibit a pair at each point, and match the conversion with the duality.

The curve determines the divergence. By Lemma 32.2, step 2, the curve fixes the law of \(L\) under \(P\), and \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) is a functional of that law.
RDP implies \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\)-DP. By the data-processing inequality the two coins of any test satisfy the constraints, so every point of the true curve is feasible and \(T(P, Q) \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).
Shape. Each constraint bounds the logarithm of a sum of terms \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\), so it bounds the sum itself, and each term is jointly convex for \(\alpha > 1\) (the paragraph after Theorem 30.2; Section F.5). So the feasible set and its lower boundary are convex. Two equal coins have divergence 0, so \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR}) \le 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(1) = 0\), and a convex function with its minimum at 1 is non-increasing. Relabelling the coins’ outcomes swaps the two constraints, so the feasible set is symmetric about the diagonal.
No higher value. For each feasible point, the pair of coins \((\mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FPR}), \mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FNR}))\) is itself a mechanism with these RDP values, and its test “fire on 1” has errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) (step 5 of the proof of Theorem 30.2). Different values of \(\mathrm{FPR}\) need different pairs.
The conversion is the conjugate. Equation 30.16 maximizes \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\), with the roles of the two errors swapped from Theorem 32.2. Since \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is symmetric the swap changes nothing, and the maximum is Equation 32.7 applied to \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\).


The results form a ladder. For the Gaussian mechanism, \(G_\mu\) is the exact curve, \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is what its RDP curve keeps, and an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair is one touching line of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\). The optimal conversion removes the gap between the line and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), but no conversion removes the gap between \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) and the true curve (Section 30.5). RDP loses because different laws of the loss share the same exponential moments at the grid’s orders, and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) must allow the worst of them. Conversions shows that the extra power it grants an attacker persists down to \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\) (Table 30.4). So GDP accounting for full-batch noisy gradient descent beats RDP accounting, although both compose exactly.

Example 32.7 For the running example, \(\mu = 1\), the RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) (Proposition 3.3). The Gaussian pair has these RDP values, so claim 2 gives \(G_1 \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), and the script, computing \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) by bisection on \(\mathrm{FNR}\), finds it strictly below \(G_1\) everywhere it looked. In Table 32.8 the best advantage \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \mathrm{FNR}\) of a symmetric curve is reached at its diagonal point, where its slope is \(-1\), and equals \(1 - 2\mathrm{FPR}\) there, which for \(G_1\) is \(1 - 2 \times 0.3085 = 0.3829\).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.1 Amplification for (ε, δ)-DP under Poisson sampling
Training a neural network with differential privacy (DP) runs stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for ten thousand steps or more, with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, a method called DP-SGD. Each step clips every example’s gradient to norm \(C\), sums the clipped gradients and adds Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) times \(C\). If every record were in every batch, ten thousand steps with \(\sigma = 1\) would cost \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (Rényi DP), a guarantee nobody would report. This chapter asks how much cheaper a step becomes when it looks only at a small random batch, and for which ways of drawing the batch the answer holds.
The one idea is that the output becomes a mixture. Neighbours differ by adding or removing one record, unless a section says otherwise. Write \(P_0\) for a step’s output distribution without the record and \(P_1\) for it with the record. If the batch contains the record only with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, the step on the dataset with the record draws from \(P_1\) with probability \(q\) and from \(P_0\) otherwise. So every likelihood ratio between the two runs is pulled toward 1: \[\frac{(1 - q)P_0 + qP_1}{P_0} = (1 - q) + q\,\frac{P_1}{P_0}, \tag{33.1}\] a weighted average of 1 and the old ratio, once the rest of the batch is fixed.
The running example is DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and up to \(T = 10{,}000\) steps. Sampling turns a step that costs \(\varepsilon = 1\) into one that costs 0.0170, and with Rényi differential privacy (RDP) the whole run costs \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) instead of 5425.5.
You have a mechanism \(M\) that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, and you run it on a random sample of the data. What are the privacy parameters of the combined mechanism? This question comes first because every later answer reuses its argument: fix everything except whether the record was drawn, compare a mixture with its parts, and average the rest back in. The tight answer below is due to Li, Qardaji & Su (2012) and Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi (2018).
The argument rests on one inequality about mixtures. Write \(P(A)\) for the probability that \(P\) gives to an event \(A\), and say that \(P\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-close to \(Q\) when \(P(A) \le e^\varepsilon Q(A) + \delta\) for every event \(A\). Picture two runs that both draw from a common distribution \(R\) with probability \(1 - q\), while with probability \(q\) the first draws from \(P\) and the second from \(P'\). In the opening’s picture, \(R\) and \(P'\) are both \(P_0\) and \(P\) is \(P_1\). Where the runs agree the likelihood ratio is 1, and where they differ it is at most \(e^\varepsilon\), up to the slack \(\delta\). So the mixture’s ratio should be at most the weighted average \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), and the slack should shrink to \(q\delta\). The one subtlety is that \(P\) must be close to \(R\) as well as to \(P'\), or a likely event of \(P\) could be one that \(R\) never produces.
Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi (2018, Theorem 2) call this advanced joint convexity. On 20,000 random triples \((R, P, P')\) on four outcomes, the chapter’s script finds some that meet it with equality to four digits. In the theorem, \(R\), \(P\) and \(P'\) will be outputs for one fixed choice of the other records, and the next lemma averages that choice back in.
This is joint convexity of the hockey-stick divergence of Definition 3.4, the largest excess \(P(A) - \gamma Q(A)\) over events, for a mixing choice that both runs share. With both lemmas the theorem follows, and it says that \(\delta\) is paid only when the record is drawn.
The formula has two regimes (Figure 33.1). For small \(\varepsilon\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\) and the logarithm is close to its argument minus 1, so \(\varepsilon' \approx q\varepsilon\). For large \(\varepsilon\) the 1 inside the logarithm stops mattering, so \(\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q)\), because in the worst case the record was drawn. At \(q = 0.01\) the switch comes near \(\varepsilon = \ln(1/q) = 4.6\), so Table 33.1 gives 0.9059 at \(\varepsilon = 5\), not the 0.05 of a factor of 100.
The \(\delta\) always shrinks by the factor \(q\), because the failure event of \(M\) only matters when the record was drawn. The bound is tight for one step, but composing per-step pairs is not, as Section 33.5 shows.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
Definition 33.1 (Poisson subsampling) Let \(q \in [0, 1]\). Poisson sampling with rate \(q\) keeps each record of a dataset \(D\) independently with probability \(q\) and returns the kept records, \(S_q(D)\). For a mechanism \(M\), the subsampled mechanism \(M \circ S_q\) runs \(M\) on \(S_q(D)\).



Lemma 33.1 (The mixture lemma) Let \(R\), \(P\) and \(P'\) be distributions on the same outputs, and let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), \(\delta \in [0, 1]\) and \(q \in [0, 1]\). Suppose that for every event \(A\), \[P(A) \le e^\varepsilon P'(A) + \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad P(A) \le e^\varepsilon R(A) + \delta. \tag{33.2}\] Then for every event \(A\), \[(1 - q)R(A) + qP(A) \le e^{\varepsilon'}\big[(1 - q)R(A) + qP'(A)\big] + q\delta, \qquad e^{\varepsilon'} = 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{33.3}\]


Proof. The plan is to treat the three probabilities of \(A\) as unknowns. Making \(P'(A)\) and \(R(A)\) smaller makes the inequality harder to satisfy, so it is enough to check it at the smallest values the assumptions allow. Fix \(A\) and write \(a = P(A)\), \(b = P'(A)\) and \(c = R(A)\). Write \(F\) for the gap, the left side of Equation 33.3 minus the bracketed term times \(e^{\varepsilon'}\). The claim is that \(F\) is at most \(q\delta\).

Expand \(F\). The two terms in \(c\) combine to \((1 - q)c(1 - e^{\varepsilon'})\), and \(1 - e^{\varepsilon'} = -q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) by the definition of \(\varepsilon'\). The term in \(b\) is \(-e^{\varepsilon'}qb\). So \[F = qa - q(1 - q)(e^\varepsilon - 1)\,c - q\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big)\,b. \tag{33.4}\]
Find the worst \(b\) and \(c\). Both coefficients are negative, so \(F\) is largest when \(b\) and \(c\) are as small as allowed. Solving each assumption for \(b\) or \(c\) gives the lower bound \(e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\) for both, and both are also at least 0, being probabilities.
Case \(a \le \delta\). Dropping the two negative terms leaves \(F \le qa \le q\delta\).
Case \(a > \delta\). Put \(b = c = e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\) into step 1. With the common factor \(q\) taken out, the two coefficients add up to \((1 - q)(e^\varepsilon - 1) + 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1) = e^\varepsilon\), so \[F \le qa - q\,e^{-\varepsilon}(a - \delta)\,e^\varepsilon = q\delta. \tag{33.5}\]




Lemma 33.2 (Averaging over a shared choice) Let \(P = \sum_tw_tP_t\) and \(Q = \sum_tw_tQ_t\) be averages of distributions with the same non-negative weights \(w_t\) summing to 1, and let \(\gamma > 0\). If \(P_t(A) \le \gamma Q_t(A) + \delta\) for every \(t\) and every event \(A\), then \[P(A) \le \gamma Q(A) + \delta \quad\text{for every event } A. \tag{33.6}\]


Proof. 

Write the excess as an average. For a fixed event \(A\), both averages use the same weights, so the excess of the averages is the average of the excesses: \[P(A) - \gamma Q(A) = \sum_tw_t\big[P_t(A) - \gamma Q_t(A)\big]. \tag{33.7}\]
Bound the average. Each bracket is at most \(\delta\), and so is any weighted average of them.




Theorem 33.1 (Amplification by Poisson subsampling) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, and let \(q \in [0, 1]\). Then \(M \circ S_q\) is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for add/remove neighbours with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{33.8}\] For every \(\varepsilon\) and \(q\), some \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism attains this \(\varepsilon'\).


Proof. The plan is to fix every random choice except whether the added record \(x\) is drawn, apply Lemma 33.1 once for each order of the pair, average with Lemma 33.2, and finally exhibit a mechanism that attains the bound. Let \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\).

Condition on the rest of the sample. Let \(\tilde D\) be the Poisson sample of \(D\). Each record has its own coin, so the sample of \(D'\) is \(\tilde D \cup \{x\}\) with probability \(q\) and \(\tilde D\) otherwise, independently of \(\tilde D\). Given \(\tilde D\), write \(P_0 = M(\tilde D)\) and \(P_1 = M(\tilde D \cup \{x\})\), so that the output on \(D'\) is the mixture \((1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\).
Bound the direction with the mixture first. Apply Lemma 33.1 with \(R = P' = P_0\) and \(P = P_1\). Both of its assumptions then hold because \(\tilde D\) and \(\tilde D \cup \{x\}\) are neighbours, and its right side becomes \(e^{\varepsilon'}P_0(A) + q\delta\). Here the dataset with the record comes first and its neighbour removes it, which Numerical accounting calls the remove direction.
Bound the direction with the mixture second. Apply the lemma with \(R = P = P_0\) and \(P' = P_1\). Its first assumption is DP of \(M\) again, and its second, \(P_0(A) \le e^\varepsilon P_0(A) + \delta\), always holds. Its left side becomes \(P_0(A)\), so \(P_0(A) \le e^{\varepsilon'}[(1 - q)P_0(A) + qP_1(A)] + q\delta\).
Average over \(\tilde D\). Both bounds hold for every \(\tilde D\), so Lemma 33.2 carries them to the subsampled mechanism.
Attain the bound. Randomized response reports a bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flipped otherwise (Theorem 18.1). Let \(M\) apply it to the bit “the sample contains a flagged record”, take \(D\) with no flagged record, and let \(x\) be flagged. Then \(P_1\) gives the output 1 exactly \(e^\varepsilon\) times the probability that \(P_0\) gives it, for every \(\tilde D\). At the output 1 the likelihood ratio of the mixture to \(P_0\) is therefore \[\frac{(1 - q)P_0(1) + qP_1(1)}{P_0(1)} = 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{33.9}\] With \(\delta = 0\), the event that the output is 1 forces \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) to be at least this ratio.

Example 33.1 Take the randomized response of step 5 of the proof of Theorem 33.1, with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(q = 0.1\). When the record is not drawn the true bit is 0, which is reported as 0 with probability \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\) and as 1 with probability 0.2689. When it is drawn the two probabilities swap. The mixture weights the two cases by 0.9 and 0.1, so it reports 1 with probability \(0.9 \times 0.2689 + 0.1 \times 0.7311 = 0.3152\) and 0 with probability 0.6848.
Without sampling the likelihood ratios are \(e\) and \(1/e\). With sampling the largest ratio of the mixture to \(P_0\) is \(0.3152/0.2689 = 1.1718 = 1 + 0.1(e - 1)\), so \(\varepsilon' = \ln 1.1718 = 0.1586\), as Equation 33.8 says, against \(q\varepsilon = 0.1\). The largest ratio the other way, \(0.7311/0.6848 = 1.0675\), is smaller. The mixture never puts less than 0.9 times \(P_0\)’s probability on any output, so this ratio can never exceed \(1/0.9\).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.2 Sampling schemes and neighbouring relations
Poisson sampling gives batches of random size, but most training code draws batches of a fixed size. Does Theorem 33.1 still apply to them? This section says which pair of outputs to account for under each scheme, because accounting for one scheme while running another can multiply \(\varepsilon\) several times over. A fixed batch size pairs naturally with replace-one neighbours, datasets of the same size that differ in one record’s value, because adding a record would change the size.

Definition 33.2 (Fixed-size batches) Sampling without replacement draws a batch of \(m\) of the \(n\) records of a dataset uniformly at random. Shuffle and partition puts the records in a uniformly random order once per epoch and uses consecutive blocks of \(m\) records as the epoch’s batches.

A uniformly random batch contains a given record with probability \(m/n\), which plays the role of \(q\). There is no independent coin for the differing record, though, so the proof uses a coupling: it builds the batch in a way that has such a coin, and shares the coin and the other records between the two datasets (Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi 2018, Theorem 9).

Theorem 33.2 (Amplification by sampling without replacement) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours on datasets of size \(m\), and let \(q = m/n\). Running \(M\) on a batch of \(m\) records drawn without replacement from \(n\) is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP for replace-one neighbours on datasets of size \(n\), with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{33.10}\]


Proof. The plan is to draw the batch in two stages that expose a coin for the differing record, write both outputs as the mixtures of Lemma 33.1, check its assumptions, and average. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in record \(i\), which is \(x\) in \(D\) and \(x'\) in \(D'\).

Build a batch that avoids \(i\). Draw \(B\), a uniform set of \(m - 1\) of the other \(n - 1\) records, then \(z\), a uniform record among the \(n - m\) others not in \(B\). Each set of \(m\) records that avoids \(i\) arises from \(m\) choices of \(z\), equally often, so \(B \cup \{z\}\) is a uniform such set.
Write both outputs as mixtures. A uniform batch contains \(i\) with probability \(q\). Given that it does, the rest of it is distributed as \(B\), and otherwise the batch is distributed as \(B \cup \{z\}\). So flip a coin with probability \(q\), and use \(B \cup \{x\}\) in \(D\) and \(B \cup \{x'\}\) in \(D'\) on heads, and \(B \cup \{z\}\) in both on tails. Given \((B, z)\), the outputs are \((1 - q)R + qP\) and \((1 - q)R + qP'\), with \(R = M(B\cup\{z\})\), \(P = M(B\cup\{x\})\) and \(P' = M(B\cup\{x'\})\).
Check the assumptions. The three batches have size \(m\) and differ pairwise in one element, so each of \(P\) and \(P'\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-close to the other two.
Apply the lemma and average. Lemma 33.1 gives the bound in each direction, and Lemma 33.2 averages over \((B, z)\).


Each combination of sampling scheme and neighbouring relation needs its own base guarantee (Table 33.2), and the zero-out relation of its last row sets the target’s gradient to 0. The last column applies them to DP-SGD’s sum of gradients clipped to norm \(C\), with noise \(\sigma C\). Replacing a record moves the sum by up to \(2C\), twice what adding one does, since the new gradient may point the opposite way. A Gaussian mechanism’s privacy depends only on the shift in units of the noise, so this is the same as a shift of \(C\) with noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\). Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke (2024, Proposition 9) show that for fixed-size batches this shift is the worst case under add and under remove too.
