Poisson sampling under replace-one neighbours is the row where both outputs are mixtures, \((1 - q)R + qP\) and \((1 - q)R + qP'\), given the rest of the sample \(\tilde D\). Here \(R = M(\tilde D)\), and \(P\) and \(P'\) add \(x\) or \(x'\), so each is one step from \(R\) but two from the other. Lemma 33.1 needs one guarantee for all these pairs, so it must use the weaker one. Group privacy (Theorem 19.2) gives \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) for datasets two steps apart, and the lemma with Lemma 33.2 then gives \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q(1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta. \tag{33.11}\] For small \(q\) this is about \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) times the add/remove value, since \(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1 = (e^\varepsilon - 1)(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). It is loose, because it charges the pairs one step apart the two-step price. For pure DP, the ratio of the two mixtures at an output is largest where \(P = e^\varepsilon R\) and \(P' = e^{-\varepsilon}R\), which gives the exact value \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big) - \ln\big(1 - q(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\big), \tag{33.12}\] which the Laplace mechanism on a sum attains. For small \(\varepsilon\) the exact value is about twice the add/remove value. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(q = 0.01\) it is 0.02338, against 0.06193 for the group-privacy bound and 0.01704 for add/remove: a ratio of 1.37, not 3.64.
Shuffle and partition is worse, because in one epoch the record is in exactly one batch, so no step’s output is a mixture with “not used”. The only uncertainty is which batch held the record, and the other records can give that away. Chua et al. (2024) build a bad case under zero-out, with scalar gradients: every other record has gradient \(-1\) and the target has \(+1\). Adding the batch size to each batch sum cancels the other records, so batches without the target output \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), while the target’s batch outputs \(\mathcal N(2, \sigma^2)\), or \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) when the target is zeroed out. A natural test says “target present” when the largest batch output exceeds a threshold \(\tau\).

Proposition 33.1 (A lower bound for shuffle and partition) In the epoch above, with \(b\) batches and noise multiplier \(\sigma\), let \(\Phi\) be the standard normal distribution function. For every threshold \(\tau\) and every \(\varepsilon\), the smallest \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for which the epoch is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP satisfies \[\delta(\varepsilon) \ge \Big[1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{\tau-2}\sigma\Big)\Phi\Big(\frac\tau\sigma\Big)^{b-1}\Big] - e^\varepsilon\Big[1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{\tau-1}\sigma\Big)\Phi\Big(\frac\tau\sigma\Big)^{b-1}\Big]. \tag{33.13}\]


Proof. 

Compute the event’s probability. The largest output stays below \(\tau\) only if every batch output does, and the batches’ noises are independent. With the target present, its batch stays below \(\tau\) with probability \(\Phi(\frac{\tau-2}\sigma)\), and each of the \(b - 1\) others with probability \(\Phi(\frac\tau\sigma)\). With the target zeroed out, the first factor becomes \(\Phi(\frac{\tau-1}\sigma)\).
Remove the batch index. Neither product depends on which batch holds the target, so averaging over the random order changes nothing.
Bound \(\delta(\varepsilon)\). The smallest \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the largest value of \(P(A) - e^\varepsilon Q(A)\) over events \(A\), the hockey-stick divergence of Definition 3.4. One particular event gives a value no larger.


Maximizing over \(\tau\) gives the best such bound, and so a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\) at a given \(\delta\). Under zero-out a Poisson step’s sum also moves by at most \(C\), so the Poisson accountant applies to the same relation. With \(\sigma = 0.4\) and \(b = 10{,}000\) batches, the script reproduces Chua et al.’s check, \(\delta(4) \ge 0.226\) for shuffling against 0.244 for a fixed batch order, where a Poisson accountant gives \(\delta(4) \le 1.18 \times 10^{-5}\).

Example 33.2 In the running example one epoch is \(b = 100\) batches, and Table 33.3 compares three batch samplers over it. Deterministic batches use the record once, in a known batch, so the epoch is a plain Gaussian mechanism with an exact \(\varepsilon\). Shuffling gets the lower bound of Proposition 33.1, and Poisson sampling the RDP upper bound.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.3 RDP of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian
Per-step \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification composes badly, as Section 33.5 will show, while RDP composes well. A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP when the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between its outputs on any two neighbouring datasets is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and these curves add under composition (Rényi DP). So DP-SGD’s accountant needs the curve of one subsampled Gaussian step, a Rényi divergence between a Gaussian mixture and a Gaussian, which has an exact finite sum at integer orders. Figure 33.3 shows the pair and its privacy loss, the logarithm of the likelihood ratio at each output.






Figure 33.3: Left: one subsampled Gaussian step with \(q = 0.1\); the mixture (dashed) is close to \(P_0\). Right: the privacy loss, flat near \(\ln(1 - q)\) on the left and \(\ln(1/q)\) below the unsubsampled loss in the right tail.



The Rényi divergence of Definition 3.2 is a log-average of a power of the likelihood ratio, in which a larger order weights large ratios more heavily. For \(\alpha > 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{y\sim Q}\Big[\Big(\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\Big)^\alpha\Big]. \tag{33.14}\] The proof below starts, like that of Theorem 33.1, by fixing the rest of the sample, so its first step needs the Rényi counterpart of Lemma 33.2.

Lemma 33.3 (Averaging cannot increase a Rényi divergence) Let \(P = \sum_tw_tP_t\) and \(Q = \sum_tw_tQ_t\) be averages with the same weights \(w_t\), and let \(\alpha > 1\). Then \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \max_tD_\alpha(P_t\|Q_t). \tag{33.15}\]


Proof. 

Write the divergence as an integral. By the definition, \(e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\) is the integral of \(Q\,g(P/Q)\) with the convex function \(g(r) = r^\alpha\).
Use joint convexity. A function of the form \(Q\,g(P/Q)\) with \(g\) convex, called the perspective of \(g\), is jointly convex in the pair \((P, Q)\), as Section F.5 in the appendices derives. So the integral at the averaged pair is at most the average of the integrals: \[\int Q\,g(P/Q)\,\mathrm d y \le \sum_tw_t\int Q_t\,g(P_t/Q_t)\,\mathrm d y. \tag{33.16}\]
Take the largest term. An average is at most its largest term, and the logarithm and division by \(\alpha - 1 > 0\) keep the order.


This is the quasi-convexity of the Rényi divergence (van Erven & Harremoës 2014, Theorem 13). The theorem and its proof are due to Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019).

Theorem 33.3 (RDP of the subsampled Gaussian) Let \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(P_1 = \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) and \(P_q = (1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\). The Poisson-subsampled Gaussian mechanism with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for add/remove neighbours, for every \(\alpha > 1\), with \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \max\big\{D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0),\ D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q)\big\} = D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0) = \frac{\ln A_\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{33.17}\] where \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}\Big[\Big((1 - q) + q\frac{P_1(y)}{P_0(y)}\Big)^\alpha\Big], \qquad \frac{P_1(y)}{P_0(y)} = e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{33.18}\] For integer \(\alpha\), \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{33.19}\]


Proof. The plan is to remove every coordinate except the one along which the record moves the output, compare the two directions of the remaining pair, and evaluate the larger one.

Condition on the rest of the sample. Let \(f\) be the clipped gradient sum divided by \(C\), so that its sensitivity is 1, and let \(\tilde D\) be the rest of the sample. Given \(\tilde D\), one output is \(\mathcal N(f(\tilde D), \sigma^2I)\) and the other mixes it, with weight \(1 - q\), with \(\mathcal N(f(\tilde D\cup\{x\}), \sigma^2I)\). By Lemma 33.3 it suffices to bound one \(\tilde D\).
Reduce to one dimension. Shifting or rotating both distributions changes no likelihood ratio, so rotate the difference of the means onto the first axis. The other coordinates are identical in both runs and independent of the first, and Rényi divergences of independent coordinates add (Theorem 3.2), so they contribute 0.
Reduce to length 1. Rescaling the output by \(1/c\) turns a difference of length \(c < 1\) into one of length 1 with noise \(\sigma/c > \sigma\). That is the length-1 pair with extra independent noise added, which cannot increase a divergence (Theorem 3.5). What is left is the pair \((P_q, P_0)\) in both orders.
Compare the two directions. Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019, Theorem 5) prove that the order with the mixture first is the larger, for every \(\alpha \ge 1\), using the reflection \(y \mapsto 1 - y\), which swaps \(P_0\) and \(P_1\). This step is cited, and Section L.1 in the appendices derives it.
Write the first direction as an expectation. The definition with \(Q = P_0\) makes \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0)\) the logarithm of the average of \((P_q/P_0)^\alpha\) under \(P_0\). Dividing the mixture by \(P_0\) gives \((1 - q) + q\,P_1/P_0\), which is Equation 33.18. In the Gaussian ratio the normalizing constants cancel, leaving \[\frac{P_1(y)}{P_0(y)} = \exp\Big(\frac{y^2 - (y-1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = e^{(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{33.20}\]
Expand for integer \(\alpha\). Write \(r\) for the ratio \(P_1/P_0\). The binomial theorem expands \((1 - q + qr)^\alpha\) into the sum of \(\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha-j}q^jr^j\) over \(j\), and the average of a sum is the sum of the averages.
Compute each moment. By the definition of \(D_j\), the average of \(r^j\) under \(P_0\) is \(e^{(j-1)D_j(P_1\|P_0)}\). Two normals one unit apart have \(D_j(P_1\|P_0) = j/(2\sigma^2)\), by Equation 3.19. So the \(j\)-th moment is \(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}\), which gives Equation 33.19.


For fractional \(\alpha\) the sum does not terminate, so the script integrates Equation 33.18 numerically, and the reverse direction too. The dominance of step 4 holds for Rényi divergences only, and for \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) Numerical accounting computes both directions.
The curve has two regimes (Figure 33.4). Low orders average the privacy loss over the bulk of the outputs, where sampling flattens it, so the curve stays close to the \(j = 2\) term of Equation 33.19, the lowest power of \(q\) that costs anything. High orders look at the far tail, where sampling saves only \(\ln(1/q)\). Every term of Equation 33.19 is positive, so \(A_\alpha\) is at least its last term, and taking logarithms makes this precise: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \ge \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1} + \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{33.21}\] the unsubsampled curve minus about \(\ln(1/q)\), a bound Concentrated DP also uses.






Figure 33.4: The RDP curve of the subsampled Gaussian with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) (black), against the unsubsampled curve, the small-\(q\) term and Abadi et al.’s leading term, whose range ends at the solid vertical line. The dashed line marks \(\alpha = 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\).




Example 33.3 Take \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\). At \(\alpha = 2\), Equation 33.19 has three terms, one for each number \(j\) of factors \(r\). Their coefficients are \((0.99)^2 = 0.9801\), \(2 \times 0.99 \times 0.01 = 0.0198\) and \((0.01)^2 = 0.0001\), which add up to \((1 - q + q)^2 = 1\). The exponential factors are 1, 1 and \(e\), so they change only the last term, which becomes 0.000272. So \(A_2 = 1 + 0.0001 \times 1.71828 = 1.00017183\) and \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln A_2 = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\), against 1 without sampling. The terms \(j = 0\) and 1 cost nothing, because they have the factor 1 that a mixture of identical distributions would have.
The binomial sum is exact but exists only at integer orders, while the integral covers every order but could be wrong if its grid were too coarse. Table 33.4 compares them, and gives the reverse direction \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q)\) beside them.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
section: 33.4 Small q and the moments accountant
text:
33.4 Small q and the moments accountant
Abadi et al. (2016) introduced DP-SGD together with the moments accountant, which tracks the cumulant generating function \(K_M(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]\) of the privacy loss \(L\), the log-likelihood ratio of an output. Rényi DP shows that this is the RDP curve in disguise, \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1)\). Abadi et al. bounded \(K_M\) for small \(q\), and this section derives the leading term and where it stops holding. The idea is that of Example 33.3: the terms \(j = 0\) and 1 cost nothing, and every term from \(j = 3\) on carries \(q^3\) or a higher power.

Proposition 33.2 (The subsampled Gaussian for small q) For \(q \to 0\) at fixed \(\alpha\) and \(\sigma\), the RDP curve of Theorem 33.3 is \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}{2} + O(q^3) \approx \frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\quad\text{for large }\sigma. \tag{33.22}\]


Proof. The plan is to subtract the part of the sum that costs nothing, keep the lowest power of \(q\), and expand the logarithm.

Subtract what costs nothing. Without the exponential factors, Equation 33.19 is \((1 - q + q)^\alpha = 1\). Subtracting this 1 leaves each term multiplied by its factor minus 1, and the terms \(j = 0\) and 1 vanish because their factor is \(e^0 = 1\): \[A_\alpha = 1 + \sum_{j=2}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\big(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)} - 1\big). \tag{33.23}\]
Keep the lowest power of \(q\). The \(j = 2\) term is \(\binom\alpha2q^2(1 - q)^{\alpha-2}(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and every other term carries \(q^3\) or more.
Take the logarithm. For small \(y\), \(\ln(1 + y) = y + O(y^2)\), and \((1 - q)^{\alpha - 2} = 1 + O(q)\), so \[\ln A_\alpha = \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2}q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big) + O(q^3). \tag{33.24}\]
Divide by \(\alpha - 1\). This gives Equation 33.22 by Equation 33.17. For large \(\sigma\), \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\).


The cost per step is quadratic in \(q\), not linear as in Theorem 33.1, so the total over \(E\) epochs of \(E/q\) steps is about \(E\,q\,\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), which shrinks as batches get smaller. Abadi et al. (2016, Lemma 3) prove a bound of the same shape for \(\sigma \ge 1\), \(q < 1/(16\sigma)\) and integer \(\lambda \le \sigma^2\ln\frac{1}{q\sigma}\). Divided by \(\lambda\), with \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\), its leading term reads \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \lesssim \frac{q^2\alpha}{(1 - q)\sigma^2}\quad\text{for }\ \alpha \le 1 + \sigma^2\ln\frac{1}{q\sigma}. \tag{33.25}\] For large \(\sigma\) this is about twice Equation 33.22, a valid but loose bound, and the source of the “\(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx q^2\alpha/\sigma^2\)” you will see quoted.
The real limit of the expansion is its range of orders. Each next term multiplies the power of \(q\) by \(q\) and the exponential by \(e^{j/\sigma^2}\), so the terms first fall and later grow. The expansion fails when the last term, \(q^\alpha e^{\alpha(\alpha-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\), overtakes the \(j = 2\) term, about \(q^2e^{1/\sigma^2}\). Ignoring the binomial coefficients, the difference of their logarithms factors as \((\alpha - 2)\big(\frac{\alpha + 1}{2\sigma^2} - \ln\frac1q\big)\), which turns positive at \(\alpha = 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q) - 1\). So the expansion holds up to about \[\alpha \approx 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q), \tag{33.26}\] and the curve leaves the quadratic regime abruptly there. Abadi et al.’s range has the same form with about half the constant, so it is conservative.

Example 33.4 At \(q = 0.01\), \(\ln(1/q) = 4.605\), so Equation 33.26 puts the breakdown at 9.2 for \(\sigma = 1\) and 147.4 for \(\sigma = 4\). Table 33.5 compares the exact curve with Equation 33.22 and Equation 33.25. For instance, at \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\sigma = 1\) the Abadi column is \(0.0002/0.99 = 2.0202 \times 10^{-4}\).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.5 Accounting for DP-SGD
Everything is now in place to account for the running example. How large is its \(\varepsilon\), and how much does the accounting route matter? The RDP accountant adds the per-step curve over the \(T\) steps and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once. Mironov’s conversion adds \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) to the RDP value, and the improved conversion of From RDP to (ε, δ) subtracts two small corrections. Section C.4 and Section C.5 in the appendices derive the result from scratch.

Theorem 33.4 (The RDP accountant for DP-SGD) Let DP-SGD run \(T\) steps that may each depend on the earlier outputs. Each step draws a Poisson sample with rate \(q\), clips every per-example gradient to norm \(C\) and adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\) to the sum. With \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) from Equation 33.17, DP-SGD is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours with \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha}\Big[T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \quad\text{(Mironov)}, \qquad \varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \quad\text{(improved)}, \tag{33.27}\] with the minimum over the grid of orders shared by this part.


Proof. 

Identify one step. Dividing the noisy sum by \(C\) makes one step the mechanism of Theorem 33.3, whose curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\).
Compose. RDP curves add under adaptive composition (Rényi DP), so the \(T\) steps have the curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\).
Convert. Mironov’s conversion is Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda L}\) and solved for \(\varepsilon\), and the improved one is Balle et al. (2020, Theorem 21). Each holds at every order, so the smallest value over the grid holds too.


The naive routes amplify each step in \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form and then compose. Each step gets a share \(\delta_0\) of \(\delta\), and is \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\)-DP for the \(\varepsilon_0\) that solves the exact Gaussian profile of Theorem 20.3. Then Equation 33.8 turns this into \((\varepsilon_1, q\delta_0)\). Basic composition (Theorem 19.3) adds the parameters to \((T\varepsilon_1, Tq\delta_0)\), which fixes \(\delta_0 = \delta/(Tq)\). Advanced composition (Corollary 21.1) grows like \(\sqrt T\) at the price of an extra slack \(\delta'\), whose share of \(\delta\) the script optimizes.
For one step RDP loses, 0.96 against 0.20, because the conversion costs \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) however small the curve is. RDP pays that cost once, so it wins from \(T = 4\) on (Figure 33.5). The best order falls from 9.9 to 4.1 as \(T\) grows, because the growing term \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) pulls the minimum toward the low orders, where the exact curve is 1.06 times the quadratic term at \(T = 10{,}000\), against 30.61 at \(T = 1\).
The improved conversion saves from 27.5% at \(T = 1\) to 9.6% at \(T = 10{,}000\), where it gives 6.71 against 7.43, still an upper bound. Numerical accounting computes the tight value, and Choosing an accountant compares all the accountants of this part.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.6 Amplification for a general mechanism
For \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, Equation 33.8 is one formula, tight over the whole class of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms. Is there an RDP analogue, a map from any mechanism’s RDP curve and \(q\) to the subsampled curve that is tight? No, and the reason is also why accountants treat the Gaussian as a special case. The expansion of Theorem 33.3 still works for one direction of any mechanism.

Proposition 33.3 (The first direction for any mechanism) Let \(M\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for add/remove neighbours at every order, let \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) be its outputs on a neighbouring pair, and let \(\alpha \ge 2\) be an integer. Then \[D_\alpha\big((1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\big\|P_0\big) \le \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[(1 - q)^{\alpha-1}(\alpha q - q + 1) + \sum_{j=2}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha-j}q^je^{(j-1)\varepsilon(j)}\Big]. \tag{33.28}\]


Proof. 

Expand. Steps 5 and 6 of the proof of Theorem 33.3 never used the Gaussian, so they expand the divergence into the moments of \(r = P_1/P_0\) under \(P_0\).
Bound each moment. By the definition of \(D_j\), the \(j\)-th moment is \(e^{(j-1)D_j(P_1\|P_0)}\), which RDP of \(M\) bounds by \(e^{(j-1)\varepsilon(j)}\) for \(j \ge 2\).
Collect the first two terms. The moments for \(j = 0\) and 1 are 1, and their terms add to \((1 - q)^\alpha + \alpha q(1 - q)^{\alpha - 1} = (1 - q)^{\alpha - 1}(\alpha q - q + 1)\).


This is not a tight general answer, for two reasons. Each \(\varepsilon(j)\) is a maximum over pairs, taken separately for each \(j\), so the bound is attained only if one pair is the worst at every order at once, as for the Gaussian. And the other direction has no finite expansion and can be the larger one.

Theorem 33.5 (General RDP amplification (Zhu & Wang 2019)) Let \(M\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP for add/remove neighbours at every order, and let \(q\) be the Poisson rate. For every integer \(\alpha \ge 2\), \(M \circ S_q\) is RDP at order \(\alpha\) with at most \[\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[(1 - q)^{\alpha-1}(\alpha q - q + 1) + \binom\alpha2q^2(1 - q)^{\alpha-2}e^{\varepsilon(2)} + 3\sum_{j=3}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha-j}q^je^{(j-1)\varepsilon(j)}\Big]. \tag{33.29}\]


The proof is Zhu & Wang’s (2019, Theorem 5). It bounds the first direction as Proposition 33.3 does and covers the second with the factor 3. Without that factor the expression is a lower bound for some mechanisms (their Theorem 6), and exact for the Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms (their Theorem 8 and Proposition 10). Wang, Balle & Kasiviswanathan (2019) give a bound of the same form for fixed-size batches.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.9 References

Kasiviswanathan, Lee, Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith, “What Can We Learn Privately?” (FOCS 2008; SIAM Journal on Computing 2011). The first use of sampling to amplify privacy, in private learning. Read it for the origin of the idea; the bound there is not tight.
Li, Qardaji & Su, “On Sampling, Anonymization, and Differential Privacy: Or, k-Anonymization Meets Differential Privacy” (ACM Symposium on Information, Computer and Communications Security, ASIACCS 2012). The first proof of the tight \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification for Poisson sampling.
Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi, “Privacy Amplification by Subsampling: Tight Analyses via Couplings and Divergences” (NeurIPS 2018). Advanced joint convexity (Theorem 2), the tight \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification for Poisson sampling (Theorem 8), fixed-size sampling with replace-one neighbours (Theorem 9) and sampling with replacement, and tightness via randomized response (Theorem 13). The reference for Section 33.1 and Section 33.2.
Abadi, Chu, Goodfellow, McMahan, Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016). DP-SGD and the moments accountant; Lemma 3 is the small-\(q\) bound of Section 33.4. Read it to see where the practice started and which assumptions it made, including Poisson sampling.
van Erven & Harremoës, “Rényi Divergence and Kullback-Leibler Divergence” (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2014). The properties of the Rényi divergence, including joint quasi-convexity (Theorem 13), used in Lemma 33.3.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (arXiv 2019). The reduction to one dimension (Theorem 4), the dominance of the first direction (Theorem 5 and Corollary 7), and the numerically stable computation of \(A_\alpha\) (Section 3.3). The reference for Section 33.3 and the basis of most RDP accountants.
Wang, Balle & Kasiviswanathan, “Subsampled Rényi Differential Privacy and Analytical Moments Accountant” (AISTATS 2019). General RDP amplification for sampling without replacement (Theorem 9) and a lower bound (Proposition 11).
Zhu & Wang, “Poisson Subsampled Rényi Differential Privacy” (ICML 2019). General RDP amplification for Poisson sampling (Theorem 5), the matching lower bound (Theorem 6), and exactness under a condition that the Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms satisfy (Theorem 8 and Proposition 10).
Steinke, “Composition of Differential Privacy & Privacy Amplification by Subsampling” (arXiv 2022). A self-contained survey chapter with clean proofs of composition and of subsampling; the best second reading after this chapter.
Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?” (ICML 2024). Shows that shuffle-and-partition batching can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports, with the largest-batch-output test of Proposition 33.1.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (arXiv:2405.20769, 2024; IEEE SaTML 2025). Fixed-size against Poisson sampling (the factor two in the shift, and \(\varepsilon \approx 1\) against \(\varepsilon > 10\)), and worst-case datasets that fail under composition.
Zhu, Dong & Wang, “Optimal Accounting of Differential Privacy via Characteristic Function” (AISTATS 2022). Dominating pairs for subsampled mechanisms (Theorem 11), used by Lebeda et al. and by Numerical accounting.
Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato, “Hypothesis Testing Interpretations and Rényi Differential Privacy” (AISTATS 2020). The improved conversion used in Equation 33.27 (Theorem 21).

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.1 The privacy loss distribution
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP) by 10,000 steps of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). In this algorithm, DP-SGD, each step sampled every record independently with probability \(q = 0.01\), clipped each gradient to a fixed norm, and added Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is \(\sigma = 1\) times that norm. You need the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which the whole run is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP for datasets that differ by adding or removing one record. Rényi differential privacy (RDP), from Rényi DP, gives an upper bound of unknown slack, 6.7127, and the Gaussian central limit theorem (CLT) of f-DP and Gaussian DP gives an approximation, 6.0071. This chapter brackets the truth, here between 6.1377 and 6.2377, and a finer grid narrows the bracket at a known cost.
The one idea is to track the whole distribution of the privacy loss. Composition showed that \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is an average of a non-decreasing function of the loss, and that the loss of a composition is the sum of the step losses. For independent steps the total loss therefore has a convolution as its distribution, which a computer can evaluate once the loss sits on a grid of width \(h\). Rounding every loss up can only raise \(\delta\) and rounding down can only lower it, so the two roundings bracket the truth, and after \(k\) steps the bracket is at most \(kh\) wide in \(\varepsilon\).
The running example is this run, for up to \(T = 10{,}000\) steps. Because \(q\) is the sampling rate, the densities of the two output distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) are written \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\) rather than \(p\) and \(q\). Table 34.1 lists the symbols.
The guarantee you report is \(\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\), the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences, the smallest \(\delta\) for which \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\) holds for every set \(S\) of outputs. Computed directly it is a sum over outputs, and the output space of a training run is enormous. This section shows that the one-dimensional distribution of the privacy loss (Definition 21.1) carries all of \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).
An output adds to \(\delta\) only if its loss \(\ell\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then it adds the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell}\) of its probability, so \(\delta\) is an average of that weight over the PLD. Equivalently, it is the gap \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) on the set \(S\) of outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), which is the set that makes the gap largest. The \(Q\)-probability of that set needs no extra information, because reweighting by the likelihood ratio recovers it from \(\omega\).
So two pairs with the same PLD have the same \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), whatever their output spaces. The weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) is 0 up to \(\ell = \varepsilon\) and then rises towards 1, so \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the upper tail of the PLD beyond \(\varepsilon\), down-weighted near \(\varepsilon\) (Figure 34.1). Because the weight is at most 1, \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\), and because losses just above \(\varepsilon\) get a weight close to 0, that tail bound is loose.
Not every distribution is a PLD. By step 5, \(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\) is a \(Q\)-mass, so it is at most 1. Section 34.3 will round a PLD and must know that the result still belongs to a real pair, so it needs the converse, that every distribution with this property is a PLD.
For the Gaussian pair \(P = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(s, \sigma^2)\) of a query whose answer moves by \(s\) between the neighbours, write \(\mu = s/\sigma\) for the shift in noise standard deviations. The loss is then linear in the output, so it is normal, with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\) under \(P\) and mean \(-\mu^2/2\) under \(Q\) (Lemma 20.3). Inserting the two normal tails into Equation 34.1 gives the exact profile of Theorem 20.3, which is also the curve of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\) in f-DP and Gaussian DP: \[L \sim \mathcal N\big(\tfrac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2\big)\ \text{under } P, \qquad \delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{34.4}\] The law under \(Q\) agrees with Theorem 34.1, since tilting a normal density by \(e^{-\ell}\) moves its mean down by its variance.

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
Definition 34.1 (Privacy loss distribution) Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the output distributions of a mechanism on neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\), with densities \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\), which is \(+\infty\) where \(Q(y) = 0 < P(y)\) and \(-\infty\) where \(P(y) = 0 < Q(y)\). The privacy loss distribution (PLD) \(\omega\) of the pair is the law of \(L(Y)\) with \(Y \sim P\). Its atom \(\omega(\{+\infty\})\) is the \(P\)-mass of the outputs that are impossible under \(D'\).



Theorem 34.1 (δ is an average over the PLD) Let \(\omega\) be the PLD of a pair \((P, Q)\), including its atom at \(+\infty\). Then for every real \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E_{L\sim\omega}\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr_Q[L > \varepsilon], \tag{34.1}\] where \((x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}\) and an infinite loss gets the weight 1. The law of \(L\) under \(Q\) is fixed by \(\omega\): it is \(e^{-\ell}\,\omega(\mathrm d\ell)\) on the finite losses, plus an atom at \(-\infty\) of size \(1 - \mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\).


Proof. The plan is to take the first form from the composition chapter, split its weight into two terms, and move the second term from \(P\) to \(Q\) by reweighting.

The first form. Lemma 21.1 proved it: each term \((P(y) - e^\varepsilon Q(y))_+\) of the hockey-stick sum equals \(P(y)(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)})_+\), and outputs with \(Q(y) = 0 < P(y)\) add their whole probability.
Split the weight. When \(L > \varepsilon\) the bracket \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) is positive, and otherwise its positive part is 0, so \[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+ = \mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon\,e^{-L}\,\mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{34.2}\] The first term averages to \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\).
Reweight from \(P\) to \(Q\). An output with \(P(y) > 0\) has \(Q\)-probability equal to its \(P\)-probability times \(Q(y)/P(y) = e^{-L(y)}\). This is the change of measure of Lemma 3.2 with the roles of \(P\) and \(Q\) swapped, and it reaches only the outputs that \(P\) can produce. For any function \(g\) of the loss it gives \[\mathbb E_Q\big[g(L)\,\mathbf 1[P > 0]\big] = \mathbb E_P\big[g(L)\,e^{-L}\big]. \tag{34.3}\]
The second form. Take \(g\) to be the indicator of a loss above \(\varepsilon\). The outputs with \(P(y) = 0\) have \(L = -\infty\) and are not in that event, so the factor \(\mathbf 1[P > 0]\) can be dropped, and the second term of step 2 averages to \(e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[L > \varepsilon]\).
The law under \(Q\). With \(g\) the indicator of a set \(A\) of finite losses, step 3 gives \(\Pr_Q[L \in A] = \int_A e^{-\ell}\omega(\mathrm d\ell)\). With \(g = 1\) it gives the \(Q\)-mass of the outputs where \(P > 0\), which is \(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\). The rest of \(Q\) sits where \(P = 0\), at \(L = -\infty\).









Figure 34.1: The Gaussian PLD for \(\mu = 1\) (blue), the weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (orange, scaled by 0.4 to fit), and their product (green). The green area is \(\delta(1) = 0.1269\).





Proposition 34.1 (Which distributions are PLDs) A distribution \(\omega\) on \(\mathbb R \cup \{+\infty\}\) is the PLD of some pair of distributions if and only if \(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}] \le 1\), where \(e^{-\infty} = 0\).


Proof. 

Necessity. By Theorem 34.1, \(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\) is the \(Q\)-mass of the outputs where \(P > 0\), and no mass exceeds 1.
Build \(P\). For the converse, let the outputs be the losses themselves, and take \(P = \omega\) on the real line, with its atom at \(+\infty\), if any, on an extra point \(y_+\).
Build \(Q\). Put \(Q(\mathrm d\ell) = e^{-\ell}\omega(\mathrm d\ell)\) on the finite losses, of total mass at most 1 by assumption, and the missing mass \(1 - \mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}]\) on a second extra point \(y_-\), where \(P\) is zero.
Check the loss. At each finite \(\ell\) the ratio of the two masses is \(1/e^{-\ell}\), so the loss is \(\ell\), and at \(y_+\), where \(Q\) is zero, it is \(+\infty\). So the loss under \(P\) has law \(\omega\).




Example 34.1 With sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 1\), \(\mu = 1\) and the PLD is \(\mathcal N(0.5, 1)\). A million samples in the chapter’s script (Section 34.7) give a mean loss of 0.4990, a variance of 1.0013 and \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = 1.0015\), against the exact 0.5, 1 and 1. The green area of Figure 34.1 is Equation 34.4 at \(\varepsilon = 1\): \[\delta(1) = \Phi(-0.5) - e\,\Phi(-1.5) = 0.3085 - 0.1816 = 0.1269. \tag{34.5}\] Table 34.2 checks Equation 34.4 against numerical integration over the PLD density and against Monte Carlo. Solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) shows that the mechanism is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP.

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.2 Composition is convolution
DP-SGD releases \(T\) noisy gradients, and more generally a composition of \(k\) mechanisms outputs a tuple \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\), whose \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) you want. The bounds of Composition, including the optimal composition theorem (Theorem 21.4), see each step only through its pair \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\), so they must cover the worst PLD with those values. With the PLDs themselves, composition is exact. The loss of a tuple is the sum of the per-step losses (Lemma 21.2), and the law of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their laws.

Theorem 34.2 (Composition is convolution) Let \(k\) steps run independently, step \(i\) with the pair \((P_i, Q_i)\) and the PLD \(\omega_i\). The product pair \((P_1 \times \dots \times P_k,\ Q_1 \times \dots \times Q_k)\) has PLD \[\omega_{1..k} = \omega_1 * \omega_2 * \dots * \omega_k, \qquad \omega^{*k} \text{ for } k \text{ identical steps}, \tag{34.6}\] where \(*\) is the convolution of distributions and a sum that contains \(+\infty\) is \(+\infty\). For \(k\) Gaussian steps with shift \(\mu\) the result is again Gaussian, \[\mathcal N\big(\tfrac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2\big)^{*k} = \mathcal N\big(\tfrac{k\mu^2}2, k\mu^2\big), \tag{34.7}\] the PLD of one Gaussian pair with shift \(\sqrt k\,\mu\).


Proof. The plan is to follow the probability of the tuple from a product, to a sum of losses, to a convolution.

Losses add. By Lemma 21.2, the loss of the tuple is \(\sum_iL_i(y_i)\), with \(L_i = \ln(P_i/Q_i)\). A sum that contains \(+\infty\) is \(+\infty\), because once one step gives the dataset away, the whole run does.
The terms are independent. Under the product of the \(P_i\), the outputs \(Y_i\) are independent with \(Y_i \sim P_i\), and each \(L_i(Y_i)\) depends only on its own \(Y_i\), with law \(\omega_i\).
A sum’s law is the convolution. The chance that two independent terms sum to \(\ell\) adds, over every split \(\ell = a + b\), the chance of \(a\) times the chance of \(b\), which is what convolution computes. Adding one term at a time gives Equation 34.6.
Gaussian steps. A sum of independent normals is normal, with the means and the variances added, which gives mean \(k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(k\mu^2\).


In DP-SGD each gradient depends on the model, which depends on the earlier outputs, so step 2 fails: the second step’s pair, and with it its loss, depends on the first output. The way around is to replace each step by one fixed pair that is at least as easy to tell apart, whatever happened before. Comparing pairs at every level of strictness uses the hockey-stick divergence with a general weight \(\gamma \ge 0\) in place of \(e^\varepsilon\), \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(P(y) - \gamma Q(y)\big)_+. \tag{34.8}\]

Definition 34.2 (Dominating pair) A pair \((P, Q)\) dominates a mechanism \(M\) if \(E_\gamma(M(D)\|M(D')) \le E_\gamma(P\|Q)\) for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all \(\gamma \ge 0\) (Zhu, Dong & Wang 2022, Definition 7).

Every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) statement true of a dominating pair is then true of the mechanism, and domination survives adaptive composition.

Theorem 34.3 (Dominating pairs compose) Run \(k\) mechanisms in sequence, each chosen as a function of the earlier outputs. If \((P_i, Q_i)\) dominates step \(i\) for every value of the earlier outputs, then \((P_1 \times \dots \times P_k,\ Q_1 \times \dots \times Q_k)\) dominates the adaptive composition. So the convolution of the dominating PLDs gives a valid \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for the adaptive run.


Its proof is in Zhu, Dong & Wang (2022, Theorem 10), and Section K.3 in the appendices derives it step by step. It compares the adaptive run with the fixed pairs one step at a time, and that comparison needs \(E_\gamma\) for every \(\gamma \ge 0\), not only for \(\gamma \ge 1\).
Equation 34.6 has no slack at all, so the only errors in a PLD accountant are the ones you introduce to compute the convolution, by discretization (Section 34.3) and in floating point (Section 34.4). The bound is only as tight as the dominating pair, though. For the Gaussian mechanism with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity 1, the pair \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) dominates and is attained by some neighbouring datasets, so the result is tight, while a subsampled mechanism needs one pair for adding a record and one for removing it (Section 34.5).

Example 34.2 One Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) has \(\mu = 1\) and PLD \(\mathcal N(0.5, 1)\). Ten steps add ten means and ten variances, so their PLD is \(\mathcal N(5, 10)\), a single Gaussian pair with \(\mu = \sqrt{10}\). Solving Equation 34.4 with that \(\mu\) for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the composition is \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP. For 100 steps, \(\mu = \sqrt{100} = 10\) and \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\). Section 34.4 recovers both numbers from a discretized PLD.

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.3 Pessimistic and optimistic discretization
A computer cannot convolve continuous distributions, so the loss must sit on a finite grid \(\{ih : i \in \mathbb Z\}\) of width \(h\), and any rounding changes \(\delta\). The question is whether the error can have a known sign for every number of compositions, so that the answer is still a guarantee. It can, because the weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) never decreases as the loss grows, so moving every loss up can only raise \(\delta\) and moving every loss down can only lower it.

Definition 34.3 (Pessimistic and optimistic PLDs) Let \(\omega\) be a PLD, \(h > 0\) a grid width and \(\tau \ge 0\) a tail mass. The pessimistic PLD \(\omega^\uparrow\) moves every loss \(\ell \in ((i-1)h, ih]\) up to \(ih\). It may also truncate each tail, of mass at most \(\tau\), moving the top one to \(+\infty\) and the bottom one up to the lowest kept grid point. The optimistic PLD \(\omega^\downarrow\) moves every loss \(\ell \in [ih, (i+1)h)\) down to \(ih\). It may move the top tail down to the highest kept grid point, and drop the bottom tail, which leaves a total mass just below 1.

To compare averages before and after such moves, the next proof builds the rounded loss from the same random draw as the true one, a coupling, and its step 3 needs one lemma.

Lemma 34.1 (Monotone coupling) Let \(g\) be non-decreasing, and let \(X\) and \(X'\) be random variables built on the same random draw with \(X \le X'\) for every outcome. Then \(\mathbb E[g(X)] \le \mathbb E[g(X')]\).


Proof. For every outcome \(g(X) \le g(X')\), because \(g\) is non-decreasing. Averaging an inequality that holds outcome by outcome keeps it.

Write \(\delta_\nu(\varepsilon)\) for Equation 34.1 evaluated on a distribution \(\nu\).

Theorem 34.4 (The discretization sandwich) Let \(\omega\) be the PLD of a pair \((P, Q)\). For every number of steps \(k\) and every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta_{(\omega^\downarrow)^{*k}}(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta_{\omega^{*k}}(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta_{(\omega^\uparrow)^{*k}}(\varepsilon), \tag{34.9}\] and the same holds for convolutions of different PLDs, each rounded the same way. Moreover:

\(\omega^\uparrow\) is the PLD of a pair that dominates \((P, Q)\), so the upper bound also holds for adaptive composition.
Without truncation, let \(\varepsilon^\uparrow(\delta)\) and \(\varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta)\) be the values of \(\varepsilon\) at which the composed pessimistic and optimistic curves reach \(\delta\). Then \(\varepsilon^\uparrow(\delta) \le \varepsilon^\downarrow(\delta) + kh\).



Proof. The plan is to build both roundings from the same draw of the loss, add up \(k\) steps, and apply Lemma 34.1 to the weight of Equation 34.1. Validity, domination and the width then follow from the same coupling.

Couple one step. Draw \(L \sim \omega\) and set \(L^\uparrow = h\lceil L/h\rceil\) and \(L^\downarrow = h\lfloor L/h\rfloor\), which have the laws \(\omega^\uparrow\) and \(\omega^\downarrow\). A number lies between its two roundings, which are at most one grid step apart, so for every outcome \[L^\downarrow \le L \le L^\uparrow \le L^\downarrow + h. \tag{34.10}\]
Add \(k\) steps. Coupling each of \(k\) independent steps as in step 1 and adding the inequalities gives \[\sum_i L_i^\downarrow \le \sum_i L_i \le \sum_i L_i^\uparrow \le \sum_i L_i^\downarrow + kh, \tag{34.11}\] and by Theorem 34.2 each sum has the convolved law of its PLDs.
Apply the lemma. By Equation 34.1, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the average of \(g_\varepsilon(\ell) = (1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) at the total loss, and \(g_\varepsilon\) is non-decreasing. Lemma 34.1 applied to the first two inequalities of step 2 gives Equation 34.9.
Truncation keeps the sign. The pessimistic truncation moves mass up, so Lemma 34.1 still applies. The optimistic truncation moves mass down, which the lemma covers in the other direction, or deletes it, which removes a non-negative term from \(\delta\). Both can be repeated after every convolution.
The pessimistic PLD belongs to a pair. Rounding up raises every loss and so lowers \(e^{-L}\), and mass moved to \(+\infty\) contributes \(e^{-\infty} = 0\). So \(\mathbb E_{\omega^\uparrow}[e^{-L}] \le \mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L}] \le 1\), and Proposition 34.1 builds a pair \((P^\uparrow, Q^\uparrow)\) with PLD \(\omega^\uparrow\) (Doroshenko et al. 2022, Lemma 4.2, prove it for this rounding).
That pair dominates. Step 3 with \(k = 1\) says \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) \le E_{e^\varepsilon}(P^\uparrow\|Q^\uparrow)\) for every real \(\varepsilon\), that is for every \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon > 0\). At \(\gamma = 0\) both divergences are the total mass 1. So \((P^\uparrow, Q^\uparrow)\) dominates \((P, Q)\) at every \(\gamma \ge 0\), and Theorem 34.3 extends the bound to adaptive composition.
The width. Write \(\delta^\uparrow\) and \(\delta^\downarrow\) for the composed pessimistic and optimistic curves. Adding a constant \(c\) to the loss shifts its \(\delta\) curve to the right by \(c\), because \(g_\varepsilon\) sees only the difference \(\varepsilon - \ell\): \[\mathbb E[g_\varepsilon(X + c)] = \mathbb E[g_{\varepsilon - c}(X)]. \tag{34.12}\] The last inequality of step 2 and Lemma 34.1 then give \(\delta^\uparrow(\varepsilon) \le \delta^\downarrow(\varepsilon - kh)\). So wherever the optimistic curve has dropped to \(\delta\), the pessimistic curve has dropped to it at most \(kh\) further right.


Rounding down raises \(e^{-L}\), so \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}]\) can exceed 1, and then \(\omega^\downarrow\) is no pair’s PLD. Its \(\delta\) still lies below that of \(k\) non-adaptive copies of \((P, Q)\), so it bounds the mechanism’s \(\delta\) from below whenever some neighbours actually produce \((P, Q)\), as they do for the Gaussian and the subsampled Gaussian. Each truncation of mass \(\tau\) adds at most \(\tau\) to \(\delta\), since a weight never exceeds 1, and a few dozen truncations at \(\tau = 10^{-15}\) are far below any reported \(\delta\).
For a continuous PLD the width is almost exactly \(kh\). Such a PLD puts no mass on the grid points, so every loss moves by exactly \(h\) between its two roundings, and a fixed width at \(10^4\) steps needs a grid \(10^4\) times finer than for one step. When the losses spread evenly inside each cell, each rounding moves a loss by about \(h/2\) on average, so the midpoint of the two sides is a nearly unbiased estimate, but only the two sides are guarantees.

Example 34.3 Randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) (The definition of differential privacy) reports the true bit with probability \(\frac34\). The true report has loss \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\), with probability 0.7500, and the flipped one has loss \(-1.0986\), with probability 0.2500. On the grid \(h = 0.5\), rounding up gives the losses \(\{-1, 1.5\}\) and rounding down gives \(\{-1.5, 1\}\). The rounded-up PLD is valid: \[\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = 0.75\,e^{-1.5} + 0.25\,e^{1} = 0.1673 + 0.6796 = 0.8469 \le 1. \tag{34.13}\] The rounded-down one has \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = 1.3963\), which no pair can have.
Table 34.3 follows the four outcomes of three steps, indexed by the number \(j\) of steps with a positive loss. The exact total is \((2j - 3)\ln 3\), the rounded-up total is \(1.5j - (3 - j)\), and the rounded-down total is \(j - 1.5(3 - j)\). The gap between the two roundings is \(3 \times 0.5 = 1.5\) in every row, as step 7 of the proof predicts.

title: 34  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
34.4 Composition by FFT
A discretized PLD is a vector of masses \(m_0, \dots, m_{n-1}\) at the losses \((o + i)h\), where the integer offset \(o\) says where the vector starts on the grid, plus an atom at \(+\infty\). Convolving two such vectors directly costs a number of operations proportional to the product of their lengths. On the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\), one DP-SGD step of the running example already has 329590 bins, and after 10,000 steps the composed PLD has 2103251. The fast Fourier transform (FFT), brought to PLD accounting by Koskela, Jälkö and Honkela (2020), makes this cheap.
The proof of Proposition 34.2 below needs one tool, which turns a convolution into a pointwise product. The discrete Fourier transform attaches to index \(i\) the power \(\zeta^i\) of a fixed complex number \(\zeta\), and powers multiply by adding exponents, so indices add the way losses add.

Lemma 34.2 (The discrete convolution theorem) For a length \(N\), let \(\zeta = e^{-2\pi\mathrm i/N}\), and let the discrete Fourier transform of \(a_0, \dots, a_{N-1}\) be \(\hat a_m = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_i\,\zeta^{im}\). Then \(\hat a_m\hat b_m\) is the transform of the circular convolution \[c_n = \sum_{i + j \equiv n \bmod N}a_ib_j. \tag{34.15}\]


Proof. 

Multiply the transforms. Expanding the product \(\hat a_m\hat b_m\) gives one term per pair \((i, j)\), and the powers combine as \(\zeta^{im}\zeta^{jm} = \zeta^{(i+j)m}\).
Group by the index sum. Since \(\zeta^N = 1\), exponents matter only modulo \(N\), so grouping the pairs by \(i + j\) modulo \(N\) gives \[\hat a_m\,\hat b_m = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Big(\sum_{i + j \equiv n \bmod N}a_ib_j\Big)\zeta^{nm}, \tag{34.16}\] which is the transform of \(c\).


The FFT computes a transform of length \(N\) in \(O(N\log N)\) operations instead of \(O(N^2)\). Two discretized PLDs on a common grid then compose as follows.

Proposition 34.2 (Convolution of discretized PLDs) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be the mass vectors of two discretized PLDs on the same grid, with lengths \(n_a\) and \(n_b\), offsets \(o_a\) and \(o_b\), and atoms \(a_\infty\) and \(b_\infty\) at \(+\infty\). Their convolution has offset \(o_a + o_b\), atom \(a_\infty + b_\infty - a_\infty b_\infty\), and masses \[c = \mathrm{IDFT}_N\big(\mathrm{DFT}_N(a)\cdot\mathrm{DFT}_N(b)\big), \qquad N \ge n_a + n_b - 1, \tag{34.17}\] where \(\mathrm{DFT}_N\) transforms the vectors padded with zeros to length \(N\) and \(\mathrm{IDFT}_N\) is its inverse. For \(k\) copies of one vector \(m\) of length \(n\), with \(N \ge k(n - 1) + 1\), \[\omega^{*k} = \mathrm{IDFT}_N\big(\mathrm{DFT}_N(m)^k\big). \tag{34.18}\] If \(N\) is smaller, the result is the PLD of the total loss reduced modulo \(Nh\) into the window of \(N\) grid points.


Proof. The plan is to turn adding losses into adding indices, handle the atom, and then apply Lemma 34.2.

Grid losses add as indices. A loss \((o_a + i)h\) plus a loss \((o_b + j)h\) is \((o_a + o_b + i + j)h\). So the mass at index \(n\) of the sum collects every pair with \(i + j = n\), which is the discrete convolution \(c_n = \sum_{i + j = n}a_ib_j\).
The atom. The sum is finite only when both terms are, which has probability \((1 - a_\infty)(1 - b_\infty)\). So it is \(+\infty\) with probability \(a_\infty + b_\infty - a_\infty b_\infty\).
Padding. By Lemma 34.2 the product of transforms gives the circular convolution. With \(N \ge n_a + n_b - 1\), every pair of nonzero entries has \(i + j \le n_a + n_b - 2 < N\), so no index sum wraps and the circular convolution is \(c\).
Powers. Each further convolution multiplies the transform by one more copy, which gives \(\mathrm{DFT}(m)^k\). The composed vector’s largest index is \(k(n - 1)\), so it has \(k(n - 1) + 1\) entries, and that is the padding needed.
Wraparound. With \(N\) too small, Lemma 34.2 still holds but indices add modulo \(N\). Mass at total index \(n \ge N\) lands at \(n - N\), so the total loss is reduced modulo \(Nh\).


The one-shot \(k\)-th power needs a window \(k\) times wider than one step. The script instead uses repeated squaring, which lets it trim the vector between convolutions. It forms \(\omega^{*2}, \omega^{*4}, \omega^{*8}, \dots\) by convolving each with itself and multiplies the powers in the binary expansion of \(k\), so that \(\omega^{*10} = \omega^{*8} * \omega^{*2}\), at most \(2\log_2k\) convolutions in all. After each one it truncates both tails at mass \(\tau = 10^{-15}\) in the safe directions of Definition 34.3. Since all but \(\tau\) of the mass lies within a fixed number of standard deviations of the mean, the vector then grows like the composed PLD’s standard deviation, \(\sqrt k\) times one step’s, and not like the worst-case range \(k(n - 1)\).
The FFT is not exact in floating point, since each mass has an absolute error of order \(10^{-16}\) times the largest mass. Tiny tail masses therefore come out as noise, sometimes negative, which the script sets to zero. Summed over millions of bins, that noise alone can exceed \(\tau\), so a truncation that may cut only a tail of mass at most \(\tau\) never trims the ends, and the script also cuts every loss below \(-100\) or above \(200\) in the safe direction. That noise is far below a \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\) but is not part of the certified bound, and the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant of Gopi, Lee and Wutschitz (2021) also leaves it out, as negligible for \(\delta\) above \(10^{-10}\) (their Section 6).
To choose the grid, pick \(h\) from the width \(kh\) you can accept. Pick the range of losses to keep from the tails, which Chebyshev’s inequality (Theorem 2.2) bounds from the composed variance alone. Two published refinements allow coarser grids: the PRV accountant rounds to the nearest grid point and recentres the mean, so its errors grow like \(\sqrt k\,h\) (Gopi et al., Lemma 5.3), and connect the dots (Doroshenko et al. 2022) finds the tightest pessimistic PLD on a given grid.

Example 34.4 On the grid \(h = 10^{-3}\), truncated at \(\tau = 10^{-15}\) per tail, the Gaussian PLD \(\mathcal N(0.5, 1)\) has 15884 bins. After ten steps by repeated squaring it has 50257, a ratio of \(3.16 = \sqrt{10}\), while the one-shot power needs a window of \(10 \times (15884 - 1) + 1 = 158831\). Both give the same pessimistic \(\delta(1) = 0.81891018\), against the exact 0.81851782 from Equation 34.4 with \(\mu = \sqrt{10}\). 34.5 The subsampled Gaussian
One DP-SGD step with Poisson sampling includes each record independently with probability \(q\), sums the clipped gradients of the sampled records, and adds Gaussian noise. Look at it from the one record that may be missing, and measure the noisy sum along that record’s gradient, in units of the clipping norm, the bound on each gradient’s length. Without the record, this sum is a Gaussian centred at 0. With it, the record is sampled with probability \(q\) and then shifts the centre by the sensitivity 1, so the output is a mixture. Amplification by subsampling derives this reduction, and this section gives its PLD in closed form, so that only rounding separates the grid from the truth.
Under add/remove, each direction gives its own pair. Write \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\) for the dataset that holds the record, as in the rest of the part. The remove direction puts \(D'\) first, \(P = M(D')\) and \(Q = M(D)\), because its neighbour \(D\) is obtained by removing \(x\). The add direction is the order \(P = M(D)\), \(Q = M(D')\).

Theorem 34.5 (Dominating pairs of the subsampled Gaussian) Let one step of DP-SGD use Poisson sampling at rate \(q\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and sensitivity 1, under add/remove neighbours. The pair \[P = (1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2),\qquad Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \tag{34.19}\] dominates the remove direction, and the same pair with \(P\) and \(Q\) swapped dominates the add direction.


Zhu, Dong & Wang (2022, Theorem 11 and the paragraph after it) prove each pair dominates its case, and Section L.2 in the appendices derives it step by step from two exact hockey-stick identities. Their mixture component sits at 0 and their base Gaussian at 1, and the reflection \(y \mapsto 1 - y\) turns that into the form above. By Theorem 34.3, a \(T\)-step run has the guarantee \(\max\{\delta_{\mathrm{rem}, T}(\varepsilon), \delta_{\mathrm{add}, T}(\varepsilon)\}\). Neither pair dominates the other in general, so an accountant that uses only the remove pair covers only half of the add/remove relation.
The ratio of the mixture density to the base density \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) is \(1 - q\) plus \(q\) times the ratio of the shifted Gaussian to the base, an exponential in \(y\). Swapping \(P\) and \(Q\) flips the sign of the log of that ratio.

Proposition 34.3 (The PLD of the subsampled Gaussian) For the pairs of Theorem 34.5, with \(Y \sim P\) of the respective pair, the privacy losses are \[L_{\mathrm{rem}}(y) = \ln\Big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\Big), \qquad L_{\mathrm{add}}(y) = -L_{\mathrm{rem}}(y). \tag{34.20}\] The remove loss is increasing, takes values in \((\ln(1 - q), \infty)\), and the output with loss \(\ell\) is \[y(\ell) = \sigma^2\ln\frac{e^\ell - 1 + q}{q} + \frac12, \tag{34.21}\] with \(y(\ell) = -\infty\) for \(\ell \le \ln(1 - q)\). A bin of remove losses is therefore an interval of outputs, with mass \[\Pr_P\big[L_{\mathrm{rem}} \in (a, b]\big] = (1 - q)\Big[\Phi\Big(\tfrac{y(b)}\sigma\Big) - \Phi\Big(\tfrac{y(a)}\sigma\Big)\Big] + q\Big[\Phi\Big(\tfrac{y(b) - 1}\sigma\Big) - \Phi\Big(\tfrac{y(a) - 1}\sigma\Big)\Big], \tag{34.22}\] and for the add pair \(\Pr_P[L_{\mathrm{add}} \in (a, b]] = \Phi(y(-a)/\sigma) - \Phi(y(-b)/\sigma)\). One step’s \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is a difference of two normal tails at the output \(y(\varepsilon)\).


Proof. The plan is to divide the mixture by the base, read off the loss and its inverse, and turn loss bins into output intervals; step 6 then gives the single-step \(\delta\).

Divide the mixture by the base. Write \(\varphi\) for the standard normal density, so that \(\mathcal N(c, \sigma^2)\) has density proportional to \(\varphi((y - c)/\sigma)\), with the same constant for both centres. Dividing each part of the mixture by the base gives \[\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)} = (1 - q) + q\,\frac{\varphi((y-1)/\sigma)}{\varphi(y/\sigma)}. \tag{34.23}\]
The ratio of two Gaussians. The densities are exponentials of minus a square, so their ratio is the exponential of the difference of the squares: \[\frac{\varphi((y-1)/\sigma)}{\varphi(y/\sigma)} = \exp\Big(\frac{y^2 - (y - 1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{34.24}\] Taking logs of step 1 gives \(L_{\mathrm{rem}}\), and swapping \(P\) and \(Q\) flips the sign, which gives \(L_{\mathrm{add}}\).
The loss is increasing. The exponential is positive and increasing in \(y\). As \(y \to -\infty\) it vanishes and the loss tends to \(\ln(1 - q)\), and as \(y \to \infty\) the loss tends to \(\infty\).
Invert it. To solve \(e^\ell = (1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\) for \(y\), subtract \(1 - q\), divide by \(q\), take logs, multiply by \(\sigma^2\) and add \(\frac12\).
Bins are intervals. Because the map is increasing, the bin \(\{L_{\mathrm{rem}} \in (a, b]\}\) is the interval \(\{Y \in (y(a), y(b)]\}\). Its probability under the mixture is \(1 - q\) times that under \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) plus \(q\) times that under \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). For the add pair, \(L_{\mathrm{add}} \in (a, b]\) exactly when \(Y \in [y(-b), y(-a))\), with \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\).
Single-step \(\delta\) in closed form. For the remove pair, \(L > \varepsilon\) exactly when \(Y > y(\varepsilon)\), so by Equation 34.1 \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Pr_P[Y > y(\varepsilon)] - e^\varepsilon\,\Pr_Q[Y > y(\varepsilon)], \tag{34.25}\] two normal tail probabilities. The add pair is the same with the event \(Y < y(-\varepsilon)\).


The two directions have very different losses (Figure 34.3). The remove loss is bounded below by \(\ln(1 - q)\) and has an unbounded upper tail, because a rare large output betrays that the record was used. The add loss is its mirror image, bounded above by \(-\ln(1 - q)\), so a single add step has \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 0\) once \(\varepsilon \ge -\ln(1 - q)\).
In the running example the remove direction gives the larger \(\varepsilon\) at every \(T\) of Table 34.7. That is an observation, not a theorem, so the accountant computes both and takes the larger.






Figure 34.3: Left: the densities of \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and of the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on a log scale. They differ only in the far right tail. Right: the privacy loss as a function of the output for the remove pair (red) and the add pair (blue). Both are nearly flat near zero and steep in the right tail.




Example 34.5 For \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), the lowest possible remove loss is \(\ln(0.99) = -0.0101\). Except for \(10^{-15}\) of mass, the remove loss is in \([-0.0101, 3.2858]\) and the add loss in \([-2.8926, 0.0101]\), which on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\) is 329590 and 290268 bins. The rounded-up remove PLD has \(\mathbb E[e^{-L}] = 0.999995\), below 1 and so valid, as step 5 of the proof of Theorem 34.4 requires. 34.6 Accounting for DP-SGD
To answer the opening question, the accountant discretizes each direction’s PLD up and down (Section 34.5), composes it \(T\) times by FFT (Section 34.4), and reads off \(\varepsilon\), which can be done exactly because between two grid points \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) has a simple form.

Proposition 34.4 (Reading ε off a discretized PLD) Let a discretized PLD have masses \(m_\ell\) at the grid losses \(\ell\) and an atom \(m_\infty\) at \(+\infty\), and let \(\varepsilon\) lie between two consecutive grid points. Write \(A\) for the total mass of the grid points above \(\varepsilon\), and \(B\) for the sum of those masses times \(e^{-\ell}\). Then \[\delta(\varepsilon) = m_\infty + A - e^\varepsilon B, \tag{34.26}\] so on that interval the equation \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\) has the root \(\varepsilon = \ln\big((m_\infty + A - \delta)/B\big)\).


Proof. 

The weights. Between two grid points the set of grid losses above \(\varepsilon\) does not change. So the weight of Equation 34.1 is \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell}\) on those losses, 1 on the atom, and 0 elsewhere.
Sum them. Summing the weights against the masses gives \[\delta(\varepsilon) = m_\infty + \sum_{\ell > \varepsilon}m_\ell - e^\varepsilon\sum_{\ell > \varepsilon}m_\ell\,e^{-\ell}, \tag{34.27}\] which is the stated form. It is linear in \(e^\varepsilon\), so setting it equal to \(\delta\) and solving for \(e^\varepsilon\) gives the root.


Two accountants from earlier chapters serve as comparisons. The RDP accountant of Amplification by subsampling tracks, for each order \(\alpha > 1\), the per-step Rényi divergence \(\frac1{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha\) of the remove pair. Here \(A_\alpha\) is the likelihood ratio of Proposition 34.3 raised to the power \(\alpha\) and averaged under the base, \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E_{y\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)}\Big[\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y-1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big)^\alpha\Big]. \tag{34.28}\] The script multiplies the divergence by \(T\), converts it to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with the improved conversion of From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests, and takes the best order on a grid of orders. For integer orders the binomial theorem turns \(A_\alpha\) into a finite sum, which agrees with numerical integration on \(\ln A_2 = 0.00017181\) and \(\ln A_{10} = 0.34443377\).
The GDP central limit theorem of f-DP and Gaussian DP replaces the \(T\) steps by one Gaussian pair. Heuristically, the average squared deviation of the likelihood ratio from 1 is \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) for one Gaussian step, subsampling scales it by \(q^2\), and \(\mu^2\) adds over steps, which gives the shift of Theorem 32.5 \[\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}, \tag{34.29}\] and \(\varepsilon\) then comes from Equation 34.4. At \(T = 10{,}000\) this gives \(\mu = 0.01 \times 100 \times 1.3108 = 1.3108\).

34.9 References

Sommer, Meiser & Mohammadi, “Privacy Loss Classes: The Central Limit Theorem in Differential Privacy” (Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies, PoPETs 2019). Defines the privacy loss distribution, proves that composition convolves PLDs, and shows that composed PLDs tend to Gaussians. Read it for the PLD formalism of Section 34.1 and Section 34.2.
Meiser & Mohammadi, “Tight on Budget? Tight Bounds for r-Fold Approximate Differential Privacy” (CCS 2018). The privacy buckets: discretize the loss into buckets, round up for a certified upper bound and down for a lower bound. The origin of Section 34.3.
Koskela, Jälkö & Honkela, “Computing Tight Differential Privacy Guarantees Using FFT” (AISTATS 2020). FFT-based PLD accounting on a fixed window, with error analysis for the truncation and wraparound. Read it for Section 34.4.
Koskela, Jälkö, Prediger & Honkela, “Tight Differential Privacy for Discrete-Valued Mechanisms and for the Subsampled Gaussian Mechanism Using FFT” (AISTATS 2021). Rigorous upper and lower bounds with the FFT accountant, applied to the subsampled Gaussian; the source for the setting of Section 34.5 and Section 34.6.
Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021). The PRV accountant: nearest-point discretization with a mean-matching shift, explicit error bounds, and a running time of order \(\sqrt k\) (up to logarithmic factors) for \(k\) identical steps. Read it when you need certified error bars on a fast accountant.
Doroshenko, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar & Manurangsi, “Connect the Dots: Tighter Discrete Approximations of Privacy Loss Distributions” (PoPETs 2022). Frames discretization with dominating pairs, proves rounding up gives a valid PLD (Lemma 4.2) and builds the optimal pessimistic PLD on a grid. Read it for the cleanest account of why the pessimistic bound is valid.
Zhu, Dong & Wang, “Optimal Accounting of Differential Privacy via Characteristic Function” (AISTATS 2022). Dominating pairs (Definition 7), their adaptive composition (Theorem 10), the two directions of Poisson subsampling (Theorem 11), and accounting through the characteristic function of the privacy loss.
Google, dp_accounting library documentation (the pld module). A production PLD accountant with pessimistic and optimistic estimates and connect-the-dots discretization; use it to check the numbers here.

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.1 Shuffled randomized response, exactly
Amplification by subsampling showed that uncertainty is worth privacy: a step that uses your record only with probability \(q\) leaks roughly \(q\) times as much. This chapter asks what two other kinds of uncertainty are worth. The first is uncertainty about which report is yours. In the shuffle model of Trust models, each of \(n\) users randomizes their own data with a local randomizer that satisfies differential privacy (DP) at level \(\varepsilon_0\), and a shuffler mixes the reports before the analyst sees them. The second is uncertainty about when your record was used. Noisy gradient descent (GD) on a convex loss forgets, so when only the final model is released, a record used early is better hidden than composition says.
One idea organizes every result. You show that what the adversary sees can be generated from a much simpler pair of distributions, by a procedure that does not depend on your record. By the data-processing inequality, the simple pair’s privacy then holds for the real output. For shuffling the simple pair is a pair of counts, and for iteration it is a pair of Gaussians, or a pair that a chain of noisy steps keeps close.
The numbers come from two running examples. A company asks 10,000 users a yes-or-no question through randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), a weak local guarantee, yet behind a shuffler the reports are \((0.0870, 10^{-6})\)-DP. A model is trained for 10,000 steps of full-batch noisy GD, with noise ten times as large as the change one record makes to a step. Releasing every iterate gives no guarantee at all, while releasing only the final model of a contracting run gives \(\varepsilon = 6.5534\). Throughout, neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) are replace-one: they differ in the value of one record, yours. The shuffling here is of anonymous reports, not the shuffle-and-partition batching of Amplification by subsampling, for which no comparable theorem holds.
Before bounding shuffling for every randomizer, it pays to compute it exactly for one. For binary randomized response the privacy of the shuffled reports can be computed in milliseconds, and that value is the yardstick for every general bound in Section 35.2. Randomized response, from the definition of differential privacy, reports a bit truthfully with probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\) and flipped otherwise (that chapter writes \(t\) for \(p\)). One report is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, because changing the bit makes any report likelier by a factor of at most \(p/(1 - p) = e^{\varepsilon_0}\).
Earlier chapters supply the two tools. The first computes \(\delta\): for two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) on a finite set, the smallest \(\delta\) at a given \(\varepsilon\) is the hockey-stick divergence \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\), which by Lemma 20.2 sums \(P(y) - e^\varepsilon Q(y)\) over the outcomes \(y\) whose privacy loss \(\ln(P(y)/Q(y))\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\). The exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of a pair is the larger of the two directions, \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) and \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(Q\|P)\). The second, the data-processing inequality of Theorem 3.5, says that a map that does not depend on the data cannot move two distributions further apart.
Once the order is gone, only the number of 1-reports can tell the analyst anything, and your report moves that number by at most one.
The pair assumes that the other users all hold 0. If \(m\) of them hold 1, a guarantee must hold for the worst \(m\). The chapter’s script (Section 35.6) scans every \(m\) at \(n = 1000\), and \(m \le 30\) at \(n = 10^4\) and \(10^5\). The pair \(m = 0\) is the worst or within \(10^{-4}\) of the worst found, so the chapter calls its \(\varepsilon\) exact.
Shuffling never lowers the pure-DP level. At the count \(y = 0\) the ratio \(P(0)/Q(0)\) is \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) for every \(n\), and only the probability of that outcome shrinks. So shuffling amplifies by moving the bad outcomes into \(\delta\).
How does the privacy improve with the number of users? The count is a sum of many independent bits, so it is close to normal. Two normals with the same variance are as hard to tell apart as two unit-variance normals a distance \(\mu\) apart, where \(\mu\) is their mean difference in standard deviations. Such a pair satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) of f-DP and Gaussian DP with parameter \(\mu\), written \(\mu\)-GDP, and its exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the curve of Theorem 20.3. The next result computes the two moments that set \(\mu\).
So the privacy falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), with a constant that grows like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). The approximation is good when there are many 1-reports to hide among: at \(n = 10^5\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it gives \(\varepsilon = 0.0244\) against the exact 0.0247 (Table 35.2). At \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), the others send on average only \(999/(1 + e^4) = 18.0\) 1-reports, a count far from normal, and it gives 0.9667 against the exact 1.6910. The exact computation costs milliseconds, so use it.

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
Definition 35.1 (Shuffled randomized response) Each of \(n\) users holds a bit and sends its randomized-response report to a shuffler, which outputs the \(n\) reports in a uniformly random order. The analyst sees only this shuffled sequence, whose order carries no information, so the page calls it the bag of reports.




Theorem 35.1 (The count is the whole view) In shuffled randomized response, let the other \(n - 1\) users all hold 0, and let your bit be 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\). Write \(b\) for the probability mass function of \(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1 - p)\). Then the bag has the same divergences as the number \(Y\) of 1-reports, whose distributions on \(D\) and \(D'\) are \[P(y) = p\,b(y) + (1 - p)\,b(y - 1), \qquad Q(y) = (1 - p)\,b(y) + p\,b(y - 1), \qquad y = 0, \dots, n. \tag{35.1}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that the count carries everything, then to split it into your report and the others’, and to condition on yours.

The bag is the count. Given the count \(Y\), every arrangement of \(Y\) ones and \(n - Y\) zeros is equally likely under both datasets, because the shuffle is uniform. So the bag can be rebuilt from the count with randomness that does not depend on the data, and the data-processing inequality, applied in both directions, gives the two the same divergences.
Split the count. Write \(Y = S + B\), where \(S\) counts the 1-reports among the others and \(B\) is your report. Each other user reports 1 with probability \(1 - p\), independently, so \(S \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1 - p)\) on both datasets.
Your report. You hold 0 in \(D\), so \(\Pr[B = 0] = p\), and you hold 1 in \(D'\), so \(\Pr[B = 0] = 1 - p\).
Condition on your report. The count is \(y\) either when \(B = 0\) and \(S = y\), or when \(B = 1\) and \(S = y - 1\), so by the law of total probability \[\Pr[Y = y] = \Pr[B = 0]\,b(y) + \Pr[B = 1]\,b(y - 1), \tag{35.2}\] and the two values of \(\Pr[B = 0]\) from step 3 give Equation 35.1.






Proposition 35.1 (Moments of the shuffled count) In the setting of Theorem 35.1, the count \(Y\) has variance \(np(1 - p)\) on both datasets, and its means differ by \(2p - 1\). So a pair of normals with these moments is \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = \frac{2p - 1}{\sqrt{np(1 - p)}} = \frac{2\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt n}. \tag{35.3}\]


Proof. 

The variance. Every report, yours included, is a bit that is 1 with probability \(p\) or \(1 - p\), so each has variance \(p(1 - p)\). The \(n\) reports are independent, so their variances add to \(np(1 - p)\) on both datasets.
The mean difference. Only your report changes between the datasets, and its mean moves from \(1 - p\) to \(p\), a difference of \(2p - 1\).
Simplify. In terms of \(\varepsilon_0\), the numerator is \(2p - 1 = (e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\) and the square root is \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)} = e^{\varepsilon_0/2}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\). The factors \(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1\) cancel in the ratio, and dividing top and bottom by \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\) leaves \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2} - e^{-\varepsilon_0/2}\), which is \(2\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)\).









Figure 35.1: Left: the number of 1-reports among \(n = 30\) shuffled reports with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), when you hold 0 (blue) and 1 (orange); the others hold 0. Right: the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for one unshuffled report and for \(n = 10, 100, 1000\) shuffled reports; all reach 0 only at \(\varepsilon_0\), but for large \(n\) they are negligible far earlier.




Example 35.1 Start with the smallest case, \(n = 3\) users at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), so \(p = \frac34\). The two other users hold 0, so their count has \(b = (\frac9{16}, \frac6{16}, \frac1{16})\), and Table 35.1 fills in Equation 35.1. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), where \(e^{0.5} = 1.6487\), only \(y = 0\) has a ratio \(P/Q\) above \(e^{0.5}\), so only it enters the sum: \[E_{e^{0.5}}(P\|Q) = \frac{27 - 9e^{0.5}}{64} = 0.1900. \tag{35.4}\] In the other direction the outcomes \(y = 2\) and \(y = 3\) enter and give 0.0861, so \(\delta(0.5) = 0.1900\). A single unshuffled report has \(\delta(0.5) = \frac34 - \frac14e^{0.5} = 0.3378\), so even two other users nearly halve \(\delta\).
