title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 35.2 The clone bound for any local randomizer
text:
35.2 The clone bound for any local randomizer
Randomized response on bits is one randomizer. In practice users send histograms, \(k\)-ary responses or noisy vectors, so you need one bound for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer \(R\), a randomized map from a user’s data to a report. Erlingsson et al. (2019) and Balle et al. (2019) gave early bounds. The one to use today is that of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021), and its central reduction is short enough to prove here.
The reduction rests on clones. Lemma 26.4 shows that any \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer, run on another user’s data, produces with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) a report distributed exactly like one of your two possible reports. After the shuffle, the adversary can only count the reports that look like your \(D\)-version and those that look like your \(D'\)-version, and the clones blur both counts. Write \(x^0\) and \(x^1\) for the values you hold in \(D\) and in \(D'\).

Theorem 35.2 (The clone reduction) Let every user apply the same \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer \(R\), and shuffle the reports. Let the number of clones be \(N_c \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, e^{-\varepsilon_0})\), let \(A \sim \mathrm{Bin}(N_c, \frac12)\) given \(N_c\), and let the bit \(F \sim \mathrm{Bern}\big(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\big)\) be independent of both. Then the shuffled output on \(D\) and on \(D'\) is the same post-processing of \[\tilde P = (A + F,\; N_c - A + 1 - F) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \tilde Q = (A + 1 - F,\; N_c - A + F). \tag{35.5}\] Each pair counts the reports that look like your \(D\)-version and like your \(D'\)-version, and \(F = 1\) when your own report points to your true value.


Proof. The plan is to split every other user’s report into clones and a leftover, to show that after the shuffle only the numbers of clones matter, and then to replace your own report by a randomized-response bit.

Every report contains clones of yours. By Lemma 26.4, for every value \(x\) there is a leftover distribution \(\mathrm{LO}(x)\) with \[R(x) = \frac{e^{-\varepsilon_0}}{2}R(x^0) + \frac{e^{-\varepsilon_0}}{2}R(x^1) + \big(1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0}\big)\mathrm{LO}(x). \tag{35.6}\]
Read the mixture as a three-sided coin. A mixture is sampled by first choosing a component with its weight. So each other user flips a coin with faces “0”, “1” and “leftover”, and draws from \(R(x^0)\), \(R(x^1)\) or \(\mathrm{LO}(x)\). The users flip independently, so the number of clones has the law of \(N_c\), and given \(N_c\) the number of 0-clones has the law of \(A\).
After the shuffle, only the counts matter. Give yourself the face 0 on \(D\) and 1 on \(D'\). Someone who knows every other user’s data, but not your bit, can produce the shuffled bag from the numbers of 0-faces and 1-faces alone, by drawing that many reports from \(R(x^0)\) and \(R(x^1)\), a leftover report for every other user, and shuffling. Those numbers are \((A + 1, N_c - A)\) on \(D\) and \((A, N_c - A + 1)\) on \(D'\), so by the data-processing inequality the output is no more distinguishable than these counts (Lemma 3.3 of the paper).
Your own report is a randomized response. Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath (2015) show that any \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer on two inputs is a post-processing of binary randomized response. So there are two distributions \(Q_0\) and \(Q_1\) such that \(R(x^0)\) draws from \(Q_0\) with probability \(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\) and from \(Q_1\) otherwise, and \(R(x^1)\) does the reverse. Your report therefore comes from the distribution of your true value exactly when \(F = 1\).
Recount by \(Q_0\) and \(Q_1\). The weights in step 4 are symmetric, so a clone, a fair mix of \(R(x^0)\) and \(R(x^1)\), is also a fair mix of \(Q_0\) and \(Q_1\). Count reports drawn from \(Q_0\) and from \(Q_1\) instead of faces. The clones give \((A, N_c - A)\), and your report adds 1 to the first count on \(D\) when \(F = 1\) and to the second when \(F = 0\), the reverse on \(D'\). That is Equation 35.5. This step is Lemma 3.4 of the paper, and Section L.3 in the appendices gives the full argument for a fixed randomizer.


Computing the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of this pair of two-dimensional counts, with Lemma 20.2, gives the numeric clone bound. Feldman et al. also bound it in closed form, with Chernoff bounds on \(N_c\) and on \(A\) (their Lemma 3.5), which gives Theorem 26.2 of Trust models. For any \(\delta \in [0, 1]\) with \(\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\big(\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}\big)\), the shuffled output is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right). \tag{35.7}\] Section L.3 carries out a version of the Chernoff calculation. The condition, \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0} \ge 16\ln(2/\delta)\), asks for enough expected clones that \(N_c\) stays close to its mean except with probability about \(\delta\). At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it allows \(\varepsilon_0\) up to 1.460 for \(n = 1000\), 3.763 for \(n = 10^4\) and 6.066 for \(n = 10^5\).
The closed form scales as Proposition 35.1 predicts for the count. Given \(n_c\) clones, the first coordinates of the pair, \(A + F\) and \(A + 1 - F\), have means that differ by \(2\Pr[F = 1] - 1 = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\), while \(A\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{n_c}/2\). With \(n_c \approx ne^{-\varepsilon_0}\), the ratio of the two is \(2/(1 + e^{-\varepsilon_0})\) times the \(\mu\) of Equation 35.3. The factor exceeds 1 because the clone argument counts only the fraction \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) of reports guaranteed to look like yours. In Table 35.2 the numeric clone bound is 1.44 to 2.00 times the exact \(\varepsilon\) wherever there are many expected clones, close to that factor, and 2.36 at \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), with only about \(999e^{-4} = 18.3\) of them. No general bound can go below the exact column, since binary randomized response is one of the randomizers it covers.
The closed form is looser again, because its Chernoff constants are safe but not sharp. Where its condition holds it is 3.10 to 4.75 times the numeric clone bound, and 4.47 to 7.55 times the exact \(\varepsilon\). The first bound, of Erlingsson et al. (2019), grows like \(e^{3\varepsilon_0}\) instead of \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). So reason about scaling with the closed form, and deploy with the numeric bound.

The choice of accountant can decide whether a deployment is feasible. Suppose \(n = 10^5\) users send a bit and you want central \(\varepsilon \le 0.2\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). The closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) (0.1862), but the numeric clone bound allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) (0.1698), where each report is the truth with probability \(p = 0.9820\). If a fraction \(\pi\) of the population holds 1, the debiased estimate of \(\pi\) has variance \[\frac1n\left(\pi(1 - \pi) + \frac{p(1 - p)}{(2p - 1)^2}\right). \tag{35.8}\] The noise term is \(\frac{0.9820 \times 0.0180}{0.9640^2} = 0.0190\), against up to 0.25 for the sampling term you would pay without any privacy, so it costs little accuracy.

title: 35  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
35.3 Amplification by iteration
The second half of the chapter turns from hiding which report is yours to hiding when your record was used. Projected noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) makes one pass over the data. At step \(t\) it takes a gradient step on record \(x_t\), adds Gaussian noise and projects back onto a convex set. If every iterate is released, \(x_t\) is protected only by the noise of step \(t\), but if only the final iterate is released, the noise of every later step also covers it. The obstacle is that the later steps are maps applied to random points, so their variances do not simply add. Feldman, Mironov, Talwar & Thakurta (2018) overcame it with a divergence that allows a bounded shift.
The argument needs every step to be a map that never pushes two points further apart.

Definition 35.2 (Contractive noisy iteration) A map \(\psi\) is a contraction if \(\|\psi(u) - \psi(v)\| \le \|u - v\|\) for all points \(u\) and \(v\). A contractive noisy iteration is a sequence \(X_t = \psi_t(X_{t-1}) + Z_t\), for \(t = 1, \dots, T\), where each \(\psi_t\) is a contraction and \(Z_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\) is fresh noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\).

A gradient step \(\theta \mapsto \theta - \eta\nabla\ell(\theta)\) on a convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss \(\ell\) with learning rate \(\eta \le 2/\beta\) is a contraction, by Lemma 7.2. So is the projection \(\Pi_K\) onto a closed convex set \(K\), which maps each point to its nearest point of \(K\), and so is their composition.

Lemma 35.1 (Projection is a contraction) Let \(K\) be a closed convex set with projection \(\Pi_K\). Then \(\|\Pi_K u - \Pi_K v\| \le \|u - v\|\) for all points \(u\) and \(v\).


Proof. 

Two obtuse angles. Step 2 of the proof of Lemma 6.2 shows that the nearest point makes an obtuse angle with every other point of the set: \(\langle u - \Pi_K u, \theta - \Pi_K u\rangle \le 0\) for every \(\theta \in K\). Take \(\theta = \Pi_K v\), and then exchange the roles of \(u\) and \(v\).
Add them. Adding the two inequalities and collecting terms gives \[\|\Pi_K u - \Pi_K v\|^2 \le \langle u - v, \Pi_K u - \Pi_K v\rangle. \tag{35.9}\]
Cauchy–Schwarz. The right side is at most \(\|u - v\|\,\|\Pi_K u - \Pi_K v\|\). Dividing by \(\|\Pi_K u - \Pi_K v\|\), when it is not 0, gives the claim.


The two runs, on \(D\) and on \(D'\), are pushed apart at the step that uses your record, and after that the contractions keep the gap from growing while the noise blurs it. So the quantity to track is how far apart the runs might be, a shift, and the divergence that would remain if one run could be moved by that shift. To move a random variable by at most \(z\) means to pair each of its values with one at most \(z\) away, a pairing called a coupling.

Definition 35.3 (Shifted Rényi divergence) For random vectors \(X\) and \(X'\), an order \(\alpha > 1\) and a shift \(z \ge 0\), the shifted Rényi divergence is \[D_\alpha^{(z)}(X\|X') = \inf\big\{D_\alpha(Y\|X') : \text{some coupling of } X \text{ and } Y \text{ has } \|X - Y\| \le z \text{ almost surely}\big\}, \tag{35.10}\] where \(D_\alpha\) is the Rényi divergence of Divergences. With \(z = 0\) it is \(D_\alpha\) itself.

The noise pays off a shift at the price it charges for hiding one. Two normals of standard deviation \(\sigma\) whose means are \(a\) apart have, by Proposition 3.3, \[R_\alpha(a) = D_\alpha\big(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N(a, \sigma^2)\big) = \frac{\alpha a^2}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{35.11}\] Lemmas 20 and 21 of Feldman et al. drive everything. The first lets the noise pay off part of the shift at this price.

Lemma 35.2 (Shift reduction) Let \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\) be independent of \(X\) and of \(X'\). For all \(z \ge 0\) and \(a \ge 0\), \[D_\alpha^{(z)}(X + Z\,\|\,X' + Z) \le D_\alpha^{(z + a)}(X\|X') + R_\alpha(a). \tag{35.12}\]


The proof couples the two variables and splits each displacement into a part carried forward and a part of length at most \(a\) that the noise pays for. Section L.4 in the appendices derives it step by step. On two point masses, \(X = 0\) and \(X' = z\), the lemma is exact: moving \(X + Z\) by \(z - a\) towards \(X' + Z\) leaves two normals a distance \(a\) apart, at divergence \(R_\alpha(a)\).
The second lemma handles the gradient steps, which differ between the two runs at the step that uses your record. Different maps can only add the gap between them to the shift, at no cost.

Lemma 35.3 (Contraction) Let \(\psi\) be any map and \(\psi'\) a contraction, with \(\|\psi(u) - \psi'(u)\| \le s\) at every point \(u\). Then for every \(z \ge 0\), \[D_\alpha^{(z + s)}\big(\psi(X)\,\|\,\psi'(X')\big) \le D_\alpha^{(z)}(X\|X'). \tag{35.13}\]


Proof. 

Start from a coupling. Take any \(Y\) coupled with \(X\) so that \(\|X - Y\| \le z\) almost surely.
Map it. By the triangle inequality through \(\psi'(X)\), and because \(\psi'\) is a contraction, \[\|\psi(X) - \psi'(Y)\| \le \|\psi(X) - \psi'(X)\| + \|\psi'(X) - \psi'(Y)\| \le s + z. \tag{35.14}\]
Data processing. So \(\psi'(Y)\) is an admissible move of \(\psi(X)\) for the shift \(z + s\). Applying the same map \(\psi'\) to \(Y\) and to \(X'\) cannot increase their divergence (Theorem 3.5), so \(D_\alpha^{(z + s)}(\psi(X)\|\psi'(X')) \le D_\alpha(Y\|X')\). Taking the infimum over \(Y\) gives the claim.


Chained over \(T\) steps, the lemmas become a piece of bookkeeping. The shift grows by \(s_t\) when the two maps differ at step \(t\), and at each step you choose how much of it, \(a_t\), the noise pays off.

Theorem 35.3 (Amplification by iteration) Let \(X_t = \psi_t(X_{t-1}) + Z_t\) and \(X'_t = \psi'_t(X'_{t-1}) + Z'_t\) be contractive noisy iterations from the same starting point, with noise of the same distribution, and let \(s_t = \sup_u\|\psi_t(u) - \psi'_t(u)\|\). Choose payments \(a_1, \dots, a_T \ge 0\) such that the unpaid shift \(z_t = \sum_{i \le t}(s_i - a_i)\) is never negative and \(z_T = 0\). Then \[D_\alpha(X_T\|X'_T) \le \sum_{t = 1}^{T}R_\alpha(a_t). \tag{35.15}\]


Proof. The proof is an induction on the claim that, with the unpaid shift allowed, the divergence after step \(k\) is at most what has been paid so far: \(D_\alpha^{(z_k)}(X_k\|X'_k) \le \sum_{i \le k}R_\alpha(a_i)\).

Start. At \(k = 0\) both runs sit at the same point and \(z_0 = 0\), so both sides are 0.
Peel off the noise. Step \(k + 1\) adds noise to \(\psi_{k+1}(X_k)\) and to \(\psi'_{k+1}(X'_k)\), so shift reduction with payment \(a_{k+1}\) gives \[D_\alpha^{(z_{k+1})}(X_{k+1}\|X'_{k+1}) \le D_\alpha^{(z_{k+1} + a_{k+1})}\big(\psi_{k+1}(X_k)\,\|\,\psi'_{k+1}(X'_k)\big) + R_\alpha(a_{k+1}). \tag{35.16}\]
Peel off the maps. By the definition of the unpaid shift, \(z_{k+1} + a_{k+1} = z_k + s_{k+1}\). So the contraction lemma, with the gap \(s_{k+1}\), bounds the shifted divergence on the right by \(D_\alpha^{(z_k)}(X_k\|X'_k)\).
Close the induction. The claim for step \(k\) bounds that by \(\sum_{i \le k}R_\alpha(a_i)\), which proves the claim for step \(k + 1\). At \(k = T\) the shift is \(z_T = 0\), and the shifted divergence is the ordinary one.


The contractions never enter the cost. For one pass of noisy SGD the runs differ at a single step, and because the price is quadratic, small equal payments are cheapest. The theorem states its guarantee in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), and measures the noise per unit of the gradient’s replace-one sensitivity \(2G\), as the noise multiplier \(\tilde\sigma = \sigma/(2G)\).

Theorem 35.4 (One pass of noisy SGD) Let the losses \(\ell(\cdot\,; x)\) be convex, \(G\)-Lipschitz and \(\beta\)-smooth, and let \(K\) be a closed convex set. Run projected noisy SGD once over \(x_1, \dots, x_n\), with \(\theta_t = \Pi_K\big(\theta_{t-1} - \eta(\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; x_t) + Z_t)\big)\), \(Z_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\) and \(\eta \le 2/\beta\). Then releasing only \(\theta_n\) is \(\big(\alpha, \frac{2\alpha G^2}{\sigma^2(n - t + 1)}\big)\)-RDP for the record \(x_t\), for every \(\alpha > 1\) (Theorem 23 of Feldman et al.). With \(\sigma = 2G\tilde\sigma\), the RDP curve of the record at step \(t\) is \[\varepsilon_t(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\tilde\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n - t + 1}: \tag{35.17}\] one step’s Gaussian RDP curve, divided by the number of noisy steps from \(t\) to the end.


Proof. We write the pass as a contractive noisy iteration, find the one step where the runs differ, and pay as cheaply as possible.

A contractive noisy iteration. Write \(X_t\) for the iterate before projection, so that \(\theta_t = \Pi_K(X_t)\). Then \(X_t = \psi_t(X_{t-1}) - \eta Z_t\), with \(\psi_t(u) = \Pi_K(u) - \eta\nabla\ell(\Pi_K(u); x_t)\). That map is a projection followed by a gradient step, a contraction by Lemma 35.1 and Lemma 7.2. The noise \(-\eta Z_t\) has standard deviation \(\eta\sigma\), and \(\theta_n = \Pi_K(X_n)\) is a post-processing of \(X_n\).
The shift. The runs on \(D\) and \(D'\) use different records only at step \(t\). There the maps differ by at most \(s_t = 2\eta G\), since each gradient has norm at most \(G\), and at every other step they agree.
Equal payments are cheapest. Pay nothing before step \(t\), and pay \(a_t, \dots, a_n\) with \(\sum_ka_k = s_t\) from step \(t\) on. Cauchy–Schwarz, applied to \((a_t, \dots, a_n)\) and a vector of \(n - t + 1\) ones, gives \[\Big(\sum_k a_k\Big)^2 \le (n - t + 1)\sum_k a_k^2, \tag{35.18}\] with equality for the even schedule \(a_k = s_t/(n - t + 1)\). That schedule keeps every unpaid shift non-negative.
Add up the price. Each payment costs \(\alpha a_k^2/(2\eta^2\sigma^2)\) by Equation 35.11 with noise \(\eta\sigma\). So Theorem 35.3 with the even schedule gives \[D_\alpha(X_n\|X'_n) \le \frac{\alpha s_t^2}{2\eta^2\sigma^2(n - t + 1)}. \tag{35.19}\]
Put in the shift. With \(s_t = 2\eta G\) the learning rate cancels, because it scales the shift and the noise alike, and the bound is \(\frac{2\alpha G^2}{\sigma^2(n - t + 1)}\). Substituting \(\sigma = 2G\tilde\sigma\) gives Equation 35.17.


The even schedule loses nothing when the maps after step \(t\) are translations and the runs start from one point at step \(t\). The last iterates are then Gaussians a distance \(s\) apart, and Table 35.3 and Figure 35.3 show the even schedule matching their exact divergence, while uneven schedules cost more.
The bound is exact in the worst case, when step \(t\) maps every point to one point and erases the noise added before it. For typical runs it is loose, because that earlier noise also hides the shift, and a map that strictly shrinks distances shrinks the shift for free. Read as a Gaussian pair, the bound gives the record at step \(t\) the parameter \(\mu = s/(\sigma\sqrt{n - t + 1})\). Figure 35.4 compares it with the exact \(\mu\) of a one-dimensional run of 100 steps with \(s/\sigma = 1\), computed in Section 35.5. When each step shrinks distances by the factor 0.95, the exact \(\mu\) at \(t = 50\) is 0.0240, against the bound’s \(1/\sqrt{51} = 0.1400\).
Early records are safe and late ones are not. A uniformly random stopping time spreads this out, and Theorem 26 of Feldman et al. then gives every record \(2\ln n\) times the guarantee of the first (Section L.5 derives a version). Several passes need Theorem 35.3 with several shifts, and Altschuler & Talwar (2022) combine iteration with subsampling.

Mironov’s conversion from From RDP to (ε, δ) turns an RDP curve into \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\), minimized over a grid of orders \(\alpha\) up to 512, and at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) each position gets its own answer.
The last record gets \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\), from the RDP curve \(\alpha/2\) of a single Gaussian mechanism, which is also what every record gets if all iterates are released (its exact value by Theorem 20.3 is 4.3772). The record used 100 steps before the end gets \(\varepsilon = 0.4849\), the record in the middle gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0707\), and the first record gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0481\), at the largest order of the grid. So a report must state the worst record’s value, or randomize the order and the stopping time.

section: 35.4 Many steps on a bounded set
text:
35.4 Many steps on a bounded set
Full-batch noisy GD uses every record at every step, so the RDP of \(T\) steps grows linearly in \(T\) under composition. Theorem 35.3 does not help by itself, because every step adds a fresh shift \(s\) and the cheapest schedule pays \(s\) at every step, which is composition again. Yet if the parameters live in a bounded set, two runs can never be further apart than its diameter, however long they run. Altschuler & Talwar (2022) turned this into a bound that stops growing, and this section derives its full-batch form.
The idea is to ignore everything before some late step. At that step the two runs are at most the diameter \(d_K\) apart, and only the later steps need to pay off that distance plus the new shifts.

Proposition 35.2 (A bounded set caps the cost) Let two contractive noisy iterations have noise standard deviation \(\sigma\) and maps \(\psi_t = g_t \circ \Pi_K\) and \(\psi'_t = g'_t \circ \Pi_K\). Here \(\Pi_K\) projects onto a closed convex set \(K\) of diameter \(d_K\), and \(g_t\) and \(g'_t\) are contractions that differ by at most \(s\) at every point. After \(T\) steps, from a common start, \[D_\alpha(X_T\|X'_T) \le \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\min\left\{Ts^2,\ \min_{m \in \{1, \dots, T\}}\frac{(d_K + ms)^2}{m}\right\} \le \frac{2\alpha d_Ks}{\sigma^2}\quad\text{when } d_K/s \text{ is an integer}. \tag{35.20}\]


Proof. We start the accounting \(m\) steps before the end, pay evenly, compare with composition, and choose \(m\).

Start the accounting late. Fix \(\tau = T - m\). The projected points \(\Pi_K(X_\tau)\) and \(\Pi_K(X'_\tau)\) both lie in \(K\), at most \(d_K\) apart, so moving each onto its partner shows that their shifted divergence with shift \(d_K\) is 0. This is the only place where boundedness enters.
Run the induction from there. The induction in the proof of Theorem 35.3, started at step \(\tau\) from shift \(d_K\) and divergence 0, applies with the contractions \(g_t\). Its payments must total \(d_K + ms\), the starting gap plus \(s\) per step.
Pay evenly. Paying \(a = (d_K + ms)/m\) at every step pays \(d_K/m\) more than the step adds, so the unpaid shift falls from \(d_K\) to 0 and never goes negative. The total price is \[m\cdot\frac{\alpha a^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\alpha(d_K + ms)^2}{2m\sigma^2}. \tag{35.21}\]
Or start at the beginning. From the common start, paying \(s\) per step costs \(\alpha Ts^2/(2\sigma^2)\), the composition of \(T\) Gaussian steps. The better of the two choices gives the first bound.
Choose \(m\). A short window means few, large payments, and a long one means more shift to pay. Expanding the square shows the trade-off: \[\frac{(d_K + ms)^2}{m} = \frac{d_K^2}{m} + 2d_Ks + ms^2. \tag{35.22}\] Over real \(m > 0\) the falling and the growing terms balance at \(m = d_K/s\), where the sum is \(4d_Ks\). When \(d_K/s\) is an integer and \(T \ge d_K/s\), that \(m\) is allowed. When \(T < d_K/s\), the composition branch \(Ts^2\) is below \(d_Ks\). Either way the bound is at most \(\frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\cdot 4d_Ks = \frac{2\alpha d_Ks}{\sigma^2}\).


The bound follows composition until \(T = 4d_K/s\) and stays flat after that. For other \(d_K/s\), taking \(m = \lceil d_K/s\rceil\) gives at most \(\frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}(4d_Ks + s^2)\). For full-batch GD on \(n\) records the shift is \(s = 2\eta G/n\). Theorem 3.1 of Altschuler & Talwar proves the same shape for mini-batch noisy SGD, and their Theorem 4.1 shows it tight up to constants. All these results need only the last iterate to be released. Checkpoints or a model released after each epoch show the run before it has forgotten, and the accounting is back to composition. They also need contractive steps, and so convexity. For non-convex losses, Annamalai (2024) constructs a loss for which the last iterate of differentially private SGD (DP-SGD) leaks as much as all iterates together. Nasr et al. (2021) found that their attacks fall short of the DP-SGD bound when the adversary sees only the final model, but that observation is not a guarantee. So do not report an \(\varepsilon\) that relies on a hidden state for deep learning.

Example 35.4 Take the parameter set \(K = [0, 1]\), so \(d_K = 1\), with per-step shift \(s = 0.01\) and noise \(\sigma = 0.1\), so that \(d_K/s = 100\) is an integer. Each composed step costs \(\frac{\alpha s^2}{2\sigma^2} = 0.01\) at \(\alpha = 2\). The plateau of Equation 35.20 is \(2\alpha d_Ks/\sigma^2 = 2\alpha\), which is 4.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\), reached at \(T = 4d_K/s = 400\) steps. After 2000 steps composition charges 20.0000, five times the bound.
How loose is the constant? With a linear loss the two runs are random walks drifting in opposite directions and projected onto the interval, the construction behind Altschuler & Talwar’s lower bound. The script computes their \(D_2\) on a grid of 1000 cells (500 cells give 0.3779 against 0.3786 at \(T = 2000\)). It flattens at 0.3786 after about 100 steps (Table 35.4 and Figure 35.5, right). This walk is one pair of datasets, so its divergence is a lower bound on the worst case, and the constant of the bound is at most \(4.0000/0.3786 = 10.57\) times too large.

section: 35.5 Noisy gradient descent on a quadratic
text:
35.5 Noisy gradient descent on a quadratic
All the results so far are bounds. In one dimension with a quadratic loss, each step of noisy GD is a linear map plus Gaussian noise, so the last iterate is Gaussian on both datasets and its privacy can be computed exactly. The computation shows the plateau directly, shows that it needs contraction, and gives a yardstick for the bounds on strongly convex losses.
Full-batch noisy GD on the loss \(\ell(\theta; x) = \frac\lambda2(\theta - x)^2\) has the averaged gradient \(\lambda(\theta - \bar x)\), where \(\bar x\) is the mean of the records. So a step multiplies \(\theta\) by a contraction factor \(c = 1 - \eta\lambda\) and adds the offset \(\eta\lambda\bar x\) and noise. Replacing one of \(n\) records by one that differs by \(v\) moves the offset by \(s = \eta\lambda v/n\), at every step from the one where the record joins.

Theorem 35.5 (Exact privacy of the last iterate) Let \(\theta_k = c\,\theta_{k-1} + b_k + \xi_k\) for \(k = 1, \dots, T\), from a fixed \(\theta_0\), with \(0 < c \le 1\), offsets \(b_k\) and independent noise \(\xi_k \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). Let the offsets on \(D\) and \(D'\) differ by \(s\) at every step \(k \ge t\) and agree before. Then the last iterate is exactly \(\mu_T\)-GDP, with \[\mu_T = \frac{s}{\sigma}\cdot\frac{\sum_{k=t}^{T}c^{T-k}}{\sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}c^{2j}}}, \qquad\text{and for } t = 1,\ c < 1:\qquad \lim_{T\to\infty}\mu_T = \frac{s}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{1 + c}{1 - c}}. \tag{35.23}\] Releasing all iterates instead is \(\sqrt{T - t + 1}\,s/\sigma\)-GDP, and for \(c = 1\) and \(t = 1\) the two agree.


Proof. Unroll the run into a sum, read off its mean and variance, and divide; then take the limit.

Unroll. Substituting each step into the next shows, by induction on \(T\), that each step’s offset and noise are multiplied by \(c\) once for every later step: \[\theta_T = c^T\theta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{T}c^{T-k}(b_k + \xi_k). \tag{35.24}\]
The noise. The noise part is a sum of independent normals, so it is normal with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}c^{2j}\), the same on both datasets.
The means. The start and the offsets before step \(t\) are the same in both runs and cancel, so the means differ by \(s\sum_{k \ge t}c^{T-k}\).
A Gaussian pair. Two normals with the same variance are \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu\) their mean difference in standard deviations, which gives the first formula.
The limit. For \(t = 1\) both sums are geometric, \((1 - c^T)/(1 - c)\) on top and \((1 - c^{2T})/(1 - c^2)\) under the root. As \(c^T \to 0\), the ratio tends to \(\sqrt{1 - c^2}/(1 - c)\), and writing \(1 - c^2 = (1 - c)(1 + c)\) gives \(\sqrt{(1 + c)/(1 - c)}\).
All iterates. Releasing every iterate composes \(T - t + 1\) Gaussian steps, each \(s/\sigma\)-GDP given the past. GDP composes by adding squares (f-DP and Gaussian DP), which gives \(\sqrt{T - t + 1}\,s/\sigma\). For \(c = 1\) every power of \(c\) is 1, and step 4 gives \((T - t + 1)s/(\sigma\sqrt T)\), which for \(t = 1\) is \(\sqrt T s/\sigma\).


Contraction is what forgets. With \(c < 1\), the offset of step \(k\) reaches the end damped by \(c^{T-k}\) while fresh noise keeps arriving, so the signal saturates at \(s/(1 - c)\) and the noise at \(\sigma/\sqrt{1 - c^2}\). With \(c = 1\) the signal grows like \(T\) and \(\mu\) like \(\sqrt T\) (Figure 35.5, left). The plateau arrives after a few multiples of \(1/(1 - c)\) steps. With \(c = 0.99\), \(\mu\) is 9.6101 at \(T = 100\) and 14.1061 at \(T = 1000\), against the limit \(\sqrt{199} = 14.1067\). On a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss with \(\eta = 1/\beta\), that is the condition number \(\beta/\lambda\).
Chourasia, Ye & Shokri (2021, Corollary 1) bound the RDP of the last iterate of full-batch noisy GD on smooth strongly convex losses. In the notation of this section its limit is \(\frac{2\alpha s^2}{(1 - c)\sigma^2}\). The exact limiting RDP is \(\alpha\mu^2/2\) with the limit of Equation 35.23, so the ratio of exact to bound is \(\frac{1 + c}{4}\). At \(c = 0.99\), \(\alpha = 2\) and \(s/\sigma = 1\) that is 199.0000 against 400.0000, so the bound is within a factor of about 2.






Figure 35.5: Left: the exact \(\mu\) of the last iterate of one-dimensional full-batch noisy GD with \(s/\sigma = 1\), against the number of steps \(T\), for \(c = 1\) (dashed, on the black composition line), \(c = 0.99\) and \(c = 0.9\). Right: \(D_2\) of the last iterate for a linear loss on \([0, 1]\) with \(s = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\): composition, the bound Equation 35.20, and two projected random walks.




Example 35.5 Run \(T = 10{,}000\) steps of full-batch noisy GD with noise ten times the per-step shift, \(\sigma/s = 10\), on a quadratic with \(c = 0.99\). Releasing every iterate is \(\mu = \sqrt{10{,}000}/10 = 10.0000\)-GDP, which Theorem 20.3 turns into \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), no guarantee at all. Releasing only the final model is, after this many steps, at the limit of Equation 35.23, \(\mu = 0.1 \times 14.1067 = 1.4107\), which is \(\varepsilon = 6.5534\). The noise is the same, and the difference lies entirely in what the adversary may see.

35.8 References

Feldman, McMillan & Talwar, “Hiding Among the Clones: A Simple and Nearly Optimal Analysis of Privacy Amplification by Shuffling” (FOCS 2021; arXiv:2012.12803). Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and Lemmas 3.3–3.5 are the clone bound and reduction used here; Section 6 gives the numerical method, and their code computes it. Also covers approximate-DP randomizers (Theorem 3.8) and RDP of shuffled mechanisms.
Erlingsson, Feldman, Mironov, Raghunathan, Talwar & Thakurta, “Amplification by Shuffling: From Local to Central Differential Privacy via Anonymity” (SODA 2019; arXiv:1811.12469). The first amplification-by-shuffling theorem (Theorem 7 of the arXiv version), for adaptive randomizers; read it for the swap argument and for the encode–shuffle–analyse motivation.
Balle, Bell, Gascón & Nissim, “The Privacy Blanket of the Shuffle Model” (CRYPTO 2019). Writes each randomizer as a mixture with an input-independent “blanket” and derives amplification bounds from it, including a closed form tailored to \(k\)-ary randomized response.
Cheu, Smith, Ullman, Zeber & Zhilyaev, “Distributed Differential Privacy via Shuffling” (EUROCRYPT 2019). An early formal study of the shuffle model; its analysis of shuffled binary randomized response already has the \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}/\sqrt n\) dependence.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015). Shows that every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer on two inputs is a post-processing of binary randomized response, the fact used in step 4 of the clone reduction.
Feldman, Mironov, Talwar & Thakurta, “Privacy Amplification by Iteration” (FOCS 2018; arXiv:1808.06651). Shifted Rényi divergence, the shift-reduction lemma (Lemma 20), the contraction lemma (Lemma 21), Theorem 22, and noisy SGD (Theorems 23, 24 and 26).
Altschuler & Talwar, “Privacy of Noisy Stochastic Gradient Descent: More Iterations without More Privacy Loss” (NeurIPS 2022; arXiv:2205.13710). The bounded-domain plateau (Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.1; the full-batch form Equation 35.20 is this chapter’s specialization of Proposition 3.2), a matching lower bound (Theorem 4.1), and extensions to strongly convex losses and cyclic batches.
Chourasia, Ye & Shokri, “Differential Privacy Dynamics of Langevin Diffusion and Noisy Gradient Descent” (NeurIPS 2021; arXiv:2102.05855). Converging RDP of the last iterate of noisy GD for smooth strongly convex losses (Corollary 1), proved through Langevin diffusion and log-Sobolev inequalities.
Ye & Shokri, “Differentially Private Learning Needs Hidden State (Or Much Faster Convergence)” (NeurIPS 2022; arXiv:2203.05363). Extends the converging bound to mini-batch noisy SGD with shuffle-and-partition and sampling without replacement.
Nasr, Song, Thakurta, Papernot & Carlini, “Adversary Instantiation: Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Machine Learning” (IEEE S&P 2021; arXiv:2101.04535). Attacks that match the DP-SGD bound for strong adversaries and fall short when the adversary sees only the final model.
Annamalai, “It’s Our Loss: No Privacy Amplification for Hidden State DP-SGD With Non-Convex Loss” (ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, AISec 2024; arXiv:2407.06496). A non-convex loss for which the last iterate leaks as much as all iterates.

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.1 When the parameters are chosen during the run
Every composition theorem so far assumes that the privacy parameters of the steps are fixed before the run starts. The mechanisms may be chosen after seeing earlier outputs, as in Composition (Theorem 21.5), but the per-step budgets and the number of steps must be known in advance. Real systems break this. You train until the validation loss stops improving, or lower the noise when training stalls, so the number of steps and their budgets depend on the outputs. And when a model is trained with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD), each record’s gradient is scaled down to a maximum norm, and a record whose gradient is small costs less than the worst case, by an amount that depends on the current model.
Plugging the parameters that occurred into a fixed-parameter theorem fails, because an analyst who chooses when to stop can make the bound fail about three times as often as it claims. So the question splits in two. A privacy filter decides before each step whether the run may continue within a budget fixed in advance. A privacy odometer reports how much has been spent, and it must hold at every step at once, because you may stop at any of them. The one idea behind both is a quantity built from the privacy loss that never goes up on average, since stopping it at a time of your choosing cannot raise its mean. In Rényi differential privacy (RDP) this makes adaptivity almost free: if the spends at a fixed order add up to at most a budget on every path, the run has that budget.
The running example is full-batch noisy gradient descent whose noise has standard deviation \(\sigma = 10\) times the sensitivity, the noise multiplier. One hundred steps planned in advance are \((5.299, 10^{-5})\)-DP, best at the Rényi order 5.8, where the RDP budget is \(B = 2.900\) (Example 36.2). The chapter lowers the noise mid-run, reports the spend with an odometer, and tracks each record’s own spend. The pure-DP sections use randomized response instead, because a Gaussian step is not pure DP.
Before building anything, you need to see why the obvious approach fails. Advanced composition bounds the privacy loss of \(k\) steps of \(\varepsilon\)-DP, with \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) fixed, except with probability \(\delta\) (Equation 21.17). The shortcut is to apply it ex post, reporting advanced composition of the parameters used when you stop. Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan (2016) showed that this is not valid, because a bound that fails with probability \(\delta\) at each fixed time can fail far more often at a time chosen from the outputs.
A run has steps \(t = 1, 2, \dots\), and step \(t\) releases \(y_t\) from a mechanism chosen from the earlier outputs \(y_{<t}\). On neighbours \(D \sim D'\), which differ by adding or removing one record, write \(P_t(y_t \mid y_{<t})\) and \(Q_t(y_t \mid y_{<t})\) for the probability of \(y_t\) after that history on \(D\) and on \(D'\). The privacy loss of step \(t\) is \(L_t = \ln\big(P_t(y_t \mid y_{<t})/Q_t(y_t \mid y_{<t})\big)\), and by Lemma 21.2 the loss of the first \(t\) steps is the sum \(L_{1:t}\). Step \(t\) is \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP whatever the history, where \(\varepsilon_t\) may depend on \(y_{<t}\) but not on \(y_t\). Such a parameter is predictable. The analyst is whoever makes these choices from the outputs. Probabilities are under \(P\), the distribution of the whole transcript on \(D\), unless written otherwise.
An odometer makes a claim at every step. Since you may stop at any of them, the claim you report is only safe if it held at all times at once.
The natural candidate for \(U_t\) is advanced composition of the parameters used so far, which is correct at every fixed time and still not an odometer. The simplest mechanism shows it. Randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) reports a person’s bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flips it otherwise.
The theorem was never wrong; its use was. An analyst who stops when the loss happens to be high selects exactly the paths where a fixed-time bound fails. Rogers et al. (2016, Theorem 6.1) turn this construction into a lower bound: every valid odometer pays an extra \(\ln\ln n\) inside the logarithm, where \(n\) is the number of steps.
Basic composition does not suffer from this, because \(|L_{1:t}| \le \sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j\) holds for every output and leaves no bad event to select. Filters escape by another route. A filter fixes the budget in advance and only asks whether the next step fits, so there is no running claim to catch out, and Section 36.3 answers that question with no \(\ln\ln\) loss.

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
Definition 36.1 (Privacy filter) A privacy filter with budget \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\) is a rule that, before each step, looks at the parameters \(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_t\) so far, including the one about to run, and says continue or halt. It is valid if the stopped run \((y_1, \dots, y_T)\) is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP for every analyst, however the analyst picks the steps and their parameters.



Definition 36.2 (Privacy odometer) A privacy odometer with confidence \(\delta\) is a sequence of functions \(U_t(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_t)\) of the parameters spent so far. It is valid if, for every analyst and every pair of neighbours, the probability that the loss ever exceeds the running bound is at most \(\delta\): \[\Pr\big[\exists\, t: L_{1:t} > U_t\big] \le \delta. \tag{36.1}\]



Proposition 36.1 (The plug-in odometer fails) Let every step be randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) on the same person’s bit, and let \[U_t = t\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) + \varepsilon\sqrt{2t\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{36.2}\] At every fixed \(t\), \(\Pr[L_{1:t} > U_t] \le \delta\). But the probability that \(L_{1:t} > U_t\) at some \(t \le n\) tends to 1 as \(n \to \infty\), so \(U_t\) is not a valid odometer.


Proof. The plan is to prove the fixed-time bound with Azuma’s inequality, then to show that an analyst who stops at the first crossing turns the crossing probability into the failure probability, and that this probability tends to 1.

The loss is a walk. Take a person whose bit is 1 in \(D\) and 0 in \(D'\). A report of 1 has probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) on \(D\) and \(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) on \(D'\), so its loss is \(+\varepsilon\), and a report of 0 has loss \(-\varepsilon\). By Proposition 21.1 the mean loss per step under \(D\) is \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\). So \(L_{1:t}\) is a random walk with steps \(\pm\varepsilon\) and a slight upward drift.
Centre it. Subtracting the drift gives \(M_t = L_{1:t} - t\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), a martingale whose increments lie in intervals of length \(2\varepsilon\).
The fixed-time bound. Azuma’s inequality (Theorem 2.7) bounds the chance that such a martingale exceeds \(s\) after \(t\) steps by \(\exp(-2s^2/(4t\varepsilon^2))\). Setting this to \(\delta\) gives \(s = \varepsilon\sqrt{2t\ln(1/\delta)}\), and adding the drift back gives \(\Pr[L_{1:t} > U_t] \le \delta\).
The analyst’s rule. Run until \(L_{1:t} > U_t\), then stop. The loss is \(\varepsilon\) times the number of reports of 1 minus the number of reports of 0, a function of the outputs, so this rule decides from what has been released.
The event the odometer must control. The claim \(L_{1:T} \le U_T\) fails exactly when the walk crossed the boundary at some \(t \le n\), because that is when the analyst stops. So the failure probability is \(\Pr[\exists\,t \le n: L_{1:t} > U_t]\), a probability over the whole path.
The crossing probability tends to 1. The boundary sits \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2t\ln(1/\delta)}\) above the mean, a fixed multiple of \(\sqrt t\). The centred steps are \(\pm\varepsilon\) minus their mean, so their variance is the mean square minus the squared mean, \(v = \varepsilon^2 - \varepsilon^2\tanh^2(\varepsilon/2)\). The law of the iterated logarithm, which we cite (Durrett, in the References), says that a centred walk with step variance \(v\) exceeds \(\frac12\sqrt{2vt\ln\ln t}\) infinitely often with probability 1. That curve grows faster than any fixed multiple of \(\sqrt t\), because \(\ln\ln t\) grows without bound, so the walk crosses the boundary with probability 1.










Figure 36.1: Left: forty runs of randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the loss in units of \(\varepsilon\), and the plug-in advanced-composition bound at \(\delta = 0.01\). Red paths stop at their first crossing. Right: the exact probability of a crossing by step \(n\), for \(\delta = 0.05\) and \(0.01\) (dashed).




Example 36.1 Take randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), whose mean loss per step is \(0.1 \times \tanh(0.05) = 0.004996\). The crossing probability is exact: propagate the distribution of \(L_{1:t}/\varepsilon\), an integer walk, step by step, and remove at each \(t\) the mass above \(U_t/\varepsilon\) (Table 36.2).

In Figure 36.1 (left), a few runs cross the boundary early, where it is narrow, and the analyst freezes them there. A small \(\delta\) does not cure it: at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the factor is 3.69.

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.2 The Rényi filter
Rényi differential privacy describes a mechanism by a curve. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) is \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]\), a log of an exponential moment of the privacy loss \(L\) (Equation 31.2), and a mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP if this is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) for every pair of neighbours. RDP composition adds curves fixed in advance (Equation 29.11). This section asks what happens when the spend \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) depends on the earlier outputs. Feldman & Zrnic (2021) and Lécuyer (2021) showed that nothing is lost at a fixed order, and every later section rests on that.
The proof stops a random process at a time chosen from the outputs, so it needs two tools. The first extends Lemma 21.2 to a run whose length is decided by its outputs.

Lemma 36.1 (The loss of a stopped run) Let the run stop after step \(T\), where the decision to stop after \(y_t\) is a function of \(y_1, \dots, y_t\) alone. Then the privacy loss of the stopped transcript \((y_1, \dots, y_T)\) is \(L_{1:T} = \sum_{t \le T}L_t\).


Proof. 

Chain rule. The transcript has probability \(\prod_{t \le T}P_t(y_t \mid y_{<t})\) under \(P\), times the probability of the stopping decisions, and likewise with \(Q_t\) under \(Q\).
The stopping decisions cancel. Each decision is a function of outputs already released, so given them it has probability 1 or 0, the same under \(P\) and \(Q\), and it cancels from the ratio.
Take logs. The log of the remaining ratio of products is the sum of the step losses.


The second tool says that stopping early cannot raise the mean of a process that never goes up on average. Picture your wealth in a game that is fair or unfavourable to you, where you may quit at any time by looking at the past but not at the future.

Definition 36.3 (Supermartingale and stopping time) A process \(N_0, N_1, \dots\), with \(N_t\) a function of \(y_{\le t}\), is a supermartingale if \(\mathbb E[N_t \mid y_{<t}] \le N_{t-1}\) for every \(t\), and a martingale if equality holds. A stopping time \(T\) is a random step such that the event \(\{T \ge t\}\), “the run takes step \(t\)”, is decided by \(y_{<t}\).


Lemma 36.2 (Optional stopping) Let \(N\) be a supermartingale and \(T\) a stopping time with \(T \le n\) for a fixed \(n\). Then \[\mathbb E[N_T] \le \mathbb E[N_0]. \tag{36.3}\] If \(N_t \ge 0\) for every \(t\), the horizon can be dropped: \(\mathbb E\big[N_T\mathbf 1[T < \infty]\big] \le \mathbb E[N_0]\) for every stopping time \(T\).


Proof. The idea is to write the stopped process as a running total of the increments it collects, and to show that each has non-positive mean. Write \(T\wedge t = \min(T, t)\).

Write the stopped process as a sum. The stopped process gains \(N_t - N_{t-1}\) only if the run takes step \(t\), which the indicator \(\mathbf 1[T \ge t]\) records: \[N_{T\wedge t} = N_{T\wedge(t-1)} + \mathbf 1[T \ge t](N_t - N_{t-1}). \tag{36.4}\]
Each collected increment has non-positive mean. The indicator is decided by \(y_{<t}\), so given \(y_{<t}\) it comes out of the conditional expectation, and what remains, \(\mathbb E[N_t \mid y_{<t}] - N_{t-1}\), is non-positive. This is where the stopping decision must not look at \(y_t\).
Add up the steps. Taking expectations and summing over \(t \le n\) gives \(\mathbb E[N_{T\wedge n}] \le \mathbb E[N_0]\), and \(T \wedge n = T\).
Drop the horizon. For \(N \ge 0\), apply step 3 to \(T \wedge n\) and let \(n \to \infty\). Fatou’s lemma, which says that the mean of a limit of non-negative variables is at most the limit of their means, gives the second bound.


The horizon matters only for processes that can go negative. With both tools in hand, the result says: fix an order and a budget, add up the RDP spends as the run goes, and stop before the sum would pass the budget.

Theorem 36.1 (The Rényi filter (Feldman & Zrnic 2021; Lécuyer 2021)) Fix an order \(\alpha > 1\) and a budget \(B\). Let step \(t\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon_t(\alpha))\)-RDP conditionally on \(y_{<t}\), with \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) predictable. Run step \(t\) only if \[\sum_{j \le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha) \le B. \tag{36.5}\] Then the stopped run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP. Equivalently, if \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t(\alpha) \le B\) on every path, the adaptive composition is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP.


Proof. The proof builds a supermartingale from the privacy loss and the spends, stops it with the filter, and reads the RDP bound off its mean. The quantity to use is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), whose mean is what the Rényi divergence measures, divided by what the spends allow. Fix \(D \sim D'\) and define \[N_t = \exp\Big((\alpha - 1)\Big(L_{1:t} - \sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\Big)\Big), \qquad N_0 = 1. \tag{36.6}\]

One step’s moment is bounded by its spend. Given \(y_{<t}\), step \(t\) is a fixed mechanism, so the moment form of \(D_\alpha\) and the RDP assumption give \(\mathbb E\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L_t} \mid y_{<t}\big] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_t\|Q_t)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_t(\alpha)}\).
\(N_t\) is a supermartingale. Each step multiplies \(N\) by \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(L_t - \varepsilon_t(\alpha))}\). Both \(N_{t-1}\) and \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) are functions of \(y_{<t}\), so they come out of the conditional expectation, and step 1 bounds what remains by 1. This is where predictability is used.
Stop it. Whether step \(t\) runs depends on spends that are functions of \(y_{<t}\), so the filter’s last step \(T\) is a stopping time, and Lemma 36.2 gives \(\mathbb E[N_T] \le 1\).
Use the budget on every path. Undoing the definition, \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L_{1:T}} = N_T\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\sum_{j\le T}\varepsilon_j(\alpha)}\), and the filter keeps the spend at most \(B\) on every path. Taking expectations, \[\mathbb E\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L_{1:T}}\big] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)B}\,\mathbb E[N_T] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)B}. \tag{36.7}\]
Read off the divergence. By Lemma 36.1, \(L_{1:T}\) is the privacy loss of the stopped transcript, so the left side is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha}\) of the stopped run, and \(D_\alpha \le B\). Swapping \(D\) and \(D'\) gives the other direction.


Step 4 needs the budget on every path, not on average, because paths with a large spend may also have a large \(N_T\). When every path spends exactly \(B\) and each step’s moment equals its RDP parameter, as for Gaussian steps, \(N\) is a martingale and the bound is attained. In Figure 36.2, adaptive Gaussian steps (shift 0.3 after a positive output, 0.6 otherwise, in units of the noise) are stopped by a filter with \(\alpha = 2\) and \(B = 1\). If the last step’s shift is chosen so that it spends exactly what is left, \(10^6\) Monte Carlo paths give \(D_2 = 1.0004\). If the filter simply stops, \(D_2 = 0.9305\), because no path uses the whole budget.
The price is the order, which must be fixed before the run. You can track several orders and stop when any one is exhausted, but continuing while some order still fits is a choice made after seeing the spends, which Section 36.4 prices. At the end, Mironov’s conversion (Equation 29.24) turns a DP target \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\) into the budget \(B = \varepsilon_g - \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\).






Figure 36.2: Adaptive Gaussian steps under a Rényi filter with \(\alpha = 2\) and \(B = 1\). Left: \(\ln N_t\) along thirty paths, each frozen when stopped. Right: the mean of \(N_t\) over \(2\times10^5\) paths stays at 1.




Example 36.2 You train with full-batch noisy gradient descent and want to lower the noise when progress stalls. With \((\varepsilon_g, \delta) = (5.299, 10^{-5})\) and the order \(\alpha = 5.8\), the RDP budget is \(B = 5.299 - \ln(10^5)/4.8 = 2.900\). A Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma_t\) spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma_t^2)\) (Equation 29.5). With \(\sigma_t = 10\) throughout, each step spends \(5.8/200 = 0.0290\), which gives \(2.900/0.0290 = 100\) steps. If you switch to \(\sigma_t = 5\) after a plateau at step 60, each later step costs \(5.8/50 = 0.1160\), and the filter allows \((2.900 - 60\times0.0290)/0.1160 = 1.160/0.1160 = 10\) more. Either way the run is \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP, whatever rule decided the switch.

The filter can also beat fixed-curve composition outright when branches trade costs. Two steps, as in Table 29.5 of Rényi DP, are too few to show it, but three are enough.

Example 36.3 Take \(\alpha = 2\), so \(N_t = e^{L_{1:t} - \text{spend}}\), and one person’s bit, 1 in \(D\) and 0 in \(D'\). Step 1 is randomized response with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), keep-probability \(p = 3/4\), and RDP at order 2 (Equation 29.7) \(\ln\big(p^2/(1 - p) + (1 - p)^2/p\big) = 0.8473\). After \(y_1 = 1\), steps 2 and 3 are randomized response with \(\ln 3\) (strong) and then \(\ln 1.5\) (weak, keep-probability \(0.6\), RDP 0.1542), and after \(y_1 = 0\) they come in the other order. So every path spends \(B = 2 \times 0.8473 + 0.1542 = 1.8487\) (computed before rounding), while fixed-curve composition charges each later step its worst branch, \(3 \times 0.8473 = 2.5419\).

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.3 Filters for pure differential privacy
You run an interactive system with a global budget \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\), and each query comes with its own \(\varepsilon_t\), chosen after seeing the earlier answers. Before each query you need a rule that says whether it may run. Summing the \(\varepsilon_t\) is valid however you stop, but the total grows like the number of steps \(k\), and advanced composition, which grows like \(\sqrt k\), cannot be applied ex post. This section gives filters that grow like \(\sqrt k\). Its examples use pure-DP steps, since Gaussian steps are not pure DP.
Every filter below continues while one statistic of \(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_t\) is at most \(\varepsilon_g\). The simplest statistic is the plain sum, which works because a pure-DP step bounds the loss of every single output.

Proposition 36.2 (The basic filter (Rogers et al. 2016, Theorem 3.4)) Let each step be \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP conditionally on the past, with \(\varepsilon_t\) predictable. The filter that continues while \(\sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j \le \varepsilon_g\) gives an \(\varepsilon_g\)-DP stopped run, and \(U_t = \sum_{j \le t}\varepsilon_j\) is a valid odometer with \(\delta = 0\).


Proof. 

Each step’s loss is bounded on every output. An \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP step makes no output more than \(e^{\varepsilon_t}\) times likelier on one neighbour than on the other, so \(|L_t| \le \varepsilon_t\).
So is the stopped run’s loss. By Lemma 36.1, \(|L_{1:T}| \le \sum_{t\le T}\varepsilon_t \le \varepsilon_g\) on every path, and the same bound holds at every \(t\), which is the odometer.
A bounded loss is pure DP. A loss of at most \(\varepsilon_g\) on every transcript \(y\) means \(P(y) \le e^{\varepsilon_g}Q(y)\), and summing over the transcripts in any event \(E\) gives \(P(E) \le e^{\varepsilon_g}Q(E)\).


To grow like \(\sqrt k\), the statistic needs a mean term plus a spread term like advanced composition’s \(\sqrt{2V\ln(1/\delta)}\), where \(V = \sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\) plays the role of a variance. Because \(V\) is random, Rogers et al. pad it by a constant \(x\) and multiply it by a logarithmic factor in \(V/x\).

Theorem 36.2 (The Rogers et al. filter (2016, Theorem 5.1)) Under the assumptions of Proposition 36.2, let \(\delta < 1/e\) and \(x = \varepsilon_g^2/(28.04\ln(1/\delta))\). The filter that continues while \[K = \sum_t\frac{\varepsilon_t(e^{\varepsilon_t} - 1)}{2} + \sqrt{2(V + x)\Big(1 + \tfrac12\ln\big(\tfrac Vx + 1\big)\Big)\ln(1/\delta)} \le \varepsilon_g \tag{36.8}\] gives an \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP stopped run.


The proof is in Rogers et al.’s Section 5. Its centred loss has random increment ranges \(2\varepsilon_t\), so Azuma’s inequality no longer applies, and they use a self-normalized inequality instead (their Theorem 4.4), which bounds the martingale divided by \(\sqrt{V + x}\) whatever \(V\) turns out to be. The extra \(x\) and the logarithmic factor are its price, while the constant 28.04 and the condition \(\delta < 1/e\) are constants of their proof.
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) avoids that price. A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP if it is \((\alpha, \alpha\rho)\)-RDP at every order \(\alpha > 1\), so its RDP curve lies below a line through the origin with slope \(\rho\). In zCDP, adaptive budgets add up for free at every order by Theorem 36.1, and the conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP happens once, at the end.

Theorem 36.3 (The Whitehouse et al. filter (2023, Theorem 2)) Under the same assumptions, let \(\delta \in (0, 1)\). The filter that continues while \[\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2} + \tfrac12\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \varepsilon_g \tag{36.9}\] gives an \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP stopped run. Equivalently, it continues while \(\frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \rho^*\), where \[\rho^* = \Big(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon_g} - \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\Big)^2. \tag{36.10}\]


Proof. Measure each step in zCDP, apply the Rényi filter at every order at once, then convert. Write \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\).

Each step is zCDP. An \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP step is \((\alpha, \alpha\varepsilon_t^2/2)\)-RDP for every \(\alpha > 1\) (Equation 31.7), because its loss lies in \([-\varepsilon_t, \varepsilon_t]\). So it is \(\varepsilon_t^2/2\)-zCDP.
The rule is a Rényi filter at every order. Multiplying \(\frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \rho^*\) by \(\alpha\) gives \(\sum_t\alpha\varepsilon_t^2/2 \le \alpha\rho^*\), a Rényi filter with budget \(\alpha\rho^*\). By Theorem 36.1 the stopped run is \((\alpha, \alpha\rho^*)\)-RDP. The rule does not mention \(\alpha\), so this holds at every order, and the stopped run is \(\rho^*\)-zCDP.
Convert. A \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}, \delta)\)-DP (Equation 31.15), Mironov’s conversion at the best order.
The choice of \(\rho^*\) makes this \(\varepsilon_g\). The equation \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell} = \varepsilon_g\) completes to \((\sqrt\rho + \sqrt\ell)^2 = \varepsilon_g + \ell\), whose solution is the \(\rho^*\) of the statement (Equation 31.18).
Rewrite the rule. The map \(\rho \mapsto \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\) is increasing, so \(\rho \le \rho^*\) is the same as \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell} \le \varepsilon_g\). With \(\rho = \frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\), the square root is \(\sqrt{2\ell\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2}\), and the rule becomes Equation 36.9.


This is the budget-spending rule that Section 21.5 asked for, and adaptivity costs it essentially nothing. Its mean term \(\varepsilon_t^2/2\) lies slightly above the sharp mean \(\varepsilon_t\tanh(\varepsilon_t/2)\) of Equation 21.17 but below the \(\varepsilon_t(e^{\varepsilon_t} - 1)\) of Equation 21.9, which is why Table 36.4 puts it below fixed-\(k\) advanced composition. For the same reason, a plug-in filter on Equation 21.9 is valid: it halts no later than the Whitehouse filter, and stopping earlier is post-processing.

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.4 Odometers
Early stopping and open-ended analyses have no budget to stop at. They need a running answer to “how much have I spent?” that stays valid however the stopping time is chosen, the odometer of Definition 36.2. This section builds odometers from the Rényi filter’s supermartingale, at the cost of a union over the orders you might pick.
The tool is a time-uniform Markov inequality. Markov’s inequality (Theorem 2.1) says that a non-negative variable with mean 1 is at least \(c\) with probability at most \(1/c\). Ville’s inequality gives the same bound for the event that a supermartingale is ever that large, because stopping at the first time it reaches \(c\) leaves the mean at most 1.

Lemma 36.3 (Ville’s inequality) If \(N_t \ge 0\) is a supermartingale with \(N_0 = 1\), then for every \(c > 0\), \[\Pr\big[\exists\, t: N_t \ge c\big] \le \frac1c. \tag{36.11}\]


Proof. 

Stop at the first crossing. Fix a horizon \(n\) and let \(T\) be the first \(t\) with \(N_t \ge c\), or \(n\) if there is none. Whether \(T \ge t\) depends only on \(N_1, \dots, N_{t-1}\), so \(T\) is a stopping time bounded by \(n\).
The stopped process keeps its mean. By Lemma 36.2, \(\mathbb E[N_T] \le 1\).
Apply Markov’s argument to the stopped value. If the process reaches \(c\) by time \(n\), then \(N_T \ge c\), and elsewhere \(N_T \ge 0\). So \(N_T\) is at least \(c\) times the indicator of that event, and taking means gives \(c\Pr[\exists\,t \le n: N_t \ge c] \le 1\).
Drop the horizon. These events grow with \(n\), and their union is \(\{\exists\,t: N_t \ge c\}\).


Each odometer below turns the running RDP spend at a few orders into a running \(\varepsilon\). The orders form a finite grid \(\Lambda\) fixed in advance, with \(|\Lambda|\) orders, and \(S_t(\alpha) = \sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\) is the spend so far. The first odometer reports Mironov’s conversion at the best order in the grid, with \(\delta\) replaced by \(\delta/|\Lambda|\) to pay for choosing the order late.

Theorem 36.4 (The Ville odometer) Let step \(t\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon_t(\alpha))\)-RDP conditionally on the past for each \(\alpha \in \Lambda\), with predictable spends. With probability at least \(1 - \delta\), simultaneously for all \(t\), \[L_{1:t} \le U_t = \min_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\Big[S_t(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{36.12}\]


Proof. Ville’s inequality, applied to the Rényi filter’s supermartingale at each order, unpacks into a bound on the loss, and a union bound pays for all the orders.

A supermartingale at each order. Fix \(\alpha \in \Lambda\). Steps 1 and 2 of the proof of Theorem 36.1 showed that \(N_t\) of Equation 36.6 is a non-negative supermartingale with \(N_0 = 1\), using only that the spends are predictable.
Ville. Lemma 36.3 with \(c = |\Lambda|/\delta\) gives \[\Pr\big[\exists\,t: N_t \ge |\Lambda|/\delta\big] \le \delta/|\Lambda|. \tag{36.13}\]
Unpack. Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) turns \(N_t \ge |\Lambda|/\delta\) into \(L_{1:t} \ge S_t(\alpha) + \ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). So at this order the bound holds for all \(t\) at once, except with probability \(\delta/|\Lambda|\).
Union over the orders. By the union bound (Lemma 2.3), the bound fails at some order with probability at most \(\delta\). Outside that event it holds at every order and time, so it holds at the minimizing order, chosen after the fact.


With a single order the Ville odometer is Mironov’s fixed-time conversion, so at one fixed order a running bound is free. For Gaussian steps it is then exactly tight. In the limit of small steps the loss is a Brownian motion with drift, which crosses the boundary with probability exactly \(\delta\): \(N\) is then a martingale with continuous paths, so it equals \(1/\delta\) at the crossing, and the inequalities in the proof of Lemma 36.3 become equalities. The script checks this at \(\delta = 0.05\) and order 2, with 1000 Gaussian steps whose mean shifts by 0.2 noise widths. The crossing probability is 0.0461, a little below 0.0500 because whole steps miss crossings between them, while at any single fixed time it is at most 0.0072. Several orders add the union’s \(\ln|\Lambda|\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), with the grid of 154 orders that this part’s accountants use, \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.513\) becomes \(11.513 + \ln 154 = 16.550\).
An odometer is a tail bound, not a DP guarantee: “\(\varepsilon = U_T\)” means that this run’s loss exceeds \(U_T\) with probability at most \(\delta\). A filter that stops before \(U_T\) passes \(\varepsilon_g\) is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP, by splitting any event on whether the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon_g\) (Section 29.6).
Lécuyer (2021, Section 4) builds a second odometer from Rényi filters with doubling budgets \(B_f(\alpha) = 2^{f-1}\ln(2|\Lambda|/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), for \(f = 1, 2, \dots\) Let \(f(\alpha)\) be the first \(f\) whose budget covers \(S_t(\alpha)\). The odometer reports that budget plus a conversion term whose confidence shrinks with \(f\).

Theorem 36.5 (The Lécuyer odometer) Under the assumptions of Theorem 36.4, with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), simultaneously for all \(t\), \[L_{1:t} \le \min_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\Big[B_{f(\alpha)}(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(2|\Lambda|f(\alpha)^2/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{36.14}\]


Proof. 

One filter at one order. Fix \(\alpha\) and \(f\), and let \(T_f\) be the first step at which \(S_t(\alpha)\) exceeds \(B_f(\alpha)\). The supermartingale \(N_t\) stopped at \(T_f\) is still non-negative and starts at 1. So Lemma 36.3 with \(c = 2|\Lambda|f^2/\delta\), unpacked as in the previous proof, bounds the loss by \(B_f(\alpha) + \ln(2|\Lambda|f^2/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) at every \(t\) before \(T_f\), except with probability \(\delta/(2|\Lambda|f^2)\).
Union over filters and orders. The failure probabilities add up to \(\delta\sum_f 1/(2f^2) = \delta\pi^2/12 < \delta\).
Pick the filter. At time \(t\), filter \(f(\alpha)\) has not run out, so \(t\) comes before \(T_{f(\alpha)}\), and step 1’s bound holds at every order. Minimizing over the orders gives Equation 36.14.


Because the budgets double, the certified budget is at most twice the spend once the spend exceeds \(B_1\). For pure-DP steps, Rogers et al. (2016, Theorem 6.5) and Whitehouse et al. (2023, Theorem 3) give advanced-composition odometers.






Figure 36.4: Running privacy bounds at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for full-batch Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 10\), for the four columns of Table 36.6; the dashed fixed-time conversion is not a valid odometer.




Example 36.5 Take the running example’s steps with \(\sigma = 10\), so \(S_t(\alpha) = \alpha t/(2\sigma^2)\), at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with the part’s 154 orders. Table 36.6 and Figure 36.4 compare the fixed-time conversion with the two odometers and with a Ville odometer at the single order 5.8, chosen for \(t = 100\). That last one spends \(0.029\) per step plus \(\ln(10^5)/4.8 = 2.399\), so it is \(0.29 + 2.399 = 2.689\) at \(t = 10\) and \(29 + 2.399 = 31.399\) at \(t = 1000\).

title: 36  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
36.5 Individual privacy accounting in DP-SGD
A step of DP-SGD, the private form of SGD, clips each record’s gradient to norm at most \(C\), adds the clipped gradients and releases the sum with Gaussian noise. The usual analysis charges every record as if its clipped gradient always had norm \(C\), but once the model fits a record, its gradient shrinks. Feldman & Zrnic (2021) observed that a record’s actual cost is random and predictable, so the Rényi filter applies record by record. This section does the full-batch case, where every number is exact. A record’s cost depends on how far it moves the released sum.

Proposition 36.3 (Individual RDP of a Gaussian step (Feldman & Zrnic 2021, Section 2)) At step \(t\), let the mechanism release \(\sum_i\bar g_{i,t} + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2 I)\), where \(\bar g_{i,t}\) is record \(i\)’s gradient at the current model, clipped to norm \(C\). For the datasets with and without record \(i\), the step’s RDP at order \(\alpha\) is \[\varepsilon_{i,t}(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha\|\bar g_{i,t}\|^2}{2\sigma^2C^2} \le \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{36.15}\]


Proof. 

Reduce to one dimension. With record \(i\) the output is \(\mathcal N(m + \bar g_{i,t}, \sigma^2C^2I)\), and without it \(\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2C^2I)\), where \(m\) sums the other clipped gradients. Rotate so that \(\bar g_{i,t}\) lies along one axis. The noise is the same in every direction, so the other coordinates contribute nothing.
Use the Gaussian divergence. What remains is two normals with standard deviation \(\sigma C\), a shift of \(\|\bar g_{i,t}\|/(\sigma C)\) in units of the noise. Two normals with shift \(\mu\) in units of the noise have \(D_\alpha = \alpha\mu^2/2\) in both directions (Equation 3.19), which gives the equality.
Clip. Clipping makes \(\|\bar g_{i,t}\| \le C\), which gives the bound.


The filter then runs separately for each record: a record takes part only while its own spend fits in the budget.

Theorem 36.6 (The individual filter (Feldman & Zrnic 2021, Section 4.1)) Fix \(\alpha\) and \(B\). At step \(t\), let record \(i\) take part in the gradient sum only if \(\sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_{i,j}(\alpha) \le B\), counting only the steps it took part in. Then the whole run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP.


Proof. It is enough to check that a record’s spend is predictable and to apply the Rényi filter to each pair of neighbours.

The spend is predictable. The clipped gradient \(\bar g_{i,t}\) is a function of record \(i\) and the current model, which is a function of \(y_{<t}\). So by Proposition 36.3, \(\varepsilon_{i,t}(\alpha)\) is the RDP of step \(t\) for the pair with and without record \(i\), given \(y_{<t}\). It must not depend on the other records, or removing record \(i\) would change which of them take part.
Dropping a record costs it nothing. Whether record \(i\) takes part depends only on its own past spends. If it is dropped, the outputs with and without it have the same law at that step, and its spend is 0.
Apply the Rényi filter per record. For the pair with and without record \(i\), the spends are predictable and never sum past \(B\), so Theorem 36.1 makes the transcript \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP for this pair. Every pair of neighbours differs in one record.


The filter gives the same guarantee with more training. Since no spend exceeds \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), every record survives at least as long as the worst-case run, and records whose gradients shrink keep taking part long after. A per-record \(\varepsilon\) computed from the realized spend is only an ex post estimate, for the reasons of Section 36.1, and it is sensitive, since a small spend says the record is well fitted. For Poisson-subsampled DP-SGD the argument is unchanged, with the subsampled-Gaussian curve of Amplification by subsampling.
There is a fairness cost. Records that the model fits poorly, often from under-represented groups, keep large gradients, spend their budget first and are dropped first, so the model sees even less of them. Yu et al. (2023) find that the classes a model serves worst also get the weakest individual guarantees.

Example 36.6 The simulation has 10,000 records, clip \(C = 1\), \(\sigma = 10\) and full-batch steps. Typical records (90%) have gradient norms \(\|g_{i,t}\| = s_ie^{-t/40}e^{0.25Z_{i,t}}\), with \(s_i\) uniform between 0.3 and 2 and \(Z_{i,t}\) standard normal, so they shrink as the model fits them. Hard records (10%; 962 in this draw) have \(\|g_{i,t}\| = s_ie^{0.25Z_{i,t}}\) with \(s_i\) uniform between 0.7 and 1.5, and never shrink. The worst-case run is the running example: 100 steps, \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), order \(\alpha^* = 5.8\), budget \(B = 2.900\) and a per-step spend of at most \(0.0290\).
After the same 100 steps, record \(i\)’s \(\varepsilon\) at order 5.8 is its own spend plus \(\ln(10^5)/4.8\), a floor of 2.399 that no record can go below. Table 36.7 and Figure 36.5 show the distribution.

Optimizing the order per record lowers the typical median to 2.61, because a small spend is best converted at a larger order, where the floor is smaller. Now run the individual filter for 300 steps with \(B = 2.900\) at order 5.8. Everyone takes part in the first 100 steps, since \(100 \times 0.0290 = 2.900\). Then hard records run out: the first is excluded at step 101, the median one at step 111, and by step 200 none takes part (0.1% are back at step 300, when a small gradient fits what was left). 36.8 References

Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, “Privacy Odometers and Filters: Pay-as-you-Go Composition” (NeurIPS 2016; arXiv:1605.08294). Defines filters and odometers, proves basic composition works for both (Theorem 3.4), gives the first advanced-composition filter (Theorem 5.1), the lower bound separating odometers from filters (Theorem 6.1) and an odometer (Theorem 6.5). Read Sections 1 and 3 for the model.
Whitehouse, Ramdas, Rogers & Wu, “Fully-Adaptive Composition in Differential Privacy” (ICML 2023; arXiv:2203.05481). Filters that match advanced composition including constants (Theorems 1–2, through approximate zCDP), and odometers from time-uniform martingale concentration (Theorem 3). The place to look for steps with \(\delta_t > 0\).
Feldman & Zrnic, “Individual Privacy Accounting via a Rényi Filter” (NeurIPS 2021; arXiv:2008.11193). The fully adaptive RDP composition theorem and the Rényi filter (Sections 3–4), individual RDP and the individual filter, and private gradient descent with filtering (Section 5).
Lécuyer, “Practical Privacy Filters and Odometers with Rényi Differential Privacy and Applications to Differentially Private Deep Learning” (2021, arXiv:2103.01379). An independent proof of the Rényi filter, the filter over a set of orders, and the RDP odometer with doubling budgets; experiments with adaptive training.
Koskela, Tobaben & Honkela, “Individual Privacy Accounting with Gaussian Differential Privacy” (ICLR 2023). Individual filtering with Gaussian differential privacy and privacy loss distributions, tighter than RDP for the Gaussian mechanism.
Yu, Kamath, Kulkarni, Liu, Yin & Zhang, “Individual Privacy Accounting for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent” (TMLR 2023). Output-specific per-example guarantees for DP-SGD, and the link between a record’s training loss, its privacy and group fairness.
Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (FOCS 2010). Advanced composition with parameters fixed in advance, the theorem this chapter makes adaptive.
Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe & Sekhon, “Time-uniform Chernoff Bounds via Nonnegative Supermartingales” (Probability Surveys 2020). Ville’s inequality and the time-uniform bounds behind the Whitehouse et al. odometers.
Williams, Probability with Martingales (1991), chs. 10–11. Optional stopping (ch. 10) and martingale convergence (ch. 11), with proofs.
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (5th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2019), the chapter on Brownian motion. The law of the iterated logarithm used in Section 36.1, and Brownian hitting probabilities.
