title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.1 Every accountant on one run
You have trained a model with differential privacy (DP). The training loop was stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. At each step every record joins the batch independently with probability \(q\) (Poisson sampling), each record’s gradient is clipped to norm at most \(C\), and Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) is added to the sum. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\) thus measures the noise against one record’s largest contribution. Your run used \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, and you must now write “the model is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP” in a paper or a model card. That promises that for any two datasets \(D \sim D'\) that differ by adding or removing one record, any event about what training released is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely on one as on the other, plus \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
The run is fixed, so its true \(\varepsilon\) is one number. Nobody can compute it exactly, and a procedure that bounds or estimates it is called an accountant. This part has built several, and they disagree. Composing per-step guarantees gives 11296.93, while Rényi differential privacy (RDP) yields 7.4287 or 6.7127, depending on how its curve is converted. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) says 6.0071, and a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant brackets the truth in \([6.1377, 6.2377]\). Which one do you report, and what else must you say so that someone else can check it?
The numbers differ because the accountants make different kinds of statement. Some are upper bounds, proved for every pair of neighbouring datasets, and one is a proved lower bound, while others are approximations that may land below the truth. So the rule is short. Report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, and enough for someone else to recompute it. The sections take its clauses in turn, and the chapter’s script imports every accountant from the chapter of this part that derived it.
This is the question the part has built up to: on the running example, what does each accountant report, and which of its numbers can you trust? Earlier chapters computed some of the numbers. This section puts them in one table, adds the optimal conversion of an RDP curve, and sorts the accountants by the kind of statement each makes.
All accountants start from what one step reveals about one record. The other records contribute the same on both datasets, so look only at the noisy sum along that record’s clipped gradient, in units of \(C\). Without the record, the output is pure noise, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). With it, the record joins the batch with probability \(q\) and then shifts the output by at most 1, and the worst case is exactly 1, so the output is the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The accountants differ in what they keep of this pair and in how they combine \(T\) copies of it.
A lower bound is not a privacy guarantee, but it tells you how far any valid upper bound can fall. The six accountants of the part are these.
Table 37.2 gives every accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) on the running example.
The next theorem sorts the columns. It collects results proved earlier in the part, and what it adds is the two chains that order the bounds.
The theorem does not order the two chains against each other. The pessimistic PLD describes a rounded-up pair and may exceed the truth by up to \(Th\), so a curve-based bound very close to the truth could fall below it. All that follows is \(\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \ge \varepsilon^\uparrow_{\text{PLD}} - Th\). The script finds RDP optimal above the PLD upper bound at all nine values of \(T\) it tries, from 1 to 10,000, because the gap between them (at least 0.2677, Table 37.4) is far larger than \(Th\) (at most 0.1000), but that is an observation, not a theorem.
The CLT is missing from the theorem because it is not a bound. Equation 32.17 is a limit as \(T \to \infty\) with \(q\sqrt T\) fixed, and it keeps only the mean and variance of the per-step loss (f-DP and Gaussian DP). Neither the limit nor the two-moment summary controls its error in the tail of the loss, where \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is read, and here the CLT lies below the PLD lower bound at every \(T\).

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
Definition 37.1 (Upper bound, lower bound and approximation) An accountant maps the parameters of a run and a target \(\delta\) to a number \(\varepsilon_A\). Write \(\varepsilon_{\text{true}}\) for the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which the run is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The accountant is an upper bound if \(\varepsilon_A \ge \varepsilon_{\text{true}}\) for every run that satisfies its assumptions, and a lower bound if \(\varepsilon_A \le \varepsilon_{\text{true}}\) for every such run. It is an approximation if neither is proved.



Per step, then composition (Amplification by subsampling). One Gaussian step is \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\)-DP. Since the record is absent with probability \(1 - q\), subsampling dilutes \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) to \(1 + q(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\), giving \(\varepsilon_1\) (Equation 33.8). Then \(T\) steps compose, by basic composition to \(T\varepsilon_1\), or by advanced composition, which grows like \(\sqrt T\) at the price of an extra slack \(\delta'\).
RDP, Mironov’s conversion (Rényi DP). RDP describes one step by the curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between the two outputs (Equation 33.17). Curves add under composition, and Markov’s inequality turns the composed curve into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the best order: \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{37.1}\]
RDP, improved conversion (Equation 30.8 in From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests). A sharper analysis of the same tail (Balle et al. 2020) saves, at each order, an amount that does not depend on the curve.
RDP, optimal conversion (the same chapter). It gives the smallest \(\varepsilon\) that holds at \(\delta\) for every pair of distributions with the curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\).
GDP central-limit approximation (Equation 32.17 in f-DP and Gaussian DP). A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP if telling its two outputs apart is no easier than telling \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The loss of \(T\) steps is a sum of \(T\) small losses, so it is close to Gaussian. The approximation treats the run as \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) and reads \(\varepsilon\) off the GDP profile Equation 32.9.
PLD, pessimistic and optimistic (Numerical accounting). The privacy loss \(L\) at an output is the log of how much more likely it is on one neighbour than on the other, and the PLD is its distribution. Losses add, so the PLD of \(T\) steps is a \(T\)-fold convolution, computed with the fast Fourier transform (FFT) on a grid of width \(h = 10^{-5}\). Rounding every loss up gives the pessimistic PLD, whose \(\varepsilon\) is the “PLD upper” column below, and rounding down gives the optimistic one, “PLD lower”. Each is converted to \(\varepsilon\) with the record in the first dataset and in the second, and the larger value is kept (Section L.2 in the appendices).

Theorem 37.1 (Which accountants are bounds) Assume that the run samples each record independently with probability \(q\), clips each per-example gradient to norm \(C\), adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to the sum, releases every noisy gradient, and fixes \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) in advance, with add/remove neighbours. Then per-step composition, RDP with each conversion and the pessimistic PLD are upper bounds, and the optimistic PLD is a lower bound. They satisfy \[\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, Mironov}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, improved}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{true}}, \qquad \varepsilon^{\uparrow}_{\text{PLD}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{true}} \ge \varepsilon^{\downarrow}_{\text{PLD}}, \tag{37.2}\] and if the accountant drops no far tail of the loss distribution, the two PLD values differ by at most \(Th\).


Proof. The plan is to ask, for each accountant, whether what it keeps of the per-step pair still supports a proof, and then to order the RDP conversions.

Per-step composition. One step is \((\varepsilon_1, q\delta_0)\)-DP by the amplification theorem. Basic composition (Theorem 19.3) and advanced composition (Theorem 21.1) hold even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs (Theorem 21.5), which is how SGD works.
RDP with Mironov’s or the improved conversion. The curve Equation 33.17 is the exact Rényi divergence of the pair. Curves add under adaptive composition (Equation 29.11), because the Rényi divergence is the log of a moment of the likelihood ratio, and given the earlier outputs each step adds fresh noise, so the moments multiply step by step. Both conversions are proved for every pair with the curve (Proposition 30.1, Theorem 30.1). The accountant minimizes over a finite grid of orders, which can only raise the minimum, so it costs tightness, never validity.
The optimal conversion. For each \(\varepsilon\) it takes the largest privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), the smallest \(\delta\) that works at \(\varepsilon\), over all pairs with the curve (Theorem 30.2). The real pair is one of them, so its profile is no larger, and \(\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{true}}\).
The PLD sandwich. Rounding every loss up describes a pair that leaks at least as much as the real one, a dominating pair, and composing dominating pairs gives a dominating pair (Section K.3 in the appendices). Rounding down works the other way, so the error keeps its sign through all \(T\) convolutions, which is Equation 34.9.
The width. Each step’s loss moves by less than \(h\) between rounding down and up. After \(T\) steps the two composed losses differ by at most \(Th\) at every outcome, and \(\varepsilon\) is read off the loss, so the two \(\varepsilon\) values differ by at most \(Th\) too, unless a tail was dropped (Numerical accounting).
Mironov above improved. At every order the improved conversion is smaller by the saving of Corollary 30.1, \[s(\alpha) = \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{37.3}\] whose two terms are positive for \(\alpha > 1\). An expression that is larger at every order has a larger minimum.
Improved above optimal. The optimal conversion is the smallest \(\varepsilon\) valid for every pair with the curve, and the improved one is such an \(\varepsilon\).

Right: RDP, the CLT and the PLD lower bound divided by the PLD upper bound; per-step composition is off the scale. Only the PLD lower bound may lie in the shaded region below 1, and the CLT lies there at every \(T\).

Per-step composition is right only at \(T = 1\), where there is nothing to compose. At \(T = 10{,}000\) it is off by a factor of over a thousand, because adding \(\varepsilon\)’s assumes that every step leaks its worst case, while the loss of each step is positive on some outputs and negative on others, so the losses mostly cancel. Advanced composition is worse still, because besides its \(\sqrt T\) term it has a term \(T\varepsilon_1(e^{\varepsilon_1} - 1)\) that grows like \(T\), and the amplified \(\varepsilon_1\) is too large for that term to be negligible.

The conversion slack dominates short runs, 0.4656 of the 0.7561 excess at \(T = 1\), because every conversion pays \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), about \(11.5/(\alpha - 1)\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), however small the curve is. That toll is also why basic composition (0.20) beats RDP (0.9555) at \(T = 1\), though both are valid. After many steps the curve term is large, so the best order trades it against a toll that is now small in comparison, and the conversion slack fades, to 0.0005 at \(T = 1000\). The last 7.6% at \(T = 10{,}000\) is curve slack, which only an accountant that keeps the whole distribution removes.
So after 1,000 steps a paper might say \(\varepsilon = 2.54\) (RDP with Mironov’s conversion, as in older code), 2.10 (the improved conversion, as in Opacus’s RDP accountant), 1.83 (a PLD accountant) or 1.62 (the CLT). The first three are true, and 1.83 is the most informative. The fourth is false, because the optimistic PLD proves \(\varepsilon \ge 1.8232\). At \(T = 10{,}000\) the PLD bracket has width \(6.2377 - 6.1377 = 0.1000\), exactly \(Th\), and only a finer grid narrows it.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.2 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
37.2 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
Practitioners rarely compute \(\varepsilon\) after the fact. They fix a budget, say \(\varepsilon = 3\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), fix the steps and the batch size, and ask how much noise to add. This section asks what each accountant’s slack costs in noise. Dividing the noisy sum by the expected batch size \(qn\) leaves noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C/(qn)\) in the averaged gradient. A loose accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\) at every \(\sigma\), so it asks for a larger \(\sigma\), and its slack turns directly into noise.

Definition 37.2 (The noise an accountant requires) For an accountant \(A\), with \(q\) and \(T\) fixed, write \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma)\) for the \(\varepsilon\) it reports at \(\delta\) when the noise multiplier is \(\sigma\). The noise it requires for a target \(\varepsilon^*\) is \[\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*) = \min\{\sigma > 0 : \varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\}. \tag{37.4}\]

This minimum is easy to find if more noise never raises the reported \(\varepsilon\), because then it is where a decreasing function crosses a level. The reason to expect it is that a noisier run can be made from a less noisy one without touching the data.

Proposition 37.1 (More noise never raises a bound) Let \(\sigma < \sigma'\). Per-step composition, RDP with each conversion and the exact PLD report \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma') \le \varepsilon_A(\sigma)\). The discretized PLD does so up to grid effects of order \(Th\), and the CLT’s \(\varepsilon\) falls strictly as \(\sigma\) grows.


Proof. 

Post-processing. Variances of independent Gaussians add, so adding fresh \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma'^2 - \sigma^2)\) noise to each output of the run with \(\sigma\) gives exactly the run with \(\sigma'\), by a map that does not look at the data.
Data processing. By Theorem 3.5, such a map can only lower every divergence between the two outputs, including the Rényi divergences behind the curve and the hockey-stick divergence that defines \(\delta(\varepsilon)\). Each listed accountant computes \(\varepsilon\) from these by a map that rises with them, so its \(\varepsilon\) falls.
Grid and CLT. Rounding can move the composed loss against the trend by up to \(Th\). The CLT’s \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) falls as \(\sigma\) grows, and Equation 32.9 gives a smaller \(\varepsilon\) for a smaller \(\mu\).


So any bracketing method finds \(\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*)\). The script uses false position, which places each guess where the line through the two ends crosses the target, with the Illinois modification that stops one end from getting stuck, so it needs only a handful of evaluations. That matters for the PLD, where each is two FFT compositions of 10,000 steps.
The solver stops when the bracket is narrower than \(10^{-4}\) and returns the upper end, where \(\varepsilon_A \le \varepsilon^*\) was checked, so the returned \(\sigma\) meets the budget even if grid effects make it slightly larger than the minimum. For the PLD the bracket runs from 90% of the smaller of the RDP and CLT values to the RDP value, and since Theorem 37.1 does not order RDP against the PLD, the solver checks that the target really lies between the two ends. The optimal conversion is left out because it costs a search of its own at every \(\sigma\). The CLT needs no search over \(\sigma\): find the \(\mu^*\) whose GDP profile gives \(\varepsilon^*\), and invert Equation 32.17 for \(\sigma\): \[\sigma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln\big(1 + \mu^{*2}/(q^2T)\big)}}. \tag{37.5}\]

Figure 37.2 shows each \(\sigma\) of Table 37.5 relative to the PLD upper bound’s. Advanced composition asks for 6.19 to 6.63 times the noise, a level at which DP-SGD rarely trains a useful model. Mironov’s conversion costs 8.6 to 24.7% more, most at the strictest target, where its fixed toll is the largest share of \(\varepsilon\), and the improved conversion 3.4 to 4.9% more. That is less than RDP’s 7.6% excess in \(\varepsilon\), because here a small relative rise in \(\sigma\) buys a larger relative fall in \(\varepsilon\). Example 37.2 With \(n = 50{,}000\) records and \(q = 0.01\), the expected batch holds 500 records. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the RDP accountant sets \(\sigma = 0.917\), so the averaged gradient carries noise of standard deviation \(0.917C/500\), while the PLD accountant sets \(\sigma = 0.885\). The RDP accountant thus asks for 3.6% more noise for the same certified budget (the ratio 1.036 in Figure 37.2). Seen from the other side, at \(\sigma = 0.8851\), where the PLD certifies \(\varepsilon = 8\), the RDP accountant reports 8.6330. At a fixed \(\sigma\) the tighter accountant buys a longer run instead, 20% more epochs at \(\varepsilon = 3\).

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.3 Where each accountant is tight
DP-SGD is one mechanism. You will also release statistics with the Gaussian mechanism, answer queries with pure-DP mechanisms (\(\delta = 0\)), shuffle locally randomized reports, or stop training adaptively. This section asks which accountant is tight for which mechanism. An accountant is tight exactly when the summary it keeps describes the mechanism’s privacy loss without loss, so the answer changes with the mechanism. Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) joins the list here, summarizing the RDP curve by one line \(\rho\alpha\) above it. Table 37.6 collects the answers from the earlier chapters.

The ranking in every row follows one ladder. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair keeps two numbers, zCDP one line, RDP a curve, GDP the whole trade-off function when it is Gaussian, and the PLD the entire distribution of the loss. Each rung loses information that the next keeps, and lost information is filled in with a worst case. To measure that cost you need mechanisms whose true \(\varepsilon\) is known, and the next result gives one whose composed loss is exactly Gaussian and one whose loss takes few values.

Proposition 37.2 (Two mechanisms with an exact ε)  

\(T\) Gaussian steps of sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma\), without subsampling, are exactly \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \sqrt T/\sigma\), so Equation 32.9 gives their exact \(\varepsilon\). Their RDP curve \(\alpha\mu^2/2\) is also exact, and equals the zCDP line with \(\rho = \mu^2/2\).
\(k\) rounds of randomized response, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, have composed loss \((k - 2J)\varepsilon_0\) with \(J \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, 1/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0}))\), so the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is a finite sum.



Proof. 

One Gaussian step. The two outputs \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), divided by \(\sigma\), are exactly \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(1/\sigma, 1)\), so one step is \(1/\sigma\)-GDP with nothing lost.
Gaussian composition. Squares of \(\mu\) add under composition, as variances do (f-DP and Gaussian DP), so \(\mu^2 = T/\sigma^2\). The Rényi divergence of two normals \(\mu\) standard deviations apart is \(\alpha\mu^2/2\) (Proposition 3.3), a line through the origin, so the best zCDP line is the curve itself.
Randomized response. Each round’s loss is \(\pm\varepsilon_0\) and losses of independent rounds add (Lemma 21.2), which gives Proposition 21.1. The values lie on a lattice, so nothing is rounded, and \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), an average over the loss (Lemma 21.1), is a finite binomial sum.


So when the composed pair is exactly Gaussian, GDP costs nothing. When subsampling makes it a mixture, no closed form is exact, and only the PLD is both certified and tight. Adaptivity is where RDP is the natural tool. If the noise or the stopping time depends on released outputs, the per-step pair is not fixed in advance as Theorem 37.1 assumed, and the Rényi filter of Adaptive composition handles that while losing nothing at the order it tracks.

Example 37.3 One hundred Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 10\) compose to \(\mu = \sqrt{100}/10 = 1\), and Equation 32.9 gives the exact \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Converting the equally exact RDP curve gives 4.7285 with the improved conversion, 8.0% above, and 5.2985 with Mironov’s. One hundred rounds of randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\) have exact \(\varepsilon = 4.3068\). Against that, RDP with the exact curve reaches 4.6154. zCDP must use a \(\rho\) whose line lies above the curve, and the smallest is \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) per round, the charge that every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP step satisfies (Equation 31.11), which yields 4.7263. Advanced composition with \(\delta' = \delta\) ends at 5.8502, and basic composition at \(100 \times 0.1 = 10.0000\).
Suppose a team releases the 100 Gaussian counts and reports \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) from an old RDP accountant with Mironov’s conversion. The release is exactly \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP, so the report is 21.0% above the truth (\(5.2985/4.3772 \approx 1.210\)), and the team could have answered more queries at no cost in privacy.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.4 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
37.4 Matching the accountant to the code
Every number so far assumes a model of the training run, and the accountant cannot check it against your code. It takes \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) and trusts that the code does what the theorem assumes. Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.1) put it in one heading, “privacy accounting assumptions should match training reality”, and note that many papers since Abadi et al. (2016) have reported the Poisson number while training with shuffled fixed-size batches. This section asks what such a mismatch costs, and the answer is that the number then describes a different algorithm. Check each item of Table 37.7 against the code before reporting.



Table 37.7: A checklist for matching the accountant to the training code.





Item
What the accountant assumes
What to check
If it does not match




Sampling scheme

Fixed-size: Proposition 37.3; shuffled: Proposition 37.4

Or replace-one, or zero-out (one gradient set to 0)?
Replace-one costs about twice as much (subsampling)

Tuning

Adaptive parameters

Implementation

Floating-point sampling?

The first row is the most common mismatch. A loader that draws a random batch of exactly \(qn\) records looks like Poisson sampling. But a record cannot enter a full batch without pushing another out, so in effect one record is swapped for another, and the batch sum can move by \(2C\) rather than \(C\).

Proposition 37.3 (Fixed-size batches (Lebeda et al. 2024)) If each step draws a fresh uniformly random batch of exactly \(qn\) records, then under add/remove neighbours every \(\varepsilon\) certified for the Poisson pair with rate \(q\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\) holds for the run with noise multiplier \(\sigma\).


The proof is Proposition 9 of Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke (2024), which shows with Zhu, Dong & Wang (2022, Theorem 11) that the shift of \(2C\) is the worst case under the add and the remove relation separately. A shift of \(2C\) against noise \(\sigma C\) is a shift of \(C\) against \((\sigma/2)C\), and Amplification by subsampling derives the coupling behind it.
A loader that shuffles once per epoch and cuts the data into batches uses each record exactly once per epoch. The record is then never absent by chance, which is what amplification feeds on, and no amplification theorem holds for every dataset. What stays certain is the record’s own steps, one per epoch, under the zero-out relation, in which one record’s gradient is replaced by zero.

Proposition 37.4 (The guarantee without amplification) Suppose each of \(E\) epochs shuffles the data and cuts it into consecutive batches, with noise multiplier \(\sigma\). Under zero-out neighbours the run is \(\sqrt E/\sigma\)-GDP, and under replace-one neighbours it is \(2\sqrt E/\sigma\)-GDP.


Proof. The plan is to fix the shuffles, find the one step per epoch that differs, and compose those steps.

Fix the shuffles. They do not depend on the data. Publishing them too can only help an observer, and the real run drops them, a post-processing (Theorem 19.1), so it suffices to prove the bound with them fixed.
One step per epoch differs. With the shuffles fixed, only the batch that holds the record differs, and its sum moves by at most \(C\) under zero-out. Every other step, given the earlier outputs, has the same distribution on both datasets.
That step is Gaussian. A shift of \(C\) against noise \(\sigma C\) is \(1/\sigma\)-GDP, by part (a) of Proposition 37.2.
Compose. The \(E\) differing steps compose adaptively to \(\mu^2 = E/\sigma^2\) (f-DP and Gaussian DP). Under replace-one, the old gradient leaves and a new one comes in, so the shift is up to \(2C\) and \(\mu\) doubles.


Under add/remove there is no clean bound, because inserting a record shifts every later batch. Ponomareva et al. recommend reporting this guarantee whenever the sampling assumption fails. Tuning breaks the accountant’s assumptions differently, because the release depends on several runs while the accountant counts one.

Proposition 37.5 (Tuning on the private data composes) Training \(m\) configurations on the private data and releasing the best costs at most the \(m\) runs composed. With RDP, that is the curve \(mT\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\).


Proof. 

Post-processing. The best run is a function of the \(m\) trained models, so by Theorem 19.1 releasing it is no less private than releasing all \(m\).
Composition. The \(m\) runs use the same data, so their RDP curves add (Equation 29.11).


Papernot & Steinke (2022) do much better when the number of configurations is random, and NIST SP 800-226 (Section 4.3) recommends tuning on non-sensitive data.

Example 37.4 At \(T = 10{,}000\), fixed-size batches accounted honestly by Proposition 37.3 give 47.42 with RDP instead of 6.71, and 43.42 with the PLD instead of 6.24. Shuffle and partition for 100 epochs at \(\sigma = 1\) is \(\mu = \sqrt{100} = 10\) by Proposition 37.4, and Equation 32.9 gives \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\) for zero-out neighbours, or 284.39 at \(\mu = 20\) under replace-one. Ten tuning runs compose to \(\varepsilon = 27.23\) with RDP, and 100 runs to 145.17.
So a script whose DataLoader has shuffle=True and batch_size=500 on 50,000 records for 100 epochs, calling an RDP accountant with sample_rate=0.01, fails the checklist’s first row, and its certified guarantee is 91.8173, not 6.71. Switching the loader to Poisson sampling, a few lines, makes the assumptions true and the guarantee 6.24 with a PLD accountant.

The sampling scheme is the largest single risk. Its factor of 6.96 (\(43.42/6.24\)) from one line in the data loader exceeds the choice between RDP and the PLD, at most 1.19 here (Table 37.3). The other rows decide what the number means. Example-level DP-SGD protects each example, not each user, which NIST SP 800-226 (Section 2.4) calls a privacy hazard, and floating-point noise can break a mechanism that is correct on paper (Section 4.3).

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.5 What to report
An \(\varepsilon\) without its assumptions cannot be checked, compared or even read, since the same number means different things for one example or one user, with or without tuning, at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) or \(10^{-10}\). This section asks what a statement must contain so that a reader can interpret and recompute it. NIST SP 800-226, “Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees” (Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, 2025), answers for anyone evaluating a claim, and Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.3) answer for machine learning.

Definition 37.3 (A privacy statement) Following Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.3), a privacy statement gives four things.

The DP setting: central or local, and who is trusted.
The instantiated definition: which data accesses are covered (one run, or tuning too), the mechanism’s output, the unit of privacy, and the neighbouring relation.
Accounting details: the type of accounting, its assumptions and whether they hold, and the formal guarantee for the final model and for the tuning.
Transparency: code when possible, using standard libraries.

For DP-SGD it adds what the accountant needs: the sampling scheme, \(q\) (or the batch size and \(n\)), \(T\) (or the epochs), \(\sigma\), the clipping norm \(C\), and the accountant’s version and discretization.

The clipping norm is listed although \(\varepsilon\) does not depend on it, because \(C\) and \(\sigma\) together give the actual noise \(\sigma C\) and let a reader check the implementation.
The second parameter needs as much care. Both documents want \(\delta\) much smaller than \(1/n\) for \(n\) units of privacy, because \(\delta\) is a chance that the promise fails. A mechanism that publishes each record in full with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, yet at \(\delta = 1/n\) it exposes someone with probability about \(1 - 1/e = 0.632\) (Proposition 18.3). Ponomareva et al. (Section 5.3.2) suggest \(\delta = n^{-1.1}\). NIST (Section 2.3) gives \(\delta \le 1/n^2\) as a common recommendation, calls values above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious, and asks for the original RDP, zCDP or GDP parameters alongside any conversion.
So a report should give \(\varepsilon\) at more than one \(\delta\), and these cannot be derived from one pair. Many mechanisms share a single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair and behave differently below it; one can be \((0, \delta)\)-DP but satisfy no guarantee at all at a smaller \(\delta\). A PLD accountant composes the distribution once, and each further \(\delta\) costs one more evaluation of \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).



Table 37.8: The running example’s privacy profile: \(\varepsilon\) at several \(\delta\) for \(T = 10{,}000\), \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(n = 50{,}000\).

Example 37.5 With \(n = 50{,}000\) records, the expected batch is \(qn = 500\), and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps are \(Tq = 100\) epochs. The conventions give \(1/n = 2.0\times10^{-5}\), \(n^{-1.1} = 6.8\times10^{-6}\) and \(1/n^2 = 4.0\times10^{-10}\), and Table 37.8 gives \(\varepsilon\) at each. The usual \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is half of \(1/n\), so it is not “much smaller than \(1/n\)”, and at \(1/n^2\) the certified \(\varepsilon\) rises to 9.0502. The PLD bracket has width 0.1000, the \(Th\) of Theorem 37.1, down to \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). At \(1/n^2\) it is \(9.0502 - 8.9378 = 0.1124\), because the accountant cuts off the far tails of each step’s PLD and moves up to \(10^{-15}\) of mass to the side that keeps each bound safe, of order \(10^{-11}\) over \(10^4\) steps, a few percent of \(4\times10^{-10}\). The RDP accountant’s original parameter is its curve, \(\varepsilon(4.1) = 3.7336\) at the best order, which converts to 6.7127.

Privacy guarantee. The model was trained with DP-SGD in the central model: the training server is trusted to run the code below, and the guarantee covers every intermediate noisy gradient, hence every checkpoint and the final model. Unit of privacy: one training example; each person contributes at most one example. Neighbouring relation: add or remove one example. Training: Poisson sampling with rate \(q = 0.01\) (\(n = 50{,}000\) examples, expected batch size 500), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps (100 epochs), per-example clipping norm \(C = 1\), Gaussian noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). Accountant: privacy loss distributions, pessimistic discretization on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\), both add and remove directions (this book’s numerical_accounting.py). Guarantee: \((6.24, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((9.06, 4.0\times10^{-10})\)-DP. The optimistic discretization gives 6.1377 and 8.9378, so the accountant’s own error is at most 0.1000 and 0.1124. Not covered: hyperparameters were tuned on a public proxy dataset. If the sampling assumption failed (for example, shuffled fixed-size batches), the guarantee without amplification is \((91.82, 10^{-5})\)-DP for zero-out neighbours.

Upper bounds are rounded up, never to the nearest value, so 9.0502 becomes 9.06, because 9.05 would be a claim the accountant has not certified.

The statement gives the accountant’s error bar, which RDP cannot give for lack of a lower bound, and the fallback for a reader who doubts an item of Table 37.7.

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.6 Checking your accountant
An accountant is code, and code has bugs. This section asks how to test one, yours or a library’s, before you trust its number. A good test is a case where the truth is known exactly, or a property every correct accountant must have, so that a failure is a bug and not slack. The results of this chapter supply four.

Proposition 37.6 (Four properties of every correct accountant) Under the assumptions of Theorem 37.1:

With \(q = 1\) the run is exactly \(\sqrt T/\sigma\)-GDP, and every upper bound is at least the \(\varepsilon\) that Equation 32.9 gives.
On the plain Gaussian pair, the PLD bracket contains that exact \(\varepsilon\), if no tail is truncated.
The chains of Equation 37.2 hold at every \(T\), and no upper bound falls below the optimistic PLD.
The composed pessimistic PLD, evaluated at its own \(\varepsilon\), gives back \(\delta\), and no accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) decreases as \(T\) grows.



Proof. The plan is to derive each property from a result already proved, so that a violation can only be a bug.

Full batches. With \(q = 1\) every step is the plain Gaussian mechanism, so Proposition 37.2 gives the truth, and an upper bound is at least the truth (Definition 37.1).
The Gaussian PLD. By Theorem 37.1 the two PLD values bracket the truth, here the closed form.
The chains. Theorem 37.1 proves them, and an upper bound below a lower bound would put the truth on both sides.
Round trip and growth. Solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\) and evaluating \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) at the solution are inverse operations on one decreasing profile. The \(T\)-step transcript is the \((T + 1)\)-step one with its last output dropped, a data-independent map, so by Theorem 3.5 it is no easier to tell apart.



Example 37.6 For \(\sigma = 1\), \(T = 10\) and \(q = 1\), the exact \(\mu\) is \(\sqrt{10} = 3.1623\) and the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 17.8566. The RDP accountant gives 19.0536, above it as a bound must be. The CLT formula gives \(\mu = \sqrt{10(e - 1)} = 4.1452\) and \(\varepsilon = 25.5853\), and fails because its derivation assumes a small \(q\). On the plain Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\), \(T = 10\) and \(h = 10^{-3}\), the PLD bracket \([17.8516, 17.8616]\) contains the closed form 17.8566. Both chains hold at all nine values of \(T\), the round trip gives back \(\delta = 1.000\times10^{-5}\), and the PLD upper bound increases with \(T\).


37.6.1 Comparing with independent libraries
How closely should two independent implementations agree? This book’s accountants use no library, so that every line can be read, but production code should use a maintained one and compare it with a second: Google’s dp_accounting (RDP and PLD), Opacus (RDP, GDP and its default, the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant), or Microsoft’s prv_accountant (Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz 2021), which returns a lower bound, an estimate and an upper bound. Two RDP accountants differ only in their orders and their conversion. Opacus uses the improved conversion and the same orders as this book’s accountant except the three largest (128, 256 and 512), and the running example’s best orders, 4.1 to 9.9, lie in both grids. A gap of about \(s(\alpha)\) (Equation 30.14), 0.3612 at order 10, means that one of them uses Mironov’s conversion.
Fractional orders are a known weak spot, because there the subsampled Gaussian’s RDP is an infinite series with terms of both signs. dp_accounting 0.6.0 counts the negative terms as positive and returns a loose bound, so the fixed-size value 47.42 of Example 37.4 comes out as 49.43 there, while Opacus keeps the signs. PLD and PRV brackets from two libraries must overlap, since every certified upper bound lies above every certified lower bound. A cross-check run outside this book’s scripts agrees. Opacus 1.6.0, dp_accounting 0.6.0 and prv_accountant 0.2.0 match this chapter’s RDP and PLD numbers to the printed precision, and their tight PLD estimate at \(T = 10{,}000\) is about 6.19, inside the bracket. These values, like the 49.43, come from the libraries, not from the book’s scripts.

37.9 References

Ponomareva, Hazimeh, Kurakin, Xu, Denison, McMahan, Vassilvitskii, Chien & Thakurta, “How to DP-fy ML: A Practical Guide to Machine Learning with Differential Privacy” (Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 77, 2023; arXiv:2303.00654). Section 5.3.1 on matching accounting to data processing (Table 3), Section 5.3.2 on setting \(\delta\), Section 5.3.3 on what to report, Section 5.2.1 on target \(\varepsilon\) tiers. The practical companion to this chapter.
Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, “Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees” (NIST Special Publication 800-226, March 2025). The unit of privacy (Section 2.4), the choice of \(\delta\) and reporting original parameters of RDP, zCDP and GDP guarantees (Section 2.3), floating-point and hyperparameter-tuning hazards (Section 4.3). Read it for what an evaluator will ask.
Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021). The PRV accountant with certified error bounds, and examples where the CLT under-reports; the basis of prv_accountant and Opacus’s default accountant.
Doroshenko, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar & Manurangsi, “Connect the Dots: Tighter Discrete Approximations of Privacy Loss Distributions” (PoPETs 2022). The pessimistic PLD discretization used in Google’s dp_accounting.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (arXiv 2019). The RDP of the subsampled Gaussian, computed exactly; the core of every RDP accountant for DP-SGD.
Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato, “Hypothesis Testing Interpretations and Rényi Differential Privacy” (AISTATS 2020). Theorem 21 is the improved conversion that Opacus and dp_accounting use.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 2022), and Bu, Dong, Long & Su, “Deep Learning with Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2020). The GDP CLT for DP-SGD; read with this chapter’s warning that it is not a bound.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (arXiv:2405.20769, 2024; IEEE SaTML 2025). Fixed-size batches versus Poisson sampling, and the factor that the wrong accountant costs.
Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?” (ICML 2024). Shuffled batches can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports.
Papernot & Steinke, “Hyperparameter Tuning with Renyi Differential Privacy” (ICLR 2022). Privacy cost of tuning with a random number of trials, far below naive composition.
Google, dp_accounting library; Meta, Opacus; Microsoft, prv_accountant. Documentation of the production RDP, PLD and PRV accountants to check this book’s numbers against.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
Who this part is for
The previous parts built the guarantee and the tools to account for it. This part trains models with it. It asks the questions that decide whether a private model is worth deploying: how do you train with differential privacy (DP), how much accuracy does it cost, which knobs move that cost, and how do you check that the trained model is as private as the accountant claims? The answers are mostly about one algorithm, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, and about everything around it: how its hyperparameters are chosen, what replaces it when its assumptions fail, how public data and the choice of privacy unit change it, who pays for its noise, which \(\varepsilon\) to target, and how to audit the result. The last chapter turns the guarantee to a different use: the same noise that protects people also keeps a reused validation or test set honest.
You are expected to have read the earlier parts. From Optimization you need SGD, strong convexity and the sensitivity of regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM). From Membership inference you need the likelihood-ratio attack (LiRA) and the true and false positive rates of an attack. From the DP foundations you need the Gaussian mechanism (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), clipping (Beyond global sensitivity), the exponential mechanism and report-noisy-max (Selection) and the lower bounds of Lower bounds. From the accounting part you need Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) and trade-off functions (f-DP and Gaussian DP), amplification by subsampling and the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant for DP-SGD (Amplification by subsampling), and what to report (Choosing an accountant). The last chapter also uses the replace-one argument of Algorithmic stability and generalization and the sparse vector technique of Selection. Each chapter restates the facts it uses and links to them.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The common thread
A private training algorithm has two halves. The privacy half says which quantity has bounded sensitivity and how much noise covers it; it is a theorem, and the accountants of the previous part turn it into a number. The utility half says how much the noise and the bounding cost; it is mostly measured, rarely proved. Every chapter of this part moves one of the two.
The first two chapters build the algorithm: Private ERM compares three places to inject noise into training and shows why, in practice, only noise on the gradients survives non-convex models, and DP-SGD adds clipping, minibatches and accounting. The next three ask what else spends the budget or could spend it better: hyperparameter search; mechanisms that do not rely on random batches, such as the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm run on noisy gradient sums, DP-FTRL; and private prediction instead of private training, such as private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE). The next three change the setting: public data, a different privacy unit, and the effect on under-represented groups. The next two close the loop between theory and practice: which \(\varepsilon\) to choose, and how to test a claim empirically. The last chapter uses the privacy half for a different purpose. A mechanism that reveals little about any one record cannot be overfitted, so DP also lets one holdout set answer many adaptively chosen questions, the situation of every hyperparameter search and leaderboard. Table 1 lists them.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The running examples
Two models recur. The first is regularized logistic regression in \(d = 10\) dimensions on synthetic data, where the exact minimizer can be computed and every method can be compared with the non-private optimum; Private ERM introduces it. The second is a small neural network trained with DP-SGD on synthetic data, small enough that every experiment of the part runs on a laptop in seconds, yet non-convex, so that clipping and noise behave as they do in deep learning; DP-SGD introduces it. The full-scale experiment, DP-SGD on CIFAR-10 audited with LiRA, needs a GPU and PyTorch, which are not dependencies of the repository; the chapters scale it down and say how.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
How to read this part
Order. Read chapters 38 and 39 first, in order: every later chapter uses DP-SGD. Chapters 40 and 41 change how the algorithm is run, and can be read in either order. Chapters 42 to 45 are independent of each other. Chapter 46 uses the vocabulary of all the earlier ones, and chapter 47 should come after the others, because it checks what the others claim. Chapter 48 can be read at any point after chapter 40, whose hyperparameter search is its motivating example. It needs DP-SGD only for that example.
Structure of a chapter. The chapters have the shape of the earlier parts. Each opens with the question it answers and its running example, then gives one section per topic, whose definitions, theorems and worked examples are numbered, each theorem followed by its proof. A Code section, a Summary table of the chapter’s results and References close it.
Run the code. Each chapter has a script in code/ that prints every number its text quotes, except values attributed to a paper, and regenerates its figures, for example
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/dp_erm.py
Every model is written in NumPy, gradients included, so you can see exactly what each algorithm computes.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
section: What you will be able to do

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.1 Output perturbation
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM). You choose the parameters \(\theta\) that minimize the average loss on the training data, usually plus a ridge penalty on the squared length of \(\theta\). The trained weights are a function of every training record, and Membership inference showed that they give some of those records away. An exact minimizer can even release a record outright: the median of an odd number of values minimizes the average absolute loss, and it is one of the values. Differential privacy (DP) promises the opposite: the distribution of whatever you release changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a slack \(\delta\), when one record is replaced. So randomness has to enter somewhere between the data and the released weights, and this chapter asks where.
The idea that organizes the answer is the one behind every mechanism of this book. Find a quantity that one record can move only by a known amount, its sensitivity, and add noise large enough to hide a move of that size. There are three natural places for the noise. Output perturbation trains as usual and adds noise to the minimizer, which a ridge penalty keeps from moving far. Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to the objective and minimizes it exactly, which needs a bound on how far one record moves the objective’s gradient. Gradient perturbation adds noise to every gradient during training, so it needs that bound only at the points it visits. The earlier in training the noise enters, the fewer assumptions it needs, and the third needs no convexity at all, which is why the next chapter builds on it.
The running example is regularized logistic regression in \(d = 10\) dimensions, with a ridge of weight 0.01. The features are uniform on the unit sphere, and the labels come from a logistic model whose true weights have length 5. Every method targets \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for those that need a \(\delta\), on 1,000 to 100,000 records. At 10,000 records, output perturbation with Gaussian noise raises the training loss above the exact minimizer’s by \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\), and objective perturbation by ten times less.
The simplest private trainer computes the exact minimizer and adds noise to it, as Chaudhuri & Monteleoni (2008) did for logistic regression. This section asks how much noise hides one record’s effect on the minimizer, what the noise costs in accuracy, and what changes when the minimizer is only approximate.
A training set \(D\) holds \(n\) records. Each record \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\) pairs a feature vector \(x_i \in \mathbb R^d\) with a label \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), and \(\ell(\theta; z)\) is the loss of the parameters on one record. The objective adds a ridge penalty of weight \(\lambda\) to the average loss, \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \tag{38.1}\] and its minimizer is \(\theta^*(D)\).
Neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) differ by replacing one record, \(z\) in \(D\) by \(z'\) in \(D'\), so both have size \(n\). The excess risk of a released \(\tilde\theta\) is \(\mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), how much worse it fits the objective than the exact minimizer.
Two earlier results do most of the work. First, if each loss is convex with gradients of length at most \(L\), replacing one record moves the minimizer by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\) (Theorem 6.5 in Optimization). That is because the objective’s gradient moves by at most \(2L/n\), and the ridge’s curvature \(\lambda\) turns a small gradient into a small distance: where the gradient has length \(g\), the minimizer is within \(g/\lambda\).
The second result says how much Gaussian noise hides a move of \(\Delta_2 f\), the most that one record can move a function \(f\) in Euclidean length. With normal noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) per coordinate, only the ratio \(\mu = \Delta_2 f/\sigma\) matters, because a rotation puts the move along one axis without changing the noise. The release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \[\delta \ge \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{38.2}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function (Theorem 20.3). The right side grows with \(\mu\), so each budget has a largest admissible ratio, written \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), and the least noise is \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) (Corollary 20.1). For \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\mu = 0.2681\), so \(\sigma = 3.7306\,\Delta_2 f\), while the classic formula \(\Delta_2 f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) of Theorem 20.2 gives 30% more, \(4.8448\,\Delta_2 f\).
Gaussian noise can never give pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, with \(\delta = 0\), because the log ratio of two shifted Gaussian densities grows without bound in the tails. Pure DP needs a density that falls off only exponentially in every direction, and the theorem below offers this noise as its pure option.
A Gaussian vector’s squared length has mean \(d\sigma^2\), against \(d(d + 1)s^2\) here, so in high dimension the pure-DP noise is longer by a factor that grows with \(d\).
How much accuracy does the noise cost? Section M.1 answers exactly, and a second-order answer is simpler. Near the minimizer the objective is a bowl, whose shape is given by the Hessian \(H = \nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*)\), the matrix of second derivatives. A small random step costs half its squared length times the bowl’s curvature averaged over the step’s direction.
Every solver stops at an approximate minimizer, so the theorem’s exact \(\theta^*\) never exists in practice. What a solver can guarantee is that the gradient’s length is below a tolerance \(\tau\), and the next result adds that slack to the sensitivity.
The noise is calibrated to the worst case, and the damage is measured on the actual case. The sensitivity uses only the ridge’s curvature \(\lambda\), while the damage is weighted by \(H\), which includes the data’s own. If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to some \(h\), then \(\operatorname{tr}H \approx dh\), and substituting the \(\sigma\) of Equation 38.5 into \(\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}H\) gives a Gaussian excess risk of about \(\frac{2dL^2}{\mu^2n^2}\cdot\frac{h}{\lambda^2}\), so a small ridge buys a better non-private fit and costs a lot of noise. The excess risk falls like \(1/n^2\), faster than the error of order \(1/n\) that sampling causes even without privacy, so for large \(n\) privacy costs less than sampling does.
The method also needs a nearly exact solution. To keep the extra term of Equation 38.9 below the exact one, the optimizer must reach \(\tau \le L/n\), a tolerance that shrinks with the dataset. The stopping rule must be a gradient check, not a step count, because a fixed number of steps may leave a large gradient on some dataset, and the proof needs the bound on every one. Wu et al. (2017) bound the sensitivity of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) run for a fixed number of passes instead.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
Lemma 38.1 (Noise with density proportional to \(e^{-|b|/s}\)) Let a noise vector \(b \in \mathbb R^d\) have density \(\nu(b) \propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\), with scale \(s > 0\). If \(f\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\) and \(s = \Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\), then \(f(D) + b\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The length \(\|b\|\) has the gamma distribution with shape \(d\) and scale \(s\), the direction is uniform and independent of the length, and \[\mathbb E\|b\| = ds, \qquad \mathbb E\|b\|^2 = d(d + 1)s^2. \tag{38.3}\]


Proof. 

Privacy. At an output \(y\) the two densities share their constant, so their ratio is \(e^{(\|y - f(D')\| - \|y - f(D)\|)/s}\). By the triangle inequality the difference of distances is at most \(\|f(D) - f(D')\| \le \Delta_2 f\). So the ratio is at most \(e^{\Delta_2 f/s} = e^\varepsilon\) at every output, which is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP by the pointwise criterion of the definition of differential privacy.
Length and direction. The density depends on \(b\) only through its length \(r\). The sphere of radius \(r\) has surface area proportional to \(r^{d-1}\), so the length has density proportional to \[r^{d - 1}e^{-r/s}, \tag{38.4}\] the gamma density with shape \(d\) and scale \(s\). At a given length every direction has the same density, so the direction is uniform and independent of the length.
Moments. A gamma variable with shape \(d\) and scale \(s\) has mean \(ds\) and variance \(ds^2\). The second moment is the variance plus the squared mean, \(ds^2 + d^2s^2 = d(d + 1)s^2\).




Theorem 38.1 (Output perturbation) Let each loss \(\ell(\cdot; z)\) be convex and differentiable, with gradients of length at most \(L\), let \(\lambda > 0\), and let neighbours replace one record. Release \[\tilde\theta = \theta^*(D) + Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N\big(0, \sigma^2I\big), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{\lambda n\,\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{38.5}\] This release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Replacing \(Z\) by noise \(b\) with density \(\propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\) and \(s = 2L/(\lambda n\varepsilon)\) gives pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

Sensitivity. By Theorem 6.5 the minimizer moves by at most \(\Delta_2\theta^* = 2L/(\lambda n)\) when one record is replaced.
Gaussian noise. With \(\sigma = \Delta_2\theta^*/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) the ratio of sensitivity to noise is \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), which satisfies Equation 38.2, so the release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Pure noise. With \(s = \Delta_2\theta^*/\varepsilon\), Lemma 38.1 makes the release \(\varepsilon\)-DP.




Proposition 38.1 (Excess risk of output perturbation) Let \(\mathcal L\) be twice differentiable with Hessian \(H\) at \(\theta^*\), and let the noise \(Z\) have a uniformly random direction, independent of its length. To second order in \(Z\), \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \frac12\,\mathbb E\big[Z^\top HZ\big] = \frac{\mathbb E\|Z\|^2}{2d}\operatorname{tr}H, \tag{38.6}\] which is \(\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}H\) for the Gaussian.


Proof. 

Expand around the minimizer. The gradient vanishes at \(\theta^*\), so a second-order Taylor expansion leaves only the quadratic term, \[\mathcal L(\theta^* + Z) - \mathcal L(\theta^*) \approx \tfrac12Z^\top HZ. \tag{38.7}\]
Average over the direction. Write \(Z = \|Z\|u\) with \(u\) a unit vector. The \(d\) squared coordinates of \(u\) add up to 1 and are exchangeable, so each averages \(1/d\). Flipping the sign of one coordinate leaves a uniform direction uniform, so the product of two different coordinates averages to zero. Hence \[\mathbb E[u^\top Hu] = \frac1d\sum_iH_{ii} = \frac{\operatorname{tr}H}{d}. \tag{38.8}\]
Put the length back. The length is independent of the direction, so \(\mathbb E[Z^\top HZ] = \mathbb E\|Z\|^2\operatorname{tr}H/d\). For the Gaussian \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2 = d\sigma^2\).




Proposition 38.2 (Sensitivity of an approximate minimizer) In the setting of Theorem 38.1, let the optimizer return, on every dataset, a point \(\theta\) with \(\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta; D)\| \le \tau\). Then its outputs \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\) on two neighbouring datasets satisfy \[\|\theta - \theta'\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n} + \frac{2\tau}{\lambda}. \tag{38.9}\]


Proof. 

Each output is near its minimizer. The objective is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, so part (a) of Corollary 6.1 puts \(\theta\) within \(\tau/\lambda\) of \(\theta^*(D)\), and \(\theta'\) within \(\tau/\lambda\) of \(\theta^*(D')\).
The minimizers are near each other. By Theorem 6.5 they are at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\) apart.
Add the three distances. The triangle inequality along the path \(\theta \to \theta^*(D) \to \theta^*(D') \to \theta'\) gives Equation 38.9.










Figure 38.1: Left: two neighbouring regularized logistic objectives in one dimension (\(n = 20\), \(\lambda = 0.5\)), their minimizers (vertical lines) 0.083 apart, below the bound \(2L/(\lambda n) = 0.2\). Right: the released weight’s density under each dataset with Gaussian noise for \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); the noise must hide a shift as large as the bound, not the actual shift.




Example 38.1 Start with one feature, \(n = 20\) records and \(\lambda = 0.5\) (Figure 38.1). Replacing the last record, which has \(x = 1\), by the same feature with the opposite label moves the minimizer from 0.2128 to 0.1296, by 0.0832. With \(L = 1\), since a logistic gradient is never longer than its unit feature, the bound is \(2/(0.5 \times 20) = 0.2\), and the noise is calibrated to the bound, \(\sigma = 3.7306 \times 0.2 = 0.7461\), so the two output densities overlap almost completely.
In the running example (\(d = 10\), \(\lambda = 0.01\), \(L = 1\)), \(n = 10{,}000\) gives sensitivity \(2/(0.01 \times 10{,}000) = 0.02\) and \(\sigma = 0.07461\) per coordinate, next to a minimizer of length 2.886. The Hessian at \(\theta^*\) has eigenvalues between 0.0263 and 0.0330, and trace 0.3129. Equation 38.6 predicts \(\frac12 \times 0.07461^2 \times 0.3129 = 8.711 \times 10^{-4}\), and 20 simulated releases average \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\). The pure-DP version, with \(s = 0.02\), predicts \(6.885 \times 10^{-4}\) and averages \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\). The gap is wider because the squared length of gamma noise varies a lot, and 20 draws average it only roughly.
Stopping early is costly. A gradient tolerance of \(\tau = 10^{-6}\) gives sensitivity 0.0202, essentially exact, and \(\tau = 10^{-4}\) doubles it to 0.04. At \(\tau = 10^{-3}\) it is 0.22, eleven times the exact value, which multiplies the excess risk by about 121.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.2 Objective perturbation
Output perturbation wastes the data’s curvature, because it pays for the worst case \(\lambda\) and is judged on the actual \(H\). Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate (2011) put the noise inside the optimization instead. This section asks whether a randomly tilted objective, minimized exactly, is private, and what it costs.
The tilt is a random linear term \(\frac1n\langle b, \theta\rangle\). It acts as a constant force, and all of the objective’s curvature resists it, so where the data add curvature the minimizer moves less. The output is no longer something fixed plus noise, so the proof must track how the minimization stretches the noise. It bounds that stretching only when each record’s Hessian has rank one, so that replacing a record changes it by little. So the loss must depend on \(\theta\) through one inner product, \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = \psi(y\langle \theta, x\rangle)\), for a scalar function \(\psi\) of the margin \(m = y\langle\theta, x\rangle\). Logistic regression has \(\psi(m) = \ln(1 + e^{-m})\), whose derivative lies in \((-1, 0)\) and whose second derivative is at most \(c = \frac14\). The budget \(\varepsilon\) is split in two. One part pays for the difference in stretching between the two datasets, which the bound \(c\) on \(\psi''\) controls, and the rest, written \(\varepsilon'\), goes to the noise.

Theorem 38.2 (Objective perturbation) Let the loss be \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = \psi(y\langle \theta, x\rangle)\), with \(\psi\) convex and twice differentiable, \(|\psi'| \le 1\) and \(0 \le \psi'' \le c\), and let every feature have \(\|x\| \le 1\). Let \(\lambda > 0\) and let neighbours replace one record. Set \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big), \tag{38.10}\] draw \(b\) with density \(\nu(b) \propto e^{-\varepsilon'\|b\|/2}\), and release \[\tilde\theta = \arg\min_\theta\Big[\mathcal L(\theta; D) + \frac1n\langle b, \theta\rangle\Big]. \tag{38.11}\] If \(\varepsilon' > 0\), the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP (Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate 2011, Algorithm 2). If \(\varepsilon' \le 0\), adding \(\lambda_+ = \frac{c}{n(e^{\varepsilon/4} - 1)} - \lambda\) to the ridge and drawing the noise with \(\varepsilon/2\) in place of \(\varepsilon'\) makes it \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to write the density of \(\tilde\theta\) explicitly, then bound the ratio of the two densities, for \(D\) and \(D'\), at every point. The ratio splits into a noise factor and a stretching factor, and each consumes part of \(\varepsilon\).

From the output back to the noise. The perturbed objective is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, so it has exactly one minimizer, where its gradient is zero: \(\nabla\mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) + b/n = 0\). Solving for \(b\) gives \[b = \phi_D(\tilde\theta) = -n\nabla\mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) = -\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla\ell(\tilde\theta; z_i) - n\lambda\tilde\theta. \tag{38.12}\] Every \(\theta\) is the output for exactly one noise vector, \(\phi_D(\theta)\), so the map from noise to output is invertible and \(\phi_D\) is its inverse.
The density of the output. When a random vector with density \(\nu\) is mapped smoothly and invertibly, the image has density \(\nu\) at the preimage times the absolute determinant of the inverse map’s Jacobian. The determinant corrects for stretching: a small box around \(\theta\) and its preimage around \(b\) carry the same probability, so their densities differ by the ratio of their volumes. Applied to \(D\) and \(D'\), the ratio of the two output densities at any \(\theta\) is \[\frac{p_D(\theta)}{p_{D'}(\theta)} = \underbrace{\frac{\nu(\phi_D(\theta))}{\nu(\phi_{D'}(\theta))}}_{\text{noise}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{|\det\nabla\phi_D(\theta)|}{|\det\nabla\phi_{D'}(\theta)|}}_{\text{Jacobian}}. \tag{38.13}\]
The noise factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon'}\). The sums in \(\phi_D\) and \(\phi_{D'}\) share every term except the replaced record’s, so \(\phi_{D'}(\theta) - \phi_D(\theta) = \nabla\ell(\theta; z) - \nabla\ell(\theta; z')\), of length at most 2, since each gradient \(\psi'(m)\,y\,x\) has length at most \(|\psi'|\,\|x\| \le 1\). This is the setting of Lemma 38.1 with sensitivity 2 and scale \(s = 2/\varepsilon'\), so the noise factor is at most \(e^{2/s} = e^{\varepsilon'}\).
The Jacobian is the Hessian. Differentiating \(\phi_D\) gives \(\nabla\phi_D(\theta) = -A\), with \[A = \sum_i\psi''(m_i)\,x_ix_i^\top + n\lambda I, \tag{38.14}\] where \(m_i\) is the margin of record \(i\). The chain rule gives each loss’s Hessian as \(\psi''(m_i)\) times \(y_i^2x_ix_i^\top = x_ix_i^\top\). Every term is positive semi-definite, so all eigenvalues of \(A\) are at least \(n\lambda\). For \(D'\) the matrix is \(A' = A + E\), with \(E = \psi''(m')x'x'^\top - \psi''(m)xx^\top\): one rank-one term in, one out.
The Jacobian factor is at most \((1 + c/(n\lambda))^2\). The factor is \(\det(A)/\det(A')\). Bound first its reciprocal, \(\det(A')/\det(A)\), which is \(\det(I + A^{-1}E)\), which equals \(\det(I + K)\) for the similar, symmetric matrix \(K = A^{-1/2}EA^{-1/2}\). With \(\tilde x = A^{-1/2}x\), \(K\) is the difference of the rank-one terms \(\psi''(m')\tilde x'\tilde x'^\top\) and \(\psi''(m)\tilde x\tilde x^\top\). A rank-one matrix \(vv^\top\) has one nonzero eigenvalue, \(\|v\|^2\), and here \(\|\tilde x\|^2 = x^\top A^{-1}x \le 1/(n\lambda)\). So \(K\) has at most two nonzero eigenvalues \(\kappa_1\) and \(\kappa_2\). The term added has one eigenvalue, \(\psi''(m')\|\tilde x'\|^2 \le c/(n\lambda)\), and can raise no eigenvalue by more than that. The term subtracted can likewise lower none by more than \(c/(n\lambda)\). So each \(\kappa\) lies between \(-a\) and \(a\), with \(a = c/(n\lambda)\). Hence \[\det(I + K) = (1 + \kappa_1)(1 + \kappa_2) \le (1 + a)^2. \tag{38.15}\] The same argument with \(D\) and \(D'\) exchanged bounds \(\det(A)/\det(A')\), the Jacobian factor itself, by \((1 + a)^2\), because \(A'\) also has all eigenvalues at least \(n\lambda\).
Add the two budgets. The log of the density ratio is at most \(\varepsilon' + 2\ln(1 + c/(n\lambda))\), which is \(\varepsilon\) by Equation 38.10, at every \(\theta\) and in both directions. A bound on the density ratio everywhere is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
When \(\varepsilon' \le 0\). The Jacobian factor alone would then exceed \(\varepsilon\), and a larger ridge shrinks it. With \(\lambda + \lambda_+\) in place of \(\lambda\), \(a = e^{\varepsilon/4} - 1\), so the Jacobian takes \(2\ln(1 + a) = \varepsilon/2\) and the noise gets the other half.


The analysis is safe but not tight. The noise factor reaches \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) only if both records have full-length gradients in opposite directions. A logistic gradient has full length only at a very negative margin, and two records whose gradients point in opposite directions have margins of opposite sign, so at most one of them can. The Jacobian bound charges both records the full curvature \(c\), but the record that arrives raises the determinant while the one that leaves lowers it, so \(\ln(1 + a)\) suffices, half the charge.
The method needs exact minimization, which no computer delivers, and even rounding can leak (Discrete mechanisms). It also needs twice-differentiable losses, so a support vector machine’s hinge loss must be smoothed first. Iyengar et al. (2019) tolerate inexact solvers by adding a little output noise.
The excess risk follows the second-order argument of output perturbation, except that the noise now enters as a force, which the curvature \(H\) converts into a displacement by dividing by it.

Proposition 38.3 (Excess risk of objective perturbation) Under the assumptions of Proposition 38.1, with the noise \(b\) of Theorem 38.2, to second order in \(b\), \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \frac{1}{2n^2}\mathbb E\big[b^\top H^{-1}b\big] = \frac{\mathbb E\|b\|^2}{2dn^2}\operatorname{tr}H^{-1}. \tag{38.16}\]


Proof. 

The displacement. To first order in \(b\) the gradient of \(\mathcal L\) at \(\tilde\theta\) is \(H(\tilde\theta - \theta^*)\), and the perturbed minimizer makes it cancel the force: \[\tilde\theta - \theta^* = -\frac1nH^{-1}b. \tag{38.17}\]
Its cost. Substituting the displacement into the quadratic of step 1 of Proposition 38.1 gives \(\frac{1}{2n^2}b^\top H^{-1}HH^{-1}b = \frac{1}{2n^2}b^\top H^{-1}b\).
Average over the direction. The direction of \(b\) is uniform and independent of its length (Lemma 38.1), so step 2 of Proposition 38.1 applies with \(H^{-1}\) in place of \(H\).


Curvature now helps. Output perturbation’s noise scales like \(1/(\lambda n)\) and is weighted by \(H\), while here the noise does not depend on \(n\) or \(\lambda\), is divided by \(n\), and is weighted by \(H^{-1}\). If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to \(h\), pure-DP output perturbation’s excess risk is about \((h/\lambda)^2\) times objective perturbation’s, when \(\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon\), because both use the same noise shape. When the ridge supplies all the curvature the two are equivalent, and when the data supply more, objective perturbation wins quadratically.






Figure 38.2: Objective perturbation in one dimension, \(n = 5\), \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: the exact densities of the released weight under a dataset and its neighbour, computed by change of variables. Right: their log ratio, the privacy loss, which stays well inside \(\pm\varepsilon\).




Example 38.2 In one dimension the chapter’s script computes both output densities exactly on a grid. Take logistic loss (\(c = \frac14\)) on \(n = 5\) records with features in \([-1, 1]\), \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). Then \(c/(n\lambda) = 0.5\), the Jacobian budget is \(2\ln 1.5 = 0.8109\), and the noise gets \(\varepsilon' = 0.1891\) (Figure 38.2). Over 500 random datasets and replacements, the largest log ratio anywhere on the grid is 0.3779. Its noise part never exceeds 0.0992, about half its budget of 0.1891, and its Jacobian part never exceeds 0.3395, below even \(\ln 1.5 = 0.4055\), which is half the Jacobian budget of 0.8109.
In the running example at \(n = 10{,}000\), the Jacobian budget is \(2\ln(1 + 0.25/100) = 0.0050\), so the noise gets \(\varepsilon' = 0.9950\). The noise has \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2 = d(d+1)(2/\varepsilon')^2\), and \(\operatorname{tr}H^{-1} = 320.7\), so Equation 38.16 predicts an excess risk of \(7.127 \times 10^{-5}\), and 20 simulated releases average \(8.156 \times 10^{-5}\). Pure-DP output perturbation with the same \(\varepsilon\) had \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\), so objective perturbation is ten times better. The rule \((h/\lambda)^2\) predicts this, because the objective’s curvature, between 0.0263 and 0.0330, is about three times the ridge’s 0.01, and \(3^2 = 9\).

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.3 Gradient perturbation: noisy gradient descent
The first two methods need the exact minimizer, but real training is iterative and stops early. Gradient perturbation, proposed by Williams & McSherry (2010), makes each step of the optimizer private and composes the steps. This section asks how much noise per step makes a whole run of full-batch gradient descent private, and how accurate the run is.
Each step will be a Gaussian mechanism applied at a point that earlier steps chose. \(T\) such adaptive Gaussian mechanisms, with ratios \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_T\), are exactly as private as one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_T^2}\) (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy). Given the past, each step’s privacy loss is normal with variance \(\mu_t^2\) and mean \(\mu_t^2/2\), so their sum is normal with variance \(\sum_t\mu_t^2\) and half that as its mean, which is the privacy loss of one Gaussian mechanism.

Theorem 38.3 (Noisy gradient descent) Let every per-record gradient have length at most \(L\), with the loss convex or not, and let neighbours replace one record. Start from \(\theta_0 = 0\) and run \(T\) steps of \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\big(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I)\ \text{independent}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}, \tag{38.18}\] with learning rate \(\eta\). Releasing all the iterates \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

One step is a Gaussian mechanism. Given \(\theta_t\), the step releases \(\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\). The ridge term \(\lambda\theta_t\) is the same on both datasets, and the averages differ only in the replaced record. So the gradient moves by at most \(\frac1n\|\nabla\ell(\theta_t; z) - \nabla\ell(\theta_t; z')\| \le 2L/n\), and the step’s ratio is \(\mu_{\text{step}} = 2L/(n\sigma)\). The point \(\theta_t\) depends on the data only through earlier released outputs, which is what adaptive composition allows.
Compose. By the composition of Gaussian mechanisms, the \(T\) steps are as private as one Gaussian with ratio \(\sqrt T\cdot 2L/(n\sigma)\). Setting this to \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) gives the \(\sigma\) of Equation 38.18. The iterates are computed from the noisy gradients and \(\theta_0\) alone, so releasing them is post-processing.
No convexity was used. Steps 1 and 2 bounded the gradient’s change by \(2L/n\) at the point \(\theta_t\), whatever \(\theta_t\) is. Nothing required a minimizer, convexity or smoothness.


Convexity enters only for accuracy. On a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth objective, one whose curvature lies between \(\lambda\) and \(\beta\) everywhere, gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) shrinks the error by a fixed factor per step, while the noise keeps the iterate from settling.

Proposition 38.4 (Excess risk of noisy gradient descent) Let the objective be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and \(\beta\)-smooth, and let \(\eta = 1/\beta\). The excess risk of the last iterate is approximately \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\theta_T) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \Big(1 - \frac\lambda\beta\Big)^T\big(\mathcal L(\theta_0) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big) + \frac{d\sigma^2}{4\beta}. \tag{38.19}\]


Proof. 

Optimization error. Without noise, each step shrinks \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\) by at least a factor \(1 - \lambda/\beta\). Theorem 6.1 proves the same factor for the distance on a quadratic, and Section G.1 proves it for the excess risk of every such objective. Over \(T\) steps this gives the first term.
How the noise moves the error. Near the minimizer the gradient is about \(H(\theta_t - \theta^*)\), so the error \(e_t = \theta_t - \theta^*\) evolves as \[e_{t+1} \approx (I - \eta H)e_t - \eta\xi_t. \tag{38.20}\]
The steady state in one direction. Along an eigenvector of \(H\) with curvature \(h\), the error’s variance \(v\) settles where one step leaves it unchanged, \(v = (1 - \eta h)^2v + \eta^2\sigma^2\). Solving gives \(v = \eta\sigma^2/(h(2 - \eta h))\).
Its cost. That direction costs \(\frac12hv = \eta\sigma^2/(2(2 - \eta h))\), about \(\eta\sigma^2/4\) when \(\eta h\) is small and at most twice that when \(\eta h\) reaches 1. Summing over the \(d\) directions with \(\eta = 1/\beta\) gives \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\).


The curvature \(h\) cancels in step 4, because flat directions wander farther but cost less per unit of wandering. What does not cancel is \(T\), so the step count is a privacy parameter: every step spends budget, so the noise floor grows like \(T\), while too few steps leave optimization error (Figure 38.3). Equation 38.19 can be minimized from public quantities: \(\lambda\), the curvature bound \(\beta = \frac14 + \lambda\) of logistic loss with unit features, \(\mathcal L(\theta_0) = \ln 2\) at \(\theta_0 = 0\), \(d\), \(n\) and the budget. This public rule for \(T\) is pessimistic, because it knows only that the curvature is at least \(\lambda\). Picking \(T\) by validation score is itself a computation on the data (Hyperparameter tuning).






Figure 38.3: Excess risk of noisy gradient descent at \(n = 10{,}000\), \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), against the number of steps \(T\), averaged over datasets, with the same steps without noise (dashed). The noiseless error falls geometrically and reaches machine precision; the noisy run is limited by noise that grows with \(T\), so its error is smallest near \(T = 50\).




Example 38.3 For \(n = 10{,}000\), the public rule picks \(T = 218\). That gives per-step noise \(\sigma = 0.01102\) on the mean gradient and an estimated excess risk of \(1.301 \times 10^{-3}\), and simulated runs average \(1.384 \times 10^{-3}\). Table 38.1 gives the rule’s choice at every dataset size. The step count grows slowly, like \(\ln n\), because the optimization error shrinks geometrically while its target, the noise floor, shrinks like \(1/n^2\).
