title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.4 Noisy projected gradient descent without a ridge
text:
38.4 Noisy projected gradient descent without a ridge
Every method so far leaned on the ridge, for its privacy or for its accuracy. But a linear classifier trained without a ridge inside a fixed ball of weights is convex with bounded gradients, not strongly convex. This section asks how accurate a private trainer can be on such a model, and where the dimension enters.
The tool is the guarantee of projected SGD from Optimization. Projected SGD keeps the weights in a closed convex set \(\mathcal W\) fixed in advance, here the ball of radius \(R\), by replacing each new point with its projection \(\Pi_{\mathcal W}\), the nearest point of the set. It steps along a random vector \(g_t\) that is right on average given the past, with squared length at most \(G^2\) on average. If the objective is convex and its minimizer over \(\mathcal W\) lies within \(R\) of the start, then \(T\) steps with learning rate \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) make the average \(\bar\theta_T\) of the visited points satisfy \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T)\big] - \mathcal L(\theta^*) \le \frac{RG}{\sqrt T} \tag{38.21}\] (Theorem 6.2). Independent noise with mean zero only adds its second moment to \(G^2\) (Proposition 6.4).

Theorem 38.4 (Noisy projected gradient descent) Let the loss be convex in \(\theta\) with per-record gradients of length at most \(L\), let the objective be the plain average \(\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell(\theta; z_i)\), with no ridge, and let neighbours replace one record. Keep the weights in the ball \(\mathcal W = \{\|\theta\| \le R\}\). Start from \(\theta_1 = 0\) and run \(T\) steps of \[\theta_{t+1} = \Pi_{\mathcal W}\Big(\theta_t - \eta\big(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\big)\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}, \tag{38.22}\] with \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) and \(G^2 = L^2 + d\sigma^2\), and release \(\bar\theta = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\theta_t\). The release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and its excess risk over the best weights in the ball is at most \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)\big] - \min_{\theta\in\mathcal W}\mathcal L(\theta; D) \le RL\sqrt{\frac1T + \frac{4d}{n^2\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)^2}}. \tag{38.23}\] Once \(T \ge n^2\mu^2/(4d)\) this is at most \(2\sqrt2\,RL\sqrt d/(n\mu)\), and for \(\varepsilon < 1\) \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)\big] - \min_{\theta\in\mathcal W}\mathcal L(\theta; D) \le \frac{4RL\sqrt{d\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}. \tag{38.24}\]


Proof. The plan is to prove privacy as for noisy gradient descent, check the two conditions of the SGD guarantee for the noisy gradient, and then see that the step count drops out of the noise term.

Privacy. Each step releases a noisy gradient whose noiseless part moves by at most \(2L/n\), as in step 1 of the proof of Theorem 38.3, and the \(T\) steps compose into one Gaussian with ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). The projection uses only the public ball, and the average uses only the iterates, so both are post-processing.
The noisy gradient is unbiased. Write \(g_t = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\). Given the past, \(\xi_t\) is fresh noise with mean zero, so \(g_t\) averages to the true gradient.
Its second moment is at most \(L^2 + d\sigma^2\). The gradient of \(\mathcal L\) is an average of vectors of length at most \(L\), so its squared length is at most \(L^2\). The noise is independent with mean zero, so by Proposition 6.4 it adds its own second moment, one \(\sigma^2\) per coordinate, \(d\sigma^2\) in all.
Apply the SGD guarantee. The minimizer over the ball and the start \(\theta_1 = 0\) both lie in the ball, so they are at most \(R\) apart. With \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\), Theorem 6.2 bounds the excess risk of \(\bar\theta\) by \[\frac{RG}{\sqrt T} = R\sqrt{\frac{L^2 + d\sigma^2}{T}}. \tag{38.25}\]
The step count cancels from the noise term. By Equation 38.22, \(\sigma^2 = 4L^2T/(n^2\mu^2)\), so \(d\sigma^2/T = 4L^2d/(n^2\mu^2)\) whatever \(T\) is. Factoring out \(L^2\) gives Equation 38.23.
Choose \(T\). The first term under the root falls with \(T\) and the second does not. When \(T \ge n^2\mu^2/(4d)\) the first is at most the second, and the root is at most \(\sqrt{8d/(n^2\mu^2)} = 2\sqrt2\,\sqrt d/(n\mu)\).
In terms of \(\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon < 1\) the classic noise \(\Delta_2 f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP (Theorem 20.2). The exact calibration uses the least noise that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, so its ratio is at least the classic one, \[\frac1\mu \le \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{38.26}\] Substituting this into step 6 gives \(2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2 = 4\) in front, which is Equation 38.24.


Privacy noise is just more gradient variance. The SGD guarantee cares only about the second moment of \(g_t\), and Gaussian noise raises it by one \(\sigma^2\) for every coordinate the optimizer moves, which Public data and private fine-tuning exploits by training fewer coordinates. Unlike in Section 38.3, more steps never hurt, because step 5 cancels the growth of the noise. The step count only has to reach \(n^2\mu^2/(4d)\), but each full-batch step costs \(n\) gradient evaluations, so Bassily, Smith & Thakurta use one random record per step instead, which by Amplification by subsampling also needs less noise.
The rate cannot be beaten. As long as \(\sqrt d \le n\varepsilon\), every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm has excess risk of order \(RL\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) on some dataset, by the fingerprinting argument of Lower bounds (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014). Section M.1 derives this lower bound with explicit constants, and Equation 38.24 matches it up to \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\) and constants. It is a worst case, reached by losses nearly linear near their minimizer.






Figure 38.4: Noisy projected gradient descent on unregularized logistic regression in the ball of radius 5, \(d = 10\), \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP, with \(T = \lceil n^2\mu^2/(4d)\rceil\) steps: the measured excess risk over the best weights in the ball (circles) against the bound Equation 38.23 (squares), averaged over 3 datasets drawn separately from those of the table. The bound falls like \(1/n\); the measured excess risk falls faster.




Example 38.4 Take the running example’s data, with \(d = 10\) and \(L = 1\), drop the ridge, and keep the weights in the ball of radius \(R = 5\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the exact ratio is \(\mu = 0.2681\), and the classic ratio \(\varepsilon/\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\) is smaller, 0.2064, as step 7 requires. With a thousand records the rule \(T = \lceil n^2\mu^2/(4d)\rceil\) gives 1,797 steps, and the noise on the mean gradient is \(\sigma = 0.3163\). The noise adds \(d\sigma^2 = 10 \times 0.3163^2\) to the second moment, so \(G^2 = 2.0004\), about twice the noiseless \(L^2 = 1\). The learning rate is then 0.0834, and Equation 38.23 evaluates to 0.1668.
As \(T\) grows, the first term under the root vanishes and the bound falls to \(2RL\sqrt d/(n\mu) = 0.1180\), a factor \(\sqrt2\) below its value at the threshold. It is 0.5137 after 100 steps, 0.1973 after 1,000 and 0.1190 after 100,000, within 1% of that limit. Table 38.2 runs the algorithm for three dataset sizes, five datasets each.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.5 How the three compare
Each method is private by its own argument, so which should you use? Theory answers by rates, how the excess risk falls with \(n\), \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\), and simulation answers for the running example. This section shows that they agree on the rate and differ in the constant, which is what you choose by.
With a guaranteed curvature the rate improves. The convex rate of Section 38.4 falls like \(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\). For a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex objective the rate squares this to \(d/(n\varepsilon)^2\) and divides it by \(\lambda\).

Theorem 38.5 (Optimal rate for strongly convex objectives) For \(\lambda\)-strongly convex objectives whose losses have gradients of length at most \(L\), the best expected excess risk achievable under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is of order \[\frac{L^2\,d}{\lambda\,n^2\varepsilon^2}, \tag{38.27}\] up to logarithmic factors in \(n\) and \(1/\delta\).


Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) prove both sides, the upper bound with noisy stochastic gradient descent and the lower bound with fingerprinting codes, and Section M.1 proves both with explicit constants. Output and objective perturbation fall at this rate in \(n\) because their noise has second moment proportional to \(1/n^2\). Noisy gradient descent loses a logarithm, because pushing its optimization error below a noise floor \(\propto T/n^2\) takes \(T \propto \ln n\) steps.

On the running example (Table 38.3, Figure 38.5) all four releases fall like \(1/n^2\), and noisy gradient descent a little slower, \(-1.79\), because its step count grows with \(\ln n\). Objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation at every \(n\), the \((h/\lambda)^2\) of Section 38.2. Noisy gradient descent with the public step rule is the worst of the three for \(n \ge 10{,}000\), and tuned privately to \(T \approx 50\) it would sit between the two perturbation methods. Accuracy on held-out data suffers even less. The non-private model has accuracy 0.747 at \(n = 1{,}000\), which output perturbation drops to 0.681, noisy gradient descent to 0.695 and objective perturbation only to 0.736. By \(n = 10{,}000\) all four private releases are within 0.002 of the non-private 0.753.
The pure-DP column is slightly better because, by Lemma 38.1, at \(d = 10\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) its noise has mean squared length \(d(d + 1)(\Delta_2 f)^2 = 110\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\), against \(d \times 3.7306^2(\Delta_2 f)^2 = 139.2\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\) for the Gaussian. At \(d = 100\) it is \(10{,}100\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\) against \(1{,}392\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\), the price of \(\delta = 0\) that Lower bounds proves unavoidable.
A deployed model is judged not on the training objective but by its population risk, the expected loss on a new record from the same distribution. For convex Lipschitz losses over a ball, Bassily, Feldman, Talwar & Thakurta (2019) show that the best population excess risk is of order \[LR\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt n} + \frac{\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{38.28}\] The first term is what any learner pays for seeing only \(n\) samples, so once \(n\) exceeds about \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\), privacy adds less than sampling already costs.






Figure 38.5: Excess risk of the four private releases against the dataset size on the running example, log-log, with a line of slope \(-2\). All fall like \(1/n^2\); objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation throughout.




Example 38.5 Equation 38.27 predicts how much data you need. Suppose an excess risk of \(10^{-4}\) is acceptable, and output perturbation gives \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(n = 10{,}000\). The rate \(1/n^2\) says that multiplying \(n\) by \(\sqrt{9.274} = 3.05\) brings it to about \(10^{-4}\), and Table 38.3 confirms it, with \(9.973 \times 10^{-5}\) at \(n = 30{,}000\). Halving \(\varepsilon\) costs as much as halving \(n\), because every noise scale in this chapter is proportional to \(1/(n\varepsilon)\).

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.6 When the model is not convex
text:
38.6 When the model is not convex
A neural network’s loss is not convex in its parameters, and the privacy proofs of output and objective perturbation both need a unique minimizer that moves only a little when one record changes. This section asks what survives of the three methods, and why the next chapter keeps only one.
Without convexity the minimizer can jump. Optimization averages the per-record loss \(\frac14(\theta^2 - 1)^2 - y\theta\), with labels \(y = \pm1\), into a risk with two wells, minimized in the well of the majority label. With 501 labels \(+1\) and 500 labels \(-1\), changing one label flips the majority and moves the minimizer by 2.0010. No \(1/n\) appears, so output perturbation would need noise whose scale does not shrink with the dataset.
Objective perturbation breaks at step 1 of its proof, because the perturbed objective can have several minimizers and the map from noise to output is no longer invertible. Neel, Roth, Vietri & Wu (2020) prove a variant private without convexity, but only when an oracle returns the global minimizer of the perturbed objective. Gradient descent on a neural network finds a local minimum, about which that guarantee says nothing. Gradient perturbation survives, once clipping supplies the gradient bound its proof needs, just as Beyond global sensitivity clips a value before averaging it.

Proposition 38.5 (Noisy gradient descent with clipping) For any differentiable loss, convex or not, replace each per-record gradient by its clipped version \(\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i)\min(1, C/\|\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i)\|)\), for a clipping norm \(C\). Noisy gradient descent with the average of clipped gradients in place of \(\nabla\mathcal L\), and with \(L = C\) in Equation 38.18, is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours.


Proof. 

The clipped gradients are bounded. A clipped gradient has length at most \(C\), and is unchanged when it is already shorter.
The step’s sensitivity. The average of clipped gradients loses one term of length at most \(C/n\) and gains another, so it moves by at most \(2C/n\).
The rest of the proof. The proof of Theorem 38.3 used only this bound at the visited points (its step 3), so it goes through with \(L = C\).


The non-convex case loses the guarantee of accuracy, not of privacy, so whether a network learns becomes an empirical question. Clipping also changes what is optimized, because the average of clipped gradients is not the gradient of \(\mathcal L\), and the next chapter measures that bias. Random minibatches, which make each step cheaper and more private, complete DP-SGD, stochastic gradient descent with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise.

Example 38.6 Take the double-well loss with \(n = 1{,}001\) records. Output perturbation at \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs \(\sigma = 3.7306 \times 2.0010 = 7.465\), more than three times the distance between the wells, whatever the dataset size. The release hides which well the data chose, as privacy demands when one record decides it, and so is useless. Noisy gradient descent with clipping still moves toward the well the noisy average gradient points to. When many records agree, that gradient is large compared with the noise, and the method finds the majority well with high probability.

Excess risk \(\approx\mathbb E\Vert b\Vert^2\operatorname{tr}H^{-1}/(2dn^2)\)
Beats output perturbation by about \((h/\lambda)^2\) when the data add curvature \(h\)


Theorem 38.3
Noise \(\sigma = (2L/n)\sqrt T/\mu\) on the mean gradient; all iterates \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, convex or not
The privacy argument of DP-SGD; every iterative private trainer


Proposition 38.4
Optimization error shrinking like \((1 - \lambda/\beta)^T\), plus a noise floor \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\)
The step count is part of the budget; choose it from public quantities, or pay for choosing it


Theorem 38.4
No ridge, ball of radius \(R\): excess risk \(\le 4RL\sqrt{d\ln(1.25/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon)\)
The \(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) rate, optimal up to logarithms; noise is more gradient variance; Public data


Theorem 38.5
Strongly convex: \(L^2d/(\lambda n^2\varepsilon^2)\), up to logarithms
All three methods reach it; halving \(\varepsilon\) costs as much as halving the data


Proposition 38.5
Clipped noisy gradient descent is private for any loss
Why deep learning uses gradient perturbation, with clipping

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.1 The algorithm and its guarantee
Private empirical risk minimization ended with one method left standing for non-convex models: gradient descent with Gaussian noise on every step. This chapter asks what that method computes exactly, why it is private for any model, and what its privacy costs in accuracy. The method is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, which Abadi et al. (2016) introduced to give deep learning a guarantee of differential privacy (DP), and which is called DP-SGD. Nearly every private deep-learning system runs it, through libraries such as Opacus, TensorFlow Privacy and JAX Privacy.
The one idea is that the privacy analysis never looks inside the model. Each step releases a noisy sum of clipped per-example gradients. Clipping rescales each record’s gradient to length at most \(C\), the clipping norm, so adding or removing one record changes the sum by at most \(C\), whatever the network, the loss or the current parameters. The privacy proof needs nothing more, so everything else affects only accuracy, and the knobs fall into two groups. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\), which is the noise’s standard deviation in units of \(C\), the sampling rate and the number of steps set the privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\) through an accountant, and nothing else does. The clipping norm and the learning rate leave \(\varepsilon\) alone, and decide how much of the gradient survives and how far the noise moves the weights. Privacy then costs accuracy in two ways: a bias from clipping, which changes the direction of the average gradient, and a variance from the noise, which makes each step partly random.
The running example takes a configuration whose privacy Part 4 computed without training anything: a sampling rate of 0.01, a noise multiplier of 1 and 10,000 steps. Amplification by subsampling reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for it, and this chapter uses it to train a network. Inputs are 50-dimensional standard normal vectors, and each label is the sign of the output of a fixed random teacher network with 8 hidden tanh units, so a perfect classifier exists. The student has one hidden layer of 64 tanh units and a logistic loss, with \(d = 3{,}329\) parameters including biases. It trains on \(n = 10{,}000\) records and is tested on 20,000 more. DP-SGD runs with a clipping norm of 0.5 and a learning rate of 0.5. Each step draws on average 100 records, so an epoch is 100 steps and the 10,000 steps make 100 epochs. The dataset is fixed, and only the training randomness changes between runs. Table 39.1 lists the symbols of the chapter.
What exactly does DP-SGD compute, and which \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) does it satisfy? The answer has to be precise, because each detail of the algorithm is a hypothesis of the proof, and an implementation that changes a detail can lose the guarantee without any visible symptom. Two datasets are neighbours here when one is the other with one record added or removed. Write \(D \sim D'\) for such a pair, with \(D' = D \cup \{z\}\) the dataset \(D\) with the record \(z\) added. The previous chapter used replacement instead. Add/remove suits DP-SGD because its batches are drawn by an independent coin for each record, so adding a record just adds one more coin.
The algorithm takes the noisy gradient descent of the previous chapter and changes three things. Each step uses a random batch instead of the whole dataset, each record’s gradient is clipped, and the noise is scaled to the clipping norm.
The proof needs one fact about step 4: how far one record can move the clipped sum. Its answer is why the guarantee ignores the model.
With the sensitivity fixed at \(C\) and the noise at \(\sigma C\), a step on which \(z\) is drawn is a Gaussian mechanism whose shift, measured in noise standard deviations, is \(C/(\sigma C) = 1/\sigma\). Its privacy depends on that ratio alone (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, Theorem 20.3), so the clipping norm cancels.
Poisson sampling then makes the step’s output on \(D'\) a mixture. The record \(z\) is left out with probability \(1 - q\), and then the output is distributed as on \(D\). It is drawn with probability \(q\), and then the output is shifted. Amplification by subsampling computes the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve of that mixture against the unshifted Gaussian. That curve is the Rényi divergence between the two distributions as a function of its order \(\alpha > 1\), which the accountant chooses later. At order \(\alpha\) the divergence is the logarithm of the \(\alpha\)-th moment of the ratio of the two densities, divided by \(\alpha - 1\). For integer orders the mixture’s ratio is \(1 - q\) plus \(q\) times a Gaussian ratio, so its \(\alpha\)-th power expands by the binomial theorem, with one term for each number \(j\) of the \(\alpha\) factors that take the shifted component, and \[\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^je^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}, \tag{39.4}\] and a numerical integral gives the other orders. Abadi et al. (2016) introduced this curve as the moments accountant.
The accountant tracks a curve rather than one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair because curves add under composition. A pair only bounds the probability that the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and says nothing about how large the loss is on that rare event, so pairs compose loosely. The theorem below composes the curves and converts the total. Section C.5 derives the same result from scratch, from clipping to the final \(\varepsilon\), with worked numbers.
Each assumption is a condition on the code, and each has a common way to fail. Batch normalization computes means and variances over the batch, so one record changes every other record’s gradient and the sum can move by much more than \(C\). Private models therefore use normalizations that act on one example at a time, such as group or layer normalization. Choosing \(C\) as the median gradient norm of the current batch makes the noise depend on the data, so \(C\) must come from public data or a private estimate. Dividing by the realized batch size \(|S_t|\) instead of \(B\) also breaks the proof, because \(|S_t|\) changes when \(z\) is added. Shuffling the data and cutting it into fixed batches is a different mechanism, which Amplification by subsampling shows can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports. Finally, the accountant must see every step, including the steps of runs discarded during tuning, which is the subject of Hyperparameter tuning.
The guarantee is for one record. A person with many records needs user-level privacy, and preprocessing that uses the data, such as normalizing features by their mean, must itself be private or use public statistics.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
Definition 39.1 (DP-SGD) Fix in advance the clipping norm \(C > 0\), the noise multiplier \(\sigma > 0\) and the sampling rate \(q \in (0, 1]\), as well as the number of steps \(T\) and the learning rate \(\eta\). Write \(B = qn\) for the expected batch size. Start from initial parameters \(\theta_0\) chosen independently of the data. For each step \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Sample. Put each record in the batch \(S_t\) independently with probability \(q\). This is Poisson sampling.
Per-example gradients. For each record \(i\) of the batch, compute its per-example gradient \(g_i = \nabla_\theta\ell(\theta_t; z_i)\) from the record \(z_i\) and \(\theta_t\) alone.
Clip. Rescale each gradient to length at most \(C\), \[\bar g_i = g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big). \tag{39.1}\]
Noisy sum. Add fresh Gaussian noise \(\xi_t\), with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) in every coordinate, to the clipped sum, and call the result \(G_t\): \[G_t = \sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i + \xi_t, \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I_d). \tag{39.2}\]
Step. Set \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,G_t/B\). The divisor is the expected batch size, a public number, not the size of the batch actually drawn.

The output is the sequence of parameters \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\).



Lemma 39.1 (The clipped sum has sensitivity C) Fix the parameters \(\theta_t\) and the set of other records drawn into the batch. If a record \(z\) is added to the batch, the clipped sum \(\sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i\) changes by a vector of length at most \(C\), whatever the model, the loss and \(\theta_t\).


Proof. 

The other terms do not move. Each term \(\bar g_i\) is computed from its own record and \(\theta_t\) alone, by step 2 of Definition 39.1, so every term of the other records is the same with or without \(z\).
The new term is short. The only change is the extra term \(\bar g_z\). Clipping multiplies the length of \(g_z\) by \(\min(1, C/\|g_z\|)\), so the new term’s length is \[\|\bar g_z\| = \min(\|g_z\|, C) \le C. \tag{39.3}\]






Theorem 39.1 (Privacy of DP-SGD) Run DP-SGD (Definition 39.1) with neighbours \(D \sim D'\) that differ by adding or removing one record. Assume that:

each per-example gradient depends only on its own record and the current parameters;
the initial parameters \(\theta_0\) and the values of \(C\), \(\sigma\), \(q\), \(T\) and the denominator \(B\) are fixed before the data are read;
every batch is drawn by Poisson sampling.

Then for every \(0 < \delta < 1\), releasing all of \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha > 1}\Big[T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}\alpha - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{39.5}\] The guarantee does not depend on the loss, the model, \(C\) or \(\eta\).


Proof. The plan is to show that one step is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(1/\sigma\), that the parameter update is post-processing of it, and then to compose the \(T\) steps and convert the total.

One record moves the clipped sum by at most \(C\). This is Lemma 39.1, and it uses the first assumption.
One step is the subsampled Gaussian. Only the shift between the two outputs matters, by Lemma 20.1, and rotating the space puts that shift on one axis, where the other coordinates carry the same noise under both datasets. A shift shorter than \(C\) gives a pair that is a post-processing of the pair with shift \(C\), by adding extra noise, so it is at least as private, as in step 4 of the proof of Theorem 20.3. So after rescaling by \(C\), the worst case is the one-dimensional pair of the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) and \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), whose curve is Equation 39.4. Poisson sampling is what makes the step on \(D'\) this mixture, because \(z\) is drawn with probability \(q\) independently of the other records. The reverse direction, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against the mixture, has a smaller curve at every order (Amplification by subsampling), so Equation 39.4 covers both.
The update is post-processing. The denominator \(B = qn\) is a fixed public number, so \(\theta_{t+1}\) is computed from \(\theta_t\) and \(G_t\) alone. Post-processing cannot raise an RDP curve, by Theorem 29.3.
Compose. Step \(t\) is evaluated at \(\theta_t\), which depends on the earlier noisy sums. Its curve is bounded by \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}\) whatever \(\theta_t\) is, and that bound is fixed in advance, so adaptive composition applies (Theorem 29.2). The \(T\) steps together have the curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\).
Convert. The conversion of Balle et al. (2020) turns a curve value at each order into an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee. From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) proves it. Taking the best order gives Equation 39.5. Every iterate is a function of the released noisy sums, so releasing all of them, or only the last, is covered.





Example 39.1 For the running example’s configuration, Equation 39.5 gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the same value Part 4 reports. The best order is \(\alpha = 4.1\). Table 39.2 gives the noise multiplier that the same \(q\) and \(T\) need for other budgets.



Table 39.2: The noise multiplier that DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps needs for each budget, from the RDP accountant.

How large is the noise? The averaged update \(G_t/B\) carries noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C/B = 1 \times 0.5/100 = 0.005\) on each of the 3,329 coordinates. A Gaussian vector with \(d\) independent coordinates has length close to \(\sqrt d\) times their standard deviation, so the noise has length about \(0.005 \times \sqrt{3{,}329} = 0.288\). The signal is the averaged clipped gradient, whose length is at most \(C = 0.5\). In the run its length is 0.070 at the first step, and between 0.015 and 0.027 from step 1,000 on, so from then on the noise is about ten times longer than the signal.
Training works anyway, because the signal points in roughly the same direction from one step to the next, while the noise is independent. So over \(t\) steps the signals add up to about \(t\) times their length, while the noise adds up to only about \(\sqrt t\) times its length, since independent vectors add in squares. With a typical signal length of 0.026, signal overtakes noise when \(t \cdot 0.026 > \sqrt t \cdot 0.288\), that is after \(t > (0.288/0.026)^2 \approx 123\) steps. The final model reaches test accuracy 0.9589, against 0.9627 for non-private SGD.

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.2 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
text:
39.2 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
The clipping norm does not affect privacy, but it controls both forms of cost. A small \(C\) clips more gradients, which biases the update, and a large \(C\) adds more noise, because the noise is \(\sigma C\). To choose \(C\) you need to know what the update estimates on average, and how a run changes when \(C\) changes.
Averaged over the sampling and the noise, each record enters the update with a weight that clipping sets. The denominator \(B\) is chosen so that the sampling rate cancels.

Proposition 39.1 (The expected update) In DP-SGD (Definition 39.1), with \(\theta_t\) fixed, the averaged update is an unbiased estimate of the average clipped gradient, \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{39.6}\] and its noise has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\) in each coordinate.


Proof. 

Average over the sampling. Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\), so the expected clipped sum is \(\sum_{i=1}^n q\,\bar g_i\). The noise has mean zero.
Divide by \(B = qn\). The \(q\) cancels and leaves \(\frac1n\sum_i\bar g_i\), which is Equation 39.6 by the definition of \(\bar g_i\).
The noise. The noise \(\xi_t\) has standard deviation \(\sigma C\) in each coordinate, and dividing by \(B\) divides it by \(B\).


The update is therefore not the gradient of the training loss but of a reweighted one. Each record’s weight \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\) falls as its gradient grows, so records the model fits badly, such as rare examples, members of small groups or mislabelled points, are down-weighted, while well-fitted records keep their full weight. The weights change as training proceeds, and Disparate impact measures who pays for them. Dividing by \(|S_t|\) instead of \(B\) would not give this average, because the expectation of a ratio of random quantities is not the ratio of their expectations.
When \(C\) is below every gradient norm, clipping turns each gradient into \(C\) times a unit vector. The clipping norm then plays the same role as the learning rate.

Proposition 39.2 (Scale invariance) Suppose that every per-example gradient of a run is clipped, that is \(\|g_i\| \ge C\) at every step. Write the noise as \(\xi_t = \sigma C\zeta_t\) with \(\zeta_t \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\). Then the update is \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta C}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}\frac{g_i}{\|g_i\|} + \sigma\zeta_t\Big), \tag{39.7}\] which depends on \(\eta\) and \(C\) only through their product \(\eta C\). So two runs with the same \(\eta C\) and the same seed, in both of which every gradient is clipped, produce the same parameters.


Proof. 

Clipped gradients are scaled unit vectors. If \(\|g_i\| \ge C\), then \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|) = C/\|g_i\|\), so \(\bar g_i = Cg_i/\|g_i\|\).
Factor out \(C\). Every term of the noisy sum now carries the factor \(C\), so \(G_t = C\big(\sum_{i \in S_t}g_i/\|g_i\| + \sigma\zeta_t\big)\).
Substitute into the step. Step 5 of Definition 39.1 subtracts \(\eta G_t/B\), which gives Equation 39.7. The batch, the unit vectors and \(\zeta_t\) involve neither \(\eta\) nor \(C\), so the run depends on them only through \(\eta C\).


Below the gradient norms, DP-SGD is normalized SGD, which averages unit vectors, plus noise. Lowering \(C\) further changes nothing once \(\eta\) is scaled up to match. This is why practitioners often clip aggressively and tune only the learning rate, and it explains why De et al. (2022) find that small clipping norms work well. With the Adam optimizer, \(C\) drops out of the step length altogether, because Adam divides each coordinate of the update by its own running scale, which carries the same factor \(C\).
Above the gradient norms, noise grows and signal does not. Once \(C\) exceeds most gradient norms, the clipped average stops growing with \(C\), but the noise \(\sigma C/B\) keeps growing in proportion, so the signal-to-noise ratio falls like \(1/C\). So raising \(C\) beyond the point where it clips almost nothing only adds noise.

Example 39.2 Gradient norms change during training, so a fixed \(C\) visits both regimes. In the DP-SGD run of the running example the median per-example gradient norm is 3.592 at the first step and 0.006 at step 1,000, and it rounds to 0.000 from step 3,000 on. Non-private training behaves the same way (Figure 39.1, right). The logistic loss flattens on records classified with a wide margin, so their gradients vanish. With \(C = 0.5\), every gradient is clipped at the start, and later between 9% and 25% of the batch are, the few records still near the decision boundary. So a fixed \(C\) is in the scale-invariant regime early, and later above most gradient norms, where clipping changes little.
Table 39.3 trains the running example at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) with seven clipping norms, once with the learning rate fixed at 0.5 and once with \(\eta C\) fixed at \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\).

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.3 Batch size and the number of steps at a fixed budget
text:
39.3 Batch size and the number of steps at a fixed budget
Suppose the privacy budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and the compute budget, a number of epochs \(E\), are both fixed. Each epoch is \(1/q\) steps, so \(T = E/q\). Should you take many small steps or few large ones? The accountant says how much noise each choice needs, and the noise on the averaged gradient decides how useful each step is.
For small \(q\), the terms \(j = 0\) and \(j = 1\) of Equation 39.4 cost nothing. Their exponent \(j^2 - j\) is zero, and with every exponential set to 1 the sum is the binomial expansion of \(\big((1 - q) + q\big)^\alpha = 1\), whose logarithm is zero. Among the other terms the term \(j = 2\), which carries \(q^2\), dominates (Amplification by subsampling derives the approximation). That term is enough to see the trade.

Proposition 39.3 (Batch size at a fixed budget) Assume that the per-step RDP curve is approximately \[\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) \approx \frac\alpha2q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big), \tag{39.8}\] as it is for small \(q\) and orders that are not too large. Fix \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and the number of epochs \(E\), so that \(T = E/q\). Where \(\sigma\) is well above 1, keeping \(\varepsilon\) fixed as \(q\) changes requires \[\sigma \propto \sqrt q, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{qn}\,\sqrt n} = \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}, \tag{39.9}\] and the noise on the averaged gradient falls like \(1/\sqrt B\). Where \(\sigma\) is near or below 1, the per-step cost is larger by the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) > 1\), so small batches need more noise than Equation 39.9 says.


Proof. The plan is to approximate the per-step cost and add it over all the steps. The total gives the noise multiplier that keeps \(\varepsilon\) fixed, and the last step measures what the approximation leaves out.

Per-step cost. For \(\sigma\) well above 1, the exponent \(1/\sigma^2\) is small and \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\). So the per-step curve is about \(\frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\).
Total cost. Curves add under composition, so \(T = E/q\) steps have the curve \[\frac{E}{q}\cdot\frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\alpha Eq}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{39.10}\] The conversion Equation 39.5 depends on the run only through this curve, so \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(q/\sigma^2\) does, that is when \(\sigma \propto \sqrt q\).
Noise per averaged gradient. The noise on the averaged gradient is \(\sigma C/B\) with \(B = qn\). With \(\sigma \propto \sqrt q\) and \(n\) fixed it is proportional to \(\sqrt q/q = 1/\sqrt q\), and since \(q = B/n\) that is Equation 39.9.
Small \(\sigma\). The exponential grows faster than its tangent at 0, so \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) exceeds the approximation \(1/\sigma^2\) of step 1. The ratio of the two is the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), which is above 1 and grows as \(\sigma\) falls. By step 2, small batches need small \(\sigma\), so they are the ones that pay this factor, as extra noise beyond the \(\sqrt q\) law.


The accountant’s numbers, in Table 39.4 of the example below, show that amplification is most efficient at large \(\sigma\). The ratio \(\sigma/\sqrt q\), which Equation 39.9 says is constant, falls from 22.3 at \(B = 10\) to 10.8 at \(B = 10{,}000\). Over the same range the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) falls from 3.23 to 1, so the small batches pay most of the extra noise through it. The rest comes from the high orders that the conversion uses, where the approximation of Proposition 39.3 does not hold and sampling buys little (Amplification by subsampling).
Large batches help, but not for free. For a fixed number of epochs they give less noise per step and fewer steps, and fewer steps means less progress unless the learning rate grows in proportion. The best learning rate does grow with the batch: in Table 39.5, below, it goes from 0.25 at \(B = 30\) to between 1 and 2 at \(B = 100\) to \(B = 1{,}000\). De et al. (2022) and Anil et al. (2022) train with batches of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and report that large batches are a main ingredient of accurate private models. Large batches also parallelize well, which matters more on accelerators than in this small example.






Figure 39.2: DP-SGD at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), for 100 epochs on \(n = 10{,}000\) records, as a function of the expected batch size. Left: the noise multiplier the accountant requires, against the \(\sqrt B\) law of Equation 39.9 (\(\sigma \propto \sqrt q\) at fixed \(n\)). Right: the noise standard deviation on the averaged gradient, in units of \(C\), against the \(1/\sqrt B\) law. Small batches need more noise than the law predicts.

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.4 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
text:
39.4 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
Ordinary backpropagation computes the gradient of the sum of the batch’s losses, never the gradient of each record. Clipping needs each record’s gradient norm, and forming all \(B\) per-example gradients costs \(B\) times the memory of the model’s gradient, which for large models is prohibitive. Can the norms, and the clipped sum, be had more cheaply?
The tool is the shape of a dense layer’s gradient. Take a dense layer that maps an input \(a\) to \(Wa\), and write \(v\) for the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output, the back-propagated error. The gradient with respect to the weights \(W\) is then the outer product \(va^\top\) (Gradient inversion, Proposition 14.1). That chapter uses the outer product to reconstruct inputs from gradients, and here it makes per-example norms cheap.

Proposition 39.4 (Ghost norms) Consider a dense layer, and for record \(i\) write \(a_i\) for its input to the layer and \(v_i\) for its back-propagated error, so that the record’s gradient for the layer is \(v_ia_i^\top\). Then \[\big\|v_ia_i^\top\big\|_F = \|v_i\|\,\|a_i\|, \tag{39.11}\] where the Frobenius norm \(\|\cdot\|_F\) is the square root of the sum of squared entries. The whole network’s per-example gradient norm is the square root of the sum of these squared norms over the layers. Write \(c_i\) for the clipping factor of record \(i\), \[c_i = \min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big). \tag{39.12}\] Stack the errors as the rows of a matrix \(V\) and the inputs as the rows of a matrix \(A\). If \(c \circ V\) is \(V\) with row \(i\) multiplied by \(c_i\), the clipped sum for the layer is \(\sum_ic_iv_ia_i^\top = (c \circ V)^\top A\). Now let the layer act on a sequence of \(N\) tokens, with input \(a_{is}\) and error \(v_{is}\) at token \(s\). Record \(i\)’s gradient is then \(\sum_sv_{is}a_{is}^\top\), and \[\Big\|\sum_sv_{is}a_{is}^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \sum_{s, s'}(a_{is}\cdot a_{is'})(v_{is}\cdot v_{is'}). \tag{39.13}\]


Proof. The plan is to compute the norm of one outer product, add over layers, write the clipped sum as one matrix product, and expand the square for sequences.

One token. The entry \((j, k)\) of \(va^\top\) is \(v_ja_k\), so the squared Frobenius norm factors into two sums, \[\sum_{j,k}v_j^2a_k^2 = \Big(\sum_jv_j^2\Big)\Big(\sum_ka_k^2\Big) = \|v\|^2\|a\|^2. \tag{39.14}\]
Layers. The full gradient is the concatenation of the layers’ gradients, so its squared length is the sum of theirs.
The clipped sum. The sum \(\sum_ic_iv_ia_i^\top\) is linear in the errors, so it is the usual batch product of errors and inputs with each record’s error scaled by \(c_i\). One backward pass computes the errors, the norms come from Equation 39.11, and one more matrix product per layer gives the clipped sum.
Sequences. Drop the record index \(i\). The squared Frobenius norm of a matrix \(M\) is the trace of \(M^\top M\), so the square of a sum of outer products expands into one trace per pair of tokens, \[\Big\|\sum_sv_sa_s^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \sum_{s, s'}\operatorname{tr}\big(a_sv_s^\top v_{s'}a_{s'}^\top\big). \tag{39.15}\] Inside each trace, \(v_s^\top v_{s'}\) is the number \(v_s\cdot v_{s'}\), and what remains is \(\operatorname{tr}(a_sa_{s'}^\top) = a_s\cdot a_{s'}\). That gives Equation 39.13, the entrywise product of two \(N \times N\) Gram matrices, summed.


This is ghost clipping, in which the per-example gradients are “ghosts” that are never formed. Goodfellow (2015) gave the norms for single inputs, Lee & Kifer (2021) clipped with them, and Li et al. (2022) extended them to sequences. For one token per record, ghost clipping stores \(B(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) numbers per layer instead of \(Bd_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\), where \(d_{\text{in}}\) and \(d_{\text{out}}\) are the layer’s input and output widths. For sequences the Gram matrices cost \(2BN^2\), which beats the explicit gradients only when \(2N^2 < d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\). So long sequences in narrow layers favour forming the gradients, and Bu, Mao & Xu (2022) choose per layer. A convolutional layer’s per-example gradient is a sum of outer products over spatial positions, so Equation 39.13 applies with positions in place of tokens.
Either way, privacy is untouched. Ghost norms are exact computations of the same quantities, so the clipped sum, and with it Theorem 39.1, is unchanged.

Example 39.4 For the 256 records of a test batch of the running example, the norms from Equation 39.11 agree with explicitly formed per-example gradients to a relative difference of \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\), which is rounding error. For a random 16-token sequence, Equation 39.13 gives 33.144228, and the explicit gradient’s norm is the same. Table 39.6 compares the memory for several layers.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.5 Microbatches and vectorized per-example gradients
Deep-learning frameworks are built to compute the gradient of a batch’s summed loss in one parallel pass, and per-example clipping breaks that pattern. Computed naively, one record at a time, DP-SGD can run tens or hundreds of times slower than ordinary training. Ghost norms (Section 39.4) are one remedy, and two others are common. Vectorization computes the per-example gradients in parallel after all, while microbatching clips groups of records instead of single records. Vectorization changes nothing about privacy or accuracy, so the question is what microbatching costs.

Definition 39.2 (Microbatched DP-SGD) Choose a group size \(m\), and fix in advance a rule that assigns every record to one of \(B/m\) groups, for example a hash of a record identifier. A Poisson batch of expected size \(B\) then splits into about \(B/m\) microbatches of about \(m\) records each. Microbatched DP-SGD runs Definition 39.1, but clips the mean gradient of each microbatch instead of each record’s gradient. It adds Gaussian noise to the sum of the clipped means and divides the result by \(B/m\).

Under per-example clipping, the added record’s term goes from absent to present, a change of at most \(C\). A microbatch’s clipped mean instead goes from one vector of length at most \(C\) to another, and that change can be twice as long.

Proposition 39.5 (What microbatches cost) Under add/remove neighbours, the sum of clipped microbatch means has sensitivity \(2C\) as soon as a record can share its group with others. So the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) for the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) holds only with noise of standard deviation \(2\sigma C\). The update’s noise then has standard deviation \[\frac{2\sigma C}{B/m} = 2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B} \tag{39.16}\] per coordinate, \(2m\) times that of per-example clipping.


Proof. The plan is to locate the one microbatch a record can change, bound how far its clipped mean moves, and then scale the noise to match the accountant.

One record touches one microbatch. The assignment of records to groups is fixed before training and does not depend on which other records are present. A position in the dataset would not do, because adding a record shifts the positions of the records after it. So adding or removing \(z\) changes only the microbatch of \(z\)’s group, and every other clipped mean is the same on both datasets.
That clipped mean moves by up to \(2C\). If the group has other sampled records, its clipped mean changes from one vector of length at most \(C\) to another. The two can point in opposite directions, so they differ by up to \(2C\). Only when \(z\) is alone in its group does the change shrink to \(C\), the per-example case, and a worst-case bound must take \(2C\).
The accountant. Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 39.1 needs the noise to be \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, so the noise must be \(\sigma \cdot 2C\). The rest of that proof is unchanged.
Per coordinate. The update divides the noisy sum by the public number \(B/m\), and dividing \(2\sigma C\) by it gives Equation 39.16.


Microbatching trades accuracy for speed at a steep rate. A batch now has only \(B/m\) clipped terms to carry signal instead of \(B\), while the total noise has doubled to \(2\sigma C\). A microbatch’s mean gradient is also shorter than its records’ gradients when they disagree, so clipping removes less of it, but that does not make up for a factor \(2m\) in the noise. Some libraries offer microbatches as a speed option, so check what yours assumes. Whether its accounting uses sensitivity \(C\) or \(2C\), and whether its microbatches are fixed in advance or cut by position from the sampled batch, decides whether the reported \(\varepsilon\) is valid. Cut by position, adding one record shifts every later record into a different microbatch, and step 1 fails.
Vectorization costs nothing, because it keeps per-example clipping. JAX’s vmap computes the per-example gradients in parallel by vectorizing over the examples of a batch, and Opacus by attaching hooks that record the per-example quantities during backpropagation. These are exact computations of the same per-example gradients, so they change neither the privacy nor the accuracy. Subramani, Vadivelu & Kamath (2021) show that vectorization combined with just-in-time compilation in many cases brings DP-SGD’s running time close to that of ordinary training.

Example 39.5 At the running example’s \(\sigma = 1\), \(C = 0.5\) and \(B = 100\), the noise on the averaged update is 0.0050 per coordinate with per-example clipping. With microbatches of \(m = 4\) records it is 0.0400, eight times more, and with \(m = 16\) it is 0.1600, thirty-two times more, at the same \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). The test accuracy falls with it, from 0.9589 for per-example clipping (Example 39.1) to 0.9336 with microbatches of 4 and 0.7459 with microbatches of 16, one run each.

39.6 The running example: privacy against accuracy
The earlier sections each changed one knob. This one puts the pieces together and asks, for the running example, how much accuracy each budget costs and where the loss comes from.

Example 39.6 Table 39.7 trains the running example with \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, at each budget’s noise multiplier from Table 39.2, three times each. Each run starts from a fresh random initialization. The non-private baseline uses the same sampling and learning rate with neither clipping nor noise. In a single run its accuracy is already at its best after 1,000 steps, at 0.9627, and stays there, at 0.9617 after 10,000 steps. Part 4 asked how private the running configuration is, and answered \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). This example adds the other half: on this task it costs 0.4 points of accuracy, 0.9589 against 0.9627 in the single runs of Example 39.1. Halving \(\varepsilon\) to about 3 needs \(\sigma\) between 1.36 and 2.28, and by the table costs about one more point of accuracy, while reaching \(\varepsilon = 1\) costs four points. Choosing ε asks which of these trades is worth making, and Auditing checks whether the trained model is as private as the accountant says.

Clipping costs nothing here, and noise costs everything. Clipping without noise reaches 0.9649, slightly above non-private SGD, because on this problem clipping only limits the influence of the few records with large gradients. The whole loss comes from the noise, and it is steeply non-linear in \(\varepsilon\). From \(\varepsilon = 8\) to 4 the accuracy drops by half a point, from 2 to 1 by 2.7 points, and from 1 to 0.5 by almost 10. The signal-against-noise argument of Example 39.1 explains the collapse. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise multiplier is 4.13, so the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \(4.13 \times 0.5/100 \times \sqrt{3{,}329} = 1.19\), against a signal of about 0.026 if the signal stays near its length at \(\sigma = 1\). Signal then overtakes noise only after about \((1.19/0.026)^2 \approx 2{,}100\) steps, so the 10,000 steps contain only a few independent useful moves. Figure 39.4 shows the result: with \(\sigma = 4\) the model reaches its accuracy early and then wanders.
Run-to-run variation grows with the noise. The standard deviation over runs is 0.0019 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and 0.018 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). A single private run is a sample from a wide distribution, so comparing two configurations by one run each, as Table 39.3 does, is reliable only for differences well above that spread.
Architecture choices change under privacy. The running example uses tanh units deliberately, because Papernot, Thakurta, Song, Chien & Erlingsson (2021) find that bounded activations such as tanh train better than ReLU under DP-SGD. With the same guarantee, \((2.93, 10^{-5})\) on the handwritten digits of MNIST, their tanh network reaches 98.1% test accuracy against 96.6% for ReLU. On the CIFAR-10 images at \((7.53, 10^{-5})\) it reaches 66.2% against 61.6%. Model size changes too. The noise vector has length about \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\), which grows with the number of parameters, while the clipped signal cannot exceed \(C\). So the best private model is often smaller than the best non-private one, unless pretraining on public data has already done most of the work (Public data and private fine-tuning). Larger models can still win when the batch size and the clipping norm are tuned with them. De, Berrada, Hayes, Smith & Balle (2022) train a 40-layer wide residual network from scratch on CIFAR-10 to 81.4% test accuracy at \((8, 10^{-5})\). Very large batches and small clipping norms are among their practices. These numbers come from the papers, not from this chapter’s script.






Figure 39.3: Test accuracy of DP-SGD on the running example at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) against \(\varepsilon\) (log scale), with the non-private model dashed. Accuracy is close to non-private above \(\varepsilon = 4\) and falls steeply below \(\varepsilon = 1\).









Figure 39.4: Left: test accuracy during training with clipping alone, with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 6.71\)) and with \(\sigma = 4\). Right: the length of the averaged clipped gradient at each step (solid, log scale) against the length of the noise on it (dotted). The noise is about ten times longer than the signal at \(\sigma = 1\), and about forty times at \(\sigma = 4\).

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.1 The cost of releasing the best run
The previous chapter proved a guarantee for one training run. The algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise. Run once with a fixed learning rate, clipping norm, batch size and number of steps, it satisfies differential privacy (DP) with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) reported by its accountant, the routine that adds up the privacy cost of the steps, and it is called DP-SGD. But in practice nobody trains once. A practitioner tries a grid of learning rates, scores each trained model on a validation set, and ships the best one. The validation set and the training set are private data, and every run touched them. So this chapter asks how much the search leaks, and how to pay for it honestly.
The answer turns on one idea. The model you ship was chosen by comparing all the runs, so it is a function of all of them, and with a fixed number of runs it can cost as much as all of them together. If instead the number of runs is random, drawn before the search starts, then the event “every run came out badly” is mostly explained by “there were few runs” rather than by the data. The cost then falls to a constant multiple of one run, plus a term that grows only with the logarithm of the expected number of runs.
The running example is that of DP-SGD: a network with 3,329 parameters trained on \(n = 10{,}000\) records, with a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01, a clipping norm \(C\) of 0.5, a noise multiplier \(\sigma\) of 1 and 10,000 steps. One run costs \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Charging for every run in Rényi differential privacy (RDP) turns a grid of 10 runs into \(\varepsilon = 27.23\), less than ten times 6.71 because the conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pays its \(\delta\) term once. A random number of runs with mean 10 costs between 10.08 and 13.67, depending on its distribution (Section 40.4).
A choice among eight learning rates carries at most three bits, which seems harmless. But the released model is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out, and the comparison depends on every run. This section measures how much that can cost, because the rest of the chapter is about avoiding it.
Call one run a randomized algorithm \(Q\) that trains a model on the private data with hyperparameters taken from a fixed set of candidates, and outputs the model with its score, such as a validation accuracy. Outputs are ordered by score, and \(Q(D)\) also denotes the distribution of one run’s output on the dataset \(D\).
The best-of-\(K\) algorithm \(M\) draws a number of runs \(K\), independently of the data, runs \(Q\) independently \(K\) times, and releases the best output. Each run draws its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, as random search does. Neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) differ by adding or removing one record. Every result of this chapter needs the distribution of the best of \(K\) draws, which the next lemma gives.
A die shows the lemma at work. The best of two rolls is a 6 with probability \(1 - (5/6)^2 = 0.3056\). If you roll once or twice with probability \(\frac12\) each, then \(f(x) = \frac12x + \frac12x^2\), and the best is a 6 with probability \(f(1) - f(5/6) = 0.2361\), the average of the one-roll and two-roll answers.
The simplest run that shows the cost has two outcomes, as in randomized response (Definition 18.4). With “bad” the worse outcome, Lemma 40.1 says that the best of \(k\) is bad only when all \(k\) runs are bad, so the likelihood ratios of the \(k\) independent runs multiply.
The proposition below also bounds the cost in Rényi terms, to show that large orders see it too. For distributions \(P\) and \(P'\) on a finite set, the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) is \[D_\alpha(P\|P') = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_y P(y)^\alpha P'(y)^{1 - \alpha}, \tag{40.4}\] and an RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds it between outputs on neighbours (Rényi differential privacy, Definition 29.1).
The whole loss sits on one event, that every run failed, whose ratio is the product of \(k\) per-run ratios. Figure 40.1 (right) shows the privacy loss, the log ratio of an output’s probabilities on \(D\) and \(D'\), for \(\varepsilon = 1\). One run has losses \(\pm1\), while the best of 10 has a loss of 10 with probability 0.0436. A DP-SGD run that sometimes diverges is such a run, with a “bad” outcome whose probability depends a little on the data.
The bound for a fixed \(k\) is therefore tight. Composition says that the best of \(k\) costs at most \(k\varepsilon\) (Section 40.2), and Proposition 40.1 exhibits a run that attains it. No analysis that knows only each run’s guarantee can promise less, so a better guarantee needs a different procedure. The next sections change one thing about it: the number of runs.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
Lemma 40.1 (The best of a random number of draws) Let one draw have a distribution \(Q\) on outcomes ordered from best to worst. Write \(Q(\preceq y)\) for the probability that a draw is no better than \(y\), and \(Q(\prec y)\) for the probability that it is strictly worse. Let the number of draws \(K\) be random and independent of the draws, with generating function \[f(x) = \mathbb E[x^K] = \sum_k \Pr[K = k]\,x^k. \tag{40.1}\] If \(K = 0\), the release is a fixed output that does not depend on the data. Then for every other outcome \(y\), the best of the \(K\) draws is \(y\) with probability \[\Pr[M = y] = f\big(Q(\preceq y)\big) - f\big(Q(\prec y)\big). \tag{40.2}\] A fixed \(K = k\) has \(f(x) = x^k\), and a Poisson number of draws with mean \(\mathbb E[K]\) has \(f(x) = e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\). A geometric number on \(\{1, 2, \dots\}\), with \(\Pr[K = k] = \omega(1 - \omega)^{k - 1}\) for a stopping probability \(\omega \in (0, 1)\), has \(f(x) = \omega x/(1 - (1 - \omega)x)\).


Proof. The plan is to count outcomes for a fixed number of draws, then average over \(K\), then sum the three series.

A fixed number \(k\) of draws. The best of \(k\) independent draws is no better than \(y\) exactly when every draw is, which has probability \(Q(\preceq y)^k\).
The best is exactly \(y\). That happens when every draw is no better than \(y\) but not every draw is strictly worse. The second event is contained in the first, so subtracting its probability gives \[\Pr[\text{best of } k = y] = Q(\preceq y)^k - Q(\prec y)^k. \tag{40.3}\]
Average over \(K\). The number of draws is independent of the draws, so averaging step 2 over \(K\) replaces each power \(x^k\) by its average \(\sum_k \Pr[K = k]\,x^k = f(x)\). The term for \(K = 0\) is the same constant in both generating functions and cancels.
The three generating functions. A fixed \(k\) gives one term, the Poisson weights sum by the exponential series, and the geometric weights by the geometric series.






Proposition 40.1 (The best of k randomized responses) Let one run be randomized response with two outcomes, “good” and “bad”, with good the better. On \(D\) the run comes out good with probability \(\frac{1}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\), and on its neighbour \(D'\) with probability \(\frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\), so one run is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Releasing the best of \(k\) runs is exactly \(k\varepsilon\)-DP, because \[\frac{\Pr_D[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]}{\Pr_{D'}[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]} = \frac{\big(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\big)^k}{\big(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\big)^k} = e^{k\varepsilon}. \tag{40.5}\] At every order \(\alpha > 1\) the release also has (Papernot & Steinke 2022, Proposition 17) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big) \ge k\varepsilon - \frac{k\ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{40.6}\]


Proof. We compute the probability of “bad” on each dataset, compare the other outcome, and then keep only the bad term of the Rényi sum.

Bad needs every run bad. No outcome is worse than “bad”, so Lemma 40.1 with \(f(x) = x^k\) gives \(\Pr[\text{best is bad}] = Q(\text{bad})^k\) on each dataset.
The ratio for bad. One run is bad with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) on \(D\) and \(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) on \(D'\). Raising both to the power \(k\) gives Equation 40.5.
The ratio for good. The good outcome has the ratio \((1 - Q_D(\text{bad})^k)/(1 - Q_{D'}(\text{bad})^k)\), which lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and 1. The two datasets play symmetric roles, so the largest log ratio over outcomes and over both orders of the pair is \(k\varepsilon\).
The Rényi version. Every term of the Rényi sum is positive, so the sum is at least its bad term. With the probabilities of step 2, \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha} \ge \Pr_D[\text{bad}]^\alpha\,\Pr_{D'}[\text{bad}]^{1 - \alpha} = e^{k\varepsilon\alpha}(1 + e^\varepsilon)^{-k}. \tag{40.7}\] Taking logarithms, dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) and writing \(\ln(1 + e^\varepsilon) = \varepsilon + \ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})\) gives the bound.










Figure 40.1: Left: the exact \(\varepsilon\) of releasing the best of \(K\) randomized-response runs, each \(1\)-DP, against the expected number of runs, for a fixed number of runs, a Poisson, a geometric and a logarithmic number. A fixed number grows linearly; the geometric and logarithmic numbers stay below their bounds \(3\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon\). Right: the privacy loss of the released outcome under \(D\) for one run, the best of 10 runs and the best of a Poisson number with mean 10; the best of 10 puts a loss of 10 on an event of probability 0.0436.




Example 40.1 With \(\varepsilon = 1\), a run is good with probability 0.2689 on \(D\) and 0.7311 on \(D'\). The largest log ratio is 2.0000 for \(k = 2\), 3.0000 for \(k = 3\) and 10.0000 for \(k = 10\), exactly \(k\varepsilon\). At order \(\alpha = 2\), the Rényi divergence of the best of 10 is 6.8683. That lies between the lower bound of Proposition 40.1, 6.8674, and the composition bound, ten times one run’s 0.7353, which is 7.3533. Composition overstates the exact value by only 7%, so the best of 10 costs almost as much as all 10 runs.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.2 Paying by composition
The safe answer is to charge for every run. This section says what that costs, because it is the baseline every cleverer method must beat. The best output is computed from the \(k\) outputs alone, so it leaks no more than all of them, and they together cost the sum of their RDP curves.

Proposition 40.2 (Composition of k runs) Let each of \(k\) runs have RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and let the runs use independent randomness. Then releasing anything computed from the \(k\) outputs alone, in particular the best, has RDP curve \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le k\,\varepsilon(\alpha), \tag{40.8}\] even if each candidate is chosen after seeing the earlier results. For DP-SGD, \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps at noise multiplier \(\sigma\) have the curve of one run of \(kT\) steps.


Proof. 

The runs compose. The curves of adaptively chosen mechanisms add (Theorem 29.2), so the \(k\) outputs together have curve \(k\varepsilon(\alpha)\).
The release is post-processing. The best output is computed from the \(k\) outputs without reading the data, so its curve is no larger than theirs (Theorem 29.3).
DP-SGD. Write \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) for the curve of one subsampled Gaussian step. One run of \(T\) steps then has curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), so \(k\) runs have \(kT\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), the curve of one run of \(kT\) steps.


Every \(\varepsilon\) in this chapter comes from a curve by the conversion of From RDP to (ε, δ) (Theorem 30.1), minimized over the order. In \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) terms, \(k\) runs cost less than \(k\) times one run’s \(\varepsilon\), because the conversion pays its \(\ln(1/\delta)\) term once. So 10 runs of the running example cost 4.06 times one run, not 10. But the curve grows linearly, and so does \(\varepsilon\) once the budget is large: from 30 to 100 runs, \(\varepsilon\) grows by a factor of 2.5.
Raising the noise keeps the budget: at a total of \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), each of 10 runs needs \(\sigma = 2.45\) instead of 1, which costs accuracy (DP-SGD). For two or three candidates, composition costs little more than the alternatives below. Figure 40.2 shows that the methods with a random number of runs pull away from composition only from a few runs on.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.3 Random stopping
Liu & Talwar (2019) asked whether the best of many \(\varepsilon\)-DP runs can cost a constant multiple of \(\varepsilon\), whatever the number of runs. They found that it can, with one change to the procedure: the number of runs becomes random. This section proves their result for pure DP runs, where the mechanism behind the Rényi versions of Section 40.4 is easiest to see.

Definition 40.1 (Random stopping) Fix a stopping probability \(\omega \in (0, 1)\). Repeat the following: run \(Q\) on the data and keep its output, then, with probability \(\omega\), stop and release the best output kept so far. The number of runs \(K\) is then geometric, with \(\Pr[K = j] = \omega(1 - \omega)^{j - 1}\) for \(j \ge 1\) and mean \(1/\omega\).

The probability of each output turns out to be a ratio built from three probabilities of one run. Each moves by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours, and the stopping probability cannot amplify those moves.

Theorem 40.1 (Random stopping is 3ε-DP (Liu & Talwar 2019, Theorem 3.2)) Let \(Q\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and let \(M\) be random stopping with probability \(\omega\). For an outcome \(y\), write \(p\) for the probability that one run outputs \(y\), \(p_>\) for the probability that one run is strictly better than \(y\), and \(p_\ge = p_> + p\). Then \[\Pr[M = y] = \frac{\omega\,p}{\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\big)\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge\big)}, \tag{40.9}\] and \(M\) is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP for every \(\omega\). For every fraction \(\pi \in (0, 1]\), the release falls below the top \(\pi\)-quantile of one run’s score with probability \[\Pr[\text{miss}] = \frac{\omega(1 - \pi)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)\pi} \le \frac{\omega}{\pi}. \tag{40.10}\]


Proof. The plan is to apply Lemma 40.1 with the geometric generating function, simplify the result to Equation 40.9, bound each of its three factors between neighbours, and finally sum a geometric series for the utility.

Apply the lemma. One run is no better than \(y\) with probability \(1 - p_>\) and strictly worse with probability \(1 - p_\ge\). With \(f(x) = \omega x/(1 - (1 - \omega)x)\), and since \(1 - (1 - \omega)(1 - p_>) = \omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\), Equation 40.2 gives \[\Pr[M = y] = \frac{\omega(1 - p_>)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>} - \frac{\omega(1 - p_\ge)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge}. \tag{40.11}\]
Simplify. Over the common denominator, the numerator is \(\omega\) times \((1 - p_>)(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge) - (1 - p_\ge)(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>)\). The terms with \(\omega\) give \(\omega(p_\ge - p_>) = \omega p\), and the terms with \(1 - \omega\) give \((1 - \omega)(p_\ge - p_>) = (1 - \omega)p\). Their sum is \(p\), which gives Equation 40.9.
Bound each factor. Write primes for the same quantities on \(D'\). Each of \(p\), \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge\) is the probability of an event about one run’s output, so \(\varepsilon\)-DP gives \(p \le e^\varepsilon p'\), \(p'_> \le e^\varepsilon p_>\) and \(p'_\ge \le e^\varepsilon p_\ge\). The constant \(\omega\) does not depend on the data, so \(\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_> \le e^\varepsilon\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\big)\), and the same holds with \(p_\ge\).
Multiply. The ratio of output probabilities is the product of the numerator ratio and the two inverted denominator ratios, each at most \(e^\varepsilon\) by step 3: \[\frac{\Pr[M(D) = y]}{\Pr[M(D') = y]} = \frac{p}{p'}\cdot\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_>}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>}\cdot\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_\ge}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge} \le e^{3\varepsilon}. \tag{40.12}\] The same argument with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped bounds the inverse ratio, and this holds for every outcome, so the release is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP.
Utility. The release is below the top \(\pi\)-quantile only if every run is. Summing over the number of runs with the geometric series gives \[\Pr[\text{miss}] = \sum_{j \ge 1}\omega(1 - \omega)^{j - 1}(1 - \pi)^j = \frac{\omega(1 - \pi)}{1 - (1 - \omega)(1 - \pi)}, \tag{40.13}\] and the denominator equals \(\omega + (1 - \omega)\pi\).
The simple bound. The miss probability is at most \(\omega/\pi\) exactly when \(\pi(1 - \pi) \le \omega(1 - \pi) + \pi\), which holds because \(\pi(1 - \pi) \le \pi\).


This is why the disaster of a fixed \(k\) disappears. With \(f(x) = x^k\) the ratio for the worst outcome is a \(k\)-th power, while here it is a product of three bounded ratios. The event “every run was bad” is now mostly the event “the coin stopped early”, which does not depend on the data. The factor 3 is attained in the limit, by an outcome with something above it and something below it (Example 40.3). On randomized response the good outcome has nothing above it, so one factor cannot move and the cost tends to \(2\varepsilon\).
The utility guarantee is about quantiles, and it costs runs. Equation 40.10 does not promise the best candidate, only a release in the top \(\pi\) fraction of one run’s outcomes with probability at least \(1 - \omega/\pi\). To land in the top \(1/m\) of a grid of \(m\) with probability 0.9, set \(\pi = 1/m\) and \(\omega/\pi = 0.1\), which gives \(\omega = 0.1/m\), a mean of \(10m\) runs.

Example 40.3 On randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\), geometric stopping has an exact \(\varepsilon\) of 1.3106 at \(\omega = 0.5\), 1.7957 at \(\omega = 0.1\), 1.9769 at \(\omega = 0.01\) and 1.9977 at \(\omega = 0.001\), approaching 2. To reach 3, take three outcomes, best first, with probabilities \((a, b, 1 - a - b)\) on \(D\) and \((ae^\varepsilon, be^{-\varepsilon}, \dots)\) on \(D'\), and let \(\omega \ll b \ll a\) be small. For the middle outcome, the numerator ratio of Equation 40.9 is \(e^\varepsilon\). Since \(\omega\) is negligible next to \(p_>\), and \(p_\ge\) is close to \(p_>\), both denominator ratios approach \(e^\varepsilon\) too. Table 40.2 shows the exact \(\varepsilon\) approaching 3, and that of the logarithmic number of runs of Section 40.4 approaching 2.
