title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.4 Rényi bounds for a random number of runs
text:
40.4 Rényi bounds for a random number of runs
DP-SGD is not usefully \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any small \(\varepsilon\), because its guarantee is an RDP curve that converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Papernot & Steinke (2022) extended random stopping to RDP and to a family of distributions for the number of runs, which lets you trade more runs against a lower privacy cost. This section proves their generic bound and its Poisson case, and states a third case. (They write \(\lambda\) for the order, \(\mu\) for the Poisson mean and \(\gamma\) for the stopping probability.)
The generic bound separates one run’s divergence from a factor that depends only on the derivative \(f'\) of the generating function at two points. Those points are acceptance probabilities of a test that reads only a run’s output, which is what makes the bound useful: any privacy guarantee of the run keeps them close.

Theorem 40.2 (The generic bound (Papernot & Steinke 2022, Lemma 7)) Let \(K\) have generating function \(f\) and be independent of the runs, and let \(M\) release the best of \(K\) independent runs of \(Q\). For a pair of neighbours, write \(Q, Q'\) for the two run distributions, and \(M, M'\) also for the two best-of distributions. Then for every order \(\alpha > 1\) there are numbers \(s, s' \in [0, 1]\) such that \[D_\alpha(M\|M') \le D_\alpha(Q\|Q') + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}\Big], \tag{40.14}\] where \(s\) and \(s'\) are the probabilities that one and the same randomized test (step 5 of the proof) accepts a run’s output, on \(D\) and on \(D'\).


Proof. Take the outputs finite and \(\Pr[K = 0] = 0\) to keep the steps short; the paper handles the general case, including the Poisson distribution, for which \(K\) can be 0. We write each best-of probability as one run’s probability times an average of \(f'\), put that into the Rényi sum, bound the averages by their worst case, and recognize the worst case as a test.

The best-of probability is an average of \(f'\). By Equation 40.2 and the fundamental theorem of calculus, \[M(y) = f\big(Q(\preceq y)\big) - f\big(Q(\prec y)\big) = \int_{Q(\prec y)}^{Q(\preceq y)}f'(x)\,\mathrm dx. \tag{40.15}\] The interval has length \(Q(y)\), so \(M(y) = Q(y)\,c(y)\), where \(c(y)\) is the average of \(f'\) over that interval, the expectation of \(f'(X)\) for \(X\) uniform on it. Likewise \(M'(y) = Q'(y)\,c'(y)\).
Put it in the Rényi sum. Substituting step 1 into the definition of the divergence gives \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(M\|M')} = \sum_yM(y)^\alpha M'(y)^{1 - \alpha} = \sum_yQ(y)^\alpha Q'(y)^{1 - \alpha}\,c(y)^\alpha c'(y)^{1 - \alpha}. \tag{40.16}\]
Bound the averages by a worst case. Couple \(X\) and \(X'\) at the same relative position \(t \in [0, 1]\) in their two intervals. The function \((u, v) \mapsto u^\alpha v^{1 - \alpha}\) is jointly convex for \(\alpha > 1\), so by Jensen’s inequality \(c(y)^\alpha c'(y)^{1 - \alpha}\) is at most the average of \(f'(X)^\alpha f'(X')^{1 - \alpha}\). That average is at most the largest value of \(f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}\) over \(t\), with \(s = Q(\prec y) + tQ(y)\) and \(s' = Q'(\prec y) + tQ'(y)\).
Pull the worst case out of the sum. Bounding every factor \(c^\alpha c'^{1 - \alpha}\) by the largest one over \(y\) and \(t\) leaves \(\sum_yQ(y)^\alpha Q'(y)^{1 - \alpha} = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(Q\|Q')}\) times that maximum. Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation 40.14.
The pair comes from one test. The test “accept an output worse than \(y\), accept \(y\) itself with probability \(t\), reject anything better” accepts with probability \(s\) under \(Q\) and \(s'\) under \(Q'\). The test reads only the run’s output, so any privacy guarantee of \(Q\) constrains the pair \((s, s')\), by post-processing (Theorem 19.1, Theorem 29.3).


The first term is one run’s divergence. The second is what the distribution of \(K\) adds, and each bound below comes from choosing \(f\) and bounding it.
For a Poisson number of runs, \(f'\) is an exponential, so the second term is linear in \(s\) and \(s'\). An \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP guarantee of the run, applied to the event that the test rejects, then bounds it.

Theorem 40.3 (A Poisson number of runs (Papernot & Steinke 2022, Theorem 6)) Let \(K\) be Poisson with mean \(\mathbb E[K]\). Let \(Q\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP, and also \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP for some \(\hat\varepsilon\) with \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\). Then \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) + \mathbb E[K]\hat\delta + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{40.17}\]


Proof. 

Compute \(f'\). With \(f(x) = e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\), the derivative is \(f'(x) = \mathbb E[K]e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\). Taking the logarithm of the second term of Equation 40.14 and regrouping the exponents gives \[\ln\Big[f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}\Big] = \ln\mathbb E[K] + \mathbb E[K]\big[(\alpha - 1)(1 - s') - \alpha(1 - s)\big]. \tag{40.18}\]
Use the DP guarantee on the rejection event. The numbers \(1 - s'\) and \(1 - s\) are the probabilities that the test of Theorem 40.2 rejects, on \(D'\) and on \(D\). The run is \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP, so \(1 - s' \le e^{\hat\varepsilon}(1 - s) + \hat\delta\), and the bracket is at most \[(1 - s)\big[(\alpha - 1)e^{\hat\varepsilon} - \alpha\big] + (\alpha - 1)\hat\delta. \tag{40.19}\]
The condition removes the first term. The condition \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\) is the same as \((\alpha - 1)e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le \alpha\), so the first term is not positive and the bracket is at most \((\alpha - 1)\hat\delta\). Dividing by \(\alpha - 1\), and adding \(D_\alpha(Q\|Q') \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) in Equation 40.14, gives Equation 40.17.


The Poisson bound pays \(\mathbb E[K]\hat\delta\) for the chance of many runs. That is linear in the expected number of runs, but multiplied by the run’s \(\hat\delta\) at a small \(\hat\varepsilon\), so it is small only when one run is very private. On randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and mean 10, the run has \(\hat\delta = 0\) at \(\hat\varepsilon = 0.5\), so Equation 40.17 applies at the order where \(e^{0.5} = 1 + 1/(\alpha - 1)\), which is \(\alpha = 2.5415\). There the exact divergence is 0.4421, the bound 1.7654 and composition of 10 runs 2.7165.
A bound that stays a constant multiple of one run, whatever the run’s \(\hat\delta\), needs another distribution for \(K\), from a family that contains the geometric distribution.

Definition 40.2 (Truncated negative binomial number of runs) For a shape \(\nu > -1\) and \(\omega \in (0, 1)\), the truncated negative binomial distribution on \(\{1, 2, \dots\}\) has \[\Pr[K = k] = \frac{(1 - \omega)^k}{\omega^{-\nu} - 1}\prod_{i = 0}^{k - 1}\frac{i + \nu}{i + 1}, \qquad \mathbb E[K] = \frac{\nu(1 - \omega)}{\omega(1 - \omega^\nu)}. \tag{40.20}\] The shape \(\nu\) sets how skewed \(K\) is: the smaller \(\nu\), the more often \(K = 1\). The case \(\nu = 1\) is the geometric distribution. The limit \(\nu = 0\) is the logarithmic distribution, with \(\Pr[K = k] = \frac{(1 - \omega)^k}{k\ln(1/\omega)}\) and mean \(\frac{1/\omega - 1}{\ln(1/\omega)}\).

The theorem for this family uses the run’s RDP guarantee at a second order \(\hat\alpha\), chosen freely, to keep the rejection probabilities close.

Theorem 40.4 (A truncated negative binomial number of runs (Papernot & Steinke 2022, Theorem 2)) Let \(K\) follow the distribution of Definition 40.2, and let \(Q\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP and \((\hat\alpha, \varepsilon(\hat\alpha))\)-RDP for a second order \(\hat\alpha \ge 1\). Then \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) + (1 + \nu)\Big(1 - \frac1{\hat\alpha}\Big)\varepsilon(\hat\alpha) + \frac{(1 + \nu)\ln(1/\omega)}{\hat\alpha} + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{40.21}\] If \(Q\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, letting both orders grow gives \((2 + \nu)\varepsilon\)-DP (their Corollary 3). That is \(3\varepsilon\) for the geometric distribution, as in Theorem 40.1, and \(2\varepsilon\) for the logarithmic.


The proof follows that of Theorem 40.3, now with \(f'(x) = \omega^{\nu + 1}\mathbb E[K]\,(1 - (1 - \omega)x)^{-\nu - 1}\). Step 2 now bounds the rejection probabilities through the run’s RDP guarantee at the order \(\hat\alpha\). Papernot & Steinke (2022, Appendix B.2) carry out the algebra, and Appendix Section M.3 does it step by step, with their Corollaries 3 and 4.
Each term of Equation 40.21 pays for something. The first is one run. The last is the price of the number of runs, and it is logarithmic, so ten times more runs in expectation adds only \(\ln 10/(\alpha - 1)\). The middle terms pay for how far the distribution of \(K\) lets an adversary tell “many runs, all bad” from “few runs”, and they are a constant times the run’s own privacy at another order. For a run with a linear RDP curve, \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), Papernot & Steinke’s Corollary 4 turns the bound into a closed form whose overhead grows like \(\sqrt{\ln\mathbb E[K]}\).
The bounds hold for every run with the given curve, so they can be loose for one run. On randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and a logarithmic number of runs with mean 10, Table 40.3 compares the exact Rényi divergence of the release with Equation 40.21 and with composition of 10 runs. Randomized response is pure DP, so the bound keeps falling as \(\hat\alpha\) grows, and the table gives its limit, in which the two middle terms become \((1 + \nu)\varepsilon = 0.5\). At order 2, Equation 40.21 is worse than composition, because its constant terms dominate at small orders. At orders 5 and 20 it is 2.6 and 4.3 times below composition, and 3.7 and 1.7 times above the exact value.

section: 40.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
40.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
The methods so far treat each run as a black box that outputs a model and its score. Often, though, the candidates are already fixed, such as public pretrained checkpoints, and only the choice among them uses private data, a held-out validation set. That is a selection problem, which Selection solved. This section says how those tools apply to tuning, and what they leave out: the cost of training the candidates, and the protection of the validation set.
Let the score of candidate \(r\) be its number of correct predictions \(u(r)\) on a private validation set of \(m\) records. Adding or removing one validation record adds or removes one prediction, which is right or wrong, so every count moves by at most \(\Delta u = 1\). The exponential mechanism picks \(r\) from the candidate set \(\mathcal R\) with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon u(r)/(2\Delta u)}\). It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP in the validation records (Theorem 22.1). Its expected gap to the best count is at most \(\frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1)\) (Theorem 22.2), an accuracy gap of \(\frac{2}{\varepsilon m}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1)\).
When the candidates were themselves trained on private data, the cost has two parts, which fall on different records.

Proposition 40.3 (Trained candidates and a disjoint validation set) Let \(k\) candidates be trained on a private training set by runs with RDP curves \(\varepsilon_1(\alpha), \dots, \varepsilon_k(\alpha)\). Let a selection mechanism choose among them on a private validation set disjoint from the training set, with RDP curve \(\varepsilon_{\text{sel}}(\alpha)\) in the validation records for every fixed set of candidates. Then releasing the selected model costs \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \max\Big(\sum_{j = 1}^k\varepsilon_j(\alpha),\ \varepsilon_{\text{sel}}(\alpha)\Big). \tag{40.22}\]


Proof. 

A training record. If the neighbours differ in a training record, the validation set and the selection’s noise are the same on both and do not depend on it. The release is then a post-processing (Theorem 29.3) of the \(k\) trained models, which compose (Theorem 29.2) to \(\sum_j\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\).
A validation record. If the neighbours differ in a validation record, the trained models have the same distribution on both. Given the models, the release is the selection applied to fixed candidates, with curve at most \(\varepsilon_{\text{sel}}(\alpha)\), and mixing both sides over the same distribution of models keeps the divergence below that worst case.
Combine. Neighbours differ in one record, which lies in one of the two sets, so the larger bound covers every pair, as in parallel composition (Theorem 19.4).


Selection is cheap, and training is not. The expensive part is that each candidate was trained on private data, which Equation 40.22 still charges by composition. If the candidates do not depend on private data, as with public checkpoints, that term vanishes, and choosing among them costs \(\ln|\mathcal R|\) in utility and no linear cost in privacy.
The validation set needs protection under every method. The best-of methods of Section 40.3 and Section 40.4 assume that the score is part of each run’s private output. If the score is an exact validation accuracy, the validation records are not protected at all. Adding Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma_{\text{val}}\) to each validation count makes each score a Gaussian mechanism with curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma_{\text{val}}^2)\) (Theorem 29.1). By step 3 of the proof of Proposition 40.3, the counts then cost the larger of the training curve and their own composed curve. With \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\) correct predictions, one noisy count alone has \(\varepsilon = 0.182\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and the eight counts of a search, composed, have \(0.546\), far below eight training runs.

Example 40.5 In the experiment of Section 40.6, eight DP-SGD runs at \(\sigma = 2.07\), with learning rates from 0.0625 to 8, get these counts out of \(m = 5{,}000\): 4,486, 4,604, 4,681, 4,694, 4,600, 4,470, 4,232 and 4,123. Table 40.5 selects among them with the exponential mechanism.

text:
40.6 Tuning the running example
This section puts the strategies side by side on the running example, at the same total budget, and asks what each delivers in accuracy, which is the comparison a practitioner faces.

Definition 40.3 (Six ways to tune the learning rate) Each run trains the running example’s network with DP-SGD (\(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\)) for 1,000 steps, with one of eight learning rates \(\eta \in \{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\), and is scored by its correct predictions on 5,000 private validation records plus Gaussian noise with \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\). Each strategy releases one model and chooses its noise multiplier \(\sigma\) so that the whole procedure meets \(\varepsilon = 2\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

No tuning: one run with the learning rate 0.5 that DP-SGD used.
The reporting bug: the eight runs at the \(\sigma\) of one run, the best released, and the single-run \(\varepsilon\) reported, though the search really spends more.
Proxy data: the grid run on a related public task, then one private run with its best learning rate.
Composition: the eight runs at the \(\sigma\) for which eight runs together cost 2 (Proposition 40.2).
Poisson random search: \(K\) runs with learning rates drawn uniformly from the grid, \(K\) Poisson with mean 8 (Theorem 40.3).
Logarithmic random search: the same with \(K\) logarithmic (Theorem 40.4).


Runs take 1,000 steps instead of 10,000 to keep the script fast. Of the running example’s 20,000 held-out records, 5,000 form the validation set and 15,000 the test set. The proxy task is labelled by a different random network and touches no private data, so it costs nothing (Theorem 19.1). The script trains three runs per learning rate for each \(\sigma\) and repeats each procedure 4,000 times by drawing from this pool, with fresh validation noise and a fresh \(K\), which understates the variety of a real search a little.

Suppose one paper reports “test accuracy 0.948 at \(\varepsilon = 1.97\)” for a model chosen from eight learning rates, and another 0.943 at \(\varepsilon = 1.99\) after an honest grid search. section: 40.7 What to do and what to report
text:
40.7 What to do and what to report
The results of this chapter turn into a short procedure, and into a rule for what a reported \(\varepsilon\) must cover.

Definition 40.4 (An honest tuning procedure)  

Spend private runs only where you must. Tune on public or proxy data when it exists, and reuse hyperparameters from similar tasks. Shrink the search: below the typical gradient norm only the product of learning rate and clipping norm matters (DP-SGD).
Fix the search before touching the private data. Write down the candidate set, the distribution of the number of runs, the score and the validation set.
Make the score private. Use a held-out validation set and a noisy count.
Account for the whole search. For a few candidates, compose (Proposition 40.2). For more, use random search with Theorem 40.3 or Theorem 40.4. Count every run on the private data, including crashed runs, debugging runs and evaluations for early stopping.
Report both numbers. Give the \(\varepsilon\) of the released run, and the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure with how it was computed: the candidate set, the distribution of \(K\), the accountant, \(\delta\) and the neighbouring relation.


The cheapest fix is usually upstream: in Table 40.6, the strategies that spend the whole budget on one private run beat every honest search. Tuning without noise does not escape the problem, because the hyperparameters are then a non-private function of the data. Papernot & Steinke (2022, Section 2) build a support vector machine whose best regularization weight reveals whether a few outliers were in the training set, a membership inference through a single number. Retraining the chosen configuration with fresh noise does not make the tuning free either, because the configuration is still a function of the tuning runs.
Fixing the search in advance is part of the guarantee. The theorems of Section 40.3 and Section 40.4 require that each run draws its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, which is random search, and that \(K\) is drawn independently of the data. Adaptive methods such as Bayesian optimization, which pick the next candidate from the scores so far, are not covered and need Adaptive composition. An engineer who looks at the first results and decides to “try a few more” has changed the procedure, and the theorem no longer applies.
Both numbers in step 5 matter. The released run’s \(\varepsilon\) says what the model alone would leak if its hyperparameters were public, while the procedure’s \(\varepsilon\) is what the release guarantees. Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.3) ask for both. Auditing cannot catch the bug, because an audit tests the trained model, not how it was chosen.

Example 40.7 For the Poisson row of Table 40.6, a complete report reads: “DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate 0.01, clipping norm 0.5, noise multiplier 1.53, 1,000 steps; one run satisfies \((0.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The learning rate was selected by random search over \(\{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\) with a Poisson number of runs with mean 8, scored by correct predictions on a disjoint validation set of 5,000 records with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20; the whole procedure satisfies \((1.99, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022, Theorem 6), add/remove neighbours, record level.”

40.10 References

Liu & Talwar, “Private Selection from Private Candidates” (STOC 2019; arXiv:1811.07971). Random stopping and the \(3\varepsilon\) bound of Section 40.3; threshold and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) variants; the fixed-\(k\) counterexample (their Appendix B).

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.1 Training is a stream of prefix sums
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), the DP-SGD of the previous chapter, owes much of its privacy to Poisson sampling. A record is in each batch only with probability \(q\), and the accountant credits the run for that uncertainty. On the running example of this part, with \(q = 0.01\), this amplification turns a noise multiplier of 1 into \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) over 10,000 steps. But fixed batches, streaming pipelines and federated servers cannot honestly claim Poisson sampling, and Amplification by subsampling shows that the Poisson accountant then understates \(\varepsilon\). Without amplification, for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over five passes, the noise multiplier grows from 0.928 to 4.458 and test accuracy falls from 0.9460 to 0.8941.
This chapter asks how to train privately without trusting random batches. The one idea is that training releases running sums of gradients, so noise added at one step may partly cancel the noise added before it. Releasing all running sums is described by a matrix \(A\), and writing \(A = LR\) splits the release into an encoder \(R\), which sets the privacy, and a decoder \(L\), which sets the error. The first such algorithm ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer on sums noised through a binary tree, and is called DP-FTRL. That tree, the square-root factorization and the best known mechanisms are all choices of \(L\) and \(R\).
The running example is the part’s network from DP-SGD, with \(d = 3{,}329\) weights, \(n = 10{,}000\) records, clipping norm \(C = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The fixed-order runs cut one public random permutation, drawn independently of the data, into 100 batches of 100, so each record takes part once per epoch, 100 steps apart. Table 41.1 lists the symbols.
What does a training run have to release, and what does privacy cost when nothing is sampled? The answer turns training into the private release of running sums, a classic problem with much better mechanisms than fresh noise on every step. The reason is that gradient descent adds up its steps. Write \(B\) for the batch size and \(\eta\) for the learning rate.
Why release every prefix sum, and not only the last? Training is adaptive, since the gradient \(x_t\) is computed at \(\theta_{t-1}\), which depends on the earlier noisy prefix sums. So the intermediate models must be private too, and the workload is all \(T\) rows of \(A\), released one at a time as the stream arrives. With momentum or a learning-rate schedule the weights are still fixed linear combinations of the noisy gradients, with another lower-triangular matrix in place of \(A\), which Denisov, McMahan, Rush, Smith & Thakurta (2022) factor too. This chapter keeps plain gradient descent.
Two facts from earlier chapters price every mechanism here. The first is about privacy. Release a matrix \(f(D)\) plus independent normal noise of standard deviation \(sC\) on every entry, and measure the change in \(f\) between neighbours in the Frobenius norm, the length of the matrix read as one long vector. Then only the ratio \(\mu\) of that change to \(sC\) matters, and the release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least the Gaussian privacy profile of Theorem 20.3 at \(\mu\). Such a release satisfies \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). The profile grows with \(\mu\), so each target allows a largest ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), and at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) these are \(\mu(2, \delta) = 0.502\) and \(\mu(8, \delta) = 1.666\).
The second fact is about error. A weighted sum of independent normals is normal, with variance the sum of the variances times the weights squared (Proposition 1.11). So if \(z\) has independent entries of standard deviation \(sC\) and \(\ell\) is a fixed row vector, each coordinate of \(\ell z\) is normal with variance \[s^2C^2\|\ell\|^2 = s^2C^2\sum_j\ell_j^2. \tag{41.3}\]
Neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) differ by adding or removing one record, whose slot in the public order is then empty in one stream. (Under replace-one neighbours, a contribution could change by \(2C\), and every sensitivity would double.) The two obvious mechanisms put the noise at opposite ends, on each step’s gradient sum or on each prefix sum.
DP-SGD run in a fixed order without sampling is the first mechanism, so its model at step \(t\) carries a random walk of \(t\) noise vectors. Neither mechanism uses the structure of \(A\), because the first ignores that the noise accumulates and the second that most of \(S_t\) was already released in \(S_{t-1}\).

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
Proposition 41.1 (Training releases prefix sums) Run gradient descent from \(\theta_0\) with a constant learning rate \(\eta\) and no momentum, \(\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \frac\eta B\hat x_t\), where \(\hat x_t\) is the possibly noisy clipped gradient sum of step \(t\). Then \[\theta_t = \theta_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t, \qquad \hat S_t = \sum_{s \le t}\hat x_s, \tag{41.1}\] so every model is post-processing of the prefix sums, and its noise is \(\eta/B\) times theirs. The FTRL algorithm with linear losses \(\langle\hat x_s, \theta\rangle\), \(\theta_t = \arg\min_\theta\big(\langle\hat S_t, \theta\rangle + \frac B{2\eta}\|\theta - \theta_0\|^2\big)\), produces the same weights. Releasing all \(T\) prefix sums is the linear workload \[S = Ax, \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & & & \\ 1 & 1 & & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb R^{T \times T}, \tag{41.2}\] where the \(x_t\) are stacked as the rows of the \(T \times d\) matrix \(x\), and row \(t\) of \(Ax\) is \(S_t\).


Proof. 

Unroll the recursion. The updates \(\theta_u - \theta_{u-1} = -\frac\eta B\hat x_u\) for \(u = 1, \dots, t\) telescope when added, which gives Equation 41.1.
FTRL. The FTRL objective is a linear term plus a quadratic. Its gradient is \(\hat S_t + \frac B\eta(\theta - \theta_0)\), and setting it to zero gives \(\theta = \theta_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t\), the same point.
Post-processing. Every model is a fixed function of the released prefix sums, and post-processing never weakens a guarantee (Theorem 19.1).







Proposition 41.2 (The two naive mechanisms) Let a record take part in one step \(\tau\), fixed in advance, and add a vector of length at most \(C\) to \(x_\tau\). Then each of the following is \(\mu\)-GDP.

Independent noise on each step, \(\hat S_t = \sum_{u \le t}(x_u + z_u)\) with noise of standard deviation \(C/\mu\) per coordinate. The error of \(\hat S_t\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt t\,C/\mu\).
Independent noise on each prefix sum, \(\hat S_t = S_t + z_t\) with noise of standard deviation \(\sqrt T\,C/\mu\) per coordinate, which is also the error of every \(\hat S_t\).



Proof. The plan is to find, for each mechanism, how far one record moves the noisy quantities, which fixes the noise by the first fact, and then to read the error off Equation 41.3.

Independent noise on each step: privacy. The record changes only \(x_\tau\), by a vector of length at most \(C\), so the noisy gradients \(x_u + z_u\) form one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\mu\), and the prefix sums are post-processing of them.
Its error. The error is \(\hat S_t - S_t = z_1 + \dots + z_t\), which is Equation 41.3 with \(\ell = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0)\), carrying \(t\) ones. So its standard deviation is \(\sqrt t\,C/\mu\).
Independent noise on each prefix sum: privacy. The record’s gradient appears in every \(S_t\) with \(t \ge \tau\). So \(T - \tau + 1\) of the released vectors move by the same vector, and the total Frobenius change is \(\sqrt{T - \tau + 1}\,C\). The worst position, \(\tau = 1\), gives \(\sqrt T\,C\), and the noise must be \(\sqrt T\,C/\mu\).
Its error. Each \(\hat S_t\) carries one noise vector of that standard deviation.




Example 41.1 Take one epoch, \(T = 100\) steps, and normalize \(\mu = 1\) and \(C = 1\). Independent noise on each step gives the final prefix sum an error standard deviation of \(\sqrt{100} = 10\). Averaged over the 100 prefix sums, its root-mean-square error is \[\sqrt{(1 + 2 + \dots + 100)/100} = \sqrt{50.5} = 7.11. \tag{41.4}\] Independent noise on each prefix sum has error 10 on every one.
At \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(\mu = 0.502\), so the first mechanism needs a noise scale of \(1/0.502 = 1.994\) per step, and its final prefix sum carries noise of standard deviation 19.94, both in units of \(C\). DP-SGD with Poisson sampling at the same \(\varepsilon\) needs only \(\sigma = 0.827\), and its final prefix sum carries \(0.827\sqrt{100} = 8.27\). Amplification buys a factor of 2.4 here, and correlated noise can beat even that without any sampling.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.2 The matrix mechanism
The two naive mechanisms put the noise on the inputs or on the answers. The matrix mechanism of Li, Hay, Rastogi, Miklau & McGregor (2010) puts it in between, on a linear transformation of the inputs from which the answers can be recovered linearly. This section asks how private and how accurate such a release is, even on an adaptive stream, and how accurate any such release can be.

Definition 41.1 (Matrix mechanism) A factorization of the prefix-sum matrix is a pair \(A = LR\), with an encoder \(R \in \mathbb R^{m \times T}\) and a decoder \(L \in \mathbb R^{T \times m}\). Write \(r_j\) for column \(j\) of \(R\) and \(\ell_t\) for row \(t\) of \(L\). The matrix mechanism with noise scale \(s\) releases \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz, \qquad z_{jk} \sim \mathcal N(0, s^2C^2) \text{ independent}. \tag{41.5}\] It is streaming when \(L\) and \(R\) are lower-triangular, so that \(\hat S_t\) needs only the inputs and noise up to step \(t\).

The encoder decides where each step’s gradient lands, so it sets the privacy, and the decoder decides how much noise reaches each answer, so it sets the error.

Theorem 41.1 (Privacy and error of the matrix mechanism) Let a record take part in one step, at a position fixed in advance. Then the release Equation 41.5 is \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = \frac{\Delta_2 R}{s}, \qquad \Delta_2 R = \max_j\|r_j\|, \tag{41.6}\] the largest Euclidean length of a column of \(R\). If the factorization is streaming, this holds even when each \(x_t\) is chosen after seeing \(\hat S_1, \dots, \hat S_{t-1}\). Each coordinate of \(\hat S_t - S_t\) is normal with mean zero and standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_t\|\). At a fixed privacy level \(\mu\) this is \[\frac C\mu\,e_t, \qquad e_t = \Delta_2 R\,\|\ell_t\|, \tag{41.7}\] and the error per unit of privacy \(e_t\) does not change if \(R\) is multiplied by any number \(c > 0\) and \(L\) divided by it.


Proof. The plan is to compute how far one record moves the noisy encoding \(Rx + z\), extend that to adaptive inputs, and then read the error off the decoder.

Reduce to the encoding. \(L\) is fixed, so \(\hat S\) is post-processing of \(Rx + z\) (Theorem 19.1), and \(LRx = Ax\) by the factorization.
Sensitivity for fixed inputs. Neighbouring streams differ in the record’s contribution \(g\) to \(x_\tau\), a vector of length at most \(C\), so row \(\tau\) of \(x\) changes by \(g\) and nothing else. Then \(Rx\) changes by \(r_\tau g^\top\), column \(\tau\) of \(R\) times the row \(g\). Its entries are \(r_{j\tau}g_k\), so its squared Frobenius norm factorizes, and its Frobenius norm is \(\|r_\tau\|\,\|g\| \le \|r_\tau\|C\). The worst position gives \(\Delta_2 R\,C\), and with noise of standard deviation \(sC\) the ratio is \(\Delta_2 R/s\).
Adaptive inputs. With lower-triangular factors, row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\) depends on \(x_1, \dots, x_j\) only, so it can be released at step \(j\). Because \(R\) is lower-triangular, rows before \(\tau\) do not involve \(x_\tau\), so the earlier outputs have the same distribution under both streams, and conditioning on them fixes \(g\). Given the same history, the other records’ gradients agree in both runs, so each later row of \(Rx + z\) has its mean shifted by the matching row of \(r_\tau g^\top\). These are Gaussian mechanisms released one after another, with squared shifts adding up to at most \(\|r_\tau\|^2C^2\). Adaptive Gaussian steps compose into one Gaussian mechanism whose squared ratio is the sum of theirs (Gaussian DP), so the ratio is at most \(\Delta_2 R/s\) again. Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1) prove the general statement, and Section H.5 in the appendices proves the Gaussian case for several participations.
Error. The error is \(\hat S_t - S_t = \ell_tz\), so Equation 41.3 gives standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_t\|\). Substituting \(s = \Delta_2 R/\mu\) from Equation 41.6 gives Equation 41.7. Replacing \(R\) by \(cR\) and \(L\) by \(L/c\) multiplies \(\Delta_2 R\) by \(c\) and \(\|\ell_t\|\) by \(1/c\), so their product is unchanged.


So privacy lives in the columns and error in the rows. Insisting on streaming factors costs nothing, because any factorization has a lower-triangular one with the same distribution of \(\hat S\) (Denisov et al. 2022, Proposition 2.2), which Section H.5 derives by Gram–Schmidt.
When \(R\) is square and invertible, the mechanism is noisy SGD with correlated noise. Then \(L = AR^{-1}\) and \(\hat S = A(x + R^{-1}z)\), so the mechanism adds the noise \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\) to the gradients and then sums. An implementation generates each \(\zeta_t\) on the fly from the stored past noise.
How small can the error be? The squared row lengths of \(L\) add up to its squared Frobenius norm \(\|L\|_F^2\), so the root-mean-square error over the \(T\) prefix sums is \[\Big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\Big)^{1/2} = \frac{\Delta_2 R\,\|L\|_F}{\sqrt T}. \tag{41.8}\] The bound below uses the trace norm \(\|A\|_* = \sum_k\nu_k(A)\), the sum of the singular values \(\nu_k(A)\) of \(A\).

Theorem 41.2 (The trace-norm lower bound) For every factorization \(A = LR\), \[\frac{\Delta_2 R\,\|L\|_F}{\sqrt T} \ge \frac{\|A\|_*}T. \tag{41.9}\] For the prefix-sum matrix, \(\nu_k(A) = 1/\big(2\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}\big)\) for \(k = 1, \dots, T\).


Proof. The plan is to bound \(\|A\|_*\) by the product \(\|L\|_F\|R\|_F\), then bound \(\|R\|_F\) by its longest column.

Duality. For any matrix \(U\) whose largest singular value is at most 1, \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) \le \|A\|_*\), with equality for a \(U\) built from the singular vectors of \(A\). This dual description of the trace norm is proved in Section H.3 in the appendices.
Cauchy–Schwarz. The trace \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top LR)\) is the Frobenius inner product of \(L^\top U\) and \(R\), so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[\operatorname{tr}(U^\top LR) \le \|L^\top U\|_F\,\|R\|_F. \tag{41.10}\]
Remove \(U\). The matrix \(U^\top\) does not lengthen any vector, since its singular values are at most 1. Applied to each column of \(L\), this gives \(\|L^\top U\|_F = \|U^\top L\|_F \le \|L\|_F\). With step 1, \(\|L\|_F\|R\|_F \ge \|A\|_*\).
Bound \(\|R\|_F\) by the sensitivity. \(R\) has \(T\) columns, each of length at most \(\Delta_2 R\), so \(\|R\|_F^2 \le T(\Delta_2 R)^2\). With step 3, this gives \(\Delta_2 R\,\|L\|_F \ge \|A\|_*/\sqrt T\), which is Equation 41.9 after dividing by \(\sqrt T\).
The singular values. The inverse \(A^{-1}\) has 1 on the diagonal and \(-1\) just below it. The eigenvalues of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) are \(4\sin^2\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}\), because that product is the second-difference matrix with a 1 in its last diagonal entry, whose eigenvectors are sine waves; Section H.3 derives them. The singular values of \(A\) are the reciprocals of their square roots.


Step 4 is tight only when all columns of \(R\) are equally long, so unequal columns waste privacy on the short ones. The chapter’s script (Section 41.7) checks the closed form of the singular values against a numerical decomposition at \(T = 256\), and they agree to \(2.0 \times 10^{-13}\).

Example 41.2 Table 41.2 collects the error per unit of privacy for one participation. At \(T = 100\) the naive mechanisms have root-mean-square errors 7.11 and 10, while Equation 41.9 says no factorization can go below 2.18. The other rows are derived in Section 41.3 and Section 41.4.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.3 Tree aggregation and DP-FTRL
The first mechanism with error far below \(\sqrt T\) was the binary tree, found independently by Dwork, Naor, Pitassi & Rothblum (2010) and by Chan, Shi & Song (2010) for counting events in a stream. Kairouz, McMahan, Song, Thakkar, Thakurta & Xu (2021) used it to release the prefix sums of gradients, with FTRL as the optimizer, and called the result DP-FTRL. This section asks how the tree works as a factorization and how good it is.

Definition 41.2 (Binary tree mechanism) Build a binary tree over the steps \(1, \dots, T\). Level 0 has one node per step, and a node at level \(l\) covers one of the blocks \(1, \dots, 2^l\), then \(2^l + 1, \dots, 2\cdot2^l\), and so on, of \(2^l\) consecutive steps. There are \(H = \lceil\log_2T\rceil + 1\) levels. The mechanism releases each node’s sum of gradients plus independent noise, and estimates each prefix sum as \[\hat S_t = \sum_{\text{nodes in the decomposition of }t}(\text{node sum} + \text{noise}), \tag{41.11}\] where the decomposition of \(t\) takes one node for each 1 in the binary expansion of \(t\).


Proposition 41.3 (Error of the tree) The binary tree is a streaming factorization of \(A\), with \[\Delta_2 R = \sqrt H, \qquad e_t = \sqrt H\sqrt{\operatorname{popcount}(t)}, \tag{41.12}\] where \(\operatorname{popcount}(t)\) is the number of 1s in the binary expansion of \(t\), at most \(H - 1\) for \(t \le T\). Both factors grow like \(\sqrt{\ln T}\), so the error grows like \(\ln T\).


Proof. The plan is to check the decomposition, write the tree as an encoder and decoder, and count.

The decomposition. Write \(t\) in binary. Going from the highest bit down, each 1 at bit \(l\) takes the next block of \(2^l\) steps. That block starts right after the sum of the higher bits, which is a multiple of \(2^{l+1}\), so it is a node of the tree. For example, \(7 = 4 + 2 + 1\) uses the nodes covering steps 1 to 4, 5 and 6, and 7, while \(8\) uses a single node covering 1 to 8.
The factorization. \(R\) has one row per node, with 1 in the columns of the steps the node covers, so it is \(m \times T\) with \(m\) about \(2T\). Row \(t\) of \(L\) has a 1 for each node of the decomposition of \(t\). Then \(LR = A\), because by step 1 those nodes cover each step \(1, \dots, t\) exactly once.
Sensitivity. A step lies in exactly one node per level, so column \(j\) of \(R\) has \(H\) ones and length \(\sqrt H\).
Error. Row \(t\) of \(L\) has \(\operatorname{popcount}(t)\) ones, so \(\|\ell_t\| = \sqrt{\operatorname{popcount}(t)}\), and Equation 41.7 gives Equation 41.12.
Streaming. Each node can be released once its last step has arrived, and \(\hat S_t\) uses only completed nodes. With the rows of \(R\) ordered by completion time, the factors are streaming, so Theorem 41.1 applies to adaptive training.


The tree sums at most \(\log_2t + 1\) noise terms for the \(t\)-th prefix instead of \(t\), each somewhat larger because every step is hidden in \(H\) nodes. That trade is a large win for long runs but not for short ones: the tree first wins at \(T = 28\).
The tree is not the end. Its error jumps around, since \(t = 127 = 1111111_2\) uses seven nodes and \(t = 128\) uses one (Figure 41.2, left), and every step pays for being in top-level nodes that few prefixes use. Honaker (2015) combined all nodes with weights to reduce the variance, but that estimator uses nodes completed after step \(t\), so it cannot be used during training. The square-root factorization of the next section has smaller error everywhere.

Example 41.3 For \(T = 100\) the tree has \(H = 8\) levels, so \(\Delta_2 R = \sqrt8 = 2.828\). The largest popcount up to 100 is 6, at \(t = 63\), so the largest error per unit of privacy is \(\sqrt8\sqrt6 = 6.93\). The root-mean-square error is 5.05 (Table 41.2). For \(T = 10{,}000\) there are 15 levels and \(\Delta_2 R = 3.873\). The maximum error is then 13.96 and the root-mean-square error 9.84, against 70.71 for independent noise.

DP-FTRL runs FTRL, which by Equation 41.1 is gradient descent on noisy prefix sums, with the prefix sums released by the tree. Kairouz et al. (2021) also add momentum and restart the tree after a number of steps, and they report that DP-FTRL without amplification compares favourably with amplified DP-SGD. Xu et al. (2023) train production language models for the Gboard keyboard with it in federated learning, where devices cannot be Poisson-sampled.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.4 The square-root factorization
The tree has a tall, thin encoder and a sparse decoder. A symmetric choice is \(L = R\), a matrix whose square is \(A\). This section asks whether \(A\) has a lower-triangular square root, what it looks like, and how close it comes to the best possible factorization.
Power series find the square root. A lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix is constant along each diagonal, so it is fixed by its first column \((c_0, \dots, c_{T-1})\), identified with the series \(c(u) = \sum_kc_ku^k\) in a formal variable \(u\). The proof of the next theorem needs one fact, which turns a matrix equation into an equation between series.

Lemma 41.1 (Lower-triangular Toeplitz matrices multiply like power series) The product of the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrices of two series \(a(u)\) and \(b(u)\) is the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix of \(a(u)b(u)\), truncated after \(u^{T-1}\).


Proof. 

Entry \((i, k)\) of the first matrix is \(a_{i-k}\) and entry \((k, j)\) of the second is \(b_{k-j}\), both zero above the diagonal. So entry \((i, j)\) of the product is \(\sum_ka_{i-k}b_{k-j}\) over \(j \le k \le i\). This sum depends only on \(i - j\), and it is the coefficient of \(u^{i-j}\) in \(a(u)b(u)\).



Theorem 41.3 (The square-root factorization) The lower-triangular matrix \(R = A^{1/2}\) with \(R^2 = A\) is the Toeplitz matrix with entries \[R_{ij} = c_{i-j} \text{ for } i \ge j, \qquad c_k = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}: \quad c = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac38, \tfrac5{16}, \tfrac{35}{128}, \dots, \tag{41.13}\] the coefficients of the power series \((1 - u)^{-1/2} = \sum_kc_ku^k\), computed by \(c_0 = 1\) and \(c_k = c_{k-1}\frac{2k - 1}{2k}\). With \(L = R\), \[(\Delta_2 R)^2 = \|\ell_T\|^2 = \sum_{k<T}c_k^2, \qquad 1 + \frac{\ln\frac{2T+1}3}\pi \le \sum_{k<T}c_k^2 \le 1 + \frac{0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5}\pi, \tag{41.14}\] and the largest error per unit of privacy is \(\max_te_t = e_T = \sum_{k<T}c_k^2\), which grows like \(\ln(T)/\pi\). As noisy SGD, the noise added to the gradients is \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\), where \(R^{-1}\) is the Toeplitz matrix of the coefficients \(h_k\) of \((1 - u)^{1/2}\), \(h = 1, -\frac12, -\frac18, -\frac1{16}, -\frac5{128}, \dots\).


Proof. The plan is to write \(A\) as a series, take its square root as a series, and then read the sensitivity and the error off the coefficients.

\(A\) is the series \(1/(1 - u)\). Its first column is all ones, and \(1 + u + u^2 + \dots = 1/(1 - u)\).
A square root. The series \((1 - u)^{-1/2}\) squares to \(1/(1 - u)\), so by Lemma 41.1 its Toeplitz matrix squares to \(A\). Its coefficients come from the binomial series. The \(k\)-th one is \[\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac32\cdots\frac{2k-1}2}{k!} = \frac{1\cdot3\cdots(2k - 1)}{2^kk!}. \tag{41.15}\] Multiplying top and bottom by \(2\cdot4\cdots2k = 2^kk!\) gives \(\frac{(2k)!}{4^k(k!)^2} = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}\), and the ratio of consecutive terms is \(\frac{2k-1}{2k}\).
The inverse. By Lemma 41.1 again, \(R^{-1}\) is the matrix of \(1/(1 - u)^{-1/2} = (1 - u)^{1/2}\). The binomial series gives its coefficients \(1, -\frac12, -\frac18, -\frac1{16}, -\frac5{128}, \dots\), all negative after the first.
Sensitivity and error. Column \(j\) of \(R\) holds \(c_0, \dots, c_{T-j}\), so the first column is the longest, with squared length \(\sum_{k<T}c_k^2\). Row \(t\) of \(L = R\) holds \(c_{t-1}, \dots, c_0\), so its squared length is \(\sum_{k<t}c_k^2\), largest at \(t = T\).
Bounds. A Wallis-type inequality gives \(\frac1{\pi(k + 1/2)} \le c_k^2 \le \frac1{\pi(k + 1/4)}\) for \(k \ge 1\). Section H.3 in the appendices proves it, and since both bounding functions decrease, each sum compares with an integral. For the lower bound, \[\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}\frac1{k + 1/2} \ge \int_1^T\frac{\mathrm dv}{v + 1/2} = \ln\frac{2T + 1}3. \tag{41.16}\] For the upper bound, the first term is kept apart and the rest is bounded by an integral, \[\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}\frac1{k + 1/4} \le \frac1{5/4} + \int_1^{T-1}\frac{\mathrm dv}{v + 1/4} = 0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5. \tag{41.17}\] Multiplying both sums by \(1/\pi\) and adding the \(k = 0\) term, 1, gives Equation 41.14.


The noise added to step \(t\)’s gradient is \(z_t - \frac12z_{t-1} - \frac18z_{t-2} - \dots\), fresh noise minus a decaying share of the noise already injected. Each step’s noise is a little larger than independent noise, by the factor \(\big(\sum_kh_k^2\big)^{1/2}\) at the same noise scale. The script sums 100,000 coefficients and finds \(\sum_kh_k^2 = 1.2732 = 4/\pi\), so the factor tends to 1.128. But the negative coefficients pull the accumulated noise back toward zero, so the running sums no longer drift (Figure 41.1).
The square root is close to optimal. Against the lower bound of 2.18 at \(T = 100\) and 3.63 at \(T = 10{,}000\), its root-mean-square error is 2.37 and 3.84, within 9% and 6%, and Section H.3 proves that the ratio tends to 1. Fichtenberger, Henzinger & Upadhyay (2023) and Henzinger, Upadhyay & Upadhyay (2023) bound its maximum and mean squared errors, and note that the factorization already appears in Bennett (1977). The closed form in Theorem 1 of the arXiv version of the first paper, \(1 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5/\pi\), omits the first term of the upper comparison in step 5, so it gives 2.392 against the true 2.531 at \(T = 100\). A finer expansion, stated here without proof, gives \(\sum_{k<T}c_k^2 \approx (\ln T + \gamma + 4\ln 2)/\pi\) with \(\gamma\) Euler’s constant, which is 2.532 at \(T = 100\).






Figure 41.1: Left: one coordinate of the noise added to each of the first 60 steps’ gradients, independent (identity factorization) and square-root correlated, both calibrated to \(\mu = 1\) for one participation. Right: the noise in the prefix sums over 1,000 steps, for independent noise, the binary tree and the square root, with bands of two standard deviations. Independent noise drifts like a random walk; the square root’s stays within a narrow band.




Example 41.4 At \(T = 4\) the coefficients are \(c = (1, \frac12, \frac38, \frac5{16})\), so \[R = \begin{pmatrix}1 & & & \\ \frac12 & 1 & & \\ \frac38 & \frac12 & 1 & \\ \frac5{16} & \frac38 & \frac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{41.18}\] Row 4 times column 1 of \(R\) is \(\frac5{16} + \frac38\cdot\frac12 + \frac12\cdot\frac38 + \frac5{16} = 1\), as \(R^2 = A\) requires, and the script confirms \(R^2 = A\) exactly. The first column has squared length \[1 + \frac14 + \frac9{64} + \frac{25}{256} = \frac{381}{256} = 1.488, \tag{41.19}\] so \(\Delta_2 R = 1.220\), and the last prefix sum has error 1.488 per unit of privacy, against \(\sqrt4 = 2\) for independent noise. At \(T = 100\) the same computation gives \(\sum_kc_k^2 = 2.531\), so \(\Delta_2 R = 1.591\). The final prefix sum’s error is then 2.53, a quarter of independent noise’s 10.


41.4.1 The optimal factorization
How much better than the square root can any factorization do? By scale invariance the best encoder may have columns of length at most 1, and it then minimizes \(\|L\|_F\). Write \(X = R^\top R\) for the inner products of the columns of \(R\). For a given \(X\) the best decoder, the least-squares solution of \(LR = A\), gives \(\|L\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1})\), which is convex in \(X\).

Theorem 41.4 (The optimal factorization) The problem of minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1})\) over positive definite \(X\) with diagonal at most 1 has the solution \[X = V^{-1/2}(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2})^{1/2}V^{-1/2}, \tag{41.20}\] where \(V\) is the diagonal matrix of a positive vector \(v\) that is a fixed point of \(v \mapsto \operatorname{diag}\big((V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2})^{1/2}\big)\). The optimal value is \(\sum_iv_i\). In words, the optimal \(X\) is the matrix square root of \(A^\top A\), rescaled on both sides by a diagonal matrix chosen so that every column of \(R\) has length exactly 1.


The proof is Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 3.2), who iterate the fixed-point map to find \(v\), and Section H.4 in the appendices gives it in full. A lower-triangular \(R\) with \(R^\top R = X\) comes from a Cholesky factorization of \(X\) with rows and columns reversed.
The script’s iteration converges in 155 steps at \(T = 100\), to a root-mean-square error of 2.24 against 2.37 for the square root, and in 193 steps at \(T = 256\), to 2.52 against 2.67. Each iteration costs cubic time, so the square root, free and nearly as good, is the usual default for long runs. Figure 41.2 shows the errors across one run and against the horizon, and Figure 41.3 shows that the square root and the optimal factors look alike at \(T = 16\).






Figure 41.2: Left: standard deviation of the error of each released prefix sum \(S_t\) for \(T = 256\), one participation, at \(\mu = 1\) and \(C = 1\), for five factorizations. Right: the root-mean-square error over a run against its length \(T\), with the trace-norm lower bound of Equation 41.9 dotted; the optimal factorization is computed up to \(T = 256\).









Figure 41.3: The encoder \(R\) (top) and decoder \(L\) (bottom) of three factorizations of the \(16 \times 16\) prefix-sum matrix. The tree’s encoder has one row per node (31 rows), and its decoder picks the nodes of each prefix. The square root uses the same matrix for both; the optimal factorization’s encoder has columns of length exactly 1.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.5 Several participations
So far each record took part in one step. Training usually makes several passes, and then a record’s gradient enters \(x\) at several steps, each time through a different column of \(R\). This section asks how large the sensitivity is then, and how the factorization should change to keep it small. The answer depends on which steps a record can occupy and on how the columns of \(R\) overlap.

Definition 41.3 (Participation pattern, separation and band) A record’s participation pattern is the set of steps \(\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_k\) at which it contributes, with vectors \(g_1, \dots, g_k\) of length at most \(C\), possibly chosen adaptively. The pattern has \(b\)-min-separation if any two participations are at least \(b\) steps apart. A lower-triangular encoder is \(b\)-banded if its nonzero entries lie on the main diagonal and the \(b - 1\) diagonals below it, that is \(R_{ij} = 0\) whenever \(i - j \ge b\).


Theorem 41.5 (Sensitivity under several participations) For a record with participation pattern \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_k\), the change in \(Rx\) is \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\). If \(R^\top R \ge 0\) entrywise, the sensitivity in units of \(C\) is \[(\Delta_2 R)^2 = \frac1{C^2}\max_{\text{patterns}}\ \sup_{\|g_i\| \le C}\Big\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \max_{\text{patterns}}\Big\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}\Big\|^2, \tag{41.21}\] the largest length of a sum of participating columns, and the release is \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \Delta_2 R/s\). For independent noise, \(R = I\), this gives \(\Delta_2 R = \sqrt k\). For a \(b\)-banded encoder and patterns with \(b\)-min-separation, whatever the sign of the entries of \(R^\top R\), \[\Delta_2 R = \Big(\sum_i\|r_{\tau_i}\|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le \sqrt k\max_j\|r_j\|. \tag{41.22}\]


Proof. The plan is to expand the squared norm of the change into inner products, find the worst contributions, and evaluate the two special cases.

The change in \(Rx\). Row \(\tau_i\) of \(x\) changes by \(g_i\), so \(Rx\) changes by \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\), a sum of the column-times-row products of Theorem 41.1.
Expand the norm. The Frobenius inner product of two such products, \(ab^\top\) and \(a'b'^\top\), is \((a\cdot a')(b\cdot b')\). So \[\Big\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j}(r_{\tau_i}\cdot r_{\tau_j})(g_i\cdot g_j). \tag{41.23}\]
The worst contributions. Each \(g_i\cdot g_j\) lies in \([-C^2, C^2]\). The entries of \(R^\top R\) are the inner products of columns, so if they are nonnegative, the sum is largest when every \(g_i\cdot g_j = C^2\), that is when all \(g_i\) are the same vector of length \(C\). The sum is then \(C^2\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}\|^2\). The condition holds for the identity, the tree and the square root, because their \(R\) has nonnegative entries. Adaptive choices of the \(g_i\) cannot exceed this supremum, and Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1) state their adaptive result for exactly this sensitivity, and Section H.5 in the appendices proves it for Gaussian noise and a lower-triangular \(R\).
Independent noise. The columns of \(I\) are orthonormal, so the squared length of a sum of \(k\) of them is \(k\).
Banded encoders. Column \(\tau\) of a \(b\)-banded \(R\) is nonzero only in rows \(\tau, \dots, \tau + b - 1\). Participations at least \(b\) apart have columns with disjoint supports, so the cross terms of step 2 vanish whatever the \(g_i\), leaving \(\sum_i\|r_{\tau_i}\|^2\|g_i\|^2\).


Correlated noise makes repeated participation more expensive. Under independent noise, \(k\) participations cost \(\sqrt k\), as Gaussian composition says. Under the square root, the columns of nearby steps overlap and point in similar directions, so a record’s contributions pile up and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt k\). Under the tree it is worse still, because a top node holds several participations of the same record. For the optimal factorization Equation 41.21 applies only if \(X\) has no negative entries. Banding restores \(\sqrt k\) by cutting the square root’s encoder to its first \(b\) diagonals, which removes the overlaps. Its decoder \(L = AR^{-1}\) is less accurate for one participation, but with many the saving in sensitivity dominates. Choquette-Choo and coauthors (2023) optimize factorizations under a participation constraint and add amplification to banded ones.
So the data order is part of the mechanism. A fixed permutation repeated every epoch guarantees a separation of exactly \(n/B\) steps, while reshuffling every epoch can put a record one step apart across an epoch boundary, which breaks the banded bound. The order must be fixed independently of the data, but it need not be random.

Example 41.5 Table 41.3 takes the running example’s order, with separation \(b = 100\), so over \(E\) epochs every record takes part \(E\) times. The banded encoder keeps the first 100 coefficients of the square root. Each cell gives the sensitivity and then \(e_T\) of Equation 41.7 with that sensitivity.

section: 41.6 The running example: matrix mechanisms against DP-SGD
text:
41.6 The running example: matrix mechanisms against DP-SGD
The previous sections compared mechanisms by the error in released sums. This section asks whether that ranking carries over to trained networks, and how mechanisms without sampling compare with DP-SGD with sampling at the same \(\varepsilon\). The comparison needs one number per method computed before training, the noise its final model carries.

Proposition 41.4 (Noise at equal privacy) Fix a target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and \(E\) participations 100 steps apart, so \(T = 100E\). A fixed-order mechanism with encoder \(R\) and the multi-epoch sensitivity \(\Delta_2 R\) of Theorem 41.5 needs the noise scale \[s = \frac{\Delta_2 R}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}, \tag{41.24}\] and its final prefix sum carries noise of standard deviation \(s\|\ell_T\|\) per coordinate, in units of \(C\). For independent noise this is \(s = \sqrt E/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). DP-SGD with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) carries \(\sigma\sqrt T\) in its final prefix sum.


Proof. 

Noise scale. By Theorem 41.5 the release is \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \Delta_2 R/s\), and it meets the target exactly when \(\mu \le \mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). The smallest such \(s\) is the one stated, and for \(R = I\) the sensitivity is \(\sqrt E\).
Final prefix noise. By Theorem 41.1 the error of \(\hat S_T\) has standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_T\|\), which is \(s\|\ell_T\|\) in units of \(C\).
DP-SGD. Its final prefix sum is a sum of \(T\) independent noise vectors of standard deviation \(\sigma\) in units of \(C\), so by Equation 41.3 it carries \(\sigma\sqrt T\).


For DP-SGD, the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant of DP-SGD finds the smallest \(\sigma\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(T\) steps and the target \(\varepsilon\). Training then runs Equation 41.1 with each factorization’s noise added to the gradients. For the square-root and banded encoders that noise is \(R^{-1}z\), a convolution in time, and for the tree it is the difference of consecutive tree estimates.

Example 41.6 Table 41.4 gives the noise each method needs for \(\varepsilon = 2\) and 8 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and the noise its final prefix sum carries. Table 41.5 gives the test accuracy at the better of two learning rates, 0.5 and 2, averaged over three runs.

At \(\varepsilon = 2\), fixed-order SGD with independent noise loses 2.8 points to DP-SGD after one epoch and 8.5 points after ten. It gets worse with more epochs, because its noise scale grows like \(\sqrt E\), from 1.994 to 6.305. The tree recovers between a quarter and a half of the gap, and the square-root encoders nearly all of it. At ten epochs the banded encoder reaches 0.9491, within 0.0002 of DP-SGD.

Matrix mechanisms can even beat amplified DP-SGD for short runs at large \(\varepsilon\), where amplification gains little. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) and one epoch, the square root’s final prefix sum carries 1.52 against DP-SGD’s 5.01, and it wins outright. DP-SGD keeps its lead at small \(\varepsilon\) over many epochs, where its noise multiplier grows only from 0.827 to 1.03 while every fixed-order mechanism pays for ten participations, and only banding keeps up. In every row, the method with the least final-prefix noise is the most accurate or within the run-to-run spread of it.
The comparison is slightly tilted toward the fixed-order methods. DP-SGD is accounted with the RDP accountant, which overstates \(\varepsilon\) and so gives it more noise than it needs (Choosing an accountant), while the others use the exact Gaussian curve. Choosing the learning rate by test accuracy is itself a leak (Hyperparameter tuning), used here only to compare methods at their best. The runs are short, but the gaps of Table 41.3 widen with more epochs. Figure 41.4 shows the same pattern across budgets at five epochs.






Figure 41.4: Test accuracy of the running example after 5 epochs (500 steps of batch 100) at learning rate 1, against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run per point. DP-SGD uses Poisson sampling; the other four use a fixed data order and differ only in how their noise is correlated.



A federated server cannot sample devices with a known rate, but if it can ensure that a device contributes at most once every \(b\) rounds, the banded matrix mechanism gives a provable guarantee, and at the running example’s scale it is as accurate as DP-SGD with sampling would be. The privacy unit there is a user, which User-level differential privacy treats.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.1 The noisy vote: LNMax and GNMax
Training with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped and noisy gradients, DP-SGD, makes the weights private, so every later query to the model is free post-processing. The price is paid during training, and sometimes it cannot be paid. The model may be a large language model (LLM) that you can prompt but not train, or a model with no gradients. This chapter asks when it is better to make each answer private instead, and how.
The idea that organizes the chapter is one record, one vote. Split the private records into disjoint shards, train an ordinary model, a teacher, on each, and answer a query by a noisy vote of the teachers. A record lives in one shard, so it moves at most one vote, whatever the teachers are, as in the subsample-and-aggregate idea of Beyond global sensitivity. Privacy is therefore easy, and accuracy comes down to the gap between the top two vote counts against noise that grows like the square root of the number of answers. Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE), by Papernot, Abadi, Erlingsson, Goodfellow and Talwar (2017), turns a few private answers into a private model.
The running example is the part’s task (DP-SGD): 50-dimensional standard normal inputs labelled \(\pm1\) by a fixed random network, with \(n = 10{,}000\) private records. Its 20,000 test records are split into a public pool, whose inputs are treated as public and unlabelled, and an evaluation set, 10,000 each. The teachers are regularized logistic regressions (Private empirical risk minimization), each fitted on one shard of consecutive records. Neighbours \(D \sim D'\) differ by adding or removing one record, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout, and Table 42.1 lists the symbols.
A query arrives, the teachers vote, and you must release one label. This section asks which mechanism releases it and how the cost of many answers grows with their number, since that growth is what limits private prediction.
Every privacy statement below starts from one fact: one record can move the vote histogram \((N_1(x), \dots, N_m(x))\) only a little, whatever the teachers do. The cost theorem below needs this in the \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of absolute changes, and the \(\ell_2\) norm, their Euclidean length.
The cost of many answers is counted in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), whose curves add under composition. The improved conversion of Theorem 30.1 then turns a composed RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, adding to the curve at each order the price of the conversion and keeping the best order: \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{42.2}\] A curve that is a line \(\rho\alpha\) enters only through its slope, so write \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest slope that converts to a given budget. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) it is \(\rho = 0.0306\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\rho = 0.3731\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\).
What the teachers are never enters the cost, so a teacher can even be a human annotator. Only the label may be released, though, because the winner’s noisy count would publish the noise that the report-noisy-max proof keeps hidden.
An LNMax answer enters the RDP accountant as an \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP step with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2/b\), charged the curve of randomized response, which Theorem 31.3 shows bounds every such step. That charges every answer for its worst case, while Gaussian curves add without slack, so Gaussian noise wins for many answers. The RDP accountant is itself a little loose for GNMax, whose \(Q\) answers are exactly one Gaussian shift (f-DP and Gaussian DP). At the \(\sigma\) the accountant picks for \(\varepsilon = 1\), the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 0.915, and for \(\varepsilon = 4\) it is 3.698, so the accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\) by about 9% and 8%.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
Definition 42.1 (Teacher ensemble and noisy vote) Split the private dataset \(D\) into \(k\) disjoint shards by a rule fixed before looking at the data, such as a hash of a record identifier, and train one teacher on each shard. On a query \(x\) with \(m\) possible labels, let \(N_i(x)\) be the number of teachers that vote for label \(i\). The label with the most votes is the plurality \(i^*\), and the gap \(g\) is the top count minus the runner-up. LNMax (Laplace noisy max) releases \[\arg\max_i\big(N_i(x) + Z_i\big), \qquad Z_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b), \tag{42.1}\] and GNMax (Gaussian noisy max) releases the same label with \(Z_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), the noise independent across labels. Only the label is released, never the noisy counts.



Lemma 42.1 (One record changes one vote) With the shards fixed in advance, adding or removing one record changes at most one teacher. On every query, the vote histogram then moves by at most 2 in \(\ell_1\) norm and by at most \(\sqrt2\) in \(\ell_2\) norm.


Proof. 

The record lands in the one shard its hash points to, and every other shard, and so every other teacher, is unchanged. Shards cut by position would not do, since one inserted record would shift every later record into the next shard. The script cuts by position only because, on its one fixed dataset, that is the same as a fixed assignment.
The changed teacher may vote differently, so one count goes down by 1 and another goes up by 1, or nothing changes. One vote is replaced, so this is the change of a histogram under replace in Proposition 20.2, with \(\ell_1\) norm \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(\ell_2\) norm \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2\).




Theorem 42.1 (The cost of noisy votes) Under add/remove neighbours, with the shards fixed in advance:

Each LNMax answer is \((2/b)\)-DP (Papernot et al. 2017).
Each GNMax answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP for every \(\alpha > 1\) (Papernot, Song, Mironov, Raghunathan, Talwar & Erlingsson 2018, Proposition 8).
\(Q\) GNMax answers, even on adaptively chosen queries, are \((\alpha, Q\alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP. A budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) therefore needs the noise \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{42.3}\]



Proof. The plan is to read LNMax as report-noisy-max and GNMax as a Gaussian mechanism followed by post-processing, then to compose and solve for the noise.

LNMax. LNMax is report-noisy-max (Theorem 22.4) with the counts as scores, each moving by at most 1. By Lemma 42.1 one count may go up while another goes down, so the scores are not monotone, and the theorem’s scale \(b = 2/\varepsilon\) applies. Solving for \(\varepsilon\) gives \(2/b\).
GNMax. Adding \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to every count is the Gaussian mechanism on a histogram of \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt2\), so its noise multiplier is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\). The Gaussian curve of Theorem 29.1, \(\alpha\) over twice the squared multiplier, gives \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2(\sigma/\sqrt2)^2} = \frac{\alpha}{\sigma^2}. \tag{42.4}\] The argmax reads only this output, so by post-processing (Theorem 29.3) it cannot raise the curve.
Compose. Each answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP whatever the earlier answers were, so by adaptive composition (Theorem 29.2) the curves of \(Q\) answers add to \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\).
Calibrate. That curve is the line with slope \(Q/\sigma^2\). Setting the slope to \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) and solving for \(\sigma\) gives Equation 42.3.





Example 42.1 Table 42.2 gives the noise for four numbers of answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\), with the Laplace scale also shown as a standard deviation, \(\sqrt2b\).

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.2 How accurate is a noisy vote
text:
42.2 How accurate is a noisy vote
The cost of an answer does not depend on the teachers, but its accuracy depends almost only on them. This section asks how likely the noisy vote is to return the plurality label and the right label, which you need to choose the number of teachers. Whether GNMax picks one label over another depends only on the difference of their two noises, and that difference is \(\mathcal N(0, 2\sigma^2)\), because the variances of independent variables add.

Proposition 42.1 (Accuracy of a noisy vote) Let \(\Phi\) be the standard normal distribution function. On two labels with gap \(g\), GNMax returns the plurality label with probability \[\Pr[\text{plurality}] = \Phi\Big(\frac{g}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}\Big). \tag{42.5}\] On \(m\) labels, it misses the plurality with probability at most \[\tilde\beta = \sum_{i \ne i^*}\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\Big(\frac{N_{i^*} - N_i}{2\sigma}\Big), \tag{42.6}\] where \(\operatorname{erfc}\) is the complementary error function (Papernot et al. 2018, Proposition 7). If a fraction \(a(x)\) of the teachers vote for the correct label on a two-label query \(x\), the answer is correct with probability \(\Phi\big(k(2a(x) - 1)/(\sqrt2\sigma)\big)\), and the expected accuracy is the average of this over queries.


Proof. 

Two labels. GNMax returns label 1 when \(N_1 + Z_1 > N_2 + Z_2\), that is, when the noise difference \(Z_2 - Z_1\) is below \(N_1 - N_2\). That difference is \(\mathcal N(0, 2\sigma^2)\), so the event has probability \(\Phi((N_1 - N_2)/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), and with label 1 the plurality, \(N_1 - N_2 = g\).
Many labels. GNMax misses the plurality only if some other label beats it, and the chance of a union of events is at most the sum of their chances. By step 1, label \(i\) beats the plurality with probability \(\Phi(-(N_{i^*} - N_i)/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), which equals \(\frac12\operatorname{erfc}((N_{i^*} - N_i)/(2\sigma))\) because \(\Phi(-u) = \frac12\operatorname{erfc}(u/\sqrt2)\).
Toward the truth. The gap toward the correct label is the number of teachers that are right minus the number that are wrong, \(ka - k(1 - a) = k(2a - 1)\). Step 1 with this signed gap gives the chance of a correct answer, and averaging over queries gives the expected accuracy.


For a fixed number of answers and budget, \(\sigma\) is fixed, while the signal \(k(2a - 1)\) grows with \(k\). But each teacher then sees \(n/k\) records and is right less often, so \(2a - 1\) shrinks, and which effect wins depends on how fast a teacher’s accuracy falls with its shard size.
The noiseless plurality vote is an ordinary ensemble, and its accuracy is the ceiling of every private answer, since noise only pulls answers toward a coin flip. Equation 42.5 is exact, because two labels have one competitor, while Equation 42.6 is loose when many labels are nearly tied with the plurality.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.3 Private answers against a private model
text:
42.3 Private answers against a private model
You have a budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). You can spend it on training one model with DP-SGD, whose answers are then free, or on answering queries one at a time with a teacher ensemble. This section asks which gives more accurate answers, and how the choice depends on the number of queries you expect. Write \(A_{\mathrm{model}}(\varepsilon)\) for the accuracy of a privately trained model and \(A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon)\) for the expected accuracy of \(Q\) private answers at the same budget.

Proposition 42.2 (The break-even number of queries) Suppose that \(A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon)\) decreases in \(Q\), as it does when the plurality is correct on most queries. Then private answers are more accurate than a private model exactly when \[Q < Q^*(\varepsilon) = \max\{Q : A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon) \ge A_{\mathrm{model}}(\varepsilon)\}, \tag{42.7}\] with \(Q^* = 0\) when even one answer is worse than the model.


Proof. 

The model is constant in \(Q\). Every query to a released model is post-processing of its weights (Theorem 19.1), so it costs nothing and is as accurate as the model.
The vote falls toward \(\frac12\). By Equation 42.3, \(\sigma\) grows like \(\sqrt Q\), and by Proposition 42.1 each answer is correct with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\) for its signed gap \(g\). That chance falls toward \(\frac12\) as \(\sigma\) grows when the gap is positive, which is why the hypothesis holds when most gaps are positive.
Break-even. A decreasing function crosses a constant at most once, and the last \(Q\) before the crossing is \(Q^*\).


DP-SGD pays a fixed price, which at small \(\varepsilon\) is a much worse model, while the vote’s first answers are almost as good as the noiseless ensemble. So private prediction wins when the budget is small and the queries are few. At large \(\varepsilon\) the ensemble’s ceiling decides, and a million queries are out of reach either way, since they need a \(\sigma\) a hundred times that of 100 answers.
The comparison assumes that you can run DP-SGD. With LLMs behind an interface, or parties who will not pool their data, private prediction is the only private option.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.4 PATE: from private answers to a private model
text:
42.4 PATE: from private answers to a private model
Private answers cost budget forever, while a private model costs it once. PATE spends the budget on labelling a fixed number of public, unlabelled inputs with private answers, then trains a new model on them and releases only that model. This section asks how private the released model is, and how good it can be.

Definition 42.2 (PATE) Train teachers as in Definition 42.1 and label \(Q\) public inputs \(x_1, \dots, x_Q\) by GNMax with noise \(\sigma\). Then train a student on these inputs and labels, by any algorithm, possibly with other public data. The student is released, and the teachers never are.

The student never sees a private record, only public inputs and private labels, so its privacy should be that of the labels.

Theorem 42.2 (Privacy of the PATE student) The student of Definition 42.2, and every prediction it ever makes, is \((\alpha, Q\alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP, and so \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 42.2, even when each input to be labelled is chosen after seeing the earlier labels. The cost depends on nothing about the student.


Proof. 

The only private output is the labels. The student’s training sees the public inputs, which do not depend on the private data, and the \(Q\) labels, never the teachers or the records.
The labels are \(Q\) GNMax answers. By Theorem 42.1 they cost \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\), and adaptive composition lets the student choose which inputs to ask about.
Post-processing. The student’s weights are a function of the labels and of public data, so by Theorem 29.3 they are as private as the labels, and so is every prediction computed from them.


Three things limit the student. It is trained on \(Q\) examples rather than \(n\), its labels are noisy, and the plurality vote has the ensemble’s ceiling. More labels mean more noise per label by Equation 42.3, so each \(\varepsilon\) has a best \(Q\). The semi-supervised students of Papernot et al. (2017, 2018) also learn from unlabelled public inputs, which this chapter’s student does not.
PATE needs public, unlabelled inputs from the same distribution as the private data. The teachers are non-private models of their shards and must stay secret (Part 2 attacks them).

Example 42.4 Take \(k = 250\) teachers, whose plurality vote labels the public pool with accuracy 0.9322. The student is the part’s network, trained non-privately for 2,000 steps on the first \(Q\) public inputs and their GNMax labels (Table 42.6; the first two rows have no privacy).
