title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.3 User-level DP-SGD
Accounting for users after the fact charges a heavy user for every one of their records, and Table 44.2 shows the bill. The alternative changes the algorithm, so that the unit DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for is the user. McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang (2018) introduced it for federated learning, where each user’s device computes an update on its own data. This section states the algorithm and asks what it guarantees.

Definition 44.2 (User-level DP-SGD) Fix \(U\) users, a user sampling rate \(q\), a clipping norm \(C\), a noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and a learning rate \(\eta\), and start from weights \(\theta_0\) chosen independently of the data. For \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Sample users. Put each user in the set \(S_t\) independently with probability \(q\).
Per-user update. For each \(u \in S_t\), compute one vector \(\bar g_u\) from user \(u\)’s records alone. It can be their average gradient \(\bar g_u = \frac1{n_u}\sum_{i \in u}\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta_t; z_i)\), or the change in weights after a few local steps of SGD on those records.
Clip per user. Set \(\tilde g_u = \bar g_u\min(1, C/\|\bar g_u\|)\).
Noisy sum. Set \(G_t = \sum_{u\in S_t}\tilde g_u + \xi_t\) with \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\).
Step. Set \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,G_t/(qU)\).


The proof of DP-SGD used four properties of the clipped sum. Each one still holds with users in place of records, so the accountant should not change.

Theorem 44.2 (User-level DP-SGD keeps the record-level accountant) In Definition 44.2, suppose each \(\bar g_u\) is computed from user \(u\)’s records alone and the number of users \(U\) is public. Then releasing \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with \(\varepsilon\) given by Equation 44.4 and \(q\) the user sampling rate.


Proof. The plan is to check the four properties that the proof for records uses, one at a time.

One user moves the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Fix the weights \(\theta_t\) and the other sampled users. Each \(\tilde g_v\) is computed from user \(v\)’s records alone, so adding user \(u\) leaves every other term unchanged and adds \(\tilde g_u\), of length at most \(C\). However many records \(u\) has, they enter only through \(\tilde g_u\).
One step is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism over users. User \(u\) enters \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), independently of the other users. So the output with \(u\) is a mixture: the same as without \(u\) with probability \(1 - q\), and shifted by \(\tilde g_u\) with probability \(q\). After rescaling by \(C\) and rotating the shift onto one axis, the worst case is the record-level pair, whose curve is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\).
The division is post-processing. Dividing by \(qU\) uses only public numbers, as dividing by \(n\) does in example-level DP-SGD.
Compose and convert. RDP composition over the \(T\) adaptive steps and Equation 44.4 finish the proof.


The count that matters is the number of units. User-level DP-SGD has the privacy of example-level DP-SGD on a dataset of \(U\) records. To keep an expected batch of \(B\) units, its sampling rate must be \(B/U\), larger than \(B/n\) by the average number of records per user, so amplification is weaker. On the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 units, a record-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) at \(q = 0.01\). A user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 3.78\) at \(q = 0.1\). With \(C = 0.5\), the noise on the averaged update, \(\sigma C/B\), is then 0.0189 against 0.00389, about five times larger. That is the honest price of protecting people. There are ten times fewer of them than records, so the sampling rate is ten times larger, and the noise must grow to make up for the weaker amplification.
In return, the records inside a user are free. The guarantee does not depend on \(n_u\), so a user’s records can be averaged, used for several local steps or subsampled, as long as the result is one clipped vector computed from that user’s data alone. More records per user then improve each \(\bar g_u\) while the noise stays fixed (Levy et al. 2021). The proof does assume two things. Step 1 rules out any computation that mixes users, such as normalizing features by an average over users, and it fails if one person’s records are spread over several accounts, since the unit is then the account and the person is again a group. Step 2 needs users to be Poisson-sampled, and iterating over users in a shuffled order is a different mechanism, as it is for records.
A common variant keeps the code for per-example gradients. It replaces steps 2 and 3 by per-record clipping and a cap: keep at most \(k\) records per user, clip each record’s gradient to \(C\), and sum them. One user can then move the sum by \(kC\), so the variant should pay for the cap in noise.

Proposition 44.3 (Per-record clipping inside user sampling) Run Definition 44.2 with users sampled whole at rate \(q\), but let each user’s vector be the sum of at most \(k\) of their records’ gradients, each clipped to \(C\). Then each step has the RDP curve of noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), whose Rényi moment at integer order \(\alpha\) is \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{k^2(j^2 - j)}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{44.14}\]


Proof. 

The user’s shift. The user’s vector is a sum of at most \(k\) vectors of length at most \(C\), so its length is at most \(kC\). The user is still sampled as a whole with probability \(q\).
The pair. In units of \(C\), step 2 of the proof of Theorem 44.2 now compares \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) with \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(k, \sigma^2)\).
Rescale. Dividing the output by \(k\) is an invertible map, so it changes no divergence. It gives the pair with shift 1 and noise \(\sigma/k\), whose moment is Equation 44.3 with \(\sigma/k\) in place of \(\sigma\), which is Equation 44.14.


This chapter’s script checks Equation 44.14 at \(k = 2\) and \(\alpha = 3\), where it and the binomial sum at \(\sigma/k\) both give \(8.219438 \times 10^{-2}\). So clipping each record and summing at most \(k\) of them reuses existing code but pays a factor \(k\) in noise multiplier. Averaging before clipping costs no extra noise, whatever the user’s size, and it gives every user a vector of the same kind whatever their size, which keeps the clipping norm meaningful across users. Summing a user’s gradients and then clipping the sum is also valid, with sensitivity \(C\), and Section 44.5 shows that it gives heavy users more weight.

Example 44.3 Table 44.3 gives the noise multiplier for four user-level budgets, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 sampled units. The column “record-level” is the noise that protects only records. Column (a) is example-level DP-SGD on all 10,000 records at \(q = 0.01\), accounted by Theorem 44.1 for the largest user, with \(k = 348\). Column (b) is user-level DP-SGD at \(q = 0.1\). title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.4 Contribution bounding
User-level DP-SGD needs a data pipeline that groups records by user and computes one vector per user. Many training pipelines are built around records instead, with shuffled files of examples, per-example gradient code and fixed-length batches. This section asks whether you can keep such a pipeline and still protect users. You can, if you limit how many records each user contributes, and the question becomes what limit to choose.

Definition 44.3 (Contribution bounding) Contribution bounding with cap \(k\) keeps at most \(k\) records of each user and discards the rest. The records kept for user \(u\) are chosen from \(u\)’s own records, with randomness independent of everything else, for example uniformly at random. The bounded dataset has \(n_k = \sum_u\min(n_u, k)\) records.

After bounding, a user-level neighbour is a group of at most \(k\) records of one user, and Theorem 44.1 already accounts for exactly that.

Theorem 44.3 (Bounding gives a user-level guarantee) Run example-level DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q\) on the dataset bounded at cap \(k\). The result is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with \(\varepsilon\) given by Equation 44.4 applied to the curve \(T\varepsilon_k(\alpha)\) of Theorem 44.1 for a user with \(k\) records.


Proof. 

Bounding acts on each user separately. Write the bounded dataset as the union over users of \(\pi(D_u)\), where \(D_u\) is user \(u\)’s records and \(\pi\) keeps at most \(k\) of them. Adding user \(u\) adds \(\pi(D_u)\) and changes nothing else, because \(\pi\) looks only at \(u\)’s records and uses independent randomness. So user-level neighbours become datasets that differ in at most \(k\) records, all of one user. A rule that looked at other users’ data, such as keeping the records most similar to the rest of the dataset, would break this step.
Account for those records. Example-level DP-SGD draws each of the user’s at most \(k\) records independently with probability \(q\), so Theorem 44.1 gives the pair Equation 44.5 for one step. A user with fewer records is a \(k\)-record user some of whose clipped gradients are 0, and the worst case of Theorem 44.1 covers every gradient of length at most \(C\), including 0.
Compose and convert, as in Theorem 44.1 and Equation 44.4.


The cap trades the noise the accountant requires against the data you throw away. Both sides of the trade follow from results above, the noise from Corollary 44.1 and the data from how the expected update weights each record.

Proposition 44.4 (What the cap costs) Under contribution bounding with cap \(k\), two things change as \(k\) grows. When \(kq\) is small and \(\sigma\) large, holding the user-level budget fixed at a fixed \(q\) requires a noise multiplier that grows in proportion to \(kq\). And the expected update gives user \(u\) weight \(\min(n_u, k)/n_k\) instead of \(n_u/n\), so every user with more than \(k\) records loses weight.


Proof. 

The noise. For large \(\sigma\), \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\), so the per-step curve of Equation 44.12 becomes about \(\frac\alpha2(kq/\sigma)^2\). It depends on \(k\), \(q\) and \(\sigma\) only through \(kq/\sigma\), so holding it fixed means \(\sigma \propto kq\). Doubling \(k\) then requires either halving \(q\), which halves the batch, or doubling \(\sigma\).
The weights. Before bounding, the expected update of DP-SGD averages over all \(n\) records, each with weight \(1/n\). After it, the average is over the \(n_k\) kept records, of which user \(u\) has \(\min(n_u, k)\). A user with \(n_u > k\) therefore loses weight, and their records beyond \(k\) are not used at all.


Choosing \(k\) is a bias–variance trade-off. Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina & Vassilvitskii (2019) studied this choice for private empirical risk minimization, and showed that the best cap depends on the distribution of user sizes. A cap above most users’ sizes buys little data at a large noise cost, and a cap below them throws away most of the data, the same trade as choosing a clipping norm. The cap depends on the data, so it should come from public knowledge of the population or be chosen privately. Choosing it by trying several caps and reading test accuracy, as the example below does to show the trade-off, spends privacy that the accountant does not see (Hyperparameter tuning).
Which records to keep also matters. By step 1 of the proof of Theorem 44.3, any rule that looks only at the user’s own records is allowed, and Chua et al. (2024) report that keeping each user’s longest records worked best on one of their language datasets. Bounding also combines with user-level DP-SGD that averages each user’s records, where a cap bounds compute and costs data but no noise.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.5 Heterogeneous users
User sizes are rarely equal. In the running example’s population, the 30 users with at least 50 records each hold 30.6% of the records, while the smallest half of the users hold 10.3% (Figure 44.1). Example-level training weights each user by their number of records, and user-level training does not. This section asks what objective user-level DP-SGD optimizes, and what that means for heavy users.
Averaging over the sampling cancels the factor \(q\), and the noise has mean zero, so the expected update should be a plain average over users of their clipped vectors.

Proposition 44.5 (The expected user-level update) In Definition 44.2, averaged over the user sampling and the noise, the update direction is \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{qU}\Big] = \frac1U\sum_{u=1}^U\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|\bar g_u\|}\Big)\bar g_u, \tag{44.15}\] in which each user’s term has length at most \(C/U\), whatever their number of records. Example-level DP-SGD gives user \(u\)’s records together the weight \(n_u/n\) instead.


Proof. The plan is to average over the sampling and the noise, then bound one user’s weight, then compare it with example-level training.

Average over the sampling. User \(u\) is in \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), so the expected sum of the sampled \(\tilde g_u\) is \(q\sum_u\tilde g_u\). The noise has mean zero.
Divide by \(qU\). The \(q\) cancels, which leaves \(\frac1U\sum_u\tilde g_u\). That is Equation 44.15, by the definition of \(\tilde g_u\).
The weight of one user. Clipping gives \(\|\tilde g_u\| \le C\) for every user, so each term has length at most \(C/U\). The share of any group of users in the update is therefore at most their share of the users.
Example-level. The same computation for DP-SGD over records (DP-SGD) gives each record weight \(1/n\), so user \(u\)’s records together have weight \(n_u/n\).


User-level training therefore changes the objective, not only the noise. With averaged per-user gradients, the model minimizes a clipped version of the average over users of each user’s average loss, \(\frac1U\sum_u\frac1{n_u}\sum_{i\in u}\ell(\theta; z_i)\), rather than the average over records. For a keyboard model, weighting people equally keeps a few very active users from defining everyone’s suggestions. For a model meant to fit the overall distribution of records, it under-weights heavy users’ content, which matters when heavy users differ from light ones.
Clipping caps heavy users a second time. A heavy user’s average gradient is a good estimate, typically short once the model fits their data. But if their data are unusual, the gradient is long and is clipped to \(C\), the user-level analogue of what clipping does to records with large gradients (Disparate impact). Summing a user’s gradients before clipping sits between record weighting and user weighting. A heavy user’s vector is then up to \(n_u\) times longer than one record’s, so their influence rises with \(n_u\) until it reaches \(C\).

Example 44.5 The 30 users with at least 50 records hold 30.6% of the records, and so 30.6% of the weight in the expected example-level update. Under user-level DP-SGD, Proposition 44.5 caps their weight at \(30/1{,}000 = 3.0\%\). To see whether that hurts the model where heavy users’ data are, the script splits the test set by the owner of each test point’s nearest training record. A heavy user’s records were chosen as the nearest neighbours of one seed in 50 dimensions, so they spread widely, and 68.3% of test points have a heavy user’s record as their nearest neighbour. At user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), user-level DP-SGD reaches 0.9361 on those points and 0.9319 on the others, against 0.9607 and 0.9622 for the non-private model. On this task, down-weighting heavy users costs nothing measurable, because one teacher network labels every record, so the light users’ records teach the same function. On data where heavy users’ records follow their own patterns, the same reweighting would cost accuracy on those patterns.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
section: 44.6 Comparing the strategies on the running example
text:
44.6 Comparing the strategies on the running example
Three ways to train the running example with a user-level guarantee are now on the table. Strategy (a) runs example-level DP-SGD on all records, accounted for the heaviest user by Theorem 44.1 with \(k = 348\). Strategy (b) is user-level DP-SGD, with the guarantee of Theorem 44.2. Strategy (c) bounds contributions to two records per user and runs example-level DP-SGD, with the guarantee of Theorem 44.3 at \(k = 2\). This section asks which model is best at the same user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).

Example 44.6 Table 44.5 trains each strategy for 1,000 steps with an expected batch of 100 units, \(C = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 0.5\), at the noise multipliers of Table 44.3, one run each.

Run-to-run variation is of the order of a point at these budgets, which is why the cap of 2 scores 0.8810 here and 0.8920 in its separate run of Table 44.4. The cap \(k = 1\) and user-level DP-SGD on one random record per user are the same algorithm with the same \(\sigma\), and two runs of it gave 0.8917 and 0.9070.

User-level DP-SGD is best at every budget; example-level DP-SGD on all records, accounted for its heaviest user, stays near chance.



Keeping the record as the unit fails. Strategy (a) is at chance, between 0.53 and 0.57, at every budget up to \(\varepsilon = 8\), because the heaviest user dictates the noise for everyone, and a \(\sigma\) between 70.3 and 449 drowns every gradient. This is Figure 44.2 in practice: an example-level pipeline on data with heavy users needs either an enormous \(\varepsilon\) or a cap.
Changing the unit wins. User-level DP-SGD is the best strategy at every budget, with 0.9347 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) against 0.9612 for the non-private model. It needs a little less noise than the cap of 2, and unlike the cap it uses every record, through the per-user average. Its advantage is largest at small budgets, 9.8 points at \(\varepsilon = 1\) against 1.1 points at \(\varepsilon = 8\). Its cost is compute, since each step processes the records of about 100 users, about 1,000 records, ten times what the example-level strategies process. Bounding is the fallback, and strategy (c) keeps the example-level pipeline and loses 5 to 10 points against (b) below \(\varepsilon = 8\). It comes close at \(\varepsilon = 8\), where the noise is small enough that the discarded data, not the noise, limits accuracy.
Published comparisons on language models agree. Chua et al. (2024) find that user-level DP-SGD generally beats contribution bounding, especially at small budgets, and Charles et al. (2024) find that user-level sampling usually wins, though not always.
At \(\varepsilon = 4\) user-level DP-SGD loses 2.7 points against the non-private model, while the record-level model of DP-SGD reached 0.9548 at the same \(\varepsilon\). The difference between 0.9548 and 0.9347 is the price of the unit, since the guarantee now covers the person with 348 records as well as the one with a single record.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.1 Measuring disparate impact
The chapter on private gradient descent trained the part’s running example with differential privacy (DP) at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and lost less than one point of test accuracy: 0.9548 against 0.9610 without privacy. That number is an average over the test set, so it says nothing about who loses the point. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) asked that question. They found that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, concentrates the accuracy it loses on the classes and subgroups that are under-represented in the training data. In their gender classifier the drop was much larger on Black faces than on white faces. They called this the disparate impact of DP on model accuracy. This chapter asks why it happens, how to measure it honestly, and what can be done about it.
The answer lies in the two rules of DP-SGD, which are blind to groups and for that very reason are not neutral. Clipping caps each record’s pull, its contribution to the update, so a group’s pull is at most its share of the records times the cap, however badly the model fits it. The noise is the same for everyone, while the part of the update that serves a group grows with the group’s size, so a small group’s signal is weaker against the same noise. A small group the model finds hard suffers from both, and the two effects compound, because the noise then acts on a pull that clipping has already shrunk.
The running example is the part’s two-layer network on 50-dimensional inputs, with a minority added. Of the \(n = 10{,}000\) training records, 9,500 come from the running example’s training set. The other 500, a share of 5%, lie in another region of input space, where inputs are longer, 8.89 on average against 7.04, which lengthens their gradients. They also follow a rule of their own, one the majority does not teach. Without privacy the model reaches 0.9529 on the majority and 0.9411 on the minority, each measured on 20,000 fresh test records. DP-SGD keeps the running example’s settings from DP-SGD, with neighbours that differ by adding or removing one record. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the majority loses 0.59 points of accuracy and the minority 9.34. Table 45.1 lists the symbols of the chapter.
Before explaining the effect, you need to say what exactly to measure, and to check that it happens on the running example. A gap between the groups’ accuracies is not enough, because the non-private model may already have one, and DP did not cause that part. The right quantity compares each group with itself, trained with and without privacy.
Esipova et al. (2023) use this definition, and Bagdasaryan et al. (2019) compare the same differences. The experiment below is designed to make the comparison fair. Every row trains on the same records with the same recipe, and differs only in the clipping and in the noise multiplier that the accountant of DP-SGD sets for each \(\varepsilon\). Test records are drawn independently, so a measured accuracy near 0.9 on 20,000 of them is a binomial proportion with standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/20{,}000} = 0.0021\), far below the differences in Table 45.2. Training is random, so each row averages three runs. And because the non-private model serves both groups within 1.2 points, the private model is compared with a baseline that is already fair.
Both causes of the effect are already visible in the table. The clipping-only row has no noise at all, yet the minority loses 4.04 points while the majority gains 0.51, so clipping alone is disparate. Adding noise then widens the gap steadily as \(\varepsilon\) falls (Figure 45.1), and the next two sections explain each part. The minority’s runs also vary more, a point Section 45.4 returns to.
The published experiments found the same pattern. Esipova et al. (2023) undersampled class 8 of the MNIST digits to about 1% of the training set. At \(\varepsilon = 5.90\), DP-SGD cost class 2, which kept its usual size, 8.9 points, but class 8 57.9 points (their Table 2).

title: 45  Disparate impact

Definition 45.1 (Privacy cost and disparate impact) Train a model on the same data with the same recipe, once without privacy and once with DP. The privacy cost of group \(g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the recipe is made private, \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big], \tag{45.1}\] where the expectation is over the randomness of private training. DP has disparate impact on groups \(g\) and \(h\) when \(\pi_g \ne \pi_h\), and the privacy cost gap \(|\pi_g - \pi_h|\) measures how much.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.2 Clipping reweights the groups
Clipping without noise gives no privacy at all, yet in Table 45.2 it costs the minority 4.04 points. This section asks how a rule that treats every record the same way can treat groups differently. Each DP-SGD step adds up the clipped gradients of a Poisson batch, adds Gaussian noise, and divides the noisy sum \(G_t\) by the public expected batch size \(B = qn\). Because each record enters the batch with probability \(q\), DP-SGD shows that the average update is the average gradient with each record weighted by how much of it clipping keeps: \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac C{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i. \tag{45.2}\]
The factor in front of each gradient is what the rest of the chapter tracks, record by record and then group by group.

Definition 45.2 (Clipping weights) A record’s clipping weight is \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\), the factor clipping multiplies its gradient by. A group’s clipping weight \(w_g\) is the average of its records’ clipping weights. Group \(g\)’s average gradient and average clipped gradient are \[\bar g_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}g_i, \qquad m_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}\min\Big(1, \frac C{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i. \tag{45.3}\]

Splitting the average update by group shows each group’s pull. Because each clipped gradient is at most \(C\) long, a group’s pull is capped by its share, however large its gradients are. When the gradients within a group point the same way, the cap turns into a reweighting of the groups.

Proposition 45.1 (Clipping reweights the groups) For any gradients, the expected update of DP-SGD is a share-weighted sum of the groups’ average clipped gradients, and each group’s term is at most its share times \(C\) long: \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \sum_gs_g\,m_g, \qquad \|s_g\,m_g\| \le s_g\,C. \tag{45.4}\] Suppose in addition that the records within each group have parallel gradients, and let \(c_g = \|m_g\|/\|\bar g_g\|\) be the fraction of group \(g\)’s average gradient that survives clipping. Then the expected update is the gradient of a reweighted mixture of the groups, \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \Big(\sum_hs_h\,c_h\Big)\sum_g\tilde s_g\,\bar g_g, \qquad \tilde s_g = \frac{s_g\,c_g}{\sum_hs_h\,c_h}, \tag{45.5}\] where the effective shares \(\tilde s_g\) are non-negative and add up to 1. If all of group \(g\)’s records also have the same gradient norm, then \(c_g = w_g\).


Proof. The plan is to regroup the sum, bound each group’s part, and then use parallel gradients to pull a scalar out of each group’s part.

Split the sum. Group the records of the expected update and multiply and divide each group’s part by \(n_g\): \[\frac1n\sum_g\sum_{i\in g}\min\Big(1, \frac C{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i = \sum_g\frac{n_g}n\cdot m_g = \sum_gs_gm_g. \tag{45.6}\]
Bound the pull. Each clipped gradient has length at most \(C\), and the length of an average is at most the average of the lengths, by the triangle inequality. So \(\|m_g\| \le C\), and \(\|s_gm_g\| \le s_gC\).
Parallel gradients. If every \(g_i\) in group \(g\) points along the same unit vector \(e_g\), then \(g_i = \|g_i\|e_g\) and its clipped version is \(\min(\|g_i\|, C)\,e_g\). Averaging, \(m_g\) and \(\bar g_g\) both point along \(e_g\), so \(m_g = c_g\bar g_g\).
Factor out the total. Substituting step 3 into step 1 and multiplying and dividing by \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) gives Equation 45.5. Each \(\tilde s_g\) is a non-negative term divided by the sum of all such terms, so they add up to 1.
Equal norms. If all of group \(g\)’s records have the same norm, the ratio of clipped length to length is the same for each record, namely its clipping weight. So \(c_g\) is that common weight, which is also the group’s average \(w_g\).


Equation 45.5 separates two things clipping does. The factor \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) shortens the update, which a larger learning rate can undo. The effective shares change which mixture of the groups is being descended, and no learning rate undoes that. Esipova et al. (2023) find this error of direction far more harmful than the error of length, especially to the under-represented class (their Table 1). The effective shares also move the end point. Clipped gradient descent stops where \(\sum_gs_gm_g = 0\), so it stops at the optimum of the reweighted mixture, which leans toward the groups whose gradients clipping cuts least.
A group’s effective share falls when its gradients are long compared with \(C\), for two reasons. The model may fit the group badly, since a misclassified record has a large loss derivative and a record classified with a wide margin a small one. Or the group’s inputs may be large, since a dense layer’s per-example gradient norm is the error’s norm times the input’s norm (DP-SGD). Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) identify both factors, and a small group the model has not yet learned has both. That sets up a feedback loop. As the majority is learned, its gradients fall below \(C\) and its weight rises toward 1, while the minority keeps long gradients and a low weight. So the minority is learned more slowly, and its gradients stay long.






Figure 45.2: The clipping example in two dimensions: 95 majority records with gradient (0.2, 0) and 5 minority records with gradient (0, 4). Without clipping the two groups pull about equally hard (black); clipping at C = 0.5 cuts the minority’s pull eightfold and turns the update toward the majority (red). Scaling every gradient by the same factor 1/8 instead keeps the direction (blue).



The smallest case shows the reweighting exactly, before the network shows the feedback loop.

Example 45.2 Take 95 majority records whose gradient is \((0.2, 0)\), already short, and 5 minority records whose gradient is \((0, 4)\), long because the model fits them badly (Figure 45.2). Without clipping the average gradient is \((0.95 \times 0.2, 0.05 \times 4) = (0.19, 0.2)\), of length 0.2759. The five minority records pull as hard as the ninety-five others, since the minority’s component is a fraction \(0.2/0.39 = 0.513\) of the sum of the two components. Clipping at \(C = 0.5\) leaves the majority’s gradients untouched and shrinks the minority’s to length 0.5, so the average becomes \((0.19, 0.05 \times 0.5) = (0.19, 0.025)\), of length 0.1916, and the minority’s fraction falls to 0.116. The update has turned by 39.0 degrees toward the majority.
Here \(c_{\text{maj}} = 1\) and \(c_{\text{min}} = 0.5/4 = 0.125\), so Equation 45.5 gives the minority an effective share of \(0.05 \times 0.125/(0.05 \times 0.125 + 0.95) = 0.0065\) instead of 0.05. Scaling every gradient by \(C/C_{\max}\) instead, with \(C_{\max} = 4\) the largest norm, gives \((0.0238, 0.0250)\). That update is eight times shorter, but at an angle of 0.0 degrees to the true average.

At step 0 both groups are fully clipped, with similar weights, and the minority’s effective share, 0.0495, is its true share. By step 2,500 the majority’s median gradient norm has fallen to \(3.8 \times 10^{-4}\), while the minority’s is still 2.7 and 70% of its records are clipped. The minority’s effective share has fallen to 0.0251, half its true share, exactly while it most needs to be learned, with test accuracy 0.6724 against the majority’s 0.9569. The share recovers only as the minority is learned, to 0.0387 at the end.

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.3 The noise floor of a small group
text:
45.3 The noise floor of a small group
Clipping explains the clipping-only row of Table 45.2, but not why the gap keeps widening as \(\varepsilon\) falls. The noise is added to the sum and is the same for everyone, so this section asks why it should hurt a small group more than a large one. The reason is that the noise competes with each group’s signal, and a group’s signal in the sum is proportional to its size. On the averaged update the noise has standard deviation \(\tau = \sigma C/B\) per coordinate, whatever the data. In the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\tau = 1.36 \times 0.5/100 = 0.0068\).
DP-SGD explains why training works at all when each step’s noise is ten times longer than its signal. The signal keeps pointing the same way, so it adds up in proportion to the number of steps, while independent noise adds up only in proportion to its square root. Apply the same argument to the part of the signal that serves one group. That part is proportional to the group’s share when each of its records pulls about as hard as any other, and the argument gives a first law.

Proposition 45.2 (Break-even time of a group’s signal) Suppose each step moves the weights by a signal that keeps pointing the same way, plus noise that is independent from step to step, has mean zero and has root-mean-square length \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\). Let \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) be the length of the signal the whole population shares, and suppose the part that serves group \(g\) has length \(s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\). Then after \(t\) steps the group’s accumulated signal is longer than the root-mean-square length of the accumulated noise exactly when \(t > t_g\), where \[t_g = \frac1{s_g^2}\Big(\frac{\ell_{\text{noise}}}{\ell_{\text{sig}}}\Big)^2. \tag{45.7}\] That is \(1/s_g^2\) times as many steps as a signal the whole population shares needs.


Proof. 

The signal adds up. The group’s signal points the same way at every step, so after \(t\) steps its length is \(t\,s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\).
The noise adds up more slowly. The noise vectors are independent with mean zero, so the cross terms of the squared length of their sum average to zero, and the squared lengths add. The sum has mean squared length \(t\,\ell_{\text{noise}}^2\), so its root-mean-square length is \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt t\).
Compare. The signal is longer when \(t\,s_g\ell_{\text{sig}} > \ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt t\). Dividing both sides by \(\sqrt t\,s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\) and squaring gives \(t > t_g\).


The law compares the group’s signal with the whole noise vector, as DP-SGD does for the full signal, so it is a rough clock, not an exact threshold.
The break-even law says when a group’s signal can emerge, but not where training settles once it has. For that, take a model simple enough to solve exactly. Each group has its own block of weights, which no other group’s loss touches, and its loss is quadratic in them. Step 3 of the proof below needs one fact about a number that is pulled toward zero at each step and kicked by fresh noise.

Lemma 45.1 (A shrinking recursion with noise settles at a fixed variance) Fix a pull strength \(a\) with \(0 < a < 2\). Let the noise terms \(\zeta_t\) be independent of each other and of the start \(x_0\), with mean zero and variance \(\omega^2\), and let a number evolve as \[x_{t+1} = (1 - a)x_t + \zeta_t. \tag{45.8}\] Then the variance of \(x_t\) converges to \[V = \frac{\omega^2}{a(2 - a)}, \tag{45.9}\] and the distance of the variance from \(V\) shrinks by the factor \((1 - a)^2\) at every step, so the starting point is forgotten after about \(1/a\) steps.


Proof. 

One step of variance. The noise \(\zeta_t\) is independent of \(x_t\), so the variances of the two terms add, and the constant factor \(1 - a\) multiplies the variance by its square. Writing \(V_t\) for the variance of \(x_t\), \[V_{t+1} = (1 - a)^2V_t + \omega^2. \tag{45.10}\]
The fixed point. The \(V\) of the statement solves \(V = (1 - a)^2V + \omega^2\), because \(1 - (1 - a)^2 = a(2 - a)\).
Convergence. Subtracting the fixed-point equation from step 1 gives \(V_{t+1} - V = (1 - a)^2(V_t - V)\). Since \(0 < a < 2\), the factor \((1 - a)^2\) is below 1, so \(V_t\) converges to \(V\). For small \(a\) the factor after \(t\) steps is \((1 - a)^{2t} \approx e^{-2at}\), which is small once \(t\) is a few times \(1/a\).


A weak pull lets the noise accumulate, and halving the pull roughly doubles the variance. The theorem below applies the lemma to each weight of a group, and the variance it settles at is the group’s noise floor. Section M.5 in the appendices derives a per-step decomposition of a group’s loss change, due to Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021), and recovers the same floor from it.

Theorem 45.1 (The noise floor of a group) Suppose group \(g\)’s loss depends only on its own block \(\theta_g\) of \(d_g\) weights, which no other group’s loss touches, as \(L_g = \frac\lambda2\|\theta_g - \theta_g^*\|^2\) with curvature \(\lambda > 0\) and optimum \(\theta_g^*\). The training objective is the share-weighted average \(\sum_gs_gL_g\), and gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta\), where \(0 < \eta s_g\lambda < 2\), adds independent noise of standard deviation \(\tau\) per coordinate to the averaged gradient at each step. Then group \(g\)’s expected loss settles at \[\mathbb E[L_g] = \frac{d_g\,\eta\,\tau^2}{2\,s_g\,(2 - \eta s_g\lambda)} \approx \frac{d_g\,\eta\,\tau^2}{4\,s_g}, \tag{45.11}\] and it takes about \(1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps to get there. If clipping multiplies the group’s gradient by a constant factor \(c_g\), as in Proposition 45.1, the same holds with \(s_gc_g\) in place of \(s_g\).


Proof. The plan is to write one step for a single weight of the group, recognize the recursion of Lemma 45.1, and add up the resulting variances into a loss.

The group’s gradient. Only group \(g\)’s loss depends on \(\theta_g\), and it enters the objective with weight \(s_g\). So the objective’s gradient with respect to \(\theta_g\) is \(s_g\lambda(\theta_g - \theta_g^*)\).
One step. Write \(x = \theta_g - \theta_g^*\) for the distance from the optimum and \(\tau\xi\) for the noise, with \(\xi\) standard normal. The update \(\theta_g \leftarrow \theta_g - \eta(s_g\lambda x + \tau\xi)\) moves each coordinate as \[x \leftarrow (1 - \eta s_g\lambda)x - \eta\tau\xi. \tag{45.12}\]
Stationary variance. This is the recursion of Lemma 45.1 with \(a = \eta s_g\lambda\) and noise variance \(\omega^2 = \eta^2\tau^2\). So each coordinate settles at variance \[\frac{\eta^2\tau^2}{\eta s_g\lambda(2 - \eta s_g\lambda)} = \frac{\eta\tau^2}{s_g\lambda(2 - \eta s_g\lambda)}, \tag{45.13}\] and gets there after about \(1/a = 1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps.
Excess loss. The loss is \(\frac\lambda2\) times the sum of the squared coordinates over the group’s \(d_g\) weights, so its expectation is \(\frac\lambda2d_g\) times step 3’s variance, which is Equation 45.11. For a small group \(\eta s_g\lambda\) is small, so \(2 - \eta s_g\lambda \approx 2\), which gives the approximate form.
With clipping. If clipping multiplies the group’s gradient by \(c_g\), the group’s term in step 1 becomes \(s_gc_g\lambda(\theta_g - \theta_g^*)\), while the noise is unchanged. Steps 2 to 4 then hold with \(s_gc_g\) in place of \(s_g\).


The floor scales like one over the share. A group with a twentieth of the records sits at about twenty times the excess loss of a group with all of them, and takes twenty times longer to get there. The curvature \(\lambda\) cancels, because a sharper loss is pulled back harder but also pays more for each unit of noise. The share does not cancel, because it scales the group’s pull back to the optimum while the noise stays the same size. Waiting does not help either, because at a fixed budget more steps need more noise per step. DP-SGD shows that, for a small sampling rate, doubling the steps doubles the noise variance per step. The break-even count of Equation 45.7 is proportional to that variance, so it doubles too, and grows as fast as the run. Finally, the two mechanisms compound, so a group that is 5% of the data and whose gradients clipping halves pays the floor of a group of 2.5%.
The quadratic model is exact for what it assumes, as the simulation below confirms, but a network is not quadratic and its groups do not use disjoint weights. Where the minority’s task overlaps the majority’s, the majority’s gradient does part of the minority’s work, and the penalty is smaller. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto’s decomposition needs no disjoint weights, but it leaves the role of the share implicit, while the quadratic model makes it explicit.

Example 45.4 Take the noise of the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\tau = 0.0068\), with \(d_g = 51\) weights per group, \(\lambda = 1\) and \(\eta = 0.5\). Table 45.4 compares Equation 45.11 with a simulation of 40,000 noisy steps, averaged over the second half.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.4 Measuring per-group accuracy
Every number so far was measured on 20,000 test records per group. Real evaluations are not so generous. A test split of 2,000 records with a 5% minority holds 100 minority records. This section asks how precisely a group’s accuracy, and the gap between two groups, can be measured, and how much a single training run says.
Given the trained model, each test record of a group is classified correctly or not, independently, with probability equal to the group’s true accuracy \(p_g\). This needs the test records to be drawn independently from the group. Then the number correct is binomial, and the Clopper–Pearson interval of Theorem 4.7, built from exact binomial tail probabilities, covers the true accuracy with probability at least 95%. For the gap between two groups, the two counts come from different test records, so their variances add. Training adds a second source of variation, since a different run gives a different model.

Proposition 45.3 (Measuring a gap between groups) Fix a trained model with true accuracies \(p_g\) and \(p_h\) on groups \(g\) and \(h\), and measure them as \(\hat p_g\) and \(\hat p_h\) on disjoint sets of \(n^{\text{test}}_g\) and \(n^{\text{test}}_h\) test records. Then \(\hat p_g - \hat p_h\) has mean \(p_g - p_h\) and variance \(p_g(1 - p_g)/n^{\text{test}}_g + p_h(1 - p_h)/n^{\text{test}}_h\), and for large counts an approximate 95% interval for the gap is \[(\hat p_g - \hat p_h) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_g(1 - \hat p_g)}{n^{\text{test}}_g} + \frac{\hat p_h(1 - \hat p_h)}{n^{\text{test}}_h}}. \tag{45.14}\] If the model itself is the output of a random training run, the variance of one run’s measured accuracy on group \(g\) is the average test-set variance plus the run-to-run variance of the true accuracy: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat p_g) = \mathbb E\Big[\frac{p_g(1 - p_g)}{n^{\text{test}}_g}\Big] + \operatorname{Var}(p_g). \tag{45.15}\]


Proof. 

The gap. Given the model, each count is binomial, so \(\hat p_g\) has mean \(p_g\) and variance \(p_g(1 - p_g)/n^{\text{test}}_g\). The two counts come from disjoint test records, so they are independent, and the variance of a difference of independent estimates is the sum of their variances. For large counts the difference is approximately normal by the central limit theorem, and 1.96 standard deviations on each side cover 95%. Replacing the true accuracies by the measured ones in the variance gives Equation 45.14.
Two sources. Over training runs the true accuracy \(p_g\) is itself random. The law of total variance splits the variance of \(\hat p_g\) into the average of its variance given the model, which is step 1’s test-set variance, plus the variance of its mean given the model, which is \(\operatorname{Var}(p_g)\).


The second term is the one a larger test set cannot touch, because only repeated training estimates it. In Table 45.2 the run-to-run standard deviation at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is 0.0211 for the minority against 0.0037 for the majority, almost six times as large. So a comparison of two training recipes on one run each can easily be reversed for the small group. DP-SGD draws the same lesson for overall accuracy, and for a small group it is sharper. The first term, the test-set variance, grows as the group’s test records shrink, so small groups need intervals. A 5-point gap between groups can be seen only with a few hundred minority test records, and a 1-point gap only with thousands. Per-group accuracies on private test data are themselves statistics of that data, and publishing them needs its own privacy analysis (Choosing ε).






Figure 45.5: Width of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval for a group’s accuracy against the number of test records in the group, for observed accuracies 0.95 and 0.7, on log scales. The width falls like one over the square root of the number of records.




Example 45.6 Train the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\) once. On all 20,000 minority test records its accuracy is 0.8641. Table 45.6 measures it on random subsets.

With 100 minority records, the split that a 2,000-record test set with a 5% minority would give, the estimate is 0.880. That is 1.6 points above the true 0.8641, and the interval is 13.6 points wide. The non-private model’s 0.9411 from Table 45.2 lies only just above its upper end, 0.936. So on this test set alone the minority’s privacy cost could be anywhere from about half a point to fourteen points. With 500 records the interval is 6.5 points wide, and the majority’s, from 1,900 records at a higher accuracy, is 2 points wide.
By Equation 45.14 the gap between the groups, measured on the 1,900 and the 100 records, is \(0.954 - 0.880 = 0.074\), with a standard error of \(\sqrt{0.954 \times 0.046/1{,}900 + 0.88 \times 0.12/100} = 0.0329\). Its 95% interval is therefore \(0.074 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0329 = 0.074 \pm 0.064\), from 0.010 to 0.138. The gap is real, but it could be anywhere from one point to fourteen. And this is one training run. By Table 45.2 the minority’s accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 4\) varies by 0.0211 from run to run on top of this.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.5 Mitigations and what they cost
Both mechanisms come from DP-SGD’s two knobs, the clipping norm and the noise. This section asks whether you can set the knobs, or change the algorithm, so that small groups pay less without spending more privacy. Each fix moves cost around rather than removing it, and it is worth knowing where to.
The first idea is to stop clipping from turning the update. Global scaling multiplies every per-example gradient by the same factor \(C/C_{\max}\), where \(C_{\max}\) is a bound that no gradient’s norm exceeds, and then adds noise \(\sigma C\) to the sum. Nothing is clipped, so the direction is right, as the blue arrow of Figure 45.2 shows. Write \(S_t\) for the batch and \(\xi\) for a standard normal vector.

Proposition 45.4 (Global scaling is a large clipping norm) Suppose no per-example gradient is longer than \(C_{\max}\). Then one step of global scaling with learning rate \(\eta\) is one step of DP-SGD with the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and learning rate \(\eta C/C_{\max}\): \[\frac\eta B\Big(\frac C{C_{\max}}\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma C\xi\Big) = \frac{\eta C/C_{\max}}B\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma C_{\max}\xi\Big). \tag{45.16}\] Both have the same privacy guarantee.


Proof. 

Factor out the scale. Both terms inside the left-hand bracket carry the factor \(C/C_{\max}\), since \(\sigma C = (C/C_{\max})\,\sigma C_{\max}\). Moving it in front of the bracket gives the right-hand side.
Recognize DP-SGD. With the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\) and no gradient longer than \(C_{\max}\), DP-SGD clips nothing, so its clipped sum is \(\sum_ig_i\) and its noise is \(\sigma C_{\max}\xi\). That is the right-hand bracket, with learning rate \(\eta C/C_{\max}\).
Privacy. Each scaled gradient is at most \(C\) long and the noise is \(\sigma C\), so the ratio of sensitivity to noise is \(1/\sigma\), as for DP-SGD at the same \(\sigma\), and the same accountant applies.


So global scaling gets the direction right and pays in noise. It is the large-\(C\) end of the clipping-norm curve of DP-SGD with \(\eta C\) fixed, where the noise is as large as possible relative to the gradients. The bound must be fixed in advance, because a bound read off the training data would make the sensitivity depend on the data. Esipova et al. (2023) instead clip the rare gradients above \(C_{\max}\) and adapt it from a privately estimated count of the gradients that exceed it. They report a smaller privacy cost gap than DP-SGD and earlier mitigations, without group labels.
Group-aware methods do need group labels. Xu, Du & Wu (2021) give groups that are clipped more a larger clipping norm, and Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) penalize the differences between groups in the terms of their decomposition. Both need each training record’s group, which is itself sensitive and may not be lawful to collect, and their per-group statistics must be computed privately. The simplest group-aware fix, multiplying a group’s loss by a weight, fails outright, because clipping scales each long gradient back to length \(C\) whatever the weight.
To give a group more pull, you can give it more records in each batch instead, by sampling its records at a higher rate. Clipping does not undo that, but privacy charges for it. Write \(\varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(q, \sigma, T, \delta)\) for the \(\varepsilon\) that the accountant of DP-SGD gives at sampling rate \(q\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\), \(T\) steps and slack \(\delta\).

Proposition 45.5 (Oversampling a group costs that group’s privacy) Suppose group \(g\)’s records are sampled at rate \(vq\), with \(v > 1\), and the others at rate \(q\), by a rule fixed in advance, and the noisy sum is still divided by \(B = qn\). Then group \(g\)’s term in the expected update grows by the factor \(v\), to \(v\,s_gm_g\). Each of its records has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian mechanism (Gaussian noise on a Poisson-sampled batch) at rate \(vq\), and the algorithm is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_g = \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(vq, \sigma, T, \delta) \;>\; \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(q, \sigma, T, \delta). \tag{45.17}\] So a fixed target \(\varepsilon\) requires the noise multiplier for rate \(vq\).


Proof. 

The pull. Record \(i\) enters the batch with probability \(q_i\), so the expected clipped sum is \(\sum_iq_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\). With \(q_i = vq\) for group \(g\) and division by \(qn\), regrouping as in Proposition 45.1 gives group \(g\) the term \(v\,s_gm_g\).
One record’s privacy. The add/remove analysis of a record \(x\) in DP-SGD compares the output with and without \(x\). With \(x\) present, the output is a mixture of two distributions, one for the steps where \(x\) is in the batch and one for the steps where it is not. The other records’ terms are the same in both, so the mixture’s weights are \(x\)’s own inclusion probability and its complement. A record sampled at rate \(vq\) therefore has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\). The rate may depend on the record’s own group, which is part of the record, but not on anything learned from the data.
The guarantee. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP must hold for every record, so the algorithm’s \(\varepsilon\) is the largest of the per-record values, which is the oversampled group’s. It exceeds the others’ because the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) grows with the sampling rate.


Oversampling therefore buys little at a fixed budget. Fixed at \(\varepsilon = 4\) for every record, sampling the minority four times as often requires \(\sigma = 4.71\) instead of 1.36. The minority’s pull grows by 4 and the noise by \(4.71/1.36 = 3.46\), so its signal-to-noise ratio improves by only \(4/3.46 = 1.16\), while the majority’s falls by 3.46. The majority’s records end at \(\varepsilon = 0.86\), which is wasted budget. Oversampling without changing \(\sigma\) would silently give the minority \(\varepsilon = 20.96\), the weakest privacy for the group already worst served.

None of the three changes helps the minority. A ten times smaller clipping norm clips the minority more, and its accuracy falls by 1.64 points while the majority’s rises by 0.71, the clipping mechanism at work. A ten times larger one clips almost nothing, so the direction is right. But with \(\eta C\) fixed, the learning rate is ten times smaller, so the noise in each step, \(\eta\sigma C/B\), is unchanged while every gradient shorter than 0.5 moves the weights ten times less. By the end of training more than half of the minority’s gradients are that short (Table 45.3), so its signal falls against the noise and it loses 3.44 points, the noise mechanism at work. These differences are of the size of the run-to-run spread, 0.0157 to 0.0211, so their sizes are uncertain.
Oversampling narrows the gap from 9.93 to 3.99 points, but by levelling down. The minority’s accuracy is 2.07 points lower than without it, and the majority’s 8.01 points lower. A smaller gap is not by itself a fairer model, so report both groups’ accuracy and privacy cost, never the gap alone.

Some of the cost is unavoidable. Learning a group’s own rule privately includes estimating statistics of that group’s \(n_g\) records, such as its average features, and private estimation has a price that no algorithm avoids. The fingerprinting bound, Theorem 27.3 in Lower bounds, shows that releasing the means of \(d\) attributes with constant accuracy under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP needs at least about \(\sqrt d/(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) records, whatever the mechanism. A smaller group is a smaller dataset, and no clever clipping makes it larger. Feldman (2020) argues the deeper point for any learner. When the data have a long tail of small subpopulations, fitting them well requires memorizing their few examples, which is exactly what DP forbids. What helps is more data from the group, a larger \(\varepsilon\) with its own costs, or a starting point that already serves the group, such as a public pretrained model (Public data and private fine-tuning).

\(\mathbb E[G_t/B] = \sum_gs_gm_g\), \(\Vert s_gm_g\Vert \le s_gC\); effective shares \(s_gc_g/\sum_hs_hc_h\)

Proposition 45.2

Training longer at a fixed \(\varepsilon\) does not help a small group


Lemma 45.1
\(x_{t+1} = (1 - a)x_t + \zeta_t\) settles at variance \(\omega^2/(a(2 - a))\)
Any noisy descent near an optimum

\(\mathbb E[L_g] \approx d_g\eta\tau^2/(4s_g)\), with \(s_gc_g\) under clipping

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.8 References

Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov, “Differential Privacy Has Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy” (NeurIPS 2019). The observation this chapter explains: DP-SGD’s accuracy loss falls on under-represented and complex groups, and existing gaps grow.
Tran, Dinh & Fioretto, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization under the Fairness Lens” (NeurIPS 2021). Per-step decompositions of a group’s excess risk into clipping and noise terms, for output perturbation and DP-SGD, and the role of gradient norms, input norms, the loss Hessian and the distance to the decision boundary.
Esipova, Ghomi, Luo & Cresswell, “Disparate Impact in Differential Privacy from Gradient Misalignment” (ICLR 2023). Separates clipping’s direction error from its length error, finds the direction error the main cause, and proposes global scaling with an adaptive threshold.
Xu, Du & Wu, “Removing Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy in Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent” (KDD 2021). Group-dependent clipping that equalizes the groups’ clipping bias.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020). Why fitting small subpopulations well requires memorizing their examples, and so conflicts with privacy.
Clopper & Pearson, “The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial” (Biometrika, 1934). The exact interval of Section 45.4.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1 What one (ε, δ) pair says about a membership test
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a budget \(\varepsilon\). DP is the guarantee that one record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), up to a slack \(\delta\). An earlier chapter trained the part’s running example, a small neural network on 10,000 records, with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made private by clipping and Gaussian noise, which is DP-SGD. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) its test accuracy was 0.9175 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9441 at \(\varepsilon = 2\), 0.9548 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and 0.9604 at \(\varepsilon = 8\), against 0.9610 without privacy. Those accuracies are half of a decision. The other half is what each budget means for the people in the data: what an attacker who sees the model can learn about one of them, and how sure it can be.
The one idea of this chapter is that \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is one straight line above a curve. An attacker who asks whether a record was in the training set runs a test with two error rates, and DP bounds the true positive rate by a line in the false positive rate. A training algorithm has a whole trade-off curve, the best true positive rate at each false positive rate, which lies below that line. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the line allows a test that catches every member while almost never accusing a non-member, yet the curve of DP-SGD caps the true positive rate at 0.0589 when the false positive rate is \(10^{-3}\). So choosing \(\varepsilon\) well means computing the curve and reading it where your threat lies, as a bound on membership tests, on beliefs or on reconstruction.
The running example is DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps and \(n = 10{,}000\) records, at six budgets from \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) to 16. Each budget has the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) that the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant of DP-SGD requires at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table 46.1 lists the symbols that recur.
A model card says “trained with \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (8, 10^{-5})\)”. What does that number alone forbid an attacker to do? This question comes first because it is the only one you can answer for a model whose training algorithm you have not seen.
Both rates are probabilities of one event, so DP bounds them directly. By Theorem 18.3, a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when every test obeys two lines, the definition applied to \(S\) and to its complement with the pair swapped. That theorem names the errors \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), but this page keeps \(\alpha\) for the Rényi order of Section 46.2. Since a probability is also at most 1, every membership test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{46.1}\] The advantage \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) measures how much a test beats guessing. It is largest where the two lines cross, and Corollary 18.1 bounds it there: \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{46.2}\]
The line that matters is \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\), which binds at low FPR. Membership inference judges attacks by their TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or below, because an attack that flags members while almost never flagging non-members confidently identifies people. Once \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) reaches 1, the pair allows a perfect TPR, and at \(\varepsilon = 8\) that happens from an FPR of \((1 - 10^{-5})e^{-8} = 3.35\times10^{-4}\) on. So at \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair says nothing where attacks are judged. An audit refutes a claimed budget only when its measured point lies above the line.
The advantage, by contrast, is read where the two error rates are equal. It is 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.9640 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), numbers that make \(\varepsilon = 4\) sound hopeless. But they are tight only for randomized response, whose curve is exactly the two lines, and DP-SGD is not that mechanism.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
Definition 46.1 (Membership test) Fix the training set without the target, \(D^-\), and a target record \(z^*\), so that \(D^-\) and \(D^- \cup \{z^*\}\) are add/remove neighbours, the relation DP-SGD with Poisson sampling uses. The attacker sees an output \(y\), the model or all its iterates, drawn from \(Q = M(D^- \cup \{z^*\})\) if \(z^*\) is a member and from \(P = M(D^-)\) if not. A membership test says “member” on a set \(S\) of outputs. Its false positive rate (FPR) is \(P(S)\), and its true positive rate (TPR) is \(Q(S)\). A randomized test, which says “member” with probability \(\phi(y)\), has rates \(\mathbb E_P[\phi]\) and \(\mathbb E_Q[\phi]\). The privacy loss of an output is \(L(y) = \ln(Q(y)/P(y))\), with \(Q(y)\) and \(P(y)\) the two densities.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.2 The whole curve of DP-SGD
The pair is one point of a privacy profile, the \(\delta\) an accountant reports at each \(\varepsilon\). The accountant could equally have reported \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) or \(10^{-3}\), and each such pair is another line that every test obeys. The best TPR an attacker can reach is the curve that all those lines enclose, and for DP-SGD it can be computed. Here it is computed exactly and compared with the line and with two cheaper summaries, from RDP and from a Gaussian limit.
DP-SGD reduced a run to one pair of distributions per step, the worst case over models, data and directions. In units of the clipping norm, a step’s output is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) without the target and the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) with it. The log of the ratio of the two densities is the privacy loss of one step, \[L_1(y) = \ln\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big). \tag{46.3}\]

Definition 46.2 (Trade-off curve, privacy profile and privacy loss distribution) Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be as in Definition 46.1. The trade-off curve \(\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR})\) is the largest TPR of any test whose false positive rate is at most \(\mathrm{FPR}\). The privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest \(\delta\) with \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\). The privacy loss distribution (PLD) \(\omega\) is the distribution of \(L(y)\) when \(y\) is drawn from \(Q\).

The PLD fixes the other two, because the best tests compare the loss with a threshold. Theorem 32.2 proved a version for curves that treat adding and removing the record alike. A membership test needs only adding, which the proof below handles (Dong, Roth & Su 2022).

Theorem 46.1 (The trade-off curve from the privacy loss) Let \(P\) and \(Q\) have positive densities, privacy loss \(L\) and PLD \(\omega\), and write \(\mathbb E_\omega[X;\ A]\) for the average of \(X\) times the indicator of the event \(A\). The best tests say “member” when \(L\) exceeds a threshold \(\tau\), and they trace the trade-off curve \[\big(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau), \mathrm{TPR}(\tau)\big) = \big(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L};\ L > \tau],\ \omega(L > \tau)\big), \qquad \tau \in \mathbb R. \tag{46.4}\] The curve is the lower envelope of the lines of the privacy profile, \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \inf_{\varepsilon \in \mathbb R}\big(e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big), \qquad \delta(\varepsilon) = Q[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon P[L > \varepsilon], \tag{46.5}\] and the line at \(\varepsilon\) touches it at the threshold test with \(\tau = \varepsilon\), whose FPR is at most \(e^{-\varepsilon}Q[L > \varepsilon]\). For \(T\) steps of DP-SGD, \(\omega\) is the \(T\)-fold convolution of the one-step PLD. Rounding each one-step loss up, or down, to a grid gives a curve above, or below, the true one.


Proof. The plan is to find the best tests, show that every line of the profile lies above them and touches them once, and then compute the PLD of the composed run.

The best tests threshold the loss. The likelihood ratio \(Q(y)/P(y)\) is \(e^{L(y)}\), which increases with \(L\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1), the test with the largest TPR at a given FPR says “member” where \(L(y) > \tau\), randomizing where \(L = \tau\). Its TPR is \(Q[L > \tau]\), which is \(\omega(L > \tau)\).
Its FPR by a change of measure. Both densities are positive, so the definition of \(L\) gives \(P(y) = e^{-L(y)}Q(y)\). The \(P\)-probability of an event is therefore the \(Q\)-average of \(e^{-L}\) over it (Lemma 4.2): \[P[L > \tau] = \mathbb E_Q\big[e^{-L};\ L > \tau\big]. \tag{46.6}\] With step 1, this is Equation 46.4.
Every line lies above the curve. By the definition of the profile, every test has \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\). Taking the smallest right-hand side over \(\varepsilon\) gives “\(\le\)” in Equation 46.5.
The profile is a tail of the loss. We want the event that makes \(Q(S) - e^\varepsilon P(S)\) largest. Since \(P(y) = e^{-L(y)}Q(y)\), adding an output with \(L(y) \le \varepsilon\) adds \(Q(y) - e^\varepsilon P(y) = Q(y)(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)})\), which is not positive, and removing one with \(L(y) > \varepsilon\) removes a positive amount. So the best event is \(\{L > \varepsilon\}\), which gives the formula for \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), as in Lemma 20.2.
Each line touches the curve. By step 4 the threshold test with \(\tau = \varepsilon\) has \(\mathrm{TPR} = e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\), so it lies on the line. Every FPR is reached by some threshold test, with randomization at the threshold, so the infimum is attained at every FPR. On its event \(e^{-L} < e^{-\varepsilon}\), so by step 2 its FPR is at most \(e^{-\varepsilon}Q[L > \varepsilon]\).
Composition adds losses. The steps use independent noise, so the total loss is the sum of the per-step losses (Lemma 19.2). The worst-case pair is the same at every step, so under \(Q\) these losses are independent with one distribution, and \(\omega\) is its \(T\)-fold convolution (Numerical accounting).
A guaranteed bracket. Rounding each one-step loss up to a grid makes every output look more revealing, so the rounded pair is less private and its curve lies above the true one (Numerical accounting). Rounding down gives a curve below it.


The RDP accountant that set \(\sigma\) also gives a curve, at no extra cost. A test turns the two distributions into two coins, and processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence, so the coins must stay within the run’s RDP budget at every order \(\alpha\).

Proposition 46.1 (A trade-off bound from the RDP curve) If \(D_\alpha(Q\|P) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) at each order \(\alpha > 1\), as the RDP accountant of the whole run certifies, then every test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min_{\alpha > 1}\big(\mathrm{FPR}\cdot e^{\varepsilon(\alpha)}\big)^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}. \tag{46.7}\]


Proof. 

Reduce the test to two coins. The test maps \(Q\) to a coin that says “member” with probability TPR, and \(P\) to one that does so with probability FPR. Post-processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence (Theorem 29.3), so at each order \[e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} \ge \mathrm{TPR}^\alpha\mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{TPR})^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha}. \tag{46.8}\]
Drop a term. The second term is not negative, so dropping it keeps the inequality, and \(\mathrm{TPR}^\alpha \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\mathrm{FPR}^{\alpha - 1}\).
Solve for TPR. The power \(1/\alpha\) gives the bound at order \(\alpha\), and since it holds at every order, it holds at the best one.


Theorem 32.6 keeps the dropped term and gives the best curve that RDP allows; Equation 46.7 is looser but closed-form at each order. The Gaussian summary is a limit. By Theorem 32.5, as \(T\) grows with \(q\sqrt T\) fixed, the curve approaches that of \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) (Theorem 4.3). With \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, this Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation is \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \approx 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big), \qquad \mu = q\sqrt{T\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}, \tag{46.9}\] and it is not a bound. Table 46.3 gives each run’s \(\sigma\) and what the three accountants report. Against the upper end of the PLD bracket, the RDP accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\) by between 0.035 (at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\)) and 0.264 (at \(\varepsilon = 4\)), and by 0.58 at \(\varepsilon = 8\).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.3 The Bayesian reading
People who are not statisticians rarely think in error rates. They ask “if someone sees the model, how sure can they be that I was in the data?”, which is a question about posterior probabilities. Read as beliefs, the curve answers it, and the answer depends on what the attacker believed before.
Bayes’ rule in odds form says that the posterior odds of membership are the prior odds times the likelihood ratio \(e^{L(y)}\) (Theorem 4.6). So an attacker with prior \(p\) believes afterwards that the target is a member with probability \(pe^L/(pe^L + 1 - p)\), which grows with the loss. Wherever the loss is at most \(\varepsilon\), Theorem 18.4 bounds this posterior: \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid y] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{46.10}\] Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP the same theorem lets the bound fail only on rare outputs, those whose loss exceeds a higher level. An attacker who acts only on a flag, the test’s verdict “member”, also faces the base rate \(p\), by the same odds rule.

Proposition 46.2 (The precision of a flag) Let a membership test have rates TPR and FPR, and let the attacker’s prior be \(p\). A flag (“the test said member”) is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}} \le \frac{p\,(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta)}{p\,(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta) + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}, \tag{46.11}\] where the bound holds if the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. With \(\delta = 0\) the bound equals Equation 46.10.


Proof. 

The odds of a flag. A flag has probability TPR for a member and FPR for a non-member, so the posterior odds are \(\frac{p}{1 - p}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{TPR}}{\mathrm{FPR}}\). Odds \(o\) convert to the probability \(o/(1 + o)\), which gives the equality.
The bound. The precision increases with TPR, so replacing TPR by its bound from Equation 46.1 can only increase it.
Pure DP. With \(\delta = 0\) the FPR cancels, leaving \(pe^\varepsilon/(pe^\varepsilon + 1 - p)\). A flag is never more convincing than the most convincing single output.


DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief, as Table 46.7 shows at three priors. An attacker who thinks there is a 1% chance that you are in the data can reach at most 2.67% at \(\varepsilon = 1\), but 35.55% at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and 96.79%, near certainty, at \(\varepsilon = 8\).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.4 Reconstruction
Membership is a strict standard for the defender, because the attacker is handed the target record and only has to decide whether it was used. Many harms need more, such as recovering a diagnosis or a face the attacker does not know. The same curve bounds them too, read at a false positive rate set by the attacker’s uncertainty beforehand.

Definition 46.3 (Reconstruction robustness (Balle, Cherubin & Hayes 2022)) An informed adversary knows every training record except the target \(Z\), knows a prior \(\pi\) from which \(Z\) was drawn, sees the trained model, and outputs a guess. It succeeds if the guess is within an error radius \(\xi\) of \(Z\), as measured by an error function \(\mathrm{err}\). The baseline is the best success without the model, \[\kappa = \sup_{z_0}\Pr_{Z \sim \pi}\big[\mathrm{err}(Z, z_0) \le \xi\big], \tag{46.12}\] for example \(\kappa = 1/m\) when \(Z\) is uniform over \(m\) candidates and only an exact guess counts.

The proof below averages one membership test per candidate over the prior, and moving that average inside the curve needs the curve to be concave. Theorem 4.2 proved that every trade-off function, the smallest false negative rate at each FPR, is convex and non-increasing, and \(\mathrm{TPR}^*\) is one minus such a function, so it is concave and non-decreasing.

Theorem 46.2 (Reconstruction is membership at the baseline) If every neighbouring pair of \(M\) has trade-off curve at or below \(\mathrm{TPR}^*\), then every informed reconstruction attack succeeds with probability at most \[\Pr[\text{success}] \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\kappa). \tag{46.13}\] With the pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) this is \(e^\varepsilon\kappa + \delta\), and with one RDP order it is \((\kappa e^{\varepsilon(\alpha)})^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\).


Proof. The plan is to bound each candidate’s test by the curve, then average over the prior, using concavity to bring the average inside.

One test per candidate. Fix \(D^-\) and the attack \(\mathcal A\). For a candidate \(z\), let \(S_z\) be the set of models \(\theta\) for which \(\mathcal A(\theta)\) is within \(\xi\) of \(z\). The attack succeeds on \(z\) exactly when the model trained on \(D^- \cup \{z\}\) falls in \(S_z\).
Bound each test by the curve. “Say member when \(\theta \in S_z\)” is a membership test for \(z\), with \(Q_z = M(D^- \cup \{z\})\) and \(P = M(D^-)\). Its FPR is \(\mathrm{FPR}_z = P(S_z)\), so \(Q_z(S_z) \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}_z)\).
Average over the prior. The success probability is the average of \(Q_Z(S_Z)\) over \(Z \sim \pi\). Because the curve is concave, Jensen’s inequality moves the average inside it: \[\mathbb E_Z[Q_Z(S_Z)] \le \mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}_Z)] \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{FPR}_Z]). \tag{46.14}\]
The average FPR is at most the baseline. The average FPR is the chance that the attack succeeds on a model trained without \(Z\). That model is independent of \(Z\), and for each fixed model the guess is a fixed \(z_0\) (a randomized attack averages such guesses), which succeeds with probability at most \(\kappa\). Since the curve is non-decreasing, Equation 46.13 follows.
The special cases. Substituting the line of Equation 46.1, or Equation 46.7 at one order, for \(\mathrm{TPR}^*\) gives the closed forms.


Balle, Cherubin & Hayes state the pure-DP and RDP forms, and the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form is a corollary given here. With the exact curve of DP-SGD it is the bound of Hayes, Mahloujifar & Balle (2023), who found it close to their best attack. They also found that hyperparameters with the same \(\varepsilon\) have different curves and so different reconstruction success. A large prior uncertainty is a small FPR, which is where the curve of DP-SGD lies far below the line.
A small baseline is an honest assumption only if you can defend it. If the attacker can narrow the target to two candidates, \(\kappa = 0.5\) and reconstruction is as easy as membership at an FPR of 0.5, so a defensible claim states the prior. Guo, Karrer, Chaudhuri & van der Maaten (2022) bound continuous targets differently. Under RDP of order 2 at level \(\varepsilon\), an unbiased reconstruction of a target in an interval of width \(w\) has expected squared error at least \(w^2/(4(e^\varepsilon - 1))\), and Fisher information gives a tighter bound. Section N.4 derives the first and shows why it needs unbiasedness.

Example 46.4 Choosing one of \(m\) equally likely candidates is reconstruction with \(\kappa = 1/m\), so its success bound is the curve at an FPR of \(1/m\), read from Table 46.4 and Table 46.5. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair gives no bound for any \(m\) up to 1,000, but the curve caps the success among 1,000 candidates at 0.0589, against 0.001 by guessing. With only ten candidates the attacker already knows a lot: at \(\varepsilon = 4\) the curve allows 0.3416 against a baseline of 0.1. Among a thousand candidates even \(\varepsilon = 16\) keeps the success at 0.2808, as Balle, Cherubin & Hayes also observed in experiments.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.5 Interpreting δ
Every number so far was at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). What does \(\delta\) mean, how small must it be, and what does a smaller one cost in \(\varepsilon\) for DP-SGD? The answer depends on the losses at which a mechanism uses up its \(\delta\).
The worst way to spend it is to publish records. Proposition 18.3 showed that the mechanism that publishes each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\), is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. On \(n\) records it publishes at least one with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{46.15}\] So \(\delta = 1/n\) permits exposing a record with probability about 0.63, and a meaningful guarantee needs \(n\delta\) well below 1. That mechanism spends \(\delta\) at infinite loss, since a published record is identified with certainty. So the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) prefers guarantees that rule out such failure, such as zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP). DP-SGD spends \(\delta\) at moderate losses, because \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is at most the tail \(Q[L > \varepsilon]\) (Theorem 46.1), which is thin (Table 46.8). So for DP-SGD \(\delta\) is not a probability of catastrophe, and shrinking it raises \(\varepsilon\) only moderately.
How small? NIST SP 800-226 (Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth 2025) calls \(\delta \le 1/n^2\) a common recommendation and \(\delta\) above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious. The running example has \(n\delta = 0.1\), acceptable for DP-SGD but not by the \(1/n^2 = 10^{-8}\) rule. If one person can contribute many records, \(n\) is the number of people, and a per-record guarantee is not a per-person one (User-level differential privacy).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Deployed values and their units
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” is a common justification. What have real deployments published, and in which units? Comparing your budget with theirs needs one notion first, because an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing without it.

Definition 46.4 (Privacy unit and period) The privacy unit of a guarantee is what one neighbouring change is: one record, one user’s data for a day, or one user’s data forever, under add/remove or replace-one. The period is the time over which the budget is spent, counting every release and training run that touched the data.

Table 46.10 lists deployments documented in a primary source. The unit, period and accounting differ from row to row, so the values are not comparable without conversion. A zCDP guarantee with parameter \(\rho\) converts by the simple bound of Theorem 31.4 (Bun & Steinke 2016), \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{46.16}\] and tighter numerical conversions give somewhat smaller values. The Gboard models were trained on users’ devices by follow the regularized leader (FTRL) with noise on sums of gradients (DP-FTRL and matrix factorization).
