The conversions are short. With \(\rho = 2.56\) and \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), Equation 46.16 gives \(2.56 + 2\sqrt{2.56 \times 23.026} = 17.915\), the persons’ figure of Kazan & Reiter (2022); the Bureau’s 17.14 uses a tighter conversion. Local reports add up over time, so QuickType’s two donations of \(\varepsilon = 8\) cost up to 16 per day, and Tang, Korolova et al. (2017) found that this budget resets daily. RAPPOR reuses one randomized answer for a value that does not change, so all its reports cost at most \(\varepsilon_\infty = 2H\ln\frac{1 - f/2}{f/2}\), for \(H\) hash functions and a probability \(f\) of replacing a bit by a coin. At \(H = 2\) and \(f = 0.75\) that is \(4\ln(5/3) = 2.043\), but a value that changes is reported afresh (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models). In the Facebook release a user with \(k\) actions costs \(k\) times one action, because zCDP composes by adding \(\rho\).
Only the Gboard rows train a model. They give device-level guarantees for a whole run, with \(\varepsilon\) between about 1 and 14 at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), while the running example’s 1 to 8 are at a much larger \(\delta\) and per record. NIST notes that many deployments have used \(1 < \varepsilon \le 20\), but practice is no evidence that a value is safe. To compare budgets, convert both to the same unit, neighbouring relation, accounting and \(\delta\), as Desfontaines’ list of real-world uses does, or say that you did not.
The deployments also show what a published \(\varepsilon\) leaves out, as four questions to ask of any budget. Does it renew? Rogers et al. (2021) count one RAPPOR report every 30 minutes as \(0.534 \times 48 \times 30 = 769\) per month for a user whose value changes, and Microsoft’s four rounds a day as \(0.686 \times 4 \times 30 = 82.3\). What sits outside it? Apple’s encrypted channel and stripped IP addresses protect users, but \(\varepsilon\) does not count them. What does it assume? LinkedIn’s budget per analyst holds only if analysts do not collude, which a contract enforces, not noise. Whom does it cover? The Facebook release protects whole users only up to the 99th percentile of activity. LinkedIn even chose its value from an attack, accepting the 0.115 chance that an analyst who averages a count over 30 days recovers it.

Example 46.6 Is the \(\varepsilon = 8\) run “less than half the Census budget”? The Census 17.14 is replace-one at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), the run’s 7.997 add/remove at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). At \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) the run is at 11.627 (Table 46.9). Replacing a record is a removal and an addition, so in the worst case replace-one doubles an add/remove guarantee (Proposition 18.2). Doubled, the run’s 11.627 exceeds 17.14, so after converting the two are of the same order, a weaker claim than the slogan.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.7 Justifying a choice
You must now pick a target for the running example and write a statement that a sceptical reviewer will check. The earlier sections supply the pieces, and a good statement states what is claimed before giving the number.

Definition 46.5 (A defensible privacy statement) A defensible privacy statement for a trained model gives six things.

The unit, with the period, counting every run and hyperparameter search that touched the data (Hyperparameter tuning).
The threat: membership, attribute inference or reconstruction, the attacker’s prior, and what it observes.
The whole guarantee: the curve from a tight accountant, with \(\delta\) well below \(1/n\), read at the threat’s operating points.
The evidence: an audit (Auditing private training) consistent with the claim, and a check of the code against the proof’s assumptions (DP-SGD).
The utility: the accuracy curve against \(\varepsilon\), and the smallest budget beyond which accuracy stops rising steeply.
The comparison: the tiers of Ponomareva et al. (2023), in which \(\varepsilon \le 1\) is strong, \(\varepsilon \le 10\) is reasonable for many applications, and above 10 the guarantee alone is not enough.


The first four items answer failures seen earlier. Without the unit, one number can mean protection of a single click or of a whole history. The threat decides where to read the curve, and the pair alone can overstate the attacker 17-fold, which tempts a reader to dismiss DP as vacuous. Whether the code runs the algorithm of the proof is an empirical fact, which audits check.
The utility item matters because the accuracy curve is steeply non-linear (Figure 46.5). Each doubling of \(\varepsilon\) buys less accuracy and more risk, read as the exact TPR at an FPR of 1%. Going from \(\varepsilon = 1\) to 2 gains 2.66 percentage points and moves that TPR from at most 0.01893 to at most 0.03141, while the step from 2 to 4 gains 1.07 points for a TPR of at most 0.0724. The step from 4 to 8 gains only 0.56 points yet nearly triples the TPR, to at most 0.2092. So past \(\varepsilon = 4\), accuracy is bought with a much larger increase in worst-case risk. This is also why the tiers are reasonable: below 1 every mechanism is strong by Equation 46.1, from 1 to 10 DP-SGD’s curve lies far below the line, and above 10 even the curve allows a TPR above 0.27 at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), at \(\varepsilon = 16\).






Figure 46.5: Left: test accuracy of the running example against \(\varepsilon\), with the non-private model dashed. Right: the same accuracies against the largest membership TPR at FPR 1%, from the exact curve (circles) and from the pair (squares).




Example 46.7 Following Definition 46.5, a team might choose the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run and write:

The model was trained with DP-SGD (Poisson sampling rate 0.01, noise multiplier 1.36, clipping norm 0.5, 10,000 steps) on 10,000 records, one record per person. The privacy unit is one record under add/remove neighbours; no other run touched the training data. The RDP accountant gives \((3.993, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((5.209, 10^{-8})\)-DP; a PLD accountant gives \(\varepsilon \le 3.729\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Against an attacker who knows every other record and sees every iterate, any membership test has TPR at most 0.01312 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and at most 0.0724 at FPR \(10^{-2}\), and any attack that picks a record out of 100 equally likely candidates succeeds with probability at most 0.0724. Test accuracy is 0.9548, against 0.9610 without privacy.

Every number in it is checkable, and a reviewer who thinks \(\varepsilon = 4\) is too large can now argue with the TPR at a specific FPR rather than with the number.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.1 From an attack to a lower bound on ε
Every chapter of this part ended with a number. Train with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), that is, with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise (DP-SGD), and an accountant turns the configuration into a guarantee. That guarantee concludes a proof about an algorithm on paper, but what ships is code, and the code can quietly differ from the algorithm in a dozen places. The noise may be scaled for the averaged gradient but added to the sum, or the accountant may be handed the wrong dataset size. None of these changes the accuracy much, so the usual tests miss them. This chapter asks whether the trained model is as private as the accountant says.
An audit answers by attacking. It plants records of its own, called canaries, trains with and without them, and runs a membership test. It measures the test’s true positive rate (TPR), how often it flags a canary that was trained on, and its false positive rate (FPR), how often it flags one that was not. The one idea is that DP caps how often any test can be right, so measured error rates imply a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\). Such a bound cannot prove privacy, but it disproves any claim below it. The chapter then makes the bound bite. It puts confidence intervals on the measured rates, chooses the strongest attack, and gets many trials out of one or two training runs.
The running example is the part’s network, a two-layer tanh network trained on the 10,000 records of DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), clipping norm \(C = 0.5\), noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\), learning rate 0.5 and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and this is the claim every audit below tests. Neighbours \(D \sim D'\) differ by adding or removing one record, and Table 47.1 lists the symbols.
You ran an attack and counted how often it was right. This section asks what that lets you conclude about \(\varepsilon\), with what confidence, and how much \(n\) trials could ever conclude. Every later audit reports its result through this bound.
The definition of DP limits these rates. By Theorem 18.3 in The definition of differential privacy, if \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP then every test, randomized or not, satisfies both \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{47.2}\] The first inequality caps how often the test flags present canaries against how often it flags absent ones. The second swaps the two datasets and applies the cap to the verdict “canary out”.
The audit sees only counts, not rates. If the trials are independent, \(k_0\) is a binomial count whose success probability is the FPR, and Theorem 4.7 in Hypothesis testing turns such a count into an interval. Its proof shows that each end, on its own, misses the true rate with probability at most half the interval’s failure probability. So write \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) for the lower bound on the TPR, each at level \(\beta/2\). They solve \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(n, \overline{\mathrm{FPR}}) \le k_0\big] = \frac\beta2, \qquad \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(n, \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}) \ge k_1\big] = \frac\beta2. \tag{47.3}\] Putting these pessimistic ends into Equation 47.2, and taking the larger of the two caps, gives a bound that holds with probability \(1 - \beta\).
The bound says that no smaller \(\varepsilon\) is possible, never that this \(\varepsilon\) is enough. A weak attack gives a small \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\) for a leaky model as easily as for a private one. So a bound above the claim refutes it, while a bound below it says only that this attacker did no better. The second form in the maximum rewards tests that rarely miss present canaries.
The hypothesis on the threshold matters in practice. Sweeping the threshold over the same trials and reporting the best bound makes the confidence level wrong, because among many thresholds one is lucky. Every audit in this chapter chooses its threshold on half of the trials and counts on the other half.
Even an attack that never errs certifies only a limited \(\varepsilon\), because the bound uses the pessimistic end of each interval. The next result computes that ceiling, which tells you how many trials to budget.
So each factor of \(e\) in the bound costs a factor of \(e\) in trials. The reason is that a false positive rate cannot be told apart from zero with fewer than about \(3/\mathrm{FPR}\) trials, the rule of three. For example, with no false positive in 3,000 trials the 95% upper bound is \(9.9808 \times 10^{-4}\). Table 47.2 shows what that means. Certifying the running example’s 6.71 needs at least 3,038 trials per hypothesis, so 6,076 training runs, even for an attack that never errs. For a real network each run is a full training job.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
Definition 47.1 (Audit trials and error rates) Let \(M\) be a training algorithm, \(D\) a dataset and \(z^*\) a canary record, and write \(D' = D \cup \{z^*\}\). A trial runs \(M\) on \(D\) or on \(D'\) with fresh randomness and computes a score \(s\) from the output. The attack says “canary in” when \(s \ge \tau\), for a threshold \(\tau\). Its false positive rate and true positive rate are \[\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[s \ge \tau \mid D], \qquad \mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[s \ge \tau \mid D'], \tag{47.1}\] and its false negative rate is \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{TPR}\). An audit runs \(n\) trials on each dataset and counts \(k_0\) false positives and \(k_1\) true positives.




Theorem 47.1 (A certified lower bound on ε) Suppose the \(2n\) trials are independent and the threshold \(\tau\) was chosen without looking at them. Let \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) be the one-sided Clopper–Pearson bounds at level \(\beta/2\), and let \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} - \delta}{\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}},\ \ln\frac{1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}} - \delta}{1 - \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}}\Big\}. \tag{47.4}\] Then, with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), \(M\) is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\).


Proof. The plan is to solve the two caps for \(\varepsilon\), check that pessimistic rates can only lower the result, and then bound the probability that the rates are not pessimistic.

The true rates bound \(\varepsilon\). Dividing each inequality of Equation 47.2 by the factor in front of \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \[e^\varepsilon \ge \frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}, \qquad e^\varepsilon \ge \frac{1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \delta}{1 - \mathrm{TPR}}. \tag{47.5}\]
Pessimistic rates lower both fractions. Both fractions grow with the TPR and shrink with the FPR. So a larger FPR and a smaller TPR can only lower them.
The two bounds hold together with probability \(1 - \beta\). Each bound fails with probability at most \(\beta/2\), so by the union bound at least one fails with probability at most \(\beta\). This needs binomial counts, which is why the trials must be independent and the threshold fixed before the counting.
Combine. When both bounds hold, step 2 says that \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\) is at most the larger logarithm of the two fractions at the true rates. Step 1 says that this is at most the \(\varepsilon\) of any valid guarantee. So, over the randomness of the trials, the bound exceeds the \(\varepsilon\) of a valid guarantee with probability at most \(\beta\).






Corollary 47.1 (The ceiling of an audit) Under the hypotheses of Theorem 47.1, the largest bound that \(n\) trials per hypothesis can certify is that of a perfect attack, with \(k_0 = 0\) and \(k_1 = n\): \[\varepsilon_{\max}(n) = \ln\frac{(\beta/2)^{1/n} - \delta}{1 - (\beta/2)^{1/n}} \approx \ln\frac{n}{\ln(2/\beta)}. \tag{47.6}\]


Proof. 

A perfect attack gives the best ends. Fewer successes push both Clopper–Pearson ends down, so \(k_0 = 0\) gives the smallest \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) and \(k_1 = n\) the largest \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\). By step 2 of the proof of Theorem 47.1, these give the largest bound.
Solve for the ends. With \(k_0 = 0\) the upper bound solves \((1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}})^n = \beta/2\), so \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 1 - (\beta/2)^{1/n}\). With \(k_1 = n\) the lower bound solves \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}^n = \beta/2\), so \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = (\beta/2)^{1/n}\). Substituting into either form of Equation 47.4 gives the exact expression.
Approximate. Write the power as an exponential, \((\beta/2)^{1/n} = e^{-\ln(2/\beta)/n}\), which is about \(1 - \ln(2/\beta)/n\) for large \(n\). So \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) is about \(\ln(2/\beta)/n\) while \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) is about 1, and their ratio is about \(n/\ln(2/\beta)\). With \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\ln(2/\beta) = \ln 40 = 3.69\).






Table 47.2: The most a perfect attack can certify with \(n\) trials per hypothesis, at 95% confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Conversely, certifying \(\varepsilon = 1\), 2, 4, 6.71 and 8 takes at least 12, 30, 204, 3,038 and 10,999 trials per hypothesis.

Example 47.1 Suppose 1,000 runs with the canary and 1,000 without give 500 true positives and 1 false positive. The point estimate is \(\ln\frac{0.5 - 10^{-5}}{0.001} = 6.21\). The Clopper–Pearson bounds at \(\beta/2 = 0.025\) are \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 0.00556\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = 0.4685\), so one false positive in 1,000 is consistent with a true FPR five times larger. The certified bound is \(\ln\frac{0.4685 - 10^{-5}}{0.00556} = 4.43\), almost two less than the point estimate. With ten times the trials and the same rates, the bounds are \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 0.00184\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = 0.4902\), and the certified bound rises to 5.59. The price of confidence falls, slowly, as the counts grow.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.2 Canaries and threat models
A bound is only as strong as the attack behind it, and DP is a promise about the worst pair of datasets and the worst test. A typical training record scored by its loss gives a valid but nearly useless bound, since Membership inference shows that most records are barely exposed. This section asks which canary and which view of training make the strongest audit of DP-SGD, and what that audit faces.

Definition 47.2 (Canaries and threat models) An input-space canary is a record \((x, y)\) inserted into the training data like any other, such as a mislabelled example, chosen so that its gradient is large and points where few others do. A gradient-space canary is a gradient the auditor writes directly, as if it controlled the training code. A Dirac canary (Nasr et al. 2023) is a gradient-space canary equal to \(C\) on one coordinate and zero elsewhere, on a coordinate where the other records’ gradients are zero. In the black-box threat model the attacker sees only the final model, and in the white-box model it sees every iterate \(\theta_0, \dots, \theta_T\).

A white-box gradient audit tests the mechanism, that is, whether the code clips and adds the noise the proof assumes. A black-box input audit tests the deployment, what an attacker with a released model can learn. A white-box attacker can recover every step’s noisy gradient sum \(G_t\), which the lemma below defines. DP-SGD moves the weights by the learning rate \(\eta\) times \(G_t\) divided by the expected batch size \(B\), so \(G_t = -B(\theta_{t+1} - \theta_t)/\eta\). The proof of the next theorem needs to know what this sum looks like along one direction, and the lemma below works it out.

Lemma 47.1 (One DP-SGD step seen along one direction) Let one DP-SGD step release \(G_t = \sum_i\bar g_i + \xi_t\), the sum of the clipped gradients \(\bar g_i\) of the records sampled at step \(t\) plus noise \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\), with Poisson sampling at rate \(q\). Let \(u\) be a fixed unit vector. Suppose one record’s clipped gradient is exactly \(Cu\) at every step, while no other record’s gradient has a component along \(u\). Then the projection \(x_t = u^\top G_t/C\) satisfies \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the record}, \qquad x_t \sim (1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}, \tag{47.7}\] independently over the steps.


Proof. 

The noise and the other records. The projection of an isotropic Gaussian vector on a unit vector is a one-dimensional Gaussian with the same standard deviation, so \(u^\top\xi_t/C\) is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). The other records add nothing, because their gradients have no component along \(u\).
The record. Its gradient \(Cu\) adds exactly 1 to \(x_t\) when it is sampled, which happens with probability \(q\), independently of the noise.
Independence. The sampling coin and the noise are drawn afresh at every step, and the record’s contribution does not depend on the weights, so different steps are independent.


This is the pair that the accountant of Amplification by subsampling analyses, the worst case for one step under add/remove neighbours. A Dirac canary meets the lemma’s hypotheses exactly. The strength of a test against this pair is measured on the scale of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP (Definition 32.2) when no test separates its neighbours better than one separates two unit-variance normals whose means are \(\mu\) apart. That pair’s best true positive rate at a given false positive rate is \[\mathrm{TPR}_\mu(\mathrm{FPR}) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big), \tag{47.8}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.

Theorem 47.2 (The white-box Dirac audit) Let a Dirac canary sit on a coordinate \(j\) that no other record’s gradient touches, let the attacker see every iterate, and let \(x_t = G_{t,j}/C\). Then \(x_1, \dots, x_T\) follow Equation 47.7 independently, and the most powerful test at every FPR thresholds the likelihood-ratio statistic \[\Lambda = \sum_{t=1}^T\ln\Big(1 - q + q\,e^{(x_t - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{47.9}\] No attacker who sees the whole training run does better. For large \(T\) with \(q\sqrt T\) fixed, the trade-off curve of \(\Lambda\) approaches that of \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\). The sum of projections \(\sum_tx_t\) has a curve close to \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = q\sqrt T/\sigma\).


Proof. The plan is to show that the projections follow the lemma’s pair, to multiply the steps’ likelihood ratios, to check that the rest of the run adds no evidence, and then to read off both statistics’ strength.

The canary is the only difference. Every other record contributes 0 to coordinate \(j\). The canary’s gradient has norm exactly \(C\), so clipping leaves it unchanged, and it is the same at every step whatever the weights are. So Lemma 47.1 applies with \(u\) the unit vector of coordinate \(j\).
The likelihood ratio of one step. The squares \(x^2\) cancel in the ratio of two normal densities with the same variance, so \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) over \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) at \(x\) is \(e^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\). The mixture puts weight \(1 - q\) on the null density and \(q\) on the shifted one, so its ratio to the null is \[1 - q + q\,e^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2}. \tag{47.10}\]
Multiply over the steps. Independence makes the joint likelihood ratio the product of the per-step ratios, and its logarithm is Equation 47.9. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1), thresholding it is the most powerful test at every FPR.
The rest of the run carries no evidence. The whole run is a function of the \(x_t\) and of randomness with the same distribution under both hypotheses, namely the other records’ sampling and the noise on the other coordinates. The weights depend on past \(x_t\), but given those, everything else is drawn the same way with or without the canary.
The two statistics in Gaussian terms. For \(\Lambda\), the subsampled Gaussian central limit theorem (CLT), Theorem 32.5 in f-DP and Gaussian DP, gives the curve of \(T\) steps of this pair, which the most powerful test attains. For the sum, the mean shifts by the expected number of times the canary is sampled, \(qT\), while the noise has standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt T\), and their ratio is \(q\sqrt T/\sigma\). With the canary the sum also has a little extra variance, \(Tq(1 - q)\).


The likelihood ratio beats the sum because it weighs each step by its evidence. A step with \(x_t = 3\) is much stronger evidence than three steps with \(x_t = 1\), since a value three noise standard deviations out is very unlikely without the canary. The ratio of the two \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), which is 1.311 at \(\sigma = 1\) and tends to 1 as \(\sigma\) grows.
Black-box audits with input canaries are weaker for three reasons. The final model is one function of all the noisy sums, so by post-processing it carries at most as much information as they do, and usually much less. An input canary’s gradient shrinks or turns once the model fits it or gives up on it. And it shares directions with the other records’ gradients, which act as extra noise. Nasr, Song, Thakurta, Papernot & Carlini (2021) built a ladder of adversaries for DP-SGD and found the bound tight only for the strongest, which sees every iterate and chooses a worst-case dataset and canary.

Example 47.2 At \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), the likelihood-ratio statistic has \(\mu = 0.01 \times \sqrt{10{,}000 \times 1.7183} = 1.3108\). The sum of projections has \(\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = 0.01 \times 100 = 1.00\), or 0.9951 with the extra variance. The Gaussian privacy profile of Corollary 32.1 converts these to \(\varepsilon = 6.01\) and \(4.35\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). So choosing the sum lowers the \(\varepsilon\) the audit can ever reach from 6.01 to 4.35, before a single trial is run.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.3 Tight audits of the mechanism
The white-box Dirac audit faces the accountant’s own pair. This section asks whether, with enough trials, it recovers the accountant’s 6.71, and how close it gets with the trials an auditor can afford. The answer explains why audits stop short of their claims.
The smallest \(\varepsilon\) that a pair of output distributions allows can be read straight off the definition. Only likelihood-ratio thresholds need to be checked, because the Neyman–Pearson lemma says they are the best tests.

Theorem 47.3 (A perfect audit measures the true ε) Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the distributions of the training output without and with the canary. The smallest \(\varepsilon\) such that \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\) is \[\varepsilon^*(\delta) = \sup_S\ \ln\frac{Q(S) - \delta}{P(S)}, \tag{47.11}\] the supremum over events with \(Q(S) > \delta\), and it may be taken over likelihood-ratio thresholds only. So an audit that thresholds the likelihood ratio, and knows its rates exactly, computes \(\varepsilon^*(\delta)\).


Proof. 

The supremum is the definition solved for \(\varepsilon\). If \(\varepsilon\) is at least the supremum, every event’s log-ratio is at most \(\varepsilon\), which rearranges to \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\). If \(\varepsilon\) is below it, some event violates the inequality.
Only likelihood-ratio thresholds matter. For a fixed \(P(S)\), the ratio grows with \(Q(S)\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 4.1), among events with a given \(P(S)\) the one with the largest \(Q(S)\) is a likelihood-ratio threshold, randomized on ties.
A perfect audit. Reading off exact rates at every likelihood-ratio threshold evaluates the ratio of step 1 at every candidate of step 2, so it computes the supremum.


For the Dirac canary this pair is the one the accountant bounds, so a perfect audit converges to the true \(\varepsilon\) of DP-SGD, not to what an accountant reports. The RDP accountant’s 6.71 is a loose upper bound. The numerical accountant of f-DP and Gaussian DP puts the true value between 6.14 and 6.24, and the CLT approximation gives 6.01. So even an audit with infinitely many trials stops about half a unit below 6.71, and that gap belongs to the accountant.
Real audits fall much further short, because of where on the curve the supremum is reached. For a \(\mu\)-GDP curve that point is explicit.

Proposition 47.1 (Where ε lives on a Gaussian curve) Let a mechanism’s trade-off curve be the \(\mu\)-GDP curve Equation 47.8, and let \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon^*(\delta)\). The supremum Equation 47.11 is reached at the threshold whose rates are \[\mathrm{FPR}^* = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big), \qquad \mathrm{TPR}^* = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{47.12}\]


Proof. 

The supremum is a tangent. By Equation 47.11, \(\varepsilon\) is set by the steepest line through \((0, \delta)\) that still meets the concave curve of TPR against FPR. At the optimum that line touches the curve, so the curve’s slope there is \(e^\varepsilon\).
The slope is the likelihood ratio. By Proposition 4.1 in Hypothesis testing, the slope at a threshold is the likelihood ratio there. For \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) at threshold \(\tau\) it is \(e^{\mu\tau - \mu^2/2}\).
Solve for the threshold. Setting the slope to \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(\tau = \varepsilon/\mu + \mu/2\). Its FPR is \(1 - \Phi(\tau) = \Phi(-\tau)\), and its TPR is \(1 - \Phi(\tau - \mu) = \Phi(\mu - \tau)\).


For the running example, \(\mu = 1.3108\) and \(\varepsilon = 6.01\) give \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\) and \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = 4.3 \times 10^{-5}\). So certifying the full \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) means measuring a false positive rate below one in ten million. With \(n\) trials you can measure rates down to about \(3/n\), and there the curve’s log-ratio of TPR to FPR is far below \(\varepsilon\). For \(\mu = 1.3108\), Equation 47.8 gives 2.74 at FPR \(10^{-2}\), 3.63 at \(10^{-3}\) and 4.38 at \(10^{-4}\). Seeing ten false positives near \(10^{-7}\) takes about \(1.2\times10^{8}\) trials without the canary. Figure 47.1 shows the measured curve well inside the \((6.71, 10^{-5})\) limit.






Figure 47.1: Left: the trade-off of the white-box audit of the running example on log axes, from 30,000 trials per hypothesis. The black line is the most any test can achieve under \((6.71, 10^{-5})\)-DP; the dashed grey curve is \(\mu\)-GDP with the CLT’s \(\mu = 1.31\). The blue curve is the likelihood-ratio statistic, the orange one the sum of projections; boxes are 95% Clopper–Pearson regions at four thresholds. Right: the \(\varepsilon\) a threshold would certify if its rates were known exactly, \(\ln((\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR})\), against its false positive rate. The Gaussian curve reaches its \(\varepsilon\) of 6.01 only at FPR \(8 \times 10^{-8}\) (dotted line), far below the rates a feasible audit can measure.



Nasr, Hayes, Steinke, Balle, Tramèr, Jagielski, Carlini & Terzis (2023) avoid the tail by assuming the curve’s shape. If the mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP, one test at a moderate FPR, where trials are cheap, bounds \(\mu\) from below, and the Gaussian shape carries that bound into the tail.

Proposition 47.2 (A lower bound on μ from one test) If \(M\) is \(\mu\)-GDP, every test satisfies \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{47.13}\] Under the hypotheses of Theorem 47.1, the value \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) of the right-hand side at \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) satisfies \(\mu \ge \mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. 

Rearrange the curve. Under \(\mu\)-GDP every test’s TPR is at most Equation 47.8. The normal distribution is symmetric, so \(1 - \Phi(a) = \Phi(-a)\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - p) = -\Phi^{-1}(p)\), and the cap becomes \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}) + \mu\big). \tag{47.14}\] Applying the increasing function \(\Phi^{-1}\) to both sides gives Equation 47.13.
Pessimistic rates. The right-hand side of Equation 47.13 grows with the TPR and shrinks with the FPR, so the Clopper–Pearson ends can only lower it. They hold together with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), as in step 3 of the proof of Theorem 47.1.


The bound on \(\mu\) is rigorous, but its conversion to \(\varepsilon\) is valid only if the curve really is Gaussian. The subsampled Gaussian of DP-SGD has a heavier tail, so the \(\mu\) that Equation 47.13 gives depends on where you read it. In the example below, the measured rates give 1.300 at FPR \(10^{-1}\), 1.303 at \(10^{-2}\), 1.371 at \(10^{-3}\) and 1.492 at \(2 \times 10^{-4}\), against the CLT’s 1.3108. For this reason Nasr et al. mostly insert the canary at every step, which makes each step an exact Gaussian mechanism, as Section 47.6 does.

Example 47.3 The script simulates the white-box Dirac audit directly from Equation 47.7. Each trial draws 10,000 projections, adds the canary on a \(\mathrm{Bin}(10{,}000, 0.01)\) number of steps when it is present, and computes \(\Lambda\). By Theorem 47.2 this is statistically identical to training the network with a Dirac canary, and thousands of times cheaper.
With 50,000 trials per hypothesis, the measured curve is heavier-tailed than the Gaussian. At FPR \(10^{-2}\) the point value of \(\ln((\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR})\) is 2.73, as the Gaussian predicts, but at \(10^{-4}\) it is 4.84, above the Gaussian’s 4.38. Table 47.3 gives the certified bounds, with thresholds chosen on the first half of the trials and counts taken on the second.

The bounds grow roughly like the logarithm of the number of trials.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.4 One-run auditing
The audits so far need one training run per trial, thousands in all, which is out of the question for a model that takes a day to train. Can a single training run give a valid bound? It can, if each canary is a trial.

Definition 47.3 (One-run audit) Insert \(m\) canaries, each independently with probability \(\frac12\), and write \(S_i = +1\) if canary \(i\) is in the training set and \(S_i = -1\) if not. Train once and score every canary. Guess \(\hat S_i = +1\) (“in”) for the \(r/2\) highest scores and \(\hat S_i = -1\) (“out”) for the \(r/2\) lowest, and abstain, \(\hat S_i = 0\), on the rest. Let \(W\) be the number of correct guesses among the \(r\) made.

Each guess is about one fair coin, made from an output that is private in that coin. DP lets the output make one value of the coin at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely as the other, so no guess can be right more often than \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\). Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023) turn that into a bound on the total count.

Theorem 47.4 (One-run auditing under pure DP) If training is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then for every \(v\) \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{47.15}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that each guess is right with probability at most \(p_\varepsilon\), even given the earlier guesses, and then to compare the count with a binomial.

Each inclusion bit is protected. Fix every inclusion bit except \(S_i\). Changing \(S_i\) adds or removes one record, so the run is \(\varepsilon\)-DP as a function of \(S_i\), and by post-processing (Theorem 19.1) so are the guesses. For every vector of guesses \(s\), \[\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = +1, S_{-i}] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = -1, S_{-i}]. \tag{47.16}\]
Average over the later bits. Order the guessed canaries in a fixed order, and condition only on the earlier bits \(S_{<i}\). The later bits are independent of \(S_i\), so averaging step 1 over them puts the same weights on both sides, and the inequality holds given \(S_{<i}\).
No guess is right more than \(p_\varepsilon\) of the time. Given \(S_{<i}\), write \(a\) for the probability of \(s\) when \(S_i = +1\) and \(b\) for it when \(S_i = -1\). With the prior \(\frac12\) on \(S_i\), Bayes’ rule gives \(\Pr[S_i = +1 \mid \hat S = s, S_{<i}] = a/(a + b)\). The fraction grows with \(a\), and step 2 says \(a \le e^\varepsilon b\), so \[\frac{a}{a + b} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon b}{e^\varepsilon b + b} = p_\varepsilon. \tag{47.17}\] The same holds for \(S_i = -1\). The earlier bits fix whether the earlier guesses were right, so each guess is right with probability at most \(p_\varepsilon\) given the earlier outcomes.
The count is dominated by a binomial. Write the \(j\)-th guess’s correctness as \(\mathbf 1[U_j \le p_j]\), with \(U_j\) independent uniform numbers and \(p_j \le p_\varepsilon\) its conditional probability from step 3. Then \(\mathbf 1[U_j \le p_j] \le \mathbf 1[U_j \le p_\varepsilon]\), and the right-hand indicators sum to a \(\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon)\) count, so Equation 47.15 follows. Section N.1 in the appendices builds this coupling step by step and proves the domination lemma it relies on.


Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP each guess can be right a little more often. Write \(F(v) = \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v]\) for the binomial tail of Equation 47.15.

Theorem 47.5 (One-run auditing under approximate DP) If training is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then for every \(v\) \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le F(v) + 2m\delta\max_{i = 1, \dots, m}\frac{F(v - i) - F(v)}{i}. \tag{47.18}\]


The proof is Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023, Corollary 5.4), which tracks how the additive \(\delta\) of step 1 accumulates over the guesses. Either theorem gives an audit in the same way. Observing \(v\) correct guesses rejects every \(\varepsilon\) whose right-hand side is below \(\beta\), and the largest such \(\varepsilon\) is the bound.
The binomial is exactly the count of \(\varepsilon\)-randomized response on the true bits (Theorem 18.1), so the bound is tight for that mechanism. In the paper’s worked example, 75 correct guesses out of 100 give the lower bound 0.702 at 95% confidence. The script reproduces it, and the paper’s 0.699 and 0.673 for \(\delta = 10^{-4}\) with 100 and 1,000 canaries. The ceiling is again logarithmic, about \(\ln(r/\ln(1/\beta))\) when all guesses are right, with \(\ln(1/\beta)\) because the test is one-sided. That is 3.49 for 100 canaries, 5.81 for 1,000 and 8.11 for 10,000 at \(\delta = 0\), and certifying 6.71 needs about 2,500 perfect guesses. So a one-run audit saves runs, not trials.
The \(\delta\) term grows with the number of canaries, since the correction is at most \(2m\delta\). With 10,000 canaries all guessed right it lowers the bound from 8.11 to 7.83, and when \(2m\delta\) approaches \(\beta\) it swallows the whole failure probability. Even with white-box Dirac canaries, one run is not tight for DP-SGD. Each canary is guessed once, so the audit reads the trade-off curve near FPR \(1/m\) at best. And the binomial is calibrated to randomized response, whose curve has a sharp corner, while the curve of DP-SGD is smooth.

Example 47.4 Simulate one run of the running example with 1,000 Dirac canaries on distinct untouched coordinates, about half of them included, each scored by \(\Lambda\). The auditor tries six list lengths \(r\) and pays for trying them with a Bonferroni correction. Each test runs at level \(\beta/6\), so that the chance that any of the six is wrong is at most \(\beta\). Table 47.4 gives the result.

section: 47.5 Black-box audit of the trained network
text:
47.5 Black-box audit of the trained network
The white-box Dirac audit tests the mechanism. What does an attacker learn from the released network itself, with canaries planted as ordinary records? This section runs the one-run audit of Section 47.4, so each audit costs one training run. The canaries must be records the model can learn only by memorizing them, since a correctly labelled record has nearly the same loss whether or not it was trained on.

Definition 47.4 (Black-box audit with mislabelled canaries) Take 1,000 records from the held-out test set of the running example and flip their labels, which makes them mislabelled canaries. Include each in the 10,000 training records with probability \(\frac12\), train once with DP-SGD at the claimed configuration, and score each canary by minus its loss on the final model. Guess with the six list lengths of Example 47.4, and bound \(\varepsilon\) with Equation 47.18, Bonferroni-corrected. As controls, audit a model trained with clipping but no noise, and one trained without clipping or noise.

The bound is valid, because including a canary is adding a record, and DP-SGD’s guarantee holds for every dataset. But it should be far below 6.71. The attacker sees one function of the 10,000 noisy sums, the canary’s gradient changes as it is fitted, and the 10,000 real records pull the other way. The no-noise control separates the attacker’s weakness from the noise. A model trained without noise has no finite \(\varepsilon\), so if its audit also gives a small bound, the audit is what keeps the bound small.

The non-private model memorizes the canaries it trained on. Their mean loss is 0.023, against 9.041 for those it did not see, so 967 of 1,000 guesses are right and the audit certifies 2.96. A thousand perfect guesses would certify 5.78 even without the Bonferroni correction, so 33 mistakes cost almost three units. Memorizing also costs almost five points of test accuracy, 0.9155 against 0.9645.
DP-SGD does not memorize. The mean losses of included and excluded canaries differ by less than half a unit, 59 of the 100 most confident guesses are right, and the certified bound is 0.13, from 293 of 500. The clipping-only model is barely easier, at 0.24. Clipping alone bounds each canary’s pull on the weights to \(C\) per step, against the combined pull of 10,000 correctly labelled records, and that is what defeats this attacker. It does not make clipping private, since a white-box Dirac canary would identify membership in that model perfectly. The black-box bound of 0.13 says that a realistic attacker with one model extracts very little, while the white-box audits of Section 47.3 say that an attacker who sees every step extracts much more. An honest privacy statement reports both, with the threat model of each, and Definition 46.5 lists what else it must contain.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.6 Finding bugs
An audit bound below the claim proves nothing, but a bound above it proves, with confidence \(1 - \beta\), that the claim is false. That makes audits a test suite for private training code, which passes silently on a correct implementation and fails loudly on a broken one. This section asks which bugs such a test catches, and how cheaply.

Definition 47.5 (Per-step and end-to-end audits) A per-step audit inserts a Dirac canary at every step in one run and leaves it out in another, and treats each step’s projection \(x_t\) as one trial, so it gets \(T\) trials per hypothesis from two runs. An end-to-end audit runs the many-trial protocol of Section 47.3, with one training run per trial.

With the canary always present there is no sampling coin to blur it, so each step of a correct implementation is a plain Gaussian mechanism. Its privacy is then known exactly, and a measured \(\mu\) above it is evidence of a bug.

Proposition 47.3 (A per-step audit tests the noise) In a per-step audit of a correct implementation, the projections are independent across steps, with \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}, \tag{47.19}\] so each step is exactly \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). If the bound \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) of Proposition 47.2, computed from these trials with a threshold chosen on other trials, exceeds \(1/\sigma\), the implementation does not add the noise it claims, with confidence \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. 

One step is a Gaussian mechanism. With the canary in every batch, Lemma 47.1 with \(q = 1\) gives Equation 47.19. The means differ by 1 in noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), so by Theorem 4.3 the trade-off curve is Equation 47.8 with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\).
The steps are independent trials. The noise is fresh at every step and the canary’s gradient is fixed, so the counts at a fixed threshold are binomial and Proposition 47.2 applies.
A refutation. By Proposition 47.2, a correct implementation gives \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} \le 1/\sigma\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). So observing \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} > 1/\sigma\) rejects, at level \(\beta\), the hypothesis that the code adds noise \(\sigma C\) to a sum with sensitivity \(C\).


A per-step audit tests the noise and the clipping, but it never exercises the sampling code, and it compares the measured noise with the claimed \(\sigma\), not with the claimed \(\varepsilon\). So a bug in how batches are drawn, or in what the accountant is told, passes it. Nasr et al. (2023) used per-step audits to catch clipping applied after averaging, noise drawn from a seed with only 100 possible values, and a wrong noise scale. An end-to-end audit tests the claimed \(\varepsilon\) directly, so it catches an accounting bug as readily as a noise bug, but only when the true \(\varepsilon\) exceeds the claim by more than the audit’s shortfall. For the running example that shortfall is about three units at 100,000 runs. Tramèr, Terzis, Steinke, Song, Jagielski & Carlini (2022) used such an audit to refute the guarantee of an open-source implementation, at a confidence they report as \(1 - 10^{-10}\).
No canary audit catches everything, because it tests one dataset, one canary and one attack. Batches drawn by shuffling but accounted as Poisson can have an \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one, by a lower bound in Amplification by subsampling. Yet a per-step audit never sees the sampling, and an end-to-end audit sees the gap only where it exceeds the shortfall. Audits also catch errors only in the unsafe direction. Noise \(\sigma C\) added to the averaged gradient is \(B\) times more noise than claimed, so every audit passes, although the bug wastes accuracy. Passing an audit is evidence, never a certificate.

The correct implementation passes, with 0.886 below the claimed 1. The two noise bugs fail decisively. Passing the variance \(\sigma^2C^2 = 0.25\) where the code expects the standard deviation \(\sigma C = 0.5\) halves the noise, and the audit measures 1.745. Scaling the noise for the averaged gradient, whose sensitivity is \(C/B\), and adding it to the sum makes the noise \(B = 100\) times too small. Then 10,000 steps separate the hypotheses perfectly, and 6.359 is the most Equation 47.13 can certify from the 5,000 error-free trials per hypothesis of the evaluation half. The same bug also fails an end-to-end audit with the sum of projections, which with 10,000 runs per hypothesis gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = 7.21 > 6.71\). Figure 47.4 shows why the two noise bugs are easy to see.
A fourth bug lies in the accounting and leaves the code correct. The accountant is told that the dataset has 20,000 records instead of 10,000, as can happen when augmented copies are counted. It computes \(q = 0.005\) and reports \(\varepsilon = 3.06\). The per-step audit measures the noise, which is right, and composing its \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) at the claimed \(q = 0.005\) gives 2.47, which does not contradict 3.06. The end-to-end audit of Table 47.3 does, because the code really samples at \(q = 0.01\) and its 3.63 exceeds 3.06.

The titles give the certified lower bound on the per-step \(\mu\); the claim is 1.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.1 Reusing a holdout set overfits
Every chapter so far has used differential privacy (DP) to protect the people in a dataset. This chapter uses it for a different purpose: to keep a data analysis honest. Machine learning reuses its evaluation data all the time. You tune hyperparameters on a validation set, look at the scores, and try new settings, and competition teams adjust to every leaderboard score. In each case the next question asked of the data depends on the answers to the previous ones. How many such questions can one holdout set answer before its answers stop telling you anything about new data?
The idea that organizes the answer is that a question chosen from answers that reveal little about any one record cannot be overfitted to the holdout set. Overfitting a holdout set means choosing questions that fit its particular records, and to do that the analyst must learn something about those records from the earlier answers. A DP mechanism limits what any sequence of answers reveals about a single record, and that limit survives whatever the analyst computes from the answers. So the proof of Algorithmic stability and generalization, which replaces one record at a time by a fresh one, still works with privacy in place of stability.
The running example is a search over 1,000 hyperparameter configurations on a validation set of 10,000 records, each configuration chosen from the scores of the earlier ones. The error of a score is how far it lies from the model’s accuracy on new data. If the scores were questions fixed in advance, their largest error would be at most 0.0195 on average. Chosen adaptively, they can be much worse: an analyst who attacks the set can make a model that only guesses at random score 0.0712 above its true accuracy. Of the guarantees that hold for any analyst, splitting the set so that each record answers one question bounds the largest error only by 0.6165, and Gaussian noise on each answer by 0.4095. When the analyst also has a training set, the reusable holdout does better in practice, because it adds noise only when the two sets disagree. The chapter’s symbols are collected in Table 48.1.
A holdout set gives an unbiased verdict on a model that was fixed before the holdout set was drawn. The trouble starts on the second question, once the analyst has seen an answer and lets it shape the next one. This section makes the setting precise and shows how quickly exact answers go wrong.
The questions are averages over records, such as an accuracy, so they are the questions of Part 1’s stability chapter (Definition 7.4), here called queries.
When the queries are all fixed before the sample is drawn, exact empirical answers are accurate, and the number of queries enters only through its logarithm. Theorem 7.5 proves that the expected largest error then obeys \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|f_j(D) - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{48.2}\] A version with high probability follows from Hoeffding’s inequality (Theorem 2.5), which bounds the chance that one error exceeds \(\alpha\) by \(2e^{-2n\alpha^2}\), and the union bound over the \(k\) queries (Lemma 2.3). So all \(k\) errors stay below \(\alpha\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) once \[n \ge \frac{\ln(2k/\beta)}{2\alpha^2}. \tag{48.3}\] At \(\alpha = \beta = 0.05\), ten queries need 1,199 records. A thousand queries need 2,120, and a million need only 3,501.
That argument needs each query to be fixed while the records are drawn, so that its values on the records are independent draws with mean \(f_j(\mathcal D)\). One query built from earlier answers is enough to break it.
The bound holds for every sample, and it stays above \(\frac12\) until \(n \ge (k - 1)/2\). So with exact answers \(n\) must grow linearly in \(k\), against \(\ln k\) for fixed queries. Each point query is harmless, but together they reveal the sample, and a later query exploits it.
Real analysts leak more slowly than this attack, but they leak. In Freedman’s paradox (Freedman 1983), which Part 1 runs in Example 7.9, features screened and then tested on the same sample look predictive even when all are noise. The leaderboard version is an attack of Blum & Hardt (2015).
Each kept labelling agrees with the holdout labels slightly more often than chance, and the vote adds these small agreements up. A normal approximation predicts that the vote’s reported accuracy exceeds its true accuracy of \(\frac12\) by about \[\frac{\sqrt{k/(2n)}}{\pi}. \tag{48.5}\] So the overfitting grows like \(\sqrt{k/n}\), while the bound Equation 48.2 for fixed queries grows only like \(\sqrt{\ln k/n}\).

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
Definition 48.1 (Statistical queries and adaptive analysis) The dataset \(D = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) is a sample of \(n\) records drawn independently from a distribution \(\mathcal D\), the population. Each record holds features and label together. A statistical query is a function \(f\) from one record to \([0, 1]\), such as “does this classifier get this record right?”. Its empirical value and its population value are \[f(D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_i), \qquad f(\mathcal D) = \mathbb E_{x \sim \mathcal D}\big[f(x)\big]. \tag{48.1}\] An analyst asks \(k\) queries \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) one at a time, and a mechanism \(M\) answers query \(f_j\) with a number \(a_j\). The analysis is adaptive when each query may depend on the earlier answers. The answers are accurate to a target \(\alpha\) when the largest error \(\max_j|a_j - f_j(\mathcal D)|\) is at most \(\alpha\), either on average or with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) for a small failure probability \(\beta\).




Proposition 48.1 (The point-query attack) Let the records be uniform on \(N\) values, labelled \(1, \dots, N\), and let a mechanism answer every query with its exact empirical value. An analyst asks the \(N\) point queries \(f_v(x) = \mathbf 1[x = v]\), which are fixed in advance. Then it asks one query chosen from their answers: “is this record’s value one of those that occur in the sample?”. With these \(k = N + 1\) queries, the largest error is \[\max_j\big|a_j - f_j(\mathcal D)\big| \ge 1 - \frac nN = 1 - \frac{n}{k - 1}. \tag{48.4}\]


Proof. 

The last query can be built. The answer to \(f_v\) is positive exactly when the value \(v\) occurs in the sample, so the point queries’ answers name the set of values that occur.
Its empirical value. Every record’s value occurs in the sample by definition, so the last query is 1 on every record, and its answer is 1.
Its population value. The last query is 1 exactly on the distinct values of the sample, of which there are at most \(n\). A fresh record takes each value with probability \(1/N\), so the population value is at most \(n/N\).
The error. The last answer exceeds its population value by at least \(1 - n/N\), which is Equation 48.4.




Example 48.1 With \(n = 1{,}000\) records on \(N = 2{,}000\) values, the 2,000 point queries are all within 0.0035 of their population values in one run of the chapter’s script. The last query has empirical value 1 and population value 0.3905, against an expected \(1 - (1 - 1/2{,}000)^{1{,}000} = 0.3935\). So its error is about 0.61, while Equation 48.2 would bound the average largest error of 2,001 fixed queries by 0.0644. With \(N = 10{,}000\) values the error is about 0.90.



Definition 48.2 (The boosting attack) The holdout labels are \(n\) fair coins, independent of everything else, so no submission can beat an accuracy of \(\frac12\) on new data. The attacker submits \(k\) random labellings of the holdout records and reads each one’s exact accuracy. It keeps the labellings that scored above \(\frac12\), and submits their majority vote on each record.



Example 48.2 Table 48.2 runs the attack, averaged over 20 runs. In the running example’s regime, 1,000 submissions to a holdout set of 10,000 records, the final submission reports 0.5712 for a coin flip. Its overfitting of 0.0712 is more than three times the bound 0.0195 for 1,001 fixed queries, the 1,000 submissions and the vote.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.2 Sample splitting and its cost
The attacks work because a query can depend on the records that answer it. The obvious fix is to make that impossible, by never letting a record answer a query it helped to choose. This section asks how much data that costs, because every later method must beat it.

Definition 48.3 (Sample splitting) Split the sample into \(k\) parts \(D_1, \dots, D_k\) of \(n/k\) records each, and answer query \(j\) with its empirical value on part \(j\) only, \(a_j = f_j(D_j)\).

Fixing the earlier parts and the analyst’s own coins fixes query \(j\), while part \(j\) is still a fresh sample. So the argument for fixed queries applies to each part with \(n/k\) records, and Proposition 7.3 proves that, however the queries are chosen, \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|f_j(D_j) - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{k\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{48.6}\] In the same way, Hoeffding’s inequality and the union bound make all errors below \(\alpha\) with probability \(1 - \beta\) once \(n \ge k\ln(2k/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\). The data needed grows linearly in \(k\).
Splitting buys validity by using each record once, as if it collected fresh data for every query, so it suits analyses with few rounds of adaptivity. If the queries come in \(r\) rounds, and each round is fixed before its answers are seen, one part per round suffices, and the bound becomes \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\). A final test set, used once after all decisions are made, is the extreme case \(r = 1\).
When every query is adaptive, though, the cost is steep. At \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(k = 1{,}000\), the bound Equation 48.6 needs 1,520,181 records, against 1,521 for the bound Equation 48.2 on average if the queries were fixed in advance.

Example 48.3 In the running example, 1,000 configurations are scored one after another on 10,000 records. If each score were a query fixed in advance, Equation 48.2 would bound the average largest error by 0.0195. The search is adaptive, so that bound does not apply. Splitting the set into 1,000 parts of 10 records restores validity, but Equation 48.6 is then \(\sqrt{1{,}000\ln 2{,}000/20{,}000} = 0.6165\), which is useless for scores between 0 and 1.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.3 Differential privacy implies generalization
The point-query attack learns individual records from the answers and then asks a query that fits them. A mechanism that hides individual records should stop it without throwing away data, and this section proves that it does. Every later section applies the result.
The proof swaps one record for a fresh one, so the guarantees here are for the replace-one relation. Two samples are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ in one record. Write \(D^{(i)}\) for the sample with \(x_i\) replaced by an independent fresh draw \(x_i'\), so that \(D \sim D^{(i)}\). Under this relation every statistical query has sensitivity \(1/n\), since one record moves an average of \(n\) values in \([0, 1]\) by at most \(1/n\). A mechanism that is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for adding or removing a record is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP for replacing one (Proposition 18.2).
Three facts about DP from Part 3 carry the proof. The first says that DP bounds averages as well as probabilities. For an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism \(M\), neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and every function \(g\) of the output with values in \([0, 1]\), Lemma 19.1 gives \[\mathbb E\big[g(M(D))\big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E\big[g(M(D'))\big] + \delta. \tag{48.7}\] The second is post-processing (Theorem 19.1): any computation on the output that does not touch the data is as private as the output. The third is adaptive composition (Theorem 19.3): mechanisms chosen one after another from earlier outputs have parameters that add up, or grow more slowly under the sharper bounds of Composition. The analyst’s choices are post-processing of earlier answers, so the transcript, the whole list of queries and answers, inherits the answering mechanism’s guarantee, however clever the analyst is.
The first result says that a query chosen privately has nearly the same expected value on the sample as on the population. Its proof needs one tool from Part 1, Lemma 7.1: swapping two independent draws from one distribution, both independent of everything else, leaves the expectation of any function of all of them unchanged. Write \(f_{W(D)}\) for the query that a randomized algorithm \(W\) outputs on the sample \(D\), shortened to \(f_W\) when the sample is clear.

Lemma 48.1 (Transfer lemma) Let \(W\) be an algorithm that reads a sample and outputs a statistical query \(f_W\), and let \(W\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP under the replace-one relation. Then, with expectations over the sample and the coins of \(W\), \[\mathbb E\big[f_W(D)\big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E\big[f_W(\mathcal D)\big] + \delta, \qquad \mathbb E\big[f_W(\mathcal D)\big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E\big[f_W(D)\big] + \delta, \tag{48.8}\] and therefore, since a query’s values lie in \([0, 1]\), \[\Big|\mathbb E\big[f_W(D)\big] - \mathbb E\big[f_W(\mathcal D)\big]\Big| \le e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.9}\]


Proof. The plan is to write both expectations as averages over records \(x_i\) of a chosen query’s value on \(x_i\). On the sample side the query was chosen with \(x_i\) in the sample, and on the population side without it, so DP can compare the two choices.

The empirical value is an average over records. By definition \(f_W(D) = \frac1n\sum_if_W(x_i)\), so linearity of expectation gives \[\mathbb E\big[f_W(D)\big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\big[f_{W(D)}(x_i)\big]. \tag{48.10}\]
The population value is the same average after a swap. The fresh record \(x_i'\) is one that \(W\) never saw, so averaging over \(x_i'\) alone turns its value on \(x_i'\) into the population value: \[\mathbb E\big[f_{W(D)}(\mathcal D)\big] = \mathbb E\big[f_{W(D)}(x_i')\big]. \tag{48.11}\] The records \(x_i\) and \(x_i'\) are independent draws from \(\mathcal D\), independent of the other records and of the coins of \(W\). So by Lemma 7.1, exchanging them, which turns \(D\) into \(D^{(i)}\) and \(x_i'\) into \(x_i\), leaves the expectation unchanged: \[\mathbb E\big[f_{W(D)}(x_i')\big] = \mathbb E\big[f_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)\big]. \tag{48.12}\] In words, the population value of a query chosen from \(D\) equals the value on \(x_i\) of a query chosen without \(x_i\).
DP compares the two choices. Hold \(D\) and \(x_i'\) fixed. Then \(D \sim D^{(i)}\), and \(g(f) = f(x_i)\) is a function of the output of \(W\) with values in \([0, 1]\). So Equation 48.7, with \(\mathbb E_W\) averaging over the coins of \(W\), gives \[\mathbb E_W\big[f_{W(D)}(x_i)\big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_W\big[f_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)\big] + \delta, \tag{48.13}\] and averaging over \(D\) and \(x_i'\) keeps the inequality.
Combine. Averaging step 3 over \(i\) turns its left side into \(\mathbb E[f_W(D)]\) by step 1, and its right side into \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[f_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta\) by step 2. That is the first bound. Subtracting \(\mathbb E[f_W(\mathcal D)]\) from both sides leaves \((e^\varepsilon - 1)\,\mathbb E[f_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta\), which is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) because a query’s value is at most 1.
The other direction. The replace-one relation is symmetric, so steps 3 and 4 hold with \(D\) and \(D^{(i)}\) exchanged, which gives the second bound. The two directions together give Equation 48.9.


Steps 1 and 2 together are Part 1’s identity for the expected gap (Theorem 7.1), with the chosen query in place of a trained model: the gap is an average over records of how much the chosen query’s value on a record changes when that record is replaced. Part 1 bounded each term by uniform stability, the largest change in one fixed algorithm’s loss when one record is replaced, while DP bounds it through the distribution of the output. Uniform stability does not survive the analyst. Keeping the best of several nearly tied queries is a choice that one record can flip, and then the chosen query’s value on that record jumps, much as for the 1-nearest-neighbour rule of Proposition 7.2. DP survives post-processing and adaptive composition, so every query the analyst builds from private answers is chosen privately, which is all the lemma needs.
For small \(\varepsilon\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) is about \(\varepsilon\), so the lemma’s cost is linear in \(\varepsilon\), and that is the right order in general. Take a sample of one record, a fair bit, and let \(W\) release the bit with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and its flip otherwise. If \(W\) then outputs the query “is the record equal to the released bit?”, that query’s empirical value exceeds its population value by about \(\varepsilon/4\) on average. Because the cost grows with \(\varepsilon\), a guarantee to within 0.05 needs \(\varepsilon\) around 0.05 or below.
The theorem turns the lemma into accuracy for every answer of a private mechanism. Its idea is to let a private algorithm pick the query with the worst error. The lemma then says that this worst query cannot be much further from the population than from the sample.

Theorem 48.1 (Transfer theorem) Let \(M\) answer \(k\) adaptively chosen statistical queries, and let the whole interaction be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in the sample under the replace-one relation. Suppose its answers are accurate on the sample on average, \(\mathbb E[\max_j|a_j - f_j(D)|] \le \alpha\). Then they are accurate on the population up to the lemma’s term: \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|a_j - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.14}\]


Proof. The plan is to turn the largest absolute error into the signed error of one query, to choose that query privately, and to split its error into the lemma’s part and the sample’s part.

Add the complements. For each query \(f_j\), also consider \(1 - f_j\), answered by \(1 - a_j\). These answers are computed from the original ones, so by post-processing they cost no privacy. A complement’s signed error is the original’s with the sign flipped, \((1 - f_j(\mathcal D)) - (1 - a_j) = -(f_j(\mathcal D) - a_j)\). So over the \(2k\) queries, the largest signed error \(f(\mathcal D) - a\) equals the largest absolute error of the original \(k\).
Pick the worst query privately. Let \(W\) read the transcript of queries and answers and output the query, among the \(2k\), with the largest \(f(\mathcal D) - a\). DP restricts only how an output depends on the sample. \(W\) also uses the distribution \(\mathcal D\), but that is a fixed constant, like a number written into its code, and \(W\) exists only inside the proof, so no one has to run it. Its only input that depends on the sample is the transcript, so by post-processing it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Split the worst error. By step 1 the left side of Equation 48.14 is \(\mathbb E[f_W(\mathcal D) - a_W]\), where \(a_W\) is the answer to the chosen query. Adding and subtracting its empirical value gives \[\mathbb E\big[f_W(\mathcal D) - a_W\big] = \mathbb E\big[f_W(\mathcal D) - f_W(D)\big] + \mathbb E\big[f_W(D) - a_W\big]. \tag{48.15}\]
Bound each part. The first part is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) by the second bound of Lemma 48.1, since \(W\) is DP. The second is at most \(\mathbb E[\max_j|f_j(D) - a_j|] \le \alpha\), because a complement’s error on the sample equals the original’s. Adding them gives Equation 48.14.


The theorem holds only on average, and Section 48.4 cites versions with high probability.
Step 1 of the proof is its least obvious move, and Table 48.3 shows it on two queries. The largest absolute error, 0.12, is on \(f_1\), whose answer is too high, so among \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) alone the largest signed error would be 0.05. The complement \(1 - f_1\) carries the error 0.12 with a positive sign, and \(W\) picks it.

Example 48.4 The lemma is easiest to see on picking the best-looking candidate, with a small sample so that the bias is visible. Take \(k = 1{,}000\) queries that are all pure noise, each the rate at which a random feature agrees with a random label on \(n = 1{,}000\) records. Every population value is \(\frac12\), and the empirical values are independent with standard deviation \(1/(2\sqrt n) = 0.0158\). Choosing the query with the largest empirical value, with no privacy, overstates it by 0.0509 on average over 2,000 runs. The queries themselves are fixed in advance, so this is at most their largest error, and Equation 48.2 bounds that by 0.0616.
Now choose with the exponential mechanism of Selection, which picks query \(j\) with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon nf_j(D)/2}\). Its score has sensitivity \(1/n\), so it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Theorem 22.1. title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
section: 48.4 Answering with Gaussian noise: the \(\sqrt k\) rate
text:
48.4 Answering with Gaussian noise: the \(\sqrt k\) rate
The transfer theorem makes any private mechanism that is accurate on the sample accurate on the population, and the simplest such mechanism adds Gaussian noise to each empirical value. This section asks how many records that needs for \(k\) adaptive queries, and how it compares with splitting.
The privacy of Gaussian answers is easiest to track in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which measures privacy by one number \(\rho\). It bounds the Rényi divergence between the outputs on neighbours, at every order, by \(\rho\) times that order. By Theorem 31.1, Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) on a query of sensitivity \(1/n\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = 1/(2n^2\sigma^2)\), and the values of \(\rho\) add under adaptive composition. By Theorem 31.4, a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta > 0\) with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{48.16}\]

Theorem 48.2 (Gaussian answers to adaptive queries) Answer each query with \(a_j = f_j(D) + \xi_j\), where the noises \(\xi_j\) are independent and normal with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\). Then for every \(\delta > 0\), \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_j\big|a_j - f_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)} + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta, \qquad \varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \quad \rho = \frac{k}{2n^2\sigma^2}. \tag{48.17}\]


Proof. 

Privacy. Each answer is the Gaussian mechanism on a query of sensitivity \(1/n\), so it is \(\rho_1\)-zCDP with \(\rho_1 = 1/(2n^2\sigma^2)\). The analyst chooses each query from earlier answers, and adaptive composition adds the \(k\) values to \(\rho = k\rho_1\). Equation 48.16 converts this to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Accuracy on the sample. The errors on the sample are the noises \(\xi_j\). A normal variable with variance \(\sigma^2\) has moment generating function exactly \(e^{s^2\sigma^2/2}\). The proof of Theorem 7.5 bounds an expected maximum of \(2k\) variables using only such a bound for each, \(e^{s^2/(8n)}\) there, and not their independence. Run with \(e^{s^2\sigma^2/2}\) for the \(2k\) values \(\pm\xi_j\), its steps give \(\mathbb E[\max_j|\xi_j|] \le \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\).
Transfer. Theorem 48.1, with the accuracy of step 2 and the privacy of step 1, gives Equation 48.17.


More noise lowers the transfer term but raises the noise term, so there is a best noise level, and it sets the rate. To see it, keep only the leading part of the transfer term. For small \(\varepsilon\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) is about \(\varepsilon\), and for small \(\rho\) the conversion is dominated by its square-root term.

Corollary 48.1 (The square-root rate) Replace the transfer term of Equation 48.17 by its leading part \(2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\), and leave the \(\delta\) term aside. The resulting bound is smallest at \(\sigma = (k\ln(1/\delta)/\ln(2k))^{1/4}/\sqrt n\), and there it equals \(\alpha\) when \[n = \frac{8\sqrt{k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}}{\alpha^2}. \tag{48.18}\] With \(\delta\) of order \(\alpha\), so that the \(\delta\) term also stays below \(\alpha\), the number of records grows like the square root of \(k\): \[n = O\Big(\frac{\sqrt{k\,\ln k\,\ln(1/\alpha)}}{\alpha^2}\Big). \tag{48.19}\]


Proof. 

The leading transfer term. With \(\rho = k/(2n^2\sigma^2)\), the leading part is \[2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)} = \frac{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}}{n\sigma}. \tag{48.20}\]
Balance the two terms. The bound is now \(\sigma A + B/\sigma\), with \(A = \sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\) from the noise and \(B = \sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}/n\) from step 1. Its derivative \(A - B/\sigma^2\) vanishes at \(\sigma = \sqrt{B/A}\), which is the stated noise level, and there the bound equals \(2\sqrt{AB}\).
Solve for \(n\). Setting \(2\sqrt{AB} = \alpha\) gives \(AB = \alpha^2/4\). Since \(AB = 2\sqrt{k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}/n\), this is the stated \(n\), and \(\ln(1/\delta)\) of order \(\ln(1/\alpha)\) gives Equation 48.19.


The \(\sqrt k\) is the \(\sqrt k\) of composition. Under zCDP, \(\rho\) grows like \(k\), so the \(\varepsilon\) of \(k\) answers grows like \(\sqrt k\) times that of one. So the best error grows like \(k^{1/4}/\sqrt n\), up to logarithms, and keeping it at \(\alpha\) needs \(n\) to grow like \(\sqrt k\), while splitting needs \(n\) to grow like \(k\). The approximate \(n\) is slightly below the exact optimum, because the proof dropped terms that add to the bound.
The constants are large. Table 48.5 solves each expected-error bound for the smallest \(n\) that reaches \(\alpha = 0.05\). For one query the Gaussian bound needs 7,300 records, against 139 for the other two, and splitting stays cheaper up to a few hundred adaptive queries. Beyond that the square root wins: at a million queries, 33 million records against 2.9 billion. At the optimum the error splits almost equally between the noise, 0.0242, and the transfer term, 0.0258, with \(\varepsilon = 0.0236\) and \(\delta = 0.0019\) for every \(k\). Here \(\delta\) protects no one, because it is only a parameter of the bound.
