For a density the list of ways becomes an integral. The first variable takes a value \(x\), the second must make up the rest, \(s - x\), and independence multiplies the two densities. That is Equation E.1. Each identification in the chapter is one such integral, and each is short.
Rotation invariance has a different reason. The joint density of \(X\) depends on the point \(x\) only through its distance from the origin, so in two dimensions its contours are circles, and in \(d\) dimensions they are spheres. A rotation moves every point along its sphere and keeps every volume, so it leaves the density where it was. So a rotation that carries two perpendicular directions onto the first two coordinate axes does not change the distribution. Along the axes the coordinates are independent by definition, so they are independent along the two directions too.


E.1.3 Derivation

Why Equation E.1 holds. Fix a small width \(\kappa > 0\) and the interval of that width around \(s\). The sum lands in it when \(X\) is near some value \(x\) and \(Y\) lands within \(\kappa\) of \(s - x\). Given \(X = x\), that has chance about \(g(s - x)\kappa\), because \(Y\) is independent of \(X\) and so its density does not change. Averaging over \(x\) with the density \(f\) gives \(\kappa\int f(x)g(s - x)\,dx\), and dividing by \(\kappa\) gives the density. For counts the same step reads \(\Pr[X + Y = k] = \sum_j\Pr[X = j]\Pr[Y = k - j]\), as in the dice.
Poisson. Take independent \(N_1 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_1)\) and \(N_2 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_2)\). The sum of step 1, with \(\Pr[N = j] = e^{-\mu}\mu^j/j!\), is \[\Pr[N_1 + N_2 = k] = \sum_{j=0}^k e^{-\mu_1}\frac{\mu_1^j}{j!}\,e^{-\mu_2}\frac{\mu_2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!} = \frac{e^{-(\mu_1+\mu_2)}}{k!}\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj\mu_1^j\mu_2^{k-j}. \tag{E.3}\] The second form multiplies and divides by \(k!\), and \(\binom kj = k!/(j!(k-j)!)\). The binomial theorem says that the last sum is \((\mu_1 + \mu_2)^k\). So \(\Pr[N_1 + N_2 = k] = e^{-(\mu_1+\mu_2)}(\mu_1 + \mu_2)^k/k!\), which is the \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_1 + \mu_2)\) probability.
Exponential minus exponential. Let \(Y_1, Y_2 \sim \mathrm{Exp}(b)\) be independent, each with density \(f(y) = \frac1be^{-y/b}\) for \(y \ge 0\) and 0 for \(y < 0\). The difference \(Y_1 - Y_2\) equals \(x\) when \(Y_1 = y\) and \(Y_2 = y - x\), so the density of the difference at \(x\) is \(\int f(y)f(y - x)\,dy\). Here \(y\) is the integration variable and \(x\) is the value of the difference. This is Equation E.1 for the sum \(Y_1 + (-Y_2)\), whose second term has density \(f(-z)\), so the copy of \(f\) appears shifted but not flipped. The integrand is non-zero only where both \(y \ge 0\) and \(y - x \ge 0\), that is for \(y \ge \max(0, x)\), and on that range \[f(y)f(y - x) = \frac{1}{b^2}e^{-y/b}e^{-(y - x)/b} = \frac{1}{b^2}e^{x/b}e^{-2y/b}. \tag{E.4}\] Integrating \(e^{-2y/b}\) from a point \(c\) to infinity gives \(\frac b2e^{-2c/b}\), so with \(c = \max(0, x)\) the density of the difference is \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{x/b}e^{-2\max(0, x)/b}\). When \(x \ge 0\) this is \(\frac1{2b}e^{-x/b}\), and when \(x < 0\) it is \(\frac1{2b}e^{x/b}\). Together they make \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|x|/b}\), which is the \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) density.
Sums of exponentials. Write \(f_n(x) = x^{n-1}e^{-x}/(n-1)!\) for \(x \ge 0\), the \(\mathrm{Gamma}(n, 1)\) density. For \(n = 1\) it is \(e^{-x}\), the \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) density. Suppose the sum of \(n\) independent \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) variables has density \(f_n\), and add one more. Use Equation E.1 with the sum at \(x\) and the integration variable \(y\) for the first term. Both terms are non-negative, so \(y\) can only lie between 0 and \(x\): \[\int_0^x\frac{y^{n-1}e^{-y}}{(n-1)!}\,e^{-(x - y)}\,dy = \frac{e^{-x}}{(n-1)!}\int_0^xy^{n-1}\,dy = \frac{e^{-x}}{(n-1)!}\cdot\frac{x^n}{n} = \frac{x^ne^{-x}}{n!}. \tag{E.5}\] The exponentials combine to \(e^{-x}\), which does not depend on \(y\), so it leaves the integral. The result is \(f_{n+1}\). By induction, the claim holds for every \(n\).
Sums of normals. Start with two independent normals with mean 0, \(X_1 \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_1^2)\) and \(X_2 \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_2^2)\), and write \(v = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2\). In Equation E.1 the two exponents add to \(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac{(s - y)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\). Completing the square in \(y\) rewrites this sum as \[-\frac{v}{2\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}\Big(y - \frac{\sigma_1^2}{v}s\Big)^2 - \frac{s^2}{2v}, \tag{E.6}\] which you can check by expanding both forms. The first term is the exponent of a normal density in \(y\) with variance \(\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2/v\), and integrating it over \(y\) gives \(\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2/v}\). The two normalizing factors \(1/(\sigma_1\sqrt{2\pi})\) and \(1/(\sigma_2\sqrt{2\pi})\) remain. Multiplying the three numbers leaves \(1/\sqrt{2\pi v}\), so the sum has density \(e^{-s^2/(2v)}/\sqrt{2\pi v}\), the \(\mathcal N(0, v)\) density. Two simpler facts extend this to weighted sums with any means. First, multiplying \(X \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) by a constant \(a > 0\) gives \(\mathcal N(a\mu, a^2\sigma^2)\). The reason is that \(aX \le t\) is the event \(X \le t/a\). Differentiating its probability in \(t\) gives the density of \(X\) at \(t/a\) times \(1/a\), and that is the \(\mathcal N(a\mu, a^2\sigma^2)\) density. A negative \(a\) also flips the sign, which the symmetry of the normal about its mean absorbs. Second, adding a constant only moves the mean. With these two facts, applying the two-term rule one term at a time gives the rule for \(\sum_ia_iX_i\).
Rotation invariance. The coordinates of \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\) are independent, so its joint density is the product of \(d\) normal densities. The exponents add up to the squared length \(\|x\|^2 = x_1^2 + \dots + x_d^2\): \[p(x) = \prod_{i=1}^d\frac{e^{-x_i^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}e^{-\|x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{E.7}\] In this appendix a rotation means any square matrix \(O\) whose rows are perpendicular unit vectors, which is also called an orthogonal matrix (it includes reflections). It keeps every length, \(\|Ox\| = \|x\|\), because the coordinates of \(Ox\) are the components of \(x\) along the rows of \(O\). It also keeps every volume, because the factor by which a matrix scales volumes is \(|\det O|\), and \(\det O = \pm1\) since \(O^\top O = I\). In two dimensions, for example, \(O\) turns the plane by an angle \(\phi\), and \(\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi = 1\) is the reason lengths are kept. Now let \(Y = OX\). For any region \(A\), \(Y\) lands in \(A\) exactly when \(X\) lands in the region \(O^{-1}A\) that \(O\) maps onto \(A\). Substituting \(x = O^{-1}y\), which keeps volume, gives \(\Pr[Y \in A] = \int_A p(O^{-1}y)\,dy\). By Equation E.7, \(p(O^{-1}y)\) depends only on \(\|O^{-1}y\| = \|y\|\), so it equals \(p(y)\). So \(Y\) has the same density as \(X\).
Perpendicular projections are independent. Let \(u\) and \(v\) be perpendicular unit vectors. Choose a rotation \(O\) whose first row is \(u\) and whose second row is \(v\); the other rows are any unit vectors that complete a perpendicular set. The first two coordinates of \(Y = OX\) are then \(\langle u, X\rangle\) and \(\langle v, X\rangle\). By step 6, \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\), so these two coordinates are independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) variables. This also proves the chapter’s general remark, if “jointly normal” means “linear functions of one vector of independent standard normals”. Two such variables \(A = \langle a, G\rangle\) and \(B = \langle b, G\rangle\), with \(G \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), have covariance \(\mathbb E[AB] = \sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\,\mathbb E[G_iG_j] = \sum_ia_ib_i = \langle a, b\rangle\), because \(\mathbb E[G_iG_j]\) is 1 when \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. When that is 0, \(a/\|a\|\) and \(b/\|b\|\) are perpendicular unit vectors, so \(A\) and \(B\) are multiples of two independent normals, and adding constant means keeps them independent.
Two Laplace variables with the same scale. The density \(\frac\varepsilon4(1 + \varepsilon|z|)e^{-\varepsilon|z|}\) is the equal-scale case of the convolution in Section E.6 (step 5 there).

One more claim of the chapter needs no new proof. It says that the sum of two independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variables is not Laplace, because its MGF \(1/(1 - b^2\lambda^2)^2\) is not a Laplace MGF. That argument needs only the easy direction, which is that two variables with the same distribution have the same MGF. So it does not depend on the uniqueness theorem.


E.1.4 Checking it
The script of this appendix (see the Code section at the end) evaluates each convolution numerically and compares it with the closed form. For the sum of two Poisson counts with means 2 and 3, the largest gap to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(5)\) is \(3.3 \times 10^{-16}\), which is rounding error. The difference of two exponential densities, integrated on a grid, is within \(7.2 \times 10^{-5}\) of the Laplace density. Similarly, five exponential densities convolved on a grid are within \(1.1 \times 10^{-3}\) of the Gamma density. Both of these gaps are the error of the grid, so they shrink as the grid gets finer. Finally, the sum of normals with variances 1 and 4 matches the normal density with variance 5 to \(1.2 \times 10^{-12}\).
Figure E.1 draws the integral of step 3. In each of the first three panels, the blue curve is \(f(y)\) and the orange curve is its copy shifted by \(x\). The green area under their product is the density of the difference at \(x\). At \(x = 0\) the two curves coincide and the overlap is largest, 0.5. Moving the copy either way shrinks the overlap at the same exponential rate, which is why the result is the two-sided Laplace shape in the last panel.






Figure E.1: The density of \(Y_1 - Y_2\) for independent \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) variables at \(x = -1\), 0 and 1.5, as the area under \(f(y)f(y - x)\) (green), next to the \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) density with those three areas marked.



For rotation invariance, the script draws a million points from \(\mathcal N(0, I_2)\) and projects them onto \(u = (\cos\phi, \sin\phi)\) and the perpendicular \(v\), with \(\phi = \pi/6\). The two projections have variances 0.9983 and 1.0010 and correlation \(-0.0005\). Independence is a stronger claim than zero correlation, so the script also checks a joint probability. The chance that both projections exceed 1 is 0.0251, and the product of the two separate chances is \((1 - \Phi(1))^2 = 0.0252\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF). Figure E.2 shows the circular contours and the two matching histograms.






Figure E.2: Left: contours of the \(\mathcal N(0, I_2)\) density, which are circles, with 400 sample points and two perpendicular unit vectors \(u\) and \(v\). Right: histograms of the projections \(\langle u, X\rangle\) and \(\langle v, X\rangle\) over 200,000 draws, against the \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) density.





E.1.5 What it does not cover
The derivations identify each sum that the book needs, one at a time. They do not prove the general theorem that an MGF finite near 0 determines the distribution. That theorem needs a way to recover a distribution from its transform, through complex numbers or a limit argument, and it stays cited to Blitzstein & Hwang (2019) and Billingsley (1995). Nothing in the book depends on it beyond the cases proved here.

title: Appendix E — Sums, limits and counting
section: E.2 Stirling’s formula and the peak of a binomial
text:
E.2 Stirling’s formula and the peak of a binomial

E.2.1 What the chapter uses
Four sections in the attacks part count with binomial probabilities. Write \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\) for the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials with success probability \(p\). Write \(\bar p = 1 - p\) and \(p_k = \Pr[X = k] = \binom nkp^k\bar p^{n-k}\).

Section 9.5 (Equation 9.17) says that the binomial weights “rise up to the middle value and fall after it”. From that it shows that shifting \(\mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\) by one has total variation (TV) distance equal to the largest weight, \(\binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\). It then says that this is about \(\sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\), without proof.
Section 9.3 releases the exact sum \(K\) of \(m\) fair secret bits. Given \(K\), the best guess sets every bit to the majority value, which gets \(\max(K, m - K)\) bits right, so the expected fraction recovered is \(\frac12 + \mathbb E|K - \frac m2|/m\). It approximates the fraction by \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\) through the central limit theorem and the mean absolute value \(\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\) of a normal variable. That step assumes that the average distance \(\mathbb E|K - \frac m2|\) follows the normal one, which the CLT alone does not give, because the CLT is a statement about probabilities, not averages.
Section 12.2 (Equation 12.7) states that a binomial is unimodal. It then argues that the probability of the most likely count is close to the height \(1/\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\) of the normal curve, because “the density is nearly flat over a unit interval at the top”.
Section 13.3 (Equation 13.11) uses \(\ln N! = N\ln N - N + O(\ln N)\), “Stirling’s approximation of the factorial”, without proof.

This section proves all of these. First, the binomial probabilities rise and then fall, with the most likely count at \(\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor\). Second, Stirling’s formula holds with an explicit error \(r_n\): \[n! = \sqrt{2\pi n}\,\Big(\frac ne\Big)^ne^{r_n}, \qquad 0 < r_n \le \frac{1}{12n}. \tag{E.8}\] Third, the fraction of bits recovered from the sum of \(m\) fair bits is exactly \[\frac12 + \frac12\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}, \qquad j = \lfloor m/2\rfloor, \tag{E.9}\] and \(\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}\sqrt{\pi j} \to 1\), so the fraction is \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\) up to a relative error that vanishes.
Fourth, the height of the mode is close to the peak \(1/\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\) of the normal curve with the same mean and variance. The proof needs the count to have some spread, so it assumes \(np\bar p \ge 4\), and then \[\Big|\ln\big(\max_kp_k\cdot\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\big)\Big| \le \frac{3.5}{np\bar p}. \tag{E.10}\]


E.2.2 The idea
The shape of the binomial comes from comparing each probability with the next one. Going from \(k\) to \(k + 1\) successes multiplies the probability by a ratio that gets smaller as \(k\) grows. While the ratio is above 1 the probabilities climb, and once it drops below 1 they fall, so there is one peak. With \(n = 4\) and \(p = \frac12\) the ratios are \(4, \frac32, \frac23, \frac14\), and the probabilities \(\frac1{16}, \frac4{16}, \frac6{16}, \frac4{16}, \frac1{16}\) climb twice and fall twice.
For the factorial, compare a sum with an integral. The logarithm \(\ln n! = \ln 1 + \ln 2 + \dots + \ln n\) is a sum of values of the slowly growing function \(\ln x\), so it is close to \(\int\ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x\). That gives \(n\ln n - n\) with an error of order \(\ln n\). Part of the error is exactly \(\frac12\ln n\), which becomes the \(\sqrt n\) in Stirling’s formula. What remains changes from \(n\) to \(n + 1\) by an amount that is always positive and adds up to a finite total, so it settles to a constant. A classical integral of \(\sin^n\), due to Wallis, then shows that the constant is \(\ln\sqrt{2\pi}\).


E.2.3 Derivation

The ratio of neighbours. Dividing the binomial formula at \(k + 1\) by the one at \(k\), most factors cancel: \[\frac{p_{k+1}}{p_k} = \frac{n - k}{k + 1}\cdot\frac p{\bar p}. \tag{E.11}\] As \(k\) grows the numerator \(n - k\) falls and the denominator \(k + 1\) rises, so the ratio decreases. It is above 1 exactly when \((n - k)p > (k + 1)\bar p\), which rearranges to \(k < (n + 1)p - 1\). So the probabilities rise while \(k + 1 < (n + 1)p\) and do not rise after. The last count reached by a rise is the largest whole number not above \((n + 1)p\), so the largest probability is at \(k^* = \lfloor(n + 1)p\rfloor\). When \((n + 1)p\) is a whole number the ratio there is exactly 1, and \(k^* - 1\) ties with \(k^*\).
Shifting by one costs the height of the peak. This is the argument of Section 9.5, which step 1 completes. The shifted list is the distribution of \(X + 1\), with \(\Pr[X + 1 = k] = p_{k-1}\), and the TV distance is the total of \(p_{k-1} - p_k\) over the \(k\) where it is positive. By step 1 those are exactly the \(k\) after the peak, \(k = k^* + 1, \dots, n + 1\), with \(p_{n+1} = 0\). In the sum \((p_{k^*} - p_{k^*+1}) + (p_{k^*+1} - p_{k^*+2}) + \dots + (p_n - p_{n+1})\), each negative part cancels the positive part of the next difference, and only \(p_{k^*}\) survives. So the TV distance equals \(\max_kp_k\).
A rough Stirling formula. The function \(\ln x\) increases, so on the interval \([k - 1, k]\) it lies below \(\ln k\), and on \([k, k + 1]\) it lies above. Summing over \(k = 2, \dots, n\) therefore gives \[\int_1^n\ln x\,dx \le \ln n! \le \int_1^{n+1}\ln x\,dx, \tag{E.12}\] since \(\ln 1 = 0\). The integral of \(\ln x\) is \(x\ln x - x\), so the two sides are \(n\ln n - n + 1\) and \((n + 1)\ln(n + 1) - n\). The upper side exceeds \(n\ln n - n\) by \(\ln(n + 1) + n\ln(1 + 1/n)\), and the second part is at most 1 because \(\ln(1 + u) \le u\). So \(\ln n!\) is \(n\ln n - n\) up to an error between 0 and \(\ln(n + 1) + 1\), which gives the form Section 13.3 uses: \[\ln n! = n\ln n - n + O(\ln n). \tag{E.13}\]
The error settles to a constant. Define \(d_n = \ln n! - (n + \frac12)\ln n + n\), the error left after taking out \(n\ln n - n\) and also \(\frac12\ln n\). The extra \(\frac12\ln n\) is chosen because, as the next lines show, it makes the remaining error change by a summable amount. Subtracting \(d_{n+1}\) from \(d_n\), the factorials leave \(-\ln(n + 1)\) and most terms cancel: \[d_n - d_{n+1} = \Big(n + \frac12\Big)\ln\frac{n + 1}{n} - 1. \tag{E.14}\] Write \(u = 1/(2n + 1)\). Then \(\frac{n + 1}{n} = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u}\) and \(n + \frac12 = \frac1{2u}\). The power series \(\ln\frac{1 + u}{1 - u} = 2(u + \frac{u^3}3 + \frac{u^5}5 + \cdots)\) comes from subtracting the series of \(\ln(1 - u)\) from that of \(\ln(1 + u)\), where the even powers cancel. Multiplying by \(\frac1{2u}\) and subtracting 1 gives \[d_n - d_{n+1} = \frac{u^2}{3} + \frac{u^4}{5} + \frac{u^6}{7} + \cdots. \tag{E.15}\] Every term is positive, so \(d_n\) decreases. The denominators 5, 7, … are larger than 3, so the sum is at most \(\frac{u^2}3(1 + u^2 + u^4 + \cdots) = \frac{u^2}{3(1 - u^2)}\). Since \(1 - u^2 = \frac{4n(n+1)}{(2n+1)^2}\), this equals \(\frac{1}{12n(n + 1)}\), which is \(\frac1{12}\big(\frac1n - \frac1{n+1}\big)\). Adding these steps from \(n\) onwards, the right sides telescope, so \(d_n - d_{n+k} < \frac1{12n}\) for every \(k\). A decreasing sequence that never drops more than a fixed amount has a limit, so \(d_n\) tends to a constant \(d_\infty\), with \(0 < d_n - d_\infty \le \frac1{12n}\). This is Equation E.8 with \(r_n = d_n - d_\infty\), once \(d_\infty = \ln\sqrt{2\pi}\).
Wallis’s integrals. Let \(I_n = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx\), so \(I_0 = \pi/2\) and \(I_1 = 1\). Integrating by parts, with \(\sin^nx = \sin^{n-1}x\cdot\sin x\), gives \(I_n = (n - 1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx\). Writing \(\cos^2x = 1 - \sin^2x\) turns this into \((n - 1)(I_{n-2} - I_n)\), so \(I_n = \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}\). Running this down to \(I_0\) or \(I_1\) gives products of fractions such as \(\frac{1\cdot3\cdots(2j-1)}{2\cdot4\cdots2j}\), which equals \(\binom{2j}j4^{-j}\). So \[I_{2j} = \frac\pi2\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}, \qquad I_{2j+1} = \frac{1}{(2j + 1)\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}}. \tag{E.16}\] Since \(0 \le \sin x \le 1\), the integrals decrease in \(n\). So \(1 \le I_{2j}/I_{2j+1} \le I_{2j-1}/I_{2j+1} = \frac{2j+1}{2j}\), and the ratio tends to 1. The ratio is \(\frac\pi2(2j + 1)\big(\binom{2j}j4^{-j}\big)^2\), so \[\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j} = \frac{1 + o(1)}{\sqrt{\pi j}}, \tag{E.17}\] where \(o(1)\) is a quantity that tends to 0 as \(j\) grows.
The constant. Write \(\ln\binom{2j}{j} = \ln(2j)! - 2\ln j!\) and replace each \(\ln n!\) by \(d_n + (n + \frac12)\ln n - n\), which is the definition of step 4 solved for \(\ln n!\). Writing \(\ln(2j) = \ln 2 + \ln j\), the terms in \(j\ln j\) and \(j\) cancel, and what is left is \[\ln\Big(\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}\Big) = d_{2j} - 2d_j + \tfrac12\ln 2 - \tfrac12\ln j. \tag{E.18}\] As \(j\) grows, \(d_{2j} - 2d_j \to -d_\infty\). By Equation E.17 the left side is \(-\frac12\ln(\pi j) + o(1)\). Matching the two gives \(-d_\infty + \frac12\ln 2 = -\frac12\ln\pi\), so \(d_\infty = \frac12\ln(2\pi) = \ln\sqrt{2\pi}\).
The fraction recovered, exactly. For \(K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\) one identity does all the work: \[\Big(k - \frac m2\Big)\binom mk = \frac m2\Big[\binom{m-1}{k-1} - \binom{m-1}{k}\Big]. \tag{E.19}\] It holds because \(\binom{m-1}{k-1} = \frac km\binom mk\) and \(\binom{m-1}{k} = \frac{m-k}m\binom mk\). By symmetry about \(\frac m2\), \(\mathbb E|K - \frac m2|\) is twice the sum of \((k - \frac m2)\binom mk2^{-m}\) over \(k > \frac m2\). Let \(k_0\) be the first whole number above \(\frac m2\). Replacing each term by the identity, the sum from \(k_0\) to \(m\) telescopes as in step 2, because the second binomial of each term cancels the first binomial of the next, and only \(\frac m2\binom{m-1}{k_0-1}2^{-m}\) is left. So \(\mathbb E|K - \frac m2|/m = \binom{m-1}{k_0-1}2^{-m}\). Now write \(j = \lfloor m/2\rfloor\). When \(m = 2j\) is even, \(k_0 = j + 1\) and \(\binom{2j-1}{j} = \frac12\binom{2j}{j}\). When \(m = 2j + 1\) is odd, \(k_0 = j + 1\) again and \(\binom{2j}{j}2^{-2j-1}\) appears directly. Either way \(\mathbb E|K - \frac m2|/m = \frac12\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}\), which is Equation E.9. For \(m = 10\) the fraction recovered is \(\frac12 + \frac12 \cdot 252/1024 = 0.62305\). By Equation E.17 and \(j \approx m/2\), the excess over \(\frac12\) is \(\frac{1 + o(1)}{2\sqrt{\pi m/2}} = \frac{1 + o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi m}}\), which is the chapter’s approximation, now proved.
The height of the peak for any \(p\). Write \(k = k^*\) for the mode and \(a = k/n\) for the fraction of successes there. Replace each of \(n!\), \(k!\) and \((n - k)!\) in \(p_k\) by Equation E.8. The square roots give \(\sqrt{n/(2\pi k(n - k))}\), and the powers \(n^n\), \(k^k\), \((n-k)^{n-k}\), \(p^k\) and \(\bar p^{n-k}\) combine into \(\exp\big(-k\ln\frac{k}{np} - (n - k)\ln\frac{n-k}{n\bar p}\big)\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\) and grouping gives three factors: \[p_k\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p} = \underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{p\bar p}{a(1 - a)}}}_{A}\cdot\underbrace{e^{-n\,\mathrm{kl}(a\|p)}}_{B}\cdot\underbrace{e^{r_n - r_k - r_{n-k}}}_{R}, \tag{E.20}\] where \(\mathrm{kl}(a\|p) = a\ln\frac ap + (1 - a)\ln\frac{1-a}{\bar p}\) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between coins with success probabilities \(a\) and \(p\), which is never negative. The mode is within one count of the mean. By step 1, \(k^*\) lies between \((n + 1)p - 1\) and \((n + 1)p\), so the offset \(\xi = k^* - np\) satisfies \(|\xi| < 1\). Each factor is then close to 1.

Factor \(B\). The logarithm is concave, so by Jensen’s inequality \(\mathrm{kl}(a\|p) \le \ln\big(\frac{a^2}p + \frac{(1-a)^2}{\bar p}\big) = \ln\big(1 + \frac{(a-p)^2}{p\bar p}\big) \le \frac{(a-p)^2}{p\bar p}\). With \(a - p = \xi/n\), this gives \(0 \le -\ln B = n\,\mathrm{kl}(a\|p) \le \xi^2/(np\bar p) < 1/(np\bar p)\).
Factor \(R\). By Equation E.8, \(|\ln R| \le \frac1{12}\big(\frac1n + \frac1k + \frac1{n-k}\big)\). When \(np\bar p \ge 4\), \(k > np - 1 \ge np/2\) and \(n - k > n\bar p - 1 \ge n\bar p/2\), so \(|\ln R| \le \frac{1}{12}\cdot\frac{5}{np\bar p}\), using \(\frac1n, \frac1{np}, \frac1{n\bar p} \le \frac1{np\bar p}\).
Factor \(A\). With \(a = p + \xi/n\) and \(1 - a = \bar p - \xi/n\), multiplying out gives \(a(1 - a) = p\bar p(1 + x)\) with \(x = \frac{\xi(\bar p - p)}{np\bar p} - \frac{\xi^2}{n^2p\bar p}\), so \(|x| \le \frac{2}{np\bar p} \le \frac12\). For \(|x| \le \frac12\), \(|\ln(1 + x)| \le 2|x|\), so \(|\ln A| = \frac12|\ln(1 + x)| \le \frac{2}{np\bar p}\).

Adding the three logarithms gives \((2 + 1 + \frac5{12})/(np\bar p) < 3.5/(np\bar p)\), which is Equation E.10. With \(n - 1\) trials and the chapter’s subgroup share \(t\) as the success probability, it gives Equation 12.7, and for \(p = \frac12\) the height \(\sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\) of Section 9.5.



E.2.4 Checking it
Figure E.3 shows step 2 for \(\mathrm{Bin}(10, \frac12)\). The green bars, where the shifted list is larger, start right after the peak and add up to 0.2461, the height of the mode. For \(\mathrm{Bin}(100, \frac12)\) the same total is 0.0796, the value in Section 9.5. The script also checks step 1 by brute force. For every \(n \le 60\) and eight values of \(p\), \(\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor\) is a most likely count in all 480 cases.






Figure E.3: Top: the \(\mathrm{Bin}(10, \frac12)\) probabilities and the same list moved one place right. Bottom: their difference at each \(k\). The positive differences (green) all lie after the peak and add up to the height of the mode.



Stirling’s error is close to its bound everywhere (Figure E.4). At \(n = 10\) the error \(r_n\) is \(8.331 \times 10^{-3}\) against \(1/(12n) = 8.333 \times 10^{-3}\), and at \(n = 1\) it is 0.0811 against 0.0833. So \(1/(12n)\) is nearly the exact error, not just a bound. The rough bounds of step 3 are far weaker, since at \(n = 10\) they only place \(\ln 10! = 15.1044\) between 14.0259 and 16.3768.






Figure E.4: The error of Stirling’s formula, \(r_n = \ln n! - \ln\big(\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n\big)\), against \(n\) on log axes, with the bound \(1/(12n)\) and the gap between the rough bounds of step 3.



For the fraction of bits recovered, Equation E.9 gives 0.62305, 0.53979 and 0.51261 for \(m = 10\), 100 and 1000, matching the sums over the binomial table to the digits shown. The approximation \(\frac12 + 1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\) gives 0.62616, 0.53989 and 0.51262. The script also confirms that \(m = 11\) recovers the same fraction as \(m = 10\), as Equation E.9 says. The ratio \(\binom{2j}{j}4^{-j}\sqrt{\pi j}\) is 0.97535 at \(j = 5\) and 0.99750 at \(j = 50\), so it approaches 1 with an error close to \(1/(8j)\).
Figure E.5 shows Equation E.10. The ratio of the mode height to \(1/\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\) approaches 1 for \(p = 0.5\), 0.2 and 0.05. At \(n = 100\) it is 0.9975, 0.9956 and 0.9834. The right panel shows that the error falls like \(1/(np\bar p)\). The constant 3.5 of the proof is loose: over every \(n \le 20{,}000\) and six values of \(p\) with \(np\bar p \ge 4\), the script finds \(np\bar p\,|\ln(\text{ratio})|\) at most 0.187.






Figure E.5: Left: the height of the binomial mode divided by the normal peak height \(1/\sqrt{2\pi np\bar p}\), against \(n\), for three values of \(p\). Right: the absolute logarithm of that ratio against \(np\bar p\), with the proved bound \(3.5/(np\bar p)\).

title: Appendix E — Sums, limits and counting
section: E.3 How fast a Poisson count falls far above its mean
text:
E.3 How fast a Poisson count falls far above its mean

E.3.1 What the chapter uses
Section 1.4 in Probability distributions defines a Poisson count \(N \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\) with mean \(\mu > 0\). It takes each value \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) with probability \[\Pr[N = k] = e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^k}{k!}. \tag{E.21}\] The chapter says that far above the mean these probabilities fall like \((e\mu/k)^k\), faster than any exponential but slower than the tail of a normal variable with the same variance, and it points here for the proof. This section proves that for every count \(k \ge 1\), \[\Pr[N = k] \le \Big(\frac{e\mu}{k}\Big)^k. \tag{E.22}\] It then shows that the whole tail beyond \(k\) obeys the same bound up to a constant factor, once \(k\) is larger than \(e\mu\): \[\Pr[N \ge k] \le \frac{(e\mu/k)^k}{1 - e\mu/k}. \tag{E.23}\]


E.3.2 The idea
The probability of the count \(k\) has \(k!\) in its denominator, so how fast the tail falls depends on how fast \(k!\) grows. A lower bound on \(k!\) gives an upper bound on the probability, and the lower bound comes from the power series of the exponential. That series writes \(e^k\) as a sum of positive terms \(k^j/j!\), one for each \(j = 0, 1, 2, \dots\), and the term with \(j = k\) is \(k^k/k!\). A sum of positive terms is at least any one of its terms, so \(k^k/k!\) is at most \(e^k\). For \(k = 3\), for example, the term is \(27/6 = 4.5\), while the whole sum is \(e^3 \approx 20.09\).
For the whole tail, each probability beyond \(k\) is at most the matching power of the single number \(e\mu/k\). Once that number is below 1, the powers form a geometric series, and a geometric series adds up to its first term divided by one minus its ratio.


E.3.3 Derivation

A lower bound on the factorial. The power series of the exponential at \(k\) is \(e^k = \sum_{j \ge 0}k^j/j!\). Every term is positive, so the sum is at least its term \(j = k\), which is \(k^k/k!\). Solving \(k^k/k! \le e^k\) for \(k!\) gives \[k! \ge \Big(\frac ke\Big)^k. \tag{E.24}\]
Bound one probability. Replacing \(k!\) in the denominator by this smaller number can only make the fraction larger, so \[\Pr[N = k] \le e^{-\mu}\mu^k\Big(\frac ek\Big)^k. \tag{E.25}\]
Drop the constant. The mean \(\mu\) is positive, so the factor \(e^{-\mu}\) is below 1, and dropping it gives Equation E.22.
Faster than any exponential. To compare the bound with an exponential decay, write it as an exponential, using \(x^k = e^{k\ln x}\) and \(\ln(1/x) = -\ln x\): \[\Big(\frac{e\mu}{k}\Big)^k = e^{-k\ln(k/(e\mu))}. \tag{E.26}\] The exponent is \(k\) times a logarithm that keeps growing with \(k\). So for any constant \(c > 0\), once \(k > e\mu\,e^c\) the logarithm exceeds \(c\) and the bound is below \(e^{-ck}\). That is what “faster than any exponential” means: the exponent grows like \(k\ln k\), while that of \(e^{-ck}\) grows only like \(k\).
A matching lower bound. The comparison with the normal needs to know that the probabilities are not much smaller than the bound. The factorial \(k! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots k\) is a product of \(k\) numbers, none larger than \(k\), so \(k! \le k^k\). Putting this larger number in the denominator gives \[\Pr[N = k] \ge e^{-\mu}\Big(\frac{\mu}{k}\Big)^k = e^{-\mu - k\ln(k/\mu)}. \tag{E.27}\] So the exponent of \(\Pr[N = k]\) lies between \(k\ln(k/(e\mu))\) and \(\mu + k\ln(k/\mu)\), and both grow like \(k\ln k\).
Slower than a normal. A normal variable with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\mu\), the Poisson’s own mean and variance, has density proportional to \(e^{-(k - \mu)^2/(2\mu)}\) at \(k\). Expanding the square, the leading term of the exponent is \(k^2/(2\mu)\), so far out its tail falls like \(e^{-k^2/(2\mu)}\). An exponent that grows like \(k^2\) eventually overtakes one that grows like \(k\ln k\), so by step 5 the Poisson probabilities fall more slowly than the normal tail.
The whole tail. Assume \(k > e\mu\) and write \(q = e\mu/k\), which is then below 1. The tail \(\Pr[N \ge k]\) is the sum of \(\Pr[N = j]\) over \(j \ge k\), and by Equation E.22 each term is at most \((e\mu/j)^j\). For \(j \ge k\) the base \(e\mu/j\) is at most \(q\), so each term is at most \(q^j\). These terms form a geometric series with first term \(q^k\) and ratio \(q\), so \[\Pr[N \ge k] \le \sum_{j \ge k}q^j = \frac{q^k}{1 - q}, \tag{E.28}\] which is Equation E.23. Once \(k \ge 2e\mu\), the ratio \(q\) is at most \(\frac12\), and the factor \(1/(1 - q)\) is at most 2.



E.3.4 Checking it
Take \(\mu = 4\), the chapter’s example of a count with standard deviation 2. Then \(e\mu \approx 10.87\), so the tail bound Equation E.23 applies from \(k = 11\), and its factor \(1/(1 - q)\) is at most 2 from \(k = 22\). Table E.3 compares the bounds with the exact values at \(k = 20\) and \(k = 40\).

The bound on one probability is loose by a factor of several hundred, and the loss is easy to account for. By Stirling’s formula Equation E.8, \(k! = \sqrt{2\pi k}\,(k/e)^ke^{r_k}\), so step 1 drops the factor \(\sqrt{2\pi k}\,e^{r_k}\) and step 3 drops \(e^\mu\). Their product is exactly the ratio in the table: \(e^4\sqrt{40\pi} \approx 612.0\) at \(k = 20\), and the factor \(e^{r_{20}}\), which is at most \(e^{1/240}\), brings it to 614.6. That factor grows only like \(\sqrt k\), so in the exponent it is a small constant beside \(k\ln(k/(e\mu))\), and the bound has the right rate. The tail bound adds the factor \(1/(1 - q)\), which is 2.19 at \(k = 20\) and 1.37 at \(k = 40\).
The comparison with the normal is stark. Take the normal variable with the same mean 4 and standard deviation 2. It lies above 20, eight standard deviations out, with probability about \(6.22 \times 10^{-16}\), while the exact Poisson tail there is \(1.02 \times 10^{-8}\). Above 40 the normal gives \(9.74 \times 10^{-73}\), against \(3.01 \times 10^{-26}\) for the Poisson count. So a normal approximation to a count understates its far tail by many orders of magnitude. Figure E.6 draws all of these against \(k\) on a log scale. The two bounds run parallel to the exact tail, a constant factor above it, while the normal tail bends away below it.






Figure E.6: The tail \(\Pr[N \ge k]\) of \(N \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(4)\) on a log scale (black), with the bound Equation E.22 on one probability (dashed), the tail bound Equation E.23 from \(k = 11\) (orange), the Chernoff bound \(e^{-\mu}(e\mu/k)^k\) (dotted), and the tail of a normal variable with mean 4 and variance 4 (dash-dotted).





E.3.5 What it does not cover
The Chernoff method of Concentration inequalities gives a sharper tail bound. It bounds the tail by the moment generating function \(\exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\big)\) of the count, at the value of the free parameter \(\lambda\) that makes the bound smallest. Steps 3 and 4 of the proof of Theorem 2.4 do exactly that for the Poisson MGF, and give, for every \(k > \mu\), \[\Pr[N \ge k] \le e^{-\mu}\Big(\frac{e\mu}{k}\Big)^k. \tag{E.29}\] That keeps the factor \(e^{-\mu}\) that step 3 here drops, and it does not need \(k > e\mu\). For the count with mean 4 it gives \(9.32 \times 10^{-8}\) at \(k = 20\), about 9 times the exact tail. This section’s bound is the simpler one, and it shows where the rate \((e\mu/k)^k\) comes from: the growth of \(k!\).

title: Appendix E — Sums, limits and counting
section: E.4 The central limit theorem, by swapping one term at a time
text:
E.4 The central limit theorem, by swapping one term at a time

E.4.1 What the chapter uses
The normal section of Probability distributions states the CLT, illustrates it with sums of exponential variables, and cites the Berry–Esseen theorem (Shevtsova, 2011) for its rate. It gives no proof. Almost every normal approximation in the book rests on it, including the CLT for composition in Section 32.5, where the summands are not identically distributed.
Take independent \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) with means \(\mu_i\), variances \(\sigma_i^2\), and finite third moments. Write \(Y_i = X_i - \mu_i\) for the centred terms and \(s^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_n^2\) for the variance of their sum. The quantity that controls the error is the Lyapunov ratio \[L = \frac{\mathbb E|Y_1|^3 + \dots + \mathbb E|Y_n|^3}{s^3}. \tag{E.30}\] For \(n\) copies of one distribution with variance \(\sigma^2\), it is \(L = \mathbb E|X - \mu|^3/(\sigma^3\sqrt n)\), which falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). The theorem proved here says that the standardized sum \(S = (Y_1 + \dots + Y_n)/s\) has a CDF within \(2L^{1/4}\) of the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\): \[\big|\Pr[S \le z] - \Phi(z)\big| \le 2L^{1/4} \quad\text{for every } z. \tag{E.31}\] So the CDF gap tends to 0 whenever \(L\) does, at least as fast as \(n^{-1/8}\) for identical terms. That proves the CLT when the third moments are finite.


E.4.2 The idea
Compare the sum with a sum of normals, one term at a time. Next to each \(Y_i\), put a normal variable \(G_i\) with the same mean 0 and the same variance \(\sigma_i^2\). The sum of all the \(G_i\), divided by \(s\), is exactly \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), by the normal-sum rule of Section E.1. Now swap the terms one at a time. Start with all normals, replace \(G_1\) by \(Y_1\), then \(G_2\) by \(Y_2\), and so on, until only the \(Y_i\) remain. The total change is the sum of the \(n\) changes from single swaps, so it is enough to show that each swap changes little.
A probability \(\Pr[S \le z]\) is the average of an indicator, which jumps, and jumps are hard to expand. So the proof first compares averages \(\mathbb E h(S)\) of a smooth test function \(h\), and handles the indicator at the end. A single swap changes such an average little, because \(Y_i\) and \(G_i\) agree in their first two moments. Expand \(h(W + Y_i/s)\) around the rest of the sum \(W\) as a Taylor series. The first-order and second-order terms depend on \(Y_i\) only through its mean and variance, so they are the same for \(Y_i\) and \(G_i\) and cancel. What is left is a third-order term of size \((\mathbb E|Y_i|^3 + \mathbb E|G_i|^3)/s^3\). There are \(n\) swaps of size about \(n^{-3/2}\) each, so the total is about \(n^{-1/2}\). The last step squeezes the indicator between two smooth ramps and pays for the width of the ramp.


E.4.3 Derivation

The hybrids. Let \(G_1, \dots, G_n\) be independent normal variables, independent of the \(X_i\), with \(G_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_i^2)\). For \(k = 0, \dots, n\), let \[H_k = \frac{Y_1 + \dots + Y_k + G_{k+1} + \dots + G_n}{s}. \tag{E.32}\] Then \(H_n = S\), and \(H_0 = (G_1 + \dots + G_n)/s\) is exactly \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) by step 5 of Section E.1, since its variance is \(s^2/s^2 = 1\). Write \(Z = H_0\).
Telescoping. For any test function \(h\), the change from \(Z\) to \(S\) is a sum of single swaps, because the middle terms cancel in pairs: \[\mathbb E h(S) - \mathbb E h(Z) = \sum_{k=1}^n\big(\mathbb E h(H_k) - \mathbb E h(H_{k-1})\big). \tag{E.33}\]
One swap. The hybrids \(H_k\) and \(H_{k-1}\) differ only in term \(k\). So if \(W\) stands for the other terms divided by \(s\), then \(H_k = W + Y_k/s\) while \(H_{k-1} = W + G_k/s\). The rest \(W\) is independent of both \(Y_k\) and \(G_k\). Now suppose that \(h\) has two derivatives, and that its second derivative \(h''\) changes by at most \(\gamma|a - b|\) between any two points \(a\) and \(b\), for a constant \(\gamma\). Taylor’s theorem with this condition says that, for every \(w\) and \(y\), \[\Big|h(w + y) - h(w) - h'(w)y - \tfrac12h''(w)y^2\Big| \le \frac\gamma6|y|^3. \tag{E.34}\] Apply it with \(y = Y_k/s\), take expectations, and do the same with \(G_k\). The term \(h(W)\) is common to both. The first-order term averages to 0 for both, because \(W\) is independent of \(Y_k\) and \(Y_k\) has mean 0, so \(\mathbb E[h'(W)Y_k] = \mathbb E[h'(W)]\,\mathbb E[Y_k] = 0\), and likewise for \(G_k\). The second-order term averages to \(\frac12\mathbb E[h''(W)]\,\sigma_k^2\) for both, because \(Y_k\) and \(G_k\) have the same variance. So these terms cancel and \[\big|\mathbb E h(H_k) - \mathbb E h(H_{k-1})\big| \le \frac{\gamma}{6s^3}\big(\mathbb E|Y_k|^3 + \mathbb E|G_k|^3\big). \tag{E.35}\]
Sum the swaps. For a normal variable, \(\mathbb E|G_k|^3 = 2\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma_k^3 \approx 1.596\,\sigma_k^3\), which you get by integrating \(|x|^3\) against the normal density. And \(\sigma_k^3 = (\mathbb E Y_k^2)^{3/2} \le \mathbb E|Y_k|^3\) by Jensen’s inequality, because \(x \mapsto x^{3/2}\) is convex. So each swap costs at most \(\frac{\gamma}{6s^3}(1 + 2\sqrt{2/\pi})\mathbb E|Y_k|^3\). By step 2, with \(c = (1 + 2\sqrt{2/\pi})/6 \approx 0.433\), \[\big|\mathbb E h(S) - \mathbb E h(Z)\big| \le c\,\gamma\,L. \tag{E.36}\]
A smooth ramp. The function \(\rho(u) = 6u^5 - 15u^4 + 10u^3\) rises from \(\rho(0) = 0\) to \(\rho(1) = 1\). Its first two derivatives are 0 at both ends, and its third derivative is at most 60 in size on \([0, 1]\). Set \(\rho = 0\) below 0 and \(\rho = 1\) above 1. For a width \(\kappa > 0\) and a point \(z\), the upper ramp \(h^+(x) = 1 - \rho((x - z)/\kappa)\) is 1 up to \(z\) and 0 beyond \(z + \kappa\). Its second derivative changes by at most \(\gamma = 60/\kappa^3\) per unit, so Equation E.36 applies with that \(\gamma\). The lower ramp \(h^-(x) = h^+(x + \kappa)\) is the same ramp moved left by \(\kappa\).
Sandwich the indicator. At every point, \(h^-(x) \le \mathbf 1[x \le z] \le h^+(x)\). Averaging keeps the order, so \[\Pr[S \le z] \le \mathbb E h^+(S) \le \mathbb E h^+(Z) + c\gamma L \le \Phi(z + \kappa) + c\gamma L. \tag{E.37}\] The last step uses \(h^+ \le \mathbf 1[x \le z + \kappa]\). The normal density is at most \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), so \(\Phi(z + \kappa) \le \Phi(z) + \kappa/\sqrt{2\pi}\). The lower ramp gives the matching bound from below, so \[\big|\Pr[S \le z] - \Phi(z)\big| \le \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{2\pi}} + \frac{60\,c\,L}{\kappa^3}. \tag{E.38}\]
Choose the width. A narrow ramp fits the indicator closely but has a large third derivative. The best balance sets the derivative in \(\kappa\) to zero, which gives \(\kappa^4 = 180\,c\,L\sqrt{2\pi}\). At that width the second term is a third of the first, and the bound is \(\frac43\kappa/\sqrt{2\pi} = 1.99\,L^{1/4}\). That proves Equation E.31.

Many dimensions. Section G.6 and other sections use the CLT for random vectors. It follows from the one-dimensional theorem by the Cramér–Wold device: a sequence of random vectors converges in distribution to a normal vector if and only if every fixed linear combination of the coordinates converges to the matching normal variable. Each linear combination is a sum of independent scalar terms, so the theorem above applies to it. The Cramér–Wold device itself rests on a uniqueness theorem for the Fourier transform of a distribution, a relative of the MGF, so it stays cited (Billingsley, 1995).


E.4.4 Checking it
Figure E.7 follows the swaps for \(n = 30\) \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) summands, with \(h = \sin\), whose third derivative is at most 1 in size. Every hybrid’s average \(\mathbb E\sin(H_k)\) is computed exactly from a closed form, with no simulation. The error grows in steps of at most 0.00122 to a total of 0.0365. Step 3 bounds each step by 0.00407 and the total by 0.1220, about three times the truth. For \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) the bound uses \(\mathbb E|X - 1|^3 = 12/e - 2 = 2.4146\), against \(\mathbb E|G|^3 = 1.5958\) for the normal.






Figure E.7: The error \(|\mathbb E\,h(H_k) - \mathbb E\,h(Z)|\) after swapping \(k\) of \(n = 30\) normal terms for centred \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) terms, with \(h = \sin\), computed exactly, against the sum of the per-swap bounds of step 3.



Figure E.8 draws the sandwich of step 6 at \(z = 0\). The ramps lie on either side of the indicator, and the shaded area under the normal density is the price \(\Phi(\kappa) - \Phi(0)\) of a ramp of width \(\kappa = 0.5\).






Figure E.8: The indicator \(\mathbf 1[x \le 0]\) between the upper and lower smooth ramps of widths \(\kappa = 0.5\) and \(0.2\), over the \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) density. The shaded area is \(\Phi(0.5) - \Phi(0)\).



The CDF bound is valid but slow. For 30 \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) terms the Lyapunov ratio is \(L = 0.4408\), and Equation E.31 gives 1.6201, which says nothing, while the true largest gap is 0.0243. Even at \(n = 10^8\) the bound is still 0.2478. The Berry–Esseen bound \(0.48L\) gives 0.2116 at \(n = 30\). The proof gets the right answer in the limit, but not the right rate.


E.4.5 What it does not cover
The proof assumes finite third moments, but the CLT holds with finite variance alone. Lindeberg’s original argument handles that case by cutting each term into a bounded part and a small remainder. The rate the proof gives is also weak. The Berry–Esseen theorem improves \(L^{1/4}\) to a constant times \(L\), with a constant below 0.48 for identical terms (Shevtsova, 2011) and a constant of the same size for terms that are not identical. Its proof uses Fourier analysis, so it stays cited. The sandwich loses the rate because a smooth ramp of width \(\kappa\) must pay \(\kappa^{-3}\) in its third derivative.

title: Appendix E — Sums, limits and counting
section: E.5 The length of a normal vector stays near \(\sqrt d\)
text:
E.5 The length of a normal vector stays near \(\sqrt d\)

E.5.1 What the chapter uses
Section 28.4 needs the chance that a standard normal vector in \(d\) dimensions is much longer than \(\sqrt d\). Let \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), a vector of \(d\) independent standard normal coordinates, and let \(t \ge 0\). The chapter uses \[\Pr\big[\|Z\| \ge \sqrt d + t\big] \le e^{-t^2/2}. \tag{E.39}\] It uses the bound to choose two lengths in its algorithm: a radius \(\tau_d\) that every record stays within, and a margin for the noise in each round of Equation 28.12. The chapter cites Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart (2013, ch. 5), whose proof uses a general theorem for functions that change slowly when their input changes. This section proves Equation E.39 using only the Chernoff method.


E.5.2 The idea
The squared length \(S = \|Z\|^2 = Z_1^2 + \dots + Z_d^2\) is a sum of \(d\) independent terms, each with mean 1, so its mean is \(d\). A sum of independent terms is the setting of the Chernoff bound: apply Markov’s inequality to \(e^{\lambda(S - d)}\), which splits into a product of \(d\) identical factors. Each factor has a closed form, and a short series bound turns it into a simple expression. A well-chosen \(\lambda\) then makes the exponent of the bound exactly \(-x\) at the level \(2\sqrt{dx} + 2x\), for any \(x > 0\). That gives a bound on the squared length, due to Laurent & Massart (2000). Taking square roots turns it into Equation E.39.


E.5.3 Derivation

One factor. For \(\lambda < \frac12\), combining the two exponents in the normal integral gives \[\mathbb E\,e^{\lambda Z_1^2} = \int\frac{e^{-(1 - 2\lambda)x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dx = (1 - 2\lambda)^{-1/2}. \tag{E.40}\] The integrand is a normal density with variance \(1/(1 - 2\lambda)\), without its factor \(\sqrt{1 - 2\lambda}\). So the logarithm of the MGF of \(Z_1^2 - 1\) is \(-\lambda - \frac12\ln(1 - 2\lambda)\).
A simple upper bound. The series \(-\frac12\ln(1 - 2\lambda) = \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{(2\lambda)^k}{2k}\) starts with the term \(\lambda\), which the \(-\lambda\) cancels. For \(0 \le \lambda < \frac12\) each later term is at most \(\frac14(2\lambda)^k\), because \(2k \ge 4\). Summing the geometric series gives \[-\lambda - \tfrac12\ln(1 - 2\lambda) = \sum_{k\ge2}\frac{(2\lambda)^k}{2k} \le \frac{\lambda^2}{1 - 2\lambda}. \tag{E.41}\]
The Chernoff bound. The \(d\) terms are independent, so the MGF of \(S - d\) is the product of \(d\) factors. Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda(S - d)}\) gives, for any level \(\ell > 0\) and any \(0 < \lambda < \frac12\), \[\Pr[S - d \ge \ell] \le \exp\Big(-\lambda\ell + \frac{d\lambda^2}{1 - 2\lambda}\Big). \tag{E.42}\]
Choose the level and \(\lambda\). The level is written through a free parameter \(x > 0\) because that makes the final exponent simple. Take \(\ell = 2\sqrt{dx} + 2x\). Write \(r = \sqrt{x/d}\), so that \(\sqrt{dx} = dr\) and \(x = dr^2\). Choose \(\lambda = r/(1 + 2r)\), which is below \(\frac12\), so that \(1 - 2\lambda = 1/(1 + 2r)\). Then \(\frac{d\lambda^2}{1 - 2\lambda} = \frac{dr^2}{1 + 2r}\) and \(\lambda\ell = \frac{2dr^2(1 + r)}{1 + 2r}\). The exponent of step 3 is \[\frac{-2dr^2(1 + r) + dr^2}{1 + 2r} = -dr^2\,\frac{1 + 2r}{1 + 2r} = -x. \tag{E.43}\] So \(\Pr[S - d \ge 2\sqrt{dx} + 2x] \le e^{-x}\).
Back to the length. Take \(x = t^2/2\). If \(\|Z\| \ge \sqrt d + t\), then squaring gives \(S \ge d + 2\sqrt d\,t + t^2\). Since \(2\sqrt{dx} = \sqrt2\sqrt d\,t\), which is at most \(2\sqrt d\,t\), and \(2x = t^2\), it follows that \(S - d \ge 2\sqrt{dx} + 2x\). So the event \(\|Z\| \ge \sqrt d + t\) lies inside the event of step 4, and its probability is at most \(e^{-x} = e^{-t^2/2}\).



E.5.4 Checking it
The squared length \(\|Z\|^2\) has the chi-squared distribution, whose tail the script computes exactly with the incomplete gamma function. Table E.4 compares it with the bound.

At \(t = 3\) it is 175 times the exact value for \(d = 1\) and about 810 times for \(d = 1000\). As \(d\) grows, \(\|Z\| - \sqrt d\) settles to a normal distribution with variance \(\frac12\), so the spread of the length stays of order 1 while \(\sqrt d\) grows. title: Appendix E — Sums, limits and counting
section: E.6 The difference of two Laplace variables
text:
E.6 The difference of two Laplace variables

E.6.1 What the chapter uses
Section 42.6 compares a Laplace noise \(\nu \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b_1)\) with another, independent noise \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b_2)\), where \(b_1 = 4/\varepsilon_0\) and \(b_2 = 2/\varepsilon_0\) for a budget \(\varepsilon_0\). It runs a test on each of \(P\) queries and wants the chance that any test wrongly passes to be at most a small number \(\delta_{\text{bad}}\). So it sets a threshold \(\tau\) with \(P\cdot\Pr[\nu - \rho > \tau] \le \delta_{\text{bad}}\), using the tail of the difference given by Equation 42.13: \[\Pr[\nu - \rho > \tau] = \frac{b_1^2e^{-\tau/b_1} - b_2^2e^{-\tau/b_2}}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}, \qquad \tau \ge 0,\ b_1 \ne b_2. \tag{E.44}\] The chapter says that the formula “comes from integrating the density of a sum of two Laplace variables, and the script checks it by simulation”. Section 27.1 uses the case of equal scales, \(b_1 = b_2 = 1/\varepsilon\), where the difference has density \(\frac\varepsilon4(1 + \varepsilon|z|)e^{-\varepsilon|z|}\). This section does the integral.


E.6.2 The idea
A Laplace variable is symmetric, so \(-\rho\) is again \(\mathrm{Lap}(b_2)\), and the difference \(\nu - \rho\) is a sum \(\nu + \rho'\) of two independent Laplace variables, with \(\rho' = -\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b_2)\). Its density at \(s\) is the convolution Equation E.1. Each Laplace density has a corner at 0, so the integral splits into three ranges of the first variable \(y\): below 0, between 0 and \(s\), and above \(s\). On each range both absolute values have a fixed sign, the integrand is a single exponential, and its integral is one line. Integrating the density from \(\tau\) outwards then gives the tail.


E.6.3 Derivation

Three pieces. Fix \(s \ge 0\), and write the density of \(\nu + \rho'\) at \(s\) as \(\frac{1}{4b_1b_2}\int e^{-|y|/b_1 - |s - y|/b_2}\,dy\).

For \(y < 0\), the exponent is \(y/b_1 - (s - y)/b_2\). Its integral over \(y < 0\) is \(e^{-s/b_2}\cdot\frac{b_1b_2}{b_1 + b_2}\), because \(\int_{-\infty}^0e^{y(1/b_1 + 1/b_2)}\,dy = \frac{1}{1/b_1 + 1/b_2}\).
For \(y > s\), the exponent is \(-y/b_1 - (y - s)/b_2\), and the same computation gives \(e^{-s/b_1}\cdot\frac{b_1b_2}{b_1 + b_2}\).
For \(0 \le y \le s\), the exponent is \(-y/b_1 - (s - y)/b_2 = -s/b_2 + y(1/b_2 - 1/b_1)\). With \(b_1 \ne b_2\) its integral is \(\frac{b_1b_2}{b_1 - b_2}\big(e^{-s/b_1} - e^{-s/b_2}\big)\).

The density. Dividing the three pieces by \(4b_1b_2\) and collecting the two exponentials, the coefficient of \(e^{-s/b_1}\) is \(\frac14\big(\frac1{b_1 + b_2} + \frac1{b_1 - b_2}\big) = \frac{b_1}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}\), and that of \(e^{-s/b_2}\) is \(-\frac{b_2}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}\). By symmetry, for every \(s\), \[f(s) = \frac{b_1e^{-|s|/b_1} - b_2e^{-|s|/b_2}}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}. \tag{E.45}\] As a check, at \(s = 0\) this is \(\frac{1}{2(b_1 + b_2)}\), which is positive.
The tail. For \(\tau \ge 0\), integrate \(f\) from \(\tau\) to infinity, using \(\int_\tau^\infty b\,e^{-s/b}\,ds = b^2e^{-\tau/b}\). This gives Equation E.44. At \(\tau = 0\) it gives \(\frac12\), as symmetry requires.
Far out, the wider noise wins. For large \(\tau\) the term with the larger scale \(b_1\) dominates, and the tail is about \(\frac{b_1^2}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}e^{-\tau/b_1}\). With \(b_1 = 2b_2\) that is \(\frac23e^{-\tau/b_1}\), which is \(\frac43\) times the tail \(\frac12e^{-\tau/b_1}\) of \(\nu\) alone. So the narrower noise \(\rho\) adds only a constant factor. To make \(P\cdot\Pr[\nu - \rho > \tau] \le \delta_{\text{bad}}\) for \(P\) queries, the threshold must be about \(b_1\ln\big(2P/(3\delta_{\text{bad}})\big)\), which is the \(4\ln(P/\delta_{\text{bad}})/\varepsilon_0\) growth the chapter describes.
Equal scales. When \(b_1 = b_2 = b\), the middle piece of step 1 has the constant integrand \(e^{-s/b}\) over an interval of length \(s\), so it is \(s\,e^{-s/b}\). The other two pieces are \(\frac b2e^{-s/b}\) each. Dividing by \(4b^2\), \[f(s) = \frac{1}{4b}\Big(1 + \frac{|s|}{b}\Big)e^{-|s|/b}. \tag{E.46}\] With \(b = 1/\varepsilon\) this is the density \(\frac\varepsilon4(1 + \varepsilon|z|)e^{-\varepsilon|z|}\) that Section 27.1 uses. Integrating from \(\tau\) gives the tail \(\frac14(2 + \tau/b)e^{-\tau/b}\). It is also the limit of Equation E.44 as \(b_1 \to b_2\). At \(\tau = 3\) and \(b = 1\), for example, it is 0.0622, and Equation E.44 with \(b_1 = 1.001\) gives 0.0623. The factor \(1 + |s|/b\) is why this density is not a Laplace density, as Section E.1 noted.



E.6.4 Checking it
At the chapter’s budget \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), so \(b_1 = 4\) and \(b_2 = 2\), and at \(\tau = 8\), Equation E.44 gives 0.0872. Numerical integration of the density of step 2 also gives 0.0872, and a million simulated pairs give 0.0867. Solving \(P\cdot\Pr[\nu - \rho > \tau] = 5 \times 10^{-6}\) by bisection gives the chapter’s thresholds, \(\tau = 74.8\) for a pool of \(P = 1{,}000\) queries and \(\tau = 84.0\) for \(P = 10{,}000\). The equal-scale density of step 5 matches a numerical convolution to \(7.5 \times 10^{-9}\).
Figure E.11 shows the tail on a log scale. It runs parallel to the tail of \(\nu\) alone and slightly above it, as step 4 says, while the tail of \(\rho\) alone falls away. The threshold sits where the tail reaches \(\delta_{\text{bad}}/P = 5 \times 10^{-10}\), far beyond the reach of a simulation. That is why the closed form matters: it is the only way to set the threshold accurately.






Figure E.11: The tail \(\Pr[\nu - \rho > \tau]\) for \(\nu \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4)\) and \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2)\) on a log scale: the formula (line), one million simulated pairs (dots), and the tails of \(\nu\) and \(\rho\) alone (dashed). The dotted lines mark the threshold for a pool of 10,000 queries and the level \(5 \times 10^{-10}\).

The norm bound loses a factor of 2 in the exponent for large \(d\), and the CLT bound is far too weak to use for numbers. In the chapters, the CLT is used for its limit, while concrete error sizes come from the exact computations or from Berry–Esseen.

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
text:
F.1 Bernstein’s inequality: the variance sets the width
Several chapters state a fact about tails, tests or divergences and then use it without a full proof. Some cite a book for the proof, some give a sketch that needs an extra condition, and one gives a reason that does not hold in general. This appendix derives six of these facts step by step. They belong together because they are built from the same three tools. The first is the moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable and its logarithm. The second is a change of measure, which rewrites a probability under one distribution as an average under another. The third is Jensen’s inequality for convex functions.
Table F.1 lists the six results, where a chapter states each one, and where the book relies on it.
crumbs: F  Tail bounds, tests and divergences

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
text:
F.1.1 What the chapter uses
Concentration inequalities states Bernstein’s inequality as Theorem 2.6, in its section on sub-Gaussian variables and Hoeffding’s inequality. It says that “the proof is the same Chernoff recipe” and cites Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart (chapter 2) for the derivation.
The setting is an average of independent measurements. Take a number \(n\) of independent variables \(X_1, \dots, X_n\), all with the same mean \(\mu\) and the same variance \(\sigma^2\). Assume that each one stays within a distance \(R\) of its mean, so that \(|X_i - \mu| \le R\), and write \(\bar X_n\) for their average. Then for every deviation \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\big[\bar X_n - \mu \ge t\big] \le \exp\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2 + \frac23 Rt}\right). \tag{F.1}\] The chapter also turns this into a width. For a failure probability \(\beta\), the width is a deviation that the average exceeds with probability at most \(\beta\). The chapter says that the width is about \[\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ln(1/\beta)}{n}} + \frac{2R\ln(1/\beta)}{3n}. \tag{F.2}\] The derivation below shows that this expression is more than an approximation: it is a valid width.


F.1.2 The idea
Hoeffding’s lemma bounds the MGF of a bounded variable as if it were the worst variable the range allows, a fair coin on the two ends, which has the largest variance of any variable in the interval. Bernstein’s inequality keeps the true variance instead. To see how, expand the MGF of a centred variable as a series. After the constant 1 and the mean, which is 0, its terms are the moments times powers of \(\lambda\): first the variance, then the third moment, the fourth, and so on. A variable that never strays more than \(R\) from its mean has small higher moments, each at most the variance times a power of \(R\). So the variance and the range together control the whole MGF. After that, the Chernoff recipe runs as usual: bound the MGF of each term of the sum, multiply these MGFs, choose the free parameter \(\lambda\) and simplify.
A rare event shows why this matters. Let \(X\) be a Bernoulli(0.01) variable, which is 1 with probability 0.01 and 0 otherwise. Its centred version \(Y = X - 0.01\) is \(0.99\) with probability 0.01 and \(-0.01\) otherwise. Its variance is \(0.01 \times 0.99 = 0.0099\), while Hoeffding’s lemma, which knows only that \(X\) lies in an interval of width 1, treats it as if its variance were \(\frac14\), about 25 times more. Its higher moments are just as small, as Table F.2 shows, and each stays below the bound \(\sigma^2R^{k-2}\) used in step 2 below.



Table F.2: Roments of the centred Bernoulli(0.01) variable \(Y\) and the bound of step 2.











Roment \(k\)
2
3
4

0.0097020
0.0096060


Bound \(\sigma^2R^{k-2}\), with \(R = 0.99\)

F.1.3 Derivation

Centre the variables. Subtract the mean from each variable, \(Y_i = X_i - \mu\), so that each \(Y_i\) has mean 0, variance \(\sigma^2\) and \(|Y_i| \le R\). Then the event \(\bar X_n - \mu \ge t\) is the event that the sum \(S = Y_1 + \dots + Y_n\) is at least \(nt\).
Bound each moment. For \(k \ge 2\), split \(|Y|^k\) as \(Y^2 |Y|^{k-2}\). The second factor is at most \(R^{k-2}\), because \(|Y| \le R\). Averaging gives \[\mathbb E[Y^k] \le \mathbb E\big[|Y|^k\big] \le \mathbb E[Y^2]\,R^{k-2} = \sigma^2R^{k-2}. \tag{F.3}\]
Bound the MGF of one term. Take \(\lambda \ge 0\) and expand \(e^{\lambda Y} = 1 + \lambda Y + \sum_{k \ge 2}\lambda^kY^k/k!\). Because the variable is bounded, you may average the series term by term. The linear term then averages to 0, because \(Y\) has mean 0. Each later term is at most \(\lambda^k\sigma^2R^{k-2}/k!\) by step 2, and the direction of the inequality is kept because \(\lambda^k \ge 0\). Writing \(\lambda^k\sigma^2R^{k-2}\) as \((\sigma^2/R^2)(\lambda R)^k\), the terms from \(k = 2\) on add up to at most \(\sigma^2/R^2\) times the sum \(\sum_{k\ge2}(\lambda R)^k/k!\), which is the exponential series without its first two terms, \(e^{\lambda R} - 1 - \lambda R\). So \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda Y}\big] \le 1 + \frac{\sigma^2}{R^2}\big(e^{\lambda R} - 1 - \lambda R\big) \le \exp\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{R^2}\big(e^{\lambda R} - 1 - \lambda R\big)\right). \tag{F.4}\] The second inequality is \(1 + x \le e^x\). It holds because the line \(1 + x\) is the tangent of the convex curve \(e^x\) at 0, and a convex curve lies above its tangents.
Simplify the series. Write \(u = \lambda R\) and take \(0 \le u < 3\). Every factor of \(k!\) from 3 up to \(k\) is at least 3, so \(k! \ge 2\cdot 3^{k-2}\). Each term of the series is therefore at most \(\frac{u^2}{2}(u/3)^{k-2}\), and these terms form a geometric series with ratio \(u/3 < 1\). Summing it gives \[e^u - 1 - u \le \frac{u^2}{2(1 - u/3)}. \tag{F.5}\] Put back \(u = \lambda R\), multiply by \(\sigma^2/R^2\) and take the logarithm of step 3’s bound. The log-MGF of one term then satisfies \[\ln\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda Y}\big] \le \frac{\sigma^2\lambda^2}{2(1 - \lambda R/3)}, \qquad 0 \le \lambda < 3/R. \tag{F.6}\] This is the Gaussian log-MGF \(\sigma^2\lambda^2/2\) with the variance inflated by the factor \(1/(1 - \lambda R/3)\), which is close to 1 for small \(\lambda\).
Chernoff for the sum. The MGF of a sum of independent terms is the product of their MGFs, so the log-MGFs add and \(S\) has log-MGF at most \(n\) times the bound of step 4. Rarkov’s inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda S}\) (the master bound of the Chernoff method) then gives \[\Pr[S \ge nt] \le \exp\left(-\lambda nt + \frac{n\sigma^2\lambda^2}{2(1 - \lambda R/3)}\right). \tag{F.7}\]
Choose \(\lambda\). Take \(\lambda = t/(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)\). It is positive, and \(\lambda R/3 = (Rt/3)/(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)\) is below 1, so step 4 applies. With this choice \(1 - \lambda R/3 = \sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)\). The second term of the exponent becomes \(nt^2/\big(2(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)\big)\), and the first is \(-nt^2/(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)\). Their sum is \[-\frac{nt^2}{2(\sigma^2 + Rt/3)} = -\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2 + \frac23Rt}, \tag{F.8}\] which is Equation F.1. This \(\lambda\) is not the exact minimizer of step 5, but it is the one that gives a clean formula.
The width. Write \(\ell\) for \(\ln(1/\beta)\). The bound equals \(\beta\) when \(nt^2 = \ell(2\sigma^2 + \frac23Rt)\), which is a quadratic equation in \(t\) with the positive root \[t^* = \frac{R\ell}{3n} + \sqrt{\Big(\frac{R\ell}{3n}\Big)^2 + \frac{2\sigma^2\ell}{n}}. \tag{F.9}\] The exponent \(nt^2/(2\sigma^2 + \frac23Rt) = nt/(2\sigma^2/t + \frac23R)\) grows with \(t\), so every \(t \ge t^*\) has a bound of at most \(\beta\). To simplify the root, use the fact that the square root of a sum of two non-negative numbers is at most the sum of their square roots, which you can see by squaring both sides. Applied to the square root in \(t^*\), it gives \[t^* \le \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ell}{n}} + \frac{2R\ell}{3n}, \tag{F.10}\] the chapter’s width. So with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the average exceeds \(\mu\) by less than this amount.

The proof also works when the variables have different variances \(\sigma_i^2\). Step 5 then adds the individual bounds, and \(\sigma^2\) becomes their average.


F.1.4 Checking it
The appendix’s script, apx_tails.py (see the Code section), checks steps 3 and 4 for the centred Bernoulli(0.01) on a grid of \(\lambda\) from 0.01 to 2.99, which is just below \(3/R = 3.03\). The exact log-MGF never exceeds the series bound \(\frac{\sigma^2}{R^2}(e^{\lambda R} - 1 - \lambda R)\) of step 3, and the series bound never exceeds the simpler bound of step 4. Figure F.1 shows the three curves together with Hoeffding’s \(\lambda^2/8\). For small \(\lambda\) both Bernstein curves lie on the exact one, far below Hoeffding’s, because they use the variance 0.0099 rather than \(\frac14\). Only near \(\lambda = 3/R\) does the simplification of step 4 blow up.






Figure F.1: The log-MGF of the centred Bernoulli(0.01) variable as a function of \(\lambda\) (black), with Hoeffding’s bound \(\lambda^2/8\) and the two Bernstein bounds of steps 3 and 4 of the derivation, on a log scale.



Figure F.2 shows what this buys for the mean of \(n = 1{,}000\) such variables, whose expected count is 10. Take \(t = 0.01\), which asks for a count of 20 or more, twice the expected count. The exact binomial tail is \(3.29\times10^{-3}\). Bernstein’s bound is \(2.26\times10^{-2}\), within a factor of 7 of it and close to the optimized Chernoff bound, \(2.00\times10^{-2}\). (That bound uses the exact binomial MGF. Section F.2 shows that its exponent is the binary Kullback–Leibler divergence.) Hoeffding’s bound is \(0.819\), which says almost nothing. The same holds for widths. At \(\beta = 0.05\) the exact root \(t^*\) of step 7 is 0.00875, the chapter’s simpler formula gives 0.00968, and Hoeffding’s one-sided width \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)/(2n)} = \sqrt{\ln(20)/2000}\) is 0.0387, four times larger.






Figure F.2: Tail of the mean of 1,000 Bernoulli(0.01) variables on a log scale: exact (black), and the Hoeffding, Bernstein and optimized Chernoff bounds.

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.2 Chernoff’s exponent is exact, for tails and for tests
text:
F.2 Chernoff’s exponent is exact, for tails and for tests

F.2.1 What the chapter uses
Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent copies of a variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\), and let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\). Write \(K_X(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\) for the log-MGF of one copy. The Chernoff method of Concentration inequalities bounds the chance that the sum reaches \(nt\), for a level \(t\) above the mean, by \[\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \le e^{-nK_X^*(t)}, \qquad K_X^*(t) = \sup_{\lambda > 0}\big(\lambda t - K_X(\lambda)\big). \tag{F.11}\] The chapter then says that “Cramér’s theorem says that … the probability of a large deviation decays exponentially in \(n\) with exactly the rate the optimized Chernoff bound gives, so no method can improve its exponent for large sums”. It does not prove this. In symbols, for every \(t\) between the mean \(\mu\) and the largest value \(x_{\max}\) that \(X\) can take, \[\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] = K_X^*(t). \tag{F.12}\]
Section 4.2 makes the same kind of claim about tests, and cites Cover & Thomas (chapter 11) for it. You observe \(n\) independent draws and test \(H_0\), that they come from \(P\), against \(H_1\), that they come from \(Q\). Hold the type I error at a level \(\mathrm{FPR}\) in \((0, 1)\), and write \(\mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR})\) for the smallest type II error of any test, randomized or not, whose type I error is at most \(\mathrm{FPR}\). The Chernoff–Stein lemma says that \[\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q), \qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\Big[\ln\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\Big], \tag{F.13}\] where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. The errors \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\) are the type I and type II errors of Section 4.2, renamed because this page needs \(\alpha\) for a Rényi order and \(\beta\) for a failure probability.


F.2.2 The idea
Chernoff’s bound shows that the probability is at most about \(e^{-nK_X^*(t)}\). To show that it is also at least about that, change the distribution so that the rare event becomes typical, and then pay for the change. The change is the tilted distribution of Divergences, which multiplies the probability of each outcome \(x\) by \(e^{\lambda x}\) and renormalizes. With \(\lambda > 0\) it moves mass toward large values. Pick \(\lambda\) so that the tilted mean sits just above \(t\), so that most of the tilted sums land in a narrow window just above \(nt\). Under the tilt, \(S_n\) then lands near \(nt\) most of the time, by Chebyshev’s inequality. The price of switching back is the ratio of the two distributions on those samples, which is about \(e^{-n(\lambda t - K_X(\lambda))}\), and that is the Chernoff exponent.
Here is a concrete case. A coin lands heads with probability 0.1, and you ask how likely 100 tosses are to give at least 20 heads, twice the expected number. Tilting by \(e^{\lambda x}\), with \(x = 1\) for heads and 0 for tails, turns it into a coin with heads probability \(0.1e^\lambda/(0.9 + 0.1e^\lambda)\). With \(\lambda = \ln 2.25 = 0.8109\) that probability is exactly 0.2, so for the tilted coin 20 heads in 100 is the typical outcome, not a rare one.
The Chernoff–Stein lemma uses the same trick, with the two distributions already given. Under \(P\), the evidence \(\sum_i\ln(p(x_i)/q(x_i))\) of a sample is close to \(n\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\), by the law of large numbers. So on most samples that \(P\) produces, \(Q\) gives a probability about \(e^{-nD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\) times smaller. A test with a small type I error must accept \(H_0\) on most of \(P\)’s typical samples. So under \(Q\) it accepts with probability about \(e^{-nD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\). No test can do better, because every test of small type I error must accept those samples. And the test that accepts exactly the samples with large evidence does that well.


F.2.3 Derivation
Two facts from the chapters do the work. The first is the change of measure (Lemma 3.2, Lemma 4.2). If \(P\) and \(Q'\) give positive probability to the same outcomes, then for any event \(A\), \[\Pr_P[X \in A] = \sum_{x \in A}p(x) = \sum_{x\in A}q'(x)\frac{p(x)}{q'(x)} = \mathbb E_{Q'}\Big[\frac{p(X)}{q'(X)}\mathbf 1[X \in A]\Big], \tag{F.14}\] because multiplying and dividing by \(q'(x)\) changes nothing. The second is the tilted distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), whose probabilities are \[q_\lambda(x) = p(x)\,e^{\lambda x - K_X(\lambda)}. \tag{F.15}\] They add up to 1 because \(e^{K_X(\lambda)} = \sum_xp(x)e^{\lambda x}\). Its mean is \(K_X'(\lambda)\) and its variance is \(K_X''(\lambda)\), as the Rényi section of Divergences shows for the log-likelihood ratio. Here you only need these facts for a bounded \(X\), where the sums are finite and the derivatives can be taken term by term.
Cramér’s lower bound. Assume that \(X\) is bounded and not constant, and that \(\mu < t < x_{\max}\).

Tilt to just above \(t\). Fix a small \(\kappa > 0\) with \(t + \kappa < x_{\max}\). The tilted mean \(K_X'(\lambda)\) equals \(\mu\) at \(\lambda = 0\). It increases with \(\lambda\), because its derivative is a variance, which is positive for a variable that is not constant. It tends to \(x_{\max}\) as \(\lambda \to \infty\), because the weight \(e^{\lambda x}\) favours the largest values more and more. So there is one \(\lambda > 0\) with \(K_X'(\lambda) = t + \kappa/2\).
Change the measure of the whole sample. Tilt each of the \(n\) copies. The ratio of the two probabilities of a sample is the product of the ratios of its draws, \(\prod_ip(x_i)/q_\lambda(x_i) = e^{-\lambda S_n + nK_X(\lambda)}\). The change of measure therefore gives, for any event \(A\) about the sample, \[\Pr[A] = \mathbb E_{Q_\lambda}\big[e^{-\lambda S_n + nK_X(\lambda)}\,\mathbf 1[A]\big]. \tag{F.16}\]
Restrict to a window. Let \(A\) be the event \(nt \le S_n \le n(t + \kappa)\). It is part of the event \(S_n \ge nt\). On \(A\), the sum is at most \(n(t + \kappa)\), and \(\lambda > 0\), so \(e^{-\lambda S_n} \ge e^{-\lambda n(t + \kappa)}\). Hence \[\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \ge \Pr[A] \ge e^{-n(\lambda(t + \kappa) - K_X(\lambda))}\,\Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A]. \tag{F.17}\]
The window is likely under the tilt. Under \(Q_\lambda\), the average \(S_n/n\) has mean \(t + \kappa/2\) and variance \(K_X''(\lambda)/n\). The window contains every average within \(\kappa/2\) of that mean. Chebyshev’s inequality bounds the chance of falling outside, so \[\Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A] \ge 1 - \frac{4K_X''(\lambda)}{n\kappa^2}, \tag{F.18}\] which tends to 1 as \(n\) grows.
Let \(n\) grow. Take logarithms in step 3 and divide by \(-n\). The term \(-\frac1n\ln \Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A]\) tends to 0, so \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \le \lambda(t + \kappa) - K_X(\lambda). \tag{F.19}\]
Let \(\kappa\) shrink. As \(\kappa \to 0\), the chosen \(\lambda\) tends to the \(\lambda_0\) with \(K_X'(\lambda_0) = t\), because \(K_X'\) is continuous and increasing. The right side of step 5 then tends to \(\lambda_0t - K_X(\lambda_0)\). The function \(\lambda t - K_X(\lambda)\) is concave, since \(K_X\) is convex, and its slope \(t - K_X'(\lambda)\) is zero at \(\lambda_0\). So \(\lambda_0\) is where it is largest, and \(\lambda_0t - K_X(\lambda_0) = K_X^*(t)\).
Combine with Chernoff. Chernoff’s bound gives \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \ge K_X^*(t)\) for every \(n\). Step 6 gives the matching upper limit, which proves Equation F.12.

For the coin, \(K_X(\lambda) = \ln(1 - p + pe^\lambda)\) with \(p = 0.1\), and solving \(K_X'(\lambda_0) = t\) gives \(e^{\lambda_0} = t(1 - p)/\big(p(1 - t)\big)\). Substituting, the exponent is the binary KL divergence \[K_X^*(t) = \mathrm{kl}(t\|p) = t\ln\frac tp + (1 - t)\ln\frac{1 - t}{1 - p}. \tag{F.20}\] With \(t = 0.2\) this is \(\lambda_0 = \ln 2.25 = 0.8109\), \(K_X(\lambda_0) = \ln1.125 = 0.11778\), and \(K_X^*(0.2) = 0.2 \times 0.8109 - 0.11778 = 0.04440\).
Chernoff–Stein, achievability. Assume that \(P\) and \(Q\) give positive probability to the same outcomes. Write \(L(x)\) for the evidence \(\ln(p(x)/q(x))\) of one draw \(x\). Under \(P\) its mean is the divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\), written \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) below, and assume that its variance \(V\) is finite. For a whole sample \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), write \(p^n(x)\) and \(q^n(x)\) for its probabilities under the two hypotheses. Each is a product over the draws, so the change of measure becomes \[q^n(x) = p^n(x)\,e^{-\sum_iL(x_i)}. \tag{F.21}\]

The test. Fix \(\kappa > 0\), and accept \(H_0\) exactly when the average evidence is at least \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa\). Call that set of samples \(A_n\).
Its type I error. It rejects when the average evidence falls more than \(\kappa\) below its mean \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\). The average has variance \(V/n\), so Chebyshev gives a type I error of at most \(V/(n\kappa^2)\), which is below \(\mathrm{FPR}\) once \(n\) is large.
Its type II error. On \(A_n\) the total evidence is at least \(n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)\), so \(q^n(x) \le p^n(x)\,e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\). Summing over \(A_n\) gives \[\mathrm{FNR}_n = \Pr_{Q^n}[A_n] \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\Pr_{P^n}[A_n] \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}. \tag{F.22}\]
The best test does at least as well. So \(\mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\) for large \(n\), and \(\liminf_n -\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \ge D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa\) for every \(\kappa > 0\).

Chernoff–Stein, converse. Now take any test, described by its probability \(\phi(x)\) of rejecting \(H_0\), with type I error \(\mathbb E_{P^n}[\phi] \le \mathrm{FPR}\).

Restrict to typical samples. Let \(B_n\) be the set of samples whose average evidence is at most \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa\). On \(B_n\), \(q^n(x) \ge p^n(x)\,e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa)}\). The type II error is the probability of accepting under \(Q\), and keeping only the samples in \(B_n\) can only lower it, so \[\mathrm{FNR}_n = \sum_x\big(1 - \phi(x)\big)q^n(x) \ge e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa)}\sum_{x\in B_n}\big(1 - \phi(x)\big)p^n(x). \tag{F.23}\]
The test must accept most typical samples. The last sum is the acceptance probability under \(P\), minus the part outside \(B_n\). That part is at most \(\Pr_{P^n}[B_n^c]\), which Chebyshev bounds by \(V/(n\kappa^2)\). So the sum is at least \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\).
Let \(n\) grow. Taking logarithms, \(-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n \le D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa - \frac1n\ln\big(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\big)\), and the last term tends to 0. (For large \(n\) the factor \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\) is positive, so its logarithm is defined.) This holds for every test of level \(\mathrm{FPR}\), so \(\limsup_n-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \le D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa\). Since \(\kappa\) is arbitrary, steps 4 and 7 together prove Equation F.13.



F.2.4 Checking it
For the coin with \(p = 0.1\) and \(t = 0.2\), the script computes the exact exponent \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge 0.2n]\) from the binomial distribution. It is 0.06225 at \(n = 100\), 0.04728 at \(n = 1{,}000\) and 0.04481 at \(n = 10{,}000\), and it approaches \(\mathrm{kl}(0.2\|0.1) = 0.04440\) from above, as Chernoff’s bound requires. The right panel of Figure F.3 also draws the bound of steps 3 and 4 for each \(n\), with the window width \(\kappa = 4\sqrt{t(1 - t)/n}\). The factor 4 makes Chebyshev’s bound in step 4 leave about three quarters of the tilted mass in the window. It closes in from the other side, but slowly: 0.23163, 0.09152 and 0.05800 at the same three sizes. It is slow because the window must shrink like \(1/\sqrt n\), the size of the typical fluctuation. The left panel shows the tilt at \(n = 100\). The original count sits around 10, while the tilted count sits inside the window from 20 up.






Figure F.3: Left: the distribution of the number of heads in 100 tosses of a coin with heads probability 0.1, and of the tilted coin, with the window of step 3 shaded. Right: the exact exponent \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge 0.2n]\) (black), the bound from the tilting argument (blue) and the Chernoff exponent \(\mathrm{kl}(0.2\|0.1)\) (dashed), against \(n\).



For the Chernoff–Stein lemma the script uses the spam example of Table 4.1. An email’s count of suspicious words, capped at 3, takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1 under ham (\(P\)) and 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 under spam (\(Q\)). There \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.4564\) and the variance of the evidence is \(V = 0.8348\). The evidence of one count is \(\pm\ln4\) or \(\pm\ln1.5\), so the evidence of a sample is \(i\ln4 + j\ln1.5\) for two whole numbers \(i\) and \(j\). The script tracks the exact distribution of \((i, j)\) under both hypotheses and builds the most powerful test of size exactly 0.05, as the Neyman–Pearson lemma prescribes. Table F.3 gives its type II error. Its last column gives the two bounds of the derivation. They use \(\kappa = \sqrt{V/(0.05\,n)}\) for achievability, so that step 2 gives size 0.05, and \(\kappa = \sqrt{2V/(0.95\,n)}\) for the converse, so that the factor in step 6 is \(0.95/2\). A negative lower bound says nothing, because an exponent is never negative.



Table F.3: Type II error of the most powerful size-0.05 test on \(n\) spam-example observations, its exponent, and the two bounds of the derivation with \(\kappa\) chosen for each \(n\). The limit is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.4564\).

The exponent creeps up toward 0.4564, as Figure F.4 shows. Both bounds tend to KL, at the slow rate \(1/\sqrt n\). The exact exponent is also far from its limit at moderate \(n\). With 200 observations it is still 18% below KL, because the test must leave room for fluctuations of the evidence of order \(\sqrt n\).






Figure F.4: The type II exponent \(-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*\) of the most powerful size-0.05 test on the spam example (black), between the achievability and converse bounds of the derivation, converging slowly to \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) (dashed).





F.2.5 What it does not cover
Cramér’s theorem holds without boundedness. The upper bound is always Chernoff’s, and the lower bound needs only a tilt with the right mean, which exists in more general settings; Dembo & Zeitouni prove it in full. The Chernoff–Stein argument above uses a finite variance \(V\) only for Chebyshev’s inequality. The weak law of large numbers gives the same two limits with only a finite KL divergence, which is the version Cover & Thomas prove. Neither proof says how fast the limit is reached. The examples above show that the approach is slow, with an error of order \(1/\sqrt n\) in the exponent.
