section: F.3 The Clopper–Pearson limits exist and are unique
text:
F.3 The Clopper–Pearson limits exist and are unique

F.3.1 What the chapter uses
Section 4.9 builds the Clopper–Pearson interval for a rate from \(k\) successes in \(n\) independent trials. Write \(F_p(k) = \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, p) \le k]\) for the probability of at most \(k\) successes when each trial succeeds with probability \(p\). Step 1 of the chapter’s derivation says that \(F_p(k)\) is continuous and strictly decreasing in \(p\) for \(k < n\), and concludes that for each \(k\) there is a single rate \(u(k)\) with \(F_{u(k)}(k) = \beta/2\). Here \(1 - \beta\) is the confidence level, which the chapter writes \(1 - \alpha\). The chapter gives a reason in one phrase, that a larger success probability makes small counts less likely, and points here for the proof. Theorem 47.1 in Auditing relies on the same step for its one-sided bounds.
The precise statement is this. For \(0 \le k \le n - 1\), the function \(p \mapsto F_p(k)\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on \([0, 1]\), from \(F_0(k) = 1\) to \(F_1(k) = 0\). So for every level \(c\) in \((0, 1)\) exactly one rate \(u(k)\) in \((0, 1)\) solves \(F_{u(k)}(k) = c\). Moreover, \[F_p(k) = \int_p^1 n\binom{n-1}{k}s^k(1 - s)^{n-1-k}\,ds. \tag{F.24}\] For \(k = n\), \(F_p(n) = 1\) for every \(p\), and the chapter sets \(u(n) = 1\).


F.3.2 The idea
Picture all the trials driven by one set of random numbers. Draw \(n\) numbers \(U_1, \dots, U_n\) uniformly from \([0, 1]\), and say that trial \(i\) succeeds at rate \(p\) when \(U_i \le p\). Each trial then succeeds with probability \(p\), independently, so the count \(K_p\) of successes is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\). Now raise \(p\) while keeping the same numbers. A trial that succeeded still succeeds, and some new ones may join, so the count never goes down. For example, with \(n = 3\) and \(U = (0.15, 0.62, 0.40)\), Table F.4 shows the count as \(p\) grows.



Table F.4: One draw of three uniform numbers, and the count of successes they give at four rates. The count can only go up as \(p\) grows.

On every draw the event “at most \(k\) successes” can only stop happening as \(p\) grows. So its probability \(F_p(k)\) never increases. The count leaves that event when one more trial crosses over while exactly \(k\) of the other \(n - 1\) have already succeeded, and that has positive probability for every \(p\) strictly between 0 and 1. So the decrease is strict. The derivation makes this exact by differentiating.


F.3.3 Derivation

The endpoints. At \(p = 0\) no trial succeeds, so \(F_0(k) = 1\). At \(p = 1\) all \(n\) succeed, so \(F_1(k) = 0\) for \(k \le n - 1\).
Continuity. \(F_p(k) = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom njp^j(1 - p)^{n-j}\) is a polynomial in \(p\), so it is continuous and can be differentiated.
The derivative telescopes. Write \(g_j(p)\) for the probability of exactly \(j\) successes in \(n - 1\) trials, \(\binom{n-1}{j}p^j(1 - p)^{n-1-j}\), and set \(g_{-1} = 0\). Differentiate one term of the sum by the product rule, and then use the identities \(j\binom nj = n\binom{n-1}{j-1}\) and \((n - j)\binom nj = n\binom{n-1}{j}\). The result is \[\frac{d}{dp}\binom njp^j(1 - p)^{n-j} = n\big(g_{j-1}(p) - g_j(p)\big). \tag{F.25}\] Summing over \(j = 0, \dots, k\), each \(g_j\) appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, except \(g_{-1} = 0\) and the last one. So \[\frac{d}{dp}F_p(k) = -n\binom{n-1}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n-1-k}. \tag{F.26}\] For example, with two trials and \(k = 0\), \(F_p(0) = (1 - p)^2\) has derivative \(-2(1 - p)\), which is what the formula gives. The formula also has a reading in words. When \(p\) rises a little, one of the \(n\) trials may cross over, and the count leaves “at most \(k\)” exactly when the other \(n - 1\) trials hold exactly \(k\) successes.
Strictly decreasing. The derivative is negative for \(0 < p < 1\). By the mean value theorem, for \(p < p'\) the difference \(F_{p'}(k) - F_p(k)\) equals \((p' - p)\) times the derivative at some point in between, which is negative.
Existence and uniqueness. A continuous function that goes from 1 to 0 takes every value \(c\) in between, by the intermediate value theorem. A strictly decreasing function takes each value at most once. So exactly one \(u(k)\) has \(F_{u(k)}(k) = c\). Strictness is also what the chapter needs when it turns the limit into a statement about the true rate: the true rate \(p\) is at least \(u(K)\) exactly when \(F_p(K) \le F_{u(K)}(K)\).
The lower end. For \(k \ge 1\), the probability of at least \(k\) successes is \(1 - F_p(k - 1)\). By steps 1 to 4 it is continuous and strictly increasing in \(p\), from 0 to 1. So the chapter’s lower limit \(l(k)\), the rate at which at least \(k\) successes have probability \(c\), also exists and is unique.
The Beta form. Integrate the derivative of step 3 from \(p\) to 1, and use \(F_1(k) = 0\). This gives Equation F.24. The integrand is the density of the \(\mathrm{Beta}(k + 1, n - k)\) distribution, because its normalizing constant \(1/B(k + 1, n - k) = n!/\big(k!\,(n - 1 - k)!\big)\) equals \(n\binom{n-1}{k}\). So \(F_p(k)\) is the probability that a \(\mathrm{Beta}(k + 1, n - k)\) variable exceeds \(p\). The upper limit \(u(k)\) is therefore the point that such a variable exceeds with probability \(c\). This is how statistical software computes Clopper–Pearson limits.



F.3.4 Checking it
Figure F.5 draws \(F_p(k)\) against \(p\) for \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(k = 0\), 1 and 10. Each curve falls from 1 to 0 and crosses the level \(0.025\) exactly once, at the upper limit: \(u(0) = 0.003682\), \(u(1) = 0.005559\) and \(u(10) = 0.018313\). The first has a closed form, because \(F_p(0) = (1 - p)^n\) gives \(u(0) = 1 - 0.025^{1/1000}\). The script checks the derivative of step 3 against finite differences, and the integral of step 7 by numerical integration. It also recomputes the limits that the chapters quote, by bisection. For 10 successes in 10,000 trials the interval is \([0.00048, 0.00184]\). For 1 success in 1,000 the one-sided 95% bound is 0.0047, and for none in 3,000 it is \(9.9808\times10^{-4}\).






Figure F.5: The probability \(F_p(k)\) of at most \(k\) successes in 1,000 trials, as a function of the true rate \(p\), for \(k = 0\), 1 and 10. Each curve crosses the level 0.025 (dotted) once, at the upper limit \(u(k)\).



Figure F.6 shows what the interval delivers. For \(n = 100\) it gives the exact coverage of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval at each true rate \(p\), the probability that the interval built from a \(\mathrm{Bin}(100, p)\) count contains \(p\). The curve is a sawtooth, because it jumps each time \(p\) crosses an endpoint of one of the 101 intervals. It never drops below 0.95: its smallest value on the grid is 0.9504 and its average is 0.9645. The Wald interval \(\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}\) of Section 4.9 falls far below 0.95 near the edges. At \(p = 0.01\) it covers only 63.34% of the time, against 98.16% for Clopper–Pearson.






Figure F.6: Exact coverage of 95% intervals for a rate from 100 trials, as a function of the true rate: Clopper–Pearson (blue) stays above the nominal 0.95 (dashed), and Wald (orange) falls far below it near 0 and 1.

section: F.4 Rényi divergence tends to KL at order 1
text:
F.4 Rényi divergence tends to KL at order 1

F.4.1 What the chapter uses
Section 3.2 writes the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) through the likelihood ratio \(r = p/q\) and the log-MGF of the evidence \(\ln r\) under \(P\), \[K_L(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P\big[r^\lambda\big], \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{K_L(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{F.27}\] That is Equation 3.13. Here \(K_L\) is the log-MGF of the evidence \(L = \ln r\), not of a sum as in the previous section. Property 1 there says that \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) as \(\alpha \to 1\), where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P[\ln r]\) is the KL divergence. The chapter proves it as the slope of \(K_L\) at 0, by passing a derivative inside an average. It adds: “This needs \(K_L\) to be finite near 0. van Erven & Harremoës prove the limit in general.” Write \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\). This section proves two statements without derivatives: \[\lim_{\alpha \uparrow 1}D_\alpha(P\|Q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \text{ always}, \qquad \lim_{\alpha\downarrow1}D_\alpha(P\|Q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \text{ if } D_{\alpha_0}(P\|Q) < \infty \text{ for some } \alpha_0 > 1. \tag{F.28}\] The first holds even when the KL divergence is infinite.
Section 5.4 states the matching facts for the Rényi entropy \(H_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1 - \alpha}\log_2\sum_xp(x)^\alpha\), measured in bits, of a variable with finitely many values. It says that \(H_\alpha\) tends to the Shannon entropy \(H\) as \(\alpha \to 1\), and to the min-entropy \(H_\infty\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\). Both follow from the divergence limits.


F.4.2 The idea
The divergence \(D_{1+\lambda}\) is \(K_L(\lambda)/\lambda\), and two simple inequalities trap it between the KL divergence and a quantity whose limit is easy. The first is Jensen’s inequality for the concave logarithm: the log of an average is at least the average of the log. The second is the tangent-line bound \(\ln m \le m - 1\). Applied to the average \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda]\), they give \[\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \mathbb E_P[\ln r^\lambda] \le K_L(\lambda) \le \mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] - 1. \tag{F.29}\] Dividing by \(\lambda\), with care for its sign, puts \(D_{1+\lambda}\) between \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) and the average of the power slope \[h_\lambda(r) = \frac{r^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}. \tag{F.30}\] For each fixed value of the ratio \(r\), the power slope moves steadily toward \(\ln r\) as \(\lambda\) tends to 0. So its average moves toward the average of \(\ln r\), which is the KL divergence, and no derivative of \(K_L\) is needed.
On the die of Table 3.1, \(r\) is 3 on a six and 0.6 otherwise. Table F.5 shows \(h_\lambda\) at both values. Each row increases from left to right, and the middle column, \(\lambda = 0\), is \(\ln r\).

F.4.3 Derivation
The derivation uses one theorem about averages, the monotone convergence theorem. Suppose random variables \(Z_1 \le Z_2 \le \dots\) increase to a limit \(Z\) at every outcome, and \(\mathbb E[Z_1] > -\infty\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z_k] \to \mathbb E[Z]\), and the limit may be \(+\infty\). The same holds for a decreasing sequence if \(\mathbb E[Z_1] < \infty\). For finitely many outcomes this is just the limit of a finite sum. For densities, it is a standard theorem of integration.

The power slopes. For a number \(x > 0\), write \(z = \ln x\), so that \(x^\lambda = e^{\lambda z}\). Then the power slope is an integral, \[h_\lambda(x) = \frac{e^{\lambda z} - 1}{\lambda} = \int_0^z e^{\lambda s}\,ds, \tag{F.31}\] which runs backward when \(z < 0\). At \(\lambda = 0\) the integral is \(z = \ln x\), and it changes continuously with \(\lambda\). It is also non-decreasing in \(\lambda\). If \(z > 0\), every \(s\) in the integral is positive, so \(e^{\lambda s}\) grows with \(\lambda\). If \(z < 0\), the integral is \(-\int_z^0e^{\lambda s}\,ds\) with negative \(s\), so \(e^{\lambda s}\) shrinks with \(\lambda\) and its negative grows. So as \(\lambda \uparrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(x)\) increases to \(\ln x\), and as \(\lambda \downarrow 0\) it decreases to \(\ln x\).
Below order 1, an upper bound. Take \(\lambda \in (-1, 0)\). Then \(r^\lambda = (q/p)^{|\lambda|}\), and Jensen’s inequality for the concave power \(|\lambda| < 1\) gives \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] \le \big(\mathbb E_P[q/p]\big)^{|\lambda|} \le 1\), so \(K_L(\lambda)\) is not \(+\infty\). (If \(P\) and \(Q\) share no outcome, \(K_L(\lambda) = -\infty\) and every divergence is infinite, so there is nothing to prove.) Next, the logarithm is concave, so Jensen’s inequality gives \[K_L(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] \ge \mathbb E_P[\ln r^\lambda] = \lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}. \tag{F.32}\] Dividing by the negative \(\lambda\) flips the inequality, so \(D_{1+\lambda}\) is at most \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\). When the KL divergence is infinite this says nothing, and nothing is needed.
Below order 1, a lower bound. Since \(\ln m \le m - 1\), \(K_L(\lambda) \le \mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] - 1 = \lambda\,\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)]\). Dividing by the negative \(\lambda\) flips it again: \[\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)] \le D_{1+\lambda} \le D_{\mathrm{KL}}, \qquad -1 < \lambda < 0. \tag{F.33}\]
The limit from below. As \(\lambda \uparrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(r)\) increases to \(\ln r\) by step 1. The sequence starts above an integrable variable: at \(\lambda = -1\), \(h_{-1}(r) = 1 - 1/r\), and \(\mathbb E_P[1/r] = \sum_{x:\,p(x)>0}q(x) \le 1\), so \(\mathbb E_P[h_{-1}(r)] \ge 0\). So monotone convergence applies, and the average of the power slope tends to the average of \(\ln r\), which is the KL divergence. Both sides of step 3 tend to \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\), so \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) as \(\alpha \uparrow 1\). This includes an infinite KL divergence, where the lower bound alone grows without limit.
Above order 1. For \(\lambda > 0\) the same two inequalities hold, and dividing by the positive \(\lambda\) keeps their direction: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}} \le D_{1+\lambda} \le \mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)], \qquad \lambda > 0. \tag{F.34}\]
The limit from above. As \(\lambda \downarrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(r)\) decreases to \(\ln r\). Monotone convergence now needs a finite starting point. That is the assumption: if \(D_{\alpha_0} < \infty\) with \(\lambda_0 = \alpha_0 - 1 > 0\), then \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\lambda_0}] = e^{\lambda_0D_{\alpha_0}}\) is finite, and so is \(\mathbb E_P[h_{\lambda_0}(r)]\). Then \(\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)] \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) and \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) as \(\alpha \downarrow 1\).
Rényi entropy. Let \(U\) be the uniform distribution on the \(N\) values of \(X\), which gives each value probability \(1/N\). Measuring the divergence in bits too, with \(\log_2\) in place of \(\ln\), the definition gives \[D_\alpha(P\|U) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log_2\sum_xp(x)^\alpha N^{\alpha - 1} = \log_2 N - H_\alpha(X). \tag{F.35}\] The identity holds in any base used for both sides. In the same way, the KL divergence from the uniform distribution is \(\log_2 N\) minus the Shannon entropy \(H(X)\). On a finite set the likelihood ratio \(Np(x)\) is at most \(N\), so every \(D_\alpha(P\|U)\) is finite. Both limits of steps 4 and 6 then apply, and \(H_\alpha \to H\) as \(\alpha \to 1\). As \(\alpha \to \infty\), property 2 of Section 3.2 says that \(D_\alpha(P\|U)\) tends to the logarithm of the largest ratio, \(\log_2(N\max_xp(x))\). Subtracting it from \(\log_2 N\) leaves the min-entropy, \[\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}H_\alpha(X) = -\log_2\max_xp(x) = H_\infty(X). \tag{F.36}\]



F.4.4 Checking it
Figure F.7 draws the sandwich for the die and for the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\), whose KL divergence is \(\frac12\). The black curve is \(D_{1+\lambda}\) and the blue curve is \(\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)]\). The blue curve lies below the black on the left of 0 and above it on the right, and both meet the KL line at \(\lambda = 0\). On the die, where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0.2939\), the divergence at \(\lambda = -0.01\) is 0.2907 with the lower bound 0.2902, and at \(\lambda = +0.01\) it is 0.2971 with the upper bound 0.2976.






Figure F.7: The Rényi divergence \(D_{1+\lambda} = K_L(\lambda)/\lambda\) (black) and the bound \(\mathbb E_P[(r^\lambda - 1)/\lambda]\) (blue) as functions of \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), with the KL divergence (dashed). Left: the loaded die against the fair die. Right: \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\).



For the PIN example of Section 5.4, with 10% on one PIN and the rest uniform over the other 9,999, the Shannon entropy is \(H = 12.4278\) bits. The script finds \(H_{0.999} = 12.4310\) and \(H_{1.001} = 12.4246\) on either side of it. As the order grows, \(H_2 = 6.6322\) and \(H_{100} = 3.3555\) approach the min-entropy \(H_\infty = 3.3219\). The identity of step 7 holds to rounding error.


F.4.5 What it does not cover
Without the assumption of step 6, the limit from above can fail. Take outcomes \(k = 1, 2, \dots\) with \(p(k)\) proportional to \(e^{-\sqrt k}\), and let \(q(k) = p(k)e^{-k}\), with the rest of \(Q\)’s mass on an extra outcome that \(P\) never produces. Then \(\ln r(k) = k\), so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \mathbb E_P[k]\) is finite. But \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda]\) sums \(e^{\lambda k - \sqrt k}\) times a constant, which diverges for every \(\lambda > 0\). So \(D_\alpha = \infty\) for every \(\alpha > 1\), while the limit from below is the finite KL divergence. van Erven & Harremoës (2014) treat the general case, including orders near 0 and \(\infty\).

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.5 Perspective functions are jointly convex
text:
F.5 Perspective functions are jointly convex

F.5.1 What the chapter uses
Let \(g\) be a convex function on \((0, \infty)\). Its perspective is a function \(G\) of two positive numbers \(x\) and \(y\). It applies \(g\) to their ratio and multiplies the result by the denominator: \[G(x, y) = y\,g(x/y). \tag{F.37}\]
The perspective has three properties. The first is that it is jointly convex. Take several points \((x_t, y_t)\), indexed by \(t\), and weights \(w_t \ge 0\) that add up to 1. The value of \(G\) at the weighted average of the points is at most the weighted average of its values: \[G\Big(\sum_tw_tx_t,\ \sum_tw_ty_t\Big) \le \sum_tw_t\,G(x_t, y_t). \tag{F.38}\] The second is that it is positively homogeneous, which means that scaling both arguments by a factor \(c > 0\) scales the value by \(c\). The third follows from the first two. The perspective is subadditive, so its value at a sum of two points is at most the sum of its values: \[G(x_1 + x_2,\ y_1 + y_2) \le G(x_1, y_1) + G(x_2, y_2). \tag{F.39}\]
The Rényi divergence uses \(g(t) = t^\alpha\) with \(\alpha > 1\), whose perspective is \(G(x, y) = x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\). Write the sum in the Rényi divergence as \[F(P, Q) = \sum_yP(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha} = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}. \tag{F.40}\] Several chapters assert one of the properties above for this function, without a proof:

Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 30.2, in the chapter on converting Rényi differential privacy (RDP) guarantees, uses that a test cannot increase the Rényi divergence, citing the data-processing inequality.
The paragraph after the proof of Theorem 30.2 says that each constraint of Equation 30.15 is convex in the test’s errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), so that the region they allow is convex and its lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is a convex function. It also uses that each constraint is smallest, equal to 1, at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). Step 3 of Section 32.7 repeats the convexity claim.
Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 31.4 uses the joint convexity of \(F\) in the pair, for the pair \((Q, P)\) written as a mixture.
Step 2 of Section 33.3 uses it to show that a mixture of pairs with shared weights has a Rényi divergence no larger than the largest of its parts. It cites van Erven & Harremoës (2014, Theorem 13) for this quasi-convexity.

This section proves the three properties and these four uses.


F.5.2 The idea
The perspective is \(g\) of a ratio, weighted by the denominator. When you mix two points, the ratio of the mixture is an average of the two ratios, weighted by the denominators. A convex function of an average is at most the average of the function (Jensen), and multiplying back by the total denominator gives the joint convexity.
Take \(\alpha = 2\), so \(G(x, y) = x^2/y\), and the two points \((0.9, 0.3)\) and \((0.1, 0.9)\). Their values are \(0.81/0.3 = 2.70\) and \(0.01/0.9 = 0.0111\), and their ratios \(x/y\) are 3 and \(\frac19\). The midpoint is \((0.5, 0.6)\), whose ratio is \(0.5/0.6 = 0.833\). That is the average of 3 and \(\frac19\) with weights \(0.3/1.2 = \frac14\) and \(0.9/1.2 = \frac34\), the shares of the two denominators. At the midpoint \(G = 0.25/0.6 = 0.4167\), well below the average of the two values, \((2.70 + 0.0111)/2 = 1.3556\).
In the language of divergences, \(x\) is \(P\)’s probability of an output and \(y\) is \(Q\)’s. Merging two outputs replaces their likelihood ratios by an average weighted by \(Q\), as in the data-processing section of Divergences, and a convex summary of the ratios can only go down.


F.5.3 Derivation

Joint convexity. Fix the points \((x_t, y_t)\) and the weights \(w_t\), and let \(x = \sum_tw_tx_t\) and \(y = \sum_tw_ty_t\). The numbers \(v_t = w_ty_t/y\) are non-negative and add up to 1. They make the ratio of the mixture an average of the ratios, \[\frac xy = \sum_t\frac{w_ty_t}{y}\cdot\frac{x_t}{y_t} = \sum_tv_t\frac{x_t}{y_t}. \tag{F.41}\] Jensen’s inequality for the convex \(g\) gives \(g(x/y) \le \sum_tv_t\,g(x_t/y_t)\). Multiplying by \(y\) turns each \(y\,v_t\) back into \(w_ty_t\), which is Equation F.38.
Homogeneity. \(G(cx, cy) = cy\,g(cx/cy) = c\,y\,g(x/y)\), because the ratio does not change.
Subadditivity. By homogeneity with \(c = 2\), \(G(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2) = 2\,G\big(\frac{x_1 + x_2}2, \frac{y_1 + y_2}2\big)\). By joint convexity with weights \(\frac12\), this is at most \(G(x_1, y_1) + G(x_2, y_2)\).
Zero probabilities. For \(G(x, y) = x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\), outputs where a probability is 0 follow the conventions \(G(0, y) = 0\) and \(G(x, 0) = \infty\) for \(x > 0\). Steps 1 to 3 still hold, case by case. If some point has \(y_t = 0 < x_t\), the right side is infinite, so there is nothing to check, while a point \((0, 0)\) adds nothing to either side. With \(x_t = 0 < y_t\), the formula \(y\,g(x/y)\) still applies, since \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g\) is convex on \([0, \infty)\).
Mixtures of pairs: quasi-convexity. Let \((P_t, Q_t)\) be pairs of distributions on the same outputs, and mix them with shared weights \(w_t\). Apply step 1 at each output \(y\), to the points \((P_t(y), Q_t(y))\), and add over \(y\). Then \[F\Big(\sum_tw_tP_t,\ \sum_tw_tQ_t\Big) \le \sum_tw_t\,F(P_t, Q_t) \le \max_tF(P_t, Q_t). \tag{F.42}\] For \(\alpha > 1\), \(D_\alpha = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln F\) increases with \(F\). So the Rényi divergence of the mixed pair is at most the largest \(D_\alpha(P_t\|Q_t)\). This is step 2 of Section 33.3. For densities, replace the sum over \(y\) by an integral, and the inequality survives because it holds at every \(y\).
The pair \((Q, P)\) for a subsampled Gaussian. In Section 31.6, \(Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(P = (1 - q)Q + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The pair \((Q, P)\) is the mixture \((1 - q)(Q, Q) + q\,(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2))\), with the shared weights \(1 - q\) and \(q\). The first inequality of step 5 gives \[F(Q, P) \le (1 - q)F(Q, Q) + q\,F\big(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\big) = (1 - q) + q\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}, \tag{F.43}\] because \(F(Q, Q) = 1\), and \(D_\alpha\) between two normals with unit shift is \(\alpha\rho_0\), where \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\). That is the bound the chapter states.
Tests cannot increase the divergence. A test rejects on output \(y\) with probability \(\phi(y)\), which may lie strictly between 0 and 1. Split each output \(y\) into two pieces, “\(y\) and reject” and “\(y\) and accept”. Their probabilities are \(\phi(y)P(y)\) and \((1 - \phi(y))P(y)\) under \(P\), and likewise under \(Q\). Both pieces keep the ratio \(P(y)/Q(y)\), so by homogeneity their two terms add up to \(G(P(y), Q(y))\), and \(F\) does not change. Now merge all the “reject” pieces into one output and all the “accept” pieces into another. By subadditivity, applied one merge at a time, \(F\) can only go down. The two merged outputs are the test’s coin. It rejects with probability \(\mathrm{FPR} = \sum_y\phi(y)P(y)\) under \(P\) and \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} = \sum_y\phi(y)Q(y)\) under \(Q\), where \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\) are its type I and type II errors. So \[G(\mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FNR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) \le F(P, Q), \tag{F.44}\] which is the data-processing step of the proof of Theorem 30.2, randomized tests included. The same split-and-merge argument works for any processing that sends each output \(y\) to a random output \(z\), so it also proves the data-processing inequality for \(D_\alpha\).
The region of allowed tests is convex. The chapter’s RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) in both directions, and the coin of step 7 inherits both bounds. Written with \(G\), the two constraints of Equation 30.15 are \[c_1(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) = G(\mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FNR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}, \qquad c_2(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) = G(1 - \mathrm{FNR}, \mathrm{FPR}) + G(\mathrm{FNR}, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}) \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{F.45}\] Each term is \(G\) applied to numbers that depend linearly on \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\). Mixing two error pairs mixes those numbers with the same weights, so step 1 makes each term, and their sum, convex in \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\). The same holds for \(c_2\), which swaps the roles of the two distributions. If two error pairs satisfy a convex constraint, so does every mixture of them, because its value is at most the mixture of two values that are both within the limit. So each constraint allows a convex set of pairs, and so does their intersection.
The boundary is convex, and each constraint is smallest at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). Let \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) be the smallest allowed \(\mathrm{FNR}\) at type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\). For allowed pairs \((\mathrm{FPR}_1, \mathrm{FNR}_1)\) and \((\mathrm{FPR}_2, \mathrm{FNR}_2)\), the mixture is allowed, so \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) at the mixed \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is at most the mixed \(\mathrm{FNR}\). Taking each \(\mathrm{FNR}_i\) as small as allowed shows that \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is convex. At \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), homogeneity gives \(c_1 = G(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FPR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = \mathrm{FPR} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = 1\). Subadditivity merges the two terms, whose arguments add up to \((\mathrm{FPR} + 1 - \mathrm{FPR},\ 1 - \mathrm{FNR} + \mathrm{FNR}) = (1, 1)\), so \(c_1 \ge G(1, 1) = 1\) for every \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), so 1 is the smallest value. A convex function of \(\mathrm{FNR}\) that is smallest at \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) decreases on \([0, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}]\), which is what the chapter needs to find \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) by bisection on \(\mathrm{FNR}\).



F.5.4 Checking it
At \(\alpha = 2\), the script draws 100,000 random pairs of points and weights. It finds no violation of joint convexity or of subadditivity. It also draws 20,000 random mixtures of three pairs of distributions on five outputs, and finds no mixture whose Rényi divergence exceeds the largest of its parts.
On the die, the loaded die gives a six probability 0.5 and each other face 0.1. Take the randomized test that rejects on a six, and with probability \(\frac12\) on a five. Its type I error is \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.5 + 0.05 = 0.55\), and it rejects under the fair die with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} = \frac16 + \frac1{12} = 0.25\). Its coin has \(D_2 = 0.3920\), below \(D_2(P\|Q) = 0.5878\) for the full roll, as step 7 requires.
For the subsampled Gaussian of step 6, with \(q = 0.1\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\alpha = 2\), numerical integration gives \(F(Q, P) = 1.0115\), below the bound \(0.9 + 0.1e = 1.1718\). The bound is loose here because it charges the full Gaussian divergence to the fraction \(q\) of the mixture.
The right panel of Figure F.8 draws the region that order 2 alone allows for the Gaussian mechanism whose sensitivity equals its noise standard deviation (\(\mu = 1\) in the chapters), whose RDP curve gives \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\). At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\) the boundary is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(0.1) = 0.5068\), so the largest power is 0.4932, the order-2 value that Section 30.3 reports. The script checks convexity on a grid of 199 values of \(\mathrm{FPR}\): the smallest second difference of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is positive. In the figure, the chord between two boundary points stays inside the region. The boundary has a kink where the binding constraint switches from \(c_2\) to \(c_1\), and convexity survives it.






Figure F.8: Left: contours of \(G(x, y) = x^2/y\), the perspective of \(g(t) = t^2\), with two points, the chord between them and its midpoint, where the function value is below the average of the two end values. Right: the pairs of type I and type II errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) that order \(\alpha = 2\) with \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\) allows (shaded), its lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), and a chord between two boundary points that stays inside.

section: F.6 A noisy count has an increasing likelihood ratio
text:
F.6 A noisy count has an increasing likelihood ratio

F.6.1 What the chapter uses
The example of Section 9.5 releases a noisy count of \(m = 100\) other records plus the target’s bit \(b\). The adversary sees \(K + b + Z\), where the unknown count \(K\) of the others is \(\mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\) and the noise \(Z\) is normal with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\). Write \(w_k = \binom mk2^{-m}\) for the binomial weights and \(\varphi_\sigma\) for the normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\). In world 0 (\(b = 0\)) the observation has density \[p(y) = f(y), \qquad f(y) = \sum_{k=0}^mw_k\,\varphi_\sigma(y - k), \tag{F.46}\] and in world 1 (\(b = 1\)) it has the shifted density \(q(y) = f(y - 1)\).
The chapter says that the likelihood ratio increases with \(y\), so the best attack is a threshold, at \(m/2 + \frac12 = 50.5\) by symmetry. A tempting reason is that \(f\) is log-concave, because a binomial and a normal are both log-concave and so is their sum. That reason is not valid in general, because the rule it quotes concerns two variables that both have log-concave densities on the real line. A binomial count lives on the integers and has no density there, and for such sums the rule fails. For example, a Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) variable plus normal noise with \(\sigma = 0.2\) has two separate peaks, as the left panel of Figure F.9 shows, so it is not log-concave. With \(m = 100\) and \(\sigma = 1\) the density does happen to be log-concave, but with \(\sigma = 0.5\) it is not.
The attack needs less than log-concavity, and what it needs holds for every \(\sigma > 0\): \[\frac{q(y)}{p(y)} = \frac{f(y - 1)}{f(y)} \text{ is strictly increasing in } y. \tag{F.47}\] The proof below uses two properties. The weights \(w_k\) must form a log-concave sequence, \(w_k^2 \ge w_{k-1}w_{k+1}\), with no zero between two non-zero weights. The noise must be normal.


F.6.2 The idea
Both densities are mixtures over the unknown count of the others. Comparing the ratio at two observations \(y < y'\) therefore means comparing two double sums, over the count \(j\) in one world and the count \(k\) in the other. Pair each term \((j, k)\) with its mirror image \((k, j)\). Each pair turns into a product of two factors. One compares the binomial weights, and it is non-negative because the binomial is log-concave. The other compares normal densities, and it is non-negative because a larger observation favours a larger centre. A product of two non-negative factors is non-negative, and so is the sum.
For a single Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record (\(m = 1\)), the weights are \(w_0 = w_1 = \frac12\), and \(w_k = 0\) for every other \(k\). The pairs with \(j > k\) whose weight factor \(w_{j-1}w_k - w_{k-1}w_j\) is not zero are listed in Table F.6. All three weight factors are positive, even though the density has two peaks.



Table F.6: The weight factors of step 4 for one Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record, for the pairs \(j > k\) where they are not zero.





Pair \((j, k)\)
\(w_{j-1}w_k\)
\(w_{k-1}w_j\)
Weight factor




\((1, 0)\)
\(w_0w_0 = \frac14\)
\(w_{-1}w_1 = 0\)
\(\frac14\)


\((2, 0)\)
\(w_1w_0 = \frac14\)

\(\frac14\)


\((2, 1)\)
\(w_1w_1 = \frac14\)
\(w_0w_2 = 0\)
\(\frac14\)








F.6.3 Derivation
Set \(w_i = 0\) for \(i\) outside \(0, \dots, m\), and write \(\varphi\) for \(\varphi_\sigma\). Substituting \(j = k + 1\) in \(q(y) = f(y - 1)\) writes both densities as sums over a centre: \[p(y) = \sum_kw_k\,\varphi(y - k), \qquad q(y) = \sum_jw_{j-1}\varphi(y - j). \tag{F.48}\]

What to show. The ratio increases exactly when \(q(y')/p(y') \ge q(y)/p(y)\) for every \(y < y'\). Multiplying by the positive \(p(y)p(y')\), this is \(\Delta = q(y')p(y) - q(y)p(y') \ge 0\).
Expand. Multiplying out the sums, \[\Delta = \sum_{j,k}a_{jk}b_{jk}, \qquad a_{jk} = w_{j-1}w_k, \qquad b_{jk} = \varphi(y' - j)\varphi(y - k) - \varphi(y - j)\varphi(y' - k). \tag{F.49}\]
Pair each term with its mirror. Swapping \(j\) and \(k\) swaps the two products in \(b_{jk}\), so \(b_{kj} = -b_{jk}\) and \(b_{jj} = 0\). Split the sum into the terms with \(j > k\) and those with \(j < k\), and rename the indices in the second part. Then \[\Delta = \sum_{j > k}\big(a_{jk} - a_{kj}\big)b_{jk} = \sum_{j>k}\big(w_{j-1}w_k - w_{k-1}w_j\big)\,b_{jk}. \tag{F.50}\]
The weight factor is non-negative. Take \(j > k\). If \(w_{k-1} = 0\) or \(w_j = 0\), the subtracted product is 0 and the factor is at least 0. Otherwise \(k - 1\) and \(j\) both carry weight, and so does every index between them, because there are no internal zeros. Log-concavity, \(w_i^2 \ge w_{i-1}w_{i+1}\), says that the ratio \(w_{i-1}/w_i\) never decreases as \(i\) grows. So \(w_{j-1}/w_j \ge w_{k-1}/w_k\), which is \(w_{j-1}w_k \ge w_{k-1}w_j\). For the binomial, \(w_{i-1}/w_i = i/(m - i + 1)\), which increases with \(i\).
The kernel factor is positive. Take \(j > k\) and \(y < y'\). Compare the logarithms of the two products in \(b_{jk}\). Expanding the squares in the normal densities, the terms in \(y^2\), \(y'^2\), \(j^2\) and \(k^2\) cancel, and \[\ln\frac{\varphi(y' - j)\varphi(y - k)}{\varphi(y - j)\varphi(y' - k)} = \frac{(y - j)^2 + (y' - k)^2 - (y' - j)^2 - (y - k)^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{(y' - y)(j - k)}{\sigma^2} > 0. \tag{F.51}\] So \(b_{jk} > 0\). In words, a larger observation is relatively more likely under the larger centre.
Conclude. Every term of step 3 is a non-negative weight factor times a positive kernel factor, so \(\Delta \ge 0\). The pair \((1, 0)\) has weight factor \(w_0^2 > 0\), so \(\Delta > 0\) and the ratio is strictly increasing. This proves Equation F.47.
The best attack is a threshold. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Section 4.2), the most powerful test rejects where the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) is above a cut-off. When the ratio increases with \(y\), that region is \(\{y > \tau\}\) for some threshold \(\tau\).
The threshold. The binomial weights are symmetric, \(w_k = w_{m-k}\), and so is the noise, so \(f(m/2 + s) = f(m/2 - s)\) for every \(s\). The ratio equals 1 where \(f(y - 1) = f(y)\). That happens when \(y - 1\) and \(y\) sit symmetrically around \(m/2\), at \(y = m/2 + \frac12\). Because the ratio is strictly increasing, it crosses 1 only there. The test with the best advantage rejects exactly where \(q > p\), that is, where the ratio is above 1 (Section 4.6), which is \(\{y > 50.5\}\) for \(m = 100\).



F.6.4 Checking it
For the Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record with \(\sigma = 0.2\), the script finds two peaks in the density. On a grid of 4,001 points the log-ratio still increases at every step. It also evaluates the double sum of step 3 directly and matches \(\Delta\) to rounding error, both for this case and for \(m = 100\). For \(m = 100\) and \(\sigma = 1\), the ratio crosses 1 at 50.5000, and the advantage of that threshold is 0.0779, the exact value in Table 9.5. The largest second difference of \(\ln f\) on a grid is negative (\(-3.8\times10^{-6}\)) at \(\sigma = 1\) and positive (\(+5.5\times10^{-5}\)) at \(\sigma = 0.5\). So the density is log-concave in the chapter’s case but not for smaller noise. The ratio increases in both cases, as the right panel of Figure F.9 shows.






Figure F.9: Left: the densities of a Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) bit plus normal noise with standard deviation 0.2, in world 0 and shifted by 1 in world 1; each has two peaks. Middle: the logarithm of their likelihood ratio still increases with the observation. Right: the log-likelihood ratio of the chapter’s noisy count of 100 records for three noise levels, increasing for each and crossing 0 at 50.5.





F.6.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs the kernel inequality of step 5 for the noise. Step 5 proves it for normal noise, and it holds for every log-concave noise density, such as the Laplace density (Karlin calls such shift kernels totally positive of order 2). For other noise the argument does not apply. It also needs log-concave weights without internal zeros. A count whose other records have unequal probabilities is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, and such a count still has log-concave weights, so the result covers it too.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
text:
G.1 Convexity three ways, and the linear rate of gradient descent
This appendix proves seven results that the chapters on optimization, generalization and attacks use without deriving them in full. The first five are about gradient methods on convex functions. Convexity can be recognized in three ways, and on a strongly convex function gradient descent (GD) closes the gap to the minimum by a constant factor per step. On a convex smooth function, a small enough gradient step never pushes two points apart. On functions whose slope is bounded (Lipschitz functions), no gradient method can beat the rate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), one over the square root of the number of steps. And when SGD trains a model, the best time to stop balances that rate against the stability that the non-expanding step gives. The other results treat a trained model as a random object, random because its training set is. Here the appendix finds the limit of the error of the 1-nearest-neighbour rule, and shows that the parameters fitted by logistic regression are approximately Gaussian, with a formula for how much one record moves them. It ends by showing when the best attack on the membership of a target record looks at the parameters only through that record’s loss. Table G.1 lists where each result is stated or used.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
text:
G.1.1 What the chapter uses
Optimization defines a convex function by its chords, saying that the straight segment between two points of the graph never dips below it. It then works with its tangents, Equation 6.2, which say that the graph lies above each of its tangent planes. It proves that chords give tangents (Lemma 6.1) and points here for the other direction. In Section 6.1 it also states, citing Nesterov’s Lectures on Convex Optimization, §2.1, that convexity and strong convexity can be read off the Hessian \(\nabla^2 f\), the matrix of second derivatives, and that a strongly monotone gradient makes a function strongly convex. Strong monotonicity, Equation 6.6, says that \(\langle\nabla f(\theta) - \nabla f(\theta'), \theta - \theta'\rangle \ge \lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|^2\): moving from \(\theta'\) to \(\theta\) raises the slope along the direction of travel by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance. Its logistic-regression example uses the Hessian test to conclude that the loss is convex. Finally, it proves the linear rate Equation 6.15, a geometric shrinking of the distance to the minimizer, only for a quadratic, while its interpretation says that GD converges linearly on every strongly convex smooth function.
Write \(f\) for a differentiable function of the parameters \(\theta \in \mathbb R^d\), and \(\lambda \ge 0\) for a level of curvature. The four claims proved here are these. First, tangents give chords. Suppose \(f\) lies above all its tangents, \(f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle\) for all points \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\). Then, for every mixing weight \(\omega \in [0, 1]\), \[f(\omega \theta' + (1-\omega)\theta) \le \omega f(\theta') + (1-\omega)f(\theta). \tag{G.1}\] Second, a Hessian with every eigenvalue at least \(\lambda\) makes \(f\) lie above each tangent by a bowl of curvature \(\lambda\). In symbols, with \(I\) the identity matrix, if \(\nabla^2 f(\theta) \succeq \lambda I\) everywhere, then \[f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle\nabla f(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle + \frac\lambda2\|\theta' - \theta\|^2. \tag{G.2}\] This inequality is what \(\lambda\)-strongly convex means, and with \(\lambda = 0\) it is convexity. The Hessian test also works backwards for \(\lambda = 0\): a convex twice-differentiable \(f\) has \(\nabla^2 f \succeq 0\). Third, a strongly monotone gradient gives Equation G.2 without any second derivatives.
The fourth claim is about GD on the training objective. Take an empirical risk \(\mathcal L(\theta; D)\), written \(\mathcal L(\theta)\) here because the dataset \(D\) stays fixed. Let it be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, with minimum value \(\mathcal L^*\), and let it also be \(\beta\)-smooth, so that no curvature exceeds the number \(\beta\), and write \(\kappa = \beta/\lambda\) for its condition number. Then GD with the learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) shrinks the gap to the minimum by the factor \(1 - 1/\kappa\) at every step, where \(\theta_t\) is the point reached after \(t\) steps: \[\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^* \le \left(1 - \frac1\kappa\right)^t\big(\mathcal L(\theta_0) - \mathcal L^*\big). \tag{G.3}\] And when \(\mathcal L\) is twice differentiable with \(\lambda I \preceq \nabla^2 \mathcal L \preceq \beta I\), the chapter’s distance bound Equation 6.15 holds exactly as stated for the quadratic.


G.1.2 The idea
To get a chord from tangents, look at the mixed point \(z = \omega \theta' + (1-\omega)\theta\) and draw the tangent there. The graph lies above this tangent at both ends, \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\), so it still lies above it after you average the two endpoint values with the weights \(1 - \omega\) and \(\omega\). The tangent is a straight line, so its weighted average over the two ends is its value at the weighted average of the ends, which is \(z\) itself. So the average of the function values is at least the tangent’s value at \(z\), which is \(f(z)\). Take \(f(\theta) = \theta^2\), \(\theta = 0\), \(\theta' = 2\) and \(\omega = \frac12\), so \(z = 1\). The tangent at 1 is \(1 + 2(\theta - 1)\). At the two ends it gives \(-1\) and \(3\), below the function values 0 and 4. The two tangent values average to \(1 = f(z)\), and the function values average to 2, which is at least 1.
The Hessian test works one line at a time. Restricted to the line from \(\theta\) to \(\theta'\), the function is a function of one variable whose second derivative is at least \(\lambda\) times the squared length of the step. Its slope therefore grows at least linearly along the line, and integrating twice gives the bowl.
The linear rate combines two inequalities. The chapter shows that a GD step with the learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) (the learning rate is also called the step size) lowers \(\mathcal L\) by at least \(\|\nabla \mathcal L\|^2/(2\beta)\). Strong convexity adds that the gradient cannot be small while the gap is large: the gap is at most \(\|\nabla \mathcal L\|^2/(2\lambda)\). So each step removes at least the fraction \(\lambda/\beta = 1/\kappa\) of the gap that remains.


G.1.3 Derivation

Tangents give chords. Let \(z = \omega \theta' + (1-\omega)\theta\). The tangent inequality at \(z\), applied towards \(\theta\) and towards \(\theta'\), gives \(f(\theta) \ge f(z) + \langle\nabla f(z), \theta - z\rangle\) and \(f(\theta') \ge f(z) + \langle\nabla f(z), \theta' - z\rangle\). Multiply the first by \(1 - \omega\) and the second by \(\omega\), and add. The inner products combine into \(\langle\nabla f(z), (1-\omega)\theta + \omega \theta' - z\rangle\), which is zero because the vector on the right is \(z - z\). What is left is \((1-\omega)f(\theta) + \omega f(\theta') \ge f(z)\), the chord inequality. Figure G.1 (left) draws the two gaps and their average.
A curvature bound gives the bowl. Fix \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\), and let \(u = \theta' - \theta\) be the step between them. Walking a fraction \(s \in [0, 1]\) of that step gives the one-variable function \(g(s) = f(\theta + su)\), the values of \(f\) along the segment. By the chain rule, \(g'(s) = \langle\nabla f(\theta + su), u\rangle\) and \(g''(s) = u^\top\nabla^2 f(\theta + su)\,u\). A symmetric matrix \(A\) satisfies \(A \succeq \lambda I\) exactly when \(u^\top Au \ge \lambda\|u\|^2\) for every \(u\), so the curvature bound says \(g''(s) \ge \lambda\|u\|^2\). Now integrate twice. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the slope at \(s\) is the slope at 0 plus the integral of \(g''\) from 0 to \(s\), so \(g'(s) \ge g'(0) + \lambda s\|u\|^2\). Integrating again over \(s \in [0, 1]\) gives \(g(1) \ge g(0) + g'(0) + \frac\lambda2\|u\|^2\), which is Equation G.2 written in terms of \(f\).
And back: convexity gives a Hessian with no negative eigenvalue. Step 5 of the proof of Proposition 6.1, with \(\lambda = 0\), shows that a convex \(f\) has a monotone gradient, \(\langle\nabla f(\theta + su) - \nabla f(\theta), su\rangle \ge 0\). In terms of \(g\) this says \(s\,(g'(s) - g'(0)) \ge 0\). Divide by \(s^2\) and let \(s \to 0\): the ratio \((g'(s) - g'(0))/s\) tends to \(g''(0) = u^\top\nabla^2 f(\theta)u\), so that is at least 0 for every direction \(u\).
Strong monotonicity gives the bowl. Keep the same \(g\). Strong monotonicity Equation 6.6, applied to the points \(\theta + su\) and \(\theta\), says \(\langle\nabla f(\theta + su) - \nabla f(\theta), su\rangle \ge \lambda s^2\|u\|^2\). Dividing by \(s > 0\) gives \(g'(s) - g'(0) \ge \lambda s\|u\|^2\), which is the inequality of step 2 obtained without second derivatives. Integrating it over \(s \in [0, 1]\) again gives Equation G.2.
A small gradient means a small gap. Apply Equation G.2 at a point \(\theta\) towards every other point \(\theta'\). The right side is a parabola in \(\theta'\), and completing the square shows that its lowest value is \(\mathcal L(\theta) - \|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta)\|^2/(2\lambda)\), reached at \(\theta' = \theta - \nabla \mathcal L(\theta)/\lambda\). Every value of \(\mathcal L\) is above the right side, and so above that lowest value. In particular \(\mathcal L^* \ge \mathcal L(\theta) - \|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta)\|^2/(2\lambda)\), which rearranges to the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality: \[\mathcal L(\theta) - \mathcal L^* \le \frac{\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta)\|^2}{2\lambda}. \tag{G.4}\]
Each step removes a fixed fraction of the gap. The chapter derives from the descent lemma Equation 6.5 that one GD step with the learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) gives \(\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) \le \mathcal L(\theta_t) - \|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2/(2\beta)\). Subtract \(\mathcal L^*\) from both sides. By Equation G.4, \(\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t)\|^2 \ge 2\lambda(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*)\), so the subtracted term is at least \(\frac\lambda\beta(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*)\). Hence \(\mathcal L(\theta_{t+1}) - \mathcal L^* \le (1 - 1/\kappa)(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*)\), and repeating this \(t\) times gives Equation G.3.
The distance bound, when second derivatives exist. Write \(\theta^*\) for the minimizer. It has zero gradient, so the GD step can be written as \(\theta_{t+1} - \theta^* = (\theta_t - \theta^*) - \frac1\beta(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t) - \nabla \mathcal L(\theta^*))\). Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 6.1 writes the gradient difference as \(\bar H_t(\theta_t - \theta^*)\), where \(\bar H_t = \int_0^1\nabla^2 \mathcal L(\theta^* + s(\theta_t - \theta^*))\,ds\) is the average Hessian along the segment. For a unit vector \(u\), \(u^\top\bar H_tu\) is an average of numbers \(u^\top\nabla^2 \mathcal L\,u\) that all lie in \([\lambda, \beta]\), so it lies there too. The smallest and largest values of \(u^\top Au\) over unit vectors are the extreme eigenvalues of a symmetric \(A\), so every eigenvalue of \(\bar H_t\) is in \([\lambda, \beta]\). Substituting \(\bar H_t(\theta_t - \theta^*)\) for the gradient difference in the GD step gives \(\theta_{t+1} - \theta^* = (I - \bar H_t/\beta)(\theta_t - \theta^*)\), a matrix with eigenvalues between 0 and \(1 - 1/\kappa\) applied to the error. This is the quadratic’s step 1 with the fixed \(H\) replaced by \(\bar H_t\), and its steps 2 and 3 then go through unchanged and give Equation 6.15.

Step 7 also gives a faster rate for the gap. The gradient vanishes at \(\theta^*\), so the descent lemma at \(\theta^*\) gives \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^* \le \frac\beta2\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2\), and with Equation 6.15 the gap falls like \((1 - 1/\kappa)^{2t}\). That exponent is twice the one in Equation G.3. The slower rate is the price of an argument that uses only first derivatives.






Figure G.1: Left: the chord of \(f(\theta) = \ln(1 + e^{-\theta}) + 0.1\theta^2\) between \(\theta = -3\) and \(\theta' = 3\), the tangent at the mixed point \(z\), and the two gaps between \(f\) and the tangent at the ends (orange), whose weighted average is the gap between the chord and \(f(z)\) (blue). Right: the same function with curvature at least \(\lambda = 0.2\), which stays above its tangent plus the bowl \(\frac\lambda2(\theta' - \theta)^2\).





G.1.4 Checking it
The script uses the logistic data of the optimization chapter: \(n = 1{,}000\) records with \(x\) uniform on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^5\) and labels from a logistic model. It adds a ridge penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) with \(\lambda = 0.01\). Each \(x\) has length 1, so the logistic curvature is at most \(\frac14\), and the ridge adds \(\lambda\). So \(\beta = 0.26\) and \(\kappa = 26\). Over 2,000 random pairs of points in the ball of radius 5, the smallest ratio of the tangent gap \(\mathcal L(\theta') - \mathcal L(\theta) - \langle\nabla \mathcal L(\theta), \theta' - \theta\rangle\) to \(\frac12\|\theta' - \theta\|^2\) is 0.0372, above \(\lambda = 0.01\) as Equation G.2 requires.
GD from \(\theta_0 = 0\) satisfies both bounds with room to spare. Over the first 40 steps, the gap shrinks by a factor of at most 0.7131 per step and the distance by at most 0.8445, both below \(1 - 1/\kappa = 0.9615\). After 25 steps the gap is \(1.22\times10^{-5}\), against \(5.30\times10^{-2}\) from Equation G.3. After 50 steps it is \(2.59\times10^{-9}\), against \(1.99\times10^{-2}\).
The bounds are loose here because they know only the curvature \(\lambda = 0.01\) of the penalty, while the data add curvature of their own. At the minimizer, the smallest eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2 \mathcal L\) is 0.0404. The rate of step 7 with that curvature in place of \(\lambda\) is \((1 - 0.0404/0.26)^2 = 0.713\) per step, and the measured rate between steps 20 and 40 is 0.712. So the form of the rate is exact, and only the curvature it is given is pessimistic. Figure G.2 shows the run.






Figure G.2: The gap \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L^*\) of GD on ridge-regularized logistic regression (\(\lambda = 0.01\), \(\kappa = 26\)), with the Polyak–Łojasiewicz bound Equation G.3, the bound from the distance Equation 6.15, and the same rate computed with the smallest curvature at the minimizer, which tracks the run.





G.1.5 What it does not cover
The distance bound Equation 6.15 was proved here only for twice-differentiable \(\mathcal L\). It holds without second derivatives as well. That proof applies the co-coercivity of the next section to \(\mathcal L - \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\), which is convex and \((\beta - \lambda)\)-smooth (Nesterov 2018, Theorem 2.1.12), and it is longer than the short argument of step 7. The gap bound Equation G.3 needs only the descent lemma and Equation G.4, so it holds for any function that satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality, even one that is not convex (Karimi, Nutini & Schmidt 2016).

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.2 The gradient of a convex smooth function is co-coercive
text:
G.2 The gradient of a convex smooth function is co-coercive

G.2.1 What the chapter uses
Step 1 of the proof of Lemma 7.2 states that the gradient of a convex \(\beta\)-smooth function \(f\) is co-coercive. In words, two gradients that differ by a lot must come from points that are far apart along the direction of that difference. For all \(u\) and \(v\), \[\langle\nabla f(u) - \nabla f(v),\, u - v\rangle \ge \frac1\beta\|\nabla f(u) - \nabla f(v)\|^2. \tag{G.5}\] The chapter cites Nesterov’s Theorem 2.1.5 and points here. The lemma then derives from Equation G.5 that a gradient step \(\psi(\theta) = \theta - \eta\nabla f(\theta)\) with \(0 \le \eta \le 2/\beta\) is non-expansive, \(\|\psi(u) - \psi(v)\| \le \|u - v\|\). That fact drives the stability bound Equation 7.21 for SGD, and Section 35.3 uses the same contraction in amplification by iteration.


G.2.2 The idea
Subtract from \(f\) its tangent at \(v\). The result, \(\varphi\), is still convex and \(\beta\)-smooth, and its gradient is zero at \(v\), so \(v\) is its lowest point. Now stand at \(u\) and take a gradient step on \(\varphi\). By the descent lemma, the step lowers \(\varphi\) by at least \(\|\nabla\varphi(u)\|^2/(2\beta)\), and no step can go below the lowest value \(\varphi(v)\). So \(\varphi(u)\) must sit at least \(\|\nabla\varphi(u)\|^2/(2\beta)\) above \(\varphi(v)\). In words, a convex smooth function cannot have a steep slope close to its minimum. This gives a tangent inequality with an extra term. Writing it once from \(u\) and once from \(v\), and adding the two, gives Equation G.5.
A one-dimensional case makes the inequality concrete. Take the logistic loss \[f(\theta) = \ln(1 + e^{-\theta}), \tag{G.6}\] whose slope is \(f'(\theta) = -\sigma(-\theta)\), where \(\sigma(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s})\) is the logistic function, and whose curvature is at most \(\beta = \frac14\). At the two points \(u = 0\) and \(v = 2\) the slopes are \(-0.5000\) and \(-0.1192\). The left side of Equation G.5 is \((-0.5000 + 0.1192)(0 - 2) = 0.7616\), and the right side is \(0.3808^2/0.25 = 0.5800\), smaller as it should be. For the quadratic \(f(\theta) = \frac\beta2 \theta^2\) the slope difference is \(\beta(u - v)\), so both sides equal \(\beta(u - v)^2\), and the inequality is tight.


G.2.3 Derivation

Shift the minimum to \(v\). Define \(\varphi(\theta) = f(\theta) - \langle\nabla f(v), \theta\rangle\). Subtracting a linear function changes neither the curvature nor the differences between gradients, so \(\varphi\) is convex and \(\beta\)-smooth. Its gradient is \(\nabla\varphi(\theta) = \nabla f(\theta) - \nabla f(v)\), which is zero at \(\theta = v\). The tangent inequality Equation 6.2 for \(\varphi\) at \(v\) then reads \(\varphi(\theta) \ge \varphi(v)\) for every \(\theta\), so \(v\) minimizes \(\varphi\).
A gradient step from \(u\) cannot go below the minimum. Apply the descent lemma Equation 6.5 to \(\varphi\) at \(u\), with the step \(\theta' = u - \nabla\varphi(u)/\beta\). The computation is the chapter’s GD step with \(\beta = \beta\), and it gives \(\varphi(\theta') \le \varphi(u) - \|\nabla\varphi(u)\|^2/(2\beta)\). Since \(\varphi(v) \le \varphi(\theta')\) by step 1, we get \(\varphi(v) \le \varphi(u) - \|\nabla\varphi(u)\|^2/(2\beta)\).
Return to \(f\). Write \(\Delta = \nabla f(u) - \nabla f(v)\), which is \(\nabla\varphi(u)\). The difference \(\varphi(u) - \varphi(v)\) is \(f(u) - f(v) - \langle\nabla f(v), u - v\rangle\), so step 2 becomes a tangent inequality with an extra term: \[f(u) \ge f(v) + \langle\nabla f(v), u - v\rangle + \frac{1}{2\beta}\|\Delta\|^2. \tag{G.7}\]
Swap and add. The same inequality with \(u\) and \(v\) exchanged is \(f(v) \ge f(u) + \langle\nabla f(u), v - u\rangle + \frac{1}{2\beta}\|\Delta\|^2\), because exchanging the points only flips the sign of \(\Delta\). Adding the two, the function values cancel and the inner products combine into \(-\langle\Delta, u - v\rangle\), which leaves \(0 \ge -\langle\Delta, u - v\rangle + \frac1\beta\|\Delta\|^2\). That is Equation G.5.
The step is non-expansive. This is the chapter’s own argument, repeated so that the page stands alone. Expand \(\psi(u) - \psi(v) = (u - v) - \eta\Delta\) as a square and replace \(\langle\Delta, u - v\rangle\) by the smaller \(\|\Delta\|^2/\beta\): \[\|\psi(u) - \psi(v)\|^2 = \|u - v\|^2 - 2\eta\langle\Delta, u - v\rangle + \eta^2\|\Delta\|^2 \le \|u - v\|^2 - \eta\Big(\frac2\beta - \eta\Big)\|\Delta\|^2. \tag{G.8}\] For \(0 \le \eta \le 2/\beta\) the subtracted term is not negative, so the distance does not grow.



G.2.4 Checking it
The script draws 500 pairs \((u, v)\) from a normal distribution with standard deviation 4 and evaluates both sides of Equation G.5 for the logistic loss. The smallest ratio of left to right side is 1.0006, so the inequality holds and is nearly tight. The tight pairs lie near 0, where the curvature of the logistic loss is close to \(\frac14\) and the loss looks like the quadratic of the example. For the five-dimensional logistic risk of the previous section, the smallest ratio over 2,000 pairs is 5.3704. That risk curves much less than \(\frac14\) in most directions, so the bound has slack there.
The non-expansive step behaves as step 5 says. Over the 500 pairs, the largest ratio \(|\psi(u) - \psi(v)|/|u - v|\) is 0.9993 at \(\eta = 4\) and 0.9988 at \(\eta = 8 = 2/\beta\). At \(\eta = 10\) it is 1.4985, so the step pushes some pairs apart. Figure G.3 shows both checks.






Figure G.3: Left: for 500 random pairs, \((f'(u) - f'(v))(u - v)\) against \((f'(u) - f'(v))^2/\beta\) for the logistic loss, \(\beta = \frac14\). Every point lies above the line \(y = x\). Right: the largest ratio of distances after and before one gradient step, over the same pairs, against the learning rate \(\eta\), with the quadratic’s factor \(|1 - \eta\beta|\). Both cross 1 at \(\eta = 2/\beta = 8\).





G.2.5 What it does not cover
Both convexity and smoothness are needed. Without convexity, step 1 fails, because a zero gradient no longer marks a minimum. A gradient step can then expand distances by up to the factor \(1 + \eta\beta\), as on the concave function \(-\frac\beta2\theta^2\), whose step multiplies every distance by exactly \(1 + \eta\beta\). Without smoothness there is no descent lemma, and the gradient of a function with a kink, such as \(|\theta|\), jumps by 2 between points arbitrarily close together, so no constant \(\beta\) can work.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.3 When to stop SGD: balancing optimization against stability
text:
G.3 When to stop SGD: balancing optimization against stability

G.3.1 What the chapter uses
Theorem 7.4 in Algorithmic stability and generalization bounds the stability of SGD. Two runs on training sets that differ in one record drift apart by at most \(2L/n\) times the sum of the learning rates, so with a constant step \(\eta\) and \(T\) steps the uniform stability is \[\gamma \le \frac{2L^2\eta T}{n}, \tag{G.9}\] where \(n\) is the number of training records and \(L\) bounds the slope of the loss. The chapter concludes that training longer lowers the training loss but raises \(\gamma\), which makes a case for stopping early, and points here for the balance. This section makes that precise. For a loss that is convex, smooth and \(L\)-Lipschitz, a constant step small enough for that theorem, and SGD started at \(\theta_0 = 0\), it shows that the expected excess test loss of the averaged weights \(\bar\theta\) over the best weights \(\theta^*\) is at most \[\frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{2L^2\eta T}{n} + \frac{\eta L^2}{2}. \tag{G.10}\] The first term falls with training time and the second rises with it. Their sum is smallest when \(\eta T = \|\theta^*\|\sqrt n/(2L)\), and there the excess test loss is at most \(2L\|\theta^*\|/\sqrt n\), plus the term \(\eta L^2/2\).


G.3.2 The idea
The test loss of the trained weights is worse than that of the best weights for two separate reasons. SGD has not finished minimizing the training loss, which is the optimization error, and the training loss of the trained weights is an optimistic estimate of their test loss, which is the generalization gap. Each step of training shrinks the first and can grow the second. So there is a best training time, and finding it is a matter of adding the two bounds and minimizing the sum.
The two bounds come from two chapters. Optimization bounds the optimization error by a term that falls like \(1/(\eta T)\), the cost of travelling from the starting point to \(\theta^*\) with steps of size \(\eta\). The stability chapter bounds the expected gap by \(\gamma\), which grows like \(\eta T\). A sum \(a/u + bu\) of a falling and a rising term is smallest where the two terms are equal, which is the whole calculation.


G.3.3 Derivation
The plan is to split the excess test loss into three pieces, bound each piece by a result the chapters prove, and then choose the training time that minimizes the sum of the bounds. Write \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta)\) for the test loss of weights \(\theta\), the average loss on a new record, and \(\mathcal L(\theta; D)\) for the training loss, the average loss on the training set \(D\). Let \(\theta^*\) be weights that minimize the test loss. They are fixed in advance, so they do not depend on \(D\).

Split the excess loss. Add and subtract the training loss of \(\bar\theta\) and of \(\theta^*\): \[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\bar\theta) - \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^*) = \big[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\bar\theta) - \mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)\big] + \big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D) - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\big] + \big[\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) - \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^*)\big]. \tag{G.11}\] The first bracket is the generalization gap of \(\bar\theta\), the second is its optimization error on the training set, and the third compares a fixed model’s training loss with its test loss.
The third piece has mean zero. The weights \(\theta^*\) do not depend on \(D\), so by Proposition 7.1 their training loss is an unbiased estimate of their test loss, and the third bracket averages to zero over \(D\).
The averaged weights are as stable as the last ones. Let \(\theta_0, \theta_1, \dots\) be the iterates of SGD on \(D\), and \(\theta_t'\) those of the coupled run on the neighbouring set \(D^{(i)}\), as in the proof of Theorem 7.4. That proof shows that the distance \(r_t = \|\theta_t - \theta_t'\|\) has \(\mathbb E\,r_t \le 2L\eta t/n\), which is at most \(2L\eta T/n\) for every \(t \le T\). The averaged weights are \(\bar\theta = \frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\theta_t\). The distance between two averages is at most the average of the distances, by the triangle inequality, so \(\mathbb E\|\bar\theta - \bar\theta'\|\) is also at most \(2L\eta T/n\). The loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so the averaged weights are uniformly stable with \(\gamma \le 2L^2\eta T/n\), as in step 5 of that proof.
The first piece. By Equation 7.7, a \(\gamma\)-uniformly stable algorithm has expected gap at most \(\gamma\). With step 3, the first bracket averages to at most \(2L^2\eta T/n\).
The second piece. Theorem 6.2 bounds the optimization error of SGD with constant step \(\eta\), run on a convex objective whose random gradients are unbiased and have mean squared length at most \(G^2\), from a start at distance at most \(R\) from \(\theta^*\). Here the objective is the training loss \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\), and the set is all of \(\mathbb R^d\), so there is no projection. A step that picks a record uniformly at random has a gradient whose average is the gradient of the training loss, so it is unbiased, and an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss gives \(G = L\). Starting at \(\theta_0 = 0\) makes that distance \(R = \|\theta^*\|\). The theorem compares with a minimizer of the objective, but its proof never uses that \(\theta^*\) minimizes anything: the convexity step holds for any fixed point. So, averaged over the steps’ random choices, \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D) - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\big] \le \frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{\eta L^2}{2}. \tag{G.12}\]
Add the three pieces. Taking expectations in step 1 and using steps 2, 4 and 5 gives Equation G.10.
Choose the training time. For a fixed step \(\eta\), training time enters Equation G.10 only through \(u = \eta T\), the total distance the learning rates allow. The part that depends on it is \[h(u) = \frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{2u} + \frac{2L^2u}{n}. \tag{G.13}\] Its derivative \(-\frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{2u^2} + \frac{2L^2}{n}\) is negative for small \(u\) and positive for large \(u\), and it is zero at \[u^* = \frac{\|\theta^*\|\sqrt n}{2L}. \tag{G.14}\]
The value at the balance. Substituting \(u^*\), each of the two terms of \(h\) equals \(L\|\theta^*\|/\sqrt n\), so the excess test loss is at most \(2L\|\theta^*\|/\sqrt n\), plus the term \(\eta L^2/2\). Training much longer than \(u^*\) buys optimization accuracy that the growing stability term gives back, because past \(u^*\) the rising term of \(h\) grows faster than the falling term shrinks.



G.3.4 Checking it
The chapter’s SGD experiment, Example 7.6, gives a concrete case. Its loss is the logistic loss on \(n = 100\) records of the running example, with features on the unit sphere, so \(L = 1\), and with step \(\eta = 0.25\). In the running example a label is \(+1\) with probability \(\sigma(5x_1)\), where \(\sigma\) is the logistic function and \(x_1\) the first feature. The logistic loss of weights \(\theta\) is the negative log-likelihood of a model that says \(+1\) with probability \(\sigma(\langle\theta, x\rangle)\). At every \(x\), the expected negative log-likelihood is smallest when the model’s probability equals the true one, so the best weights are \(\theta^* = (5, 0, \dots, 0)\), with \(\|\theta^*\| = 5\).
Step 7 then gives \(u^* = 5\sqrt{100}/2 = 25\). At \(\eta = 0.25\) that is \(T = 100\) steps, one pass over the 100 records, so the bound says to stop after one epoch. Its value there is \(2 \cdot 5/10 = 1\), plus \(\eta L^2/2 = 0.125\). Figure G.4 draws the two terms and their sum against \(u\): they cross at \(u^* = 25\), where each is 0.5, and the sum has its minimum there. In the experiment, though, the test loss keeps falling after one epoch, from 0.596 to 0.557 after five, and rises only after that (Table 7.4). So the bound stops too early, because its stability term is too pessimistic. After one epoch that term allows a gap of 0.5, while the measured gap is 0.036, and the measured gap grows far more slowly than linearly. The balance has the right form, but the true best time lies later than the bound says. The experiment measures the last iterate rather than the average, so the comparison is a check of the shape, not of the constant.






Figure G.4: The bound Equation G.10 against \(u = \eta T\), the learning rate times the number of steps, for \(n = 100\), \(\|\theta^*\| = 5\), \(L = 1\) and \(\eta = 0.25\), on log axes: the falling optimization term \(\|\theta^*\|^2/(2u)\), the rising stability term \(2L^2u/n\) (both dashed), and their sum plus \(\eta L^2/2\) (solid), smallest at \(u^* = 25\).





G.3.5 What it does not cover
The bound needs a convex loss, so it does not cover neural networks. Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016) also bound the stability of SGD on smooth non-convex losses, with steps that shrink like \(1/t\). Their stability term then grows like a power of \(T\) below 1. But the optimization error of a non-convex loss has no bound of the kind step 5 uses, so there is nothing to balance it against. The bound also uses a constant step. With a step that shrinks over time, the sum of the learning rates replaces \(\eta T\) in the stability term, and the balance is found the same way.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.4 No gradient method beats \(RL/\sqrt T\) on every convex Lipschitz function
text:
G.4 No gradient method beats \(RL/\sqrt T\) on every convex Lipschitz function

G.4.1 What the chapter uses
The section on SGD for convex Lipschitz objectives in Optimization proves Equation 6.25, an error of at most \(RL/\sqrt T\) after \(T\) steps. Here \(R\) is the distance from the start to the minimizer, and \(L\) is the Lipschitz constant, the largest size of a gradient. Its interpretation then says that the rate cannot be improved: “there are convex \(L\)-Lipschitz functions on which every method that only queries gradients has error at least of order \(RL/\sqrt T\) after \(T\) queries (Bubeck 2015, §3.5).”
This section proves that claim for the methods the book uses. A method is span-restricted if it starts at \(\theta_1 = 0\) and every point it queries or outputs is a combination of the gradients it has received so far. Gradient descent and SGD, with a constant or a changing learning rate, with projection onto a ball centred at 0 (which only rescales a vector), and with averaged iterates, are all span-restricted. The claim is that in dimension \(d \ge T + 1\) there is a convex function that is \(L\)-Lipschitz on the ball \(\{\|\theta\| \le R\}\), with its minimizer at distance \(R\) from the start, on which every span-restricted method, after \(T\) gradient queries, outputs a point \(\theta\) with \[f(\theta) - f^* \ge \frac{RL}{2(1 + \sqrt{T + 1})}. \tag{G.15}\] The right side is close to half of \(RL/\sqrt T\) for large \(T\), so the SGD guarantee is optimal up to a factor of about 2.


G.4.2 The idea
The hard function hides its minimum in many coordinates and reveals them one gradient at a time. It uses one more coordinate than the method has queries, \(k = T + 1\). Its first term is a positive constant \(\gamma\) times the largest of the first \(k\) coordinates, and its second is a small bowl with a positive weight \(\alpha\). Both constants are chosen below: \[f(\theta) = \gamma\max_{i \le k} \theta_i + \frac\alpha2\|\theta\|^2. \tag{G.16}\] Its lowest point spreads equal negative values over all \(k\) coordinates, which brings the largest coordinate down. But the gradient at a point whose later coordinates are all zero involves only one new coordinate, the first place where the largest value is reached. So after \(T\) gradients the method has touched at most \(T\) coordinates. The last coordinate is still zero, so the largest coordinate is at least zero, and \(f\) is at least zero. The minimum is negative, and its distance below zero is the bound.
Take \(T = 2\), so \(k = 3\), with \(R = L = 1\). The constants are then \(\gamma = 0.6340\) and \(\alpha = 0.3660\), and the minimum is \(f^* = -0.1830\). The first query is at \(\theta_1 = 0\), where all three coordinates tie at 0, so the gradient points along the first coordinate. The method’s next point has the form \((a, 0, 0)\). Whatever \(a\) is, the largest coordinate is first reached at the first or the second position, so the second gradient involves only the first two coordinates. Any output is then of the form \((a', b', 0)\), its third coordinate makes the largest coordinate at least 0, and \(f \ge 0\). The error is at least \(0.1830\), which is \(1/(2(1 + \sqrt3))\), the right side of Equation G.15.


G.4.3 Derivation

The minimum. The largest of \(k\) numbers is at least their average, so \(f(\theta) \ge \sum_{i \le k}\big(\frac\gamma k\theta_i + \frac\alpha2\theta_i^2\big) + \frac\alpha2\sum_{i > k}\theta_i^2\). Each term of the first sum is a parabola in \(\theta_i\) whose lowest value is \(-\gamma^2/(2\alpha k^2)\), at \(\theta_i = -\gamma/(\alpha k)\). The terms of the second sum are at least 0. Adding up, \(f(\theta) \ge -\gamma^2/(2\alpha k)\). The point with \(\theta_i = -\gamma/(\alpha k)\) for \(i \le k\) and 0 elsewhere reaches this value, because its first \(k\) coordinates are equal and so their largest equals their average. So \[f^* = -\frac{\gamma^2}{2\alpha k}, \qquad \|\theta^*\| = \frac{\gamma}{\alpha\sqrt k}. \tag{G.17}\]
The constants. The max term changes by at most \(\gamma\) times the distance moved, since no coordinate changes by more than the distance. On the ball of radius \(R\) the quadratic term changes by at most \(\alpha R\) times the distance, since \(\frac\alpha2(\|\theta\|^2 - \|\theta'\|^2) = \frac\alpha2\langle \theta + \theta', \theta - \theta'\rangle\) and \(\|\theta + \theta'\| \le 2R\). So \(f\) is \((\gamma + \alpha R)\)-Lipschitz on the ball. Asking for \(\gamma + \alpha R = L\) and \(\|\theta^*\| = R\), and solving the two equations, gives \[\gamma = \frac{L\sqrt k}{1 + \sqrt k}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{L}{R(1 + \sqrt k)}, \qquad -f^* = \frac{RL}{2(1 + \sqrt k)}. \tag{G.18}\]
The gradients the method sees. At a point \(\theta\), let \(i\) be the first index at which \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k\) reach their largest value, and return \(g = \gamma e_i + \alpha \theta\), where \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th unit vector. This is a legitimate gradient for a function with a kink, a subgradient as in the chapter: its tangent stays below the graph. The reason is that \(\max_j \theta'_j \ge \theta'_i = \max_j \theta_j + \langle e_i, \theta' - \theta\rangle\), while the quadratic term lies above its own tangent. Adding the two gives \(f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle g, \theta' - \theta\rangle\).
One new coordinate per query. Write \(V_s\) for the vectors whose coordinates after the \(s\)-th are zero. The claim is that the \(s\)-th query point lies in \(V_{s-1}\) and its gradient in \(V_s\). The first query is at \(0 \in V_0\). Suppose the \(s\)-th query point \(\theta_s\) is in \(V_{s-1}\), with \(s \le k\). Its coordinates \(s, \dots, k\) are zero, so its largest coordinate among the first \(k\) is at least 0. If that largest value is 0, coordinate \(s\) reaches it, so the first index that does is at most \(s\). If it is positive, it is reached among the first \(s - 1\) coordinates. Either way \(e_i \in V_s\), and \(\alpha \theta_s \in V_{s-1}\), so \(g_s \in V_s\). A span-restricted method then chooses \(\theta_{s+1}\) in \(V_s\).
The error after \(T\) queries. Any output lies in the span of \(g_1, \dots, g_T\), which is inside \(V_T\). Its coordinate \(k = T + 1\) is zero, so its largest coordinate is at least 0 and \(f(\theta) \ge \frac\alpha2\|\theta\|^2 \ge 0\). The error is therefore at least \(-f^*\), which by step 2 with \(k = T + 1\) is Equation G.15.



G.4.4 Checking it
The script runs the projected subgradient method of the chapter, with the learning rate \(\eta = R/(L\sqrt T)\) and the averaged iterate, against these gradients, with \(R = L = 1\). Table G.2 shows that its error always lies between the two bounds.

No iterate ever has a negative value of \(f\), as step 5 predicts. The method sits just above the lower bound, about 17% above it at \(T = 10{,}000\) (a ratio of 1.17), so the lower bound is close to exact for this method. The upper bound is about twice the lower one, as the ratio \(2(1 + \sqrt{T + 1})/\sqrt T\) approaches 2. Figure G.5 shows the three on a log scale.






Figure G.5: The lower bound \(RL/(2(1 + \sqrt{T + 1}))\), the SGD guarantee \(RL/\sqrt T\), and the error of the projected subgradient method on the hard function, against the number of gradient queries \(T\), with \(R = L = 1\).





G.4.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs the method to stay in the span of its gradients. Nemirovski & Yudin (1983) remove that condition, and prove the same order of bound for every method that uses only gradients, by hiding the coordinates in a random rotation that the method cannot know in advance; their argument is longer and stays cited. The dimension must also be at least \(T + 1\), because in low dimension, methods that cut away part of the space at each query, such as the ellipsoid method, have an error that shrinks like \(e^{-cT/d}\) for a constant \(c\) (Bubeck 2015, ch. 2). Finally, the bound is for functions that are not smooth. On a smooth function GD with exact gradients does better than \(1/\sqrt T\), and the \(1/\sqrt T\) of SGD then comes from its gradient noise.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.5 The 1-nearest-neighbour error tends to \(\mathbb E[2p(1-p)]\)
text:
G.5 The 1-nearest-neighbour error tends to \(\mathbb E[2p(1-p)]\)

G.5.1 What the chapter uses
The nearest neighbour (NN) rule with one neighbour, 1-NN, predicts the label of the closest training point. Algorithmic stability and generalization states, citing Cover & Hart (1967), that its test error tends to \(\mathbb E[2p(x)(1 - p(x))]\) as the number \(n\) of training points grows. Here \(p(x) = \Pr[y = 1 \mid x]\) is the probability that the label at \(x\) is \(+1\). Step 3 of its proof (Proposition 7.2) says that for large \(n\) “the nearest neighbour of a test point \(x\) lies arbitrarily close to \(x\)” and cites this appendix for the precise argument. In its running example the limit is 0.338 and the Bayes error, the error of the best possible classifier, is 0.250.
The precise statement proved here is this. Let the training pairs \((x_i, y_i)\) and the test pair \((x, y)\) be independent draws from the same distribution. Assume that \(x\) lies in a closed and bounded set \(K\), and that \(p\) is continuous on \(K\). Ties between equally near neighbours may be broken by any rule that looks only at the points, not at their labels. Then the test error \(R_n\) of 1-NN, averaged over the training set and the test pair, satisfies \[\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n = \mathbb E\big[2p(x)(1 - p(x))\big]. \tag{G.19}\]


G.5.2 The idea
The argument has two parts. First, the nearest neighbour gets close. For a fixed test point, the chance that none of the \(n\) training points lands within a distance \(r\) of it is \((1 - P)^n\), where \(P\) is the chance that one point lands there. As long as \(P > 0\), this goes to zero. Second, the labels behave like two coins. Given where all the points are, the neighbour’s label is \(+1\) with probability \(p(x')\), where \(x'\) is the neighbour, and the test label is \(+1\) with probability \(p(x)\), independently. They disagree with probability \[e(x, x') = p(x)(1 - p(x')) + (1 - p(x))p(x'). \tag{G.20}\] As \(x'\) approaches \(x\), \(e(x, x')\) approaches \(2p(x)(1 - p(x))\).
Table G.3 shows the two coins at a test point with \(p(x) = 0.8\). A neighbour where \(p = 0.7\) disagrees with probability 0.38. A neighbour at the same \(p\) disagrees with probability 0.32, which is \(2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2\). Even a perfect neighbour disagrees often, because both labels are noisy.



Table G.3: The chance that the 1-NN prediction is wrong at a test point with \(p(x) = 0.8\), for two neighbours.











Neighbour’s \(p(x')\)
