G.5.3 Derivation

The error given the points. Fix all the feature vectors, of the training set and the test point. The nearest neighbour \(x'_n\) is then fixed, since it depends only on the points. Given the points, the labels are independent, each \(+1\) with probability \(p\) at its own point. The neighbour was chosen without looking at labels, so its label is still \(+1\) with probability \(p(x'_n)\). The prediction is wrong when the two labels differ, which has probability \(e(x, x'_n)\). Averaging over the points gives \(R_n = \mathbb E[e(x, x'_n)]\).
The nearest neighbour gets close. Fix the test point \(x\) and a radius \(r > 0\), and write \(P_r(x)\) for the probability that one training point lands within distance \(r\) of \(x\). The training points are independent, so the probability that none of them does is \[\Pr\big[\|x'_n - x\| > r \,\big|\, x\big] = (1 - P_r(x))^n, \tag{G.21}\] which tends to 0 whenever \(P_r(x) > 0\).
Almost every test point has \(P_r(x) > 0\). Suppose some ball around \(x\) has probability zero. Then a smaller ball inside it, with a centre whose coordinates are fractions and a radius that is a fraction, also has probability zero and still contains \(x\). Such a ball exists because fractions come arbitrarily close to any number: take a centre within \(r/3\) of \(x\) and a radius between \(r/3\) and \(2r/3\), where \(r\) is the radius of the original ball. There are only countably many such balls, and each of them that has probability zero contributes nothing, so by the union bound their union has probability zero. So the test points with a zero-probability ball around them have probability zero together. For all other test points, step 2 applies for every \(r\). The averaged probability \(\Pr[\|x'_n - x\| > r] = \mathbb E[(1 - P_r(x))^n]\) then tends to 0. This uses the bounded convergence theorem: if quantities between 0 and 1 tend to 0 at almost every point, so does their average.
The error converges. Expanding \(e\) gives \(e(x, x') - e(x, x) = (p(x') - p(x))(1 - 2p(x))\), so \(|e(x, x') - e(x, x)| \le |p(x') - p(x)|\). A continuous function on a closed and bounded set is uniformly continuous. So for every tolerance \(\xi > 0\) there is an \(r > 0\) with \(|p(x') - p(x)| \le \xi\) whenever \(\|x' - x\| \le r\). Split the average according to whether the neighbour is within \(r\). Inside, the difference is at most \(\xi\), and outside it is at most 1, so \[\big|R_n - \mathbb E[2p(1 - p)]\big| \le \mathbb E\big|e(x, x'_n) - e(x, x)\big| \le \xi + \Pr\big[\|x'_n - x\| > r\big]. \tag{G.22}\] By step 3 the last term tends to 0. The limit of the left side is therefore at most \(\xi\), for every \(\xi > 0\), which proves Equation G.19.



G.5.4 Checking it
In the chapter’s running example, \(x\) is uniform on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^{10}\) and \(p(x) = \sigma(5x_1)\). The script computes the Bayes error \(\mathbb E[\min(p, 1 - p)] = 0.250\) and the limit \(\mathbb E[2p(1 - p)] = 0.338\), by numerical integration over the first coordinate. The sphere looks the same from every point, so every test point sees the same \(P_r\), so the median distance to the nearest neighbour can be computed exactly, by solving \((1 - P_r)^n = \frac12\) for \(r\). Table G.4 shows that it shrinks very slowly.

The sphere in \(\mathbb R^{10}\) is a nine-dimensional surface, so \(P_r\) grows like \(r^9\) and the distance shrinks only like \(n^{-1/9}\). That is why the error approaches its limit slowly. In the script’s table, with 4,000 test points, the measured 1-NN error is 0.398 at \(n = 100\) and 0.356 at \(n = 4{,}000\). The average of \(e(x, x'_n)\) over the same test points, which step 1 says has the same mean, is 0.392 and 0.358. Both are still above 0.338, because at \(n = 4{,}000\) the typical neighbour is still about 0.49 away, where \(p\) differs noticeably. Figure G.6 shows both parts of the argument.






Figure G.6: Left: the median distance from a test point to its nearest neighbour against \(n\), exact (line) and simulated (dots), for points uniform on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^{10}\). Right: the measured 1-NN test error and the average of \(p(1 - p') + (1 - p)p'\) over the same 20,000 test points, with the limit \(\mathbb E[2p(1 - p)] = 0.338\).





G.5.5 What it does not cover
The limit holds without continuity of \(p\), by a longer argument that approximates \(p\) by continuous functions, which is left to Devroye, Györfi & Lugosi (1996, ch. 5). The proof says nothing about the speed of convergence, and the example shows why none can be given without more assumptions: the speed depends on the dimension of the data. Finally, \(k\)-NN with \(k\) growing and \(k/n\) shrinking converges to the Bayes error itself, because averaging many neighbours’ labels estimates \(p(x)\) rather than drawing one more coin (Stone 1977).

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.6 Fitted parameters are approximately Gaussian, and one record moves them by its gradient
text:
G.6 Fitted parameters are approximately Gaussian, and one record moves them by its gradient

G.6.1 What the chapter uses
Section 12.3 states that parameters fitted by minimizing an average loss, which statisticians call M-estimators, are approximately Gaussian, centred on the population fit with covariance \(\Sigma_1/n\). Here \(\Sigma_1 = H^{-1}GH^{-1}\) is the sandwich covariance, \(H\) is the average curvature of the loss at the population fit, and \(G\) is the covariance of one record’s gradient there. The chapter gives a four-step sketch and cites “the standard asymptotic normality of M-estimators (van der Vaart 1998, ch. 5)”. The statement feeds the attack accuracy Equation 12.16 and the constant Equation 12.17. Section 10.3 uses the same fact to explain why the margin \(\phi_z\) is close to Gaussian over retrainings. Section 10.5 explains in words which records have a large self-influence \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\), the numerator of the separation in Equation 10.12. And Section 11.3 asserts that as \(n\) grows the model approaches the population’s probabilities.
This section proves the result for logistic regression, the model all four chapters use. A record is \(z = (x, y)\), with a feature vector \(x\), which may include a constant 1 for an intercept, and a label \(y = \pm1\). (The property-inference chapter writes the whole record as \(x\); here the features get their own name.) The loss is \(\ell(\theta; z) = \ln(1 + e^{-y\langle\theta, x\rangle})\). The fit \(\hat\theta\) minimizes the training objective on the dataset \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\), here the average loss plus a ridge term, and the population fit \(\theta^*\) minimizes its average over the data distribution \(\mathcal D\): \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \qquad \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta) = \mathbb E_{z \sim \mathcal D}\,\ell(\theta; z) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2. \tag{G.23}\] The ridge weight \(\lambda \ge 0\) may be zero. (The property-inference chapter writes \(\theta\) for the fit and \(\theta(t)\) for the population fit. Here \(\theta\) is any parameter vector, \(\hat\theta\) the fit and \(\theta^*\) the population fit.) The curvature and the gradient covariance are \[H = \nabla^2 \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^*), \qquad G = \mathbb E\big[g\,g^\top\big], \quad g = \nabla\ell(\theta^*; z) + \lambda\theta^*. \tag{G.24}\] The assumptions are that the records are independent draws from one distribution, that \(\mathbb E\|x\|^6\) is finite (true for bounded or Gaussian features, and needed so that the averages in step 2 have finite variance), and that \(H\) has no zero eigenvalue. Write \(h > 0\) for its smallest eigenvalue. The claim has two parts. First, \(\hat\theta\) is within a distance of order \(1/\sqrt n\) of \(\theta^*\). Second, \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta^*)\) is approximately Gaussian. It converges in distribution to a Gaussian, which means that for large \(n\) the probability that it lands in any box or half-space approaches the probability for the Gaussian: \[\sqrt n\,(\hat\theta - \theta^*) \to \mathcal N\big(0,\ H^{-1}GH^{-1}\big). \tag{G.25}\]
The influence of one record is a statement about one fixed dataset, so it uses the membership-inference chapter’s setting, with a ridge weight \(\lambda > 0\) and the margin \(\phi_z = y\langle\theta, x\rangle\) of a record \(z = (x, y)\). Compare the fit \(\hat\theta_D\) on a dataset \(D\) that contains \(z\) with the fit \(\hat\theta_{-z}\) of the same objective with \(z\)’s term removed. Training on \(z\) raises its margin by \[\phi_z(\hat\theta_D) - \phi_z(\hat\theta_{-z}) = \frac1n\,\sigma(-\phi_z)\,x^\top H^{-1}x + O(1/n^2), \tag{G.26}\] where \(\phi_z\) on the right is the margin under \(\hat\theta_{-z}\), and \(\sigma(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s})\) is the logistic function. Here \(H\) is the Hessian of the full training objective, with \(z\)’s term included, at \(\hat\theta_{-z}\), and “removed” means that the other terms keep their weight \(1/n\).


G.6.2 The idea
The argument takes four moves. The first is that the fit is close to the population fit. With high probability the training objective curves upward by at least \(h/2\) near \(\theta^*\). Its gradient at \(\theta^*\) is an average of \(n\) independent terms with mean zero, so it has size about \(1/\sqrt n\). A function that curves up by at least \(h/2\) cannot have its minimum farther than about \(2/h\) times the gradient away. The second move is that, near \(\theta^*\), the gradient is almost linear. The condition “gradient zero at \(\hat\theta\)” then becomes, exactly, \(0 = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) + \bar H(\hat\theta - \theta^*)\), where \(\bar H\) is the average Hessian between the two points. Solving it gives \(\hat\theta - \theta^* = -\bar H^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\). The third move is that the average gradient is approximately Gaussian, by the central limit theorem, with covariance \(G/n\). The fourth is that \(\bar H\) approaches \(H\), and multiplying a Gaussian vector by the matrix \(-H^{-1}\) multiplies its covariance by \(H^{-1}\) on both sides.
The simplest case shows why the covariance is a sandwich. For the loss \(\frac12(\theta - a)^2\) of a number \(a\), the fit is the sample mean. The curvature is \(H = 1\) and the gradient \(\theta^* - a\) has variance \(G = \operatorname{Var}(a)\), so the sandwich gives the familiar \(\operatorname{Var}(a)/n\). Doubling the loss to \((\theta - a)^2\) doubles the curvature and quadruples the gradient variance. The two copies of \(H^{-1}\) undo the quadrupling, so the fit’s variance does not change, as it should not, since the fit is still the mean.


G.6.3 Derivation

The curvature of the logistic loss changes slowly. The Hessian of one record’s loss is \(s(\langle\theta, x\rangle)\,xx^\top\), with \(s(m) = \sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m))\). Its derivative is \(s'(m) = \sigma(1 - \sigma)(1 - 2\sigma)\), whose largest size is \(c = 1/(6\sqrt3) \approx 0.0962\). To see this, write \(\sigma = \frac12 + v\), so that \(|s'| = 2|v|(\frac14 - v^2)\), which is largest at \(v = 1/(2\sqrt3)\). The matrix \(xx^\top\) stretches no vector by more than \(\|x\|^2\), and \(|\langle\theta - \theta', x\rangle| \le \|\theta - \theta'\|\,\|x\|\), so the Hessian moves by at most \(c\|x\|^3\|\theta - \theta'\|\). Averaging over the records, with \(\hat M_3 = \frac1n\sum_i\|x_i\|^3\), \[\big\|\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta; D) - \nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta'; D)\big\| \le c\,\hat M_3\,\|\theta - \theta'\|. \tag{G.27}\]
Three averages settle down. Each of \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), \(\hat M_3\) and \(\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\) is an average of \(n\) independent terms. Their means are \(H\), the third moment \(M_3 = \mathbb E\|x\|^3\), and 0. The last mean is 0 because \(\theta^*\) minimizes \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}\), so \(\mathbb E g = \nabla \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^*) = 0\). Their variances are finite, because the sixth moment is. By Chebyshev’s inequality, an average of \(n\) terms with variance \(v\) strays from its mean by more than \(a\) with probability at most \(v/(na^2)\). (For a matrix, apply it to the sum of the squared entries, which is at least the square of the largest factor by which the matrix stretches a vector.) So each average is near its mean with probability tending to 1. Choose the radius \(r = h/(8cM_3)\), whose role step 3 shows, and call \(E_n\) the event that all three are near their means in the following sense: \[\big\|\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) - H\big\| \le \frac h4, \qquad \hat M_3 \le 2M_3, \qquad \big\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\big\| < \frac{hr}4. \tag{G.28}\] Then \(E_n\) holds with probability tending to 1. For the gradient there is even an exact formula for the mean square. The cross terms of independent mean-zero vectors average to zero, so \[\mathbb E\big\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\big\|^2 = \frac{\operatorname{tr}G}{n}. \tag{G.29}\]
The objective curves up near \(\theta^*\). On \(E_n\), take any \(\theta\) within distance \(r\) of \(\theta^*\). By step 1 its Hessian differs from \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\) by at most \(c \cdot 2M_3 \cdot r = h/4\), and that one differs from \(H\) by at most \(h/4\). Since \(H \succeq hI\), every eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta; D)\) is at least \(h - h/4 - h/4 = h/2\). So, by step 2 of Section G.1 applied to segments inside the ball, \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) is \((h/2)\)-strongly convex on the ball of radius \(r\) around \(\theta^*\).
The fit is inside the ball, and close. On the sphere \(\|\theta - \theta^*\| = r\), strong convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(\mathcal L(\theta; D) \ge \mathcal L(\theta^*; D) - \|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\|r + \frac h4r^2\). This is larger than \(\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), by the third condition of \(E_n\). A convex function that is higher on a whole sphere than at its centre cannot be lower anywhere outside. If some outside point \(\theta\) had \(\mathcal L(\theta; D) \le \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), the segment from \(\theta^*\) to \(\theta\) would cross the sphere, and by the chord inequality the value at the crossing would be at most \(\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\). So the minimizer \(\hat\theta\) is inside the ball. There, part (a) of Corollary 6.1, with strong convexity \(h/2\) and \(\nabla\mathcal L(\hat\theta; D) = 0\), gives \[\|\hat\theta - \theta^*\| \le \frac{2}{h}\,\|\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\|, \tag{G.30}\] whose square has mean at most \(4\operatorname{tr}G/(h^2n)\) by step 2. So the fit is within a distance of order \(1/\sqrt n\) of the population fit, and in particular it converges to it.
An exact linear equation for the error. The fit has zero gradient. By the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from \(\theta^*\) to \(\hat\theta\), as in step 4 of the proof of Proposition 6.1, \(0 = \nabla\mathcal L(\hat\theta; D) = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) + \bar H_n(\hat\theta - \theta^*)\). Here \(\bar H_n\) is the average of \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) along the segment, whose eigenvalues are at least \(h/2\) by step 3, so it can be inverted: \[\hat\theta - \theta^* = -\bar H_n^{-1}\,\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D). \tag{G.31}\] This is the chapter’s step 2 with “\(\approx\)” replaced by “\(=\)” and \(H\) replaced by \(\bar H_n\).
The average curvature approaches \(H\). By step 1, \(\bar H_n\) differs from \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\) by at most \(c\hat M_3\|\hat\theta - \theta^*\|/2\), which tends to 0 by step 4. By step 2, \(\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\) tends to \(H\). The inverses follow, because \(\bar H_n^{-1} - H^{-1} = \bar H_n^{-1}(H - \bar H_n)H^{-1}\) has size at most \(\frac2h \cdot \frac1h\|H - \bar H_n\|\).
The average gradient is approximately Gaussian. The scaled gradient \(\sqrt n\,\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) = \frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_ig_i\) is a scaled sum of independent vectors with mean 0 and covariance \(G\). Take any fixed direction \(a\). The numbers \(\langle a, g_i\rangle\) are independent with mean 0 and variance \(a^\top Ga\), so the central limit theorem in one dimension (Section E.4) makes their scaled sum approximately \(\mathcal N(0, a^\top Ga)\). That is the distribution of \(\langle a, Y\rangle\) for \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, G)\). The Cramér–Wold device says that the distributions of all the one-dimensional views \(\langle a, \cdot\rangle\) determine the distribution of a vector, also in the limit (van der Vaart 1998, §2.2). So \(\sqrt n\,\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\) approaches \(\mathcal N(0, G)\).
Combine. Multiply Equation G.31 by \(\sqrt n\) and split it in two: \[\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta^*) = -H^{-1}\sqrt n\,\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D) + (H^{-1} - \bar H_n^{-1})\sqrt n\,\nabla\mathcal L(\theta^*; D). \tag{G.32}\] By step 7 the first term approaches \(-H^{-1}Y\). A linear map \(A\) turns a Gaussian with covariance \(G\) into one with covariance \(AGA^\top\), which here is \(H^{-1}GH^{-1}\) because \(H\) is symmetric. In the second term, the matrix tends to 0 by step 6, while the vector has mean square \(\operatorname{tr}G\) for every \(n\). So their product tends to 0 in probability, by Chebyshev’s inequality. Adding a term that tends to 0 in probability does not change the limiting distribution (Slutsky’s lemma, van der Vaart 1998, Lemma 2.8). This proves Equation G.25. The event \(E_n\) fails with probability tending to 0, so it changes no limit.
When the model is right, \(G = H\). Suppose \(\lambda = 0\) and the labels really follow the model, \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x] = \sigma(\langle\theta^*, x\rangle) = p\). One record’s gradient is \(-\sigma(-y\langle\theta^*, x\rangle)\,y\,x\), so \(gg^\top\) is \((1 - p)^2xx^\top\) when \(y = 1\), which has probability \(p\), and \(p^2xx^\top\) when \(y = -1\). On average, given \(x\), that is \(p(1 - p)^2 + (1 - p)p^2 = p(1 - p)\) times \(xx^\top\). That is exactly the Hessian’s weight \(s\). So \(G = H\) and the covariance is \(H^{-1}\), the inverse of the Fisher information. The same case answers Section 11.3. The expected log-loss at each \(x\) is smallest when the predicted probability equals the true one, so the population fit of a correct model is the true parameter. By step 4 the fitted model then converges to the population’s probabilities.
The influence of one record. Now fix the dataset \(D\) and the record \(z = (x, y)\) in it, with \(\lambda > 0\). The objective without \(z\)’s term is \(\mathcal L_{-z}\), and with it \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D) = \mathcal L_{-z} + \frac1n\ell(\cdot; z)\). At \(\hat\theta_{-z}\) the gradient of \(\mathcal L_{-z}\) is zero, so the gradient of \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) there is just \(\frac1n\nabla\ell(\hat\theta_{-z}; z)\). Step 5, applied to \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) around \(\hat\theta_{-z}\) instead of around \(\theta^*\), gives exactly \(\hat\theta_D - \hat\theta_{-z} = -\frac1n\bar H^{-1}\nabla\ell(\hat\theta_{-z}; z)\), with \(\bar H\) the average Hessian of \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) along the segment. This move is small: \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and the logistic gradient has length at most \(\|x\|\), so consequence (a) gives \(\|\hat\theta_D - \hat\theta_{-z}\| \le \|x\|/(\lambda n)\). Replacing \(\bar H\) by the Hessian \(H\) of \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) at \(\hat\theta_{-z}\) therefore changes the matrix by \(O(1/n)\), by step 1, and the move by \(O(1/n^2)\). The logistic gradient is \(\nabla\ell = -\sigma(-\phi_z)\,y\,x\), so the move is \(\frac1n\sigma(-\phi_z)\,y\,H^{-1}x\). The margin \(\phi_z = y\langle \theta, x\rangle\) changes by \(y\) times the inner product of the move with \(x\), which is \(\frac1n\sigma(-\phi_z)\,y^2\,x^\top H^{-1}x\). Since \(y^2 = 1\), that is Equation G.26.

Step 10 turns the heuristic of Section 10.5 into a formula. The factor \(\sigma(-\phi_z)\) is close to 1 when the model trained without \(z\) gets its label wrong, and close to 0 when it already predicts it confidently. The factor \(x^\top H^{-1}x\) counts the length of \(x\) twice, once for how hard \(z\) pulls the weights and once for how much a move of the weights changes \(z\)’s own margin, and divides by the curvature in that direction. In the chapter, the models without \(z\) train on the same number of records, with another record in \(z\)’s place. That record pulls the fit by its own gradient. Averaged over which record it is, the pull is the average gradient of the loss, which is close to zero near the population fit, where only the small ridge term \(\lambda \theta\) balances it. So, to first order, the self-influence \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}, z} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}, z}\) is the average of Equation G.26 over training sets.


G.6.4 Checking it
The script checks the Gaussian picture on the logistic-regression toy of Section 12.3. The features are \(x \sim \mathcal N(0, I_2)\) with an intercept. Records from the majority get the label \(+1\) with probability \(\sigma(2x_1 + x_2)\), records from a hidden subgroup with probability \(\sigma(2x_1 - x_2)\), and the subgroup makes up a share \(t = \frac12\) of the population. Numerically, the largest of \(|s'|\) is 0.09623, which is \(1/(6\sqrt3)\). Computed by quadrature, the population fit is \((1.704, 0, 0)\) for \((\theta_1, \theta_2, \text{intercept})\), and the sandwich has diagonal \((12.59, 6.94, 6.04)\), the chapter’s values. The chapter trains its models with a ridge weight \(10^{-3}\). Including it in \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}\), as the theorem allows, gives the population fit \((1.683, 0, 0)\) and the diagonal \((11.83, 6.76, 5.89)\). This is the right comparison for models trained that way.
Table G.5 compares \(n\) times the variance over 2,000 refits, with that ridge weight, against this sandwich. It also shows the share of refits whose \(\theta_2\) lands within 1.96 predicted standard deviations of its centre, which is 0.950 for an exact Gaussian.

At \(n = 1{,}000\) every variance is within 3% of the sandwich, about the sampling error of a variance estimated from 2,000 refits. At \(n = 50\) the variances are larger and the tails heavier, because the linearization of step 5 is not yet accurate. This also explains a remark in Section 12.3. There the chapter compares its refits with the sandwich without the ridge weight, and finds a gap of about 5% in \(\theta_1\). The ridge weight alone accounts for most of it, since it lowers the predicted value from 12.59 to 11.83. Figure G.7 shows the histograms becoming Gaussian, and Figure G.8 (left) shows the scaled variances settling on the sandwich.






Figure G.7: Histograms of \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_2 - \theta_2^*)\) over 2,000 logistic regressions refitted at subgroup share \(t = \frac12\), for \(n = 50\), 200 and 1,000, with the normal density whose variance is the sandwich value.



Step 9 checks out as well, with \(\lambda = 0\) as it requires. With the majority’s rule alone, \(t = 0\), the model is correct. Its population fit is \((2.000, 1.000, 0.000)\), the true weights, and \(G\) and \(H\) agree to rounding error, within \(10^{-12}\). At \(t = \frac12\) the model is wrong, because no single logistic rule describes the mixture. Then the diagonals differ: \(G\) has \((0.076, 0.191, 0.166)\) and \(H\) has \((0.078, 0.166, 0.166)\).
The influence formula is checked on the running example of the membership-inference chapter. That example has \(d = 100\) features, 950 typical points and 50 outliers with five times longer \(x\) and a random label, and \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\). One model is trained on \(n = 500\) points. For 200 of them the script removes the point’s term, refits, and compares the measured change in its margin with Equation G.26. For the 188 typical points, the mean change is 0.2287 against a predicted 0.2291, and the median ratio of measured to predicted is 1.003. For the 12 outliers, the mean change is 3.92 against a predicted 8.21, with a median ratio of 0.671. An outlier moves its own margin by several units, far outside the range where the linear expansion is accurate. The \(O(1/n^2)\) term of step 10 has a constant that grows with \(\|x\|\) and with \(1/\lambda\), and both are large for outliers. So the formula ranks the records correctly but overstates the largest influences. Figure G.8 (right) shows both groups.






Figure G.8: Left: \(n\) times the variance of each fitted parameter over 2,000 refits, against \(n\), with the sandwich values (dashed). Right: for points of the membership-inference running example, the measured change of the margin \(\phi_z\) when the point’s term is added, against the first-order prediction Equation G.26. Typical points lie on the diagonal; outliers fall below it.





G.6.5 What it does not cover
The result is a limit, so it says nothing about how large \(n\) must be; a finite-sample version (a Berry–Esseen bound) needs further moment assumptions. The proof also needs \(H\) to be invertible and a minimizer to exist. Both can fail with \(\lambda = 0\): when a line separates the classes perfectly, the loss keeps falling as the weights grow, so no minimizer exists at all. When the number of features grows with \(n\), so that \(d/n\) does not go to zero, the sandwich is wrong: the fitted weights are too large in size, pushed away from zero, and their variance is larger than predicted (Sur & Candès 2019). This matters for the membership example, where \(d/n = 0.2\). The general theory of M-estimators, for other losses and without convexity, is in van der Vaart (1998, ch. 5). For deep networks, which have many minima, the Gaussian shape of \(\phi_z\) that Section 10.3 relies on is an empirical finding of Carlini et al., not a consequence of this theorem.

title: Appendix G — Optimization and estimation
section: G.7 The best membership attack looks at the parameters through the loss
text:
G.7 The best membership attack looks at the parameters through the loss

G.7.1 What the chapter uses
Section 9.2 studies a centroid detector: the model is the mean \(\theta\) of \(n\) records, and an attacker who holds a record \(z\) plays a game against it. In the member world \(z\) is one of the \(n\) records, and in the non-member world all \(n\) records are fresh draws. The chapter gives the log likelihood ratio between the two worlds, saying only that “expanding the squares in the two Gaussian densities gives” it. It then cites Sablayrolles et al. (2019): if training draws the parameters with a probability that decreases exponentially in the training loss, the Bayes-optimal membership attack depends on the parameters, to a good approximation, only through the target’s loss, calibrated for each target, and white-box access then adds little. The chapter’s chain Equation 9.5 compares access levels, and this result explains why, in its example, access to the weights (white-box) gives no better attack than access to the loss of each query, compared with what that loss would typically be (calibrated black-box).
The setting of Sablayrolles et al. is this. There are \(n\) candidate records \(z_1, \dots, z_n\). Each is a member of the training set independently with probability \(\pi_1\), and \(m_i \in \{0, 1\}\) marks whether \(z_i\) is one. Training draws the parameters \(\theta\) from a Gibbs posterior at a temperature \(\nu > 0\), a density that falls exponentially in the total training loss: \[p(\theta \mid m) = \frac{1}{Z(m)}\exp\Big(-\frac1\nu\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,\ell(\theta; z_i)\Big), \tag{G.33}\] where \(Z(m)\) makes the density integrate to 1. Write \(m_{-1}\) for the memberships of the other candidates, and \(\sigma\) for the logistic function. The attacker knows the candidates and sees \(\theta\). The posterior probability that the target \(z_1\) is a member is then exactly \[\Pr[m_1 = 1 \mid \theta] = \mathbb E\Big[\sigma\Big(-\frac{\ell(\theta; z_1) - \tau(z_1, m_{-1})}{\nu} + \ln\frac{\pi_1}{1 - \pi_1}\Big)\,\Big|\,\theta\Big], \tag{G.34}\] with the calibration \[\tau(z_1, m_{-1}) = -\nu\ln\mathbb E_{\theta' \sim p(\cdot \mid m_1 = 0,\ m_{-1})}\big[e^{-\ell(\theta'; z_1)/\nu}\big]. \tag{G.35}\] Inside the logistic function, \(\theta\) appears only through the loss \(\ell(\theta; z_1)\). It also appears in the outer average over the unknown \(m_{-1}\), and that is where the result becomes an approximation. If \(\tau\) hardly depends on the other memberships, it can be replaced by one number \(\tau(z_1)\) per target, and the best attack thresholds \(\ell(\theta; z_1) - \tau(z_1)\). That last step is Sablayrolles et al.’s approximation, not a theorem.
For the centroid detector no approximation is needed. Write \(q(\theta \mid z)\) for the density of \(\theta\) in the member world and \(p(\theta \mid z)\) in the non-member world. The model is \(\theta = \frac1n\sum_ix_i\) for \(n\) records \(x_i \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), and its loss is \(\ell(\theta; z) = \frac12\|\theta - z\|^2\). The log likelihood ratio between the member and non-member worlds is exactly \[\ln\frac{q(\theta \mid z)}{p(\theta \mid z)} = -\frac{n}{n - 1}\big(\ell(\theta; z) - \tau(z)\big) + \frac d2\ln\frac{n}{n - 1}, \qquad \tau(z) = \frac{(n - 1)\|z\|^2}{2n}. \tag{G.36}\]


G.7.2 The idea
Fix the memberships of all the other candidates for a moment. Then the only question is whether the term of \(z_1\) is in the exponent or not. Adding it multiplies the density of \(\theta\) by \(e^{-\ell(\theta; z_1)/\nu}\) and changes the normalizing constant. The change of normalizing constant is a number that does not depend on \(\theta\), and \(\tau\) is \(-\nu\) times its logarithm. So, with the others fixed, the log of the posterior odds is a straight-line function of the loss. The attacker does not know the others, so it averages over them.
Two targets with the same loss show why the calibration matters. Take \(\nu = 1\) and \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), so that the prior term \(\ln(\pi_1/(1 - \pi_1))\) is zero. A hard target has \(\tau = 2\), because models trained without it give it a typical loss near 2. If the released model gives it loss 0.5, the posterior is \(\sigma(2 - 0.5) = \sigma(1.5) = 0.8176\), likely a member. An easy target has \(\tau = 0.3\), because every model fits it well. The same loss 0.5 gives \(\sigma(0.3 - 0.5) = \sigma(-0.2) = 0.4502\), slightly less likely than not. A low loss is evidence of membership only relative to what the target’s loss would be without it.


G.7.3 Derivation

Bayes’ rule with the others fixed. Write \(A = \pi_1\,p(\theta \mid m_1 = 1, m_{-1})\) and \(B = (1 - \pi_1)\,p(\theta \mid m_1 = 0, m_{-1})\) for the two joint weights. Bayes’ rule says \(\Pr[m_1 = 1 \mid \theta, m_{-1}] = A/(A + B)\). A ratio of this form equals \(\sigma(\ln(A/B))\), because \(1/(1 + B/A) = 1/(1 + e^{-\ln(A/B)})\). So \[\Pr[m_1 = 1 \mid \theta, m_{-1}] = \sigma\Big(\ln\frac{p(\theta \mid m_1 = 1, m_{-1})}{p(\theta \mid m_1 = 0, m_{-1})} + \ln\frac{\pi_1}{1 - \pi_1}\Big). \tag{G.37}\]
The density ratio. The two exponents differ by the target’s term only, so the density ratio is \(e^{-\ell(\theta; z_1)/\nu}\,Z_0/Z_1\), where \(Z_1\) and \(Z_0\) are the normalizing constants with and without the target. Write \(Z_1\) as the integral of \(e^{-\ell(\theta'; z_1)/\nu}\) times the unnormalized density without the target. Dividing by \(Z_0\) turns that integral into an average over \(\theta'\) drawn from the posterior without the target: \[\frac{Z_1}{Z_0} = \mathbb E_{\theta' \sim p(\cdot \mid m_1 = 0,\ m_{-1})}\big[e^{-\ell(\theta'; z_1)/\nu}\big] = e^{-\tau(z_1, m_{-1})/\nu}. \tag{G.38}\] So the log density ratio is \(-(\ell(\theta; z_1) - \tau(z_1, m_{-1}))/\nu\), a function of \(\theta\) only through the loss.
Average over the unknown others. By the law of total probability, \(\Pr[m_1 = 1 \mid \theta]\) is the average of \(\Pr[m_1 = 1 \mid \theta, m_{-1}]\) over \(m_{-1}\), weighted by \(\Pr[m_{-1} \mid \theta]\). Together with steps 1 and 2 that is Equation G.34. The weights depend on \(\theta\), which is why replacing \(\tau(z_1, m_{-1})\) by a single \(\tau(z_1)\) is an approximation.
The centroid: two Gaussians. If \(z\) is a member, \(\theta = (z + S)/n\), where \(S\), the sum of the other \(n - 1\) records, is \(\mathcal N(0, (n - 1)I_d)\). So \(\theta\) is Gaussian with mean \(z/n\) and variance \((n - 1)/n^2\) per coordinate. If it is not, all \(n\) records are fresh draws, so \(\theta\) is Gaussian with mean 0 and variance \(1/n\) per coordinate. The log of each density is minus the squared distance to the mean over twice the variance, plus \(-\frac d2\ln\) of the variance. Their difference is \[-\frac{n^2}{2(n - 1)}\Big\|\theta - \frac zn\Big\|^2 + \frac n2\|\theta\|^2 + \frac d2\ln\frac{n}{n - 1}. \tag{G.39}\]
Expand the squares. The first square is \(\|\theta\|^2 - \frac2n\langle z, \theta\rangle + \frac1{n^2}\|z\|^2\). Collecting terms, \(\|\theta\|^2\) has coefficient \(\frac n2 - \frac{n^2}{2(n - 1)} = -\frac{n}{2(n - 1)}\), and \(\langle z, \theta\rangle\) has coefficient \(\frac{n}{n - 1}\). So the log ratio is \(\frac{n}{2(n - 1)}(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2) - \frac{\|z\|^2}{2(n - 1)} + \frac d2\ln\frac{n}{n - 1}\), the chapter’s formula with its constant made explicit.
Write it with the loss. Since \(\ell(\theta; z) = \frac12\|z\|^2 - \frac12(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2)\), the bracket of step 5 equals \(\|z\|^2 - 2\ell(\theta; z)\). Substituting, the \(\|z\|^2\) terms are \(\frac{n}{2(n - 1)}\|z\|^2 - \frac{1}{2(n - 1)}\|z\|^2 = \frac12\|z\|^2\), which is \(\frac{n}{n - 1}\tau(z)\). The result is Equation G.36. It has the Gibbs form exactly, with temperature \((n - 1)/n\), and no approximation was needed. The reason is that the other records enter only through their sum \(S\), whose distribution does not depend on which records they are.

The chapter’s remark that the white-box and calibrated black-box attacks “agree to four decimals” follows from step 5. The calibrated score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\) is the bracket \(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\), so the log ratio is a fixed multiple of it minus the term \(\|z\|^2/(2(n - 1))\). That term changes from target to target, so the two scores do not rank the games (pairs of model and target) in exactly the same order. But it changes very little: its standard deviation is 0.0504, against 0.757 for the log ratio itself, at \(n = 100\) and \(d = 50\).


G.7.4 Checking it
The script checks Equation G.34 exactly on a small Gibbs posterior. It uses 10 candidates \(z_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), the loss \(\frac12(\theta - z)^2\), \(\nu = 1\), \(\pi_1 = \frac12\), and \(\theta\) on a grid of 801 points in \([-4, 4]\). Enumerating all \(2^9\) memberships of the other candidates, the exact posterior and the right side of Equation G.34 differ by less than \(10^{-12}\), which is rounding error. Replacing \(\tau(z_1, m_{-1})\) by the single value \(\bar\tau(z_1) = -\nu\ln\mathbb E_{m_{-1}}[e^{-\tau(z_1, m_{-1})/\nu}]\), an average over memberships drawn from their prior, changes the posterior by up to 0.054 over the grid points that carry 99.9% of the probability of \(\theta\), so in this small example the approximation is reasonable but visible.
For the centroid, Equation G.36 matches the log ratio computed from the two densities to within \(10^{-10}\), rounding error. Over 100,000 games per world, the best advantage is 0.2804 for the exact likelihood ratio, 0.2800 for the calibrated score and 0.0422 for the raw loss. (The chapter’s own run gives 0.2789 for the first two.) Figure G.9 shows why calibration matters. Against the raw loss, the exact log ratio is a cloud, because a target’s loss mixes its membership with how typical it is. Against \(\ell - \tau(z)\) it is a line of slope \(-n/(n - 1)\).






Figure G.9: For 1,500 member and 1,500 non-member games of the centroid detector (\(n = 100\), \(d = 50\)), the exact log likelihood ratio against the raw loss \(\ell(\theta; z)\) (left) and against the calibrated loss \(\ell(\theta; z) - \tau(z)\) (right).





G.7.5 What it does not cover
Real training is not a Gibbs posterior. SGD with a constant learning rate behaves like one only roughly, and an exactly trained model, like the centroid, is deterministic given its data. The centroid escapes the problem because, from the attacker’s view, the unknown other records make \(\theta\) random, and the result has the Gibbs form anyway. In general the per-target calibration \(\tau(z)\) must be estimated, which is what shadow models do in the per-example attacks of Membership inference.

Every bound holds where it should, and the checks also show how loose each one is. title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
text:
H.1 The average inverse of a random Gram matrix
Two chapters of the book lean on facts about matrices that they quote rather than prove. Reconstruction attacks decodes noisy answers by least squares, so its error depends on two properties of the random query matrix. The average of the inverse of its Gram matrix sets the error under random noise, and its smallest singular value sets the error under worst-case noise. The chapter on training with differential privacy (DP) by follow the regularized leader (FTRL), DP-FTRL and matrix factorization, releases the running sums of a training run by splitting the prefix-sum matrix into a product of two matrices. That chapter quotes several facts about this matrix and its factorizations, from its singular values to the form of the best factorization, and this appendix proves them. Each section starts by restating, in the chapter’s notation, exactly what it proves. They sit together because each one is a statement about how a matrix stretches or shrinks vectors, and each proof comes down to an eigenvalue, a singular value or a projection.
The two chapters both call their matrix \(A\), but it is a different matrix in each. In the first two sections, the query matrix \(A\) has one row for each of \(m\) queries and one column for each of \(n\) people. In the last three, \(A\) is the prefix-sum matrix, with one row and one column for each of \(T\) training steps. Table H.1 lists the results and where each chapter states or uses them.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
text:
H.1.1 What the chapter uses
Least squares turns noisy answers into an estimate, and under random noise its error is set by the inverse of the Gram matrix \(A^\top A\), the matrix of inner products between the columns of the query matrix. In Section 17.3, step 4 of the proof of Proposition 17.3 needs the average of that inverse. The chapter uses a result for Gaussian rows. Let \(Z\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix whose \(m\) rows are independent, each a normal vector with mean 0 and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). Then \(Z^\top Z\) is called a Wishart matrix, and, as long as \(m \ge n + 2\), \[\mathbb E\big[(Z^\top Z)^{-1}\big] = \frac{\Sigma^{-1}}{m - n - 1}. \tag{H.1}\] Here \(m\) is the number of rows, \(n\) the number of columns and \(\Sigma^{-1}\) the inverse of the covariance. The chapter cites Muirhead (1982, ch. 3) for it. It applies it to rows that are random 0/1 queries \(q\), by matching a normal row with the same second-moment matrix, \(\Sigma = \mathbb E[qq^\top]\), and it says that for 0/1 rows this is only an approximation. Section 17.5 reuses it in its step 4, which gives Equation 17.23. The chapter checks the final recovery rates by simulation but not the formula itself.


H.1.2 The idea
Start with one column, \(n = 1\). Then \(Z^\top Z\) is a single number, the sum of \(m\) squared standard normal values, and its average is \(m\). The naive guess for the average of its inverse is \(1/m\). But an average of inverses is always larger than the inverse of the average, because small values blow up under \(1/x\) much more than large values shrink. For example, a number that is 1 or 3 with equal chance has average 2, while the average of its inverses is \(\frac12(1 + \frac13) = \frac23\), not \(\frac12\). For the sum of \(m\) squared normals the exact answer is \(1/(m - 2)\), so the naive guess is off by two rows. The formula says this is \(1/(m - n - 1)\) with \(n = 1\).
With more columns, and \(\Sigma = I\) for now, there are two separate questions. Which matrix is the average? Symmetry answers that: flipping the sign of a column, or swapping two columns, does not change the distribution of \(Z\), so the average inverse cannot prefer any column or any sign, and it must be a multiple of the identity. And what is the multiple? One diagonal entry of the inverse of a Gram matrix has a meaning of its own. It is one over the squared length of the part of the first column that the other columns cannot explain, the residual of regressing column 1 on the others. With Gaussian columns, that residual is a standard normal vector squeezed into a space of \(m - n + 1\) dimensions, so its squared length is a sum of \(m - n + 1\) squared normals. The one-column calculation then gives \(1/(m - n + 1 - 2) = 1/(m - n - 1)\).


H.1.3 Derivation
Take \(\Sigma = I\) first, so that the entries of \(Z\) are independent standard normal numbers. Write \(W = Z^\top Z\) and \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) for the columns of \(Z\).

The inverse exists. With \(m \ge n\) Gaussian rows, the columns are linearly independent with probability 1. Add the columns one at a time: given the earlier ones, their span is a fixed subspace of lower dimension, and a column with a continuous distribution lands in it with probability 0. So \(W\) is invertible. (The stronger condition \(m \ge n + 2\) is needed only in step 6, to make the average finite.)
Off-diagonal entries average to 0. Flip the sign of column \(i\) of \(Z\). The flipped matrix has the same distribution, because a standard normal entry and its negative have the same distribution. Flipping column \(i\) flips the sign of every inner product between column \(i\) and another column, so it flips row \(i\) and column \(i\) of \(W\), except the diagonal entry. The inverse changes in the same way, since the flip is multiplication by a diagonal matrix \(\Lambda\) of signs on both sides, and \((\Lambda W \Lambda)^{-1} = \Lambda W^{-1} \Lambda\). So every entry of \(W^{-1}\) in row \(i\), off the diagonal, has the same average as its negative, and that average, which is finite by steps 4 to 6 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, is 0.
Diagonal entries share one average. Swapping columns \(i\) and \(k\) also leaves the distribution unchanged, and it swaps the diagonal entries \(i\) and \(k\) of \(W^{-1}\). So all diagonal entries have the same average \(c\), and \(\mathbb E[W^{-1}] = cI\).
A diagonal entry is one over a residual. Let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto the span of \(z_2, \dots, z_n\), so that \((I - P)z_1\) is the part of \(z_1\) that the other columns cannot explain. Let \(w\) be the first column of \(W^{-1}\), so \(Ww = e_1\), where \(e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\). Set \(u = Zw\), a vector of length \(m\). Then \(Z^\top u = Z^\top Zw = Ww = e_1\), and this equation says two things: \(u\) is orthogonal to \(z_2, \dots, z_n\), and \(z_1^\top u = 1\). Now \(u = w_1z_1 + (\text{a combination of } z_2, \dots, z_n)\). Applying \(I - P\) removes the combination and leaves \(u\) unchanged, since \(u\) is orthogonal to the other columns, so \(u = w_1(I - P)z_1\). Substituting this into \(z_1^\top u = 1\) gives \(w_1\|(I - P)z_1\|^2 = 1\), because \(z_1^\top(I - P)z_1 = \|(I - P)z_1\|^2\) for a projection. So \[\big[W^{-1}\big]_{11} = \frac{1}{\|(I - P)z_1\|^2}. \tag{H.2}\]
The residual is a sum of \(m - n + 1\) squared normals. Fix the other columns. Then \(I - P\) is a fixed projection onto a subspace of dimension \(k = m - n + 1\), the \(m\) dimensions minus the \(n - 1\) spanned by \(z_2, \dots, z_n\). The column \(z_1\) is independent of the others, and a standard normal vector keeps its distribution under any rotation, because its density depends only on the length of the vector. So rotate the coordinates until the subspace is spanned by the first \(k\) axes. In the new coordinates \(z_1\) is still standard normal, and \(\|(I - P)z_1\|^2\) is the sum of the squares of its first \(k\) coordinates, a chi-squared variable \(\chi^2_k\) with \(k\) degrees of freedom. This holds for every value of the other columns, so it holds without conditioning too.
The average of \(1/\chi^2_k\). The trick is to write \(1/x\) as an integral of exponentials, \(1/x = \int_0^\infty e^{-tx}\,dt\) for \(x > 0\), because exponentials of a sum of independent squares are easy to average. For one standard normal number \(g\) and a number \(t \ge 0\), \[\mathbb E\big[e^{-tg^2}\big] = (1 + 2t)^{-1/2}, \tag{H.3}\] because \(e^{-tg^2}\) times the normal density is a normal density with variance \(1/(1 + 2t)\), missing only its normalizing factor. A \(\chi^2_k\) variable \(X\) is a sum of \(k\) independent such squares, so the averages multiply and \(\mathbb E[e^{-tX}] = (1 + 2t)^{-k/2}\). Exchanging the average and the integral, which is allowed because everything is positive, \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac1X\Big] = \int_0^\infty(1 + 2t)^{-k/2}\,dt = \frac{1}{k - 2} \quad\text{for } k \ge 3. \tag{H.4}\] The integral converges only when \(k/2 > 1\). Putting in \(k = m - n + 1\) gives \(c = 1/(m - n - 1)\), and the condition \(k \ge 3\) becomes \(m \ge n + 2\).
General covariance. Write \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) for the symmetric square root of \(\Sigma\), the matrix whose square is \(\Sigma\). A normal row with covariance \(\Sigma\) can be written as a standard normal row times \(\Sigma^{1/2}\), so \(Z = Z_0\Sigma^{1/2}\) with \(Z_0\) standard. Then \(Z^\top Z = \Sigma^{1/2}Z_0^\top Z_0\Sigma^{1/2}\), its inverse is \(\Sigma^{-1/2}(Z_0^\top Z_0)^{-1}\Sigma^{-1/2}\), and averaging, with the fixed matrices taken outside the average, and using steps 3 and 6 gives Equation H.1.



H.1.4 Checking it
The script draws Gaussian matrices with \(n = 50\) columns and averages \(m\) times the diagonal of \((Z^\top Z)^{-1}\) over 4,000 draws. The formula predicts \(m/(m - n - 1)\). It also draws 0/1 matrices, as in the chapter, whose second-moment matrix is \(\Sigma = \frac14(I + \mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top)\). The diagonal of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is \(4n/(n + 1)\), as computed in Section 17.3, step 3. Dividing by it puts both kinds of rows on the same scale, so that both are predicted to give \(m/(m - n - 1)\). Table H.2 shows the result.

The Gaussian rows match the formula within the simulation noise. The 0/1 rows fall a little below it, by \(6.667 - 6.456 = 0.211\) at \(m = 60\), about 3%, and by less as \(m\) grows. So for subset queries the chapter’s approximation is slightly pessimistic: it predicts a slightly larger error than the attack suffers. Figure H.1 shows the same comparison over a range of \(m\). The gap between the curve \(m/(m - n - 1)\) and the naive line at 1 is the correction that step 4 of the chapter makes, and it is large only when \(m\) is close to \(n\).






Figure H.1: The average diagonal entry of \((Z^\top Z)^{-1}\), multiplied by \(m\), against the number of rows per column \(m/n\) for \(n = 50\). Circles are Gaussian rows and squares are 0/1 rows rescaled by the diagonal of \(\Sigma^{-1}\). The black curve is \(m/(m - n - 1)\) and the dashed line is the naive value 1, from inverting the average Gram matrix.



Steps 4 and 5 can be checked one at a time. For one Gaussian matrix with \(m = 60\) rows, the script regresses the first column on the others and finds a squared residual of 4.931982. One over the first diagonal entry of the inverse is the same 4.931982, as Equation H.2 says. Figure H.2 repeats this for 20,000 matrices and compares the histogram with the \(\chi^2\) density with \(m - n + 1 = 11\) degrees of freedom. Step 6 for \(k = 11\) predicts \(1/9 = 0.1111\), and a million simulated \(\chi^2_{11}\) values give 0.1112. Finally, the symmetry of steps 2 and 3 shows up in simulation as an average inverse whose off-diagonal entries are tiny. With \(n = 10\), \(m = 30\) and 20,000 draws, their average size is 0.0013 of the diagonal for Gaussian rows. For 0/1 rows the ratio is 0.1000, because 0/1 entries have a nonzero mean and flipping a column’s sign is no longer a symmetry. That is still the shape the approximation predicts, since \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is proportional to \(I - \frac{1}{n + 1}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), whose off-diagonal entries are \(\frac1n = 0.1\) times its diagonal ones.






Figure H.2: Histogram of \(1/[(Z^\top Z)^{-1}]_{11}\) over 20,000 Gaussian matrices with \(m = 60\) rows and \(n = 50\) columns, against the \(\chi^2\) density with \(m - n + 1 = 11\) degrees of freedom. The two agree, as steps 4 and 5 predict.





H.1.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs Gaussian rows in two places. Step 2 needs each column to keep its distribution when its sign flips, and step 5 needs rotation invariance. Rows of 0/1 entries have neither property, which is why the chapter calls the formula an approximation and checks the attack by simulation. There is also a technical gap for 0/1 rows. A 0/1 matrix is singular with a small but positive probability, for example when two columns happen to be equal, so the average of its inverse is not even defined. The rescaled values in Table H.2 are averages over draws that happened to be invertible, which at these sizes is every draw.
The condition \(m \ge n + 2\) is needed. At \(m = n + 1\) the residual is a \(\chi^2_2\) variable, whose inverse has an infinite average, because \(\chi^2_2\) puts too much probability near 0. Even for \(m \ge n + 2\), the diagonal entries of the inverse have a heavy right tail when \(m\) is close to \(n\), which makes simulations there noisy.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
section: H.2 A random subset matrix shrinks no direction much
text:
H.2 A random subset matrix shrinks no direction much

H.2.1 What the chapter uses
The worst-case bound of Section 17.3, Equation 17.13, says that least squares gets at most \(4mE^2/s_{\min}(A)^2\) bits wrong when every answer has error at most \(E\). Here \(s_{\min}(A)\), the smallest singular value, is the smallest length \(\|Ax\|\) over unit vectors \(x\). The bound is useful only if \(s_{\min}(A)\) is of order \(\sqrt m\). The paragraph after Proposition 17.2 says that for random rows \(s_{\min}\) “concentrates near \(\sqrt m - \sqrt n\) times the scale of the rows” and cites Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, ch. 4. It then suggests by a heuristic that \(s_{\min}(A) \approx \frac12(\sqrt m - \sqrt n)\) for random subsets, checks this at one size, and points here for a proof.
This section proves a version with a worse constant and an extra logarithm, but a complete proof. Let \(A\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix whose rows are independent uniformly random subsets \(q_1, \dots, q_m\), so each entry is an independent fair 0 or 1. For a failure probability \(\beta\), \[s_{\min}(A) \ge \frac{\sqrt m}{14} \quad\text{with probability at least } 1 - \beta, \quad\text{once}\quad m \ge 128\Big(n\ln(80n + 1) + \ln\frac1\beta\Big). \tag{H.5}\] Substituted into Equation 17.13, this gives at most \(4mE^2 \cdot 196/m = 784E^2\) wrong bits. So with \(m = O(n\log n)\) queries, error \(E = o(\sqrt n)\) leaves \(o(n)\) wrong bits.


H.2.2 The idea
The proof reuses a lemma from the chapter’s linear-programming section, Section 17.2, in three moves. The lemma says that one random query catches any fixed direction: for any fixed vector \(x\), the squared answer \(\langle q, x\rangle^2\) exceeds \(\|x\|^2/16\) with probability at least \(\frac3{16}\). Over \(m\) independent queries, Hoeffding’s inequality then makes it nearly certain that a good share of the queries catch \(x\), and each caught query adds a fixed amount to \(\|Ax\|^2\). That handles one direction. To handle all directions at once, round every unit vector to a nearby point of a fine grid, use the union bound over the finitely many grid points, and pay for the rounding with a crude bound on how much \(A\) can stretch the small difference. Table H.3 lists the chain of constants.

Rounding
\(\|Ax\| \ge \sqrt m/14\) for every unit \(x\)
whenever the previous row holds






The all-ones direction deserves a word, because subset queries have a nonzero mean. Every entry of \(A\) is \(\frac12\) on average, so \(A\) stretches the all-ones vector a lot: each answer \(\langle q, \mathbf 1\rangle\) is about \(n/2\). That direction gives the largest singular value, not the smallest, and the lemma already allows for it, since a nonzero mean only pushes \(\langle q, x\rangle\) away from 0.


H.2.3 Derivation

One query catches a fixed direction. This is the chapter’s lemma, whose proof holds for every vector \(x\) (the chapter adds an assumption about large coordinates only afterwards). Fix a nonzero \(x\) with \(n\) coordinates, and write a random subset as \(q_i = (1 + s_i)/2\) with independent fair signs \(s_i\), so that a person is in the subset when the sign is \(+1\). The answer \(Y = \langle q, x\rangle\) is then the constant \(\frac12\sum_ix_i\) plus the sum \(\frac12\sum_is_ix_i\) of terms with random signs. Write \(\tau\) for the standard deviation of that sum, so \(\tau^2 = \frac14\|x\|^2\). Counting which terms survive in the expansion of the fourth power shows that a random-sign sum has fourth moment at most 3 times its squared variance, as for a normal variable, and the chapter’s step 3 shows that adding the constant keeps \(\mathbb E Y^4 \le 3(\mathbb E Y^2)^2\). The Paley–Zygmund inequality (Equation 17.5) says that a non-negative variable \(W\) exceeds \(\xi\,\mathbb E W\) with probability at least \((1 - \xi)^2(\mathbb E W)^2/\mathbb E[W^2]\), for any level \(\xi\) between 0 and 1. Applied to \(W = Y^2\), the ratio of moments is at least \(\frac13\). Finally, \(\mathbb E Y^2\) is \(\tau^2\) plus the squared constant, so it is at least \(\tau^2\), and \[\Pr\big[|Y| > \sqrt\xi\,\tau\big] \ge \frac{(1 - \xi)^2}{3}. \tag{H.6}\] With \(\xi = \frac14\) the bound reads \[\Pr\Big[\langle q, x\rangle^2 > \frac{\|x\|^2}{16}\Big] \ge \frac{3}{16}. \tag{H.7}\]
Many queries catch it, by Hoeffding’s inequality. Call query \(j\) good for \(x\) when \(\langle q_j, x\rangle^2 > \|x\|^2/16\), and let \(N\) be the number of good queries. The queries are independent, so \(N\) is a sum of \(m\) independent 0/1 terms, each 1 with probability \(p \ge \frac3{16}\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) says that the average of \(m\) independent terms in \([0, 1]\) falls more than \(t\) below its mean with probability at most \(e^{-2mt^2}\). The event \(N \le m/8\) means the average falls at least \(p - \frac18 \ge \frac1{16}\) below its mean, so with \(t = \frac1{16}\) it has probability at most \(e^{-2m/256} = e^{-m/128}\).
Many good queries make \(\|Ax\|\) large. \(\|Ax\|^2 = \sum_j\langle q_j, x\rangle^2\) is a sum of non-negative terms, and each good query contributes more than \(\|x\|^2/16\). If \(N > m/8\), then \(\|Ax\|^2 > \frac m8\cdot\frac{\|x\|^2}{16} = \frac{m\|x\|^2}{128}\).
A finite grid. Every unit vector has its coordinates in \([-1, 1]\). Take the grid of points in \([-1, 1]^n\) whose coordinates are multiples of \(h = 1/(40n)\). Each coordinate takes \(2/h + 1 = 80n + 1\) values, so there are \((80n + 1)^n\) grid points. Rounding each coordinate of a unit vector \(x\) to the nearest multiple of \(h\) gives a grid point \(y\) with \(|x_i - y_i| \le h/2\), so \(\|x - y\| \le \frac h2\sqrt n = \frac{1}{80\sqrt n}\), and hence \(\|y\| \ge 1 - \frac{1}{80\sqrt n}\).
Union bound over the grid. By steps 2 and 3, each nonzero grid point fails \(\|Ay\|^2 > m\|y\|^2/128\) with probability at most \(e^{-m/128}\), and the point 0 does not matter, because no unit vector is rounded to it. The union bound says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances. So every grid point satisfies it except with probability at most \((80n + 1)^ne^{-m/128}\). Taking logarithms, this is at most \(\beta\) exactly when \(m \ge 128\big(n\ln(80n + 1) + \ln(1/\beta)\big)\), the condition of Equation H.5.
A crude bound on stretching. Every entry of \(A\) is 0 or 1, so \(\|Av\|^2 = \sum_j\langle q_j, v\rangle^2 \le \sum_j\|q_j\|^2\|v\|^2 \le mn\|v\|^2\), by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and because each query has at most \(n\) ones, so \(\|q_j\|^2 \le n\). So \(A\) stretches any vector by at most \(\sqrt{mn}\).
From the grid to every unit vector. Outside the bad event of step 5, take any unit vector \(x\) and its grid point \(y\). By the triangle inequality and steps 3 to 6, \[\|Ax\| \ge \|Ay\| - \|A(x - y)\| \ge \sqrt{\frac{m}{128}}\Big(1 - \frac1{80\sqrt n}\Big) - \sqrt{mn}\cdot\frac{1}{80\sqrt n}. \tag{H.8}\] The right side equals \(\sqrt m\) times \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{128}} - \frac{1}{80}\big(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{128n}}\big)\), which grows with \(n\), so it is smallest at \(n = 1\), where it is \(\sqrt m\,\big(\frac{79}{80\sqrt{128}} - \frac1{80}\big) = 0.0748\sqrt m\), which is more than \(\sqrt m/14 = 0.0714\sqrt m\). The smallest \(\|Ax\|\) over unit vectors is \(s_{\min}(A)\), which gives Equation H.5.
The consequence for least squares. Substituting \(s_{\min}(A)^2 \ge m/196\) into Equation 17.13 bounds the number of wrong bits by \(4mE^2/(m/196) = 784E^2\). If \(E = o(\sqrt n)\), then \(E^2 = o(n)\), so the wrong bits are \(o(n)\).



H.2.4 Checking it
The proof is far from tight. Figure H.3 plots the simulated \(s_{\min}(A)/\sqrt m\) against \(m/n\) for \(n = 50\), 100 and 200. It falls below the proved floor of \(1/14\) only at \(m = 1.25n\), and from about \(m = 4n\) on it sits on the cited asymptotic \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{n/m})\). At the chapter’s size, \(n = 500\) and \(m = 2000\), the script finds \(s_{\min}(A) = 11.44\), which is \(0.2558\sqrt m\). The asymptotic predicts \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1/4}) = 0.25\) times \(\sqrt m\), and the proof guarantees \(\sqrt m/14\). The price of the proof is the number of queries it asks for. For \(n = 100\) people and failure probability \(\beta = 0.01\), Equation H.5 asks for 115,627 queries, about 1,156 per person. The simulation shows the floor holding from \(m = 1.5n\) on.






Figure H.3: The smallest singular value of a random \(m \times n\) subset matrix, divided by \(\sqrt m\), against \(m/n\), for three values of \(n\) (three draws each). The black curve is the cited asymptotic \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{n/m})\), and the dashed line is the floor \(1/14\) proved here, which the proof guarantees only once \(m\) is of order \(128\,n\ln(80n)\).



Figure H.4 shows where the slack comes from. For one matrix with \(n = 100\) and \(m = 400\), it plots \(\|Ax\|^2/m\) for 4,000 random unit directions. Random directions land between about 0.2 and 3. For a unit vector the average of \(\langle q, x\rangle^2\) is \(\frac14\big(1 + (\sum_ix_i)^2\big)\), the variance of one entry plus a share of the mean that grows with how far \(x\) points along the all-ones direction. The weakest direction is lower, and the all-ones direction is about a hundred times higher, because of the nonzero mean of the entries. The proof’s levels, \(\frac1{128}\) for a grid point and \(\frac1{196}\) for every direction, are well below all of them. The lemma itself has slack too. For the weakest direction of this matrix, 0.3075 of the queries are good, and no random direction of the 4,000 has fewer than 0.5550 good queries. The lemma guarantees only \(\frac3{16} = 0.1875\) on average.






Figure H.4: Histogram of \(\|Ax\|^2/m\) over 4,000 random unit vectors \(x\), for one random subset matrix with \(n = 100\) and \(m = 400\) (log scale). The vertical lines mark the weakest direction \(s_{\min}^2/m\), the all-ones direction, and the two levels of the proof: \(\frac1{128}\) for each grid point after Hoeffding’s inequality, and \(\frac1{196}\) for every direction.





H.2.5 What it does not cover
The proof gives \(m = O(n\log n)\), not \(m = 4n\). The logarithm comes from the union bound over a grid fine enough to absorb the crude stretching bound of step 6. For matrices whose entries have mean 0, called centred, a sharper argument bounds the stretching by about \(\sqrt m + \sqrt n\), so it can use a much coarser grid of directions (a net), and it needs only \(m = O(n)\) (Vershynin, ch. 4). For subset matrices it would also have to treat the all-ones direction separately, and this appendix does not carry that out. The sharp constant, \(s_{\min} \approx \frac12(\sqrt m - \sqrt n)\) for large \(m\) and \(n\) at a fixed ratio, is the Bai–Yin law for matrices with independent centred entries (Bai and Yin 1993; Vershynin, ch. 4). Subset matrices are not centred, but they differ from \(\frac12\) times a random-sign matrix by the rank-one matrix \(\frac12\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), and on vectors orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1\) the two act the same. Turning that observation into a proof of the sharp constant takes a perturbation argument for the one remaining direction, which stays cited. So the chapter’s statement with \(m = 4n\) rests on the cited asymptotics and on its simulation, while the \(O(n\log n)\) version is proved here.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
text:
H.3 The prefix-sum matrix

H.3.1 What the chapter uses
In DP-FTRL and matrix factorization, \(A\) is the \(T \times T\) prefix-sum matrix: lower-triangular, with every entry on and below the diagonal equal to 1, so that row \(t\) of \(Ax\) is the running sum \(x_1 + \dots + x_t\). A factorization \(A = LR\) releases \(L(Rx + z)\), where \(z\) is Gaussian noise. Its sensitivity \(\Delta_2 R\) is the largest length of a column of \(R\), and its error per unit of privacy at step \(t\) is \(e_t = \Delta_2 R\,\|\ell_t\|\), with \(\ell_t\) the \(t\)-th row of \(L\). The chapter uses four facts about this matrix.
The first two are in the proof of Theorem 41.2. Every factorization has a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of at least \(\|A\|_*/T\) (Equation 41.9), where the RMSE is \(\big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\big)^{1/2}\), the typical error over the \(T\) released sums, where the trace norm \(\|A\|_*\) is the sum of the singular values. The proof uses the duality \[\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) \le \|A\|_* \quad\text{for every } U \text{ whose largest singular value is at most } 1, \tag{H.9}\] which the chapter states without proof. It also states the singular values, with \(\omega_k = (2k - 1)\pi/(2T + 1)\), \[\sigma_k(A) = \frac{1}{2\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}} = \frac{1}{2\sin(\omega_k/2)}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, T, \tag{H.10}\] and says that the eigenvalues of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) are \(4\sin^2(\omega_k/2)\), checking this numerically.
The other two are in Section 41.4. The square-root factorization uses the lower-triangular matrix with entries \(r_k = \binom{2k}{k}4^{-k}\) on its \(k\)-th diagonal (the chapter writes them \(c_k\), keeping \(r_\tau\) for the columns of \(R\)), and step 5 of the proof of Theorem 41.3 bounds its sensitivity and largest error, \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), with Equation 41.14. That step quotes the Wallis-type inequality \[\frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac12)} \le r_k^2 \le \frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac14)} \tag{H.11}\] from Fichtenberger, Henzinger and Upadhyay (2023) and checks it numerically for \(k < 100{,}000\). Finally, the chapter compares the square root with the lower bound at \(T = 100\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) and finds it within 9% and 6%. This section proves the duality, the singular values and the Wallis bounds, and it explains the comparison by proving that the ratio tends to 1: \[\frac{\ln(2T + 1)}{\pi} \le \frac{\|A\|_*}{T} \le \text{RMSE of any factorization}, \qquad \text{RMSE of the square root} \le 1 + \frac{0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}{5}}{\pi}. \tag{H.12}\]


H.3.2 The idea
The singular values of \(A\) are hard to see directly, but its inverse is simple. Taking running sums is undone by taking differences, so \(A^{-1}\) has 1 on the diagonal and \(-1\) just below it. Then \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) is the matrix of a second difference, \(-v_{j-1} + 2v_j - v_{j+1}\), the same matrix that describes a vibrating string. Its eigenvectors are sine waves, and the two ends of the matrix decide which frequencies fit. For \(T = 2\) the whole computation fits in a few lines: \[A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad (A^{-1})^\top A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{H.13}\] The eigenvalues of the second matrix are \((3 \pm \sqrt5)/2\), that is 2.618 and 0.382. The formula proved below gives the same two numbers, as \(4\sin^2(3\pi/10)\) and \(4\sin^2(\pi/10)\). The singular values of \(A\) are one over their square roots, the golden ratio 1.618 and its inverse 0.618.
The duality is a statement about lining up. The singular value decomposition writes \(A\) as a sum of simple pieces, one for each singular value \(\sigma_k\), and each piece maps one input direction \(v_k\) to one output direction \(u_k\). A matrix \(U\) that stretches no vector can line up with each piece at best perfectly, so it collects at most \(\sigma_k\) from each, and \(\|A\|_*\) in total. The Wallis bounds come from squeezing. Two sequences built from \(r_k^2\), one decreasing and one increasing, close in on the same limit \(1/\pi\), so each stays on its side. Finally, the near-optimality of the square root follows by putting the bounds side by side. The lower bound on every factorization and the upper bound on the square root both grow like \((\ln T)/\pi\), so their ratio tends to 1.


H.3.3 Derivation
The singular values.

The inverse. Write \(N\) for the matrix with ones just below the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so that \(Nx = (0, x_1, \dots, x_{T-1})\) shifts a vector down by one. Taking the differences \(x_t - x_{t-1}\) of running sums gives back the \(x_t\), so \(A^{-1} = I - N\).
The product. \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1} = (I - N^\top)(I - N) = I - N - N^\top + N^\top N\). The matrix \(N^\top N\) is diagonal with entries \(1, \dots, 1, 0\), because \(N\) maps the last basis vector to 0 and every other basis vector to the next one. So the product \(M = (A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) is tridiagonal, with \(-1\) next to the diagonal and \(2\) on the diagonal, except for a 1 in the bottom-right corner.
Interior rows. Try \(v_j = \sin(j\omega)\) for \(j = 1, \dots, T\). Row \(j\) of \(Mv\), for \(1 < j < T\), is \(-v_{j-1} + 2v_j - v_{j+1}\). The identity \(\sin((j - 1)\omega) + \sin((j + 1)\omega) = 2\cos\omega\sin(j\omega)\) turns this into \((2 - 2\cos\omega)v_j = 4\sin^2(\omega/2)\,v_j\). So \(\nu = 4\sin^2(\omega/2)\) is the eigenvalue, if the first and last rows agree.
The first row. Row 1 is \(2v_1 - v_2\), which is the interior formula with \(v_0 = 0\). The sine satisfies \(\sin(0) = 0\), so row 1 holds for every \(\omega\).
The last row. Row \(T\) is \(-v_{T-1} + v_T\), which is the interior formula with \(v_{T+1} = v_T\). So the sine must take the same value at \(T\) and \(T + 1\), which means it must be symmetric about \(T + \frac12\), a peak or a trough there. That requires \((T + \frac12)\omega\) to be an odd multiple of \(\frac\pi2\), that is, \(\omega_k = (2k - 1)\pi/(2T + 1)\). The values \(k = 1, \dots, T\) give \(T\) different angles in \((0, \pi)\), where \(\sin^2(\omega/2)\) increases, hence \(T\) different eigenvalues, which is all of them.
Back to \(A\). The eigenvalues of \(M = (AA^\top)^{-1}\) are the squares of the singular values of \(A^{-1}\), which are one over the singular values of \(A\). So \(\sigma_k(A) = 1/\sqrt{4\sin^2(\omega_k/2)} = 1/(2\sin(\omega_k/2))\), which is Equation H.10, largest at \(k = 1\).

The duality. Write the singular value decomposition \(A = \sum_k\sigma_ku_kv_k^\top\), with orthonormal \(u_k\) and orthonormal \(v_k\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top u_kv_k^\top) = v_k^\top U^\top u_k = \langle Uv_k, u_k\rangle\), linearity of the trace gives \[\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) = \sum_k\sigma_k\langle Uv_k, u_k\rangle \le \sum_k\sigma_k\|Uv_k\|\,\|u_k\| \le \sum_k\sigma_k = \|A\|_*. \tag{H.14}\] The middle step is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and the last uses \(\|Uv_k\| \le 1\), because \(U\) stretches no vector and \(v_k\) has length 1. Equality holds for \(U = \sum_ku_kv_k^\top\), which maps each \(v_k\) exactly onto \(u_k\). This is Equation H.9.
The Wallis bounds.

Two integrals. Let \(I_n = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx\). Integrating by parts gives \(I_n = \frac{n - 1}{n}I_{n-2}\), and \(I_0 = \frac\pi2\), \(I_1 = 1\). Unrolling the recursion, \(I_{2k} = \frac\pi2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdots\frac{2k - 1}{2k} = \frac\pi2r_k\), because the square root’s coefficients satisfy \(r_k = r_{k-1}\frac{2k - 1}{2k}\) (Equation 41.13). In the same way \(I_{2k+1} = \frac23\cdot\frac45\cdots\frac{2k}{2k + 1} = \frac{1}{(2k + 1)r_k}\).
The lower bound. On \([0, \frac\pi2]\), \(0 \le \sin x \le 1\), so higher powers are smaller and \(I_n\) decreases in \(n\). From \(I_{2k+1} \le I_{2k}\) you get \(\frac{1}{(2k + 1)r_k} \le \frac\pi2r_k\), that is, \(r_k^2 \ge \frac{2}{\pi(2k + 1)} = \frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac12)}\).
A first upper bound, and the limit. From \(I_{2k} \le I_{2k-1} = \frac{1}{2kr_k}\), the same way, \(r_k^2 \le \frac{1}{\pi k}\) for \(k \ge 1\). Together with step 2, \(k\,r_k^2\) is squeezed between \(\frac{k}{\pi(k + 1/2)}\) and \(\frac1\pi\), so it tends to \(\frac1\pi\). This is Wallis’s product in disguise.
Two monotone sequences. Let \(a_k = (k + \frac12)r_k^2\) and \(b_k = (k + \frac14)r_k^2\). Both tend to \(\frac1\pi\) by step 3. Using \(r_{k+1}/r_k = (2k + 1)/(2k + 2)\), \[\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k} = \frac{(2k + 3)(2k + 1)}{(2k + 2)^2} = \frac{4k^2 + 8k + 3}{4k^2 + 8k + 4} < 1, \qquad \frac{b_{k+1}}{b_k} = \frac{(4k + 5)(2k + 1)^2}{(4k + 1)(2k + 2)^2} = \frac{16k^3 + 36k^2 + 24k + 5}{16k^3 + 36k^2 + 24k + 4} > 1. \tag{H.15}\] So \(a_k\) decreases and \(b_k\) increases.
Conclude. A decreasing sequence stays above its limit, so \(a_k \ge \frac1\pi\), which is the lower bound of Equation H.11 again. An increasing sequence stays below its limit, so \(b_k \le \frac1\pi\), which is the upper bound. Both hold for every \(k \ge 0\).

How close the square root is to optimal.

A floor under every factorization. For \(0 < x \le \frac\pi2\), \(\sin x \le x\), so each singular value in Equation H.10 is at least \(\frac{1}{\omega_k} = \frac{2T + 1}{(2k - 1)\pi}\). The function \(\frac1{2x - 1}\) decreases, so each term \(\frac1{2k - 1}\) is at least its integral from \(k\) to \(k + 1\). Adding these up, and then dividing the sum of the singular values by \(T\), \[\sum_{k=1}^T\frac1{2k - 1} \ge \frac12\ln(2T + 1), \qquad \frac{\|A\|_*}T \ge \frac{2T + 1}{2\pi T}\ln(2T + 1) \ge \frac{\ln(2T + 1)}{\pi}. \tag{H.16}\]
A ceiling over the square root. For the square root, \(L = R\). Row \(t\) holds \(r_{t-1}, \dots, r_0\), so each row of \(L\) is no longer than the last one, whose squared length is \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2 = (\Delta_2 R)^2\) (step 4 of the proof of Theorem 41.3). So every \(e_t \le (\Delta_2 R)^2\), and the RMSE, an average of the \(e_t^2\) under a square root, is at most the largest \(e_t\), which is \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), which Equation 41.14 bounds by \(1 + (0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5)/\pi\). With the Wallis bounds proved above, that step of the chapter is now complete.
The ratio tends to 1. By Equation 41.9, the optimal RMSE lies between \(\|A\|_*/T\) and the square root’s RMSE, so all three lie in the band of Equation H.12. Both ends of the band are \((\ln T)/\pi\) plus a constant, so the square root’s RMSE divided by the lower bound tends to 1 as \(T\) grows, like \(1 + O(1/\ln T)\).



H.3.4 Checking it
The script compares Equation H.10 with a numerical singular value decomposition at \(T = 256\), and the largest relative gap is \(2.7 \times 10^{-15}\). Each \(\sin(j\omega_k)\) vector satisfies \(Mv = \nu v\) to within \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\). Figure H.5 draws the first three eigenvectors for \(T = 16\). Each starts from 0 just before position 1 and is flat across the mirror at \(T + \frac12\), which is how steps 4 and 5 select the angles.






Figure H.5: The first three eigenvectors \(v_j = \sin(j\omega_k)\) of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) for \(T = 16\), as dots, with the sine curves they sample. Crosses mark the extra points \(j = 0\), where every curve is 0, and \(j = T + 1\), where every curve repeats its value at \(j = T\), because it is symmetric about the dotted line at \(T + \frac12\).



For the duality at \(T = 16\), the trace norm is 26.0552. The largest \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A)\) over 2,000 random matrices \(U\), each scaled so that its largest singular value is 1, is 4.9448, well below it, and the aligned choice \(U = \sum_ku_kv_k^\top\) attains 26.0552, the trace norm itself.
For the Wallis bounds, the script checks the two ratio inequalities of step 4 in exact integer arithmetic for every \(k < 10^6\), and Equation H.11 itself in floating point for every \(k < 10^4\). A floating-point check cannot go much further, because \(b_k\) approaches \(\frac1\pi\) like \(1/(32\pi k^2)\), which soon drowns in rounding error. At \(k = 9999\), \(a_k\) is still above \(\frac1\pi\) by \(8.0 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(b_k\) below it by \(9.9 \times 10^{-11}\). Figure H.6 shows the two sequences closing in on \(\frac1\pi\) from either side.






Figure H.6: The sequences \(a_k = (k + \frac12)r_k^2\) and \(b_k = (k + \frac14)r_k^2\) against \(k\) (log scale). The first decreases and the second increases, and both tend to \(1/\pi\) (dashed), which squeezes \(r_k^2\) between \(\frac{1}{\pi(k + 1/2)}\) and \(\frac{1}{\pi(k + 1/4)}\).



Table H.4 gives the band of Equation H.12 and the two curves inside it. The chapter’s “within 9% and 6%” are the ratios 1.089 and 1.056. The ratio keeps falling slowly, to 1.040 at \(T = 10^6\), as the \(1 + O(1/\ln T)\) of step 3 predicts. The proved band is wide. At \(T = 100\) the ceiling divided by the floor is 1.568, so the band only guarantees a ratio below that, while the actual ratio is 1.089, because both \(\sin x \le x\) and the bound of each row by the last one give away a constant. Figure H.7 shows the band and both curves from \(T = 10\) to \(10^6\). Every factorization has its RMSE above the blue curve, and the optimal one has its RMSE between the blue and the orange curve.



Table H.4: The lower bound on every factorization and the square root’s RMSE, per unit of privacy, with the proved floor and ceiling of Equation H.12.

The grey band is the proved sandwich of Equation H.12. The optimal RMSE lies between the blue and orange curves, which approach each other in ratio.





H.3.5 What it does not cover
The chapter also quotes the finer approximation \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2 \approx (\ln T + \gamma + 4\ln2)/\pi\), with \(\gamma\) Euler’s constant. It follows from a longer expansion of \(r_k^2\) in powers of \(1/k\), and it stays unproved here, as in the chapter. The ratio of step 3 tends to 1 only slowly, so the comparison says that the square root is nearly optimal for the RMSE, not that it is optimal at any finite \(T\). The next section finds the optimum.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
section: H.4 The optimal factorization for the root-mean-square error
text:
H.4 The optimal factorization for the root-mean-square error

H.4.1 What the chapter uses
In Theorem 41.4 and the text around it, the chapter looks for the factorization \(A = LR\) with the smallest RMSE. Scaling the encoder \(R\) up and the decoder \(L\) down by the same factor changes nothing. So the chapter fixes \(\Delta_2 R \le 1\), which means that every column of \(R\) has length at most 1. It then minimizes the Frobenius norm \(\|L\|_F\), the square root of the sum of the squared entries of \(L\), and the RMSE per unit of privacy is \(\|L\|_F/\sqrt T\). The encoder enters only through the matrix \(X = R^\top R\) of inner products of its columns, whose diagonal holds the squared column lengths. The chapter states that the problem is \[\text{minimize } \operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1}) \quad\text{over positive definite } X \text{ with } X_{ii} \le 1 \text{ for every } i, \tag{H.17}\] that it is convex, and that its solution is \[X = V^{-1/2}\big(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}V^{-1/2}, \qquad v = \operatorname{diag}\Big(\big(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\Big), \tag{H.18}\] with \(V\) the diagonal matrix of the vector \(v\), so that \(v\) is a fixed point of the map on the right. It cites Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 3.2) for this, sketches the Lagrangian step and iterates the map. A matrix is positive definite when it is symmetric and \(x^\top Xx > 0\) for every nonzero \(x\), and \(Y^{1/2}\) is the positive definite square root of such a \(Y\).


H.4.2 The idea
There are four steps. First, once the encoder \(R\) is chosen, the best decoder is forced. It is the one that undoes \(R\) with no wasted motion, and its size depends on \(R\) only through \(X = R^\top R\). That turns a problem about two matrices into one about \(X\). Second, the objective is convex in \(X\): along any straight line through the positive definite matrices it bends upward, in the same way that \(1/x\) does for positive \(x\). Third, at the optimum the gradient of the objective must be balanced by a price \(\kappa_i\) on each column-length constraint, and solving that balance gives Equation H.18. Fourth, convexity makes any balanced point the global minimum.
The smallest case shows the answer. At \(T = 2\), \(A^\top A\) has rows \((2, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\). A feasible \(X\) with both columns of length 1 has rows \((1, \rho)\) and \((\rho, 1)\), and the objective is \((3 - 2\rho)/(1 - \rho^2)\). Setting its derivative to zero gives \(\rho^2 - 3\rho + 1 = 0\), so \(\rho = (3 - \sqrt5)/2 = 0.382\) and the minimum is \(2.618\), the golden ratio squared. Table H.5 compares it with the other factorizations at \(T = 2\).
